Fortix is a cracking little casual indie game thats furiously fast and ferociously fun to play.  The basic premise is something akin to 'Join the Dots' meets basic geometry.  You take control of an intrepid knight that must be manoeuvred around and across various maps in order to capture the enemy castle.  The action is displayed in birds-eye view.
The knight must be moved out from a safezone which starts on the outer border of the map.  While in the safezone the knight is immune to any deadly enemy attacks.  Rectangles must be drawn from one part of the safezone to another to cut down the enemys control of the land (map).  This must be done with all manner of obstacles ready to kill the knight, while being up against the clock.
Of course the further into the map the safezone encroaches the less space the knight has to avoid deadly obstacles.  These include: two types of cannon ball firing towers and, a multitude of dragons that swoop down or shoot fireballs in an attempt to kill your knight.  These must be avoided by ensuring that your knight is in the safezone when hit and not in the midst of drawning a rectangle.  If the knight is hit while drawning a polygon then a life is lost.  If this isnt enough of a challenge note that the map must be conquered against the clock.
Fear not for the knight has a few actions they can perform to help you win.  They can 'capture' triggers to destroy enemy towers, or trap dragons in a part of the safezone killing them instantly.  Special tokens can also be 'captured' that provide a number of neat abilities such as: temporary invincibility, stopping cannonballs, killing dragons, receiveing an extra life or stopping time.  To capture a trigger or token a polygon must be drawn around the item on the map.
There is one campaign which covers twelve maps.  It can be replayed through four difficulty levels: Easy, Normal, Hard and Impossible.  Difficulty affects time available, starting lives, the reaction speed amongst others.
With rudimentary controls the game is easy to pick-up.  While graphics are basic they are well rendered and provide a more than fitting medieval ambience that goes perfectly with the incredibly catchy music played in the background.  No bugs were encountered during twelve plus hours of play.
Overall I really enjoyed playing and beating this game. It has that 'just one more go' addictive quality, which kept me playing.  Easily worth the money.

Well the first thing to say is, if this game is on sale, and you are remotely interested in battlefield tactics/maneuver, BUY IT.
Pike and Shot Campaigns is a great game that in my situation, has the same sort of ''one more turn'' menatility that you see in the best of the life-destroyingingly relationship-ending sun-shunning quality games. It covers the less well known Italian Wars, English Civil Wars and Thirty Years Wars. The nation's have their own indiviual flavours, from the flamboyant Royalist Cavaliers to the all-but-tercio-crushing Polish Winged Hussars.
The campaign feature adds a whole new dimension to the game that concentrates more on the raising and movement of armies, so it's definitely NOT like Total War Campaigns.
The battles are in my opinion, brilliant. There are several difficulties you can choose from, from having to think about deployment and flank maneuvers to begging that kuirassier unit to destroy the enemy's horse unit so you can charge into the enemy's flanks in the next turn or your line is broken.
In this game the battle can rely on a lone skirmishing musket detachment sit atop a hill fending off a right wing attack whilst you struggle to hold your left flank, or you could watch your pike and shot unit chase their vanquished foe, leaving said flank vulnerable to exploitation to greedy hussars.
Inevitably in the endgame the battles turn to swirling melee's in the confusion of gunpowder smoke as you mop up/get mopped up by the enemy,  but it is an enchanting game in it's simplicity and effectiveness nonetheless.
It's a yes from me

If this game and Survivor Squad were to be put together, there would be one awesome game instead of 2 above average games.
But when it comes to comparing those two, Flesh Eaters is better.
I'll start with the negatives:
* The AI pathing is extremely faulty.
* Targeting for your soldiers is without priorities, meaning that you'll have deaths unless you go full-on babysitter mode.
* Awful tutorial that doesn't explain anything
* Too many typos, even though they are promising upcoming language options.
* Targeting individual zombies can be glitchy and annoying because of it.
* Once you've gotten used to the game, it becomes extremely easy.
* When looked closer into the game, all systems are extremely simple and due to that, can be exploited.
But on to the positives:
* The graphics have the crisp "high quality flash game" look, which is very pleasing to the eye.
* The concept of having resources that you scavenge as the main part of the game.
* Killing zombies, while indirect, is still satisfying.
* Trading cards
* Cheap
* Not too long as to bore the hell out of you, like most games do these days. Some gamers seem to actually want that even...
* Doesn't require too much attention from you.
And as you can see here, the cons outweigh the pros, yet I still am recommending this game.
The reason is that I was still having a blast with this. It felt awesome to do this. I completed the game and didn't regret spending any minute of it. Sometimes a game doesn't have to be perfect or even amazing overall to just make you have great fun with it. This didn't even come from low expectations, since I had high expectations instead. I just won this game, raising my hype. I had it wishlisted, raising my hype. I was just wanting to play a game like this, raising my hype even more.
This is a great game, just as long as you don't expect anything perfect.
Overall
Objective grade
4/10
Subjective grade
7/10
(All games start at a 5/10 and move upwards or downwards based on pros and cons present in the review)

When I first saw the trailer showing an old school fast paced FPS with cool graphics I was thrilled. I wanted to play it. I needed to play it. After all those story driven and military shooters, this game seems like it had so much potential to bring back something that I thought to be long last.

Unfortunately things aren't always how it seams.

I have to admit I actually enjoyed the game at first. I still do. The game offers most of what you see in the trailer: it really is an old school fast paced FPS game. It also has nice graphics and I had no problems with the sound effects and music.

However...

The first weird thing I noticed is that ..YOU CANNOT RELOAD. That's right.
Let's elaborate with an example: Your pistol in this game can carry 300 bullets: 50 per clip and 6 clips. This means 50/250. But when you finish those 50 bullets SURPRISE. No reload. So you have to change the gun. So you fill in those 50 bullets and then start filling in the other clips. Sure, this only happens once, when you get the gun. But that's when you need the bullets the most and walking over clips on the ground makes you take them but not use them. So you'll end up with 250 bullets that you cannot use and you'll have to use other gun or the super big super slow sword that's very likely to get you killed.

Another problem is the extremely small space you have when you have to fight some big guys or even the final boss. I played many old school fast paced shooters so far but non had this problem. What's worse, the game usually lags like hell when it comes to these fights BUT ONLY THESE. You won't encounter this problem nowhere else in the game. And dropping from 120 FPS to 5-10 is something I cannot accept that easy.

Another stupid problem occurs when you quick reload a game. Say you're in the middle of a fight and you save. Then you die and fast reload the game. In my case this results in a black screen with some action in background (this means the bad guys are active and are heading your way or even shooting at you) for 10-15 seconds. Then, I would experience 5-10 seconds of low FPS before the game goes up to 100+ FPS. I made the mistake of saving in the middle of a fight and I had to chose an older save point because I was killed before I was able to do something. Again, unacceptable.

I tried this game on 3 different PCs and had the same problem. And I had no issues with Bioshock Infinite, Far Cry 3, Tomb Raider, Shadow Warrior and so on, all maxed out.

But I am willing to give this game another chance, as soon as these bugs are fixed.

Yankai's Triangle is a laid-back, triangular puzzle game by Kenny Sun. Don't be deceived by its simple premise, though, this game has a very impressive amount of variety, much like Sun's previous game, Circa Infinity, which I also strongly reccomend. Yankai's triangle has an unexpected amount of content. I'm on level 250, and the game doesn't seem to be winding down, which is impressive for a 3$ game. To be honest, I'm not entirely convinced the game isn't procedurally generated and will just go on forever. The game is also very, very strange. None of the game's huge amount of mechanics are explained; it is expected for you to figure them out yourself. The triangles change too; they are always triangles, but some will- Oh, I've said too much. It's better to go in blind, but take it from me, 3$ is a bargain. Pick this game up if you're interested in a puzzle game that'll take up a few hours of your time.

More people should play this game. Really.
If you were a fan of Doom/Quake, you need to give this game a try. It has good pacing, kickass soundtrack, good mechanics, not that good of a story and a stylish antagonist.
You can move so fast (and bunnyhop) that you can beat the game in under a hour if you're good enough. There's also score runs, which can lead to doing some pretty neat jumps and chains. There's also secrets in each level, and oh boy those are difficult to find once you get into the Recycling Area.
Did i tell you that there's a sword that one-shots pretty much any enemy? Most badass thing ever. You also have a weak pistol, a overpowered shotgun, a machine gun (or pulsar) and a bazooka (yes, you can rocket jump).
During the game you can find secrets, most of them giving free score or lives, but some will give +max hp and +max armor.
Seriously, give it a try,

This game is an odd little fellow: On the one hand, "Ultimate Trash" quite hits the mark, and expecting deep and extensive game mechanics is beyond its point. But on the other hand, you will find yourself having fun with all the side blows, hidden remarks and strange events you will be facing that it lets you discover. But be warned, half the fun is finding everything there is to find, and it certainly won't present all its beauty on a silver platter for the lazy CoD-Player to be consumed. And be to look up a *lot* of stuff on wikipedia when it comes to historical and/or political references. At least I had to, and the depth of several findings in there only revealed itself after getting to know the details of e.g. McCarthy era America or "Project Paperclip".
Don't expect a lot in graphics, it is sufficient and functional, no more. As much as I want to like this game and come back to it again and again, in the end I feel disappointed and bad, and that's really a pity.
+ Beautiful artwork, colourful fairytale
+ Nice effects, visually and sound
- Map and 3D models not satisfying, especially compared to the 2D artwork
- Prestige victory feels prevalent and "cheap"
- Very high randomness with dice, random items, random quests, random dungeon results
Armello's "cards" have a beautiful artstyle and animation and in general art and the colourful, fairytale look are beautiful, but some small things and ultimately the gameplay ruin it for me.
The character models are a bit too simple which makes me question the value of "skins", as there isn't enough detail in teh 3D models anyway. This is especially a pity considering how nice the drawn 2D models and artwork look and I wonder if the game would've been even nicer if the characters would've been kept 2D throughout the game.
Another graphical thing I dislike is the sharpness and focus of the map. The map itself and mentioned colours are beautiful, but as soon as you zoom out a bit, everything is blurred with clouds which, to me, make the impression of solely being there to obscure dimishing detail and graphic quality that would otherwise be visible when zoomed further away, and on the other hand, zooming in totally sets everything out of focus, making characters as well as map seem blurry.
These things aside, the overall artwork, cards, battle animations and dice, would still make sure I consider this a beautiful game. Sadly I'm also too often disappointed by the gameplay.
I'm sure there are many tactics you can make, many "pro" tactics one has to learn first, and many beginner mistakes to figure out, but for my personal taste everything is too random. Dice rolls, as expected, quest locations, items, just everything is random to some degree. And while this is common in many "boardgames", it really feels "wrong" in one that features skill values an equipment.
Sometimes everything you do is totally easy and you gain stats and items like crazy, another time you constantly die three steps from your spawn area and never even manage to finish a single quest.
The winning conditions are another thing. Most games just seem to be won by "prestige victory", so, after the number of x turns is over. And in many cases this just seems like the easiest and least depressing way. The other ways consist of much more perils, stat grinding and item collecting needed in a game where the standard time (round) limit makes it hard to begin with. With all of that just waiting "in safety" and slowly gaining prestige just seems like the safest way.
Losing is rarely a great experience in games, but here, even if you win you might still feel bad, at least that's how it feels for me when I try to aim for a specific victory and in the end the time runs out and I win through yet another prestige victory. It's a victory, but still feels like "not having reached my goal".
So, yeah, that's basically it. It's a beautiful game that I'd wish to love, and the developers care about interaction with them and constantly make sure to add new stuff, paid and unpaid. But I, personally, can simply not play to many sessions without feeling sad and disappointed in the end. Thus, this is nothing for me or people like me, I fear.

The first thing to say about this game is that the art design and direction is beautiful, some of the best I've seen in any game. I'm not usually one that cares about graphics, but I think this deserves special mention. What's more, the game itself is intricate enough to keep your attention for many hours but not complex enough that it's difficult to get into without a lot of effort (I'm looking at you, Paradox). While it's fun to play with bots, who are competent enough to be a challenge, but far from broken, this game is best enjoyed with friends.
The only downside is that outside of the main gamemode, there is nothing else the game has to offer. This would be OK, but when the game is not on sale, the cost is far too high at £15. This isn't a game like Civ 5 that will keep you playing for hours on end; it's not deep enough to match that. The DLC packs are also pretty extortionate, £7 for a character pack of 4 and a few extra bonus rings. But the good thing about this is that if one person in the game owns the DLC, everyone in the game can access it, which puts no player at an unfair advantage, which is brilliant.
Overall, I strongly recommend this game, but with the caveat that it's on a Steam Sale for around 50% off, the asking price of £15 is too high for me.

Hey guys <3, this is my first steam game review and I hope like to apologise in advance for any details not present in this review ( p.s, my english isn't good either so plz bear with it ;~; )
1. Introduction of the game
2. Pros and Cons of the game
3. My thoughts and experience of the game
First of all, this review is not a negative review. I placed it as a negative review since it wasn't good either. :(
This game basically revolves around you being the person that guides your Survivors out of a zombie apocalypse by managing their resources and control their actions. such as controlling where they head out each day (applies for only story mode), what resources do they gather and how do they carry out their task. This game is basically a resource managment game with zombies inside XD. This games has 4 different type of game modes:
Story mode: Which is basically performing one action each day like searching the police station and try to gain resources like scrap metal and antibiotics ( basically medicine ) to give you higher chance of surviving in the zomble apocalypse and accomplishing your main task of getting out of the city.
Horde mode: In which you defend yourself against hordes of zombies ( that quickly overrun you ) and try to survive for as long as possible in one house. You lose when all your survivors die (Duh....)
Objective mode: Same thing like Horde mode except with objectives.........
Test Lab??: a place where you test out the mechanics of the game...... by spawning a bunch of zombies and see your survivors fend of their dear lifes XDDDDD or atleast for me in this case.
Pros:
It has pretty decent music:
making the atmosphere feel more creepier and immersive. It makes you a bit anxious like what could happen next. Will a zombie barge in and eat my survivors, those kinds of things
Decent Graphics:
atleast I can see clearly what everything looks like
Creepy atmosphere:
Like everytime your survivors are outside scavaging for supplies, it is always night time and you can't see♥♥♥♥♥♥outside the place that you are looting. 2creepy5me
Crafting and leveling up systems:
I can craft and level up what more can you ask for from a $2 + game
Cheap:
It is only $2.50 without the offers it can give
Cons:
Not much variety of missions, survivors or gamemode types:
You have like only three types of survivors the soldier,medic and engineer. even though there are many more jobs that can be added like scientist or even a businessman (maybe). The actions you do everyday in story mode are so repetitive since all the actions would only lead to two outcomes, either you get attacked by a zombie or you get supplies. The gamemode types are worse, since their horde mode and objective mode is almost identical with the objective mode being a bit more complicated then the other by giving your survivors mission. But i got to admit their variety of weapon is still okay, because I like looking at my survivors shoot and rekt the zombies with the rifles. Boom you dead :P
Survivors stats do almost nothing:
Health literally does nothing since your survivors would get infected and turn into a zombie in like one bite. Speed might help a bit but accuracy and critical sure doesn't. since even if my accuracy and critical is maxed out, my survivors still aim like the stormtroopers from Star Wars, Like really, John really, you miss like 20 shots to zombies in front of you. The only stat that has any use is Looting speed.
The balance of this game:
Even if you played easy mode ( not even talking about nightmare mode ), you cannot even win since it is too hard. As you are only given six survivors to survive, which is actually not enough compared to the number of zombies they are sending in. Since you would need like 4 of them to gather supplies to upgrade their equipment to survive with better guns while the other two to hold off like 20 zombies (with their terrible aim). And each waves gets harder and harder with the appearance of special zombies like the armoured zombies.
I only managed to complete easy mode on story mode in this game :(. Lastly, Medics and Engineers can't hold weapons??? (WTF) I mean like they cannot even hold a gun or a melee weapon and fight the zombies off. They can only rely on the soldier to fight the zombies for them...... >_< making them useless except for their special equipments they can use.
The melee weapons in this game are just useless:
Melee weapons would only work if you had armour or the power armour to work, since in order for you to be able to even attack the zombies with the melee weapons, you need to get close to them and take damage, which is not good since if you don't have a medic with the ability to heal infections or armour your survivor would get infected and turn into a zombie and kill your other survivors. So best bet would be a gun
No character customisation (personal opinion): I want to be able to change the look of my survivors to fits my playstyle and to look good as heck killing all of the zombies.
Low Replayability:
Since like i said it is repetitive you would last like 3hours of gameplay and never play it again
Buy this game on offer or there is an update on the game, if you buy it at full price don't expect much. Like the satisfaction when your survivors are OP as f#*k and are demoslishing the waves of zombies coming in and the funny part when I spammed the right click button on my survivor near the healing pod thing to prevent him from dying to the zombies overrunning him when searching in the hospital. If you like the time period you _will_ get carried away with the simple to learn but hard to master game mechanics, and fairly granular difficulty levels.
You won't be seeing individual sprites like you would in TW, so have a look at some playthroughs and if you aren't hooked, this may not be for you...   If you think to yourself 'that looks like fun' - dammit man, it is. I hesitated for a long time to get this game, finally taking the plunge when Campaigns came out. I never looked back. This is an awesome tactical game. There are some things that are actually an improvement over Battle Academy in my view--the slower moving units make the I-go-you-go more realistic as a game format. But really one of the main things that make it amazing is the occasional uncontrolled actions of your units on the battlefield when they rout the enemy and set off in hot pursuit, rest of the battle be damned. Also I read that some people were put off by the graphics of the pike & shot units--looking like little sheds moving around the battlefield--and I was a bit as well... until I saw that the developers had faithfully designed the images that way to replicate how those units were drawn in depictions of battles at the time. Now I think they look great, reminding me of those Renaissance pictures. Finally, the more I read about this era of warfare, the more I realize that they developed the game to nicely emulate the battlefield tactics and realities. All in all I would definitely recommend this game.

Why yes, I do judge VNs at a completely higher standard than other games, because they're supposed to entertain with their story, not want to make you jump off a bridge.

I don't really have a whole lot to say about this game, really. It's a visual novel/dating sim. I don't have a lot of experience with the genre, but this just felt meh all over.
You're Heileen, the potentially most vapid and shallow woman you'll ever meet (then again her Lust and Pride values were high), as she tries to be useful aboard Captain Morgan's vessel while at the same time getting a date with just about any character that looks half-decent, because eye-candy. You don't get to pick your character, you're always Heileen, but she's bi, so there's your choice there.
There are many characters, both potential romantic interests or not, and each romance equals to a different ending. You're not obligated to smooching anyone up though, as this game also provides you with profession endings, given a high enough value in either a Virtue or a Sin, and the high enough skill level in the needed jobs to end the game that way (example would be you finishing as a captain, so you'd need high leadership and maxed out Pride).
Virtues and Sins are gained and lost depending on your responses in the many conversations this game has, which is 40% of the game, the other 60% are just you grinding your skills for the profession endings, which is pointless if you want a romance ending anyway. I am told the Virtue and Sins levels do affect her personality, so you can make her more of a wench in her general dialogue or not (which is pretty cringeworthy at times, but I knew what I was getting into). Thankfully the characters are different to one another, they will like you more depending on who and what you actually do so the same process doesn't work for everyone.
This being a trilogy, I suppose I can't fault this game for bringing in tons of references from the previous two games I believe, since the first part of the game is just you looking for your friends. This happens naturally though, you don't get to choose where you want to go so while there are many different endings, the game's as linear as it gets.
You're wondering why I'm putting in a recommendation for this game. Well, it's short. And I didn't hate it enough, I mean there's nothing inherently wrong with it. There's not a whole lot to it in the end, but it is what it is. And if you're into this type of game, you'll probably enjoy it more than I did. Was very cheap in a recent bundle so, yeah, give it a try.

It's your first day working for Tremendous Corp, a firm that controls the whole gaming industry and churns out game after game on an assembly lane: suddendly someone raids the facility and, through a newspaper ad, you'll be recruited to find out the Secret (yes, Secret) behind the company's success.
The Secret of Tremendous Corporation is a quirky game with basic gameplay and a short length but its sense of humour and critique of the gaming industry make it well worth a playthrough.
-while they are simple I enjoyed the hand-drawn graphics and animations
-nice soundtrack
-acts as a good critique of the industry
-the game's humour- and the fact it breaks the fourth wall a few times-elicits quite a few chuckles during gameplay
-some funny references to the good games of the 80s/90s
-basic puzzles
-very short, expect 30/45 minutes to finish
-didn't work properly in full-screen, it has been submitted to the devs and should be fixed eventually though
The Secret of Tremendous Corporation was originally created in 48 hours for a Game Jam and this is clearly shown by its general lack of content, easy puzzles and short length: but there's an heartfelt and quirky critique of the gaming industry beneath the game. In fact the game itself functions as an interactive critique that shows you what the devs themselves had to say on the matter and ends up being an interesting piece of social commentary on the issues plaguing the gaming scene. The fact that so does it in a funny, light-hearted way makes it even better imho.
The game is free and I recommend you to try it and see if it clicks with you: perhaps it'll make you laugh, or think, or both but I find it hard to be left unfazed by it. And if you've enjoyed what the devs did you can buy the day-one useless DLC (another critique by itself) as a way to support them for what they did while supporting the business practices that the game criticizes...isn't it nice?

I think it's important to set your expectations to an appropriate level before going into some things. Knowing that a game has spent years in development with hundreds of man hours and (insert applicable currency and exaggerated value here) pumped into it, it's pretty fair to expect great things. Going into a game that was made by a couple of guys over 48 hours as a project for a game jam and is then offered for free... you probably know you won't need to be calling in sick to take the day off work to play it.
The Secret of Tremendous Corporation is a short point and click game about the game industry, a satire of sorts about both the creators and players. A new intern starts his first day at a large, successful game developer that has become so powerful that they've muscled all other developers, big and small, out of the business and are now literally the only game in town. But you don't make it to the top without making a few enemies, and a rebel group of indie devs have kidnapped their workforce to learn their secret and end their reign. This is where you come in, to snoop around the offices and see if you can find answers, and maybe even end their tyranny once and for all.
There's two main factors to this title really, one is as an actual game and how it plays, and the other is as a social commentery on the industry. As a game it's pretty decent without being staggering - the artwork has its own unique vibe that brings a certain charm with it, and the handful of puzzles aren't too bad, if not a tad trying at times given how directionless they can be. But as a commentery? Mmmhhhnnnggg... it's maybe not quite as on the mark? It feels like it perhaps makes too many jabs but with too few real points actually being made about their target. Or maybe that is sort of the point? I dunno, unless I misinterpreted the message, I get the sense that the moral of the story and its hyperbole is it's silly to get really worked up over stupid, small stuff and we should all stop for a minute and try to take stock, that a more reasonable sense of proportion and balanced perspective would serve us better. But maybe that's just me reading too much into it what feel like rather broad, and maybe even somewhat conflicting statements both against and in favour of certain issues.
But, even though I didnt buy it, I do really like the game's DLC. It's literally just a cra*ppy little hat. Not a fancy one with special powers or incredible animations or bonus XP or the like, just... a hat... the kind you wear on your head. That's it. Now, I can already imagine a bunch of people will be crying fowl about this, saying what a rip-off it is to give us a whole game for free, but a single, small, useless item for several of your monies (2 euros, in my case), but for me, it's probably the most genius aspect of this whole thing. Firstly, it's arguably the most biting of points it could have made about the industry, to have this be a day-one release and charge so much for it, but I also like that it provides an avenue for people to support the developers should they choose to. Whilst technically a transaction, I think it should be viewed more as a donation... with a free hat as thanks. The choice is at least there if you want it and I wouldn't be against other indie devs having fun with stuff like this for other free titles. As long as something isn't cynical or sleazy I think gamers will generally be OK with it as an option they can freely make for themselves.
So, as I seem to say with many games like this, it's short, it's free, and even if it isn't a landmark event in gaming, it's at least not bad. If you have an hour to spare and this sounds like your kind of thing, or even if you're merely curious about it, there's no harm in giving it a shot then moving on with your life.

I could only recommend this game to die-hard fans of board games and who like the presentation of the game. There's some actual fun involved in learning the mechanics and achieving your first victory in a non-tutorial game, but you'll quickly discover that the game experience varies extremely with the starting attributes of the character you play. Characters with a high initial Fight stat can dominate the board and more often reach the tiles they need than characters with a low initial FIght stat who have to completely depend on card draw luck to compete. Playing them can be very frustrating if you only draw useless cards.
Also, the idea of playing traps ("perils") for other players as a type of interaction when you can't beat them in a fight greatly suffers from you not being able to see where their current quest locations are. You might try to deduce it from their movement, but even then: more often you've had the negative effect of spending the money or magic to play a trap for them to either completely avoid it or even beat them and getting bonus prestige out of it. That's not a very good mechanic.
Last but not least there are still some negative user experience issues like awkwardly slow rolling dice or you always accidentially opening the main menu, that should have been ironed out long ago by now.
If you like board games and the game's style and it's on sale for less than 10€, you can get it ... but don't expect to get more than 3-5 hours or enjoyment out of it unless it really happens to rub the right gamer's itch in you.

Pike and Shot: Campaigns is a deceptively simple turn-based war game. This is all about putting your units on the right fronting and planning where you want to fight - don't expect the graphics to be fancy or detailed, or you'll be disappointed by the little squares of foot troops, cavalry and cannons, which don't even deteriorate as they take fire.
As a war game, it's a great purchase for fans of early modern warfare. But casual gamers beware: the big problem with the period is that in some of the campaigns there's very little to distinguish between the two sides. The English Civil War units start off largely identical (with the Royalists having better cavalry), and this can lead to grinding matches rather than games where you can show off your tactical flare. Still, a solid game worth the time of turn-based strategy fans.

"Pike and Shot" was already a fave wargame of mine. "Campaigns" offers the player even more ways to match up against a capable AI that will punish your battlefield blunders. In "campaign mode" armies gain experience in battle -- but, importantly, the victors gain confidence while the vanquished lose confidence. And so, crush the enemy two or three times and see your own small army grow in battlefield ability and "elan". That's neat. The "campaign mode" also models basic economics and attrition -- so split yout forces to keep them fed and concentrate to enagage in battle. That said, the AI will only accept battle if the odds are reasonable, so there's quite a bit of to-ing and fro-ing on the campaign map. When you're done with the various campaigns, there are many stand-alone scenarios, a random-battle generator, and a detailed scenario editor. At the higher difficulty levels, the AI is a tough opponent.

The culmination of the Heileen series, Heileen 3: New Horizons has the heroine of the series, Heileen, rescued from a shipwreck by a band of oddly sympathetic pirates. However, the developer does run several sales through the year if price is a concern.
Before purchasing, I highly recommend trying the demo (from the Dev's website as well).  This style of game is certainly not for everyone, but the demo definitely gives a good idea what to expect.
Additionally, I would be remiss not to mention the job skills.  It gets really grindy to raise those levels; additionally to unlock the final job endings, there is a Sin/Virtue system in game which must be met as well.

Did you like GTA4 and wanted more? And not quite ready for GTA5 yet or just loved Liberty City? Well this is for you. Definitely play the base GTA4 first as the events in this game are concurrent to GTA4, with the characters making cameos and references to the main story. Really this is two seperate stories in one, The Lost and the Damned, and The Ballad of Gay Tony.
The Lost and the Damned has you leading a motorcycle gang through gang wars, fighting off the government from trying to shut you down and dealing with lots of drugs. You better get used to driving a motorcycle, you'll be on it a lot. At least they made you "stickier" now, used to fly off when hitting a pebble in GTA4. It's really a fairly tragic story, I won't ruin it but it shows that gang life is tough, brutal, and destroys everyone's life. It is a fun story with plenty of action, and a shoot and destroy everything final mission.
The Ballad of Gay Tony is, well, much more fun than TLOU. You're Luis Lopez, helping your business partner Gay Tony (the game makes it quite clear that Luis is very straight, women falling over themselves to have him and he doesn't say no) keep your club afloat while short muscleheads, Russians and other gangs come to collect the debts you owe for the money you borrowed to run the Club. Plus you meet a very crass, very loud, very obnoxious, very, very rich arab man who loves guns, sex, and things money can't buy, who sets you on missions to steal outrageous things in some of the most fun missions in GTA. Seriously Yusuf missions are a treat. The only real negative of TBOGT which does hurt it some are all the helicopter missions, there's a disproportionate amount and the helicopter conrols and camera are just awful. Fortunately the missions aren't too hard, but I hate them nonetheless for the terrible controls. The story is compelling, and makes you race from one mission to the next. If you can only play this or TLOU, play this.
All in all TLOU takes about 7 hours, TBOGT takes about 10 hours (assuming you only do the story missions), and are quite fun. The graphics more or less hold up today, though I still sometimes get 15 fps dips even with my Titan X and i7-6800k, odd. I do recommend the CryENB v3 for a bit better graphics. Enjoy the game, you won't regret it.

A fleeting joy, but a joy nonetheless, is the best way to describe Fortix, which seems to be the combination-lovechild of an beginner's art project and beginner's programming project. While the art is interesting enough and carries what it needs to carry, you aren't going to be entranced, and the gameplay, while a bit repetitive, offers enough challenge to keep you on board for long enough to at least finish the game's achievements and receive the three offered card drops.
The game offers two control schemes, keyboard or mouse, each with it's own advantages, which is an interesting and not-often-seen twist. The game offers standard option controls including windowed mode (always a plus) and the ability to mute the in-game music, which you will most likely be doing after it loops the third time.
The gameplay is difficult enough to match each mode of play from easiest to hardest, with the hardest being worthy of the title. The game offers bonuses to be roped-off and captured in order to gain short-lasting special abilities such as a temporary speed boost, temporary halting of cannon fire, or the killing off of one of the infuriating dragons. The level designs vary and offer up a challenge as you gain access to higher levels. Be careful not to lose all of your lives, though! In levels with multiple castles to capture you have to restart from the first castle in that level if you run out of chances.
For the price, I recommend picking up the game, for the trading cards and easier-than-usual achievements. While you won't be returning again and again as if the game is a nasty habit, it is highly worth being a quick guilty casual-gaming guilty pleasure.

And spot-on-sounds, great music by the Bobby Prince, who also made music for Doom, because we know, we should compare everything to Doom and mention it everywhere. He still didn't lose his talent and you can go and get soundtrack right away.
The story of the game follows... somewhere in 21XX when humanity lives happily and forgot what "military" forces is, only one man remains fitting for action is you, Kain. And the action came, as the robots invaded Earth and are planning to take the amazing generator for their own use and you have to stop them. Oh wait, it's ugly alien lizard that can be blown into many gibbity gibs. Also comes with a cool villian Exo who builds robots and doesn't have "Dr." in the name.
Cue all the fun in story cutscenes, enjoying characters talk. Shame the artwork is a bit of lacking. It doesn't have satisfying ending either, but that's OK, we play for gameplay, not ending.
While graphics doesn't have much going technical-wise, the design is a stylish and colorful, quite pleasent for the eyes. It has character to it. Weapon animations are great and lively, perhaps too much for some people. But you can disable the camera movement in options, so not a big deal. And yes, when you blow or kill enemies, they leave their blood all over walls and floor, happily blowing into gibs as well. Robots have oil that works like a blood, gibs leaving it everywhere, and it makes killing robots as fun as aliens.
Corpses of enemies don't really use ragdoll, but there is a gameplay design to it, as you can blow corpses into gibs, resetting chain combo.
Yes, chains and combos. This game is arcade game all around. There is usual affair of exploring mazes, finding switches and dominating your enemies, running at the speed of fast-paced game. It got classic non-regenerating health, your usual armor (cuts damage taken by half), supply pickups and hazards to avoid like spikeballs. And best part is that the game is Arcadey-fair, you don't feel like you died cheaply. Every enemy uses projectile attack, there are absolutely no hitscan attack, excluding railgunners! It's all about maneuvering and buttkicking, not about camping and headshotting carefully. It's one of those FPS who doesn't make you quicksave every few seconds because you may get hit into head by random bullet anytime. And this alone makes it one of better FPS games around.
Not only it's properly done for once, but it has great Arcade elements to it. There is even a bit of platforming involved when it comes to secrets. It only has one physics trick, "straferunning", where running diagonally is faster. It also uses lives system, like any good arcade title, allowing you to start fresh from checkpoint upon death instead of making you wait loading same quicksave all time. Higher difficulties, the hardest one you have to unlock by beating game, don't even allow quicksaves. You can lose all lives, but you got infinitive continues, just gotta start level from beggining. Having truly arcade-like style where you get complete game over after losing lifes would have been interesting, but hardcore PC FPS gamers who use saving all time wouldn't be able to stomach that.
Survival is nice, but what will keep your replaying got to be score system. You got the usual treasures to pick up during there, but it's no much to chain combos system, where you have to kill enemies one after another in short amount of time between each kill. It's made to be addictive, as the hit sound pitch will go higher and higher, the score upon ending the chain increases pretty much geometrically. Not only that, but you can end the chain by releasing a powerful weapon's finisher, the strenght of which depends on the level of kill chain.
No, it's not some gore-full melee fatality. These Finishers take inspirations from fighting games instead, a more damaging shot that can clear out a room if positioned correctly.
They are different for each weapon, all of them getting their job done for various situations:
-Hyperblade: Melee weapon that doesn't suck but isn't quick-knife either. Gibs most enemies and just feels great to whack with. Finisher is vertical slash, sending projectiles out.
-Pistol: Gets stuff done for long range until bazooka. More ammo than you will ever need. Finisher is railgun-like shot.
-Shotgun: Main weapon for short and even medium ranges. Main weapon actually. You do most combo chaining with it. Finisher is just strong WIDE shot.
-Pulsar: Your superweapon, like in usual Arcade game, which you would want to keep for bosses and dangrous situations. Shoots fast, ammo is rare. Finisher is a slow powerful flying plasma. Huge one.
-Bazooka: Blow anything into gibs. Good for long-range and packs of baddies. Finisher is just having more powder in rocket.
All used through the levels to fend off the various enemies. That are common weak melee robot-crawlers, kamikaze variety, usual projectile-shooting weak and tough alien soldiers, including railgunner variery too, flying patrolling robots and big melee crushers who act like walls. You should ignore crushers during big fights, unless it's the last difficulty where they are "poke me for gibs". Could use more of variety but it goes nice with chain system.
You also may notice that damage is never randomized. There is no gamble if that rocket will kill you or not. It goes good and bad with bazooka, as damage is always same no matter the distance from radius of explosion. It helps and makes sense when blowing enemies up, but you are likely to get self-instakilled just because you was a little too close.
And then the levels. There aren't tons of them, but they are nicely packed, changing theme every two levels or so. They are abstract and got not many interesting details or interactivity, but damn good mazes and have different color palletes and textures. Each levels has a few secrets, with only around 2 in whole game being hidden behind usable wall, which means that it's not about tedius wallhumping like in "proper oldschool FPS".
And best? Many bosses! And they aren't lame! Like proper arcade, they have tactics to learn and you can't just outdamage them. Wrack outdoes many FPSes here. Aside from Oculus, he becomes lame-easy once you learn tactic.
And the game got Workshop support! It comes with face-based level editor and you can make mods with just a notepad, quite inspired by ZDoom. Easy to use, can do many stuff. Try it.
The game is not perfect though. Technical problems pop-up for many users, requring more PC power than one expects (the only modern FPS that doesn't remove gibs). Could use more enemy variety. 4-5 more levels with two more themes could be great. More.
But you know what? It still is one of the only arcade FPS around, it being felt in core gameplay up to bones, making you care of score. It may not be much for those who just want to beat game once with no care. But if you pick up any level after beating game and try the best, then you will not be able to put the game down until you finished it again.
Highly recommended.

Pike and Shot is a turn-based wargame set in an era of devastating wars between Protestants and Catholics, King and Parliament, Turks and Christians, Habsburg emperors and French kings.  Backbone unit of most armies being a combined Pike and Shot formation that has evolved from huge 2000 men pike squares by adding the shot and making them smaller.
Main focus of the game is on battles which are challenging and chaotic. Player choices for each unit are seemingly simple: move, shoot or charge into melee. Charging removes control from the player: melee continues until one side breaks and is automatically pursued.  Automatic pursuit can be bad or good: pursuers can run into the thick of the enemy and expose their flanks, wander off for several turns until control is regained or they can chain charge and rout a big chunk of enemy battle line.
Units have a momentum: turning takes time and can expose flanks, ZOC and priority target rules drastically reduce options when close to the enemy and charge takes all control from the player as unit tries to hammer its way through the enemy lines. Main attack directions must be well planned as opportunity to disengage vanishes rapidly.
AI is very good. Historical battles have a great variety: offensive, defensive, unit types evolving from Swiss pike squares to Swedish salvo, from Gendarmes to Cromwellian horse.  Completing all 40 historical battles in the original version took me over 100 hours.
New campaign aspect seems to be a great addition: not too complex (majority of the time is still spent fighting battles) but still offering some real choices.  Random battle generator used in campaign and skirmishes is pretty good.
Basics are learnable from the tutorial battles but these will leave some important things unclear: ZOC and priority charge target rules, cohesion effects of artillery fire, interactions between terrain and different unit types etc. Reading the pdf manual is recommended.

The key of the game is to utilize the various units you're given and to force around 60% of the enemy army to rout. The campaign is the newest addition and it operates rather simply, you've got manpower, you've got money and you've got supply limits. The more territory, the more money and manpower but because of supply limits, it's almost impossible to completely overpower your enemy with sheer numbers. You'll have to succeed with brain and unit composition. Highly recommended game!

I almost never buy games at release.  Even if I know I will enjoy a game, I typically wait for patches and a large sale.  Not with this game, though.  I bought it the morning it became available, installed it as quickly as I could, and have enjoyed it immensely.
This game is great, but not just because it offers in-depth historical detail for twenty different nations over around 6 time periods each (some nations have even more time period options than that) or because the battles with those units give so many different viable tactical options.  This game is great because there is that complexity (at both the campaign and battle level) in mechanics, yet everything still feels intuitive and easily understood, and very few games really manage to walk the line between complex and confusing.
Because of the stat system, terrain system, and excellent A.I. battles and campaigns feel more "real" than in many other video games: when a tactic works, you know why, and it seems like the same events would plausibly have happened in a real battle using the same units and tactics.
Overall, I recommend this game because of the excellent job it does both at demonstrating the warfare of the time period (which is not often represented in popular culture of any kind) and as a wargame in general.

Read more here:

I'd give it a 7.5/10.
Its graphics are beautiful, the puzzles are simple, and the sound is simple yet pleasant.
Its chief draw, however, lies in what The Search is all about - the search for
.
If you're an adrenaline junkie, maybe stay away.
If you're of an introspective bent, maybe buy it - it's only $4, and it's got some useful insights.
If you're of an introspective bent, and you're past your 30's, then the game likely won't tell you anything new - but it's still a good touchstone for reminding you of many of the fundamentals.

THE SEARCH was a mellow way to pass an evening, but got a little too woo-woo for me. As someone who's been writing and drawing and creating for a lot of my life, I have my own working philosophy about creating, art block, etc., so that probably didn't help. But while some of the quotes were all right, having the narrator expound upon them so obviously ("This is what that quote means!") immediately after made them seem kind of silly.
Imagine if the game ANTICHAMBER told you what every sign was about, instead of letting you feel your way through the puzzle itself. That's THE SEARCH.
(There were also a couple interface things I would have liked to've seen implemented, such as the ability to re-show an item's description after it has been picked up. and although the inventory would extend and then stay up from time to time, I never knew what caused that behavior. Its autoclose behavior was kind of annoying. And in some areas, it was easy to get turned around in. In other areas, you sometimes turned around to look at a blank wall. Makes me apprecaite more the craftsmanship of Myst's "slideshow"-style environs (even if their puzzles are sooooo haaaard.)
Finally: I couldn't have been the only person thinking about burning their way through some of the puzzles. BURN BABY BURN
Sorry, THE SEARCH. You're very pretty, but you weren't the game for me.

The first half of the movie seems like introduction, and it is very slow through the whole thing, even at the action points it seems to drag. There is a clear focus on character development, but it came out as over-emphasized and it defeated the purpose of character development, as there was no substance to contrast the characters to any gripping plot. Another crucial part to this film that didn't meet expectations was the audio mastering. This is something even I could easily fix with Audacity, but it was overlooked in the end.
All in all, I would say that the negatives outweighed the positives. Would I reccomend this to a firend? No, not really. But I wasn't so dissatisfied, as I got this on Halloween sale for 90 cents.

I played Sven Co-op before it became standalone game, since version 3.5. I enjoyed opposing force weapons and monsters, some maps were cool, but the co-op component felt like it's missing the point of true cooperative.
With infinite respawns you did not need to bother about yourself and teammates health. Anyway some maps were almost impossible to finish without dying, because monsters were so tough and some events leading to instant player's death are unpredictable.
But version 5 introduced survival mode. Now when you die, you can't repsawn by yourself. Only your teammates can help you. Using medkits got reasonable sense at last to not let your teammates down. Life has a value now. Ammo don't respawn, so saving ammo is important too.
Difficulty also was adjusted to be more balanced.

If 4 or more didnt ring a bell, you are wrong here.

Because it is unique, it is funny, it is intriguing - if played right.
And that means taking your time, reading the ingame notes, the mission notes (triggered by "M"), tinkering around to follow the hints, reading most of the paper pieces hidden on walls, floors, drawers, listening to the dialogues (oh my god, that voice acting alone will either brake you or make you laugh) and, most of all, trying out even the most stupid things. Like getting drunk before a fight or playing a piano in a brothel full of zombie hookers.
The reward is a mixture of excellent jokes, insane easter eggs, funny references, a trashy B-Movie-storyline, shameless backtracking, dozens of "WTF" moments, some boobs and ♥♥♥♥♥s, even more trashy cutscenes and. if you get them, some really intelligent, subversive and cynical political statements.
Plus "The Night of the Living Dead" to be seen in an ingame cinema, full lenghts, accompanied by some skeletons who claim to be extras from the movie.
I still cant tell if its

My personal opinion is that this game, in all its trashy quirkyness, is among my all-time-favorites and gave me plenty if really entertaining hours, hopefully there are more to come. Also, I am not stating "All people who dont find this game to be funny are stupid" as some other "fans" do, I go with "People who dont find this game to be funny are people I wouldnt invite to my parties".

PS: An interesting side note on the reviews. While they are mixed, there is a significant difference in the positive and negative reviews: Most positive reviews talk about the flaws, too, they warn, they tell "the recommendation depends on (insert variable)". Most negative reviews tell outright "its bad" or even (gosh!) "Its not funny" in a way that seems like the writer wants to tell others what to think. Some even bash those who like the game.
So, while they certainly failed to create a perfect game, the devs perhaps suceeded in creating a playable hater detector :D

Going through the demo before the game was released in early 2005, some good impressions were left after assuming the full game would expand upon all the mechanics on a much grander scale. Come release time, Republic Commando turned out to be a very disappointing experience. The opinion remains the same today.
The entire game plays out like a drawn-out demo to showcase a work-in-progress squad system, that even for its time, would quickly be surpassed by similar games in its genre. With the Star Wars license in mind, Republic Commando doesn't reach the same FPS experience as the Dark Forces / Jedi Knight series. It also certainly falls far behind in terms of story compared to other Star Wars games, only helping introduce the existence of clone commandos into the Expanded Universe but leaving their stories to be told in other mediums.
It was a nice way to build excitement for the then upcoming Episode III, but now, Republic Commando is an average game at best. Fan of squad based shooters or the Star Wars franchise, either way, there isn't much of a reason to play.

The German language has many wonderful compound words used to describe very specific feelings or situations.  There must be one that loosely translates into "Nuh-uh, this isn't crap, it's just the way we meant it, YOU just don't get it" (and if there isn't, may I suggest uwebollvergnügen). Republic Commando sees you commanding a squad of four clone commandos through three lenghty missions. The gameplay is quite enjoyable and challenging enough to keep you on your toes, yet it gets somewhat repetitive and lacking in variety by the end. The command mechanic is intuitive and snappy, but for the most part you'll be moving your squad to predetermined firing positions and managing their health. That being said, it's quite satisfying to pull off a well executed maneuver like assigning one of your clones to provide covering fire while a teammate sets an explosive charge on an enemy position. Often you'll be slowly chipping away at stronger enemies, so assigning targets for your squad is essential. There isn't a lot of room for tactical creativity; most of the time it's fairly obvious where you're supposed assign your clones to move so it's usually a matter of getting everyone into position in time. The AI is decent, the clones move about the enviroment quite naturally and they often fill in the gaps so there's minimal micromanagement.
The level design is rather linear and mostly consists of varying corridors and the occasional wide-open area. One of my favourite sections of the game has you defending large Star Destroyer hangar bays from waves of battle droids, but it's unfortunately short lived.
The gunplay and grenades have a nice floaty feeling to them, quite similar to the early Halo games. You've got four primary weapons and as well as a wide array of alien guns to pick up, but I mostly stuck to my blaster rifle and grenade launcher. You've also got a variety of five different grenade types.
Each member of Delta squad has a single character trait that they exemplify at opportunity - the trigger happy explosives guy, the intelligent computer specialist and the edgy sniper who's personality consists entirely of wanting to kill things. This doesn't really detract from the overall experience, but it would be nice to have actually have a reason to care about my squad members. The way your character narrates seemingly minor details is also a nice touch.
An extra mission or two to further develop the story and gameplay would have been welcomed, but I managed to complete the game on normal in just under eight hours which is a pretty decent length.
Overall I don't think Republic Commando lives up to the hype, but I would highly reccomend it for $9.99, especially if you're looking to scratch a tactical shooter or Star Wars itch.

With regards to my first complaint, I can understand pricing the Usurpers pack and Bandit clan. That was fulfilling a promise. It's harder to understand not coming up with new material to dilute the stuff you would have to pay for. The ratio (as of now) of free characters to not-free characters is 2:3, which seems a bit weird since I already payed money for the game. To get skins you would also have to pay. The characters are all balanced (which is good) but it would be nice to have more variety without having to pay all that extra money. Unfortunately, they're not expanding the free-to-play roster, they're adding another pack you have to buy. As an aside, you don't actually have to buy them to win (which is really great, especially given how easily they could make it that way). That isn't an excuse to make the characters you start out with a sample pack for a huge assortment of characters you would have to pay for, which is where I feel this game is headed. If it doesn't go that way, I'll try to remember to delete this comment but I may forget. If I do, sorry. Warning: the total value of all the content in this game is more than the value it is priced at on the store page.
With regard to my second complaint, (which may be unfounded but I'm speaking from personal experience) everyone has always seemed to win with prestige (which could be because all the friends who I pay with could just be too scared). X-Plane 11 is the "older next-gen" flight simulator. It's a brand new simulator (not game) that covers all the points a next-gen needs but time is changing and with the updates and changes to the Devetail's Flight Sim World, then on some aspects, it will dominate X-Plane. For the next X-Plane in a few or more years to come, Laminar Research will have to deal with these upcoming 'issues'.
The aircraft are superb in this simulator. Yes, there are some reviews saying there could be some more aircraft but,
1. There is enough to start with. The Boeing 737-800 and MD-80 are highly detailed (not study level) aircraft to fly and for the GA side of things then the Cessna 172, Columbo 400 and the Beechcraft Baron 58 are great aircraft to use.
And 2. You are able to download very detailed freeware aircraft or buy your own addons eg. JARDesign's Airbus A320.
For the level of smog/smoke/exhaust coming out of the engines, that is being adressed. For now, you are able to change the level of smog/smoke/exhaust in the configuration file for the aircraft you are changing it to.
The scenery is superb. This is part of the next-gen features and Laminar have done an amazing job. With the new 11.05 update, Las Vegas is quite simply brilliant. Everything is nearly modeled to perfection and the authors who built the X-Plane version of KLAS have done a ♥♥♥♥ing amazing job. Other airports which are noticibly incredible include KBOS (Boston), KJFK (New York), KLGA (New York), KEWR (New York), YSSY (Australia) and NZQN (New Zealand).
Overall, this simulator has shown imense detail and has clearly shown the hard work Laminar Research have put into this "older next-gen" simulator. I, personally, really enjoy flying nearly everyday on this simulator and I won't be stopping for an extremely long time yet.
My rating is a 9.5/10.

Valiant Hearts is one of the best singleplayer story games I've played.
This game is at its core a simple puzzler game. It will have you pulling levers, turning wheels, sending your little dog Walt to distract gaurds, trading objects to soldiers, throwing dynamite, digging tunnels, dodging artillery bombardments, and more. The actual gameplay is actually pretty fun, but the gameplay is not what makes this game great.
The (about 6 hour) story of Valiant Hearts is a beautiful journey through the hearts of four characters connected by the harrowing conflict of the Great War. During the game, you will play as Emile, an older French gentleman conscripted into the French Army, Freddie, an American volunteer soldier (and Emile's fast friend), Anna, a belgian nurse, and Karl, a young German who was originally the husband of Emile's daughter but was deported at the start of the war then forced to fight for the Germans. In addition, there is a loyal black dog called Walt that will help you complete the levels. The story brings them all together in a heart warming way. I won't go into spoilers, but the story is filled with emotional moments and is really a great part of the game.
The art style is also incredible. The cartoon/comic book style is very effective and very beautiful in some moments. Night trench battles, snowy car chases, underground factories - they all look stunning. The characters look great too, there isn't any real dialogue, but you can get a very good sense of the characters from their animation and design. While Freddie walks along with his head high and fists raised, Emile is more worn, more tired.
The game is somewhat faithful to WWI history, but there are plenty of fantastical looking vehicles such as a zeppelin, some sort of prototype tank, and a big French armoured car. However the battles and places are all realistic. The Marne, Ypres, Verdun, the Somme, Vimy Ridge, and the Nivelle Offensive are all depicted. The game also visits various towns, villages, and even a POW camp in France.
The downsides of this game are as follows:
The first main bad thing about Valiant Hearts is how it recognises controllers. Originally, it wouldn't let me use the Keyboard if I had my flight sim throttle and joystick connected, so I had to go disable them in the device manager. However, there are two specific instances in the game where you need an analog axis in order to dig a tunnel that goes in an upwards direction. (Pressing up and right on the keyboard doesn't work.) So I had to go turn the joystick back on in order to complete those levels.
The other bad thing is that it bombards you with a popup telling you to go view the myriad of historical facts in the game. It really takes away from the story if you stop all the time to look at them, so I just ignored them eventually and might go back and read them later.
Overall, this is absolutely recommended. However make sure you have something with an analog axis - I think a playstation or xbox style controller would be great to play the whole game with.

This is a relatively short singleplayer game. Well... game... There's not many functionalities in this game, and it is a very much linear experience. Most of the game play is related to puzzle solving so you may advance onward with the history of the game.
At about 4 - 6 hours of gameplay at a steady pace, the history of this game really does stand out a lot. Some games that hours and hours and hours of gameplay have often failed to make you feel attatched to the characters, wether they're important to the main plot of the game or not. This is not the case with this game, where it does a VERY outstanding job of getting you attatched to the characters from the moment it begins to the moment it ends.
Graphic wise, this game is pretty solid. The art style chosen helps set the climate for the game, in a war torn Europe where warfare has been turned into a mechanized, super efficient killing process. Though the game does not put you straight on the battlefields, it tells you the story of a family broken apart by war at its start. The first few missions and the last ones are heart wrenching as you'll see how war separates people.
The design of the puzzles in this game is quite interesting. You don't need to be a brainiac to figure them out, they're usually quite simple but they'll take a few moments/minutes to solve at most. And if you're having problems doing so, the game itself will provide you hints as to what you need, so no need to look up online guides or walkthroughs for this game.
If you enjoy being a completionist, boy are you in for quite a surprise. The game features over a hundred collectibles scattered throughout the game. What are these collectibles? Objects that were used by the soldiers, civillians and other war-related paraphernalia. From spent cartdriges, broken bayonets and gas masks to X-ray masks, hip flasks, dogtags and letters.
As for a replay value, unless you plan on getting every single collectible and every single achievement in game, the replay value is rather low. As I said, it is a very linear game, and does not give you any wiggle room to experiment with new things.
The one thing I find rather... bothersome is that this game requires Uplay, so... well... It is worth coping with such a thing in order to play this game.
All in all, I give it a 10/10. The game is solid, the plot is incredible, altough it suffers from some rather... non-sensical things. When it comes to conveying the horrors and educating the player about WWI, the game succeeds quite well, albeit, it is limited to the european setting.
It is worth a buy. Even more so if it is on sale.

is a buggy little zombie survival game with potential.  It's currently still in alpha, and that shows.
The strengths of
relate to the art assets.  The graphics are nice -- not spectacular, not anything you haven't seen before -- but they're atmospheric and get the job done.  The sound and background music are of similar quality, perhaps not award-winning material, but solidly respectable.
Where
currently falls down is on gameplay, which is still very uneven and glitchy.  Notable glitches I encountered on my playthrough included materials being consumed on the crafting table just for mousing over a potential item, even if I didn't construct it.  Character abilities are also unclear; in the tutorial an Engineer can build a turret or landmines, but in survival play he cannot.  There's not much of interest for your characters to do once a wave of zombies arrives, either, beyond huddling up in the Medic's healing radius and slowly backing up while shooting.  Much of story mode consisted of nothing more than choosing from a menu of options and randomly suffering numerical gains and losses as a result.
The art and sound suggests to me that the developers are comitted to making a quality indy title.  At this time, however, the deficiencies in gameplay make
not worth playing. Whether the final version is worthwhile will depend almost entirely on how much improvement goes into the play elements.

This is a really small game, but it still takes a bit of time to get to like it. The basic idea is very simple: capture enemy territory by moving your one character along a "baseline", where you are safe from attacks, and cutting off pieces of the territory by leaving the safe baseline. While you're out in the open, you're prone to attacks from cannonballs and dragons, so it's crucial to get a good timing, and even apply some basic strategy here and there.
There isn't much more to it, really, so the game is quite easy to master, but the intricacies of some of the later levels ask for some quick reactions while moving into the open. There is something addictive in trying to finish every level and outwit the dragons; and there are some nice steam-achievement and even trading cards on offer. So if you can pick this one up at a low price: just spend the money, but don't expect a great game in return, just a quick but tasty snack.

Listen, this sim is a serious investment. It's not easy to justify dropping £54.99 / 62 EUR / $72 on a game, but this isn't really a game. It's a full-on, commercial-grade flight simulator and one that will either make or break your commitment to learning curves.
If you do any flying, this sim is the only one worth getting. It accurately simulates flight dynamics based on real-time flight modelling; it's as realistic as you're going to get. Paired with the correct hardware and licences, it allows pilots to log hours towards ratings. So, for the best part of £60, you'll get as close to flying as you can in your home.
For someone who doesn't fly, this game presents a significant challenge. There are some basic tutorials which explain the fundamentals of flying in a Cessna 172 - after that, you're absolutely on your own. There's a few aircraft to choose from, from small GA planes like the Cessna all the way to four-engine passenger jets from Boeing. Systems are accurately modelled and interactable - you really can control everything just as you would in the real machine. So, once you've mastered some simple pootling about in your 172, you can escalate to small jets or 747s and find a whole new level of challenge. It's the only game where I've had to consult actual reference material outside the game, and when I found myself reading a flight manual in my idle time, I realised I was either very sad and or probably justifying my purchase price. It's an immersive world, and if you've got the time and the brainspace, it's rewarding too.
XP11 is endlessly expansible too; the default install package includes the WHOLE world's terrain and is impressively accurate, but with the help of mainly freeware mods online, you can accurately simulate your hometown if you so wish. There's a raft of extra aircraft (including some payware which rivals the base game price) which are unbelievably well-concieved - the community go the extra mile here to faithfully recreate their favourite airliners.
A small mention has to go to the visuals - it's a stunning engine and some of the 3D cockpits are so immersive it's easy to forget you're sitting in front of a monitor. Engaging, stimulating and satisfyingly accurate, Laminar Research have continued to impress with XP11 - but it's not a light purchase. There's a good demo, if you fancy it - and for the love of god, play with some sort of controller, it makes things a lot easier.

Into the Dark is a FPS horror game. The player takes control of Peter O’ Brannon, a detective who is sent to investigate the death of an elderly man in New England. Upon arriving at his cabin, you realise that all is not right and something sinister is going on.
The game makes a poor first impression. The game starts with ultra-low quality artwork and a surprisingly small amount of menu options, there is absolutely no configuration options. To configure the controls you have to edit a text file.
Gameplay consists of exploring bland locations, completing bland objectives and killing bland enemies. In order to complete the games puzzles, you often have to go back to rooms you have already explored to find that objects have magically spawned there. When you finally get past the obstacle, the game is kind enough to spawn an enemy directly behind you.
The graphics are bad. Into the Dark features completely antiquated visuals.
The voice acting for the game is beyond awful. For me it was nearly impossible to hear what is being said, it made it nearly impossible to follow the story.
If that is not enough, there are several technical issues; invisible walls block a door or you could stuck in such a wall. Loading up a saved game, starting a new level and even just doing nothing: all of them can cause crashes.
The best part in Into the Dark is that it includes the complete movie of Night of the Living Dead.
My advice take a look at other horror games. If you just want it for your collection wait for a big discount.

It's basically a board game. There's more randomness than I would like, to the point of being frustrating sometimes. For instance, entering a ruin might teleport you halfway across the map or spawn a monster that will kill you and worse. The "worse" is that once you get infected with the evil Rot, you get permanently weakened in several ways unless you get cured (rare) or go pure evil (also hard). You might also get cards that say "do something useful and gain 1 Rot", and you can't just discard them, so these can become random dead weight in your hand. Want to win using Spirit Stones? They appear randomly and you're unlikely to get them unless one appears nearby. Want to beat quests for Stones or other rewards? You start off with maybe a 40-50% random chance at that, so you can decide to either risk it or do the auto-win option where you solve every quest the timid way and get lesser rewards. Battles are decided by random dice as modified by your willingness to "burn" your random cards to lock dice into specific symbols. If you notice I'm saying the word "random" a lot, there's a reason.
The graphics are nice and the sound pleasant. There's a strong sense of theme, which I enjoy in board games, and a lot of detail obviously went into little animations and other effects. The rules can be confusing for new players, but there's a tutorial. The heroes have enough variety to be interesting without any seeming obviously overpowered.
To enjoy this game you should probably (1) accept that you might win or lose due to random fate regardless of skill, and (2) know that there are several ways to win and that you might need to switch strategies midway through.

Alright, so I know this isn't the newest, or the most hyped Battlefield-game out there, but trust me when I tell you, it's a good one. Now I have played the multiplayer mode on a different account, so don't mind the playtime. The multiplayer is really cool, thank's to Frostbite. Almost everything on the battlefield (pun intented) is destructible, which makes no cover 100% certain. The vehicles also bring depth to the multiplayer mode, since you can, for example ride around in a Jeep or fly a chopper. The multiplayer mode is more fun with your friend(s) (surprise), and you can make a 'squad' just for you and your friends. When you're in a squad with your friends, you can spectate them when dead, and you can also spawn next to them when you're ready, so that you don't have to run all the way back from a control point for example. The campaign mode, however, is the thing that interested me so much that I had to buy it for this account. The campaign's story isn't the most cliche one, but it isn't the most interesting one either. But that isn't even the reason why I wanted to get the game. The campaign simply gets you into a certain mood and additude when you play it. That's why I recommend you to play the campaign mode in dark, so that you can really get into it. My favorite part from the campaign so far is a mission, where you have to snipe, in a rain forest, in a thunderstorm/heavy rain, while in the dark. Playing that mission felt like heaven. So much fun. The price tag isn't too bad either, since it's a fairly old game. The PC multiplayer isn't dead either, so you won't have to worry about that. 8,5/10
