A tactical FPS that ACTUALLY feels tactical and a difficulty curve that can actually be pretty damn unforgiving at certain points in the game. Unlike so many other games that go under the vague auspices of being "realistic" and "tactical" in Republic Commando, you are actually forced to rely on your AI team mates to get you through all of the combat encounters, and fortunately the AI overall is rather competent and will always obey your orders, save for a few minor glitches that I encountered and had to end up backtracking about 20 minutes worth of gameplay, but overall an incredibly tight and satisfying game. The fact that an early 2000's game has AI this responsive and coordinated is highly indicative of how lazy our industry has become. The combat is fluid and fast paced and all of the weapons have a good amount of meat and impact to them. The level design can suffer from linearity on occasion, but as a whole they are a lot of fun to go through and constantly mowing down droids with your squad and getting to feel like a badass was a blast. Despite the fact that I vehemently despise the Clone Wars film, they actually managed to craft a rather decent narrative here and your squadmates are very memorable and it leaves you on a large narrative cliffhanger at the end. It is without question one of the best Star Wars games, full stop. I only ask: When in the name of Christ are we getting a sequel?!

To friends I normally describe this as "Game of thrones" meets "Settlers of Catan" meets "Redwall", but that doesn't really do it justice. This really is a great german-style boardgame with mechanics that takes full advantage of its digital platform.

This game comes off a standard board game with unique playstyles and expectable amount of RNG. It all starts with a variety of characters and way to empower them to seeking 1 of 4 victories, 5 if you include sabotaging one of the two combat victories to give you a prestige win.
The short and skinny. This game is a ruthless and cut throat board game to become King of Armello. Play with friends and assist each other. Play alone and make hair thread alliances that almost always end in tradgedy. Or still play with friends, and go all in for yourself when your friends feel their safest around you. The outcomes are constantly surprising for me.
It all starts with your choice of character who all are naturally attuned toward certain types of victories and ways to empower them toward a certain victory goal as well. But there's no hardline way to play any one character and you can empower them in ways players might not expect or go for victory conditions that aren't typical for a character and quickly surprise and take control of the game with a bit planning and a bit of trickery.
With 3 different core decks of cards that offer general expectations of effects, the first games you play are a bit of a learning experience as each card you draw from different decks can offer some simple yet powerful results on the board from simply stalling opponents to giving yourself a major edge in combat. The longer you play, the more you start to understand what cards are in which deck and you start to make more risky, but informed choices to obtain cards that can more directly suit your play style. And the quests can finally round out your game by giving you equipment and followers that can make or break your gameplan, or even completely change your original strategy.
Admittedly it the RNG factor can feel punishing, yet I cannot bring myself to say it brings down the game. I've played many many games, and I often realize, when the game seems stacked against you. Trying something else can have instant reward. A spirit stone victory where I'm falling behind suddenly becomes an unbelievable comeback victory via the Rot mechanic. It's truly a wonder and while that may be some sort of catch up mechanic in the game, I can't say I've ever truly felt helpless in the game. I find more often than not this game its too easy to get hung up on your original plan and it might seem hopeless to change it. And yet, I find that's the most satisfying aspect as it can lead to the most shocking successes and tide changing games.
There's definitely some tuning that can be done for the game but the Devs are constantly patching and improving the game, making certain cards better, removing lackluster or detrimental ones, and adding new ones that offer even more surprises. Being the nature of a board game I can't really say I expect the most perfectly fair result, a roll of the dice is as fair as it is fickle. And yet without the RNG, a board game like this stands to drift toward optimal setups and pre-determined planning removing any sense of cunning toward playing it. Both aspects I insist the League of Geeks has handled very well.
All I can really say is bravo League of Geeks. And give the game a try. It's worth it.

Beautiful game. The boards, character designs, and card art are all top notch, and a fairly interesting premise drives it all. Devs are generally great and as of fall 2017 are still tackling issues, releasing new content, and generally taking good care of their baby. I've been here since the Kickstarter days and still hop into a game here and there.
It's an interesting marriage of strategy game and board game. The board game element, by its very nature, introduces an element of RNG. You roll d6's and draw from various decks of cards, after all. The strategy element, then, can't be purely skill-based. But there *is* a skill in taking what the game gives you and adjusting your tack. There are 3.5 different victory types, and on occasion you may find that the one you were gunning for is being eclipsed by a better opportunity for another. Or every opportunity wilts before you and you have to try something desperate that juuust might succeed. There are the highs of drawing the exact card you need to win the game this turn, and the lows of feeling like everyone's punching bag. Sometimes both in the same game!
One aspect that might be an issue for some is the standard game length. Some adjustments have been made to speed up this process from its launch state (including Fury Fridays, a weekly ingame event that reworks the turn timers to be much snappier), but you're still looking at games that can stretch past an hour in multiplayer. This doesn't bother me but it does make Armello more of a planned pasttime than something you can just hop into for a quick session.
Armello does have a crate/key system, but they can be earned wholly ingame and the things they unlock are cosmetic. An ultimately harmless addition for people who like collecting. I've enjoyed it, as it can be fun to pair the character I want to play with a particular set of dice.... and I'm not a rabid completionist, so it's okay when a new dice set is introduced before I've finished the last.
Definitely recommended.

I really enjoyed playing the game. Since I'm not into the multiplayer (only because I don't play multiplayer on games like these) I'll talk about the single player campaign.  Probably my most favorite aspects of the campaign are the characters, the weapon system, and the unique enviornments the game sets you in.
The Characters are actually refreshingly more human than most other FPS. The game decided to plant a bunch of hilarious stereotypes together into a single unit, your leader being an old vet who's tired but still willing to fight (Who also has a big"Sgt. Johnson" thing going on too)  A redneck who loves the simplier things in life, who constantly bickers with the much more nerdy and immature technician, and finally your player character who is your run-of-the-mill protagionst.  The chemistry in the unit is some of the most human and funny I've seen.
The weapons system refers partially to the weapons themselves, with a mix of weapons and secondary functions to choose from, and partially to the customization.  At the start of most missions, you receive a crate that allows you to choose what weapons to bring with you, and the farther you go the more playstyles there are to choose from.  It's fun and much more enjoyable than other FPS where your only chance of a different playstyle is if you can find the weapon along the mission.
Finally, there are the enviornments.  While this game offers a lot of different and unique enviornments, I'd say my favorite one is probably in the mission (Sorry forgot the name) where you have to travel down a mountain while a heavy blizzard is blowing.  While of course you can hardly see, the game adds one more interesting twist in the form of forstbite damage. If you stay out and exposed for too long in the cold, you die, so you HAVE to move quickly to continue living, not to mention the enemies that love to shoot you from their WARM buildings.  It's great, and  mixes up the gameplay.
Overall I'd say the campaign is very well done and I really enjoyed playing it.  Again I don't have any experience playing multiplayer so you'll have to find other reviews for that aspect.  if you're like me and play Shooters for the campaign, this is certainly one to pick up.

TL;DR - Sandbox is okay for for a little bit, campaign is, simply, not  fun.
When I bought this in early access, it seemed to initially have a great deal of potential. However, the devs have done nothing to improve the overall gameplay experience since it first went EA. The controls are infuriating, as there is no precision when clicking on a target...Click on a zombie to shoot it, and your survivor runs straight into his loving arms to have his face eaten. The sandbox got old rather quickly due to its repetitive nature, but I had hoped the campaign might offer some change of pace.
However, the campaign mode is absurdly frustrating. Basically, an RNG decides what events are available, which determines what resources are available. For example, If you don't have any ammo, then you can't play a level that provides no ammo, or you will be killed immediately. Given that you only have 30 campaign actions (e.g. search something, play a level, save your game) before you die, and way too many objectives to complete, the campaign is ruthlessly difficult. After about 15 attempts, I decided that there really is little point in playing anymore, since it wasn't even fun by that point. I had hoped for more from this game.
Considering the low price point, I want to give the devs the benefit of the doubt, so expectations of graphics, sound, and grammar/sentence structure can be overlooked. Even so, this one is going away to the "another dissapointment" section of my library. This is mostly because the game just isn't any fun after a short while due to its RNG-ish nature.
Even though it's one of the older Battlefield games, it's still great. I play online almost all the time. I RECOMMEND buying it.

Flat Kingdom is an adventure platform game for the PC that is more adorable than I have words for. It's also incredibly frustrating, just like almost all platformers.
You are Flat, knight of the Kingdom. The Princess has been captured because of course she has. By a fox-headed person, whom I assume is wearing a mask. They are also taking all of the crystals that are keeping the Kingdom wonderful and peaceful. Your job, as Flat, is to stop the Fox, save the Princess and return the Crystals. Easy, right?
The artwork is elegant. It honestly looks like it was all cut out of paper and beautifully crafted together. All of the enemies are adorable, but the boss monsters terrifying. I adore everything about this game: the music, sound effects, story, level designs. It is all incredibly thought out and masterfully put together to create an amazing experience for the player.
As Flat, you are primarily a circle, but can also turn into a square and triangle. Each shape has their own pros and cons for each situation, including how to defeat enemies. Thankfully, the game allows you to have a Shape Legend in the bottom right corner to remind you what shape beats what. Circle beats Square; Square beats Triangle; Triangle beats Circle. This is a constant throughout the game; however, it is difficult to tell what all the monster shapes are and this doesn’t necessarily apply to the boss fights. Which are hell all on their own.
The levels, of course, increase in difficulty, starting off with the false hope that I could actually get through a platformer once in my life. Each level reminded me that I’m horrible at these games and that this is my own personal hell. Whilst still having fun and loving the game, I am cursing at the screen each time I die because I was just never good at these to begin with. I will finish this game, though, if it's the last thing I do.
Right now, I’m in the third section of the game, trying valiantly to finish it and not throw my computer out the window at the same time. My Let’s Plays have dwindled down into death montages and glares at the webcam, but I swear I love this game and, for $8, you will love this game, too. I can’t wait to see what the store has laid out for me because I feel there is so much more than meets the eye.

Very cheap game, the price of a mobile app, and yet so much more gameplay and story. A great, simple game, with fun, engaging, simple and tried-and-true gameplay mechanics. For less than a dollar you can get a game that is better than some $5+ games I own.
Simple story, you are a knight who has returned to his homeland to reclaim his family's throne from an evil wizard. However, this isn't some strategy game where you build up resources or units, nor is this an in-depth RPG or hack-n-slash. No, this game is a thing of pure beauty.
It is simple. You control a knight (Sir Fortix), and you move around the map, cutting out swathes of land. The more land you get, the higher your score. However, there are enemy turrets that can hit you or your drawn line, and dragons that fly around the map and can kill you. There are also enemies that travel around the lines, trying to hunt you down. How do you defeat them? Simple, outline them. Simply run around them so that they are trapped in the piece of land you cut out. Capture catapult triggers to shoot catapults at the enemy turrets and destroy them. You have a set number of lives and a time limit, although each is more than enough I think. This isn't as easy as it sounds, as enemies can fill your screen and multiple turrets can send cannon balls flying everywhere, while you dodge through, vanquishing enemies, capturing triggers and power up, and slowly but surely conquer the map.
Many levels, often with other levels within them, a great, simple, and cheap game that focuses on gameplay and fun. For $0.99? It is a steal and I highly reccomend it. Plus, it comes with trading cards, so you can get emoticons, backgrounds, and badges from this game, and for getting access to this, the price seems even better!
It is a little older, so the resolution is a little off, although setting it to full screen makes it more than playable imo. I've heard of issues with this game on Windows 8.1, but I run Windows 8 64 bit and it runs perfectly.
I do recommend this game, 8/10

I've played a few Board-Game games, but this one actually feels like you are telling a story with your game.

Short version - visually pleasant and fun to play board game with interesting gameplay mechanics aimed at multiplayer with no singleplayer campaign, but also too dependent on microtransactions and additional payments.
Catchy board game with nice animations and graphics. The game mechanics make the game fun to play, basically it combines turnbased movement on the map hexes (normally 3 movement points per turn) with the cards drawn from 3 different decks (items, spells and traps/trickeries. The point is simple - to get to the middle of the map and kill or heal the king before he dies (if nobody heals him or kills him and he dies because of his illness, the player with most prestige wins - it's an alternative win condition).
At first I was kind of sad, because the trailer was pointing to a story based game. But there is no story. Only the main premise in tutorial. Otherwise it's just the same board game with randomly generated tiles. At first you would like to learn the game mechanics and the tactics against AI, but after a while, you'll realize that this is a game that is supposed to be played against other players. So if you're not a multiplayer board game person, this game is probably not for you.
Even though it's fun to play, there not much content in the game. 8 characters that you can play as and one randomly generated map in winter and summer skins, with randomly generated quests (but quests are just specific tiles on the map, where you have to go and the game automatically does a skill-check on specific skill and afterwards the quest is completed).
The sad part is that for all the other stuff you have to pay more money. If you want more characters, you have to pay real money. If you want more than 2 skins for the map, you have to pay the money. If you want your character to look differently, you have to pay more money. You can either buy or collect lootboxes. The bad part is that you need both box and a key and you'll get one for finishing a game randomly. But then they change the season and there are different lootboxes and keys, so if you want to open the previous ones, you have to pay more money.
Absolutely adore the game, i love the art style and the gameplay, though it can be very time consuming...

EDIT: The culprit add-on for most of the crashes is xsquawkbox, an add-on used to fly on a virtual air traffic control network. When you enable AI Aircraft in XP11, it crashes occasionally when trying to render an aircraft from xsquawkbox. The fix is to turn off AI aircraft in XP11, which makes the TCAS not work correctly (both false-positives, and false-negatives). I honestly don't know whether it's XP11's fault or xsquawkbox, but I'm not the only one with the issue.
All my crashes aren't fixed, I still get random ones... And the other day I had to delete the scenery cache after a game update to even get the game to load. It is significantly better though.
EDIT 2: After lots and lots of playing time, I mostly like the game but a few things really frustrate me. However the game is solid enough on the latest beta that I can now recommend it.
1. No winter ground effects. You need an add on. There is snow but you won't see it accumulate on the ground.
2. "Ground suck effect", when you get a few feet from the ground, it's like you're sucked down to the ground. Makes soft landings difficult. This has gotten better over the beta versions but still exists.
3. Flight dynamics are really, really good except for the ground suck effect described above. (Yes, I fly real planes.)
The game is gorgeous. The aircraft are gorgeous. The panels are gorgeous. The Garmin 530 imitation is very accurate. Unfortunately I can't recommend the game. It crashes all the time. It might be a plugin that I have, but here's the deal on plugins:
The built in G1000 stinks.
The Cirrus SF50 lacks a transponder and it's G1000 stack is buggy and hard to use.
The built in FMS on bigger aircraft is absolutely terrible.
So if you want to do any simulations at all involving GPS in a non-prop aircraft, you need to buy addons. Most of the higher end addon planes for XP11 include redone G1000's, knock off Aspens, or other custom glass panels. This is for a reason, because XP11's defaults past the G530 are terrible.
So I have $100 in addon planes from well known names, and my XP11 crashes all the time. I haven't tried removing the planes, because why? If the game doesn't work with them, then it's only good for VFR stuff.

Really really hard to like a game like that.
I was on the beta, I moved off of it thinking maybe that's it...nope.
Who knows, but if this game doesn't have the modularity of FSX/P3D, then it's limited to it's out-of-the-box state...which aside from looks, is something that should be a free early release preview.

Introduction:
Let me start off by saying that this is no video game. This is a highly realistic flight simulator that is used recreationally. When I saw this game, I thought that it would be quite easy to just jump into. And to an extent, it is. I think the worst is that gameplay concepts are completely arbitrary and unjustified narratively. For instance, the main mechanic of the game is about switching between three shapes (circle, triangle and square). Once you are in the right shape, simply touching an enemy will destroy it. This feels really dumb. A rabbit is jumping towards you and you're a circle? Oh man, you're in trouble! But if you're a triangle, the rabbit instantly vanishes by barely touching you ... poof. Reeeeally?? In what kind of fantasy is this cool and immersive? Similarly, the game requires of you to understand that this or that object is associated with a square or circle or triangle. So you are expected to know that a moose is a square (or whatever they thought a moose is, I can't recall). Anyways, none of this resulted in a fun and immersive experience for me.
So yeah, I stopped playing after half an hour because I was not having any fun and I kept being underwhelmed by the game. If like me, you need a game to engage you quickly otherwise you give up on it and go look elsewhere for entertainment, I strongly discourage you from buying this game.

I can describe Flat Kingdom as a ligth-hearted platformer with an AWESOME art design, great music and few but important technical short-comings.
The main feature in the gameplay is that Flat, our main character, has the ability to shape-shift from a circle to a square or a triangle (all conveniantly maped to the corresponding button on a Play Station controller) each one with his own strongs and weaknesses. This mechanic keeps the platforming interesting and adds a little bit of puzzle elements to the game, even thou they're never to hard to solve.
Just like most platformers this game has enemies as well. To beat them you have to touching them while on a specific shape form determined by the shape of the enemy. Flat Kingdom is an adorable little puzzle platformer that won't break the bank.  It's competently put together and adds a bit of a gimmick that keeps the gameplay interesting, with powerups that keep the gameplay evolving throughout the game.
The art style is absolutely wonderful, and the boss fights are intimidating, clever, and fun and pretty well-designed to boot.
I have two main complaints (these aren't as bad as the length makes them seem):
First, the sound design is pretty bad.  Some sounds are way too loud, the overall composition isn't mixed very well, and the Circle form's footsteps are really annoying and actually sound like they're being distorted.
Second, the game's gimmick involves switching between three forms: a speed form, a jump form, and a heavy form.  This is an interesting mechanic, but switching between them could feel much better.  In a game like this I would have expected to be able to carry momentum through the air from one form to another, but what actually happens is that as soon as you swap forms your horizontal speed is immediately changed depending on the form you're in.  This makes the movement of the game feel very rigid.
On that same note, I think I'd have preferred being able to switch forms with L1 and R1 rather than Square (X), Triangle (Y) and Circle (B), since X (A) is bound to jump.  Having transformations bound to the same control set as the jump buttons means that it's difficult to do neat or clever aerial transformations without turning your hand into a claw.  However, it still feels pretty good when you nail a transformation mid-air and cross a gap.
All that said, the game is pretty fun if you're into puzzle platformers, and at 8 bucks, it seems like a pretty solid value.

One of the best games I have played in a very long time. After having met and interviewed Final Boss Entertainment at QuakeCon 2014 under a press event, I was very excited about this game, and my excitement has not changed since then. Even having logged quite a few hours in (on my friends account by accident), I can still say that this game is insanely fun, addictive, and will keep players around for hours. It returns to the old school fast paced-twitch shooters that we remember from back in the mid to late 90's. Great job and the fan workshop is just amazing with throwback content from games like DOOM and DOOM 2.

Fast-paced combat, interesting level design, an awesome art style, powerful weaponry that's satisfying to use, a unique soundtrack, and an addictive kill-chain mechanic - in the realm of arcadey old-school style FPS's, Wrack has a lot going for it.
I've been following the development of this game since its creator, Brad Carney, announced it about six years ago, and in some ways it's turned out better than I could have expected. Sprinting around levels at ridiculous speeds, dodging projectiles, avoiding melee attacks, mowing down hordes of enemies with guns that look and sound great - Wrack does some things that many first person shooters have done in the past, but it does it with a stylish flair that few can match. Beyond that, though, I can't think of any other FPS that does boss battles like this one does, and while there are probably other games in the genre with similar mechanics to the "kill chain/combo finisher" feature of Wrack, I don't know of any that have done it nearly as well.
There's a pure joy in taking down foes with blast after blast of your shotgun, hearing the audio counter for your kill chain getting louder and louder, then charging up a final, massive shot that clears out an entire room. Getting long combos and high scores in Wrack isn't easy, but it's rewarding and really damn fun. Speaking of shotguns, I would assert that this game has one of the best in the genre, ranking up with the others from Doom, Duke Nukem 3D, FEAR, and Halo. It also features a backup melee weapon that is available at all times but is (shockingly)
, and a rocket launcher that's a stupid amount of fun to use. The difficulty levels are also noteworthy in that harder ones do not turn enemies into bullet sponges by giving them more health; it's a matter of how deadly they are to you, not the other way around.
Special shout-out also goes to Bobby Prince for the music and sound effects. The soundtrack gets rather quirky at times, but it's definitely memorable, and everything in the game sounds excellent. That's not to say that the modellers, texture artists, and animators aren't worth mentioning either; Wrack looks damn good.
I kinda wish the pistol was easier to get kill chains with and had a more effective Finisher move, but beyond that, about the only non-nitpick complaint I have is that there isn't more of this game. It's got a solid amount of content for its price, with high replayability; I just want to see the addition of more levels, enemies, bosses, weapons, etc. in either more Episodes (free or otherwise) or a full sequel. I can only hope this game ends up being the success I feel it deserves to be.

Between Xbox and PC, I have a lot more hours than displayed here on Steam. No, I don't have my nostalgia glasses on, I never got a chance to play this game until after Battlefield 4 had been released. I have been a die-hard Battlefield fan since 1942 (Battlefield 1942 was my first First-Person-Shooter game), and played every title in the series with the exceptions of 2142, 1943, and Hardline. This game truly lives up to the hype, and I believe it is the best Battlefield experience to date. It feels like Battlefield 2, and plays as smoothly as if it were released today. There is currently a larger playerbase for this game than there is for Battlefield 3 and Hardline combined, and if you don't feel like grinding through the levels and suffering for joining late, there are a lot of modded servers that will give you thousands of XP for a single kill (I reached level 35 in a single match, being new to the Steam version). I have yet to encounter a hacker (aimbotter or something of that nature), and if I have he wasn't enough of a problem for me to notice. If you are a classic Battlefield veteran like me (you've probably played this game if you are), you'll know "baserape" was a problem in older titles, meaning one team will gain the advantage and camp around the others spawn location making it difficult to turn the game back around and often resulting in an entire team quitting. This game was made before measures against baserape were implemented to the series so occassionally that is something you will face. I recommend this game to lovers of the Battlefield franchise, and for people who want to play a game in which almost every square inch of the map is destructable.
P.S. this game has the the best singleplayer story offered in the Battlefield Series, followed second by Battlefield 1s "War Stories," (Bad Company 2s storyline is longer, and a continuation of the Bad Company storyline. The campaign has an actual progression system and feels more polished).

Flat Kingdom Paper's Cut Edition or FKPCE or maybe Flat Kingdom, whatever the name, it’s a side scrolling, platformer made by an indie developer by the name of Fat Panda Games. Upon first glance at the game, the Paper Mario series might spring to mind. You wouldn’t be completely wrong on thinking that, the games does share several features of the Paper Mario games, but not many. The graphical style has the paper-made-world idea set out pretty well and the music fits well with each stage, feeling cheery when traversing the colourful world and dangerous when fighting against bosses.
Mechanically however, the game doesn’t quite hit the spot. The idea of transforming between different shapes to fight off the varies enemies is a nice idea and fairly unique at that. The puzzles are fairly easy but are a welcome challenge to help players get to grips with the shape transformations. On the other hand there can be some fairly pointless puzzles that seem to serve no real purpose, and some sort of expect you to understand what the developer was thinking to solve them. Also on the rare occasion you can find enemies that you think were square, for example, only to realize they’re actually circular and you just wasted one of your precious hearts. Boss battles are another thing that seems to be on the iffy side. It takes several attempts to figure out what to do, if you can work it out at all, and you sometimes have to be in the mind of the developer to fully understand what’s supposed to happen.
I’ll give the developers credit though, their enemy dies are fairly different, including the bosses. Triangular rats, spherical fish and a killer whale called Hank.
The various stages are all thematically different ranging from cardboard caverns to volcanoes of paper (God knows how that works).
Flat Kingdom is fun game that tries too hard at some junctures but at the same time feels unique. The art style is very reminiscent of the Paper Mario series and it’s great. The mechanics are iffy at times but for the most part they work in the games favor. Overall I’d recommend playing Flat Kingdom even if it’s for a quick platforming fix. It’s different and fun and well worth a look. Good Day!

Good game. Tricky.
I got this game for free from the Devs, after entering a competition on twitter. I thank the devs, and ProjectMQ, for gifting me this game. So here is my review:
This game is a cute, paper-crafted platformer that follows a character called "Flat", a k-night who is ordered by the King to save his daughter and recover the mystical gem from a thief called Hex. The game focuses on shapes (like squares, traingles and circles), and how you manipulate the k-night into shapes to perform various tasks (such as becoming a circle to bounce, a triangle to run fast, and a square to become a piece of heavy rock that crushes near everything). You can change your "shape" to manipulate the enviroment around you.
The gameplay is fun, you have to think (which is asking a lot, y'know) about some of the puzzles. The bosses are pretty good, though some are somewhat bland.
This game is really tricky at first, trying to figure out how to use every shape in certain situations, which shape defeats x, which shape will help me get past y, etc. As time progresses, you learn what works best, it's really fun mucking around with shapes to complete a task.
Now, the story. Not great. Definitely not bad, it's good, but it could be better. The delivery is pretty good, but it has a mundane storyline, with what feels like a cut-out, run of the mill story. It's told very well, with likeable characters, but could've been done somewhat better.
Now, the Graphics. The game uses a paper-craft style, making to look like a foldout book you read as a child. The game looks pretty, though has some UV Wrapping issues, making some of the textures looks stretched and odd, though this was hardly a problem. The game looks stunning, and will run on even the most basic of toasters (unless you were like me and had a toaster from the year 1).
I like most everything from this game, the music, graphics, some elements could be better done, but overall, I really like it.
: 8/10

I had no idea that this game was going to be so addictive and enjoyable! It has the feeling of a boardgame in which you receive cards every turn and must decide movement, but where combat is largely determined by dice roll and strategically keeping cards in your hand that can be "burned" to result in a specific outcome on your dice. It is relatively simple to learn, but figuring out how to be clever and flexible to achieve victory in an environment that can be pretty dynamic is actually quite challenging. I've fallen in love with the game, and the variety of characters available is a lot of fun. If you are an antisocial gamer, you can enjoy solo play against AI opponents and have an excellent time. If you like multiplayer and putting yourself up against human intelligence, that is also available. A great game, and well worth the money. Be aware that there is a store within the game that sells things like DLC, skins, and that kind of thing. You can enjoy yourself without engaging with the store.

Armello is as close as we can get to a board game experience, and a great one at that. Its rules are quite deep and very well thought, providing a well-balanced mixture of luck and strategy. The game is beautiful to look at, fun to play, and challenging enough to keep you coming back for more. Even if you’ve never played a game like this before, it’s enjoyable just learning to play and finally getting a satisfying victory.

When I first entered the animal kingdom of Armello, I just had to think about Settles of Catan because of the hexagonal spaces of the board. And, to some degree, the game is a bit like that. But there's WAY more to do in this magical world than meets the eye. Here are a few exemples:
- Travelling the kingdom and completing quests
- Facing crow shaped horrors...and (possibly teaming up) players (really, focus them too hard and they strike back, just like the empire)
- Being hunted down by Royal Guards when you got a bounty on your head
- Shanking the King while he is becoming increasingly evil by a mysterious plague called the Rot
- Becoming increasingly evil yourself and kill the king with your Rot.
- Transforming the kingdom into a minefield of traps
- Making your defenses indestructible with legendary items
- And, last but not least, becoming the king (or tyrant, or just some promotod noble/priest with a lot of prestige) and hopefully lead Armello to a new age of wealth etc.
Sounds like a lot of fun things to do in this game, doesn't it? It is really fun, but be careful for people who bully/team up and pretty long match times (unless you're playing on Fury Friday).

For those wondering...
IS THIS GAME'S STORY CANON? (SPOILERS)
For the most part no, anything that was not the Movies or the Clone Wars animated series were never really canon and they everything that was not the movies or the clone wars series were offically decanonized by Lucasfilm after the company got sold.
IS THE CHARACTERS, WEAPONS, AND OTHER ELEMENTS CANON?
Some things yes, Delta Squad made an apperance in the Clone Wars animated series thus making them canon. The Trandoshon Shotgun also made an appearance in the Clone Wars along with it being in a EA's Star Wars Battlefront DLC named the "scatter gun" (loved using it in both games)
Other things no, The follow up to Battle of Kashyyyk does not line up with how it happend in Revenge of the Sith (this was made prior to the movie so that is understandable)
General Grevious resembles the 2003 cartoon so i'd assume if he had any lines in this he would sound like he did in that series thus making his role in this game non canon by default.
In canon the Trandoshons do in fact use regular blasters and when their shotgun made an appearance in the Clone Wars it did not eject any shells.

Since this is a trilogy pack, I’ll make a short review about each game.
The first in this series. You play as an amateur treasure hunter, Mark. While out at sea with your wife, you suddenly get swept away and resurface at an island shrouded in fog. From here you must figure out what’s going on and find a way to escape.
+60fps
+Good atmosphere
+Good number (although not unique) HO scenes
+Fairly sharp visuals
+Logical puzzles
+Reused HO scenes
+Boring story
+No voice acting
+Back and forth traveling (no map to fast travel)
+Music drops out a lot
+Notes in diary give away too much
A HOG that is pretty average. Would have given it 5/10, however, the lack of any voice acting and reused HO scenes multiple times knocks this down another point.
Below average
The second in the series. You play as Angel, Marks wife from the first game. This time she resurfaces and seems to have gone crazy and is in a hospital. You flip between what is supposedly real and her dreams (or nightmares).  Strangely, the intro and all cutscenes go by very quickly and makes it hard to follow along as to what the story even is. Blink and you miss it.
Improvements from the first game include; not as much backtracking, some voice acting, music didn’t seem to drop out (or I didn’t notice it)
+60fps
+Good atmosphere & eerie background music
+Good number (although not unique) HO scenes
+Fairly sharp visuals
+Logical puzzles
+Reused HO scenes
+Boring story. Intro is rushed.
+Notes in diary give away too much
Some improvements over the first game. The bonus chapter tries to explain some origins as to what is going on. Still can’t give it 5.
Below average
The third and final game in the series. You play as an investigator who goes to the island for another purpose but soon you realize the chaos that has already begun. There is some voice acting like the second game. However, this still suffers from pacing issues as character lines are spoken back to back and even cut themselves off. A strange addition to a HOG are quick time events. Yes…there are QTE’s in here. It amounts to you clicking words on the screen. Very basic and not sure why this was in the game. The music loops frequently and doesn’t match any scene.
Improvements from the second game include; locking inventory screen and a map showing where available actions are.
+60fps
+Good atmosphere & eerie background music
+Good number (although not unique) HO scenes
+Better story telling than the first two
+Fairly sharp visuals
+Reused HO scenes
+Music repetition
+Basic quick time events (why?)
+Voice over pacing
+Notes in diary give away too much
+No real conclusion to whole trilogy story
Below average
Overall, this trilogy pack struggles and I would not recommend this unless you are into this specific HOG genre. These three games are not terrible, but need more improvements to hit the average for what I expect from HOG’s.

The enemy AI can be a bit ♥♥♥♥ed at times but this is one of the most realistic shooters you can play.
I don't mean the Arma 3 type of realistic - where you have 10 different buttons for crouching at varying heights. I mean in the minmalistic UI, the difficulty, the sounds - each bullet ricochet ping hitting your cover, the graphics of bullets bursting through the window you are near and bouncing off the roof leaving faint scorch marks, how your vision fades and your guy screams for help when you are bing supressed, it all comes together to create a rather amazingly "horror" experience out of a game not intending to be a typical horror game (i.e. monsters going "blargle garble" and biting your face off).
Play this, and on the hardest difficulty, and you'll get a bit of an idea what it would be like to be in a real CQC firefight situation.

Origins is the only one of the group that has a map, which made it much easier to keep track of than the other two. Fortunately, I got the games as a bundle and didn't pay full price, so they're still worth playing. They just aren't my favorites in the genre.

With one boring, one half-decent, and one semi-enjoyable game in this package, Twisted Lands Trilogy will hardly be the crown jewel of a hidden object gamer’s library. Still, if you can get it very cheap, try the last game, as it is the only one that is worth any notice.
Probably the only good thing about Shadow Town is that it looks amazing for its age—because as a HOG, it is terrible and boring: endless walking around in circles, with hidden object scenes reused so often that you’ll know the item placements by heart.
There is also barely any story: we play as a man trying to find his wife after they were shipwrecked on an abandoned island. There is next to no plot between the intro and the ending (although the latter one is quite clever).
Insomniac is an improved carbon copy of Shadow Town with a lot less repetition, but a copy nonetheless: it even reuses many of the previous game’s assets.
To its credit, it at least tries to tell a story. Sure, it was ripped straight from Silent Hill 2—same premise, same revelation, even the same “real world/nightmare world” pairing—but playing as the wife we were looking for through the first game as she tries to escape a mental hospital finally gives some motivation to stay in the game.
Origin is a prequel, this time with a plot similar to Resident Evil 2: we play as an investigator, who arrives just in time to witness the outbreak that turned into the inhabitants of the island to those monsters we saw in the previous games, trying to save the child of the scientist who caused the trouble.
Almost all game mechanics and gameplay elements were replaced, from the user interface to the graphical style. All that remained was the reuse of the same hidden object scenes, but apart from that, Origin is just a typical average HOG. Strangely, this is why it is probably the most enjoyable of the pack.

Former Microsoft Flight Simulator flyer since FS98:
I Highly recommend X-plane 11 for aviation enthusiasts.
Go for multiplayer and hit the books before it. Forget about single player ATC, they were never meant to be realistic and with that it degrades your knowledge of real radio comunications as far as realistic as possible used in Pilot Edge network (paid subscription and used by professionals) and in some extent VATSIM network (free).
Helpful free flight planning services from websites:
- for flight planning, weather consultation resource and real life charts ranging from STARS, SIDS to Airport taxiways.
- for high density weather information of various types across real life airports in real time.
- for payload and fuel load on your flight plan conditions and fllight briefing output text file for consulting during flight.
Helpful Navigation Data updated in parallel to real life navigation data and charts (paid service from subscription to one time payment to acess navdata cycles (check the website for more info):
Get high level simulated aircraft from the X plane org store (paid) by very competent developers that spent years making them, and several community free addons including thousands of airports and orthoscenery (aerial/satellite imagery).

X-Plane 10 was definitly ahead of it's time and I still believe it is a great sim.  Since the release of the IXEG 737, and the 1.2 update officially offering XP11 support, I see no reason to go back to Microsofts platform.  Compared to version 10, the atmosphere is far improved, the lighting looks correctly saturated and appealing, the shading and colors look life like, and the entire sim is optimized beautifully (even more so in the coming update).  The flight dynamics feel better and the entire scene is more convincing.  The default clouds are greatly improved compared to XP10, although in full overcast, they are resource heavy.  Xenviro or SMP could help with this.  I am disapointed that we lost some more advanced control over the graphical settings, but it makes it easier for new users to get into it, without adjusting settings for days.  The joystick and control implementation is much better, as are the menus.  There is no annoying pauses and everything is internal.  Microstuttering seems to be no longer an issue, although I have adjusted my Nvidia settings.  I run XP11 with a GTX 970 overclocked, 16 GB of DDR4, and a 6700k at 4.6Ghz and run an average of 40-50 FPS on pretty much all scenarios, with dips into high 20s to low 30s with overcast skies.  Overall, XP11 is a massive improvment on the already great platform and it gets better with every update!

This game is well on its way to becoming huge.
The map design so far (on 8 completed official levels) is by no means simplistic - high attention to detail and layout is clearly shown in increasingly large labyrinth-like levels, with expertly placed enemies and items.
The graphics are of a cartoony-like nature, and work really well with the rest of the game. Personally, I much prefer the Wrack-style textures to that of Borderlands (and we all know how successful that was!)
The AI, pretty average in intelligence, are well animated and immersive to play against. There are a few bugs here and there, but remember, this game is not finished! Don't be fooled how some enemies are easily killed near the beginning, or even how the hyperblade can one-hit most non-boss enemies, the game is NOT a walk in the park on the harder difficulties and will satisfy your gameplay desires!
Bobby Prince, who has made the soundtrack to Wrack (as far as I know, correct me if I'm wrong), has done a particularly marvellous job on the music for the game, that really compliments the overall enjoyment of Wrack. It's really easy to get into the swing of the game when high quality instrumentals accompany your race to The Hyperion Generator!
Wrack comes with a level editor as well. If you're like me, you may attempt making a map for five minutes and get confused. We could do with some more video tutorials, Brad! :)
The fact that Wrack has a level editor creates potential for a very close-knit community, which could produce many fantastic map packs, mods and god knows what else! There have already been a few releases, and I'm excited to say the least!
I highly recommend this game to anyone with the current price tag, as the game is being worked on by reliable developers and can only get better. Carnevil made the right decision leaving SkullTag to produce this masterpiece!

The first thing that jumped out at me was the catchy music, all done by veteran game composer Manami Matsumae (Mega Man). It sets a tone for a lighthearted adventure full of puzzles and puzzling enemies!
The art that complements the excellent score is suitably vibrant, crisp, and full of personality in spite of it's simplicity. It harkens back to the days of Paper Mario and Kirby 64, and helps overall in telling the story of Flat's journey to save his kingdom and his princess. The papercraft ascetic really shines when telling a storybook style tale dealing with geometric figures and spatial dimensions, an oddly specific combo that just works well. Enemy and boss design are a combination of cute and imposing, and some of the games bigger bosses were some of the most interestingly designed "paper" enemies since Super Paper Mario.
The game play is where Flat Kingdom's originality actually shines through most.  Built around the simple idea of changing the characters shape to fit with a surprisingly logical weakness system based on the traditional "rock, paper, scissors" dynamic. Using a PS4 controller (or another of the many supported controllers) your square, triangle, and circle buttons allow you to instantly change into their respective shapes.
Learning which shape will get you out of every problem you come across is most of the fun, with enemies and environmental puzzles relying on the players pattern recognition, wit, and even reaction time to swap shapes contextually. Triangle can shuriken between wall panels, circle can double jump, square makes you immoveable against raging winds.
All of the enemies have a weakness, and the bosses have not only patterns, but also require you to switch between your multiple forms to deal with their various phases. The combat does not have the weight or satisfaction as many other platformers, but Flat Kingdom's focus is not on fighting. It usually comes down to running into the right part of an enemy with the right shape to deal a set amount of damage. It's simple, but it works well considering that the game's fights are supposed to be more akin to a puzzle themselves.
The story is a tale of bravery, loyalty, and deception...surprisingly deep for a platformer, however it all is kept minimal and light. The story and the scenery complement each other effortlessly.
I would HIGHLY recommed this game to fans of retro games and light but challenging platformers. The difficulty was never too easy, but never made me want to pull my hair out. Fat Panda has done a great job with their debut and I look foward to seeing more from them in the future.

Finished it. Pretty darn boring, the boss battles are the lowest lowpoint. Maybe ok for small children, but even little kids would get bored by the second boss. To me, this is a good example of poor level design.

+ Beautiful paper looking art style filled with color and detail. Some of the backgrounds are so wonderful. I would have to say the graphics are a joy to look at throughout the entire game and are quite charming.
+ Great level design with a variety of unique environments. The levels are short so you constantly feel encouraged to keep going and see what new creative area is coming up next. There's also lots of alternate paths to explore.
+ The boss fights are challenging, and each boss has a unique and creative way to defeat it. You will actually have to learn the mechanics of each boss, and figure out how to defeat them which I found to be a lot of fun.
+ Fantastic soundtrack
+ Unique combat mechanics. You are able to transform between a square, triangle, and circle. Enemy creatures are also shaped in similar ways. Combat sort of works like Rock, Paper, Scissors. If you are in square form you are able to defeat triangle monsters by touching them, triangle beats circle, circle beats square.
+ Great controls (at least when using a controller), and the platforming felt spot on. There are a lot of different moves you unlock as well.  Square transformation lets you walk underwater. Circle lets you double jump. Triangle let's you run "dash" very fast. Later you can even combine them, such as dashing as a triangle then turning into a square to launch yourself at a barrier to break through it.
- The story is a bit cliche. "The world was in chaos with war and monsters, a sorcerer came and sealed the chaos in jewels, the world was peaceful, some mysterious person steals the jewels (and the princess) and the world falls into chaos again" I feel like this story has been told far too often.
- The way to defeat some of the bosses is fairly vague at times, while others seem to be far too difficult. I often needed to look up a guide.
- I had problems using a Xbox One Controller with this game (other controllers work fine)
- There's a section near the end that makes you go back and find hidden levels in areas you have already been to. I felt very discouraged by this.

Flat Kingdom is a puzzle platformer with a unique combat system and interesting story. Many years ago the Kingdom was in chaos and this was due to the world being in 3D. A sorcerer came along and created 6 magical jewels which transformed the land to 2D. The chaos was banished forever.
This of course was until a thief called Hex decided he wanted to kidnap the Princess and while he was at it he also stole one of the magic jewels. The land began to transform back to 3D, bringing back chaos with it. It is up to you as the hero flat to save the Princess and the Kingdom!
Flat is the only one capable of surviving encounters with 3D objects. Flat has the special ability of being able to transform into various shapes. He can be circle, triangle or square. You must choose which shape will help you progress and solve puzzles. Circle moves at a reasonable pace and can double jump. Triangle runs very fast and square moves slow but is very heavy which is useful for smashing ledges and moving objects. The combat system as mentioned earlier is unique. Instead of firing weapons to kill enemies you simply have to come into contact with them. However you must ensure flat is the correct shape. In circle you can kill square enemies. In triangle you can kill circular enemies and in square you can kill triangular shaped enemies.
The puzzles offered, unique gameplay, graphics and original music from Manami Matsumae all warrant a look at this game. All in all a review score of 8.6 out of 10 has been awarded. You can read the full review here at OrangeBison:

Grand Theft Auto: Episodes from Liberty City is an expansion pass for GTA 4 where you have to DLC packs which both expand on the story of GTA 4. I will review both as separate games so let's get into it.
Grand Theft Auto Lost and Damned:
This expansion pass follows on the biker gang Lost and Damned who are old school gang in Liberty City. The story follows on Johny Klebitz as he tries his best to keep his chapter under falling out.
This expansion is really good, for story, but not so much for missions.
Now I know that I should have expected this, from an expansion that follows on Bikers, but I didn't really like how much of the entire expansion follows on bike rides. But the story missions were fun and challenging.
Music wise I enjoyed the rock music in this game, it's a very fitting choice of music for this expansion and it works well.
The entire expansion overall is still better than the entirety of GTA 4, I enjoyed the story and action based missions, but hated all the bike stuff, because of how bikes control in GTA 4 overall.
Next up is Grand Theft Auto The Ballad of Gay Tony:
This expansion is better than Lost and Damned and GTA 4.
This expansion follows on Luis a bodyguard who works on a business man Gay Tony. The entire expansion takes place after the Three Leaf Clover mission in GTA 4 and is all about Luis trying to save Tony's dying business by taking up different business ventures.
This expansion is incredibly fun and I had tons of fun playing through it. A lot of the missions are really fun action packed missions and it fixes a lot of the problems that Lost and Damned and GTA 4 had.
The overall atmosphere is also not as dark and lightens the tone. It's also incredibly funny, the characters are funny and it's all really fun.
Lightening the tone also helps a lot, cause GTA 4 being way too serious made the game kind of boring to play.
This expansion also paves the way to GTA 5 like the medals in missions and multiple characters.
Overall this expansion is a great addition and is overall better than the main game, but I still suggest playing all three games.
Pros:
+ Funny and cleverly written stories
+ Missions are action packed so it never gets boring to play
+ Soundtracks which fit the overall atmosphere of the expansions
Cons:
- Gameplay and Car physics aren't that good
- Gun gameplay is incredibly stiff
Final Rating:
9/10

This triology has the potential (sic) to gain maximum points in this category. But alone the potential isn't just enough. Still the story is great, if you wish to say it's a mixture of the Cthulhu Mythos beings Yig, some Shadow over Insmouth and H. G. Wells, Arthur Machen and of course Brian W. Aldiss Saliva Tree. The mix is what brings up some novelty thoughts, and makes the game in it's story worthwhile to play.
The game works like a charm, everything is in it's place and none of the games crashed during play. Especially fine is the fact that turning of the screen ratio isn't crippling the game. There are two Collectors Editions in this triology, the last game "Origins" is as it is perfect. The last part plays sometimes like an interactiv film, actually faking it, still the notion is very nice.
Yes, there are two collectors editions in this bundle. The last game is as it is, but to a collectors edition some nice adds would have been nice, like soundtrack (for MP3, Ringtone etc.), Wallpapers, and conceptuals. The last chapter would have been a brow raiser if there would have been set another "Bonus Chapter", as the last game concludes the story without an open thread.
Actually the games are far from perfect, but they are a good rendition of possibilities, they tell a good story, they work perfectly and have added content. The riddles are as challenging as you wish them to be, but actually it would be great not to skip them, because they are all solvable with some work. For me it was fun to play them.
Three games, all of them are good on the story side, nothing too pesky, the riddles are well thought, some of them aren't original others are just variations of known riddles or puzzles. You get three games for 20 Bucks, that is ok, if only the games would have a good replayability, which actually tends towards zero, and maybe just nostalgia or senility migh cause me to once again savour the nice story. The game has earned it's recommendation, because the story alone makes it a worthwhile waste of time. Besides the story, the graphics, the sound and the atmosphere as a whole is just a perfect fit. This is quite a good series of games.
VIsuals, graphics, and music are all the usual HO-game fare, nothing special and nothing too poor.  Minigames are engaging and rarely too annoying and the hidden-object scenes themselves are detailed and crisp.  Objects are not too challenging to find but they aren't too easy either.  It's a good mix.
Of the three games, I enjoyed the second the most, but they were all enjoyable.  While the plot isn't the pinnacle of literature (and what HO game offers such a plot?), I was engaged by the plot continuing through the three games and I enjoyed it as the various pieces of the plot-puzzle clicked into place as the games progressed.  I found myself genuinely curious about what was happening and how it was going to turn out.
There is only one really noticeable downside in my opinion, and that is the lack of a map.  Each game has a pretty extensive area to cover and there is a lot of backtracking, so a map would have been helpful, especially with what I call the "zoom zoom" function to jump across the map if necessary.  In games with this much area and as much backtracking as there is, not having that ability is a little annoying.
There are some other things missing that other games offer, such as achievements and extra items to find (for example, the "find all 18 seahorses" sort of extra goals).  This doesn't impact the game in the least, just something to keep in mind if you like very complex games with a lot of extras.
Game length is average for this genre, at about three hours per game and some extra time for the bonus chapters.  If you normally buy this type of game at full price, it's a decent deal; if not, it's certainly worth wishlisting and waiting on a sale.

The stories aren't bad and there's a lot of reading in the forms of journals and diaries, I mean some are 20-30 pages of reading.
I did find the game pleasantly surprised me with the plot twists that I honestly did not see coming.

There are some decent puzzles involved and some repeat the puzzle but with different circumstances, so there is some bit of repetition.
My main gripe is that you will find yourself lost and not knowing what to do next, but you can click the hint thankfully. The next gripe I have is the items, there are things that will work jsut fine logically to do a task or complete a puzzle but it won't let you so you have to find the exact thing to do it.
The final small gripe I have is the hidden object parts and the descriptions just aren't accurate or what you would expect. Example find the flask, in one part of the game the flask is a lab beaker type flask, the next part of the game the flask is the type you would carry with you with alcohol in. The next example would be find the bandage, there are several types of what I would consider bandages in the picture but only one of them is the correct one so you just have to keep clicking on them each. You'll find plenty more of those types of things in the games puzzles.
Bottom line: If you like hidden object games and can get this deeply discounted or in a bundle then go for it but I would not pay full price as they're just too short for the price.

Twisted Lands Trilogy is, as the name suggests, a collection of three games: Shadow Town, Insomniac ond Origin. The games are Hidden Object games. The overall difficulty of all three parts is ok and you'll have a help function, if you get stuck.
The Story:
Mark Brown, a tourist and hobby treasure hunter, and his girlfriend Angel are swept ashore of an unknown island near Spain after a promising treasure diving that somehow went wrong. When Mark regains conciousness, he realizes that Angel went missing and later discovers that she realy got kidnapped. The Island is somehow disturbing as it is on no maps and always under a layer of fog. Although there is a small town and even a modern looking ship in the harbour, there is now sign of any living person. In fact, the original inhabitants of the small town seem to have disappeared around 1921 when something happend that made some people go mad or simple disappear. The ship in the harbour is also deserted although it has come to the island not very long ago to follow a distress signal.
You'll have to discover as much as possible about the past events and rescue Angel.
Shadow Town also contains a bonus chapter after you've beaten the main game where you play the person who sent the distress signal that lured the ship into the harbour. Still it remains unclear how said person came to the island and why.
In this game you play as Angel, girlfriend of the character in the first part. Angel was (again) swept ashore and seems to have lost her wits due to the events in the first part. She has been brought to a hospital or, to be more specific, to a mental asylum. The game jumps back and forth between short scenes where Angel tries to escape the asylum (in modern days) and long episodes where she explores the twisted island from the first part, although the story is rather blurry and it remains unclear (at least to me) if one of those two settings or even both are just in Angels imagination. At least, the game explains the presence of the main character of the first part's bonus chapter.
Insomniac again has a bonus chapter where you play a women called Terese that lived on the island in 1920, when the evil started to spread on the island. This bonus chapter tries to explain the events on a more scientific basis as
which is not a big spoiler as you can guess this at the very beginning of this bonus chapter...
The third part tries to clear some of the yet unsolced questions from the first two parts. This time you don't play in modern times, but in 1921 when a private detective was sent to the island by Terese's father to find out why she didn't write a letter in the past three month. The moment the detective arrives on the island the evil events are already in progress. Only very few residents of the island are still there but compared to the first two parts with no character interaction at all, the town really seems somehow alive. Now, finding Terese is not too much of a problem, but you'll soon realize that everyone still on the island, including you, is in big danger, and you'll have to find a way to flee. You'll even find the origins of the main person of the first part's bonus chapter. In the end, there are still some questions unanswered, but as the triology ends here and there is no bonus chapter this time, we'll have to live with that.
As all three games are quite similar, I can sum up the pros and cons for all of them.
There are no real jump scares included, but some scenes that may come a little unexpected, you'll see some dead people with really horrific background stories as
and the games are still horror games. So you'll have to decide for yourself if this is something you can handle or not.
Overall, I can recommend this games. You might want to wait for a discount though, because 20€ for roughly 10 hours of gameplay are not overly much but also not in the low budget category.

Twisted Lands Trilogy is telling the tale of an island that disappeared under an intense fog.
Twisted Lands: Shadow Town, already present in the Hidden Bundle 5 in 1, has as hero Mark Brown, who disappeared in the middle of the sea, with his wife Angel and who resurfaced on a strange island under an intense fog. What secret will he discover?
The plot of the first game is perhaps basic but with all the questions arising during your quest and the fact you're seeing ghosts, you bet that there is a dark cult under it. Though the end tells you how Mark came on the Island, which is a shocking twist, playing it a second time had made more understanding of the story than the first time. The graphics are correct, the soundtrack is also too, but the problem is that you're doing a lot of backtracking for an object. You may not understand why a cruise boat from 2008 managed to get lost on an island left behind during the '20 but the bonus chapter is showing you a tourist that escaped monsters and that sent a SOS to the ship, which in turn, got sucked into the poisonous ambiance.
Twisted Lands: Insomniac is putting you in the mind of Angel Brown, found ashore and severely traumatized, so badly that she is in a psychiatric institute. You need to escape the hospital but each time you're sedated, you're sent back to the island that made you suffered. You're discovering a new side of it, but also, the why of the tourist in the bonus chapter from the first game.
The plot is alternating between your mind and the hospital, which is a good idea. Yet, the fate of Angel and Mark, her husband, is still kinda blurry: while Mark is probably dead since all this time, you don't know about Angel. The ending is an echo to what she dreamed.
Graphics are good, though they reused some ghosts from the first game. The soundtrack is correct. The puzzles are not too hard, though some of them are a real challenge, as in the previous story.
The bonus chapter is introducing you in the why of the island was infected, as it's more and more obvious that it was an experiment gone wrong - seen through the eyes of Teresa.
Twisted Lands: Origin is making visit the island in the '20, as a detective sent by Teresa's father. Given the fact that her husband is the culprit behind the infection of the island and that their son and she are prisoners, you'll need to rescue them and any people not infected. In the end, you're discovering the story of the ancestors of the tourist from 2008... and also how some scenes in the first game became like that.

In the end, the trilogy is a nice thing to have, though I find the price high for it, wait for a discount for them.

11/10 Gr8 B8 M8. Been simming since FS9 and I've found the best overall experience in XP11.
What I really found different about XP11 compared to those I had flown in the past were how its flight dynamics were portrayed in their engine. P3D and FSX always had a "flat" feel to its flight dynamics, whereas XP11 has a much more realistic feeling. It seems that physics between the wind and the aircraft's wings are actually modelled, so your flight will most likely feel quite a bit more "bumpy", as opposed to the "flat" experience in P3D/FSX. In this way, it is a bit more difficult to fly in XP11, but there is no greater satisfaction than when you finally get that perfect flare and soft landing.
The community in XP11 has been astonishing, with so many quality freeware addons available that would cost a fortune in P3D. I highly recommend Ortho4XP for photorealistic scenery, the numerous airport sceneries by MisterX, as well as simHeaven's VFR Landmarks.The Zibo 737-800 and the FMOD soundpack that goes along with it, is one of the best freeware addons for XP11 right now and is comparable to many payware addons I've flown in the past. Not quite a PMDG 737NGX experience, but pretty darn close and not $70. Reshade is a nice graphical enhancement, just find a preset and tune it to your liking. You'll find many more sceneries and utilities that will aid your simming experience on the org.
There are of course flaws such as the far less appealing clouds, limited weather, jagged shadows, lack of seasons, and bad ATC, but I find them to be minor and they don't harm my sim experience too much. (Pilot2ATC is a great offline ATC alternative, or just use VATSIM online)
Performance is pretty okay (i7-4790K and GTX970) and I am usually above 35 frames, but it can drop to 25 in heavy overcast/autogen.
I will admit that there is still a lack of payware addons. The FlightFactor 757, 767, IXEG 737, JAR A330 (w/ BSS Soundpack), and Rotate MD-80 are probably the best payware airliners out there currently. FlightFactor's 777 is aged and desperately needs a cosmetic update, but it is a must for my long-haul flights. XPRealistic Pro is a must have for those who want a much more immersive experience. Weather addons are very limited, but ActiveSky have announced that they will support XP11 in the future and xEnviro is available currently. Once more developers (especially PMDG) turn to XP11, this sim will simply be the best in the future. As of now, it feels limited because there aren't as many payware addons as P3D, but this may be due in part, because I largely fly airliners.
There is no perfect sim out there, but X-Plane 11 has been the most satisfying experience for me. It is my hope that Laminar Research will continue to improve this sim and that more developers will turn to XP11 to offer a better and more competitive freeware/payware market that will contribute in making this sim even better.

The limited chat options are a nice feature, in my opinion, when playing against a group of randoms. If trash talk is your thing then you might not enjoy that you can only select a handful of responses/insults to throw your opponents way. If playing with friends, then just jump on your voIP platform of choice and you'll be forming uneasy alliances with your friends in no time...only to betray them later of course. I mean c'mon there's only one winner after all and there's no way you're just gunna let Steve walk into the palace with the spirit stones you helped him get while you were buffing up your attack level the whole time...
The visuals and soundtrack are some of my favourite in years and the individual card artwork had a lot of thought and effort put into it.  You can tell that the creators of the game and the artists and everyone involved are passionate about the content they've worked on and released. The Dev's seem fairly active in supporting the game and are putting out updates in a timely manner and really seem to engage and listen to the community when issues crop up. I'd say they've done a pretty great job in supporting the game.
End of the day, if you like board games that are eays to learn but hard to master and you dont mind whe RNG just doesn't go your way, then this game is one you'll likely enjoy.

Having spent more than 500 hours flying the flag for X-Plane 11 and offering too much support in the Steam forums, I thought now would be a good time to review X-Plane 11, and explain why it beats all other flight simulators.
--
Let's start with what's in the box. You're getting a mixture of very high-quality general aviation aircraft, some good airliners and some other aircraft, such as a helicopter, glider and military aircraft. Some of these are brilliant, some need more work. But the default aircraft are good enough for any aspiring flight simmer.
The default weather is, as usual, not good. The clouds, rain and other effects don't do justice sadly, but developers are slowly moving from FSX to X-Plane, and soon we'll have the best weather plugins for X-Plane 11. That said, the new haze and fog effects, lighting, reflections and cloud shadows are really good for a default version of a simulator.
X-Plane 11 has been 64-bit the longest of any sim, and the devs themselves are years ahead of their competitors. Take P3D and FSW for example. Both are now 64-bit in 2017, whereas X-Plane has been 64-bit since 2014-2015. And it will only get better - X-Plane is moving to the Vulkan engine soon. This means not just one CPU core, but your entire CPU will be able to deliver exceptional frame rates for such a great sim. You'll also be able to SLI/Crossfire your GPUs too.
The X-Plane community is also some of the best you'll ever come across. The official forums, although now slow and a nightmare to navigate, are fuelled with both newbies and old-timers, real pilots and developers. I think the price of the sim means younger, less intelligent people are less likely to buy this sim, so you'll only come across the more professional flight simmers in X-Plane.
Additionally, the forums are PACKED with freeware. Freeware to enhance the weather and skies, some excellent payware-quality airports and aircraft, plenty of plugins and an array of other stuff that means a £1000-equivalent copy of FSX might only set you back less than £100 in X-Plane 11. This is a huge advantage - no other sim has a bigger freeware:payware ratio than X-Plane.
Moreover, X-Plane has been developed by devs who will actually listen to you. Drop them an email, they'll read it. Comment on their developer posts - they'll listen. Austin Meyer - creator of X-Plane - is still developing the sim over 20 years on, and there is so much more to look forward to. Future updates of X-Plane 11 look extremely promising, and I for one, cannot wait to see what the team has to offer.
X-Plane 11.10 has loads of new features, such as new autogen objects, fps enhancements and the G1000 naviagation system.
--
So why is X-Plane 11 better than its competitors? Well...
Flight Sim World (FSW) is too new to even think about, and to be quite frankly honest with you, should be the last sim that you should choose. After all, Dovetail Games put money before their customers.
Flight Simulator X (FSX) is the most successful simulator ever... Sorry, WAS the most successful. The fact is, FSX is slowly hitting retirement age, and requires a lot of plugins and payware to look good.
P3D is not for casual simming, so you have to be a trainee pilot or developer to play this.

Flat Kingdom is a 2d platformer/puzzler. It’s an amazing looking game and very well made. The game starts off very interestingly with a pretty nice story going on.  Basically the world has these 6 magical jewels which have sealed the evil that is “3D” away and now a thief is trying to steal these magical jewels and in the process he also kidnaps the princess. The world is becoming 3D from the usual 2D and the animals and even the trees/plants are freaking out and going berserk.  Our hero Flat must go and stop the thief.
The game features gorgeous looking 2d graphics sort of like Paper Mario. The art style is very unique and pleasing to the eyes. The enemies look very well made and the scenery is awesome as well. There aren’t many options in the graphics menu other than the ratio adjustment (for me only 16:9 and 16:10 were available) and full screen on/off. The game ran at a smooth 60FPS for me.
The game has very good soundtrack. It really suits the theme and visuals of the game. The soundtrack has that ‘charm’ of a beautiful game. I really like the sound bits as well. No complaints there in the music/sound department.
The game features our hero who can turn into different shapes. All the shapes give him different abilities. There’s square shape which makes him heavy and he can push objects, break wooden platforms and kill certain enemies. The circle one allows him to double jump and kill certain types of enemies. The triangle is his last shape which allows him to run fast, pop objects with the pointy triangle end and kill certain types of enemies.
All enemies have a weakness to a shape and you must figure that out either via trial and error or by making educated guesses e.g. the pointy/beaked enemies will get killed by the heavy square shape.  The platforming also requires you to change in to the correct shapes to get past obstacles. There are underwater parts of level too which can be accessed via the square shape as the heavy shape sinks and you can use that with the circle shape to navigate the waters.
The controls are not the best part of the game if you’re playing with a keyboard. The keys are cannot be custom mapped and in my opinion the default mappings are not so good, so a controller is highly recommended. Even the game developer recommends using a controller as you start the game this is the first thing you’ll see.
You can collect coins throughout the world and buy extra hearts with them which will help you. The game is not very difficult, the boss battles can be interesting and fun. The checkpoints are generous. The levels are long and plenty. There are hidden sections with coins, scrolls etc. and plenty of achievements, so the game’s replay value is also pretty good. This game really frustrated me with the controls as I much prefer to use keyboard. I had to use a controller to play this game as the keys cannot be remapped and the default mappings are horrible in my opinion. Other than that I found no frustrating part in the game.
I highly recommend this game due to its cute charm and awesome art style. The story is pretty good and the idea of different shapes having different abilities is quite good and unique. The soundtrack is also pretty nice. The game is cheap and will give you quite a few hours of fun.
