Flat Kingdom
2D Platformer
Fat Panda Games
Games Starter
is a 2D platformer developed by Fat Panda Games and published by Games Starter. It has been a while since I last played a platformer: when I was very little they were the primary genre that I played, especially the movie-licensed Disney games.
The Flat Kingdom is a beautiful and peaceful 2D land, but now it’s threatened by an evil thief and becoming 3D! The only who can stop the chaos is Flat, a little hero able to change into a circle, triangle or square.
The story is very fun, and it gets more complex the more you play it. But by the time you reach the ending, it is very clear that this was supposed to be a family friendly game, and I did enjoy following our hero on his journey through the Flat Kingdom. The characters that you interact with have some really short but funny lines, and they sure cheered me up.
I fell in love with the art style! While it certainly isn't mind-blowing, seeing a 2D world made entirely by circles, squares and triangles transforming into a 3D one is a marvel to watch. The animations and character design are very cute, and the 51 enemies and bosses that you fight are all varied.
Each part of the kingdom feels different from the other, and each level has been design very well: you rarely get lost, and there are always hidden secrets that expand the lore.
You have at your disposal four buttons: one to jump, one to turn into a circle, one to turn into a square, and one to turn into a triangle. As a circle, you can double jump. As a square, you move slowly but can move heavy objects around. As a triangle, you move fast. The further you go into the game, the more abilities you unlock to beat different puzzles.
I found the combat to be very original: since everything in the Flat Kingdom has a shape, you have to change shape in order to kill enemies. Square beats triangle, triangle beats circle, circle beats square. All you have to do is just to change shape and walk into the enemy.
The bosses that you encounter are very fun to beat, and a couple of them were starting to get very frustrating. Nevertheless, it is very fun to play and the controls are very smooth, making me fall in love for platformers once again.
The game might be family-friendly, but it sure isn't easy. All of the puzzles revolve around finding an object or pushing buttons, and they are never too hard. The real challenge is in the combat: when you are fighting enemies of multiple shapes, it isn't always easy to remember which shape to use. The boss fights are also very challenging, but after understanding the weak spot of an enemy, you can easily exploit your strategy.
The soundtrack is very cheerful and it will definitely appeal to younger players. The sound effects are pretty standard, and the voice acting is fine.
In each level there are hidden scrolls to find, and multiple coins to collect. There is also a secret ending unlocked at 100% completion, and 48 Steam achievements to unlock.
Overall,
is a very good platformer with effective gameplay, fun story, charming art style and great challenge. A must buy for fans of the genre.

Flat Kingdom is the Steam debut of talented Mexican developers Fat Panda Games. The team hail from the region of Yucatán which includes the city of Merida. Their mission is to deliver games that are fun and feature balanced gameplay and great graphics. They are inspired by great games of the past but have a desire to put unique personality into their games. Prior to being known as Fat Panda Games the team created mobile games under the banner of Ghost Apocalypse teaming with RCK Games and Lobo with Shotguns. The team intends to port Flat Kingdom to PlayStation 4.
The first thing that I gained a deep sense of prior to the game beginning was that the game was developed around a level of lore not usually seen in many platforming games. It is clear that the story and the world really meant a lot to the developers as they were building their game. It appears that every decision is based upon this lore and as a consequence one of the game’s greatest strengths is its cohesion.
One of the aspects of the game that I have enjoyed most to date is the papercraft art. Thanks to games such as Tearaway this art style has become increasingly popular in games and great artists have been able to create beautifully vivid games with the technology available to them. It’s a lot of work but when it pays off it does so in a dramatic fashion. The game is colorful and bright and is a real joy to watch as you play throughout the game. Another aspect of the presentation that I thoroughly appreciated was the soundtrack of the game. I’m a big fan of Manami Matsumae who created the soundtrack to games such as Mega Man and Shovel Knight.
One of the things that I wasn’t such a huge fan of – and that’s purely because of my own viewpoint – was that the game was a little more challenging in parts than what I would have liked. For example, some of the double jumps require absolute precision as it is super easy to fall just short of the mark. You wont necessarily die as a consequence but you can get stuck in places for an inordinate amount of time. I’d argue that the controls aren’t quite as tight as what they could be but that may just be subjective. In regards to the controls this is another game that is at the mercy of the Xbox One controller and Unity engine conflict with the game forcing me to roll back my drivers to a much earlier version in order to play. I wish that this was an issue that would be repaired by the Unity developers because it is a source of constant aggravation with their engine.
A review of the game would be remiss if I failed to mention just how much gameplay there is in the game and how many hidden pathways there are that often lead to lucrative awards in the shape of coins that enable the player to purchase things such as additional hearts (life) from the storekeeper that you can find before each level.
A very reasonable platformer and a game that I am quite happy to recommend. The game has a ten percent discount until April 23rd on the Steam store.

Too many modern shooters are forgetting what made the FPS genre fun: being armed to the teeth, slaughtering waves of varied enemies with different attack patterns, moving at breakneck speed while discovering hidden goodies and defeating bosses the old fashioned way: by filling them full of lead.  Wrack remembers, and boy does it deliver!  Whether racking up kill streaks for massive points or exploring the beautiful architecture, this game never stops being fun.  It stays true to classic FPS sensibilities while adding new layers with platforming and arcade-style action and never stops being fun.  Not only that, but the fully functional level editor is user friendly and easy to work with for mappers both old and new.  With new content being released every other week and an already active and friendly modding community, this is sure to be an instant classic with many years of replayability.  I highly recommend you give this game a go; you won't be disappointed.

Initial thoughts (Will write a full review once I've worked through all of the tuturials in flight school and played around for 20 or so more hours).
I'm very impressed with X-Plane 11. The tutorials are excellent and great for newcomers to the flight sim world. There's not very many dlc's available for version 11 yet, usually more aircraft and airport add-ons will be released over time. Although the base game is much more expensive than Microsoft's FSX, you won't be spending as much money on dlc's to improve various aspects of the game. The graphics are already fantastic, and much better than FSX (unless you buy all of the environmental add-ons, which will easily cost you hundreds of pounds;   and unless you have a state of the art computer,  you won't be able to run most of those add-ons together). For me FSX (now developed by Dovetail games) has become far too money grabbing with over £2.7K worth of dlc;  much like their Train Simulator (which has over £4K worth of dlc). Not to say X-Plane is that cheap. If you check out the earlier version 10, there's over £800 worth of dlc's for that game and the dlc for v11 is starting to mount up (almost £300).
Still, I've thourougly enjoyed the little time I've already spent crashing planes in X-Plane 11. Although I've been playing flight sims since F1 was released almost 30 years ago, I still consider myself a novice when it comes to flying. X-Plane has tried to make the experience as realistic as possible, which is why my first attempts at flying ended up with me nose down in the asphalt or spiraling out of control into the sea;  but with a little patience I soon was able to keep my aircraft in the air and level  and at that point  started to really enjoy the fantastic scenery that comes free with all X-Plane games (unlike with FSX).
I highly recommend buying this especially if you like flight sims. Even at full price (almost £55) it's a bargain and I guarantee you'll have hundreds of hours of enjoyment trying the various aircraft out that include light aircraft, small passenger planes, commercial airlines and fighter planes as well as helicopters. There's a wide range of airports available covering all types from farm landing strips to international airports.

X-Plane 11 is a welcome improvement on Laminar Research`s highly rated X-Plane 10 Flight simulator.
Virtually every aspect of the interface has been overhauled and is now very well laid out and easy to navigate and understand.
As a long time flight sim enthusiast I have collected  many different sims over the years including DCS, FSX, FSW, Aerofly 1 & 2, Dovetail Flight School, IL-2 BOS, Falcon BMS, CAP2 and X-plane 10.
FSX used to be my most used sim and recently I`ve been splitting my time between DCS and Aerofly 2, but based on what I`ve seen of the latest X-Plane iteration, I fully expect to gravitate towards it in preference to the older programs in the coming months.
The scenery is a big improvement on 10 and gets the perspective just right, it really does look pretty realistic and believable.
The flight envelope seems to be identical to 10`s which is good news because 10 has arguably the most realistic flight characteristics available in a consumer simulator.
The only criticism I have for this software is the price which I feel is a little expensive for the average gamer. That said, anybody who buys X-Plane 11 can relax in the knowledge that it is supported by a reputable company who will not abandon it, and the added benefit of a well established Flight sim and modding community.
It`s worth mentioning to prospective buyers that if you are at all unsure whether your rig will run X-Plane 11 you can download a demo version direct from Laminar Research`s web page.

Pros:
- High skill ceiling and skill gap, so those who love that will enjoy the goal of constantly improving your skill
- Kills are still satisfying without confirmation of the death or hitmarkers
- Good graphics for a Source engine game
- Fun loadout system
- Has its moments as a tense tactical, skill-based shooter
- Great suppression mechanic, and genuinely disturbing when you're the one being suppressed
- Vision through open air can be obstructed through many things in the map like smoke, sand blowing, lingering explosion clouds, etc
- EXCELLENT night vision, darkness, and light mechanics on night maps. What sucks though is that they're rarely in the map rotation for most servers I've played because they're rarely voted for.
Cons:
- The RPG and explosives spam can be UNBEARABLE at times, and explosives can be abused to the point where skill is almost not as important in winning a gunfight.
- Despite doing its best to escape the limitations of Source engine, they're still noticeable. Sounds are limited in processing and sound very raw, gun movement when aiming is jittery and not very smooth (though that might just be my computer or something idk), graphics are around the same quality as any other source game outside of lighting and bloom. It's just a dated engine...
- SPAWN KILLING. OH MY GOD. WHEN THIS IS DONE WITH EXPLOSIVES IT'S EVEN MORE ANNOYING.
The Verdict:
- Good shooter overall, but pick it up when it goes on one of its deep discounts during one of the massive Steam sales like the upcoming Christmas sale. It goes down to like a couple dollars sometimes and it's a steal at that price. Explosives and spawn exploitation leave a nasty gash on an otherwise polished and engaging experience, so try to find the right server to play on. Source engine limitations also hold this game back heavily, so look out for the sequel to this game coming in early 2018, which is being developed in Unreal Engine. It should be very, very, VERY good with the modern features of Unreal and the talent of this development team.

From the very first second you try out Flat Kingdom, you can notice this is a game made with passion for creating a charming world full of life and many hidden challenges. As you progress, you get a broader sense of the diversity of situations that Fat Panda, the developers of the game, created and all the references to many game old-school and modern classics. You can notice influences from Metroid, Megaman, Castlevania, Demon's Crest, Kirby series, Donkey Kong Country, Shovel Knight, Guacamelee, FEZ, Super Meat Boy and even The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.
Cannot forget to remark the huge, challenging and beautifully animated boss battles and to do a special mention to the soundtrack, by the hand of the legendary composer Manami Matsumae (Megaman, Shovel Knight, among others). If you are a fan of at least a couple of the games I cited before, jump into this papercraft world and start your way into the art of the shape shifting!

Dear potential fellow players,
As you set off on your quest and venture out into the world you quickly find yourself playing around with the various shapes and combinations of forms that your character can take in order to traverse obstacles, solve the frequent and engaging puzzles and defeat monsters and several fascinating and highly unique bosses.
The game (..when I played it..) was highly engaging, extremely fun and very challenging. This means that certain encounters, puzzles and bosses may take a while to figure out, however you get to try again fairly soon after failing the first (few) time(s).
Overall I believe this game to be on par with legendary games such as: The Lost Vikings (Blizzard Entertainment, 1992), Trine (Frozenbyte, 2009) and Trine 2 (Frozenbyte, 2011) and so on.
All the best,
Mike

My review for Game News
A review copy was provided by the publisher
We were graced with hundreds of epic 2D adventures where good defeats evil and everything in the world is beautifully flat. But oh no, the Flat Kingdom is popping out and becoming (dramatic musical key) three dimensional! It’s up to a small, nameless critter that has the power to change shape to save the day.
The main objective of Flat Kingdom’s adventure is to stop a master thief from taking several jewels in the kingdom (that keep it flat) and, for good measure, save the princess. Our little see-through blob can transform from a circle to either a triangle or a square. This works for tackling various obstacles within a beautifully colourful world and even used as a method of combat. Flat Kingdom has a neat concept at its core and one that attempts to elevate it into a more dynamic adventure game.
Changing shape plays an important part when interacting with objects. For example, our blob can push heavy items as the square and charge up a powerful dash attack as the triangle. This opens a vast amount of interactions that often rely on lateral thinking and good memory. It plays more strongly in combat where players will have to examine the shape of the NPC and use the right transformation to attack them. It’s a novel idea for combat but sadly it’s one that is too often infuriating. For most encounters it’s easy to determine the shape of the enemy but other NPCs make the whole process such an ordeal. You can’t always tell they’re made up of several shapes and don’t represent an overall particular structure. This becomes annoying when it comes to other factors in the game, namely the difficulty.
As mentioned, the game world is very colourful with a great variation of places to explore while accompanied by a beautifully melodic soundtrack. What ends up being problematic more often than not is the length of certain levels and the lack of checkpoints. So encountering enemies becomes a needless and unfair grind. Not including the various restrictions onscreen that blocks your view or won’t allow you to see ahead of your path when you’re sprinting as the tringle. The difficulty only becomes even more of an issue with little health pickups and when you’re presented with some tedious boss battles. There were moments I enjoyed, such as the giant spider, yet at the same time I was bugged out by the pin perfect projectiles it threw at me.
Flat Kingdom is, and will always be to the player, unfair. I felt as though most of the traps, projectiles and movements of the enemies were so pin-point perfect, that the game was two steps ahead of me and did so to make up for a short length of playtime.
Don’t get me wrong, Flat Kingdom is still an enjoyable experience, with some great platforming, clever puzzles that utilise the shape transformation and some fun boss encounters. Even with a short playtime it has good replay value when you go back to explore certain areas further with new powers and perks, just adding more to the overall adventure. It’s fun but also unfairly difficult at times and for smaller children, this might not be the best game for them. Worth checking out but only for those looking for a colourful and slightly less demeaning experience than Dark Souls 3.
+ Colourful and bright visuals
+ Dynamic and simple mechanics
+ Some fun plat-forming sections and boss battles
- Painfully difficult in some areas
- Unbalanced attacks and unfair factors against the player
- Overall game time is fairly short
A Steam key of Flat Kingdom was provided by the Publisher for the purpose of the review

The story is pretty standard; the princess has been kidnapped, you need to save her and stop the villain from aquiring the 6 jewels, but the story isn't why you should play the game!
The world not only looks stunning, but it feels pretty special to play. I had a few complaints with the way the game played and the occasional odd design choise, but Fat Panda Games' latest update fixed almost every issue I had.
The music goes perfectly with this well crafted world and was actually one of the things I was looking forward to. As much as I was excited to find out where I'd be going next, I was also equally as excited to hear the next theme, since the soundtrack is pretty great!
The levels are fun, the bosses are clever, the final world is phenominal! I didn't know what I would be getting into, but I can say that I immensely enjoyed my time with this game, and I'm definitely up for revisiting it in the future!
I initially gave it a 7/10. But the amount they improved easily earned them an extra point.
This game deserves an 8/10.
Thank you, Fat Panda Games! I look forward to the next one! :)

Gameplay in Flat Kingdom revolves around Flat transforming between his three shapes, Circle, Triangle, and Square in order to solve puzzles and defeat enemies throughout the level. All the shapes have different attributes, and eventually, different abilities. Overall, Flat Kingdom was an enjoyable experience, with cute and unique graphics and simple controls. The starting tutorial does a good job in teaching the basic controls and abilities for Flat. The level designs overall are very good, with an enjoyable soundtrack, colorful graphics, and filled with enough enemies and obstacles. There are special music tracks for different areas as well as for different bosses, a nice way of keeping the game “fresh.” The bosses are definitely a highlight in Flat Kingdom, exploring various mechanisms and strategies. There are bosses you can physically fight and damage, while others take up the entire screen and can be only damaged by the environment.
One lackluster portion of the game is the development of the story. The story fells very cliché, with a very typical development which can only be reinforced by hidden “pages” throughout the game. The cut scenes following the defeat of a boss felt repetitive, with almost the same dialogues. Certain areas feels slow, or forces the player to painstaking grind through a bunch of easy obstacles. Besides for solving the puzzles and the weak story, there are not any mechanisms that prompt further gameplay. Other areas involve a huge jump in difficulty, with either pixel or frame perfect jumps up ledges or a complex series of jumps. For example, the only way to make a jump across a chasm requires a transformation mid-air from Triangle to Circle, then utilizing the remaining double jump to make it up the ledge.
Overall, I would rate Flat Kingdom  a 7 / 10, as there are definitely areas in the story and gameplay that can be improved.

A lovely platformer 2D platformer at danger of turning into a 3D platformer without your help! Quite amusing idea for a story! I prefer 2D platformers over 3D ones where I get confused easily, so I was ready to take control of Flat, the cute ball of a protagonist of the game and go on an adventure!
The game presents itself as a light hearted platformer with a simple story, simple mechanics and offers a good amount of replayability. I really enjoyed the laid back nature of this game, the overall difficulty was on the lower side, so that made it a nice and relaxing experience.
The signature mechanic of the game is shapeshifting between a circle, triangle and a square. Each of these forms get additional abilities to use to overcome any obstacles. This makes for some very interesting problem solving and unique methods for defeating enemies. If you need one reason to play this game, then this is definitely it, I really enjoyed the platforming combined with trying to figure out how to approach and defeat any opposition!
The story and art style looks more appealing to the younger audiences, but not necessarily limited to that. The typical "Oh no some evil person does something that will destroy our world" story is simple enough, but as you play through the game you'll reveal extra story bits as you discover secrets. Backtracking as you get new abilities in addition to the standard ones adds that wonderful buzzing replay value :D Gotta catch em all coins!
So far there were only a few issues I had with the game that I hope they will be addressed in the future.
* First, there were some spots where the jumping was too pixel perfect. It's possible to jump up those high platforms, sure, but requires way too much time.
* Second issue was the controls. I've already messaged regarding the PS3 controller support but even the default button mapping seems a little off. I would definitely like to see an option to remap the controls.
* Third point for critique is for a few sections where you (are very likely) expected to speed through with the Triangle. I would love to do that, but the character moves so much forwards that I have almost no time to react and need to memorize.
* And finally, some of the checkpoints are pretty far distanced. It adds a little to the difficulty, which I don't mind actually, but there were some stages with segments that slow down the pace, so going back took a long time.
Overall, I would recommend this game. If you like Kirby games, then this is surely gonna interest you. At least give the demo a try and see how you like the whole concept of shapeshifting. Shapeshifting, platforming, backtracking sounds interesting? Go for it! A pick up and play game to relax and chuckle at the cuteness? Go for it!

Fortix may be described as a capture-the-map game in which the player has to capture certain areas of the map. This is done by venturing into the uncaptured map and basically fencing off a part of the terrain. Once both ends of the fence are connected to your baseline (initially surrounding the playing field) you claim the area inside. Movement is restricted to vertical and horizontal and fencing-off may be interrupted by a number of hazards of increasing difficulty (and annoyance ;) ).
If you, for whatever reason, remember the Game Boy game Qix you know the basic mechanics of Fortix. And if you enjoyed the former you will probably enjoy the latter, like I do.
What really annoyed me on the harder difficulty was that I couldn't always clearly determine whether I had started fencing off. Since part of the fence to-be-build is hidden under the player I often stepped of the baselline and got attacked without ever realizing the danger I had put myself in. Keeping enemy reactions in sight is hard when you are concentrating on inching by some tower fearing you will miss the baseline again and die.
I sort of like the way you are stopped when you run into a corner but I'd much rather prefer a more direct control over when to step off the baseline. Fortix 2 has running which incidentally keeps you on the baseline - both by holding CTRL - a technique similar to what I have in mind. I'd like to have a key like SHIFT that I have to hold to be able to step off the baseline, also canceling the stopping technique.
I could also imagine releasing SHIFT would result in the player returning to the closest point on the baseline. Although I understand that not having that return mechanism may be a deliberate decision in order to keep the overall difficulty of the game at a decent level.
At times I thought it might be useful to have a key for making the player backtrack on the current fence - a move almost impossible to make after taking the first corner.
As I said before, I recommend this game as I do its sequel which I will continue to be furious with now.

Lovingly crafted, freakishly surreal, beautifully drawn and wittily written, the Knobbly Crook's brief first chapter promises to lift point-and-click adventures to new heights while at the same time holding on to the classic item-based puzzles of the genre. And all for free.
Despite its surreal approach and the implied violence of its plot, this is the kind of the game that leaves me with the kind of warm feeling I get when I watch a
animation. It even has cute (although potentially lethal)
creatures by the boatload.
When I say surreal, I'm not just saying there are some funny colours in a few places and some “kooky” characters who say some slightly silly things.
I'm saying this is a full-on sick, warped, renaissance-era fantasy version of our world where exploring means diving into the acid-filled bowels of the giant, flying flesh-and-wood horse upon which you are travelling, where the horse-ship's captain lives in a dark hole and literally has a sextant for a head and a hammer for an arm. Where a beefy animal handler (actually, living rock handler) wears oven mitts, has a colander for a helmet, is armed with kitchen spatulas and yet still manages to look tough. And that's leaving out the weirdest things, the ones I don't even know how to describe.
When it comes to the plot, the best summary I can come up with is that once-peaceful paper farmer O'Sirus is given a mysterious quest by ... someone, to do ... something, for ... some reason. That's seriously about as clear as it gets, but that doesn't matter. It's the charm of setting out on an adventure and meeting a huge range of funny, friendly, cute or hostile characters that makes this game fun. You won't ever forget the people you meet on this journey, all distinct and memorable, from pocket sized Pokémon-types to room-filling hulks.
So it's high on intrigue factor. You will not have seen characters like this before unless you've smoked a lot of things you shouldn't, or you've played a lot of
. However, it's all too often that adventure games, especially those retro projects made with Adventure Game Studio (AGS), can't live up to the quality of their ideas with their production quality.
But Knobbly Crook's writer, artist, designer and voice actor, Ubisoft's Ethan Petty, doesn't do things half-a s s e d. (Well, other than the huge horse's a s s in the game, which he built with enough spare room to fit a bar into.) This is the kind of game you get from someone who's worked on Assassin's Creed, Watch_Dogs and Rainbow Six, now working on their passion project. That experience pays off in this little indie title that hits big with brilliant design on several counts.
Visually, we have the best-looking game I have ever seen made with AGS, with incredibly intricate mouse-drawn HD graphics that are part Mayan sculpture, part steampunk and part science textbook. You'll want to spend ages exploring every inch of each screen, not just to hunt for interactive objects as is the old-school adventure way, but to hunt for meaning in the assorted symbolism and just to appreciate the sinister beauty of it all. With the animation, we have nice multi-layered animated characters and occasional brief, endearingly weird close-up cutscenes at key points. The only things I felt were lacking were a couple more cutscenes showing the consequences of the player's actions as we were promised earlier in the chapter, possibly with a cowering captain in tow, but I'm sure that would have been lot of work for a joke lasting a few seconds.
With the sound, we have the fully-voiced, or I should say, fully-growled, dialogue that's a demonic-sounding version of English matching the deranged and murderous characters perfectly, with an amusingly contrasting jolly folk guitar soundtrack by Pitx.
With the writing, we have this intriguing parallel world with a completely different way of life, physical laws, and morality and yet that echos our world in interesting little ways that amuse and confuse in equal measure, keeping us on our toes in a really engaging way.
The adventure gameplay itself is the one area where the game doesn't try to break any moulds. You get the quests, hunt the items, mix them up in your inventory, and bring them back to advance the story. It's a pity that such a forward-looking game still has separate Walk, Look, Use, Take and Talk actions that need to be switched between by mashing your right click button, when left click and right click should do for such simple puzzles. Also, at a couple of points in the game, it's necessary to complete an action that isn't quite logically connected to the current goals in order to progress. Of course, as Petty has stated, this is a nostalgia project, so these gripes are partly a design choice and are pretty much standard for retro adventure games. I just don't feel that they add anything entertaining. The fact that this and a couple of absent cutscenes are the only significant criticisms I can make says a lot about the quality of the finished product.
If you're a point-and-click adventure game fan who remembers not just the puzzle mechanics of the 90's golden age, but also their offbeat black humour, this is the game you've been waiting for.
Excelling in design in multiple areas, notably the visuals and original story, and completely free, a gamer of any persuasion would be crazy not to download The Knobbly Crook, to take in the unique style of it all and especially to see what happens when someone finally makes the kind of game that inspired them as a kid.

My first review of a game; be gentle PCMR.
Altough my playtime pales in comparison to the real hardcore players and fans, I feel as if I've taken enough of a bite out of this title (PVP & Coop) to properly review it. So I'll just make this a list of my pros and cons to help anyone decide if this game is worth checking out this late in its life cycle (especially with Sandstorm around the corner).
PROS:
-Tactical, team-based gameplay
-Small, but dedicated and mature community
-Realistic bullet damage & gunplay
-COOP against challenging AI
-Official Steam Workshop Mod support
-Virtually no trolls (they're mostly in PVP)
CONS:
-Dated visuals due to older Source engine build
-Character models are copies of the same brown or white guy
-Lack of a real progression system
-Community that may seem cold or unwelcoming to new players
-Limited voice acting clips that repeat a lot (but mods fix this)
So that's my objective rundown of the game. This is an indie cult classic for a reason. The type of gameplay this game contains balances itself between tactical twitch shooters a la Counterstrike and the more realistic military sims such as ARMA. For some this middle ground between ultra realism and twitch/arcade style shooters will be a turn off and a learning curb that they may not see the point in grasping. However, the initial challenge of getting used to the game mechanics results in some of the most satisfying multiplayer matches I've had in a long time with similar titles. Also, I've mapped this title completely to an Xbox One controller via the Big Picture Mode overlay and I've shared my key binding template to the community.

Hello everybody, my name is Shaun Meyers and I'm the writer for a review and article website known as Universal Gaming Reviews. I recently finished writing my preview for the game Wrack and I figured I'd share it with those that are interested in the game. The game is still in active development so I only covered what's in the game currently and I'll be writing a full review for the game in the future.
The game captures the essence and fun of classic shooters perfectly already. The game features a campaign mode filled with lots of humor, lots of weapons and unique levels to fight hordes of enemies on. The game also includes a level editor that allows you to build your own levels to share with the community. Updates are also released every two weeks so there's always something new to try out.
In it's current form it's already lots of fun and I'm looking forward to seeing what's in store for the game leading up to it's release in the future.
If you'd like to read our full preview article you can find it here:

Wrack has the potential to become an exceptionally good FPS. Even while it is in Early Access, the gameplay feels solid and compelling. Most of the Early Access games I have encountered in the past have been clunky conglomerations of concepts that never seem to collect themselves into a properly focused game. That is not the case with Wrack. Wrack knows where it wants to go and what it wants to accomplish.
I recall one moment in Wrack where I turned a corner in a narrow hallway that opened up into a room that had multiple enemies on elevated platforms trying to blast my face off while I negotiated a way across a precarious lattice of narrow steel catwalks that were surrounded by threateningly open pits of radioactive sludge. If you enjoy do-or-die moments like the one I just described, you'll have fun with Wrack.

Wrack is a very addictive and fun game so far. I've played about 2 hours' worth; and I have yet to see one flaw. Very well put together for being in Beta, and I HIGHLY recommend this game. Once you start it, it's hard to put down. Plus, it has the same composer as the guy that composed Doom. What's not to like?
This game brings back the fun in FPS no more moving like a snail..guns that go boom...a fast pace fun game!

Even with only six levels as of this writing, it is an absolute masterpiece. If you're tired of modern shooters with their regenerating health, 2-weapon limits, and snail's pace movement, this is the game for you. It takes the formula Doom pioneered and vastly improves it, so although it definitely plays very similar to Doom, it's also its own game at the same time.
Fun fact: The creator of Wrack also developed Skulltag, a popular source port for Classic Doom. The music is also composed by Bobby Prince, who made the music for Doom 1 and 2!

One the best little indie games available in terms of polishing. Wrack is a fast paced and fun coloured FPS with retro controls including air control and bunny jump. For now, the beta only propose 5 weapons, but the action is there, the level design is fair, the developer updates his game twice a week and there is even bonus content like cheat codes, pictures to unlock and maps done by the community, with forecoming workshop support.
Wrack is not a big and astonishing FPS, but the game has the credit to be very playable, unlike other games came under "early access" and still stuck in bugs and crashes and give up of their developers. Here, you got a nice funny FPS without too much ambition, and a developer with passion and communication who answers community and takes notes.

A review of X-Plane 11 from the point of a newcomer to flight-sims.
I'm new to flight-sims and fly around with an Xbox-360 controller, however, i've bought, modded and played FSX:SE as well as XP11 and just comparing the vanilla FSX:SE (or even with mods) to the vanilla X-Plane 11, you'll notice the night and day difference.
Positivies▲
- Better Graphics
- Better phsyics (from what i feel)
- Growing (modding) community
- Better optimization (Very important in a sim)
- Ortho4XPL (Amazing freeware mod, fly over your IRL-house!)
- Airplanes can actually crash and simulate a somewhat realistic crash instead of bouncing like in FSX:SE
- Amazing way to edit keybindings and joystick inputs, incredibly easy to use
- User friendly interface
Negativies▼
- Not too many aircrafts
- Not any multiplayer as of yet (that i know of, hopefully they'll add a MP)
- No seasons
- Not as in-depth of a flying tutorial as in FSX
Summary:
------------
* No need to spend around €200 extra on clouds to make this game look amazing
* User friendly
* Great graphics and physics
* User-friendly UI
* Great FPS and optimization, i get a solid 40-50fps while having everything maxed except the Anti-Aliasing, specs below
* No Multiplayer sadly enough, that could be an important part for alot of people, although it's mostly used for fun
* Small number of aircrafts
* No seasons
I hope this was usefull for anyone who's new to flight sims!

Armello is a turn-based strategy game with the feel of a classic board game. If you don’t take it too seriously and can get past the inherent RNG nature of a game like this, it’s an incredible experience. It offers plenty of variety within the game to not get stale, multiple win conditions, a cast of characters each with their own unique play style, and a surplus of spells, equipment, and traps that affect how you take your turn all contribute to the total replay value of this game. With a pleasant atmosphere and a pleasing art style to compliment toward the feel of the game, it’s a game that I never tire looking at and with the gameplay it provides, it’s also a game I never tire of playing either.
If you enjoy playing board games, I recommend giving this game a look!

Despite the fact that this game has you buying characters that have their own gameplay differences with no chance of getting them for free, I have not payed a single dollar. I still love the base content of the game.
This game is actually pretty simple (even though the tutorial sort of fails), yet it takes hundreds of hours to master. Even though I *could* get more characters from the paid-DLC, the base characters are fair and balanced, and I still haven't mastered them. Getting the DLC doesn't give you an unfair advantage, as you still rely on the same skill on those characters as any other character. Despite the fact that many elements in this game are RNG-based, you can use your skills to make the tables turn in your favor.
That's not to say that the game is perfect. The biggest gripe is that some cards feel absolutely useless, and there is a victory that requires specific cards, which most of *those* are also useless. But you can actually come up with creative ways to dump them for chances of getting better ones within the game.
RNG is a complaint I hear from a lot of players, but you have ways to mitigate the damage of bad RNG, and learn to make educated decisions that can actually turn the bad consequences of RNG-based events into actual benefits. If you mastered the game, you won't get 100% chance of winning with pure skill, but it's still a high enough chance that you can actually win consistently.
Overall, fun game to play. I recommend it, even if you don't have the extra dough for the DLC characters.

Simple gameplay with refined features for dishing out commands makes for a very fun experience, full of great cinematic moments and making you feel like you might very well be Delta Squad's elite Clone leader.

Cannot recommend this enough, for both fans of Star Wars and good games.

The screenshots and videos of this edition of X-Plane really show off what the developers have been working on. Of course, there's always something that can be improved with payware addons, such as complex sceneries like big cities, which are really quite basic by default.
I have enjoyed plenty of time in flight sims from ProPilot to DCS World and I have to say this has left a lasting and ongoing impression. I have recommended it to the most hardcore flight sim fans and they have been shocked to see my screenshots of default aircraft, scenery, clouds, and sky textures. I would most certainly recommend it to anyone reading this review. X-Plane 11 is worth it.

This game has potential. Lots of potential. However in it's current state, it's too tough.
Pros:
The Art style: It's great how it's pixels.
Very tense: Personally it's really easy to feel worried when a huge horde comes knocking.
Gameplay: Making sure your surviviors are at the right place at the right time is extremely important.
Cons: Here's a bunch of tidbits on how this game can improve. Constructive criticism :)
Resource Gathering: Really, Really, REALLY slow. It makes Trove's servers look like The Flash. Obviously you need resources to do things like build guns, fire the guns, make the boards that will keep your imminent death out of reach and mend the wounds. So why does it take 10 months to grab enough metal for a gun? Building guns should be a secondary option if you can't find guns. All this, however falls into my second problem..
The Crafting System: The Crafting System fits into this kind of game like butter and bread. But my problem is that the stuff you can build is too expensive. I want to be able to build RPGs for when the Mutated zombies lose their $h!t. Instead of that, I'm fighting with two pistols, a shotgun and a baseball bat against Fat zombies. And that's just not fun. Another problem is the lack of descriptions for each weapon/tool. No mouseover text telling you what it does, so I'm not sure what each attachment does.
Engineers: Easily the least useful of the 3 classes available. There's also medics that I'm not too fond of either but I'll get to them in a bit. Engineers, according to the in game description "Can build traps and turrets. Also he can use melee weapons." In any of my games, I have not been able to build traps or turrets due to the high cost of the toolkits. The last part is false. They can't attack with melee weapons. I would love it if they could build custom weapons, heck, you could at least give a resource discount to building things with them so I can easily welcome them with open arms into the group.
The "random events": They don't do anything, so why are they in the latest build?
Medics: Medics are cool, because they put bandages on cuts. My only problem is they don't have any form of self defense against the horde.
Finally, the Difficulty spike: After the first 2 waves, no matter what, you will be in deep♥♥♥♥♥♥ Because you don't have time to get the cool weapons, you are going to lose an arm and leg unless you use efficient but boring tactics. There's no timer telling you when the next wave arrives. then again, there's no point, because they arrive too quickly for you to grab anything but ammo.
This game is in Early Access, so hopefully these problems are sorted or at least aknowledged. This game looks great, it feels great, but iron out the problems and this game will be perfect. :)
Good luck with your Early Access!

I don’t usually like writing in my reviews like this, but since I have no idea where to start, I’m going to use a pro and con format while expanding on each one.
You can take this with a grain of salt, since I’m not used to critiquing games.
Also, I haven’t experience everything in the game, and might have missed key factors.

I will probably play more in the future, and update this review/log or whatever.
These are honestly mostly suggestions on how to make the game better, more then a review, and I’m not sure if this place is appropriate or not, but oh well.
Pros
+easy and simple layout
I would appreciate if they added a bit more context for test lab, perhaps a brief explanatory for each mode. While the rest of the maps are self explanatory, the name should be changed for test lab because it isn’t self explanatory. You have no idea what’s going to happen when playing test lab. Also, a undo or back button would be nice when choosing the difficulty over constantly resetting the game.
Cons
-No time for strategy
Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ this is a huge issue I had with the game. Controlling multiple characters at the same time in such a confined area is a nightmare. It isn’t fun or engaging, it’s unfair hard.
You’re going to constantly misclick since everything is so packed tight together, and the the hotkey for choosing each character is even worse. You have no sense in which number selects one character, and constantly going through all the numbers before getting the right one within the few seconds the game demands you to execute.
It’s especially hard for new players who have no idea what’s going on. You don’t teach the player that you need wood and metal to create barricades within 50 seconds, give time for each player to examine the area and get used to it.
Don’t add a time limit, but at the beginning of the game, let the zombies come once you reached a certain point when the player is ready for zombies.
There are plenty of ways to fix this, add a pause button. No, not the one you currently have. let the player be able to pause the game and examine what to do, give them a little space to breathe. Let them be able to control where the character role fits while still in the pause menu, before the plan is taking to action after you unpause the game. It’s better than constantly managing multiple characters while having zombies after you in real time.
If you don’t understand what I’m explaining (which I understand, I explained it pretty badly), I recommended you a game called, “FTL: Faster Than Light”, it allows the player to strategize before making their actions. And no, it wouldn’t make the game easier. FTL is hard as balls, yet it’s mechanics are extremely easy to master. Create a proper learning curve and give the player a chance to get used to it’s surrounding within the first playthrough. This doesn’t mean the game has to be easy, just make it harder as the player progress.
If you don’t like that idea, how about the medic is able to slow down the game so the player can examine the area and strategize while playing? So, you can organize all of the characters properly while simultaneously fending off.
-Graphics
This is honestly just kind of a nitpick of mine, but the arms look ♥♥♥♥ing hideous.
Funny at first, but it gets distracting real fast.
-no explanation or hotkey
The game just drops you and tell you what role this character is, and put it in this certain room to gather material.
It doesn’t explain that you need wood to barricaded windows, or that you need this for that.
Neither does it explain which hotkey does what. What’s the key for healing your teammates with the medic? Do you left click him? do you right click him? Nope! I still don’t know how to ♥♥♥♥ing heal my teammates.
A little guidance would help, but don’t constantly hold my hand during the entire playthrough.
Or just let the player decided the pacing of the game in the beginning, just like how I mentioned earlier.
The only way you learn how the game works, is constantly dying and learning new mechanics. Which is fine, I love dark souls, and the foundation of the game revolves around that. But the key difference between the two is that, one is fair, and the other is not. I already explained earlier how it’s unfair. But even then, dark souls still did a good job explaining how the game works right from it’s tutorial and it felt fair when you died. Majority of the time I died in this game simply from unorganized character clustering around in one area not doing what I planned them to do because it never explained how to do this stuff or which buttons to press.
Other stuff that was on my mind when I was playing:

A multiplayer would be nice. Maybe a vs mode when one player is controlling the zombies, while the other player is defending the place.
Cheap game. Didn’t really include this in the positive because the price of the game doesn’t have any effect on the gameplay itself. Unless we're talking about DLCs or add ons

Will it just be a exactly the same ♥♥♥♥ing thing as the survival? I really hope not, just please add more depth to the story mode then just adding a new layout of the game. That’s just lazy.

Disclaimer: Types of games I play tend towards needing full working knowledge of how the system works, like roguelikes/lites, action games with a defined and designed end game, and various board games.
Cute, mildly strategic boardgame with a lot of luck involved on PC, but by barring full information about the game mechanics from being known and forcing a limited view, I'd say it isn't worth your money or time (as this was a gift from a friend, as opposed to anyone related to any development network anywhere). Take this with a grain of salt; I don't often play strategic board games, and this is only the experience of playing two games and going through the epilogue.
Gripes:
- Deck mechanics are not known publically; there are no counters or general deck indicators, no discard pile, cards just always exist and you can't count on anything, at least without dedicated study.
- Knowledge of cards' existance is locked behind actually encountering them blind.
- As a result, RNG can and has forced me into a loss at about turn 4, and there is no way for me to know how to handle it.
- The devs actually mention that the obfuscation of information at-a-glance is part and parcel of their game design [
] and as such isn't even an option to have for a modification a way to see all FREELY AVAILABLE INFORMATION in a convenient location; we must peck and hunt for every little piece of information in excrutiatingly dumb menus (Why did you design the PC game for touch screens, devs? How come? Did you want to make a poor product?).
Frankly, what I want is a refund for my friend. But since that's not an option, what would turn this around is publically addressing and fixing these items. I doubt I'll get that though, so here's a negative review.

Armello is a rich fantasy based board game come to life.  Everything about it is made with obvious care from the gorgeous character design to the deep mythology of the world and its inhabitants.  Choose a character from a varied cast, each with their own strengths and weaknesses and join in against 3 other human or CPU controlled players in a turn based contest for the throne.  Win through strength, strategy, subterfuge, or sometimes, just a bit of luck.
+ The gameplay is easy to get into, but deep enough to spend lots of time leaning to master.
+ There are plenty of variations in rules, accessories, and in how the cards and dice in each game play out that you'll never see the same game twice.
+ Animation, voice acting, character and game design is all beautiful
A great little game that has immense replayability.  If you love board games like Cataan or Dominion -- or enjoy any of the Civilization titles, or even some mixed genre games like Renowned Explorers, or just turn-based-strategy in general, this is one to try.

Star Wars Republic Commando is a squad based FPS set in the Star Wars universe right at the start of the Battle of Geonosis and ending right at the battle for Kashyyyk. Republic Commando was developed by LucasArts and released March 1, 2005.
You join up with the Delta Squad, an elite group of clones whom have been cloned from the Mandalorian Bounty Hunter Jango Fett. They were also hand picked by Jango Fett to become commando's. The Delta Squad batch of clones were all raised in the same pod group, they're actually one of the closest knit clone groups.
Okay PAUSE the review... I personally already had a vested interest in this game because I've read several of the Author Karen Traviss' Republic Commando Books. While Disney (and George Lucas) no longer accepts these books as cannon... ...Don't get me started, I'm just going to accept it and move on.
I still prefer the ties between the series. That said, there's a lot of additional character development given to the Delta Squad from her books. Honestly the Nulls are way better, ORDO ALL THE WAY BABY! ..but I digress.
The four Delta Characters are RC-1140 (Fixer), RC-1207 (Sev), and RC-1262 (Scorch) and you play as RC-1138 (Boss). Here's another reason to respect the game developers, the voice actor for Boss is the actual actor for Jango Fett himself: Temuera Morrison.
Republic Commando story on it's own is kind of shallow because there's very little character development. HOWEVER if you go read the Republic Commando Book series from Karen Traviss then you'll have a whole new level of appreciation for each of these clones.
Just a quick note about the multiplayer, it's gone. Since Gamespy was shut down the servers aren't there. There might still be communities and mod's which you can use to play it with other people though.
Before I jump right in and explain the gameplay, lets fix something real quick. When you boot the game the resolution will probably be all wrong, and your mouse will probably be traveling lightspeed all over the screen if you full screen it (ALT + Enter)
Basically you want to open your console mode with your Tilda key: ~ and then type in:
setres 1920x1200
setmousesensitivity 0.5
Even then my mouse moved super fast, and would just use arrow keys to navigate menu's... but it makes the game much more playable.
You have all of the features of a standard FPS in this game, fire, zoom, crouch. The buttons are a wee bit weird at times, like you zoom with Z, and you throw grenades with your right mouse button throws a grenade.
You Can jump too... but you really won't use that, you also can't sprint... it's the reverse, if you hit shift you move slower. Both of those were weird design choices, but I'm just going to blame it on being the 2000's when this game came out. We're probably lucky it turned out as well as it did.
I think it's pretty safe to say most people have played FPS before, and so you come to expect easy and medium difficulties to be relatively challengeless and the only real challenge come from hard mode onward... This is not the case for Republic Commando, I played on medium difficulty
Most of the challenge in this game comes from the team-oriented gameplay and game design. I normally exploited the AI's design, and let my team mates be cannon fodder while I set bombs, or knifed battle droids in the back of their armor plates... but even with that advantage the game can be down right brutally difficult. Especially if you run out of ammo! Which happened more frequently then I'd like to admit.
There's about 5 levels on each world, I took roughly 10 hours to play through the whole game, and in my opinion hearing the song "Vode An" and a few Mando'a words and curses was definitely worth the price of admission for me.
I really enjoyed my time spent with Republic Commando, unfortunately I'm disappointed there wasn't really any character development, the controls were awkward at times, and the technical problems you're bound to have with older titles.
I was very pleased with the Mando'a tribe, the cutscenes, and the effort given to small details which Fandalorians will definitely pick up on and after hearing Vode An I realized I have a new ringtone for my phone.
I hate to say it, but I don't think Republic Commando will appeal to everyone equally. But that being said anyone who enjoyed the clone wars era of star wars, and especially anyone who has read Karen Traviss' books should totally check this game out.

There are not a lot of competing products in the Flight simulator category these days, so do not expect the polish we have been used to in regular games.
Negatives:
- Roads and railroads are inaccurate. They suddenly stop and start out of nowhere, jagged turns, roadsigns with names of areas are just random ones from the same country, cars move awkwardly at the exact same speed. The roads and railroads doesnt look anywhere like the real world version. I got lost immediately when trying to fly from a local airport, as I could not recognise any man made structures.
- Very poorly optimized. My water cooled overclocked rig with 12 CPU cores and GTX 1080 Ti is struggling to maintain a good framerate. But it has no issues with any modern games that has far superior graphics to this one.
- Weird physics. For example while standing parked on the runway the ground is shaking like crazy.
- Awkward controls. It looks like the simulator requires a joystick. Steering with a mouse is not working well. For example if you navigate the map then go back to controlling the plane, it will go completely out of control as the mouse is not where the simulator expected it to be, And generally it is quite awkward. Even just taking off without weering off the runway is very hard when using a mouse.
- Some of the controls in the cockpit does not respond to touching them. I know controls controlling cabin heat and similar is not actually going to do anything in the simulation, but it would still be nice to be able to fiddle with everything to make the simulation more realistic.
- Graphical issues. It has a lot of problems with water. Reflections are shaky and water generally looks dull. Scenery has a lot of issues too, like blocky hills and ugly seams in the landscape.
- Tutorials are a bit old fashioned and clunky. Everything is based on dialogue boxes with text that is not always well thought out. For example the second dialogue box in the tutorial explains how to get to the next one. Which is silly since you obviously already made it to the next one at that point.
- Add on scenery, like airports, are very expensive.
- Not a lot to see. Do not expect to use the simulator to explore an area of earth. It is offering repeating autogenerated content, with some low resolution satellite textures.  Same buildings, road type, road signs, trees and so on. Over and over. You get no real sense of being in the area you area flying over.
Positive:
- Well, for all its flaws, probably one of the best and most accurate flight simulators on the market today. It is a niche product, so it is understandable they do not have the resources to polish it like we are used to with games for the mass market. And when covering the entire world, it is also understandable it is hard to maintain a high level of detail.
- The whole world is covered, all major airports included, although most of the man made structures are inaccurate or missing entirely.
- Flight simulation seems to be quite accurate. Looks like a good tool to familiarize yourself with flying before or while taking real flying lessons.
The simulation seems to have good support with many new improvements all the time, so I am giving this a recommendation after all. It does fulfill its intended purpose, but it is easy to see how it could improve in many ways.

Graphics are amazing and do beat FSX and all other flight simulators out there. Weather and lighting is so realistic I would defiantly give it 10/10 in this department.
Performance
Reason for giving the simulator a poor rating is due to the fact that the default aircrafts are not completely finished. No FMC and poor performance, I really wish they would of improved these prior X-Planes release. The wheels screetch, again no FMC. Performance of the aircraft isn't as good as FSX PMDG aircraft in my personal opinion.
When I say "performance" I am refering to the movement of the aircraft such as the speed, landing, take off. It does not simulate the G's, knots when taking off making it feel really unrealistic when taking off and landing which to me is a VERY important thing. FSX EZCA addon can simulate this so indeed it is a third party addon BUT for the price I would of expected a better system.
Sound
Sound is good and tolerable 6/10 however the ATC is awful. If there could be some kind of programme where users can implement their own voices or downloaded voice backs this would also take a work load off the developers/programmers.
In result of so many cons in this game I did ask for a refund to a later date where X-Plane was a further developed but unfortantly I had played more than 2 hours (trying to set everything up and fix the screetching).
Airports and Livery
Livery is amazing, the fact they have removed the flat 2D look by using 3D X64 terrain is the best thing they have done so far, shockwave lighting etc... It beats FSX and P3D even with addon software. Airports do however let X-Plane down.

Etch-a-sketch meets strategy. You draw lines to divide up territory, making sure that neither yourself nor your line is hurt by the obstacles along the way, and when you've captured specific territory or a certain amount, you succeed. The principle is simple and it's fun enough.
They certainly know how to set difficulty levels. The default of easy is just that as it allows time for correction. The impossible difficulty will give you a run for your money as, try though I did, I could not get perfect on the last level on the impossible difficulty. This makes it an adequate choice whether you are looking for a brief distraction or a challenge.
The game is very sensitive and seems to expect extremely precise timing. I say this because often enough I tried to reconnect to a previous section only to be a sliver off, usually leading to my demise. This is compounded by the fact that anything and everything, including your own character and score callouts, seems to be in the way of being able to see where you are and whether you've started a new line, exposing yourselft to danger. Often, I would accidentally end up on a border that was a sliver off of the one I had come from only to find myself dead because I had unknowingly just exposed myself to a nearby danger. There are also many random elements like which tower will fire when, where pick-ups appear and which way dragons will go making it much harder to plan things out. When all of these things are so meaningful alone that they could determine success or failure, it becomes increasingly frustrating on the impossible difficulty because you fail due to many factors seemingly beyond your control.

I've been playing and enjoying this game for quite a while now and I'm a fairly active forum goer for the game to. I'm not going to say the game is perfect because no game is. However, I will say that the game is very good for what it tries to be.
The game itself has a decent level of complexity, allowing for varied playstyles to be successful along with a moderate dash of RNG chaos to spice things up. The visuals and sound are appealing for the most part though if you play the game for a long time you might get tired of the music eventually. Singleplayer games are a good warm-up for multiplayer but the AI lacks a lot in the creativity department so you may find the challenge lacking.
I'd say the best and worst part about this game is the community. By and large other players are fun to play against in public MP but as I'm sure anyone who has played a public multiplayer game can attest you can't avoid the occasional toxic player(or group of them). The developers included a Report Player function in the game, so theres that to take a bit of the edge off.
Speaking of the developers, LoG is a pretty great group of people and they take tweaking and fixing Armello seriously. Bug reports are usually addressed within a week or two and updates come fairly frequently. Questions and concerns on their forums tend to be answered by Darcy the cinnamon roll, so if you have issues there's something to look forward to.

I played this game excessively during Early Access, then kind of forgot about it. I just recently rediscovered Armello and fell in love all over again. More characters, more cards, more items, lovingly crafted and still updated to this day.
It's a joy to play and even just to look at.

Armello is a digital board game that combines some features from games like Settlers of Cataan and Talisman with game mechanics all its own. Players compete with one another to acquire resources and build their characters up in order to successfully assault the palace and overthrow the king therein. Armello features a high amount of randomization which serves to make each playthrough feel fresh even after having put dozens of hours into the game as well as keep all players in the game; no matter how far behind a player is it is almost always possible to recover, you're never out of the game even when it feels like you are. There isn't so much randomization however that player decisions don't still feel meaningful, resource and risk managment remain important throughout. With each game running about an hour and a half Armello offers a fun not too heavy play experience.
This is a great board game. Love the design.

An arcade game that made it to steam, this is what Flesh Eaters is.
This defense game is based on using different combinations of soldiers to defend a location, you can pick between medics, soldiers or engineers, all having specific roles in your defense.
Soldiers can use heavier weapons and typically focus on health and armour upgrades. Medics heal neraby friendly units and can provide health bonuses when upgraded and engineers are your back bone, as they will build and repair all your fortifications.
Its a very simple game and can be played easily, its harder modes are a lot tougher (obviously), as they reduce the total squad from 6 (easy) to 4 (normal) and 2 (hard)
I find the controls are very laggy and don't respond very well in general, being very unrefined. These are very frustrating and can actually kill you as they will not respond to your commands when you need them too. This was a huge killer for me, as its game breaking at times.
It also has little replayability, only having two maps as of this review date.
Its cheap, and even cheaper when its on sale (holy ♥♥♥♥ im captain obvious) and I would tell you all to just not grab it either way, its cheap and has trading cards if thats your thing, but on a gaming basis its just a flash game you pay money for.

I hesitate to give this a perfect rating, and there's only one reason for that. Valiant Hearts isn't quite sure what it wants to be.
There's some moments where it's almost unbelievably heroic for the sake of its own story, with the heroes fighting the nasty German baddie, and they're full of drama and the occasional comedy, and hey, it's an adventure game, classical style! The puzzles (simple as they are, this was designed for education after all) contribute to this feeling, and the way everyone in-game reacts to the dog.
Then there's other scenes, like the opening French charge, or the second-to-last Emile misison, that are absolutely horrifying. In these scenes, Valiant Hearts goes all-out to sell the horror of the First World War, and it does that very well.
My problem is, there's not a lot of middle ground between them. If the heroic bits weren't in the game, it would be way too dark for kids and honestly too heavy to keep going, and if the horrific scenes weren't there it wouldn't be doing the War justice at all. But the transitions between the two are a little abrupt, so it feels... kind of weird.
That's the reservations out of the way. Valiant Hearts may not be able to quite decide what it wants to do, but it does everything it does wholeheartedly, one hundred percent. The artstyle lends itself very well to both the classical adventure game feel and the historical nature of the story, the characters are all charming and relatable, and it doesn't fall into the trap of having one side be "good" and the other "bad" (despite having a cackling German villain, somehow it pulls that off). As simple as the story may be, you WILL find yourself invested in it.
This is a great game. It has flaws, but everything has freakin' flaws. There's a good reason I've come back to this one multiple times despite beating it and even 100%ing it. Valiant Hearts is incredibly charming, and like a good book, even when you know the ending, it's always going to make you enjoy getting there. Worth full price.

Deity Quest had my interest for a couple of reasons: I love RPGs, strategy, any game that allows me to be a god-like figure, and any game that revolves around having minions that will fight for you. This game takes the latter point a step farther, where you do none of the fighting (with the exception of optional spells you can upgrade later on in the game, though most spells are supportive to your minions). I bought the game on sale, and expected a lengthy RPG given the larger playtimes posted on some of the reviews.
If you keep the tutorial activated in the game and play it, you'll notice the game incorrectly tells you to "tap" the screen instead of click. This was the first time, for me, that I noticed the game was developed for phones. If you're like me and usually pass games up because of this, don't fret. I actually did beat the game, and I don't support phone games if I know beforehand that they were developed for them, particularly if they are badly ported to PC. Deity Quest loses points with me here. The game is not negatively affected by this mistake; the mouse works perfectly fine as you click and drag spells and options over to your minions. However, the fact that the game was not updated in the simplest of ways to ensure it was ready for a PC release can be insulting to consumers who support it on PC, as it feels as an afterthought.
Deity Quest has a forgettable and light-hearted story, which serves, essentially, as a means to push you out on your way to the action. I was a little disappointed in the casual nature of the game; I'd been expecting a 30 hour or so playthrough based on the other reviews, and in truth, I beat the game in just 10 hours. Nonetheless, the gameplay during that time is pretty fantastic. There are bickering amongst gods, most of whom own and rule over sections of land that you must conquer over to defeat. Your goal changes over the course of the game, and you can get access to over 100 various creature types of various elements to control and switch in and out of the action at your will. Elemental play is very important here; using fire creatures against water creatures will get you demolished, and it's this type of emphasis that encourages you to try out multiple creatures in various situations to see what works. You will find that some creature types, although weaker appearing, can actually become almost overpowered (the goldfish and golden slime comes to mind).
Your selected creatures will fight for you, and it's up to you to utilize spells or items to support them. You get access to healing, recharge mana, and boost stat spells (among others), while you can also upgrade elemental attack spells later on (though these never seemed to be worth it to me). The spell/item bar can become cluttered and odd to navigate. Given the frenetic nature of the gameplay, switching between the two available item bars and selecting spells by their image, not their title, can be confusing. Once you equip spells, hovering the mouse over the spell in the bar does not offer you its name, so be sure to keep in mind which spell is what, or else you can waste mana finding the correct one. In general, however, gameplay is fast and fun, and you can sit back and watch the action for the some battles, while having to stay on top of your spells for others.
I had a lot of fun with Deity Quest, despite its disappointments and misgivings. I went into this expecting a lengthy and deep RPG, and did not get that. Deity Quest is a short, casual game that feels slightly off of the "RPG" title, but it is a lot of fun nonetheless. I think most people who enjoy strategy RPGs will still like this, because most of the foundation is there in the game, though it is casualized. If you are willing to overlook that, I'd recommend giving the game a try.

Deity Quest's story is about a rookie god who wants to become more powerful. To do that, he must convert the followers of other gods, which is done by beating those gods in battle using Pokémon-like minions. These battles are usually 6 vs 6, although you can choose to use less than 6. There's a wide variety of minions to choose from and with the Extended DLC you can make your own creatures, giving you an essentially unlimited supply. You can also get duplicates, so if you want a team of six orcs, six goblins, six human warriors etc, then you can do that.
All RPGs need a good battle system and Deity Quest's is one of the best. Your creatures fight automatically, although you can instruct them if you want. This is important because between boss battles, there's not much to do except collect new creatures (which can be accomplished quickly) so level grinding is necessary. By automating the battles, Deity Quest never feels like a chore.
Even the graphics (which look terrible in the trailer above) are surprisingly detailed in the game, clearly representing many different monsters and varied settings such as forests, tundra and dungeons.

Insurgency is a multiplayer tactical first-person shooter video game developed and published by New World Interactive. It is a standalone sequel to Insurgency: Modern Infantry Combat, a community made mod for Valve's Source engine.The game was released for Microsoft Windows, OS X, and Linux on January 22, 2014.Game doesnt require a lot of resources so , low specs pc's can handle it.
The game offers a lot of game modes i will name them all here.
Multiplayer Game Modes
1 Push
2 Firefight
3 Skirmish
4 Occupy
5 Ambush
6 Strike
7 Elimination
Cooperative Game Modes
1 Checkpoint
2 Hunt
3 Survival
4 Outpost
5 Conquer
One of Insurgency's defining characteristics is its hardcore gameplay. Unlike other first-person shooters, Insurgency has a very simple HUD, and lacks virtual crosshairs, ammunition and player health counters and minimaps. Also, all guns instantly kill with one shot to the head. This adds a considerable level of difficulty for the player.At the beginning of each game, players are able to choose a class and select a variety of weapons. Players have a certain amount of supply points to spend on purchasing weapons and modifications.
