Retro City Rampage DX is a huge love letter from the developer to the industry and the fans of the video game industry.  And that's one of it's best and perhaps worst issues.
The core idea of Retro City Rampage is to basically create a top down GTA style video game.  That's GTA as in the original GTA, which used a very similar but simplistic version of this game.    However they are vastly different games.  Where GTA is just a crime simulator, Retro City Rampage instead adds a huge sprawling story, tons of buildings you can enter, great unique experiences, and references to other games.
That last part is what I was saying is the best and perhaps worst issue.  This game just nails the nostalgia for long times fans of the industry, and I do mean long times.  There's a part of the world that is clearly based off of Mario Bros. (Again not the super mario bros), and it's brilliant and subtle.  There's a ton of these references most of the time quite subtle, such as four turtles jumping out of a sewer, the bike shop owner is recognizable from a certain boxing game.  The opening of the game is clearly a remake of a great movie with a clowned prince.  And so on.
But there's a problem here.  If you never played Mario Bros, but you played the rest, will you recognize them?  Not in this form unless you know this specific layout.     There's references to Metal Gear (the original again.. wow I'm saying that a lot), Contra, Sonic, and a ton of movies and tv shows.
The thing is much of this is hit or miss, there's a few characters which clearly are references to something but I didn't know what it was referring too, and that kind of sucked.  There's also a bunch of indie darlings such as Phil Fish and Billy Campbell, who again unless you REALLY know your stuff you'll kind of ask "Who's that?"
The problem is most of the game references though come from the original games in series, we're talking you're probably going to want 30 years of gaming history under your belt to really get these reference, and that's ok, but at the same time newer players will miss a great deal of these, and they are a big part of why I enjoyed the game, without them... I'm not sure I'd enjoy this game nearly as much.
However the gameplay in this game is mostly short levels, usually only a few screens long or a few minutes.  There's over 60 missions in the game, and they are mostly great (with a few controller breaking hard ones, looking at you splosion man knock off).
What really works though is almost every quest giver will tell a specific storyline/reference.  There's as I mentioned metal gear, but there's also the game genie, and a FANTASTIC Saved by the bell reference.  That one alone is a scream.
The controls in the game are also great, while I do have a problem with the stomp move being inaccurate, everything else feels really tight and gives the player a proper amount of control.
The one big complaint I have might seem odd but the achievements in this game feel all wrong.  20 achievements might have been enough, but it still feels like this game should have at least 30, if not 50.  There's so many little missions that could have gotten an achievement but beyond that, the game gives very odd achievements.  There's not even one for beating the whole game, and there's only a few that are really hard.
However the game does give good rewards in game for the entire playthrough, it's just that the achievements feel off in some odd way.
Overall though I will say I liked this game a lot.   But there's a few flaws, and a few frustrations.  However I really got along with the nostalgic references, if you knew half of them, I think you'd be more than fine, however if you really don't get nostalgia references or you miss the majority of them, I would say this game might not be as fun to play.   And that's be a real shame, but it would be the deciding factor to me.

The paper-thin story of Sophie's Curse is that you're a nurse who has landed a small time job providing at-home care for your friend's grandfather for one night. Since he has just moved in to his new house, instead of putting up real lighting for some reason he lugged four of these power generator lights into the home. It's your task to keep them all going, and for some spoopy paranormal reason, the lights like to lose their charge often. Don't worry, though, your friend says he'll pay you extra for this hassle.
At its very best, Sophie's Curse is a sub-par Five Nights at Freddy's clone. At its very worst, it's abhorrently atrocious. The gameplay is done in the same style as FNAF, where you click to traverse from one area to the next. There's an abysmal HUD that lets you know which light is losing power, and you go from light to light all night long, winding them back up again while avoiding Sophie. Who is Sophie? F**k knows! You get tidbits of the story here and there through instant messages if you open the laptop in the kitchen, which is used to fix generator errors with half-hearted mini-games, but who has time to read that crap when this entity could jumpscare you at any moment?
Basically, if you run in to Sophie, you have to run the other way if you're not in the designated safe zone, which can also be seen on the laptop. By the way, this safe spot only moves after checkpoints and when Sophie knocks the lights out, and you can't die while you're standing in it, so it kinda defeats the purpose of doing much else. At least it would, if the rules of the game didn't change constantly. Even if you are in the safe zone, Sophie likes to just randomly pop up with no warning and kill you. On the other hand, if you happen to see her and if you don't immediately go in the opposite direction she'll do the same; but at least that's as it should be. There are checkpoints placed at 2 hour intervals throughout the one-night stay at this guys house, and you must last the entire night from 6pm until 6am.
Sophie's Curse is just bad. It barely has any play value, let alone replay value; although it does have two difficulties, "Curse" and "Nightmare". The majority of positive reviews are very suspicious, and the hate that negative reviews like this one garner is even more reason to raise a red flag. The game is nowhere near being worth $5.49 CAD, it's closer to a $1.09 game such as Francisca. Sophie herself isn't even scary, being the cliché grey-skinned, eyes-ripped-out stereotype from a lot of modern horror movies, but when she appears out of nowhere, with zero warning, it's absolutely ridiculous.
*The amount of people who are passionately defending this game by using derogatory remarks toward reviewers is incredibly weird.

When given a choice with consequences, you have to actually spell them out. I was given a choice between one card where I'd lose 2 prestige, and another where every other player would gain 1 prestige. I chose the latter, since I was leading in prestige, and was immediately hit with a -3 prestige. Apparently theirs came from mine, but I had no way of knowing that.
If you're going to make a game that uses cards, you have to write them in a way that the rules are _very_ explicit. There shouldn't be surprises or unexpected side-effects. This is what we demand out of collectible card games (and board games), so it's what we expect out of video games that simulate them.

I want so badly to like this game. I want so many people to play it. But unfortunately, this is a board game that is meant to be a physical board game and not a computer program. The program is incredibly broken and pay-to-win which is a shame given the beautiful base they have and the potential therein.
Any multiplayer game is about balance and this game has absolutely none. If you happened to pay extra for the DLC, congrats, you win every match. The game presents strategy and alternative options for winning, but all of the non-prestige end game options are impossible due to the imbalance of the system at hand and the huge luck factor involved in drawing cards that are relevant to those win conditions on a consistent basis.
But worst of all, again, is that the game is unplayable as a video game. There is no controller support. Yes, I know, you say the game does have controller support, but only for certain functions. There are multiple parts of the game that the controller doesn't function with (in particular, the prompt for entering the palace for an end game scenario). If you reach one of these situations, you will have to find a mouse to proceed, which is a problem for people like me that stream their computer into a televsion to play and before you can find a mouse to continue the game, the timer has run out and you have forfeited your turn. This again, is another problem with the video game format. It is not conducive to multiplayer games as the timers are ridiculous. You will spend a disgusting amount of time waiting for other players to take their turns and be left with no time to take your own, as the game does not take into account the option of playing cards from your hand as a valid action that extends the timer.
I would love, love, love, love, love to play a physical board game version of this system, as it would get around the pay-to-win, broken controls, and bad multiplayer that this package offers (assuming the characters are a little more balanced as well). As it is, there are so, so many better turn-based strategy games you could play, or heck, go play tabletop simulator. There's tons of better board games in there.

I thought this would be a cute game with cute animals doing cute things.  Instead, I get a  furry thesis pondering the tribulations and malevolent complications of capitalism, the hypocritical anarch state, and the meritocracy.
In Armello, any prepossessed positive impressions of tolstoyan altruism and philosophy should be renounced upon one's first embarkment. Armello's tutorials fail to warn players of the furry world's dominant predisposition of Hobbesian theory. Noble virtues -like philanthropy, benevolence, mercy- are absent, and moreso, sorely repressed. The kingdom's economy is dismal; banditry and civil unrest plague Armello's citizens. Cities scrape only a few gold pieces of profit a day, which usually go straight into the pockets of the one of the four Players of the court. These players twist Armello into their own personal training ground. Usually contiually exiled from their home lands, the 4 Players scour the board questing for baubles, trinkets, and prestige in court. The tainted court of Armello values only individual prestige; loyalty to the court, to the tainted King, provides higher standing power. This power comes at the price of one's autonomy; the king forces the most prestigious to decide the fate of the other denizens of the Kingdom; wherein, the effect always afflicts the land with harrowing misfortune.  As the King's health fades, the 4 players plot skullduggery, coveting for control of Armello's throne. The meritocracy fails to assuage the primal desires of the 4 players. Instead of seaking to rid the lands of suffering, the 4 players repeatedly turn and antagonize each other, oftentimes going so far as murder. Each seeing themselves as harbingers of revolution, the animals gladly divulge themselves in combat, robbery, and overall debauchery. Peace, pacifism, empathy -- they are but puerile conjecture, liabilites to the present and familiar goals of advancement. Therein lies the selfish hypocrisy of these furry creatures; in their coveting of higher station, they ultimately seek to destroy the pre-established system of status, reform and revolution of the court of the Lion. The 4 players vehemently desire supremacy, they will never be satisfied with the position they have; they will always drive to have more. The 4 players power game parallels the Mad Lion King's drift into the occult Rot. He was the strongest creature in the kingdom; yet his greed for more power led to his decay. In this light, the 4 players game is easily seen as a puerile redundancy of the Mad King's lust for power. Armello now presents us with the interesting reprisal of conjecture concerning virtue vs. vice. Selfishness and wrath lead to redundancy-- the 4 players who vie for power only repeat the Mad King's vie for power. Altruism and Pacifism lead to stagnation -- the 4 players would have no meaning in Armello if they didn't vie for power. Armello identifies the futiliy and fallacy of both moral expression and meaningless survival. Pain and suffering are synonymous with life, as well as happiness and generosity, greed and jealousy. Armello is an uncanny interpretation our meandering existence.

DISCLAIMER: I received this product for no cost for the purpose of reviewing. However, this does not affect my views and opinions of the title.
X-Plane 11 is a flight simulator by Laminar Research. The title is part of a long running series and is the sixth iteration in the X-Plane franchise. As the title suggests, the software is a plane simulator, and is more of a tool than an actual game. The user will be in the front seat of an aircraft, and pilot the craft in any way they see fit. The software can be used to experience the joys of piloting a plane and can even be somewhat of a learning tool.
--------
The graphics of this title are both realistic and very beautiful. The software does a great job of capturing the likeliness of aircraft very well. Both the exterior and interior of each craft look appropriately detailed. The overall scenery of the earth, combined with the magnificent lighting effects really make the simulator look good. In vehicle simulation software, capturing the realistic movement of the mechanism is a very important aspect, this is something that X-Plane 11 does very well.
There are many different aircraft to choose from within the base title. The developers are continuously working on, and releasing downloadable content for the software which include new planes as well as scenery. The software is a bit demanding, and does require a bit of a mid to high tier setup to run. It will run on the lowest settings on most systems, though to fully experience the title, a decent GPU and CPU are required.
--------

Sound assets are another important aspect of simulation titles. X-Plane 11 does a decent job of mimicking the actual sounds of an aircraft as well as environmental noises. There are a very limited amount of sound effects in the software, although there are not that many different sounds to actually put into the title. That being said, the sounds of the planes seems to change and react to way the plane is controlled.
--------

It is difficult to asses the "play-ability" of a simulation title, as they are not really games. As mentioned earlier, X-Plane 11 markets itself an engineering tool, and is just that. There are so many options and settings to change each flight experience. Each of the plane's cockpit have the amount of functional buttons, triggers, levers and monitoring devices that it would in real life.
The user will take the place of the plane's pilot. They will lift off from the air station, fly to their destination, and land. The concept is simple, and is what one would expect from a flight simulator, though the actual controlling of the aircraft and understanding what all of the buttons and controls do, does require some practice. The title is as challenging as the user makes it.
The learning curve of the title is quite steep. If the user has experience with air planes or flight simulators, they would have a better time adjusting to this title.
--------
People who enjoy flight simulators will definitely enjoy this software. Especially those who've played the earlier iterations. The title has built upon those older versions, and now has a better user interface, albeit a little confusing sometimes, as well as greatly enhanced graphics. As someone who hasn't played many flight simulators, I did find the title a bit overwhelming and difficult to first get a grasp of. Though I do believe part of the experience is learning the controls.
I can't confidently say that someone could use this program as a learning tool, as I don't know enough about planes or the industry to make that call. I do think that it's possible to still learn about various aircraft through experiencing them within the simulator.
It's a little more of a challenge to review simulators, as they don't really PLAY (pun) by the same rules as games. I did think the software was very pretty, and the lighting effects, especially at night, were really nice to look at. The devs seems to be putting a lot of work into the title, as there's already a ton of DLC out for it, even free scenery packs. This is something flight fans would definitely love.
Thanks to team at Laminar Research for giving me the opportunity to review the title, as well as anyone who took this review into consideration, I hope it helped.

Fortix is heavily inspired by the 1981's arcade game QIX and is a simple, yet addictive medieval-themed puzzle game where you have to capture a castle by fencing it off with lines that you draw on the playfield by moving your character.
The game features 22 levels of increasing difficulty with a handful enemy types such as bats, various dragon types and also cannon towers, which can be destroyed by triggering catapults that are spread across the playfield.
Randomly appearing power ups not only help you to fight the enemies more efficiently, but also help to rack up bigger combos which result in a higher score and a potentially better ranking on the online-leaderboards.
Fortix is a relatively short game and can be beaten in around 1.5-2 hours (maybe even faster if you're not going for a 'Perfect!' on every level), but the 4 difficulty levels add quite a bit to the replayability as they provide an additional challenge.
For only one buck  you certainly can't go wrong on this one! :)

Dearest Marie,
I don’t even know where to start, this game must be one of if not the best game I’ve played in a long time, from its outstandingly emotional story to the catastrophic atmosphere of the tragic event that was World War I.
To start off, let’s talk about the characters:
-	Emile, the brave soldier who sacrificed all he had to try and secure the happiness of his family throughout the war. This was my personal favourite character, as he shows how he is willing to let go of everything he has in order to maintain those he cares about alive through this godforsaken war;
-	Freddie, the once happy man whose life was turned upside down after a German attack killed his wife on their wedding day, making him into the brave man we see giving all he has in the battlefield, in an attempt to regain his honour;
-	Ana, the nurse whose father was kidnapped by the Germans and forced to make them weapons of war. This character is perhaps the most valiant, brave and courageous warrior, who instead of killing decided to give her life in sacrifice to those in need;
-	Karl, son-in-law of Emile, is a German man who is forced to abandon his French family and return to Germany, to fight for his country. His wish to see and protect his family is what drives him to combat all adversities and face all odds.
Secondly, I’d like to refer how beautiful the art style of this game is, not only the hand-drawn scenarios of the western front, but the characteristic character design, corrupted voices of the characters and outstanding soundtrack, which I really recommend you listen whenever you can.
Then there is the gameplay aspect, which is, let’s say, a little bit complicated, as the puzzles are not your typical repetitive schemes with various difficulties, but rather different puzzles on every level, which in my opinion is a plus, though sometimes they aren’t very logic, so to speak, getting you to spend maybe too much times on just one level. By me, that isn’t all that bad, as long as it doesn’t happen in the big emotional points of the story, which it sometimes does. But that is really me just nit-picking, as the impact of these small flaws is practically none.
In addition, I really appreciated the inclusion of historical facts in the game, as well as how strictly the game follows them: taking part in Battle of the Somme, Battle of Verdun and driving a taxi to the frontline were some of the moments where the plot merges with the actual progress of World War I.
Finally, as you can expect, I need to talk about the story, because in my opinion it is what sets this game apart from any other game I have ever played. As previously stated, I won’t spoil the ending to anyone, but I’ll say the build up to it is amazing. I really think this story has enough potential to maybe become a movie/book if it really wants to. The way these different characters, each with their own motivations and objectives, help each other for the common good, in hopes of achieving glory, honour, happiness, or just surviving this apocalypse, driving to an outstandingly beautiful ending that is second to none is perhaps some of the best story writing I have ever seen in a video game.
Also, the atmosphere of the game is phenomenal and really puts you in a World War I scenario. The way you come to understand that all your sacrifices might be in vein, that the big victories you have achieved have no meaning to anyone but yourself and that everyone you’ve ever known might die fighting for what they think is right, but in reality, they gave their lives for nothing more than a meaningless conflict that will only end once everyone has suffered is what turns a simple concept into an emotional, dramatic, touching and sentimental experience that will surely make you understand what war really is at its core.
In the end, I highly recommend this game to everyone looking for an entertaining, emotional, beautiful, simple yet complex experience that will not only change your view of conflict and war, but also make you understand what freedom, justice and life really mean.
As Emile says -
– and hopefully, such a tragical event will not happen ever again.
With love,
Me

I bought this game in 2012, and I finally beat it. It's just really bad and boring. The open world environment is interesting enough, but the combat is simplistic and the lock-on is very finicky. The main problem with the game is that it doesn't sprinkle references here and there, but instead relies entirely on them. Every single mission and thing in the game relies on references, and just fail to be memorable on its own merits.

After finishing this game in 10 hours, I thoroughly enjoyed this game. I will say I am a sucker for "retro" games, such as Shovel Knight. If you are the same, then this game will please you immidiately.
As for everyone else:
- This game is hard, however I tended to find it hard during gun combat sections, which is a majority of the main story. There are side missions, however the ones that involved driving a vehicle were usually just time trials.
- There are challenges in the game, however these usually consisted of things such as "see how many people you can set on fire with this flame thrower." These were fun, however in some cases they felt almost the same, but with a different weapon. From what I could tell these were not required for completing the main story, but to 100% the game requires you to find all of these and complete them.
- The music is spot on for this game, no other comment needed. One artist to take note of here is "virt," also known as Jake Kaufman, of whom created most of the music for Shovel Knight.
- One of the selling points for this game is its collection of references, and that is something it is not lacking. There are plenty of references in here, some I got, and others that flew over my head. Some of these are pretty obvious, such as the following: there is a scientist you work with who is working on a car that travels through time, "I wonder who that could be," I thought sarcastically.
- Continuing with references, some of these go deeper with much of the game actually having a lot of mechanics that come from old NES games, such as most of the story levels having towers you climb that are layed out like Zelda dungeons. There is also a point where one of the main missions is just paying service to Zelda fans, while another does the same for Metal Gear fans, with another paying service to Batman fans.
Conclusion:
There is a lot this game offers that I was discovering towards the end of the story. This is a game I will be coming back to every so often since it is a very fun game. There are even things I have not mentioned yet, such as a taxi mini game or the variety of guns and weapons at the player's disposal. There is also a DOS version that comes with the game for free, and from what I can tell it is most of, if not possibly all of the story mode. There are a few things missing, however from what it looks like it was meant to be played from a real Floppy Disk on a real 486 processor. Either way, this game is worth buying on a sale. At its full price, however, I would say it is worth it if you desire to complete the story and not just use it as a sandbox.

As a stop-gap review, I just want to say that this game rocks. It's worth getting for the music alone, which is reminiscent of those sweet tunes you may remember from playing the first Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles game for the NES.

It's a pretty nice step up from the last sim I used, FSX. The flight and failure models are really well done for the default hardware, and it's surprisingly well-optimized (consistently 30fps at low altitudes, basically anywhere in the world, on a GTX960, with settings nearly maxed out).
Hadn't used X-Plane before this release, so a few things to take into account if you're used to MSFS:
- There's really, really limited custom scenery. Most cities are autogen, and CBDs are "plausible" based on OpenStreetMap data, and the road layouts are pretty amazing, but I couldn't actually find a built-in landmark besides the Space Needle in Seattle. Mods are king, and the good mods are pretty pricey -- and some of them are _very_ punishing for the GPU.
- Seasons are also out the window. Everything's in a state of perpetual late Spring/early Fall unless you get mods. There are a few good free ones for this, though, and they don't kill your GPU.
- The built-in ATC system's pretty lacking. Again, though, there are mods for this, free and paid.
Having said that, the detailed terrain, amazing lighting, and realistic weather and flight models are IMO plenty to offset those problem areas. Fully recommend this, just don't be afraid to hop on the forums and pull down some of those sweet, sweet mods.

X-Plane 11 is a solid upgrade from X-Plane 10, but some key improvements are missing.
Laminar Research, X-Plane's creator, did a very good visual upgrade to X-Plane 11 and brought all the things that worked fine in X-Plane 10 along. The simulation and flight model is still one of the most accurate in hard desktop simulation. They reworked the user interface into a more gamey appearance. Although I don't really like the look, but it still remains a solid upgrade in usability over the old interface.
A key new feature is the integration of ATC and AI aircraft. Something that MS-Flight Simulator has built in stock. Unfortunately in the current state this feature is lacking. You can only work with IRF flight plans. You don't know take off and landing runways to expect and the ATC get's regularly confused, if you don't hit way points exactly.
The AI aircraft are a nice addition, but you can only select a small number. There is no plausible traffic generated and the aircraft ignore your presence. (I had multiple aircraft taxi  though my aircraft.)
One further addition is the map. The map is zoomable down to the airport and contains navigation aids, such as ILS and VOR with frequencies. This removes the need to go look for additional charts before heading off for a quick flight.
The stock aircraft are well build, with he exception of the Cirrus Vision SF50, which has a half functional glass cockpit.
All in all a nice simulator, with some room for improvement.

I've seen people people calling this game funny, but I had my corncerns, then I started playing it. It just goes full bonkers. Your name is Player who's in the
Jester's band comitting ban robbery, but when escaping with the school bus you can't take a turn because of how many schoolbuses our there (even a dead Frogger on the street) so blow some up to reduce traffic! Then laters escape on foot while the TMN Turtles attack you, and this is the game's first few minutes. :)
Later the game uses the GTA formula: open world with cars, customization stores, weapon stores  (food/drink heals, coffee speeds up) and with rampage / challenge points, main and side missions. The whole game is just awesome - almost every quest has references to movies/games or even reflections about game industry and trends, the world is jampacked with jokes and funny characters and events. There are some general difference though: missions are slightly longer and often happen through multiple locations (There are checkpoint between them!) and the police is way less annoying - every cop has a ... I guess 10-15% chance to drop a police cloaking device that will remove your wanted rating. I think this is a great change, as you won't need to spend half of the gameplay time to drive to spray paint garages.
What else the game has?  Good music, multiple gameplay mode during the story, slightly casualized but more streamlined open-world gameplay, original and interesting storyline where something always happens, I loved it so, so much!   Also just a mention, but it's kind of weird how hard the final levels of the game are compared to the whole. Anyways, a superstrong recommendation for the lovers of retro games and eighties movie's style because you'll be in for a treat - I think you can count on about/more than 10 hours of gameplay just by messing around and doing the quests, without trying much for challenges.
Cheap retro-style GTA clone that does its job pretty well to provide fun and challenge while imitating a larger series. Driving could use some work though.

I didn't really have any expectations or much knowledge about the game except a small idea of how it all worked before I played. I were welcomed into a cool and adventurous world full of challenges and fun for hours. The game itself works a bit like a board game with some elements from card games and some fun character building. You choose your character and then you race for the throne. There is a bunch of things that make Armello a really great game. One of those is the way the game itself works. You have four characters that all work with the same goal in mind to be the new king of the land and dethrone the old one. It is a great game since you have these different ways of obtaining this goal and clear the win conditions. There are four ways to be the new king and despite you may have put your mind into one way of winning, will you maybe find yourself in a position to win by another strategy all of a sudden and sweep away victory. The game is very dynamic and the different elements really work together in a good way to form a really fun and interesting game experience. Other than the game itself, is the art, music, map layout, and basically all the other elements of the game I found myself enjoying, really well made and nicely polished.
The only downside I can see to the game is the lack of new elements, which I found myself hungering a bit for after winning with all four win-conditions and trying out the different characters.
Other than that is it a really fun game and despite I didn’t enjoy the online multiplayer as much because of some slow opponents can it be really fun to play with others and probably really fun with friends if you chose to do so.
I can greatly recommend it, a fun experience.

It is an incredibly well-made computer board-game. Beautiful fantastical graphics, mesmerising earworm music, varied characters and cards with outstanding animation. It brought childhood memories of fairy-tale board games back to me.
The king of Armello has been infested by the Rot, and four heroes rise to protect Armello in four different ways:
1. Prestige: through combat, cards or quests, hoard the most prestige points and survive until the king dies from the Rot, when you will rightfully take his place. In the meantime, as the most prestigious hero, you are the King's counselor and can decide the fate of Armello.
2. Spirit Stones: gather 4 spirit stones from the corners of the realm and bring them to the king, countering his deadly palace perils, to cleanse him from the Rot and bring peace to Armello.
3. Combat: build up your attack power and your luck, which will grant you more dice in combat, to challenge the corrupted ruler, defeat him and purge Armello of his terror.
4. Rot: harness the powers of evil and surpass the king's influence in the dark realm, challenge and overpower him in combat and bring Armello under your own tyranny.
You can play Armello on multiplayer with up to 4 friends. Though there is no way to co-op, players can help each other by using special cards.
I hope you enjoy this rich and intelligent game as much as I did, and I wonder if the soundtrack will ever come out of your brain ;)

Fallout as a series is primarily about roleplaying and interacting directly with the geo-politics of various post-apocalyptic civilizations that sprung up in an alternate history universe where Atomic-punk Murica and China nuked each other. Every time the series eschewed that roleplay/story focus such as in Fallout 4 or in this case Fallout Tactics the result has been negative. The default gameplay setting for Tactics is a real-time battle system but even with the tweaks and improvements over Fallout 1 and 2's interface it's still not an interface suited to a real time squad tactics game. Fortunately you can set it back to turn based ala 1&2 but the core combat gameplay mechanics expanded just a little bit over 1&2 just aren't deep or interesting enough to carry an entire game when divorced from the RPG and story elements people actually played those games for.
If you just want to sit for hours watching a bunch of anonymous unlikable scruffy idiots fire thousands of rounds at each other in a horrible brown wasteland without ever seeming to hit a damned thing you're probably better off just going online and watching footage of the Syrian civil war. You'll enjoy the same experience overall that way without the inconveience of having to click on the combatants or constantly manage their inventories.
Game also runs like♥♥♥♥♥♥ Looks like the last time it was updated it was to get it running on Windows 8 and while I can't vouch for how it ran on Windows 8 systems it certainly runs like complete trash on Windows 10. Pre-rendered cutscenes have problems, wired graphical glitches in-game and anytime I got a game-over and returned to the main menu by that route the cursor would completely flake out. I think I'll just watch the cutscenes on youtube and probably not bother circling back to this.

As a child, I never fairly completed this game (shoutout to invincibility cheats and boomerang unlocks), let alone 100% completion, but 15 years later it landed in my Library and I set out to finish what I never tried as a kid.
This game is such a joy to play. Its goofy and fun and keeps you entertained for hours. The characters are quirky, the music is excellent, the levels are beautiful, and there's plenty to collect and explore for! I'm such a fan of collect-a-thon games, because they give me a motive to explore every corner of this virtual world and appreciate the design the developers had in mind. Level objectives are laid out for you, and sometimes even marked on the maps, but they still leave plenty of room for analyzing and creative thinking.
That being said, this game isn't difficult by any means. There are moments of frustration splattered in, but it's nothing to sweat over. The levels are fairly linear, if and only if you aren't looking to 100% complete the game. End world bosses aren't painfully difficult, but I also understand the intended audience for this game isn't looking for Dark Souls rage bosses.
Overall, this game makes my child-like heart happy. I'd love to see a release the second and third installments of this game remastered too. Thanks for the blast from the past, devs.

Casual Horror
Like Horror movies, horror games have their gems (Slender Man = The Ring) and other times there are the ‘B-Grade’. What a lot of people don’t know is that all Horror movies start as a B-Grader, till it becomes enough of a cult classic, before major studios even think of taking over and doing twenty more for a franchise! Why Blair Witch has taken soooo long to spawn a sequel.
Same with horror games,  you have that one game that jumps out at you (punt) and you are seeing sequels and movies till your eye bleed. Resident Evil is a great example (Hated it myself, only because I could not get use to the ‘Alone in the Dark’ borrowed camera angles), more content there than you can poke a stick at! Then you have your B-grade copycats that just churn out at a dime a dozen (Phantasmagoria anyone?).
Well where dose Sophie’s curse stand. It is a B-grade copycat, one that you might sit through once but would never go back to again. The graphics are good and it will get a jump out of you, in the end but only because it waits till you are distracted, like my wife, who for giggles hides behind a door and as I walk past, jumps out to scare all eight colours of the rainbow from my loins (Yes honey, I will get you back for that)!
But there is no ‘Horror’ to this game, no atmosphere, no story, no…. Fear. All the points are ticked but each has no clue as to what it wants to achieve. The music was better suited for mediation than giving you the creeps (Ohmmm). Sound effects were constant and did not peak or plummet at all during play. The story, as told through one letter and some very short emails, has as much body as a single thigh bone. The graphics was iPad/Android storyboard stiff and static. And interaction with the environment was as dynamic as flossing you fingernails (Point and Click on rails)!
So here is the story in a nut shell. You, un-named person, covers for a friend who goes out to party while you stay in their house and look after their ill father. When you get there, you find the house has (so-called) bad wiring and you need to hand crank makeshift light sources (Me thinks old Pops forgot to pay his electricity bill and blew the money on a bag of trippy hooch) to keep certain room illuminated.
Oh, and your ♥♥♥♥♥ of a friend, happens to forget to tell you the house ‘might’ be hunted by a dead help desk girl, called Sophie (I promise Sophie! I did switch it on first. No I won’t yell at you again down the phone line. Just don’t gank me!).
You must check your friend’s laptop to see where each light source is and where a safe zone exists. Yes a safe zone, that some how keeps Sophie from harming you (Where’s my salt and iron bar!) which can move at any time, so you must keep running back to the computer to check where it is.
Each light source has a drainage bar that will drain slowly or fast, just depending on how much Sophie will tamper with it (she keeps trying to charge her iPhone 3 on them) and if the device fails or the bar drains right out, the room goes dark and you are more screwed than a nail board.
Each level is a set of hours from dusk, till the break of dawn (6 levels that I found at the beginning, there may be more but after three, I could not drag myself through this game to find out). Each level is supposed to get more scary and intense as you go but it quickly fails into a monotonous grind-fest and you get faced palmed by a 2D cut out of a Salvador Dali style Sophie.
In this age of modern games, the point and click style is better served on a Tablet or iPad system, not on a PC where other horror games give you a better amount of movement freedom. The true horror in this game is the POV camera, it is a fixed deal with very limited movement and when you do move from one spot to another, the camera will snap around to its pre-programmed grid position. Seeing as you are also not suppose to look at Sophie (she has some body image issues) this makes it near impossible NOT to automatically look in her direction or even to try and escape.
All in all, this game is great if you want to give a friend (or yourself) a cheap jump scare (because your too lazy to hide behind doors and do it yourself) but I say this again, wait till its an app for an iPad or tablet, it is a wast of time on a PC. For me, I am going to hand my laptop over to Sam and Dean (the Winchester boys) and have them perform an Exorcism on its drives to purge this evil.

I've barely put any hours into XP11, and I already know it's my new favourite flight sim.
Coming from FSX, it's a direct upgrade in almost every aspect (including price, but I already feel like it was money well spent).
The graphics are stunning, for example I was blown away while flying over a mountain range in Italy on a flight from Ancona to London. The sim also runs exceptionally well, running very comfortably at medium settings and no antialiasing on my kinda outdated PC. The cockpit detailing is far superior to any I've ever seen before, especially in the 737 (but the inability to test the GPWS annoys me slightly haha), but from what I've seen in the 737, 747 and Cessna Skyhawk it looks perfect.
The built in ATC is pretty bad. The default ATC in FSX just seems to work better, and also has a lot more functionality (I can't seem to be able to even request a change of flight level, and if I do change without the permission of ATC, it will repeatedly tell me to descend/ascend to my previous flight level and refuse to stop until I comply).
Apart from this minor issue, I can't find anything else I dislike about XP11. It's just fantastic compared to FSX.
I dont recommend this yet. Although graphics and performance are very nice compared to xp10. The ATC is an absolute joke. IMO it is still in beta and I will stick with xp10 for a bit longer.

Fallout Tactics is the red-headed step-child of the Fallout series. (And Fallout: Brotherhood of Steel is the senile, racist grandparent who may have commited a war crime and we just avoid talking about them) It comes from a era when Interplay was not doing great, and Fallout was their biggest earner.
Fallout Tactics opens and immediately you will encounter your first problem...the developers did no research. They may have done quick playthroughs of Fallout 1, skipping all the dialogue, but they definately didnt look into the story or lore. Otherwise this intro cutscene for a game called "Fallout Tactics: Brotherhood of Steel" wouldnt completely get the origin of the Brotherhood of Steel wrong. At least they got Ron Perlman.
After R. Lee Ermey is done giving you your first mission (yes its actually him) you encounter the second problem with the game: Real time combat. In a effort to make fallout more mainstream, kids nowadays dont like turn based combat, it has to be faster, more exciting! Thankfully you can turn that off, otherwise the game would be near impossible to play, and I never would have gotten past the first handful of missions. But I can imagine making this a default, caused many people to quit early on without realizing it can be turned off to classic fallout combat.
Now we get onto the good! The gameplay in turn-based modes is solid, and being squad-based suits both the theme of being BoS members and the fallout combat well! The two squadmates they start you with are actually very good (Hope you didnt make your player character a sniper or medic though) and I kept them the entire game.
The games difficulty however, ratchets up extremely fast, and the game is extremely long. Many people ive talked to "quit near the end, with the super mutants" and they were only actually halfway through the game.
Now of course, theres the other highlight, one people always like to mention in reference to this game: you can have Deathclaw, Ghoul, and Super Mutant squad members! Ghoul's are often fine, however you will want to avoid any with the "glowing one" trait, as they will poison your human squad members (including your player character)
However deathclaws (lets ignore the fact that their inclusion means someone skimmed fallout 2, and once again didnt look into the actual REASON those deathclaws could talk) are outright worthless. You want a death machine hell bent of tearing apart your enemies close up? Get a human in power armor, a deathclaws lack of armor makes them outright worthless at close range, they will be eviscerated instantly. I beat the game with a deathclaw in my party, however I used their unnatural strength....to throw grenades farther than humans can.
Super Mutants suffer from the same problem, your "front line" soldiers need power armor to survive, the increased health that super mutants and deathclaws have, make them worthless front line fighters.
Level Design is...uninspired, you got a handful of decent levels, otherwise you get warehouses, warehouses, more warehouses, and the occassional vault that doesnt have the classic gear shaped door, or any sign of anyone wearing a blue and yellow jumpsuit for miles. In fact one of the biggest problems, is the developers clearly didnt realize or care that Fallout takes place in a 1950's idealized future of 2077, which had been ravaged by nuclear war. You could just as easily set Tactics in 2002's idea of the future.
And lastly, the other big feature, vehicles! For the most part vehicles are quite interesting, though a tad unweildy to control. (You WILL run over squadmates while figuring out how to properly control them) you cant use them in missions, except for the mission in which you acquire them in the first place. Which means once you have your convoy of armored vehicles, you cant actually do much with them. So naturally, when the final mission of the game opens with a small driving section before you are forced to go on foot, that should be the last hurrah of your cars? Your reward for keeping all the vehicles until the end, right? Nope. Go on foot, clear the way, bring the newest car to the end, and thats it. Its hard to judge the entire mechanic, because its biggest problem is how under-utilized it is.
Overall this game really isnt worth your time, it overstays its welcome by dozens of hours, its difficult in ways that feel unfair and will have you save scumming every five minutes. The only enjoyable features are building your squad, and the voice acting by R. Lee Ermey and Kurtwood Smith (Red Foreman, Claren Boddicker) And if you are a big fallout fan who wants to know what in this game is canon: The BoS exists in the midwest, near chicago. Thats it.
But hey, at least it isnt Fallout: BoS.

TL;DR:
As a board game:
* "Rulebook" does not provide enough detail
* Interesting mechanics
* Good single player option
As a video game:
* Die rolls are psuedo-psuedo-random (uses physics implementation and die orientation/rest detection to determine result) and can be manipulated.
* Insists on playing out all animation for given actions, including AI turns.
* Limited and ambiguous ("very low" to "very high") graphical options
* Not all keybindings are changeable or even listed
* CAN NEVER VIEW ENTIRE BOARD
* Accusations of online cheatery (cannot confirm, would not be surprised; seems exploitable).
Final: can recommend within boardgame constraints.  Be wary if looking to play online with randoms.
****
Good board game, awful implementation.  The benefits afforded to the game being implemented as a video game are good enough that I can comfortably recommend it, as long as you don't mind it wasting a bit of your time in Single Player, as it, by the gods, is going to animate everything happening on AI turns, something wildly unnecessary for a video game.
The game's rulebook is how it is coded, but the only rules you get to read are the ones they thought to tell you.  How does the game break Prestige ties?  Why did I die after obtaining four Spirit Stones (would have loved to review the game log, but half a second later it was inaccessable as the cpu took their turn and won)?  Those sorts of questions don't get answers like they would in an actual board game, where *humans* have to implement the mechanics.  Additionally, unlike a physical board game, you are never afforded a full view of the board, instead having to pan around your static viewport or jump-to-location like an RTS.
Finally, damningly, you should be aware that whenever die rolls are shown, they are not random.  There is a random element, no doubt, but the game uses physics emulation and die face detection to decide what was rolled.  This sounds like a good idea from a board-game-as-video-game standpoint, but in reality it just means you've made it gameable.  Example: it is possible to roll dice additional dice during combat.  Die about to settle on a side you don't like?  Roll the rest of your dice, knock it around, and essentially get a free re-roll.  This becomes more of a nightmare if you consider what the netcode must look like for multiplayer.  I've not played a game online against random humans yet, but a cursory look at how the game works makes it incredibly easy for me to believe it when someone complains about cheaters, which undoubtedly becomes frustrating given the game includes lootboxes (multiplayer only) and microtransactions for cosmetics.  NOTE: the game does have DLC expansions.  AFAIK, lootboxes and microtransactions do not provide items that modify gameplay.
UNLESS the die shape is accurately represented in the physics engine, in which case, yes, the COSMETIC dice you have will affect the results of your rolls.
And honestly, that's the worst of it: as a self-descibed video/board-game hybrid, it managed to fall in to many traps making it inferior to either a properly implemented video or board game.  End of the day?  Sure.  Whatever.  I sit down and play a game or two when I don't have anything else to do.  I've got about half a dozen friends that play it off and on as well, and I'd be happy to play it with them.  I'm hesitant to dive into online play given some of the problems outlined above.
Still, I can comfortably recommend Armello as a board game.  Just not certain how eagerly I'd recommend it if you intend mainly to play against random people you can't reach over and backhand.

The game is okay, but I have my reasons for that. I adore games like these, with survival being the main point of the game, and this game has some good points but every good point is shot down by bad points. Let me start off with some of the pros.
-Multiple characters that you can choose to fit your play style: Feel like being a badass who doesn't need any healing? Go ahead and have only soldiers on your side. Feel like planning a bit and staying in a hole of protection? Go with a mixture of soldiers, mechanics, and healers like I do, or even if you feel like challenging yourself you can do so by getting only one soldier and the rest are medics. This is fun and varies the gameplay a bit.
-Waves give you time to do things inbetween them: You have no clue how many games I've played where the waves go by so fast that you have no time to upgrade your weapons or anything. It sucks when that happens and adds a difficulty that I don't exactly enjoy, especially when the upgrade station is so far away from where the main objective is.
-Fairly good graphics: This one seems a bit of a stretch in reaching for good things, but hear me out. So the top down perspective is hard to work with, but that's not all the graphics have to offer. There's small details in the menues that made me chuckle a bit because it's lighthearted and rather nice to see in a zombie game, and the upgrade menu has a nice feel to it too.
-The upgrade system: Now, this one is kinda nice. You can upgrade anyone at any time, if you have the materials. Even the armor can get upgrades! Your armor can break though so beware of that. The mechanics get some turrets and such, the medics I haven't touched because of reasons I'll get into later, and the soldiers get gun and armor upgrades. It's nice to see the visual change of your character too when you upgrade.
Now for the cons...
-Terrible character movement: When you click on an area for your character to go they can often flip out. You have to click on an area for the character to go there, which is normally not a bad thing, but whenever you click the character can often get stuck on something, or even slip around while trying to move, which segues into my next point.
-Glitchy movement: Your character, if you click multiple times, can spaz out. The first time I clicked three times the character slipped through the wall and out of the main map. This part sucks and I had trouble dealing with it. It happens multiple times and I feel like it's due to poor programing on the character part.
-Overpowered zombies: So this was kind of a huge issue for me. Your first wave starts out easy (Mind you that I'm playing on easy because I'm learning things) but as soon as that second wave comes around you're screwed. The zombie killed my soldier in two hits, or some really fast hits that seemed to do a lot of damage. I couldn't escape because of two issues, one is the terrible movement with the glitchy spazment, and the other is my next gripe.
-The slow character movement: Your characters are barely faster than the zombies! The rooms are about as big as a normal house, right? Then why is it that the characters walk like they took too many drinks and are hobbling slowly because they'll fall otherwise? I don't like that. I'll move on to my next issue
-The door mechanics: So this should be simple, yes? Well, it's not. Since story mode isn't available yet we have to go with sandbox, which isn't too big of an issue. The game is still in the works so I can let that slide, but when it comes to doors I can't. When you click on a character then on a door you will often get the message "The path is blocked", but you're clicking on the door, the only thing blocking the path. This is an issue because you have to click near the door to get your character over to the door and then click on the door to open it. That's confusing because why can't I do that to begin with?
My next issue is a bit more personal, but still.
-The item harvesting: So you sit in a room with some scrap matal, ammo, and some boxes. You harvest them and have to sit there, just waiting till you can upgrade your character for the next wave. I don't like this. The entire outside is a black void, why not fill that with something? Why not have the outside filled with cars and stuff that you can harvest some metal from to add to the danger? Lower the zombie strength and add some risk to the area. Maybe have some simple things inside you can harvest such as drawers from the kitchen for some wood or maybe some electronics for some metal, but have it limited till you're forced outside to harvest car parts for scrap.
Other than that you have very small nit-picks, such as limited upgrades which feel like they need more tabs, the lack of mele weapons for everyone, and the weird way of healing people.  Those aren't too big of an issue to me. Overall, it's an early access game and shows that. I want to see this become something good, and it probably will become better with the next update. Keep working on the game man. I like it thus far, and can't wait for story mode to open up

Episodes from Liberty City (EfLC) feature two separate games: The Lost and Damned (TLaD) and The Ballad of Gay Tony (TBoGT). What’s interesting about these two episodes is that they cross-over with each other and the main game GTAIV. However having said that each episode can be played stand alone and you will fully understand each story, but there is no doubt that you’ll get more out of the series if you play them in the order GTAIV, TLaD, then TBoGT.
Now for the gameplay, both episodes feature the same graphics and gameplay model of GTAIV. Each episode adds more songs and changes some of the radio stations. While you can still drive a car in TLaD, you will find yourself driving a motorcycle for most of the game which was a fun change up from the usual GTA formula.
Regarding story, in TLaD you play a biker in a biker gang, and along the way there are rival gangs that you are at war with. It features the classic GTA story elements of Power and Betrayal, but I felt that once the game was over, not all that much actually happened. There were also only two or three characters that actually felt like they had some importance or that was properly developed and the main story was quite bland.
In TBoGT you work for club manager Gay Tony and help him as he goes on a drug-fueled frenzy of bad decisions with the wrong people. In this game you will see more familiar faces from GTA IV, and a much larger variety of characters that feel more developed. TBoGT has more of that GTA humour and all in all felt more like a GTA game with serious moments and comedy throughout.
Overall, I highly recommend EfLC, and both TLaD and TBoGT are great additions to the Grand Theft Auto franchise.

Basic review of X Plane 11 from a FSX user. I have been using FSX since it came out and never used XP before.
I decided to give XP a go and its awesome and a bit frustrating.
First the good stuff.
-Graphics. For a standard sim its unbelievable!!
-Flight model. Very realistic and much better than FSX.
-The general scenery is very nice.
-Airport scenery is awesome.
The bad.
-Graphics. Don't for one moment think you are going to get anywhere near playable FPS with the recommended requirements. You need a beast of a PC to run this at max settings.
-Scenery. Don't get me wrong its amazing but at more than 60 GB there is still so much missing. For example I live in South Africa so I do most of the flying in that region. My hometown airport FARG is amazing but FAOR(OR Tamb Int airport) which is the main hub and the most busiest airport in Africa has no buildings, proper markings or ground services. Bit strange if you ask me.
-Bugs, There is a lot of bugs like a Beechcraft Baron 58 suddenly starts flying like a Cessna because one engine is just missing. Lots of random game crashes.
-Setting up of controls. The sim will id your joystick automatic but to fine tune it is very hard. 3rd party apps is what you need here but once everything is tuned its awesome.
-ATC. Just horrible. Freaks out and gives very bad directions. No taxi control with small aircraft.
-Flight planning, FSX was very easy. XP not so much.
Most of the bad stuff is just bugs that will be fixed with the first patch, hopefully.
Then a word of advice for all the FSX users. Changing to XP is not at all easy. Everything is different so you will need to take the time to read and watch a lot of videos but in the end its worth it.
I recommend this sim but rather wait till the first patch to avoid frustration.

Fans of the original Fallout games used to hate this game back in 2001, because they were all waiting for the follow up, that had been brewing for quite some time at the time, to Fallout 2 and then they got this: a bloody amazing Tactical Combat game, but without speech and dialogue..
I loved it, especially the Continous Turn Based (CTB) option coupled with the Aggressive Sentry Modes with variable Accuracy Thresholds. Awesome!! And if the combat got too messy or overwhelming you could always switch to turn-based. Splendid. Finally a game that lets you deal with all the cannonfodder in a nice and easy way. Levels, levels, levels. It was also the best looking Fallout game ever with dynamic lights, even though it was a bit less cozy, cartoony and charming, but the intro is awesome nonetheless and there is a bit of choice along the way, but it's mostly RPG at gun-point.
So, obviously the only thing missing here is the Speech skill.. And thus the use and need of Charisma is rather limited - to just the speed of your ranks and bartering.
There is also a Tough Guy mode, but the end mission is quite long in itself, which is the reason why I never finished it as Tough Guy - I simply don't have the time to finish the last mission in one session.
Combat is more flexible also in turn-based, because you are not stuck on a grid.. It's total free-form-360. There are Sentry modes with four Accuracy Thresholds: 95, 66, 33 and 1% where you team will react automatically. There are also three stance positions: Standing, Crouch and Prone. You can switch all at once, in minor teams or individually and they don't switch from one stance to the other unless you make them..
There are also both Special and Random Encounters (RE) when you travel the wasteland. It's both a blessing and a curse. A blessing because it's a source of EXP, guns and ammo and a curse because at times you'll be really annoyed by the sheer number of it. Having someone with Outdoorsman becomes quite crucial.
Every container, which includes both vehicles, boxes, lockers and rercruits at the Recruit Master can be used to store equipment. I think there is a kind of economy in the game that deflates the value of things you sell and therefore it's not a bad idea to pile up huge quantities before dropping them off at the Quarter Master shop.
As you progress the number and variation of Recruits at the Recruit Master will grow, but they will not advance unless you "tag" them all at least once. The "tagging" involves adding them all to your team, before you switch them back to the pool of Recruits. That way they will also get Experience, whenever you do and thus will never become too weak to join you. Just remember to come back and advance them.
Along the way you will also encounter different vehicles that you can actually bring with you, drive around in and use as armor with your whole team as gun mounts and they can also be used as Storage for all the loot you find - just remember to bring a member with the Repair skill, which you'll need to repair the damage it gets from accidents or RE along the way; having a Pilot is an added bonus.
Today, a truly wide-screen adjustment would have been nice, even though I think there is a mod for it I just can't be bothered to install it, somehow.. Well, there are some low res Wide-screen choices (16:9 and 16:10)..
I've played and replayed it a hell of a lot, before it appeared on Steam.
The combat of X-COM and Wasteland are just like flies on the windscreen compared to this.

A very thoughtout, interesting game. "Emily is Away" is based around the old 2006-ish AOL/AIM instant messanger. Anyone who remembers those services is likely to have some nostalgia flashbacks. The fact that this game is free makes it a must play for any indie player (or any gamer in general).
The game takes place over the course of five years: starting in senior year of high school and ending at college graduation. The relationship between the player and the titular Emily is the main focus of the messages. This leads into the only problem that I have with the game: there is no replay ability. I have spent well over an hour on a game that can be finished in about fifteen-twenty and all "choices" lead to exactly the same ending result. Despite the no cost of this product, that did annoy me.
Overall, however, "Emily is Away" is a fun way to spend an hour or so of your time. I am planning on purchasing the next game: "Emily is Away Too".

Not worth its weight in gold.
Rarely do I ever give bad reviews to games, mainly because the effort in which was placed into them needs at least a small hat-tip, but, bloody hell, this was not worth the twenty dollars I spent.
Critiques:
- The prologue misled me, which is perhaps the strongest of my irritations. I thought that this was to be a role-playing board game, where, at each map, you were given a plot scenario and you would have to fight your way through quests and competing players to win, thereby reaching the next map, and then the next, moving onto a strange story until you finally got to fight against the lion king at the final map. This was exactly how the prologue acted out for you. You played different characters, achieving different goals until the map dimmed out and you were warped to a different character. I was invested. I was interested.
- The ACTUAL game... is nothing like this. There are no new maps. It's the same map (though you can switch between seasons), with the same characters, all striving for the same goal: kill the king or cure him. You know Candy Land? How the setting, the plot, the characters never change? This is basically Candy Land.
- There is no plot. Not an ounce of interesting clan dimensions or rivalries. You can fight against your own clan if you want. Nothing makes sense. There's no substance in this game.
- The 3D models of the characters are... ah, for lack of a better word, ugly. The 2D profile pictures look marvelous, but when you zoom in on their 3D modeled faces, it's hideous.
- The AI makes no sense. Most of the time, it feels like everyone is after you. Everyone seems to be able to bypass trickeries except for you, and despite its "randomized" choices, they do their damnedest to focus at you.
- Characters are unbalanced. Some are abhorishly overpowered, with dice as far as the eye can see, whilst some only have two or three at their disposal, making combat near-impossible.
- It is so damn hard to get inside that stupid castle to cure the king with the spirit orbs. Not only is it littered with traps and guards, the king himself won't let you cure him.
Praises:
- The prologue could not have been more engaging. I'm still mad that it misled me, though.
- The 2D art style was beautiful to look at. I loved both the flat-colored images as well as the painted portraits.
- The overall world had so much potential. Animal clans fighting against each other was amazing to watch, and reminded me of Redwall.
I haven't tried the multiplayer version of the game, but I'm not wont to do so. This game is frustrating, and its story isn't captivating enough to keep you focused on your objectives. It wasn't worth the twenty dollars, and I regret giving it away.

First, let me clear the air on this one by saying I bought this game when it first came out on disc. Back then I think it was actually shipped on a CD-ROM and not even a DVD, but anyway that's why I show only 6 minutes played. I repurchased this game on Steam and it's a title I will take out every so often and play for a few days, and then set aside again to be enjoyed later. When I first bought the game, I played it pretty intensively, single and multiplayer.
The premise of this game is simple but the implementation is amazing. There is a little gem of a game called Final Fantasy Tactics that I used to play on Playstation which was one of my favorites; I think it got over-looked and disrespected to some extent because it was not a traditional Final Fantasy game. It was a game set in the world of Final Fantasy but focused on tactical battles rather than RPG elements, that would take place on small 3D maps where terrain and positioning of your warriors mattered greatly. Fallout Tactics is very much along the same lines: a game set in the world of the Fallout game series, but focused on tactical small-scale combat rather than role-playing. The developers of Tactics did this extremely well!
What you have here is a game that captures the fierce joy of the warrior risking his life and fighting to the death. In Tactics, you command a squad of warriors as they fight through a 3D map to accomplish certain objectives. You watch the action from above in isometric view, and directly move and perform actions with each of your squad members in a turn-based style. The maps can be the size of a small town; large enough that it takes some time to work your way across a single battle. Troop positioning and the "lay of the land" is vitally important for your success. Your troops can stand, crouch, and go prone, and move in all those positions, and since the map is rendered in 3D the height of various points of cover and "line of sight" principles mean you can really outmaneuver the enemy (or be outmaneuvered, if you aren't careful!)
During the course of the SP game you complete a campaign that progresses in difficulty. You get access to a pool of recruits that you can choose from with different skills, and those skills are honed and developed in combat, so the more you use particular recruits the more powerful they will become. This makes it especially painful if you lose a beloved comrade in combat, as combat deaths are final! All part of the glory, my friend.
This game has great graphics for its age and still looks good; it has lots of different weapons and skills you can use to achieve your goals; there is extreme freedom to decide how to tackle each map, just as you would expect from a Fallout title; and there is blood and gore and vicious, bullets-flying, clubs smacking, rockets-exploding combat action that will keep you entertained every minute.
I'm not sure how I can else I can say this other than: go ahead and buy this game if you like tactical combat or RTS or Rainbow Six-style squad battles or seeing a man's torso distintegrate into bloody chunks from a close-range shotgun blast.

Fallout Tactics is the unloved child of the series but it holds a special spot in my heart.
Despite the clunky ‘real time’ combat system and weird un-lore friendly story the game has real character. The devs choose to move away from the vault dweller being the main protagonist and you create a character of the waste land and join the brotherhood of steel as the most junior rank and force you to work your way up the chain of command.
The level design is solid and generally give you a variety of ways to complete the mission. This combined with a nice range of teammates to select from and gear to customise your character.
I really love the ambient sounds that bring the stages to life. The raider bases and towns are well designed and again provide you with options to exercise strategy. I like the fact that the game tries to push you to setting up ambushes rather than simple running and gunning through the enemy like so many other games.
This game is by no means perfect but I enjoyed in more than a dozen AAA titles i've played in recent years.

They won't take very good cover unless you order them to, they won't be overly aggressive or passive unless you tell them to. Odds are if you spend the entire game without touching an order key then the little details like ambushes in this game will go amiss.

This is a huge step forward for Laminar Research.  Having tried X-Plane since version 8, I can tell you that this 64bit architecture kicks everthing else in the teeth.  I've invested plenty of time and money into FSX, long before it was FSX or the Steam version, trying to get the most realistic flight simulation possible.  X-Plane 11 out of the box makes FSX obsolete.
The XP11 community is huge and free is a common word within it.  I was shocked to see such detail for my small hometown airport and the larger feeder airport nearby.  Ai traffic is now present, works very well and is adjustable.  If you can't find the details you want for your local airport, then
will get you going in the right direction with a huge database of free airports, scenery, aircraft and addons created by the community.
The flight physics are incredibly realistic and no lookup tables are used.  Blade element theory is used, which results in a much more realistic flight model.  The user interface is simple and intuitive.  It recognized both my xbox360 controller and logitech 3d pro stick.  I recommend X-Life Deluxe for an Ai traffic addon and XEnviro for a weather addon, although, you don't really need these.  Like Air Hauler 2 or FSPassengers for a professional pilot/mission type of experience? Then you're in luck because the MyPassengerX plugin is coming soon:

There are too many youtube videos out there that will convince you that this is the most affordable, expandable, realistic, friendlly flight community, TONS of FREE stuff out there flight simulator on the market.  It's a bit intimidating at first for a newcomer, but aviation isn't simple.  Once you learn a few things about how XP11 works, you'll never look back.
Beware! This kind of realism comes at a heavy price in regards to your PC performance.  I play this on an 8-year-old i7 860 CPU (2.8-3.46 GHz), an equally old motherboard, GTX 760 W/2GB VRAM, slow 1TB HDD and 20GB DDR3 RAM at 1920x1080 resolution, Process Lasso & ParkControl (Free versions) and pagefile/virtual memory turned off.  I get 30-35 FPS and this appears to be common even on high-end PC's.
The demo does not represent the actual performance of the game.  It is much better in  terms of FPS and overall experience.  The demo almost changed my purchasing decision because it SUCKED!
If you are like many lovers of the flight simulation genre, then you may find yourself tweaking many settings to find the FPS "G-Spot".  Once you're done screwing around and decided you're about to hit the refund button or throw a kitten out of a window, then go to the x-plane 11>output>preferences folder and delete everything in it and start over.  You'll thank me for that later and probably get a big FPS boost out of it as well.  Just make sure you have any payware activation keys/codes in hand when you do this.  Don't worry, it works.  Happy flying!
This is the future of flight simulation.
CHINESE LANGUAGE SUPPORT THANKS
Xplane 11 user interface is much better and useable.  Good flight physics with joystick controls etc.  Excellent multiuple monitor support and TrackIR.

I bought fsx during a steam sale while it stoked my love of aviation the programs age (32 bit ) failed to stick with me. Flying close to the ground resulted in an often times blurry un interesting mess and using add on's often resulted in VAS.
X-plane 11 right out of the box is a graphical upgrade over fsx in every way. plane models, scenery, weather scenery are breath taking at times. And all this eye candy is well optimized. I run everything maxed out AA off on a fx 8350 gtx 970 and 16 gigs of ram at 40fps.
The game is a great simulator everything is there atc, aerodynamics, actual damage to the plane if you crash it ( yep found that out the hard way)  UI dosn't get much friendlier than this. Coming off fsx I had no trouble configuring settings configuring my aircraft, weather, air ports .
There are some glaring issues however.
First and my absolute biggest pet peeve with x-plane 11. ATC and traffic around the airport. Request clearances .atc " a gate hold is in effect for a runway change please hold" 10,20,30 minutes later you are still waiting as this lone sr-71 meanders around the air port and then idles at a runway... or you do get clearances only to be stuck inline waiting for a plane to taxi onto the runway and take off.... only it never takes off just sits there waiting. Luckly this is easily fixed by downloading a bit of freeware. X-life. But it is still a bug that needs to be worked out of the game( I am pretty sure it is a bug) Also the atc with out x-life will often get stuck in an annoying loop with issuing orders to said sr-71.. constantly telling it to decend in alt. with it constantly confirming the order.... a default flight from kphl to kpit I eventually had to mute atc as it was driving me nuts.
My other gripe is the variety in aircraft. The pickings are bare bones as airliners go. The md-82 the 737 and 747. A 777 or dc-10 would have been nice. Technically there is the military version of the dc-10 and a few extra planes but over all it just feels very bare for 60bucks . I am sure the roster will be fleshed out via paid add ons...
My 3rd complaint is the air ports and locations. while air ports runways and taxi ways are all laid out correctly they are all very generic looking and major cities have no landmarks. They all still look nice but newyork looks like chicago looks like LA . It's not a deal breaker but a little more detail there would have been apperciated.
Over all I reccomend the "game " to any one who loves flight sims. Some annoyance and nit picking, aside it is a great sim and a absolute improvment over fsx in every single way. Though, if you have hunders of dollars in payware aircraft for fsx or x-plan 10 you will be dissapointed at the pickins as air craft go.

I was not impressed, game has potential as time goes on but right now the world feels empty. Airports often have no buildings and not much air traffic. The flying lesson are more detailed on FSX. If you are interested in learning more about the fundamentals of flight I would suggest FSX. They will refund you if you play less than two hours. I asked for a refund after 115 minutes of playing the game.

The First World War saw some of the, at the time, greatest atrocities and death tolls. It is hard to use this subject matter and use it delicately, harder still to create something beautiful out of it.
This game is educational (no don’t run away! trust me its brilliant!) and doesn’t pull any punches when it comes to the history and reality of this war. Trench warfare is horrifying, there is no other way to describe it.
