Short but High Quality.
I heard about this from Project Trinity and any VN they recommend is usually worth checking out. I wish there were more, honestly, but this was free and super intriguiging. Also, it's just part 1 so maybe we'll get more ~
Neat Things:
+ Neat art style. Each style was super fitting to the story (the live streaming versus Tyrone), and each story had a different way of evoking it.
+ Camera. I liked the ability to sort of look around during conversations, but not much. Gave a spoopy feel.
+ Lighthearted. 2/3 of the stories ended in a lighthearted way, true to the spoop factor.
+ Storytelling was intriguing, interesting, and surprisingly unique between all three of the stories.
+ The voice acting was fun, added a layer of spoop.
Meh Things:
+ There was some lag in the sfx/voice when you clicked too fast and the previoux sfx/voice acting would keep going.
+ "Perceptions of the Dead" the story that shares the name of the game, was intriguing but felt poorly paced and rushed. Like it was a snippet of a larger story that should just get shoved in there. Didn't feel as complete and flow as well as the other two stories.

Oh, look, some free spooky Halloweenish visual novel stories. Three of them. All tiny, albeit the "streamer vs hospital" was longer than others, I've felt. More interesting too. It's nothing that will give you nightmares. Real nice visual art style, fine music and voice acting, it's all pretty.

Perceptions of the Dead is a "western style" Visual Novel type game. I have to say In my opinion it is one of the better VN releases I have played as of late, made even better because it is free. I found the art especially enjoyable compared to what you usually get when VN games release free. Another huge plus for Perceptions of the Dead is that is has voice acting, I really cant make a judgement call on wether it was good or bad voice acting. What I can say however is that I am glad it was there to begin with, most VN games do not even offer that as a feature.
Overall I would recommend this to anyone who is a fan of Visual novels, or slower games in general and is looking for a good free to play release to hold them over. Its pretty neat.

Fun and quick little visual novels that are voice acted. You can tell that the creators enjoyed making it. If you have any interest in visual novels or something thematic for this time of year you should give it a shot!

I only played through the Jill Count scenario which is a small time streamer going to a haunted place to hopefully get more views during the spoopy season. Her dialogue and voice direction were perfect, I have to say. Her side profile did look a bit odd and make her look like a different person . There were a couple other character voices that were a bit offputting but eh it's fine.
The art itself imposes a nice unique style to the game as a whole and has some amazing effects added on in later scenarios for spoops. It's a refreshing reprieve to have something visually unlike any other. I found myself scanning each new scenario over to admire the art while the story was read to me by some good VAs.
As I said though I'm not much for VNs so not sure what to critique asides from dialogue, art and voice acting. Still, I would recommend this to anyone.

Not worth its weight in gold.
Rarely do I ever give bad reviews to games, mainly because the effort in which was placed into them needs at least a small hat-tip, but, bloody hell, this was not worth the twenty dollars I spent.
Critiques:
- The prologue misled me, which is perhaps the strongest of my irritations. I thought that this was to be a role-playing board game, where, at each map, you were given a plot scenario and you would have to fight your way through quests and competing players to win, thereby reaching the next map, and then the next, moving onto a strange story until you finally got to fight against the lion king at the final map. This was exactly how the prologue acted out for you. You played different characters, achieving different goals until the map dimmed out and you were warped to a different character. I was invested. I was interested.
- The ACTUAL game... is nothing like this. There are no new maps. It's the same map (though you can switch between seasons), with the same characters, all striving for the same goal: kill the king or cure him. You know Candy Land? How the setting, the plot, the characters never change? This is basically Candy Land.
- There is no plot. Not an ounce of interesting clan dimensions or rivalries. You can fight against your own clan if you want. Nothing makes sense. There's no substance in this game.
- The 3D models of the characters are... ah, for lack of a better word, ugly. The 2D profile pictures look marvelous, but when you zoom in on their 3D modeled faces, it's hideous.
- The AI makes no sense. Most of the time, it feels like everyone is after you. Everyone seems to be able to bypass trickeries except for you, and despite its "randomized" choices, they do their damnedest to focus at you.
- Characters are unbalanced. Some are abhorishly overpowered, with dice as far as the eye can see, whilst some only have two or three at their disposal, making combat near-impossible.
- It is so damn hard to get inside that stupid castle to cure the king with the spirit orbs. Not only is it littered with traps and guards, the king himself won't let you cure him.
Praises:
- The prologue could not have been more engaging. I'm still mad that it misled me, though.
- The 2D art style was beautiful to look at. I loved both the flat-colored images as well as the painted portraits.
- The overall world had so much potential. Animal clans fighting against each other was amazing to watch, and reminded me of Redwall.
I haven't tried the multiplayer version of the game, but I'm not wont to do so. This game is frustrating, and its story isn't captivating enough to keep you focused on your objectives. It wasn't worth the twenty dollars, and I regret giving it away.

In Armello, League of Geeks have created a wonderfully textured digital board game.  You play as an animal avatar against three others seeking the throne of a blighted King who will die in a set number of turns until you vanquish him or gain enough prestige to be awarded the throne on his death.   The King is both competitor and game master, visiting proclamations that affect gameplay each dawn (the gameboard has a day/night cycle and this also affects gameplay in various ways with certain events, cards and equipment operative only during either cycle).  The Kings "guard" (appropriately loyal dogs) and Banes, crow-like monsters, also appear on the game board to variously attack players, defend the King or carry out his insane proclamations, adding complexity to the game.
Armello's production values are quite high, especially the card artwork (the inventory/spell/peril cards are extraordinarily well-rendered and the artists are credited which is a nice touch).  Animations, sound, music and board visuals are all colorful and engaging.
It will take a few playthoughs to get a sense of the various victory pathways (hint: go for prestige victories at first, they are the easiest).  Avatars have enough distinguishing stats and traits, which, along with various jewelry choices at avatar set up make for somewhat unique builds (although those looking for deep, RPG-style customization will be disappointed).   The player must manage the gameboard's topography (with various tiles affecting movement, health and offering exploration benefits), equipment choices, perils (a symbol matching affair versus negative effect), quest system and - of course - dice-based combat.  Combat in particular is quite satisfying with tactile dice rolls including beautifully rendered dice and sound effects.  Various dice apply various offensive or defensive bonuses, explode into additional dice or count as misses.  I was surprised how much excitement the battles generate.
Armello has enough complexity to create solid replay value even in the base game (which this review pertains to).   In single play, a game can take 20-30 minutes, although you can speed up AI turns if you wish.  It's probably best to keep the game at regular speed as a beginner as it really pays to study your opponents' choices.   Multiplayer plays quite a bit longer (human players generally take longer to make their turn choices, equip inventory and study the game board, etc.); as a result, I had a few players quit my game such that by the end I was playing the AI.
Quite a few negative reviews cite the randomness of many events of the game (not sure why this surprises/enrages some people as it is a board game and such games notoriously rely on dice and card draws to advance the gameplay).  While it is true randomness arises in many aspects of Armello, I prefer to focus on my reactions to random events as a test of my adaptability.  Flexibility as a strategy as it were.  Is your current approach to victory not panning out?  Switch to another.   Is the leader offensively equipped?  Play defense or throw the King's guards at him by placing a bounty on his head.  You can be combative or stealthy, both are viable.  To be sure, the RNG monster plays no favorites, and I've won games with last minute, low probability strategies that were just as sweet when pulled off as longer, well-planned campaigns.   The good player will embrace randomness as a character on the board and remain open to varying their playstyle in response.
To sum up Armello is an outstanding game, not just an outstanding game of its type.  I do not consider myself a rabid fan of digital board/card games but this one won me over with its quality and execution.

TL;DR: Talisman on a Timer for Tots
Armello is a relatively good iteration of Talisman. It's been simplified, and has considerably more player interaction, but it boils down to nearly the same game. Players run around the board gathering stats to assault the central area of the game and eventually kill the king at the center. Like Talisman, how you go about that goal is up to you.
Armello has four paths to victory, but each game is fairly close to every other game of Armello you'll play. This is great, because it means that the powers and stats are mostly balanced. It's bad because it can feel repetitive and reductive.
While the RNG makes a huge impact on everything in the game, there are lots of ways of maximizing your percentages for positive outcomes. For example, if you start with a Fight character with low Wits, it's to your advantage to focus on physical fights and avoid wits battles. Similarly, just because you were planning on a Corruption victory, doesn't mean you shouldn't try and build up Prestige, too, just in case someone gets to the King before you do.
One of the best aspects of Armello is that the game is on a subjective timer. There are rarely going to be more than nine or 10 day/night cycles before the king dies of Rot with or without an assault by players on the board. Unlike Talisman, you will see the end of the game in about an hour or so each time you play.
If you've never played or watched the game before, definitely take time to play the tutorial and then several solo games to familiarize yourself with the cards in the three decks. Learning when to pick up each type of card and which deck can best help you towards your type of victory is really important.
Finally, it bears repeating that there are multiple paths to victory in Armello. About 75% of the time, the Prestige leader will win at the end of 9-12 cycles, but definitely try for Corruption, Spirit Stone, or straight Kill.
All in all, a fun Talisman-lite.

As a player who deeply enjoyed FSX this has been my experience so far:

This game man, it brings back so much nostalgia for me. I remember coming back from school one day and pops had a bought my brother and I an Xbox (fun fact I was scared ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ by the ambience in the main menu on the Xbox so I hurries as much as I could to start a game or have a game inside it when starting the console). The games we had were Halo CE and this game, I liked halo but this game was just so much more enjoyable for me, the simplicity but still the depth it brought forward was enough to satisfy my childish self to continue and play and grind to get all those golden cogs and eggs so I could test out all those different varieties of boomerangs and I simply had a blast.
Now when I look back I can still feel the joy I once felt purely from nostalgia, but with growing up and getting wiser and more perceptive, I also notice the games flaws. I felt it could get a bit too repetitive and some worlds were too large without really any way too get from point A to point B without running and feeling time consuming.
Gameplay wise it feels satisfying to throw the boomerangs, you can feel the weight behind the biting attack and the enemies are mildly difficult depending on your experience of these kind of games. Bosses felt original and fun to fight against (for the most part) and most levels are fun and original (except the hog riding level, that♥♥♥♥♥♥is ♥♥♥♥ing trash). The movement is good mostly but the parts where you need to walk slowly eg. Over thin ice it can feel frustrating because it is inconsistent. But the core gameplay is good for the most part. And the positives outshines the negatives.
The charming Australian caricature is funny and gives the game a sense of originality because if it didn't have the boomerang gameplay and the quirky accents it would pretty much be a rehash of every other plarform-type game that was consistently made during that time. And I think that's an strong plus.
Honestly the whole genre of platform games are old and don't really fit my taste in games anymore. I may try to pick them up to give my inner childishness some respect but I more easily get drawn to more modern games. But that doesent remove the enjoyment that I will have from these kind of games under smaller gaming sessions. So I will simply say that if you have played this game once when you were younger pick it up and play it for the nostalgic effect, and those that haven't played this game (furthermore even heard of this game) try to pick it up as I dare to say that it truly is a hidden gem of it's time when it washed released. I recommend it.

For anyone struggling to open game (error message). Open game in "Windowed Mode for windows 10[works for 10]" than once in game open up> Options > Display and click "default" than exit game and re-load. This will now work in "Play Normal" so you can play fullscreen.

This game, though non-canon in anyway, is still a must have, must play for any fan of the series. Its battle system was and is a breakaway from its previous two installments and continues, in my opinion—which I respect, hehe—to be better than some of the latest RTS, squad-based games in the market out right now.  Not to mention any names, but the current games' system is all-together turn-based (your squad then the A.I.'s squad); this one on the other hand can be setup to allow the action to flow continuously, hence CTB or continuos turn-based. Overall, I think this game is superb, always have and always will.
As far as story goes,  as mentioned earlier, the game's story has been held as non-canon to the Fallout series, but with the continous flow of Fallout titles, and huge storyline these contain, I think there is still a lot of room to include this game's story into the Fallout canon continuum. For example, making the bad ending the canon ending and making the emergent enemy public enemy number one in the next Fallout title (so many ideas, if only Bethesda didn't dismiss this game's story out completely. As mentioned earlier though: this title's a must have, for many reasons. Once you play it, you will really know why.

Have you ever played a video game so heart-pounding that you can't walk?
That is what happened to me the first time I played this breathtaking game.
With the most fluid gunplay comparable to a John Wick film, tactical play near the levels of a mil-sim, and gunshots loud enough to break your hymen twice over, this game is one of the most fluid shooters out there. After the tutorial, you can play against bots, in other games, this would be boring, but insurgency cranks it up, taking some of it's multiplayer elements of balance and throwing them out the window to put you against an unfair amount of enemies, it gives you the feel of insurgency, minus some of it's tactical points. After a few hours of coop, you might think to move over to multiplayer, where those gunshots will be inaudible while someone is shouting "Allah Akbar" before throwing a grenade. You can get around a few mutes, and you'll eventually find your place, out on the front lines rushing in with any weapon you choose, or back at the map, advising the team while clearing an area from 70 meters away. Insurgency can be the fastest game you've ever played at times, but also a much slower and thought out experience, it's weapon customisation only adds to this, maybe you want an M16 with a 4X sight, giving you a larger range while also letting you go burst fire on the enemy team, or how about a shotgun, without slugs and a laser sight, letting you charge in and hip fire a whole group of enemies, all down to that quick trigger-finger.
One thing that keeps me coming back to insurgency is it's inevitability to pump my body full of adrenaline, even just in a small moment, I'll relax around a corner, I take a moment, my heart pumping, my senses all at their peak as I listen for the footsteps around me, time slows down for just a moment before hearing 3 rounds being fired into the wall behind me, and I swiftly charge into the room, firing my sub machine gun full auto. That is what this game does! It's blood pumping action at it's finest. You remember when you first played Doom? You remember the intensity you felt? Insurgency is all that intensity turned up to 100
Put that fight-or-flight response into swing and buy yourself a copy of Insurgency.

Seven months after release, this game has serious issues that need ironing out. Most of it is polishing (smoother animations, more optimization), but the rest... the rest is a massive mess, including the game-breaking bug I am experiencing.
Currently, I am stuck in the campaign, falling through the map, eternally. I can't fast travel because I'm in the air. I can't do anything but fall. Forever. Reloading from the menu lets me restart my fall from the top. I don't even die. Just... fall... forever.
There are further issues with the game.
For example, there is an enemy base which I've been scouting out from about 700 meters away. I would LOVE to shoot into it, but is simply not possible. I can't get enemies to spawn in unless I'm around 400 meters or closer. My longest shot is 428 meters, and that was exploiting a bug:
When you scout a location with the drone, enemies spawn in. When you tag them and then recall the drone, the enemies remain spawned for three or so seconds, thus allowing me to get that 428 meter headshot in before the body depawned and the rest of the base with it- except the thirty or so civilian workers that I can see just fine. This doesn't appear to be related to draw distance settings as everything except Chromatic Abberation and Motion Blur are on and maxed out. Some areas have a different spawn radius than others.
It makes no sense to have civilians (civilians don't help anything and don't even provide a penalty if killed) rendered at 700 meters but not the enemy until half that. Why is this a sniping game if almost all of my engagements happen within 100 meters?
All your suppressors need repairing after being used enough times. This equates to about 20 rounds with any weapon (to my experience so far). This is not a feature. This is an annoyance. Maybe if it needed to be fixed, say, once a session? That wouldn't be so bad. But I end up fixing suppressors about 3-4 times if I raid a location.
I was having a frustrating time going through this game, but the eternal-falling glitch sealed it for me. I don't want to have to restart in order to progress in the game.
I feel as if this game is lacking any kind of serious support. There are plenty of bugs- clipping through the ground or walls, enemies that can sometimes see and shoot through rocks and buildings that I can't, sights being off from where the weapon actually shoots (having to aim the AKA iron sights at the shoulder level to get a headshot).
The upside to the game is that the gunplay- assault rifles, handguns- all feel very nice. When you can see enemies, it's a LOT of fun to line up a headshot, timed just right, to hit a Separatist right in the noggin' as he's sprinting for cover.
I will change my recommendation if they fix draw distance on enemies and patch the multitude of bugs. I can't play the game- literally. Unfortunate waste of $20. I would have liked to have seen this game succeed. It just needs to be fixed and polished. There is obviously a lot of time put into this game as it is. It's not a bad game when it works.
List of bugs:
- Enemies seeing through buildings, rocks, bushes.
-- Being shot by those enemies.
- Weapon sights that don't align with the direction of fire.
- Falling through terrain and getting stuck in areas that required a reload to the menu.
- Falling through the map.
- Vehicle spawning at a different fast-travel point. (Only happened once.)
- Enemies disappearing at a distance.
- Enemies disappearing at point blank range.
- Enemies detecting me and shooting me when they're facing the wrong direction.
- Headshots that don't register as headshots with the handgun. (Don't know if it's a specific handgun or not)
- Bad states on interrogations. (Grabbed an enemy to interrogate but he teleported a few meters away, thus requiring that I kill him instead because he was technically still there but I couldn't do anything BUT kill him. The prompt to take down was there still, but no interrogate, couldn't move. That messed up the mission state as I was supposed to interrogate that character.)
- Headshots with bows don't always work.
- Getting spotted by soldiers on a road who were invisible. They didn't attack. Just spotted. Lead to confusion.
Things that need polishing:
- Inventory size. It's really small. Some guns have way more on-person ammo capacity than others.
- Animations. They can be really jerky.
- Suppressors. Either buff them or remove the repair system.
- Crafting. It's complicated, which is not necessarily a bad thing, just a bit confusing.
- Optimization. I have good performance, it is just a little bit inconsistent.
- Unlocks. A lot of content is gated behind mission progression, thus requiring that I backtrack to complete certain Points of Interest once I have specific technology unlocks (like Drone hacking).

Star Wars Republic Commando is a First Person Shooter with a tactical twist, to control your squad! Not only does it deliver a solid and outstanding narrative, but it also proves that you can get a connection with characters through numbers. No pre-rendered cutscences needed!
Shooting: The game can be tough, it really can. It is in no means easy and the guns have the right amount of star-wars and unique twist. There isn't the biggest array of weapons, and i often found myself sticking with the default commando weapon(s). Oddly enough, these space weapons also have a tiny bit of a recoil. No idea how that works, i just know that i enjoy shooting them.
Controlling your squad: It's smooth, yes, but sometimes it doesn't really work because of the odd AI, your squadmates aren't always intelligent and they're often very slow. Luckily, it can be very useful to know where to put them, and once you've put them there, they'll stay there.(Unless you go down and they have to save you.). Overall, it needs a bit more depth, but it works a lot better than most games these days.
Your squad: Delta are absolutely the coolest looking clone-commandos in the galaxy! They are familiar with each other and have some rather cool and talketive interactions. People like 07(Sev) is the badass sniper who's not very talketive with a gruff voice and well, a few twists. I don't remember the other characters that much, but that's because i haven't played the game in a while. The AI however isn't that well-developed and often clunky.
Conclusion: Despite the lack of multiplayer (RIP gamespy), the weird AI and the short length of singleplayer. I encourage anyone to drop those 10 Euro's on this game. Because it really is worth it. Not only will you remember the game as something that ABSOLUTELY needs a sequel, but also one that needs to be more noticed. In short: The game is great. Seriously, if you haven't bought this game yet, i encourage you to buy it.

In theory a good idea for a game, Flesh Eaters' execution is shallow and it's full of bugs. When a large horde of zombies is attacking, I find that it's safest to pack your people together in one room. If you do this though, they'll all get stuck on the door, so you'll need to back them up and slowly move them in one-by-one. That's not good when the horde is rapidly closing on you.
When you're in the room, if that room is a small room (there's a small room with no windows or doors to the outside, for example, creating an essential chokepoint for zombies at the one entrance) then your dudes will bump against each other and push each other THROUGH the walls, leaving them outside the building entirely and easy prey for the zombies. If you manage to keep all your people inside then your chokepoint will affect the zombies the same way it affected your dudes when they tried to enter - they'll get stuck on the door, sometimes making it easier to shoot them or (more often) snagging them in a way that leaves them unable to attack you and you unable to attack them, so you'll have to leave your room to finish them off.
On top of that, there is no campaign mode, no multiplayer and there are no achievements. The characters have problems using much of what they've crafted and the engineer class seems underpowered compared to the other two. The developers say they'll be releasing the full version in three months. Judging by the slow progress of the game so far, it's going to be released in an unfinished state. It needs more than tweaks and fixes to be brought up to an acceptable standard, it needs a complete overhaul.

Flesh Eaters is a small indie zombie survival RTS. It features barricading mechanics, crafting, and zombies. Lotsa zombies. The game's story mode is not yet out. The game is fairly basic for an RTS squad based game, theres 3 classes that you can utilize, engineer(Who can make turrets and mines), medic(Who has a healing aura), and soldier(Who shoots stuff). The engineer can give himself melee weapons, but thats pointless as zombies can inflict countless debuffs on you, usually killing the inflicted within 15 seconds. The medic can't fight(I believe), making the soldier class the best offensive class. Sort of. The engineer can still make turrets, which can't be attacked and can still wipe out plenty of zombies. (I usually roll with 4 soldiers, 1 medic, and 1 engineer.)
So, in terms of gameplay, you start off in small map that may evoke wonderful memories of the original SAS: Zombie Assault flash games. Theres barricades, you fix them by using wood, which theres a box of, you use metal and wood together to craft your soldier some better armor, and eventually, some power armor. Each unit can also reecive level ups, for 5 traits(Health, speed, looting, barricading, hand combat). In early game, you should level up really quickly, and maybe even end up max rank before the special infected show up. More on that later, but there are some problems I should point out, firstly pathfinding can occansionally screw up, and when you try to correct that by pressing somewhere else, your unit continues walking on, blissfully unaware of the zombie horde about to close in on him.
Like many a zombie game, each wave progressively gets more difficult, in terms of zombie numbers and special infected popping up. Theres your regular zombie, fast zombie, fat zombie, and armored zombie. There may be more, but i've either beaten the objective mode too quickly, or died too early.
So, all together, I enjoyed this game. Its simplier than other RTS games, but thats not a problem. For a cheap price of under a dollar, i'd say you should pick it up.

The dice rolling mechanics are fun when you're at a board surrounded by people who are invested in your roll. It's fun to add your dice too the pool, convert your cards, and scrape together situational bonuses. It's not fun when the computer does it for you, and you just hit next enough times to make it happen. It doesn't feel like a representation of risk vs. reward, it just feels like RNG. It's something that's lost in translation.
The GUI isn't as responsive as I'd like. Rolling your dice involves clicking on the dice and dragging them to the center of the screen, but it doesn't feel good. The dice animate and bounce all around the screen, but sometimes the physics breaks and the dice teeter on edge and it takes way too long for the animation to finish. It's difficult to play cards from time to time because you didn't drag them quite to the center of the target area. There's a cosmetic fog that makes the board fuzzy if you pull the game's view too far out. They're minor issues, but they contributed to my not really wanting to continue.
The art-style is saccharine, and I didn't care for it much. My partner watched me play it for a few minutes, and they liked the artstyle a great deal. Just preference.
I recommend this game even though it's not something I'll keep playing because I think it's novel. I like when a board-game tries to create a gestalt narrative.

This is another case where Steam's binary review system is a little frustrating, because while my ultimate verdict is a "do not recommend," it's not because the game is completely meritless. The basic conceit here is the same kind of plate-spinning seen in games like Five Nights at Freddy's: You have a bunch of things to keep an eye on at once and have to divide your attention between them or else bad things happen of the "something pops out and screams at you" variety. You've got a basic routine (keep four different generator-powered lights going), and occasional random events throw a curveball into the process (like having to repair malfunctions, or "NOPE" directly away from the little ghost girl). One major point in this game's favor is that it's relatively fair from the standpoint of the FNaF-knockoff subgenre - at least from my experience on Curse difficulty (the lower of the two settings). The basic rules are explained reasonably well, and their fine points and exceptions don't take too long to figure out. The most egregious wrinkle may be that normally you flee to a randomly reassigned "safe point" when the lights flicker - but if this is accompanied by the ghost's appearance, you should run directly away and wait it out at the house's far end, instead. The most unfair point is that it's very, very easy for the ghost to pop up in the fraction of a second it takes to process a mouse click, leaving you blundering right into her with honestly no opportunity to do anything about it.
Unfortunately, besides averting some of the genre pitfalls, the game's not all that compelling. There's a little backstory explained piece by piece as you progress - but not very well. Who's this person messaging you on the laptop? Who brought up someone named Sophie to begin with? How did you know any of this to begin with? There are a few little deviations in the story as it arises that keep it from being COMPLETELY straightforward, but it's still fairly cliche. What finally tips this over out of recommendable range is that the game just isn't that gripping or, honestly, scary. There are only a small handful of randomized visual events to mix things up. Otherwise, you're generally just running back and forth, and occasionally dying in the exact same way with the exact same animation and scream. There's no variety. What's worse, with the game limiting itself to just one spook and just one death animation, its villain isn't even particularly scary looking. Of course it elicited jolts from me, of the "I just heard a loud sudden noise" variety, but there's absolutely nothing in here to even slightly unnerve. It doesn't do anything in the way of escalating tension or keeping you from getting too used to it. For a horror game, that's pretty deadly to the core of the game. While it may be more mechanically solid than a lot of other obvious FNaF derivatives, it won't get your pulse up.

Comparing to FSX to Xplane:
Ive been with FSX forever. Always thought xplane was a cheap knock off. Download the demo and find out how you feel about it yourself, but as for me ive noticed the following immedietely. (This is with my computer, Some people are having technical difficulties, mine runs perfectly.)
Pros of XPLANE:
-first off its new! FSX isnt, fsx is 32 bit, Xplane is 64.  We can update the scenery and textures of fsx and spend a lot of money, but off the shelf xplane has better graphics by far even with some payware addons.
-Much smoother flight control. MUCH smoother. At first it felt a little bit more "arcade" like. And i still feel this way, but its much easier to fly. I dont know which is more "realistic". Ive only got 3 hours of real flight time in a real plane, and xplane is much quicker to respond compared to fsx, id oscilate sometimes trying to land a plane in fsx, i dont have that problem in Xplane, and i didnt in real life..... so theres that, if thats worth anything. and actually that was the key selling point after playing the demo repeatedly for several hours.
-Default planes are more complex than any default FSX plane. ESPECIALLY airliners omg.... the 737 is about 60% of the pmdg 737 in FSX, which says A LOT as its a default plane.
-Runways arent always flat... and xplane accurately represents that, a small, but neat feature.
-Did i mention graphics? on my i7 2015 model gaming laptop, i was impressed
-There are actual cars on the roads! the night lighting is spectacular! Cars on the highways at night!? holy cow what a concept. This may not be new, but it is to me coming from fsx. it seriously makes the scenery come to life.
-very easy to get started. It just feels newer and modern.
CONS of Xplane:
- Do tires always smoke when you're taking off or taxiing? or is that an xplane thing?
- and airliners leave a black contrail behind them appearantly, it looks like an asteroid coming in from outer space more than a plane lol....
-Not many default planes. but a good solid basic lineup
-im seriously having to think hard here about this cons list.... navigating the menus is different and takes some getting used to...
- Not much payware out yet?... Nothing im really willing to commit to yet at least....
Ultimately the only thing i like better about FSX vs Xplane.
- Fsx is what im familiar with, and im a pmdg pilot. The fact that pmdg hasnt put anything out besides an old dc for xplane makes me wonder a bit. The pmdg models were the best thing that ever happend to fsx. The complexity and realism of the their latest 747 and 737 models are nothing that anyone anywhere yet has come close to yet... I guess what im realizing just now is that, my favorite part about FSX isnt even fsx itself hahaha.... oh man if that doesnt spell it out for you i dont know what will... Ill be playing my 737 and 747 flight simulators still (and by that i mean my pmdg planes, because they are simulators themselves, legitimately they are a running simulator within a simulator), but everything else will be xplane for sure.

Retro City Rampage (DX) is essentially a reference-packed trimmed down version of the original GTA games that manages to keep a lot of the original gameplay along with a few other bells and whistles. In it, you take on the role of “PLAYER”, a greaser caricature from the 1950s who has a lust for wanton destruction. Inevitably you are wrapped up in a plot to save the world from evil via completing random fetch quests and other minutia, even though you’re really just doing it to wreak havoc.
RCR is more of a linear game pretending to be an open world game to the point where I almost wished it was just a linear game. The world map serves almost entirely as a vector to get you from one plot point to the next and typically you will end up with an option list of “do optional quest” or “do main quest”. To be fair, this is mostly done for parody’s sake and the game doesn’t really take the whole open world concept very seriously (at one point randomly teleporting the character to save time). There are a few minigames and challenges to keep things interesting in case you decide to wander off the main plot-line and some of them can be pretty tough.
The game eventually does force you into a few very demanding action sequences as part of the main questline but with a little perseverance, and a bit of hatred for water levels, you should be able to make it through just fine. Pick this one up when you’re feeling the need to scratch that retro-gaming itch.

This was a really fun collect-a-thon 3D Platformer that a lot of people remember from their childhood PS2 days, but since I had never owned the game when I was a kid, the game reminded me of other games I loved like Spyro and Croc. Either way, it gave me a nice little dose of nostalgia while also offering solid gameplay, controls, music, and beautiful graphics that are remastered from their original PS2 version and amped up with adjustable effects synonymous with PC-originated games like water reflection and anti-aliasing. The water in this game is gorgeous. The game is also very easy to run at 60 FPS with decent video settings.
The platforming in this game feels good and sometimes varies with needing certain mechanics like using different boomerangs to activate platforms or recognizing patterns and figuring out timing. It uses the game's resources very well and tends to keep a good balance with its mechanics. When you get a new tool, the next level makes good use of it like how most games do, but it also makes plenty of use of all your other tools too. It makes nothing feel wasted or added in just for filler. Some of the bosses are counterintuitive to figure out how to beat them, but most are fine. Boss fights are more like puzzles than combat, but a lot of games from the PS2 era had similar mechanics. Each level looks really nice and has a lot of small places to explore, making it really fun to run around the world and seek collectibles and secrets. There aren't any terribly difficult parts in this game, but there is still challenge in it as well.
It's a really fun game and I definitely would recommend it, especially to gamers who are fans of PS2 era games or people who like 3D platforming and games like Spyro, Croc, and Banjo-Kazooie. If you're a hardcore gamer looking for tough as nails platforming, this game isn't for you, but someone looking for a fun little gem will find value in this.

Good God, do I love this game.
It's a part of my childhood. I probably spent the better part of one thousand hours wearing down my old PS2 disk years ago. I came back to it with the port here on Steam, and I can conclusively say that this is the best port I know to have been put on Steam, ever. The devs (the same studio from all the way back in 2002, though maybe not all the original staff) really put their hearts and souls into getting this classic to work on PCs. As near as I can tell, they even managed to convince the decade-and-a-half-old ORIGINAL GAME ENGINE to accept such modern amenities as adjustable graphics settings and, get this, re-bindable controls for keyboard. If that doesn't speak to the quality of both the game and the team behind it, then nothing does.
On to the game itself. The plot surrounds the eponymic character Ty, who is on a quest to save his family after they were imprisoned by the main antagonist, Boss Cass. The story makes somewhat little sense, but given the game's premise (anthropomorphic tiger collecting balls of light to save his family), I'll forgive it for that. Compare it to the likes of Banjo-Kazooie and you'll see that story generally came second or third to gameplay at the time this game came to be.
The game handles just like I remember from when I was young. It certainly isn't perfect; the camera can be mildly wonky and the jumping behavior is inconsistent at times, but Ty handles well and the biggest factor in the platforming is player skill, as it should be. One thing the game most certainly is NOT, is difficult. I 100%'d the game, at least as far as progress on the save is concerned (there's some extra stuff that doesn't count towards the total), in under 10 hours. But it was a blast the whole way through. I was brimming with so much nostalgia it gave me goosebumps at times.
If you liked the game when it was originally released, I can't recommend it more (at time of writing, it's even on sale!). If you're looking for a laid-back classic platformer, look no further. If you want to gallivant across a fictional Australia through worlds full of spirit filled with characters full of, well, character, then it doesn't get much better than this.
You don't get the single highest user satisfaction rating on Steam by making a bad game. Both the game itself and the quality of the port are absolutely outstanding, and the developers should be (and probably are) very proud of their work. Never before has the Internet laid eyes upon such a labor of love.

Reviewed primarily from the single player perspective.
Pros:
- Striking artwork and style. If the game cover speaks to you, there's more where that came from.
- Quests react to your decisions in small ways, making each playthrough seem more personal (priarmily if you start aggressively chasing a Rot victory).
- Solid, balanced variety among the different clan leaders.
Cons:
- Very random. Success is largely determined by how lucky you are in dice rolls, quest rewards, and card draw. Little room for tactical decision-making.
- Not all victory paths are created equal. Rot and Spirit Stone victories require lucky rolls and stone placements. Kingslayer/Renown are more player directed.
- Comeback from setbacks can be difficult. Easy to keep losing once you start losing.
- Game feels more like a vehicle for DLC then a stand alone product everyday.
Would Recommend To: Fans of games like Talisman. People entrhalled by the art style and curious to see what all the cards look like.
Would Alternatively Suggest: XCom franchise (for people into virtual board games that want something with more tactical depth), Actual board games like Mage Knight (for people who want the advenure experience). Tooth and Tail (for people who love the anthro astethic).

This was an interesting little game for sure. If you grew up in the late 90's/early 2000s there are a lot of "oh yeah, remember X" moments. But what really makes it stand out is that it captures the typically innevitable distancing of friends that occurs in the transition from high school to college. You can't pick who they hang out with, you can't be very present in their lives, and ultimately you will both grow up in directions neither of you expected. No spoilers, but there was a fun divide between what the protagonist wants to say, and what they say in a couple of key scenes, and it's a nice way to give you a little peek into their mind. I noticed a lot of people complaining about railroading, and I'd like to point out that the game is listed as story rich, but not choices matter... I think that's a good way to put it. Some situations you just don't have control over. Its realistic. Anyway, for free, it's totally worth the time to check out, IMO. =]

If I have a criticism, its the completely inadequate ATC.  It doesn't seem to follow airport operating procedures for light aircraft, and gives me some really weird routings. Stock FSX ATC and flight-planning was better, and there were some brilliant add-ons like VoxATC.  Hope to see an XP port soon!

Retro City Rampage (DX) is essentially a reference-packed trimmed down version of the original GTA games that manages to keep a lot of the original gameplay along with a few other bells and whistles. In it, you take on the role of “PLAYER”, a greaser caricature from the 1950s who has a lust for wanton destruction. Inevitably you are wrapped up in a plot to save the world from evil via completing random fetch quests and other minutia, even though you’re really just doing it to wreak havoc.
RCR is more of a linear game pretending to be an open world game to the point where I almost wished it was just a linear game. The world map serves almost entirely as a vector to get you from one plot point to the next and typically you will end up with an option list of “do optional quest” or “do main quest”. To be fair, this is mostly done for parody’s sake and the game doesn’t really take the whole open world concept very seriously (at one point randomly teleporting the character to save time). There are a few minigames and challenges to keep things interesting in case you decide to wander off the main plot-line and some of them can be pretty tough.
The game eventually does force you into a few very demanding action sequences as part of the main questline but with a little perseverance, and a bit of hatred for water levels, you should be able to make it through just fine. Pick this one up when you’re feeling the need to scratch that retro-gaming itch.

MY REVIEW:
Do I reccomend this game? Well, in it's current state... it's a no from me and I think you'll find it's a no from- now quite a numerous amount of- other players.
The game Undead Overlord pleasantly suprised me when I first played it back in 2014; upon first glance of the game I suppose it isn't difficult to mistake this for a really short, unresponsive, ugly, glitchy and really not fun to play game. I bought this game with an open mind, a mind open to the probability that this game is what could have been what I mentioned just before. I played the game and find out that the game ran smootly, apart from only a few apparent glitches and the occasional unresponsive zombie. Most of all, however, it was fun. The game looked, and still is, rough around the edges and has quite a bit of content that is not present yet (I say yet, but some things may never be added). Despite this, it was FUN.
One thing I enjoyed was commanding the shambling, blood thirsty and brain hungry zombies to attack the puny human meatsacks which attempted to run away in fear or dared to stand in the mighty Overlord's way by trying to eliminate my increasingly growing horde. There were other aspects which I enjoyed also, such as sacrificing a percentage of my horde to create a bigger badass zombie and breaking the lid (doors) of a lunch box (building) to get to the delicious food inside (the tasty human flesh) and upon entering, indulged upon a free all zombies-can-eat buffet and left with a bigger horde and a fuller stomach. In all seriousness, I liked this game.
Though however, this is ruined by the sheer lack of updates and and the fact that the developers seem to have abonded this game. This makes me concerned for the wellfare and playability of this game in future. A update hasn't been released since around Christmas, which is about over four months ago I think. If an update hasn't been released in four months, what honestly is the probability of this game being complete at all? The developers will have to pull some sort of miracle in order to complete this game, let alone repair it's reputation. The only thing I can hope for- that anyone could hope for- is that the game is due an absolutely giant update that will give players something to play for a long duration of time. Either that or the bigger stuff is only coming when the game is complete/released fully. In which case, the game would be more a demo than a game. But shouldn't a demo be free? But then again.. the don't the developers need money for development? Is this game really just a demo, but rendered a Early Access game so the developers can get money? There a few questions which can be asked about this game, but likely will not be answered.
I'm not one to decide wether the developers should be or should not be working on the development of this game, but I think that they should work on this; this game seems unique and seems to be few of a kind. If they aren't working on the game, it would be common decency for them to announce this, rather than just take up and leave without and indication in the slightest. Also, maybe even a price reduction (if they already have enough money to develop this if development is still continuing). Maybe even an apology for quiting on the game, or opposed to this an anouncement that clearly states the game is being worked on. I believe that the game probably is being worked on; community silence doesn't mean they aren't working on the game.
It kinda makes me angry how players are flaming over the fact that progress is taking too long, people need to realise developers have lives too. They are probably occupied with more important matters, or they could even be doing a really good update and are perfecting it as we speak. Still though, it is kinda likely that the game isn't being worked on.
With that said, players do still need some sign that the game is being worked on, and some new content needs to arrive eventually. Only then can I and other players properly recommend this game. The game has, or had, a lot of potential, but unfortunately potential alone is not success or a deciding factor to buy a game. I personally think that it would be worth investing time and some money else where, in another Early Access game that you know for sure is being worked on.

Details:
_The map is tiny, (9x7/8 so 68 squares, the middle 5 being the castle). Yes you encounter each other a lot with this setup.... it also means that you can't really avoid other players. Nice for mele types... casters are not so lucky.
_ Casters need 2 stats to be effective (card count and mana), mele only need attack. (every one needs health).
_The game is short, the king takes damage and gets weaker as you get stronger... feels unnecessary, almost forcing an endgame.
_There is many cards, but you tend to fall on the same ones for the same sitdown ( New card you get 3x copies of in the same game).
_ You have 2 sets of equipments: equipment and companions. The first you can just draw each turn... the second you need luck  (random dungeon explore or random quest result (you chose the quest, but the result is your stats as a % chance). I never get companions and using the "bribe" card to steal one has been fruitless so far. You have 3 slots when having 2 by endgame is already an achievement.
_ Repetitive, the variety in quest is just flavor, all quests are go to point X, chose to roll the dice for extra reward/penalty or not... so you basically pick one you can do (strong stat).
_ DLC adds a faction.... that's new quests and new heroes. So nothing really new.

This game... This game, It is beyond phenomenal, never has a game ever made me cry until I played this, I am quite a History lover and I love to see how we as a race evovled and learned from our past, this game looks back at one of the most devestating conflicts known to man, The Great War. This is no run and shooter or anything like that, it is a beautifully story driven puzzle game. The puzzles are fun and it is also fun finding the collectables. There is so much history which by my standards is pretty accurate(NOT INCLUDING THE ACTUAL GAME I MEAN THE LITTLE HISTORY NOTES YOU CAN READ ABOUT THE WAR). This game was such a breath of fresh air, I am a lover of immersive tactical first person shooters, but no game comes closer to being as immersive as this. This game perfectly captures the horrors of war and what humanity does to each other, this isn't just a shooter where you mindlessly KILL KILL KILL not thinking about the lives of whoever you just murdered. You get to experience the lives of broken souls seperated from each other in the dark times of war. We see how people become from simple farmers to a hero. This game makes you think, war is an aweful thing, just plain aweful and when I say that I mean literally it will be shoving your face with horror after horror after horror. This truly tells us that the world is no happy place, our home has been scared by its own inhabitants for centuries, she has seen death to many times to count. This game is what I call the perfect masterpiece, there is not a single flaw in this game, well worth 15$ for me to cry in the end. When you go to play this remember, your not only in for a really good puzzle game, your in for a lesson, a lesson about humanity and how we continue to mindlessly destroy each other but with this lesson comes knowlegde, that boring history class that you always hated in middle school wasn't only teaching you the history, they were giving a life lesson so then when the time comes we are ready to our worlds next leaders, and that when we look back at things like this we know that war should never be the answer because then the people must suffer, they must have their families seperated, and murderd and lost. This game doesn't look for your action-packed heartracing side of war, this goes for the heart-wrenching, terrifying side of war. I would recommend this game to anyone truly a 10/10 game...

Okay, to start I should mention that I played this game in beta before it was on Steam, so I probably have about 10-15 hours logged total. I have not yet beaten the game. I'll try to give an honest mostly non-biased review. Since I have a preference and style of games I like (as I assume everyone does), I will try to push that aside for this review.
It should be noted that this game wasn't delvoped by a team or company, it was made by one man over the course of a few years. That alone should count for something. But I digress...
To start, lets talk about the obvious. Yes it looks like crap. The graphics are pretty barren and old. It really does leave much to be desired. But if you judge a game solely on it's looks then you'll miss out on a hell of a lot of treasures! The game shouldn't be played for looks alone.. or at all. The game should be played for the story, much like any RPG.
The story is good, it's not amazing but it's not trash either. It has a unique perspective and moves at a reasonable pace. There are a few times where I personally felt the story was dragging a bit, but I think the plot unfolds well enough and the over all arch of the story suits the game.
The characters are unique and indepth. They all have their own personal back stories that helps to understand their motivation and personalities. There is enough substance to the characters that you can either relate with or against them. I have a few favorites when I play, and the nice thing about the game is that I could play with all of my favorite characters in one party. (I don't because most of my favorites are support characters... but I could!)
The system is interesting... Its out of the norm and that adds to the game play, but I personally feel it was a bit hard to understand and I struggled to pick it up quickly. It took me a while to understand how to do a lot of things in and out of combat, but I also played the majority of the game in beta before there was a tutorial... It's probably much easier to grasp now that there is a tutorial to break it down for you.
The level of difficulty in the game is pretty rough, I tend to be more of a casual gamer, and I find myself struggling a lot to finish this game. I die constantly and get frustrated when things need to be repeated because I failed at them, or when I have to back track to grind levels out to defeat a boss or quest mob. But a lot of RPGs are grindy, and this one is no exception.
So to recap:
Cons:
It is not visually appealing
The unique system can be hard to pick up and learn quickly
It's really hard and requires a lot of grinding (that's what she said?)
Some of the story elements felt drawn out or forced
Pros:
The story draws you in
It has interesting and fun characters
It doesn't have a typical battle system
You get a sense of nostalga from playing it
Overall opinion, I'd recommend this game ONLY to people who really enjoy RPGs and don't mind being ported back to the NES era of gaming. This game isn't for everyone.

A lot beneath the surface
So first and foremost, I do know the dev personally, and I played this game previously from Itch.io. If you wanna call me biased that's fine, but just wanna be open with ya on it.
I see a lot of posts here about the graphics, and to be quite frank that is the worst part. Locations look NES era FF to me a lot of the time, characters fair better, and monsters can be hit or miss, but some of the designs are pretty original and remind me of things out of Earthbound. Everyone's first impressions are going to be from the screenshots here, but personally I found a lot of enjoyment to thisgame and wouldn't judge a book by its cover alone.
The stamina system in the gameplay really encouraged me to push out further and further while grinding as I built up meter to pull off my abilities, rather than in other RPGs where I'd stay close to home and return to town to refill my HP and MP constantly. There's definitely a risk reward to this system though as you might run into something that completely wrecks you if you go too far out unprepared. That combined with a system of titles that worked similar to FFX to customize how each party member gains meter kept me fine tuning my party. Which also you get a lot of characters as you go with different skill sets so you can really customize things a great deal.
I also really enjoyed other little touches to the world. I found a lot of npc dialogue to be pretty humorous, and loved that there was both a journal and party dialogue that could help you in the right direction when you're out exploring the massive world map, or haven't played ina while and lost track of what you were doing (this is a big one for me XD) Oh! There's also a crafting system which was an unexpected but welcome surprise. Also the music is pretty snazzy, i believe that was done by someone else for the title, but I can't recall.
Anyway I'd give it a 3.5 or 4 out of 5. Visually it's a mixed bag, but the gameplay and writing are both great IMO. It gives me the feel of playing an old school rpg (which it should) but with enough changes to the game to keep things interesting and from simply being some knock off Final Fantasy or Dragon Quest.
Also wasn't sure what it'd be sold at on steam but 6 dollars is a pretty darn good rate for the amount of content you find here. So seriously, give this one a shot.
EDIT: As mentioned above I played a non steam version of this game. While I have purchased it on here, I have just barely started it in case of any technical differences.

Insurgency is, for my money at least, the best shooter currently on the market. I've put nearly 100 hours into it and my main thought is why didn't I buy this game earlier. I'd seen it on the store before and just passed on it cause it seemed like some bog standard FPS that i'd spend 20$ on play for a week and never touch again. I couldn't be more wrong. I picked it up while it was on a 3$ sale, my god was it a steal.
There are two sides, Insurgents and Security. Two different styles of games, COOP or Multiplayer. Personally I don't really play COOP much so I don't know much about it. But the one match of survival on tell I did with about five friends was incredible. Made it to wave 63 in about an hour n a half. Bloody amazing fun.
As for multiplayer you can play in three different types each with a few different modes, except for competitive. In Sustained Combat you can choose from: Strike, one team tries to destroy three weapons caches while the other team defends. Occupy, both teams try to capture and hold one point in the middle of the map. Push, where one team tries to capture a series of three objectives then destroy a weapons cache at the end. And Skirmish where both teams fight over three objectives each while simultaneously defending their and destroying their enemie's weapons cache. In tactical operations you can choose one of three modes however this one everyone only has one life except for firefight. In ambush one player is the vip and must be escorted to one of two zones and the other team has to stop him. I've honestly never played elimination before so idk what it's about. The last is firefight where there are three objectives, however you only can respawn if your team takes an objective while you're dead. The last game type, Unranked Competitive is a 5v5 version of firefight.
Now onto the guns n♥♥♥♥♥♥ Well for starters it's asymetrical balance that actually ♥♥♥♥ing works. Security can only use Security guns and the tererrists can only use tourist guns. Weapons range from the AK-74U to the MP5K to the ♥♥♥♥ing M1 Carbine. Each class has different loadouts however it stays fairly simple. MGer get MGs, riflemen get M16s or AKs, snipers get bolt actions and semi auto battle rifles, and engineers get shotguns and SMGs. Now there are a lot more roles than the ones I listed and there is overlap but that's basically it. All of the guns are useable unlike many other games. I've seen people go ham with the MP40 as much as I've seen amazing killstreaks with the UMP-45. You can choose from ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s of different attachments, optics and ammunition types. You can also choose from 4 different grenades, C4/IED or RPG/AT4. You can also take light, heavy or no armor at all. Most everything will be a one burst kill so it pays to be accurate.
Now for the maps. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ There are some absolutely amazing maps: Ministry, Embassy, Verticality, Panj, Kandagal, Siege, Tell, Station. The list goes on and on. Maps range from complete urban combat like Ministry to entire rural like Panj and many have a mix of both. Maps are also asymmetrical. Certain maps Insurgents get to this objecive faster or this map Security gets there four seconds faster. Still all of the maps are very well designed and I haven't found one that I absolutely dislike, even Buhriz which this community for some reason loves.
Random♥♥♥♥♥♥about the game. Currently the game is run on Source so it's a bit dated but works very well for potatos. Next year the Devs are planning on introducing Insurgency Sandstorm which will be on Unreal 4. The community is rather small which is the biggest problem. It's not so bad that you can't find a match but if you have a group of say 6 people and are looking to play a specfic mode with a populated server it may be a challenge. The community quality is about as good as you'd expect. I've met some really nice people, but honestly, it's 10$ there's lots of idiots around and lots of people who really don't have much FPS skill. There are also two announcers one for each side. The Insurgent one is okay, a bit bog standard. But the Security one, oh man. He's hilarious. Star Wars.  We all know it, we all love it.  A franchise that not only shaped many a childhood, but had a lasting impact on the culture of America as a whole.  Many games have come out set in the Star Wars universe, but Republic Commando is special.  It doesn't have the mass marketing of Battlefront or the force-fueld power fantasy of the Force Unleashed.  Yet to a small and very dedicated group of fans, this game holds a special place in our hearts.
The game sees you taking on the role of a Clone Commando.  You are part of an elite unit within the Grand Army of the Republic.  While the rest of the army is a mighty sword that strikes at the republic's word, you and your small squad are a precise scalple.  You handle missions that any other soldier couldn't, from assainations to VIP rescue, and always from deep within enemy held territory.
Your squadmates fight with you, assiting you with various tasks and watching your back while you strike down the enemies of the Galactic Republic.  Your skills as a soldier and a squad commander can mean the difference between success and failure.  When the stakes are the galaxy it's self, failure is not an option.
While unfortunarely fairly short, it makes up for it with excellent game play.  The controls are tight, everything flows smoothly, and you'll have to use some tactics to get past harder areas of the game.  Do you order your team to set up explosives on an important objective, or focus on clearing the area first?  Do you focus fire on the more powerful enemies, or try to pick off their much more numerous support?  How are you going to cross this bridge with a strong enemy presence waiting just on the other side?  All decisions you'll have to make.
With no known plans for a sequal, the story of Republic Commando may never be finished.  What was given to us though is a solid, well made game about one of the biggest conficts in the history of a universe we love.  I can not recomend it highly enough.  It is certainly worth your time and your money.

I remember as a kid how much I loved playing this game. TY was a huge part of my childhood and I remember stumbling across this game in one of my local game stores. I must have been around 9 years old when I first played it back in the day and I have so many fond childhood memories of this classic childhood gem. When I found out sometime last year that the developers of the series wanted to remaster and revamp the game up to today`s modern day and age technology, I couldn`t have been more thrilled and excited to see one of my favourite childhood games comeback to life. I only just got a brand new PC a few weeks ago and I couldn`t wait to buy it on Steam and sit down with this gem to take a nice stroll down memory lane.
The game feels like exactly how I remember it. The developers have done a smashing job on making this an amazing port of a classic. The visuals in the game look beautiful, the soundtracks to the levels are still the good old same fun rocking tunes that I love and remember. There`s been quite a few improvments though that I have noticed which make this port even more of a perfect hit such as the loading times which have been dramatically improved over the original game. Taken no more than 2 - 3 seconds max to load up a single level or your saved game file which is fantastic. I love how they have enhanced and revamped everything in the game and the developers have certainly put alot of hard work and effort into making this a solid good tremendous port that is well worth the valueble purchase of your wallet.
TY is a beautiful gorgeous 3D platformer that is well worth investing your money in if your a huge fan of many other great platformers out there that were great back in the day from the likes of Ratchet and Clank , Jak and Daxter , Sly Cooper then you will most certanily love this. If you`ve already played the original back in the day in your childhood then by all means this is without a doubt worth another round of replaying through. If your a newcomer to the series but are a fan of platfomers then TY is a game definitely worth giving a shot and I highly recommend it to all those platformer fans out there who have yet to discover the series as well as newcomers out there who are willing to give it a try.
For those who are new to the games TY is more of a open ended 3D platformer game that is very easy to pick up and enjoy though the game is quite linear as well. The storyline of the game is pretty much simple, you guide TY through a number of levels collecting a variety of different collectables on your travels such as opals , thunder eggs and bilbies that help you progress through the game. The main plot of the game for background purposes is to retrieve back all the talismans from the evil boss Cass who plans to use them for his own uses to rule the world.
Features in the game as a small breakdown
- Open ended charming 3D platformer with a fun cast of characters to meet
- A huge variety of boomerangs that help aid you in your quest
- Run . jump , swing and glide through 17 amazing levels full of great platforming and challenge
- Offers a nice variety of mini games
- Beautiful and updated enhanced graphics
The performance of the game is very good. It runs pretty much smooth with very little hiccups. The design of the levels are stunning and have been reworked , revamped and polished very well to golden standards. It`s amazing to see that even 15 years on after it`s release that TY still has the power of showing how good and strong the 3D platformer genre is. This is a worthy port and a prime example of a how a great port of a classic should be done. It`s been handled with great love and care by the developers and I couldn`t be more greatful and thankful to them for making this happen. It`s such a warm feeling inside and feels good to have this classic childhood franchise back in my life again. Everytihng in the original is on par with what they have done with the port.
What I will also say is as well is that TY is one of those platformers out there that is more forgiving than other hardcore platformers such as Crash Bandicoot. You will find that many parts of the game can be forgiving at times making this ease of accessible to newcomers out there who may not be familiar with the core of the game`s mechanics. Just as an example  to show how forgiving the mechanics are to those who are new and unaware the checkpoint system within the levels of the game are quite frequent and there`s quite alot them placed through out the levels which is nice since it can benefit those who may struggle in later parts of the game whereas compared to the hardcore platformer types out there such as Crash Bandicoot, you`ll find checkpoints are place very far out in between. Also the gamepad controls for the game are very easy to pick up and learn and there is no need to hassle around with controller configuration as the game has full integration support of controller gamepad`s which means all the controls are all automatically set up for you and ready to use when you boot the game up.
My conclusion summary and my final thoughts on the game
A beautiful and very well crafted port that I couldn`t recommend more. If your a fan of the old school 3D type platformers then TY is a another one of those childhood revival classics that you will love and if you have yet to dip your feet into this series then by all means give it a try if you have some cash floating around because it is a blast to play and I would recommend this to any newcomer who is just looking for a relaxing, casual and fun game to pick up. On a final note I want to say a massive thank you to Krome Studio`s for brinigng back one of my all time favourite nostalgia classics of all time. So many great childhood memories with this game and it feels so great to take a nice trip down memory lane to relive this classic. Absolutely stunning and amazing game that deserves another chance at getting rebooted in the near future. A great game with great value at a great affordable price.

Armello is a digital board game with bright and colorfull graphic and relaxing atmosphere.
You, as one of four players, lead one of animal heroes/characters in race to conquer the throne of Armello.
Players can fight among themselves, or put traps and cast spells on eachother, themselves or environment.
Board id drawn nicely and consists of central castle, with the king, and randomized types of tiles around central castle.
Four players have various options for approaching the task of taking the throne. They can figure out plans and quests of other players and put traps in places to slow the progress of adversaries in race for the throne, or maybe do heroic deeds, clear dungeons and gather prestige and resourcess, or prepare themselves and at the right time go right for the kings head...
Gameplay is turn based and involves moving your character to various tiles (with various occupants, effects and whatnot), fighting other heroes/players or banes and kings guards. Every player gets quests wich may grant good equipement or companions to your hero. There is a card game element also involved. Players get cards that can be played for a cost (be it mana or gold or something else) and have various effects, magics, equipement. Cards can be played even douring oponents turns so sometimes quick thinking is needed.
Battles are very imaginatively made with rolling dice as the main part wich can be effected by player sacraficing cards from hand or equiping equipment, casting spells prior to battle.
There is a lot of randomness involved, so be warned if you dont like very high degree of dependancy on pure luck.
But games are very fun and very tense either way. There is a lot of room for strategy and planning so you can get ahead of the other players.
And you can always try new game again. A typical game lasts between 40 minutes and an hour and a half.
I played prologues and 7 games and currently have 7.6 hours on record, so you can judge well in advance how much time a game will take. There is multiplayer as well but i havent tried it yet.
As far as tehnicalities are concerned, the game runs smoothly on my sub-average computer.
If you like board games, relaxing but challengeing strategies, fun replayable hour long games or cute animal heroes and dont mind random number generators, buy it.

Armello is a multiplayer, turn-based, board-game experience that has been translated to a digital medium. In essence, each player is attempting to solve the problem of a sick king. He's been infected with "rot," and becomes weaker every turn until he dies. You can win in three different ways:
1. You can accumulate "prestige" by completing quests. If you have the highest prestige upon the king's death, you take his place.
2. You can slay the king, simply by being strong in combat. Additionally, if you have accumulated rot yourself, this can aid you in the battle.
3. You can accumulate four spirit stones, and use these to cure the king of his malady.
Most of the game consists of traversing along a tile-based map attempting to reach your "quests," which appear randomly across the map. In the meantime, you can equip items (most of which aid you in combat), cast spells, or use "trickery" cards that seem to represent political schemes.
The sheer randomness of the game and some troubling design decisions led me to almost never enjoy myself while playing this game with my friends. First of all, some of the cards are tremendously powerful and can sway the game  substantially.
Within the game, there are settlements that a player can capture to increase the amount of gold you receive per turn. Typically, there is no drawback to having as many settlements as possible and it is a good policy to capture as many as you can as you traverse the map. However, one card in the game causes a player to lose "prestige" equal to the number of settlements they currently possess. I once lost four prestige (a tremendous amount) being on the receiving end of this card.
Another card, a pact, allows two players to each gain one prestige per turn as long as both of the players live. Perhaps this is meant to put a target on these characters, but this card has never entered play without tremendously altering the course of the game. Typically, this card puts the two characters in the pact 4-5 prestige above every other player.
In most games, due to random events and cards, I am unable to even complete two of the quests assigned to my character. Between deaths, bane spawns (rot dragons that emerge from dungeons), and perils (challenges that players must complete when landing on certain tiles), I can't even get across the map. This emotion, feeling a lack of both competency and agency, sours every experience I have with the game.
This is not even getting into how targeting is unclear, how one character can complete one of the extremely difficult perils in the king's courtyard and "clear the way" for another player to waltz into the final battle with the king, how spirit stones are sometimes far too easy to acquire with random spawns, or how the player needs to commit suicide on banes (rot dragons) to stand a chance of achieving a rot score comparable to the king's.
The game is charming, with a great visual style, production values, and no multiplayer connection issues. However, this is where my praise for the game ends.

There are some genuinely cool mechanics in this game, but too much of the game relies on random factors. It's not that Armello is a bad game - it's just not my type. I want to win because I was the most clever player, not because I won a gamble. and most of the wins I've achieved were ones I didn't deserve, but got lucky with random number generator. (No, really. The game that had me finally write a review was a round where I lost pretty much every random possibility, and still managed to win because I had a slightly higher reputation than everyone else... and that's because the king's card distributed the former prestige leader's points to everyone else.
Here's an example of a bad random thing: you can get stuck with a follower that gives you one "bonus" move to a free adjacent space at the start of your turn. Except that move is utterly random. Since you get 3 move points, that means the 1st point  will at least half the time be spent just undoing the damage from that card. Except that random move could have had other negative side effects. Something like this would be a good attack, but it persists and sticks around and basically meant that for the rest of that match, I was running in circles. Not fun.
Not a bad game but it takes a VERY long time for everyone to finish their turns. To play this game(and enjoy it), you have to be extremely patient.
