Received as part of the Humble Monthly Bundle. I'd been curious about this game for a long time, but avoided it because I had been warned of the RNG aspects and how it was supposedly only really fun playing with other people.
I'm not sure about multiplayer but I can definitely say the RNG just sucks the joy right out of this game. When you have to choose to try for the reward on a quest with a 70% chance to win, but still lose, it just feels Really Bad. It's not even unfair or anything, or too difficult; the game is just full of Feel Bad mechanics. Everything from killing an enemy too close to their spawn only to immediately be killed afterward to being struck by lightning from across the map, killing you after you barely manage to beat those two Banes blocking your Quest. It's just Not Fun.

This game is best played privately with friends. Matchmaking is a mess, and the dlc characters are absolutely stronger than the base ones. But, if anybody in the match has the dlc, everyone else can use them. There are base characters that can easily face or defeat the purchasable ones (River can automatically win if she's in the palace and the king has a single health, etc.), but the overall power difference between the groups is clear. In a way, it's become a game where you greatly hinder your experience if you DON'T own the extra characters, and while that sucks, it also means you're almost guaranteed to benefit from the dlc if you enjoy the base. If played under the right circumstances, it's a fantastic game. Unfortunately it's just not one that will be fun at every single encounter.
My suggestion is to find a way to try the game on a friend's account or something similar. If you really like it, buy it and play with your friends -- and if you can, enhance the experience with the dlc characters, since everyone in a private match is allowed to use them so long as a single player owns them.

So after having been an X-plane fan since 2007 when I bought 8.0, I can safely offer my 10 year view of this series. First off, the flight realism is the most accurate it has ever been in X-plane. These are not Xbox-ready military simulators with overdone graphics but more of a traditional flight simulation. If you were expecting Ace Combat, go buy Ace Combat. Though combat can be done on here, it is not too terribly fun. I will now offer my pros and cons:
PRO
>More realistic flight physics
>Easier startup interface
>Much improved ATC interface
>Maps are now accurate to flight maps
>Local graphics so accurate I can tell where I actually am in relation to real airports I've flown to, from, or out of when I was flying. If not, the custom scenery from their site is still backwards compatable.
CON
>No backwards compatability with aircraft (Pain in the rear to update too due to new GPS system)
>No emergency options with ATC (My right engine fell off, can I have vectors? No? ♥♥♥♥♥...)
>Stock sounds don't change volume with throttle and suck in their current state.
>Must wait for updates to get the most out of this (remeber when games came out "complete"?)
>Stock aircraft are bland and as of right now there isn't many aircraft on the site yet for V.11.
Overall, I'm glad I bought it. I've been a fan of the series for 10 years now so my view is pretty biased.

As a Star Wars nerd, clone troopers stories always appeal to me, but I feel that the game really shines in its mechanics. For starters, it hearkens back to older style shooters (like Doom), but maintains a freedom of movement like more modern shooters (specifically it reminds me of the Metroid Prime series in this way). The "One Gun" mechanic makes changing your shooting strategy easy and the shooting in itself is very gratifying. Most important to me though, you play as a member of a team. On the higher difficulty levels, you really can't be Rambo or Master Chief, and I like that it forces you to use your squad effectively. It's nice to play as a lowly grunt every once in awhile.

Ok. This is a recommendation from me, but there are some things to get out of the way first off: for some people this game runs really badly or has terrible stuttering. It doesn't for me, but that's definitely part of why this game has a bunch of bad reviews on Steam. And I get it! A game that you cannot play is not a good game, and it doesn't even seem to matter what kind of computer setup you have, either. Very strange, and unfortunate.
The other reason people give this a bad review is that this game is made by idiots who got in over their heads. More on that later.
If you've played the previous SNIPER GHOST WARRIOR games, throw all that out of the window. This game is essentially unrelated, both in story (that's a little joke there, ha ha) and in gameplay. The previous two games were essentially linear "stealth" games where you simply did whatever the voice on the headset told you to do or got shot to death by a million Russians. The redeeming part of SGW2 was that it had an interesting multiplayer mode, which even now has some population on the servers, and the Siberian DLC which added some neat freeform levels with multiple approaches. It's pretty clear that the good reception of this DLC is what inspired SGW3, because this game is an Open World Experience! Whoah! While the actual missions benefit greatly from this -- you can come into each base from different angles, and there's a bunch of gadgets to play with and towers to snipe from -- the world in-between is pretty empty and pointless. You can find crafting materials, which you will never use, antique guns which you cannot fire, the occasional actual modern rifle or shotgun to add to your arsenal, goofy camo prints for your gun... and religious art, which you steal from the victims of war crimes. Yes. Yes.
The developers listed Far Cry 2 as their inspiration for this game, by the way.
Anyway, the open world's pretty pointless, but when you're actually doing a mission and sneaking around, the stealth works well. I recommend you play on the hardest difficulty; the lack of a minimap makes your gadgets and detection equipment incredibly useful, rather than pointless. Hiding in a dumpster from soldiers, setting up alarms to defend your sniping nest, running away to find a safe place to deploy your drone and check the layout of the land -- these are all intense and pretty cool, and give the game a feeling that goes away when you play on Normal Difficulty and it's just a generic FPS where you can't take bullets. Play it like a full-on stealth game and a lot of things make sense. The enemy AI isn't brilliant because if it were, stealth would be impossible. You can buy tagging bullets because they let you detect people around corners. Luring bullets to draw someone out from cover and blow them away from your tower hideout. It's very clear that all of their effort went into this stuff and none went into anything else. The plot is asinine, Jon North is reprehensible, and the first act of missions feels somewhat unfinished compared to later ones. If you play it like a stealth game, and you give it a chance, I bet you'll like it. Or not, whichever. I like it, anyway.
Also, I used to write short jokey reviews all the time. If I did one for this, it would be:
This is the Metal Gear Solid 5 of shoddy Eastern European games about sniping people.

First time writing a review on Steam, shows how good this game is.
I vote this as the most underrated FPS game...ever
400+ hours and counting, and I have a busy personal and professional life.  TLDR: yes, I find time to play this game outside of a hectic life.
NWI made a winning formula.  It is somewhat disappointing that the game is so underrated.  If you like tactical FPS shooters like Counterstrike, I feel like this is a much better game.  It's just CS is going to have a larger community, it is CS after all.
There are three popular gaming modes: Push, Skirmish, and Co-op
Push is similar to Battlefield concept where your team needs to secure objectives but one at a time.  Push focuses on taking control of a territory while the opposing team defends.
Skirmish is actually my favorite mode.  There are defined objectives all around the map at the same time and it's up to your team to control each.  Each team has an ammo cache that, if destroyed, prevents the other team from gaining more reinforcements.
Co-op is where you team with other folks to take down AI-driven bots.
What makes this game shine:
1.  Kills are more gratifying than in CS or Battlefield or COD
2.  This is a realism tactical FPS.  Decisions count.
3.  More chess-like in strategy than in CS
4.  Communication is essential
5.  Challenging game where even after 400+ hours I learn new tactics
6.  No kill feed (some servers have kill feed) gives the game a tense atmosphere throughout
7.  Active mod community
8.  Lot of veterans
Cons
1.  Dated graphics (Source engine) but NWI really built upon it very well
2.  Pub servers generally have folks not playing the objective at the detriment of the team
Get the game though realize that NWI is releasing a more recent version of Insurgency (Insurgency: Sandstorm)

First and foremost, YES, there are servers running Sven Co-op, and NO, not all of them require a password. In fact, there are much fewer ones that do than there are ones that don't. With that out of the way, Sven Co-op is a multiplayer mod for Half-Life, the much beloved 1998 first person shooter. However, it also comes with several custom maps out of the box, or fresh off the steampipe, as it were. Additionally, servers can have their own custom maps, and mods, which usually don't take long to download, and once you've downloaded them the first time, you won't have to download them again unless you factory reset the game. An example of these mods is a pointshop I found on a server, where on that server, you could type commands in the chat to exchange points for ammunition and custom weapons, such as the ones added by the other mod on the server, which adds World War II weapons. And of course, the maps. Probably one of the more famous examples of custom maps in Sven Co-op is a map that was made somewhere in Asia, where the players work in a pizza shop, and a bunch of shenanigans happen, during which the players attempt to get the ingredients to make a pizza, and eventually the map ends with them defending the shop from aliens. This map was actually featured in a stream by Vinesauce. Basically, if you like Half-Life, and you like random bullcrap, you should give Sven Co-op a try.

This aint no Virtue's Last Reward, that's for damn sure. This is a game about two stereotypical young people who behave like clumsily-designed chatbots, all wrapped up, Gone Home style, in a nostalgia blanket to draw in people like me who recognize the aesthetic of older operating systems and AoL Instant Messenger.
There's a lot I could say that you'll see in every other negative review. Emily is a horribly shallow and uninteresting character, no real consequences, etc. I'll move to more original impressions.
No joke: At the date I'm posting this review, I played this game yesterday, fully sober, amped on caffeine, ready to engage in some riveting interactive fiction, and I don't remember how it ended. I think there maybe wasn't an ending. The game forced me to say goodbye, I think, but it wasn't like "goodbye forever".
The whole gimmick of seeing what your character really wants to say only for them to delete it and type something else is...okay I guess. It got used well enough without it feeling trite. Sadly that's about as far as I can take the positives.
Emily is Away has this really irritating, infantilizing way of taking notes on your actions (like with Telltale games), saying "You chose to go to the party." and such. This completely smashes the illusion that you're actually on your 2001 Windows XP profile AIMing it up with a friend to create a new illusion that you are going to get a different outcome because of your choices. You won't.
There's supposedly two endings, but I was too annoyed after playing it once to try and get the other. I was bored by chapter 2 because I predicted immediately what this game was going for: you and this character drift apart in one way or another from your choices. I just didn't expect it to be so ♥♥♥♥ing agonizingly boring from start to finish.
This game could have been so good if there were actual choices and good writing. People complain that she's a volatile, manipulative, indecisive teenage girl, but that's not the problem. You can make a character like that and give them really engaging positive aspects that seduce the player into liking her. Imagine how amazing that would be. Personally, I think volatile, indecisive teenage girls deserve better than Emily as representation.

Only 50 minutes in. This might seem premature for a reivew, but after a short flight in Seattle I'm sold.
I've flown most flight sims since the mid eighties and boy have they come a long way.
This is the first sim I have flown where you feel like you are flying through air, rather than a vacuum. In addition, the hazing effects are superb. Very realistic and once again add to the feeling of flying in air.
I have a pretty beefy system, which sims like Prepar3d normally brings to its knees. But here, at 4k resoution with everything except AA maxed out, it runs liquid smooth - something that's simply impossible in Prepar. The liquid smoothness and density of the terrain really add to the illusion of being there.
Even with default scenery and the default aircraft this sim looks superb. I can't wait to tinker with Ortho4XP scenery, nor can I wait to see what the third party publishers give us.
Prepar and FSX have had a good run, but finally, they have been surppased in every way. After I finish this review, I will be uninstalling Prepar3d as it is not even in the same ball park with regard to flight fidelity, looks and performance. Farewell Prepar and hello X-Plane! :D
EDIT: Just tried the built in VR - OMG!!!!!!! Unlike FlyInside, it is liquid smooth for me and that's with an nVidia 980ti. (Though I am a Vive user - I have heard that Oculus peeps currently have some issues)
The VR implementation allows you to control everything with just the wands. No external controls required! Rather bizzarely, it feels totally natural! In addition it provides functionality to allow one to change seats in the aircraft, select many external views, run replays and even walk around the entire environment! Want to go hiking? no problem.
I can't beleieve it's beta functionality. It completely blows away much of the competition.

Absolutely awesome piece of software, but a few notes of caution. This is not really a game, but a world-wide highly detailed flight model. If you are brand-new to flight sims, this product is extreamly daunting, and quite (no, VERY) complex to get your head around. Yes, if you just want to apply full power and get airbourne you can, but then you are missing out on 90% of the sim's potential. Learning how to fly properly, start planes, programme your flights plans from cold and dark and navigate your way to far away places and actually find the runway to land is most of the fun... but do not under estimate how much learning that will take!
There is a highly active 3rd party developer community who have developed some truely remarkable scenary, mods, planes and sounds much of which is free, or moderatly priced. Master this simulator and you will not just loose hours, days or weeks of your life in the virtual world - you will loose decades!
Highly recommend investing in a decent flight Yoke/Rudder peddels and get yourself airborne
Note: The software is regulary patched and updated and does require a substantial beefy PC to get the most out of it. We're talking here top spec gaming rigs to have all the bells and whistles on but boy oh boy, is it worth it.
Update: 16-Apr. I've now been flying for quite a few hours and been tinkering with the settings to get the most out of it. My PC Maxiumus IX moterboard, I7-7700k 4.2 Ghtz, overclocked to 5.0 Ghtz with a Asus Strix 1080Ti Gfx. I pretty much have everything clicked up to the Max (except reflections I don't like the effect) and I get between 25-45 frames per second (most 35+) depending on the complexity of the Scene. (New York in foggy conditions at 25fps is still very playable). Now I appriciate that is a fairly beefly PC, but with tinkering you'll still be able to get very good results on a lower spec machine.
I'm blown away by how good the gfx are out of the box, especially at dusk/dawn, but some of the textures do look a little week especially at low level flying, however I'm now just beginning to look into the community work, purchasing some extra custom scenery and it's fanstastic. Some free, some is payware... Ortho4XP looks an interesting tool that allows you to use realy google map pictures of the landscape and import them in to the game. (Free!)
I also flew from Bristol International, along the M4 and north on the A419 to locate my house yesterday - Highly amusing!

Alien Swarm : Considered as one of the best 50 f2p games for pc [Rock, Paper, Shotgun (2015)]. A top-down shooter game created by Valve which was originally a remake of a mod for Unreal Tournament 2004. This game puts you in a space suit of a marine who is tasked to find any survivors on a colonized planet after it has been taken over by swarms of all kinds of aliens. Along with 3 other people journey through the campaign and try to stop the infestation from spreading. This co-op shooter game is a perfect addition to your game collection if you are trying to find something casual and fun to spend some time especially with friends. 4 classes and over 40 different pieces of equipment will definitely keep you busy. You have to keep in mind that a major drawback of this game was that the only content that Valve provided was only one 7-mission campaign. On the other hand, the prestige system along with a quite number of achievements and a difficulty slider will bring you back to this game till you master it. If you are a sci-fi fan, you must give this game a shot right now. You won't be disappointed...

AI: I dislike how the Zombies act like foolhardy lemmings and just all charge a nearby enemy without me saying so, it's a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to try and keep them from rushing out of cover and being mowed down accordingly, it's also a pain to get a large group through a door in a timely manner.

[Fixed up & Cleaned 6/29/2017]
Upon fixing many old reviews, anything previosu reviews of this game can be discarded entirely.
The game seemed like a Cash Grab, requiring a certain amount of $$$ Raised in development to unlock specific features, which, should have been in a game like this by default (Discounting multiplayer, as that can be complicated, and must be supported).
Currently, the game is, still buggy in some regards, unpolished, and dull. It's like a cheaply done zombie game, the game has potential - but was executed very poorly. Survival is simply a try to grab enough ammunition to even survive against a bunch of zombies, hoping none of your units get infected, or that you dont run out of ammunition.
All in all, this game is not worth it, It forces playstyles, lacks depth and gameplay, and is simply - a small way to grab cash. Missing obvious features, still buggy, and not fun to play.
- - - - - - - - -
6/18/2016 Update : The games a bit still in my opinion, greatly unpolished. Like many Strategy games, while moving and clicking a target, that unit would; stop and fire. This is not implimented into Flesh Eaters, which makes you 99% of the time, lose people due to the fact the game forces you to run doctor to remove viruses. Campaign, yet i have not finished - Is a bit weird working; The concept of searching/command for getting supplies is good; though its a bit near hard-as-all-hell due to the fact you can get an impossible to kill amount of zombies. (1-30 horde vs no-ammo team) forcing you to leave and waste one day. While that concept is good, makes sense; its the fact that ammunition is not easily accessible; and if is, will take one day away from trying to escape from 20. Ive noticed you can randomly get more days for somesuch reason. Along with this; going back to ammunition, you will never get enough munitions to take down a mass horde, as everything is limited; there are supplies but theres only so much of it in one area, the only problem (as this is a good addition to the games type of playstyle) - is that guns dont do what they should to zombies.
All in all - the game is NOT really worth (In my eyes) 2$, but 1$. Coming from a small group/team of people - it makes sense as to why it costs 2$ as a bit of extra money. Though with the early-on near the start of Flesh Eaters, a mass amount of money was required just to simply add the basic of basics within a game like this (Features, though some games dont have them I would see them in a zombie game of this category requiring them to be more successful). TY the Tasmanian Tiger is one of those games that starts slow and grows on you. I never played it back in its original heyday with the other mascot games, but it does compare favorably to games such as Spyro the Dragon, Sly Cooper, and Jak and Daxter. There are nine environments, with one hub world and one boss world, with plenty of stuff to do that allows for exploration and decent combat and puzzle solving.
The only 2 problems I had that were of any substance were
1) TY literally only saying 1 liner catch phrases, with an occasional dumb question to progress the dialogue (seriously, every other character had some personality, while TY would be better off as Gordon Freeman), and
2) seemingly random patches in the environment that you aren't supposed to enter, but can anyways. Going up on that snowy mountain? Hope you don't hit a patch of rock that isn't covered in snow, because you're about to go for a slip n slide ride!
Otherwise, there was some minor stuff that is just pedantic, so I won't go over them. There is plenty of stuff to collect. You don't get punished a multitude of times for the same mistake (e.g. if you jump into a flamethrower, you take damage once and then either get knocked back to your starting position or keep going, with a short immunity, instead of getting knocked off a cliff and having to run all the way back). Most NPCs are interesting, the game doesn't unnecessarily drag on, and the boomerangs and their many varieties are integrated well enough that it is worth using most of the upgrades for a variety of situations.
Overall, it's a solid mascot/3D action platformer from the PS2 era, a rarity on the steam platform. It doesn't have much to set it apart from other mascot games, other than an Australian theme, but there are very few if any major drawbacks. If you like Spyro, Sly Cooper, Crash, Jak and Daxter, etc etc this is a solid nostalgia trip but won't be anything terribly new. If you haven't, it's a solid entry that showcases what these types of games are about. I would give it a 7/10, great for on sale to try, or even good outside of a sale to scratch that mascot game itch.

I've watched and played the game, and my view comes from an avid board gamer (especially a fan of adventure games).
The mechanics are pretty solid and the production is great. But in the end, it's just a modernized, suped up Talisman: very random, and surprisngly cutthroat. There is some adventure here, but it might be better to think of this as an arena battle game with quests thrown in.
You won't really spend much time questing, in part because the quests have randomized locations that you won't know until accepting the quest, in part because moving across the board can be very slow, and in part because there ends up being obstacles of one variety or another EVERYWHERE. You also cannot abandon the quest, and you cannot start another one.
There are several paths to victory, but most of them rely on a lot of RNG, especially the spirit stones, where you are entirely at the mercy of RNG. Spirit stones may spawn around the board (only a few per game, and other players can snatch them up), you might get a quest that can reward one, and they can be rewarded in dungeons. But you have no way to influence any of these sources.
The economy also has issues. You recieve gold every round from settlements you've claimed. Which means going first in turn order REALLY puts you at a disadvantage, as players and enemies can take back your settlements after you've had your turn, but before the next round (you only receive income at the start of the Day turn). Quests do not reward gold, dungeons have random rewards (or no reward), and collecting bounties on other players requires a strong combat character, unless you find a weakened opponent to pick off. Being gold starved greatly limits the cards you can play.
I also don't like how it handles risk-reward for the most part. There are times where you might be risking a lot (such as random perils placed all over the board), but you stand to gain nothing, you're only avoiding something bad. Exploring dungeons is totally random and can give you great rewards, very minor rewards, or just spawn an enemy. You also receive no reward for defeating guards (who will hunt you down if you have a bounty), and receive little reward for defeating Banes. Quests actually do it right. You can play it safe and take a small reward, or take a risk for greater reward.
The most annoying part about the game is the PvP aspect. It's not just that the clans are at war, you battle your own clanmates too. And playing negative cards on other players is VERY easy, and perils will quickly litter the board. Players aren't just encouraged to attack one another, they're rewarded for doing so with bounties.
The game seems to be aimed much more at the competitive video gamer audience, or old school ameritrash gamers. It's very in-your-face, lots of PvP, take-that card play, and lots of randomness. This isn't much of a strategy game, and has a lot less adventure than I was hoping for.

Based of the free-to-play weekend, I only played for a few hours, on single player. Personnally, I find that to be enough time to form a rudimentary opinion, but just FYI.
The devs seem really greedy, this game has been out for lord knows how long now and it hasn't gone on sale for anything lower than 40%, which is the reason it's been sitting on my wishlist in quite a high spot but I haven't bought it yet. It may be up to you to decide how you want to price your games, but it doesn't exist in a vacuum and the way the market functions reflect poorly on your decisions. But who knows, if I was in your shoes maybe I would have done the same, but then I would have expected a game worth the price and if anything, testing the game only lowered my desire to own it.
The tutorial was, strangely, both the best and the worst part of the game. The best because it had some really cool event chains to read through, especially the rat's part. Some really clever stuff there, but it was the worst because it was one of those insufferable hand holding ones and unfortunately the story/lore was all varnish, and rather thin at that. The real game pretty much skips most of the text and lore and boils down to mostly RNG and a bunch of stressful stuff where your opponents are seemingly always better off than you and you don't have the time to read much at all since even when it's not your turn, you're expected to follow along what your opponents are doing, whom zip around the map, stealing your settlements the turn after you've claimed them, leaving you with not enough gold to do much of anything the following turn and yet you're supposed to pick up quests during that "off-time" as well, meaning you either miss out on what your opponents are doing, or you miss out on quests seemingly.
Stress seems to be pretty prevalent in this game, robbing you of even more potential choices/strategy. For instance the burn card mechanic during combat/trials has a very quick timer, meaning you're expected to look at what symbols of dice you need burn, look at your cards, decide on whether or not it's worth burning them, weighing how many base dice you get, risk vs reward etc and then have enough time to actually roll the dice. Of course, that didn't work out at all for me, usually I was forced into making snap decisions which mostly turned out to be poor ones.
This was a pretty big thing for me, if I had gotten more time to think, maybe then I would have felt better about the things going on around me beyond my control.
And another thing, resources are very scarce (for your anyways) but without them you can't do much at all. There was I believe 3 main resources and rot, which is sort of a trade off where you get debuffs that hurt you, but can also hurt your opponents and further down the line they supposedly pay off and is even one of the win conditions, I didn't try it out very much. The other 3 are gold, magic and prestige. There might even have been a 4th one, but I can't remember it. Gold is the main one, the best cards I saw all required gold, and there's no downside to spending it other than not having enough for the next card, you pay gold to equip items which gives you more dice to give you a bigger chance of winning the many RNG based events and combat.
Magic is basically what you use when you run out of gold, I found magic to be pretty pointless since the effects were usually very limited and only lasted for a few turns.
Prestige is what you don't want to be spending, because even though there are some good cards that uses prestige, you also want your prestige to be nice and high since it's both a win-condition (I played 2 times after finishing the tutorial, both times I won it was because I had the highest prestige at the end, but more on that later) and every other turn or so the one with the highest prestige gets to pick between the king's decrees, usually they both suck anyways but you'd rather be the one making that choice than having it forced upon you.
Now things might have been different if I'd played against other players, but with the little time I played I didn't really feel up to testing my mettle against presumably more experienced people and even though I won, it felt more like I either got lucky, or that my win condition was forced upon me through sheer lack of choice. Since I was constantly out of gold, I couldn't do very much. Winning battles against other foes was all down to which random treasures I picked up, and sometimes some stupid random event stole or de-equipped my items, and sadly winning battles (throwing dice) is the biggest part of the game, more dice means you have a better chance at winning, so more luck = better results.
There are some choices to be made, I'm just not convinced they are impactful enough. For instance in my last game, even though I had planned to try out another win condition, my poor luck forced me into going for the prestige victory once again and I won that by basically spending several turns mostly inactive. I holed up in a town, trying to die as little as possible so I would keep my prestige, on occasion when I could afford it I would sabotage the other players, but I didn't get to quest or do many active things towards the end there, my success basically depended on the lack of success for the AI opponents rather than any skill from my side. And while it could be argued that was a strategic choice, it was still rather boring to be forced to do nothing rather than trying to fortify what little lead I had, again it felt like a lack of options.
TLDR: This is more of a neutral review than a negative one, but since the choice is binary I have to go with a negative thumb for now. Once the devs decides to put it up for a decent discount and I can afford it, I'll make a new review after a more thorough testing but for now, my interest in this game has cooled considerably.

I'm going to preface this review with what I think Early Access should mean. Then I'm going to tell you what "Undead Overlord" is. Early Access should be a title that, while unpolished and lacking features, is a fun experience that feels... nearly complete. Like a game that can stand on its own with maybe a little asterisk. And throughout its developmental process it should only improve, getting polished and expanded. Good examples of this are "Kerbal Space Program," "Sunless Sea," "Prison Architect..." the list goes on. Then they're released into the full-release wild, like "Betrayer" and "Sir, You are Being Hunted."
That is the expected and desired life cycle of all things Early Access. And let me add this: I think Early Access is not above criticism - even downright damnation. If a game is bad, it's bad. I'm not giving it leeway because "it isn't done yet." If you're selling a product, finished or not, I'm going to criticize it. People think criticizing Early Access is tantamount to punching a baby. I don't agree with that. Especially when the game is 30 minutes of content with an intended additional 60 minutes of content.
This game is bad. Objectively. It is a fact, like how old the universe is, how its heat death is inevitable, and how St. Paul, Minnesota is the happiest place on Earth (full disclosure: I've never been to St. Paul, Minnesota). Firstly let's address the graphics, arguably the least important feature (especially for an RTS). I feel that you have three options when developing a game: you can go the technically impressive route, the artistic route, or a wonderful fusion of both. "Undead Overlord" decided on the fourth, controversial option of terrible. This is pretty ugly. There is no artistic merit here. This is not fun to look at. This is like staring at the sun; it will cause inevitable blindness, madness, and is wholly inadvisable. It is jagged, blocky, muted, and utterly painful to look at. The levels are barren (particularly the one skirmish level). The character models look like the tourists in a "RollerCoaster Tycoon" game. I know graphics aren't that important at the end of the day, but you still have to stare at this for hours on end.
Gameplay is the real meat of any good game sandwich. Unfortunately for you, "Undead Overlord" features a single, suspicious slice of green bologna. You select your zombie, click on a target, and he runs over to jankily smack him or her around until they collapse into a pool of blood, resurrecting to join your dead ensemble or providing a snack for health and strength. Interesting concept, yes. But it's shallow and not fun. You're just clicking your increasingly unruly horde at dwindling townspeople and first responders until there's nothing left. Then you're on to the next of three levels. You'll blast through these in... five, ten minutes (the levels are small and same-y)? But don't worry, the developers plan on adding six more! That's roughly an hour and a half of entertainment potentially! And if they meet some unspecified monetary goal they're going to add such exciting features as MULTIPLAYER, HUMAN CAMPAIGN, and MAP EDITOR.
The AI is nonexistent. They react to your presence (sometimes) but don't expect them to seek you out or patrol of their own volition. This is a very one-sided RTS. The aforementioned skirmish level really shines a light on this. The level design on the single skirmish level is also pretty bland, featuring nothing but room after room stuffed with an assortment of humans and/or dog corpses.
So that's it. That's "Undead Overlord." It feels and plays like an iOS game. The trailer is admittedly cool looking, as is the concept. But I didn't see that game when I played. I'm not picking on this game or the developers. I just don't want you to be burned. This is not worth your hard-earned cash or time. When you can buy complete games for less than this, and when you can purchase Early Access titles more polished than this, what's the incentive? Do you like to gamble? To live dangerously? "Undead Overlord" is about as fun as staring into the sun. Some might disagree, shouting in disbelief while staring till their eyes melt out of their skulls. But you and me? We'll just keep walking, sunglasses on and eyes fixed squarely ahead.

This game has a lot of great stuff going for it.
First off, the gameplay is really fun and can get challenging in spots. However, it all stays fair and I never once felt like any of my deaths were cheap or unavoidable. It was always something I could've gotten myself out of if I had simply played better. The feel of the controls helps in this regard, as they're very tight & responsive, just as you would expect from a game of this style. One negative of the gameplay is... driving is a bit of a hassle, as you would expect from a top-down game like this, since you can't really see what's going to be in front of you and unless you have the city layout entirely memorized, you might end up crashing into a wall or two.
The graphics achieve the nice retro NES look that they were going for, and even when the novelty of it wears off, they let you choose from a lot of different graphics filters, many of which emulate the look of different retro game hardware. It's a really nice touch and allows you to keep the game looking new & interesting throughout the duration of the story mode.
The music is also very good. It's a bunch of catchy & memorable chiptunes made very much in the style of NES sound hardware, while not strictly adhering to it's limitations. It fits the game very well, and will likely get stuck in your head later on.
There are some challenge modes with online leaderboard support as well, which you can either find in the world (much like the "killing sprees" in GTA) or access from the main menu. These manage to be pretty fun if you're looking to compete with your friends. They even include replays for these challenges that you can watch for players on the leaderboards, or which you can save & share with your friends.
The story is probably the weakest part of the game, essentially being a string of retro game & movie parodies, which are cute at first but end up getting a bit tiring about halfway through the game's 8-or-so hour length. Still, the gameplay is fun enough that it's easy to overlook the annoyance of the parodies after a while and just enjoy the game for what it is: A fun throwback to the classic 2D top-down GTA games which has a really cool, retro style, good controls, and a nice slate of features which will keep you coming back to it.

Do you like Super Mario 64 style platformers? Do you like good remasters? Do you appreciate how silly voice acting used to be in games like this? If you answered yes to these questions, then this game is right for you.

Considering its age, this game has held up pretty well, and there's basically one reason as to why. Unlike a lot of contemporaries it doesn't shove garbage awful minigames down your throat constantly. Yeah, there are a few but they're usually both brief and really easy and the vast majority of the gameplay (95%+) is platforming and collecting.
The game does feel a little archaic at times - the camera isn't great, the glide/jump mechanic is a bit weird and inconsistent, and the boss battles are all kind of rubbish. But Ty controls decently and the game gives you all the tools you need to complete the game & find everything should you be willing to put in the effort.
The game also runs out of ideas for the last third of the game, with the three levels in the third tier of levels all reusing scenery and ideas from the first six levels. There's kind of a fresh spin on it to some degree, but it still feels kind of like filler, especially that second water level which is just... pointlessly spacious. As well there are some really annoyingly hidden things in the first water level that I wasn't a fan of (probably spent more time there than any other level). I think the length of the game is just right for this kind of game though, I got 15 hours out of it and felt pretty satisfied with that, not really craving much more but not feeling like I didn't get enough either.
It is a bit dated of a game but, honestly? I found this more enjoyable than Yooka-Laylee on the whole, even with its problems. It's just a nice, refreshing dose of 3D platforming & collecting the way I like it, without the pointless fluff that drags down a lot of contemporaries (Spyro 2 & 3 and the first Sly Cooper game both come to mind). And for $15 it's a pretty solid deal (though I got it for cheaper). Definitely pick it up if you're interested - I have zero nostalgia for this game as I'd never played it before but I can decisively recommend it.

I love this game, if you are a fan of games like 100% Orange Juice it feels fairly similar however feels more skill focused over RNG. Do not be mistaken, this game is HEAVILLY based on random number generation.
Pros:
- Well animated
- Runs well on a low spec computer, while retaining quality
- Fun, especially with friends
- Big cast of characters all feel pretty unique
- Lots of cards/quests
Neutral:
- There's a precomposed message system. Based on who you're playing you have a variety of different messages to communicate the same point. This of course is to limit the ammount of salt and toxicity to your game, which I believe in any RNG game there is bound to be. People will get mad. However, I think this is a GOOD choice.
- Microtransactions/skins/loot the sheer fact that this would even be in a game will make people mad, however I've seen people call this game Pay2Win and that just isn't true in the slightest. Anything you can buy is on the marketplace, and none of it (aside from DLC characters which really aren't any more or less broken than the vanilla characters.) Plus you get drops after every game with a chance of a key or a chest. Do not buy ANYTHING from skeeve's store, buy on the marketplace the chests are seriously like 8 cents and the keys are 18. If nothing else, just keep selling your chests and buy the die you want from the marketplace.
Cons:
- 4 win conditions, but 3 are basically the same thing. (Kill the king, fight the king with 4 spirit stones, kill the king with higher rot.)
- RNG (Often more of a negative than a positive in my experience.)
- One map (I think the locations etc change but the map is still the same.)
- Quests (There is no way to be able to predict where the next quest will be, but 90% of the time is the furthest it could possibly be from you.)
- The AI seems RNG as well (When a player drops out AI takes over and does some of the dumbest♥♥♥♥♥♥imaginable. Often times suiciding to the king while killing him to give highest prestiege the winner cause why not.)
and last but not least the biggest issue with the game.
- Disconnect Issue/Intentional Infinite Turn Griefing
I don't know what the problem is with this but in the last 6 games it's happened twice. Either a player disconnected and the game doesn't process it or they sit in their turn infinitely frozen at the drawing cards screen. This can be used to grief players into waiting and disconnecting without ANY means to skip their turn. Whether a bug or intentional it only stops when the player whos turn it is disconnects often resulting in games taking WAY too long and often making everyone else leave as well. Players leaving is already an issue with this game, and this on top of it makes it all the worse.
I want to leave it recommended if it is on sale because I have had a BLAST playing with my friends. However, in the current I couldn't justify a $20 purchase. There is simply not enough content to warrant it. I almost don't want to recommend it for anything more than free as long as that disconnection grief exists, I hope they do something about this soon because I really want more people to play and enjoy this game.

I, Gladiator is a port of the iOS action hack-and-slash game set in Ancient Rome developed by Steel Monkeys and published by Next Dimension Game Adventures Ltd.
You play as Rufus, a gladiator who is brought back from the dead after dying to be the champion of the god Hermes. You're goal is to win all the battles in the Arena and to become the ultimate gladiator while also achieving fame and being loved by the audience.
The game does not look terrible for an iOS port, and there are some video options that don't make much difference. However, there are various clipping problems and a couple of items some items where unreachable because they spawned inside rocks.
You use the mouse buttons to hack and slash, Spacebar to block and F to kick your enemies into traps. Unfortunately, the response time is really slow and some enemies take ages to be killed.
There are four chapters, each with 20 levels. In each level, your goal is to kill all the opponents. There are side objectives that grant you with additional experience and gold, which will be respectively used to upgrade your character and to buy extra items.
Multiplayer is not balanced at all, and you will find many people with better equipment and stats than yours that will kill you instantly.
The game is not very challenging: you spend most of the time hitting enemies, running around to recover your stamina and than starting over. Multiplayer is not fun and the game is only fun in short sessions (20-30 minutes max.)
Nothing exciting: typical "epic" music and sound effects that are pretty poor and repetitive. I do like that in the few cutscenes of the game, the characters speak actual latin.
There are many Steam achievements and side objectives to complete that will keep you hooked for many hours.
Overall, it is not a bad game for a mobile port. However, the unresponsive controls and the frustrating combat (both in single-player and multiplayer) really don't make this worth buying at full price.

Please kindly find my video review on youtube:
Presentation
I, Gladiator is a straight forward, combat intense, bloody gory game.
Decimating your enemies by slitting throats, cutting arms and beheading are only some of the many things you can do if you so want to relive the moments of the glorious days of the Roman Empire’s blood soaking arena.
The art style of I, Gladiator is very similar with games like The Walking Dead Series and Borderlands. However, this game does not shy from throwing some more blood at you.
Each NPC opponent does have their own uniqueness with the help from differences in equipment, body sizes and gestures. The randomness provided by the arena and traps at different levels also helped to avoid you from getting the repetitive feelings.
The Latin voice acting is unique and with the vast amount of historical weapons and armors to choose from, really helps to set the stage for this game.
However, one is easy to spot that there is a lack of details in this game. Despite the numerous equipment available and different arena settings, there is no description to the historical details of such equipment, nor would the game tell the player which part of the Roman Empire you are fighting in.
Gameplay
Placing yourself in the role of the most fearsome gladiator Rufus, brought back to life by Mercury, you are here to regain your past glory in the arena on behalf of your god.
Each stage is divided into multiple enemy waves. However, the pre-set enemy aggro at the beginning of the fight does make it feels unrealistic when the NPC just ignores the player standing right in-front and rushes towards another guy 5 meters away.
Although it is important to win the fight by defeating your fellow gladiators, you are also being handed a few objectives which will grant you bonus rewards and increase the difficulty for a perfect victory. However, the most important thing is to win the heart of the audiences. For they are willing to throw in bags of coins just to see some heads rolling actions.
One major problem of this game is the poorly written AI. It is so easy to lure your opponent to burn themselves by walking into naked flames or onto an obvious beast trap. There are a variety of game modes provided for multiplayer, including a real time quick match and a time record challenge. However, the quick match suffers greatly from unstable connection and lagging issue, which can make you feel frustrated.
Summary
In summary, I, Gladiator is a fun simplistic game which is perfect for a short gaming break.
However, I would rather buy the iPad version which costs 60% less than my current PC version.

Let's start this review off by saying that this game has a very mixed reputation, and for a very good reason.
Fallout Tactics isn't like its forefathers Fallout 1 and Fallout 2. Fallout Tactics is a strategy game, and unlike its forefathers, has no speech skill, no major RPG elements, and more straightforward, action based gameplay. It has a very unique story, and is so far the only Fallout game that has its setting in the Midwestern United States.
Fallout Tactics has voiceacted dialog, unlike Fallout 1 and 2. Fallout Tactics also offers four difficulty settings, Easy, Normal, Hard, and Insane. Easy is about what you would expect, easy, it makes the game very very easy and significantly more easygoing. Normal isn't much different, but it too offers a more story and action based game than the two harder difficulties. Hard is a minor step up from Normal, forcing you to play more adaptively, and sparringly with your supplies, as vendors either don't restock, or you have to complete a mission for them to, making supplies very restricted if you waste them. Insane is exactly what you would expect, insane. It's borderline impossibly hard if you play with Tough Guy Mode turned on, which I will touch on in a second. Insane mode drops your accuracy by a flat 20%, halves your average damage, curbs your chance to get criticals to extremely low, doubles enemy damage, resistence, accuracy, and worst of all, the enemy will get critical hits with frightening frequency. Strategy is everything on Insane. Your supplies become even more limited, and you will die many many many times, which makes Tough Guy even more bitter.
Tough Guy Mode makes it so you can only save when you are in a bunker, which makes Mission 1 extremely frustrating and bitter. You start off not in a bunker, with no autosave for the character you made, meaning if you die, you're going to have to remake your character all over again. Some people would say that's a very poor design choice, and I'm inclined to agree. Tough Guy Mode is something I have only ever played Fallout Tactics with turned on, extra difficulty and in this case, a Resident Evil style restrictive save system appeals to my nostalgia for difficulty driven older games. It's not too frustrating on all 3 of the easier difficulties, but on Insane, it's definitely going to make you angry once or twice per level, because there are going to be more than a few occassions in which you're going to either lose a character, or die and have to restart, due to bad luck with criticals or missing a shot you desperately needed to hit.
Fallout Tactics also comes with an editor which you can use to mod and edit the game yourself, and it's extremely well made, and isn't hard at all to learn how to use. Among the few things you can do with it, you can remedy the frustration of Mission 1 on Tough Guy Mode by checking a box in the editor that registers Mission 1 as a "bunker" which allows you to save after you make your character, open the editor, turn it off, and after that it's up to you, as you can save whenever you want for the duration of that specific save game's Mission 1, or you can save once immediately after making your character and never do it again out of honor, it's a way to alleviate the tedious nature of having to recreate your character multiple times if you're playing on a harder difficulty. The editor's readme.txt offers a fully comprehensible manual on what you need to do to use the editor, including details on what files you need to extract.
There is also a mod for Fallout Tactics that's very very similar to the Restoration Project in that it revamps a lot of the games issues and kinks, and all in all the Redux Mod, as it's called, is very well made, if albeit a bit more difficult in general, namely a few enemies are inserted into very cheap places, like corners, with weapons that have the potential to kill you instantly, and on Mission 1, with TG turned on, you can probably imagine why that will drive you crazy, which is namely what made me abuse the life out of savescumming on M1 with TG on on Insane, as both remaking my character, and the possibility of having to restart the level over and over again due to cheap enemy placement wore its welcome out very very quickly.
Charisma is also a significantly more important stat than in the previous games, or maybe not, that varies on if you used to have a posse of companions in F1 and 2. Charisma in Fallout Tactics dictates how quickly you will advance in ranks in the Brotherhood of Steel, which controls the quality of goods the Brotherhood Quartermasters will have, the quality of recruits you will have access to, and also, how soon you acquire Power Armor.
The level design is more straight along a single path than previous games, and the sandbox elements are extremely limited. There is also an infamous glitch that's unavoidable in which you will get several random encounters per second, which unless you have 100% Outdoorsman, will drain your already extraordinarily finite resources, which is extremely laborous, and frustrating, as you have the potential to die during one of these, and on Tough Guy, that will send you back to your last save at a bunker. These random encounters aren't particularly unique, or fun either, as they usually consist of the same general enemies that are commonplace for that area, which can range from komodo dragons, to deathclaws, and even just a bunch of ghostly looking civilians. It can be extremely frustratingly tedious.
Do I recommend this game? For people that enjoy strategy games, and even just diehard Fallout fans, definitely, it has drawbacks, and many flaws, but then again, doesn't any game?

I'll this review up with this: if Ubisoft would put 1/10th of the care that went into this game into their new games, they would probably be king of hill in the software industry today. So yes, I recommend it. Now onto the full review. Valiant Hearts is a puzzle platformer set during the First World War. Personally that caught my eye right there, as WWI is a very under represented era in video gaming. The game's story is about how the war affected the lives of the people that lived through it, from both a military veiwpoint, and a more civilian one, with a few ups, and a lot of downs. I won't give the ending away, but I will say this game really shows how the "glory" of war during the first few months quickly vanished into the muck and mire that most people remember this war for.
Gameplay wise, the game is well designed, there were a few "what am I doing" moments, but the game offers hints, and I don't remember having to go to a walkthrough to figure out what to do. Both the puzzles and platforming elements are well designed, and the mechanics work really well. I'm not sure I would give this game high replay value, as it's very heavily story based, but all the hours I have in the game were from my first playthrough, so there's quite a bit to sink into. Graphically speaking the game is well done, with a nice comic book style that's very atmospheric. Along with the era correct music and sound, everything really comes together to help the player feel like they're in WWI. They also did well with the history aspect. Although there were a few liberties taken, all the historical events and concepts were portrayed pretty acurately, with things like the first use of the tank, the use of zepplins, and the Nievelle Offensives and the following French Military riots covered well.
My only complaint is that they focused a little too much on the downsides of this war. Although the title characters and a few extras do some heroic acts, for the most part the game focuses solely on the death and destruction the war brought. Although I understand this, and I doubt they meant anything by it, it almost seems to dis the men that served in this era, showing that what they fought for was extremely pointless. Still, this is a really good game, and I feel it's worth a look, especially if you like puzzle platformers or the WWI era. Final Score 10/10

I never got to play this when it came out, but a friend of mine had it.  I saw it on steam and figured I'd give it a shot.
Boy I'm glad I did.  This game was one of the many "early 2000's" platformers / collectathons that were oh so popular back then.  Some others of note being the Jak and Daxter series, ratchet and clank, hell, even spongebob battle for bikini bottom.  A bunch more too.
Anyways, the movement is a little bit faster than you'd expect at first, but you get used to it.
Nine levels to explore with a bunch of different boomerangs to collect.  You could probably blaze through the game pretty fast if you wanted to, but it's well worth grabbing as much as you can along the way.  The maps are fairly large later on.
The game is very forgiving with some mechanics that other games are much more blunt with.  For example, you can swim underwater for a LONG time before drowning, which is really nice.  Checkpoints are frequent and deaths do not interrupt boss battles.  The boomerangs are essentially infinite ammo ranged weapons with some strings attached depending on the set you are using.
The game has a very nice flow with the animations used.  SMOOTH AS BUTTER!  The game runs pretty well on low to midrange systems, so you shouldn't have to worry about lowering settings.
Story wise, it's a little all over the place, but that's OK given it's a platformer with multiple different levels with very different settings.  The cutscenes have a sort of TV-show quality that seemed "OK" but didn't really detract from the overall experience.
to summarize:
+ 2000's era platformer, find the things to get to the next place to find the things, etc.
+ BOOMERANGS!  Fun as hell to use.
+ Diverse levels with mixed platforming and combat.
+ No major glitches of note.
+ Interesting boss fights
+ Looks fantastic, some subtle graphical updates really make this 15-year-old game shine.
+ Voice acting is great.  Get used to australian accents and words that leave the uninitiated confused.
~ Music is good, but gets repeditive.
~ Camera can get a little wonky in some areas, but is overall fine.
- 100% can be a grind if you miss certain collectibles on your first run through. There is a cheat code that reveals collectibles that you can use if you really need to.
If you are looking for that authentic early 2000's platforming experience, I highly recommend this game.

This is a game made by artists, not game designers. It's very pretty, it has an interesting story/hook. And that's about it.
Sadly, they try to use the interface force it to be a game the rules don't encourage. Apparently they wanted a different game, but couldn't figure out how to make it. Or, perhaps, they just had completely different people come up with each aspect and did their best to fuse the mish-mash together.
You can only zoom out a tiny bit, and when you do, a thick fog covers everything. It's like being forced to play chess while only being able to look at the board through a drinking straw. This isn't a realtime game, your opponents can't do anything when you are scrolling around, so why make it take longer than necessary to get the information you need to make informed decisions? You can still see everything if you scroll around enough, so it's not adding anything to the game except 'atmosphere' and annoyance.
Then, when you enter battle in this turn-based strategy game, suddenly a countdown clock starts and you have limited time to determine how to handle the current situation. Your opponent gets to do this at the same time, and suddenly the "turn-based" portion is shot right in the foot. They must want you to hurry up, right? Nope, once the timer ends, and you can no longer affect the outcome, they have a super-slow, drawn our 'roll the dice' animation/simulation that you have to sit through that is about as exciting as watching paint dry, weather, and peel away.
And you can't really avoid battle, because it's one of the best ways to get influence (a win condition). It's a double tap: they gain some and you lose some. At least one opponent is going to be using it to fulfill the victory condition. The board's not big enough to evade, and your cards don't have enough influence to really slow them down much.
You could try to complete quests: but you start at ~40% success on those (50% on your good score, 30% on your bad), or you can get a smaller reward. You can't influence the outcome other than the choice of wether to take the chance at all. This is assuming you can get to the randomly-chosen location before someone caps you for the above reasons. Also, you can only have one at a time, and if you don't like it, or it's in a bad location: too bad, you're stuck with it.
Which brings us to the cards: you have a limited hand size, which refills at the start of turn. But, if you don't use it, you're stuck with it. You can discard them by intentionally getting into fights (Oh, joy! another reason fighting is better!) or you can set off traps other people set for you to spend cards making them not hurt as much (sounds like a completely valid strategy to me). Manage to use all of yours because they rocked: you get a new hand full of goodness. Manage to not use a single one because they were all situational or outright hurt you: you get to look at those same cards sitting uselessly in your hand next turn, too!
And, of course, there's an expansion pack full of heroes with abilities that will stomp all over the base set. But really, that's just icing on the cake.

This game was a bloody bargain... I was buying a few games, had left over money, and found this. The game could have some great potential... At the current stage of development, there isn't much... But more will be added...
*Options*
At this current point, option setting are bare... Allowing you to swap from windowed to fullscreen.. Well, it's not much to say the least... This game is very early in dev, around one month old... I know the dev(s?) are working on a story mode, which is great 'n all... But I think you might want to fine tune some of the bugs, and the current content, in the game.
*Bugs I've encountered*
I've read some of the other reviews on this game, talking about encountered bugs... As others have said, sometimes I launch a new game, "Error reading Squad"... I've also had a glitch where I told my guys to use the work bench, and my mouse disappears! This also happens when I level up members of my group...
*AI*
I think the AI/Path-Finding of squad members, and zombies, needs to be looked over... Maybe making people able to open doors if you select an area through a locked door... Sometimes the zombies keep see me (well, at least I think) and carry on walking to another window/open door... But, it's a game early in development..
*Gameplay* [I played this game offline for a bit]
The game can be a bit of a cluster f**k at times, zombies spilling into rooms, being backed into corners... But that is the point of the game, staying away from those problems is what the game is about! You need to manage your meds, ammo and the health of your 'Squad', which is kinda hectic at times... But thats why it's fun... Some people say it's not very well explained, but if you go to the menu, it tells you what pretty much everything does...
*Over All Verdict*
This game is very cheap, £0.79 infact, rightfully deserving a space in any bargain bin/shelf... But not every store would accept an unfinished game... It's worth a note that at the time of this review, 13th August, the game is a month-or-so in development...
If you don't mind playing a slightly buggy game, have good hand-eye coordination when your mouse disappears, a\nd don't mind playing a game with little optimisation, then enjoy the game...

Squad-based tactical game in the universe of Fallout, with post-nuclear war havoc reigns the world, and you have to fight the hordes of Chaos in the name of Order. To be precise, you gotta kill much in the name of Brotherhood of Steel. But I guess you've figured that out by yourself, simple by reading the name of the game. I'll say even more of obvious things now, so for those who are short-in-temper for reading, I suggest to skip to the bottom right away.
I remember that at time when it was released, the plenty of critics were against it. They were very angry with that approach on beloved universe of Fallout 1&2, which ruined one of the brightest RPG experience ever... That was common thought back than.
Now it's 2016 year, it's been 15 years after game's release. What's the situation now, why there are so many positive reviews on Steam, why people still enjoying the game, that was almost completely sinked after release? There are two main answers: first, it is still branded as Fallout game, even if the story is not "canonical". Classic nonetheless, as people say. Now, the second reason... surprisingly, it is a fair tactical game! Certainly not the best in the genre, but hey! - all good games in that "tactical" genre you can count with your fingers! Every working approach there worth its money!
Certainly, Fallout Tactics is not for everyone. If you don't like games where you need to clear levels from enemies in the quite slow-paced turn-by-turn style, just pass by. And even if you are good with turn-based combats, in the most cases, I'd recommend you to buy and play Wasteland 2 instead. It is providing much better experience for much wider auditory.
Fallout Tactics has many downsides. The story tastes... not fresh, and even not-satisfying. The battle system is good, but not calculated enough. The worst part of it is moving in turn-based mode: the maps are big, and your legs are quite short! What's even worse, the bugs with way-mapping still there, just like I remember them from 2001 year. The skills and all other SPECIAL system from the original Fallout also not fitting in, considering the fact it is not a proper RPG, but rather a "shoot'em all" pattern turn-based combat simulator.
But... all of those minuses are manageble, if you have some temper and will. All but one, the final of the story there is way worse than in the Fallout 3. So, even strongest by will cannot really vouch for replayablity in that game. Unless they are not bothering with the story at all.
Multiplayer could be a mind-blowing thing, but no. Not even the possibility to ride deathclaws can fix some real difficulties with combat system and the possibility to connect with other players (its LAN only now, servers are gone)... Simply put, there is no fun. You'd be much better with XCom Enemy Unknown multiplayer, by any reason.
So. Why you can buy that game? Obviously, the main reason, for it goes in the bundle with the main games, Fallout 1&2. I even remember some events when the keys for that trio (F1, F2 and F tactics) were distributed free of charge...
Why play it? Well, if you have a thing for turn-based squad tactical games, with lots of guns, and big maps filled with all the menagerie of Wasteland... Give the game a shot, it is worth one. Like I already said, there are too few of decent squad-based tactical games, to turn up your nose against it.

As my first review of a game, I wanted to ensure it was a game that was especially dear to me. It would need to be a game that has secured a special place in my heart, and resonate with me on multiple sentimental levels.

Ty the Tasmanian Tiger can lay claim to this feat.
Ty the Tasmanian Tiger was released in 2002 for the PS2, Xbox, and Gamecube. My copy of the game was for the PS2 system. Being released alongside contemporaries Ratchet, Sly Cooper, and Jak, I saw Ty as part of this hypothetical Sony mascot tetrarchy of heroism. Wicked Australian accent? Boomerang slinger? Cool character design and art style? Ty was totally awesome. Being around 6 or 7 years old at the time, it was a flourishing era of elementary imagination and exploration. I would daydream about my video game heroes teaming up, indulge in make-believe adventures with them during recess, and make poorly-scribbled doodles on my spelling tests. It was great.
There is a decent number of "nostalgia" reviews. Which is just fine, but I wanted to give a little more information on the game and why one should check it out, especially if you are younger, and have not grown up with this game or its sequals.
For those that are more unfamiliar with this game, or have heard of it and simply not played it before, Ty the Tasmanian Tiger game is an action/adventure collect-em-up game similar to other titles such as Jak and Daxter, Banjo-Kazooie, and Super Mario 64.
Ty is a young Thylacine who discovers that an evil cassoweary (weird bird/ostrich thing) named Boss Cass has stolen a handful of mystic talismans and banished your parents to the Dreaming. The talismans are now scattered across the Outback and it is up to Ty to track them down, defeat Cass, and rescue his family!
The game is beautiful. The colors are bright and vivid, the remastered textures look excellent, the water looks refreshing, and the dynamic shadows are just the icing on the cake. Avid players of the original will also notice additional decorations and foliage in the levels as well. The FPS is superb. Never dropped below 60. It's pretty crazy remembering that the game came out 15 years ago.
The platforming in the game is very fun and diverse in nature that differs between the various levels in the game, with different tasks in these levels that provide some variety in the odd jobs you need to complete for the game's primary collectable, Thunder Eggs. There are also secondary, optional collectibles: Golden Cogs. These are acquired in order to create "techno rangs," which are separate from the boomerangs you obtain through story progression. Controls are tight and extremely refined for keyboard and mouse, making the platforming more enjoyable, and the combat fluid.
Guns, swords, spells, miracles, ninjutsu, runes... those are pretty neat and all.
However, there is a certain satisfaction that can only be achieved through hitting something in the face with a boomerang that explodes.
Ty the Tasmanian Tiger features the popular World Hub mechanic. This certainly isn't a bad thing when it works well, which it does. There are 10 primary levels, 9 of which are the levels you explore to retrieve Thunder Eggs. Each level is unique. Though some do indeed share similarities, they are very distinct from one another in design, and are all quite memorable and fun to explore.
They are all enjoyable and goofy. Some a bit more odd than others. Some may give you trust issues. They may not be super fleshed-out with deep backstory, but they have their charms, and that's enough for me.
This is the primary area in which this game shows its age. The animations for some of the enemies and NPCs look very dated, especially during the in-engine cutscenes within the levels. However, this is forgivable understanding that the game was released in 2002, and that it doesn't subtract from the gameplay itself.
On the flip side, the intro cutscene and primary story cutscenes are rendered and animated at a much higher quality, and look pretty dang awesome. They invoke a sense of "Indie animated movie" style.
Ah yes. This is one of those games. One of those few games that you play the full soundtrack on YouTube while playing other games. The music is one of the most memorable, nostalgia-trip-inducing aspects of this game. The reason that there is a soundtrack available for purchase with this game. It's style is simple, satisfying, and has a very distictive Australian twang to it. Many of the tracks delve into quite a wide range of genre styles, but come full circle and include catchy motifs in the tunes.
Understand that the soundtrack isn't the next revolutionary soundscape, and some of the enjoyment may be nostalgia-fuelled, but it is certainly catchy, addicting, and definitely worth a listen.
Ty the Tasmanian Tiger is as solid a adventure/platformer title now as it was 15 years ago. The remastered graphics and textures are awesome. 60 FPS. Tight controls even with keyboard and mouse. The in-engine animated sequences look quite dated, but are forgivable. Story cutscene animations are excellent. The characters are charming and goofy. The music is very catchy and addicting.
(For those curious, I did indeed derive part of my name from this game. You'll
guess where the other half came from.)
Would recommend this game to anyone. It is a must-buy for fans of the original that grew up with it, as well as those seeking a classic platforming, collect-em-up Outback adventure.
Very much looking forward to the future remasters of the sequels!

Most of the stuff in this review I've seen mentioned elsewhere, but I'd thought I'd reinforce them here.
The game's mechanics are admittedly novel and neat, but there are a few issues that I would like to see resolved before I'd commit any cash to this game:
1. The fog of war that appears when one zooms out too much seems pointless to me. I think zooming out shouldn't change the angle of the camera and just allow for more of the map to be seen - this would allow for the graphics and artstyle of the game to stand out more, and would give substance to the fact that this should be happening in a fantasy WORLD, and not just on a virtual 'board'.
2. The Quest system is broken, and should be fixed. Quests always require you to travel to some faraway location which you do not know beforehand. Now, this might not have been too much of a problem, were it not for the other RNG elements of the game making it a living hell to some characters to reach their quest locations. This is especially true when said location is surrounded by Marshes, Mountains or Banes, or when it is being blocked by a King's Guard for three turns straight. I've seen some people say that the results of the 'chance' part of the quest are also always fixed. I wouldn't know, seeing as I never tested it, but having failed three quests who's chance of success SHOULD have been 90%, and succeeded in two who's chances were 30% (I wanted them treasures ;D), I'm thinking they're on to something.
3. Prestige seems to be the go-to win condition, seeing as it is objectively the easiest to obtain, particularly using a certain item which can be easily unlocked by completing one prestige victory in singleplayer. There are few cards which are able to remove prestige from another player, and gaining prestige is much easier than attempting Regicide against a King who is that much stronger than you are, finding four randomly spawning spirit stones AND sneaking into the castle alive, or becoming corrupted enough (through rare cards or LOSING battles with Banes) to out-die the King in combat. Prestige-winners just have to stall for 9 turns, while killing banes and doing quests. Even Thane could pull off a Prestige victory pretty easily, despite being a combat-oriented hero, since heroes won't have the guts to take him on, and if they do he's likely to win (+1 prestige), and he'll have an easier time with banes (+1 prestige), which allows him to reach his quest locations much more easily (+1 prestige). That's not to mention the somewhat rare prestige cards which boost his prestige even further.
4. Some of the characters are objectively better than others, most notably the DLC ones. For example, Sana is awful in multiplayer battles, and Sasha is just terrible in singleplayer matches, since the AI know exactly where a stealthed character is.
So, yeah.
Buy this game at your own peril, Heroes!
(Or on a more generous Summer Sale)
