I've changed my negative review to a positive one on account of the developer making such a focused effort to respond to my criticisms of the game outlined in my original review below.
The random deaths, which were the one very major issue I had with
, are no longer in the game. Some people are disappointed with that but, personally, I don't see what joy there is to be gained from failing for absolutely no reason, especially in a title where the action is spread relatively thin in the early stages.
The 'jumpscare simulator' will never be a favourite sub-genre for me but, with the issues addressed, this is about as solid an example of one as you can hope to find on Steam.
=======================================================
Sorry to be the lone voice of dissent here but... no. Not while we're rating this as an actual playable game.
The premise is simple enough. You've got four lights to keep on, two upstairs and two downstairs, while avoiding the titular ghoul Sophie who will sneak, scuttle and slither around behind you at all times, looking for the perfect moment to grab your face and howl at it with a decibel count to rival most mid-40's war artillery.
The problem is that there's no rhyme or reason as to when she can murder you and when she can't. You're assigned a safe point at the start of the game that changes around between checkpoints but it's about as much use as nipples on a tank. By the developer's own admission, and I quote:
Except it's really not that rare. In fact, it's the most common way you'll die. At what point has randomised death ever been acceptable? Imagine trotting through Super Mario Bros and just bloody dying of an aneurysm. Imagine fighting Dr. Wily in Mega Man and spontaneously combusting because he just 'doesn't like you'. It's even more tedious here, in a game where you spend the majority of your time sitting around waiting for the clock to roll over a two hour increment while the lights slowly dwindle, daring you to expose yourself out of boredom rather than necessity.
It works as an app that you can leave running in the background to scare the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of you at completely random intervals, maybe like those maze games that walloped Linda Blair's demon face from The Exorcist at you with an ear-splitting shriek as a surprise bowel evacuator. Nothing more.
Here's what I got out of it:

If you are not a fan of Jumpscare games than this game might not be for you.
If you enjoyed games like FnaF, Boogeyman or Emily Wants to Play then you probably will enjoy Sophie's Curse as well.
You are a Nurse who is to take care of an old man in a house which has no electricity for 1 night. The lights in this house are powered by a crank that needs to be manually turned to re-generate as they loose power over time, or are interfered with by Sophie.
While it uses FnaF like mechanics I really enjoy that you "walk" around the house to different rooms, rather than being in a single room. It is not open roaming like Emily wants to play but instead clicking areas on the screen makes you walk to different rooms.
You only have to survive a single night but the night is divided into sections of 2 hours. Each 2 hours you survive will save that checkpoint to continue from.
Your Job is to ensure that the lamps keep staying bright by manual turning the handles on their generators to replenish their power. There is 4 lights, 2 downstairs and 2 upstairs, with 1 randomly being chosen to the be a "savepoint" when thinks get hairy.
As you progress through the night things get more frantic with each checkpoint with lamps not only loosing power but starting to fail completely needing you to use your laptop in the kitchen to re-activate them and solve additional tasks to do so.
Listen out for queues to know when to stop powering lights, run away from Sophie when she comes for you and hope she likes you :)

Overall a great game, got it working on Windows 10 too.
Last time I played was in Windows 7 and it worked fine, but getting it working in Windows 10 was kind of a pain. I could always play it in Windows 7 by putting GFWL on offline mode, but this time there doesn't seem to be an offline option.
First of all, install "Games For Windows Marketplace" (google it, should be the first result,
page), set up an account if you don't have one. The game may automatically direct you to the download link upon trying to launch it for the first time, it did for me. You may get a prompt from Windows 10 that it's not compatible, but install it anyway. Without Games For Windows Live/Marketplace installed, the game won't launch at all.
Make sure you put "-nomemrestrict -norestrictions" (without quotes of course) in the game's launch options (right click it in Steam library, select Properties). If you don't, the game won't let you change resolution or any graphics settings.
From the main menu, pick the LIVE option and sign in. It may take a while, maybe not, but just be patient if it seems to take a while. At some point it will also ask for your game key. Don't try to close the GFWL overlay in the game while it's signing in either, I did and the whole thing became unresponsive.
It may ask you to update GFWL, I updated but it may not be necessary. If you choose to update, it will ask you to exit and re-launch the game, just sign in again from the main menu using the LIVE option. When I tried to sign in when prompted while starting a new game, it crashed. So using the LIVE option from the main menu was necessary for me. It will also download your "Profile" this may also take a bit, again just be patient.
Once you're signed into LIVE go ahead and start a new game, it should work without any problems.
It's been a while since I played this game and it was a pain to get it working this time, but so far it was worth it. I almost gave up at one point, was gonna chalk it up to the game being incompatible with Windows 10. It actually works fine under Windows 10, it's just this Games For Windows Live/Marketplace stuff that gets in the way.
TL;DR
To get EFLC working in Windows 10:
1) Install Games For Windows Marketplace, sign up for an account if you don't have one.
2) Put "-nomemrestrict -norestrictions" (without quotes) in launch options for game.
3) Launch game, set up graphics, sign into GFWL using the "LIVE" option in the main menu. It may take a while, be patient. It may ask for the game key, just put it in and it will work.
4) Start a new game.

I had almost exclusively played turn-based strategy games or slow RTS games with empire-building, resource gathering, etc. before I saw this for sale secondhand at a very cheap price and decided to try it. Bear in mind my review is that of a rank amateur, but someone who has played this particular game all the way through several times, on Steam and off.
If there is anyone else out there like me, someone who doesn't enjoy fast-paced first-person shooter games but still wants a *little* bit of real-time pressure on your game play, this is a great game for that. The learning curve is pretty short, considering this type of game was unfamiliar to me. The post-apocalyptic setting is at time humorous and never takes itself  too seriously. By today's standards the animation is a little clunky, and graphics processing a bit cumbersome.
This was possibly the first game I've ever played where friendly fire was a real danger. At first it was frustrating that I couldn't expect my PC's to shoot around each other, but then it simply became a natural part of the tactical challenge. (Why would I ever realistically expect NOT to be injured when someone standing right behind me opens up with a .50 cal in my direction?)
For anyone working on third-person sequels to this: please do something about the ladders and stairs. Make them more  fluid and accessible. I've had many a player character shot to pieces because the computer can't figure out how to send two of them down a wide staircase at the same time!

If you are into Indie games and like Diablo or similar games,
it's definetly worth buying.
it's a no brainer as steam sale, but also worth the full price.
I have seen some minor negative reviews, who seem to ignore, this game is an indie game.
So keep that in mind and don't expect it provide features or graphics like a AAA-game like Diablo 3, etc.
Also at the beginning, you should use the filter and only play well rated adventures.
The battle system is relatively simple, although the RPG-aspects regarding your character (stats, abilities) are probably as complex as the ones in Diablo 3.
You can choose from 4 Classes (Warrior, Rogue, Ice Wizzard, Fire Wizzard), each playable as male or female.
although the wizzards feel more like one class. It's basicly the decision in Diablo 2, if you want to play as Fire or Ice sorceress.
depending on the equipment you find, you can also play all classes as melee or ranged heroes.
- the Warrior is the heavy, resistant melee class
- the Rogue is both strong in dealing ranged and melee damage
- the Wizzards are strong AoE damage dealers, with the frost wizzard being more able to kite.
The fun for someone new is definetly the loot-system, which is nearly as addicting as the loot-system of Diablo 2 or 3.
only nearly as addicting, because unfortunately there are not set-items.
And of course you leveling up gives you the opportunity to spend skill points on 4 different stats.
You basicly play short-storys or whole campaigns, created by other players, so the fun strongly depends on how good the map is, you choose to play.
that's why i recommend to use the filter-system, only playing well-rated adventures at first.
THE ACTUAL FUN BEGINS, after you have played some standard and user-generated levels,
and you start to create your very own adventures using the ACK (adventure creator kit).
there you design your own level, building dungeons, villages, forests, etc.
placing enemies, NPCs and loot chests in it.
and if you use the trigger features, you almost feel a little bit like a game developper yourself, since these triggers are basicly visualized programming functions.
Being visualized makes it even for someone, who never has programmed before easy to do basic programming and therefor make your levels more complex.
The game also has a multiplayer-feature, making it possible to play every level or campaign as a group.
Although due to the relatively small active community, I recommend to play the game with friends, if you want to actually play the multiplayer.
But even as a Single-Player, the game is a lot of fun.
In a nutshell:
it's an Indie-RPG game with a strong editor,
worth every penny!

I've nominated this game for The “Does Retro better than a Retro game” Steam Award.
At this moment, I haven't finished the game yet: I've only completed the story mode on Hardcore Mode and I'm working my way through the Challenge Mode. The Challende Mode is hard for me, because I always make a mistake or two. And to ace a level (getting 3 stars out of 3) requires a perfect run. So yeah, really difficult like the games of yesteryear? Check.
The graphics in this game also remind me of those good old games. It's 2D and nicely drawn in higher resolution. To me, the graphics invoke a more retro-inspired look than most pixel art games.
The music in this games also loops like many of my beloved C64 soundtracks. But the music itself really isn't up to par. The sound effects are sparse and underwhelming. Music and sound definitely are the weakest part of this game.
So what can I say about the gameplay? You run, you jump, you collect stars. Couldn't be more simple, couldn't be more retro. You can use the analoge stick, but the input is digital. And the controls are a bit fiddly too, in my opinion. Oozi is fast to react to your input. A bit to fast for my taste, resulting in unwanted move(ment)s at the worst possible moments.
Other than how the character controls and the lacklustre music, I really have no gripes. Challenging but fair level design. A star system to encourage masterful playthroughs. A sense of achievement when you do. It's lenghty too (depending on your skill level, offcourse) if you want to complete the three game modes and get all the achievements.

Great puzzle game depicting the depressive reality of the Great War.
It is not that big of a tear generator, compares to something else in the entertainment market (like Clannad...). But this is a story about a war, the first industrialized grand total war, it will be very bloody and depressive.
In terms of destruction and driving people mad,
War Never Changes

The story is based on people’s destinies and love during the devastating WWI (or The Great War) in the territory of France. The characters are trying to survive the horrors of war during missions, and are followed by a faithful dog companion. In the game the lives of all the characters are inextricably drawn together over the course of the game. Friendship, love, sacrifice, and tragedy befall each one as they help each other to retain their humanity against the horrors of war.

The short:
Valiant Hearts is a fantastic experience that explores the devastating effects of WWI through the eyes of several different characters. The story is superb and emotional, connecting the player to each character through arresting visuals, enjoyable gameplay, and a soundtrack that enhances rather than distracts. Discussion of the WWI era is often lost in the shadow of it's more devastating successor, but Valiant Heart brings the struggle to light in a way that is visceral, honest, and captivating. Despite it's very few flaws, this is a rare game and provides an experience that is not soon forgotten. I highly recommend it.
The long;
Writing a review worthy of this game is near impossible, so I just want to briefly address the few negatives that I have seen regarding this game. There are only two, the need for Uplay and the puzzle difficulty/frequency.
-Uplay is annoying yes, but once I was launching this game through my Steam library I never even saw UPlay. It was just like any other Steam game. The only time I dealt with it was when I felt like looking at what achievements I had or needed. Really not a deal-breaker for a prospective buyer and certainly not worthy of a negative review.
-The puzzles in the game are very easy for the most part. While some do take more thought, this is not a game about difficulty, it is about an experience. The puzzles can at times distract from this so I do get why some people have issues with them, but still it is a game and some of them are actually pretty smart. I enjoyed most of the puzzles but sometimes did feel like I was just dealing with them to see the next part of the story. As above, still a very minor gripe about a fantastic game.
Regarding the core aspects of the game:
-Graphically the game is just gorgeous to look at. Beautifully hand drawn characters and environments just pop out of the screen and give you a perspective you have never had before. The game is very unique graphically and I couldn't be happier with the direction they decided to take here.
-As we all know music can make or break a game, and in this game music amplifies an already engrossing experience considerably. In situations where it couldn't get more emotional, the music comes in and provides some serious steroids for your sadness. In times of intensity the music adds a sense of urgency and importance, with music starting and stopping on perfect queue. The timing and selection is just flawless and really well done.
-The gameplay is loads of fun and really intelligently done. This is a 2D game, but there are certain things that just felt so innovative to me. Despite how it may appear, this is not a game that plays like an old NES platformer. You are not just running and jumping through a level, you're stopping, going, interacting, collecting, and sometimes working across multiple characters in the same level (across different "layers" of that level) to achieve an objective. It really is neat. If you are into the history of what happened, there are also several collectible items scattered across the game, each providing a brief background on how the item was utilized during the war. Additionally, there are journal entries with pictures and dates of the events that you are playing through at the start of each level. As someone who is extremely interested in history I found myself looking forward to these little excerpts every time I started a new level. They are extremely enjoyable and put the devastation of the war into format that is factual and interesting to read.
-Story. I don't think I can say much here that hasn't been said already. Without spoilers, all I can say here is that this game is worth your time. To be fair though, once you play through it once you will unlikely play it again. It just isn't that kind of game that offers loads of replay value. You play it once and you're done, some folks may not like this, I am totally fine with that. Ultimately, this is a game worth buying that everyone should play and a stark reminder that war does indeed make men mad.

Definitely a fun game to play with friends. It presents an interesting mix of card abilities and RPG elements. The combat and quest systems are entertaining and give a nice fresh feel when you play multiple games. The micro transactions, while not the best thing in the world, seem to be for just vanity elements, not pay-to-win type things. Overall it seems to be alot of fun, with great art, music, and sound effects.
Many of the reviews are complaining about the quests being "all the way across the map", which is honestly not that bad. You take turns to get there and try to complete the quest. I think the real issue is people are used to the almost instant gratification of killing a few monsters and completing an objective. This game is planning intensive, so you need to make strategic choices. Another complaint was that choosing one quest eliminates the ability to choose others. This, once again is about strategy. You need to pick your best path to victory, and each quest leads you toward that path in a different way, so of COURSE you need to think carefully about picking one.
The combat system RNG is another point of contention people have. You roll an amount of dice based on your combat level and abilities. With 6 options per die, the odds aren't always going to be in your favor, which is why characters that aren't geared for combat shouldn't be picked. Once again, this is a strategy element. If you get items or abilities that benefit combat, you tend to do better. Addidtionally, you can get lucky and manage to defend well in combat, however the balancing factor is that if you end up rolling most of your dice to defend, you don't get to attack very much. Once again, it seems to be mostly complaining by people that don't have a head for strategy.

If you are looking for in depth strategic gameplay that a victory reflects, don't look here. There are 4 ways to win Armello; Rot, Killing the King, Spirit stones, and Prestiege. At first glance everything seems balanced until you play the game a little bit more to truly understand whats going on. Winning with spirit stones is impossible to do if you are playing against competent players because they will just steal your stones, and kill you out of your base until they walk up and last hit the king. To win playing rot, it relies on you getting really lucky with card draw, and items you recieve through quests or dungeons. To win prestiege, you have to have the highest prestiege in the round, and not have anyone kill the king. At first this seems like the easiest victory because you just go around killing things / doing quests, until you realize what the last win condition is... Killing the king. This is poorly balanced because in a normal game, killing the king will almost always result in someone going in the palace when the king has 1-3 hp, and last hitting him. You can make the argument about the king being able to kill someone and the person with the highest prestiege wins... but Come on. Players will go in with full health, and stack cards in order to win, all they have to do is survive and deal 1-2 damage and they win the game. This makes winning a prestiege victory litterally impossible against human players unless they get extremely unlucky. This is a real shame because this game looks ♥♥♥♥ing amazing, this game has so much potential. But if every game results in the game being decided by someone last hitting a king, then whats the point of playing?

One of the few good things to come out of the Prequel Era.
The gameplay revolves around properly managing your squad, and has interesting encounters. The scope is more focused than other, grand and epic Star Wars games, but by the end of the game, you've really connected with your squad. They may all be numbers to the Jedi, but you will remember each character's colour, number, nickname, and preferences.
The only unfortunate thing is that the game's premise could have easily made this a 4-player-co-op shooter, but it isn't. The multiplayer is generic and mostly bland, but the single player campaign is definitely worth it. The least enjoyable parts of the game are when you are separated from your squad, working independently. Without the squad management, it becomes a generic shooter set in the Star Wars universe.

This game techinically takes only a few hours to beat. However, the proper way to play is not simply to beat the game here. Nay, the true goal is to take as much tiime between missions as possible, thus increasing the playtime by at least twofold. That being said, other than the actual arcade-style games-within-a-game, the only game I've been able to come up with for this is "See How Long You Can Survive the Police". The story missions are quite enjoyable and provide the variety I cannot, although there really should have been more of them (especially the non-story missions). The endgame somehow manages to take away both the titular city and rampage, instead opting to throw in a tonne of combat. And then you reach the final boss. While I personally found it a pain to beat, I can only imagine the difficulty one would have with it if they hadn't played one of the aformentioned games-within-a-game. Have fun if you miss one of your incredibly specifically-timed attack opportunities!
In short Retro City Rampage is a fun game, as long as you don't put too much effort into beating it. It's fun, but doesn't have too much depth.

OK, so first of all, this is probably not a game a grown man looks at and thinks, oh yeah, that's the game for me. I got it as part of some big bundle and never would have bought it on my own since I don't have kids. And this definitely is a game you look at and think, will this entertain my kid for a few hours? So its marketing I'm guessing is aimed at adults buying it for their kids. So I'm going to frame this review that way: should your kid play this? And honestly my answer after a few minutes is a firm MAYBE, ONLY if they are really young. If they are not really young, no. Find a better platformer, there are plenty out there.

At first, there seems to be nothing wrong with this. I started out thinking, ok, if I was a kid again, would I be okay with this? And I start out trying to get into that frame of mind. But then I played for a few more minutes and was like, nope.

Now, I said before for the very young, this might work. That's because there's basically no concept of loss ever presented in the game (on "KID" mode). You basically can't die and even if you did you would lose no progress. You just are wandering around getting stars and you can get hurt but that hurt has no significance or consequence for the most part. OK. So if your kid is likely to throw a tantrum when they lose a game, this might be ok for that.

But compared to a game like Super Mario Bros or other classic platformers, it really fails to measure up. There's the lack of story. But the biggest issue is the controls. On a gamepad, you basically can no longer use the left analog to control movement as soon as you get the 'drop down' move, because it's so sensitive whenever you try to control movement at all it will force you down, so you take damage. Damage still has no consequence, but not being able to use the left analog is a huge distraction in a platformer.

There's a lot of stuff here that at first made me think, cool. You can look down and up in environments with the right analog. Cool. But as I played more, I realized that this was more a stopgap to deal with the poor camera positioning. A lot of the time the camera is not following where you want to go because the levels are just going in every which direction. But you can't look up and down on vines or in the air, which practically defeats the purpose or makes you move very slowly.

I think game designers should look at this game because it's a really interesting example of managing level design and UI, but I think it should be presented as a negative example because quite frankly it strikes me as a pretty bad platformer. It's not just another platformer and you shouldn't pretend it's impossible to have an opinion about it just because it's aimed at kids. It's designed by adults based on those adults expectations of kids needs and desires, and if anything that means it should be open to more scrutiny, not less.

Okay, so it's scary.  REALLY scary.  Fantastic atmosphere, both visually and aurally...very tense...but is it LOGICAL?!
Firstly, there's the usual "you've been given a really, really super-dangerous job for next-to-no pay" premise...so in spite of them never clearly stating as such, I'm assuming that all of these post-FNAF games are set in third world countries, where life is cheap and you'd basically murder your grandmother for spare change.  I mean, I accepted the premise of the first Five Nights at Freddy's as much as anyone, but the sixtieth time around this kind of set-up is pushing its luck just a tad, don't ya think?

Secondly, I do everything the game tells me to.  Run here to stop generator A, B, C, or D from running down, solve (admittedly well-done) mini-puzzles at the laptop when required, and try my best to hang around in the designated "safe-spot" for the rest of the time (quite how the laptop knows the exact place in the house to stand to avoid ghostly victimisation I have no fricking idea, but I'm happy enough to accept that I know ♥♥♥♥-all about modern technological capabilities).  And STILL I die, again and again and again.  I don't know WHY I do, but I do.  There's a bit in the game's instructions which says something about Sophie occasionally attacking because she simply "doesn't like you".  Well, apparently she ♥♥♥♥ing HATED ME, because she assailed me left, right, and centre.  No reprieve.  No logic.  Just sudden, random, rampant doom.

Don't get me wrong, I actually quite liked this one.  There's something at least slightly more assured about it than the likes of, say, Emily Wants to Play.  But I'm getting a bit sick of this recent run of horror games where sheer, dumb-arsed LUCK seems to play such a large part in how long you survive before the next fatal "jump-scare" comes your way.  I'm sure a plethora of fan-boys and fan-girls will slap up guides in no time, telling me what you have to do at each and every different hour and blah-blah-blah, but unless I can actually work this♥♥♥♥♥♥out for myself, it's not exactly LOGICAL, is it now?

I honestly look forward to all you people proving me wrong, at which point I'll revise this review and the below-given rating.  Please, tell me how my faculties are flawed, and by that I don't mean write♥♥♥♥♥♥like "dude, everyone knows that 11pm is the time when Sophie attacks you if you hang around too long at generator C", because unless the game clearly tells me this, IT ISN'T LOGICAL.  Please, thumb me down and tell me I'm wrong, but also tell me WHY I'm wrong.  Hell, even the first FNAF plays reasonably fair for at least the first few nights, but this game gave me almost no delusion of "control" over my fate whatsoever.

I've played a LOT of horror games in my time.  And almost all the "old" ones - I'm even talking up to Outlast and Alien: Isolation here! - give you sufficient indication of what you have to do to survive, then the rest is up to you.  This super-recent, post-FNAF breed of game seems to believe that &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥happens" can pass for good game design.  I beg to differ.  Having said all this, I think the dev of this game shows tremendous potential, he just needs to emulate a better - nay, FAIRER - kind of game in future.
This is far from the worst of its species, but it's also not the best, and until someone (including Scott Cawthon himself) makes a game as good as Freddy's the first, we really should just put a cork in all games of this type for the time being, whad'ya say?  (Or failing that, ♥♥♥♥wits like me could just stop buying them, haha.)  Looking forward to that veritable assault of "tips" from all you super-savvy fan-persons out there...

Verdict: 6.5/10.
UPDATE: Well, here we are a bit over a month later, and credit where credit is due...this dev has laboured long and hard to give the gaming public a much improved experience.  And, I'm pleased to say, he's MOSTLY succeeded.  We now have two difficulty levels - though the easier of the two is still much too hard in my humble opinion - and while the "random" death element has been ostensibly removed, and "cheap" deaths are far less common, I still can't help but feel that there are moments when you're damned-if-you-do-and-damned-if-you-don't, and I certainly still feel that save-points are too few and far between (once every hour would be more than challenging enough, especially for the allegedly "easy" version of the game).  Whichever way you look at it, I'm happy to concede that this is by far one of the best games of its type - i.e. the some-strategy/some-luck/jumpscare-game-with-minimal-mechanics sub-genre - though it would appear that the first Five Nights at Freddy's is destined to remain the king of its kind.  As with that game, however, I'm probably destined to never find the nerve and/or patience to fully "beat" this one, but in light of the dev's improvements I'm more than happy to adjust my rating to read (drum roll, please):
REVISED VERDICT: 7.5/10.
SECOND UPDATE: Well, I gotta hand it to Eddie the dev...after the initial doubts of myself and many other reviewers, he's worked long and hard at this little game of his, and he's finally managed to make it fair to the point where even the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ likes of yours truly can now complete the darned thing (granted, on the easiest difficulty)! I'm now willing to go on record and state that this is, in my opinion, a rival for the second-best game of its type, after the first Five Nights at Freddy's. Congrats, sir, and I hope you get some kind of Dev of the Year award for this commendable effort. ♥♥♥♥ing good game...finally.
RE-REVISED VERDICT: 9/10 (by far the biggest score hike I've given a game...EVER).

I really can't recommend this game enough.  It's not perfect, but it tells a damn good story, has a lot of fun but generally not frustrating puzzles, and looks fantastic.  It also has one of the best endings of any game I've played.
Honestly, my only complaints are that the driving segments were a little too frustrating and the game occasionally got a bit too cartoony given its generally weighty subject matter.  This was particularly true early in the game during various showdowns with a German Baron that played more like a parody than the rather dark material that the game covers during most other segments.
I really loved how the game included actual facts about the war into the menu system for each level.  It gives a sense of perspective to the events that occur, while also providing framework for what the characters are doing.  There is very little dialogue in the game, only during the occasional cut-scene, and so these tidbits really provide depth to the experience.  You can also find collectibles in each level that give additional little facts about the war, the people who fought in it, and the items they left behind.  Finally, the various playable characters (and one who isn't playable but is central to the narrative) have diary entries that you can read as you go through the story that add a bit more to their characterization.  It's nothing too deep, but it's a fine added touch.
And again, the ending is absolutely fantastic.

Valiant hearts is a very interesting and unique game because it depicts the First World War in a handdrawn art style. The game somehow manages to be both very silly and grounded in reality at the same time which is quite an accomplishment. It has characters that you care for and want to see them pull through. This game is a great history lesson for people who don’t know much about the first World War as the game depicts most of the events that happened during the war with the characters themselves experiencing it firsthand. As for the gameplay itself its very simplistic, I wasn’t a fan of the puzzles because they do bring the story to a halt and it forces you to get past a few obstacles before you continue on with the story. It can get frustrating at times when you are looking for a specific Item that you have missed in the area that you need to progress and it kind ruins the whole pacing of the game. It’s not necessarily a very fun game to play because the gameplay is very hit and miss and it’s not compelling in any way because it’s so simple but the story and characters pull you through until the end very easily.

There is a lot to like about this game, but it's a bit too grindy.
You can make your own adventures and quests with a level editor, which is very nice. There are many player-made adventures to play through, which adds to the gameplay content. Some of these adventures are not that great and for one achievement you need to do 500 adventures... which is a bit too much because you've experienced much of what the game has offered at around the 200 mark.
This brings me to the point about grinding - leveling up is very slow. Even with a few XP modifiers on your items it takes many adventures to level up once. Monsters give anywhere between a few XP to 36ish XP at around level 19 while you need about 2000 and said monsters have high health (needing up to 70+ shuriken hits each when there are many at once).
Indeed, in many adventures the enemies come in too big quantities and have too much health. They have to be kited for a good while and when the two things (xp and kiting) are combined you get this tedious leveling system.
Many of the weapons have so low range that only certain ranged weapon and long range melee weapons can perform well. For example, using daggers on moving enemies causes you to miss if you try to attack them from behind and axes only tend to hit one target for average damage when you could be using a hammer for AoE and higher single target DPS. Axes have the advantage of being able to use a shield, but using a shield is almost useless when enemies follow the first enemy they see, you can roll to evade and the shield is destroyed rather quickly.
The class abilities are fine, I guess. Each class feels different and the game is fun to play in local or online co-op (online multiplayer is almost dead).
Almost forgot - the game's soundtrack is pretty good, but the dragon boss fight is extremely disappointing. You can't properly evade its almost instant attacks and have to try again...100+ times.
I would recommend the game as something to play in local co-op for a good while.

I had almost exclusively played turn-based strategy games or slow RTS games with empire-building, resource gathering, etc. before I saw this for sale secondhand at a very cheap price and decided to try it. Bear in mind my review is that of a rank amateur, but someone who has played this particular game all the way through several times, on Steam and off.
If there is anyone else out there like me, someone who doesn't enjoy fast-paced first-person shooter games but still wants a *little* bit of real-time pressure on your game play, this is a great game for that. The learning curve is pretty short, considering this type of game was unfamiliar to me. The post-apocalyptic setting is at time humorous and never takes itself  too seriously. By today's standards the animation is a little clunky, and graphics processing a bit cumbersome.
This was possibly the first game I've ever played where friendly fire was a real danger. At first it was frustrating that I couldn't expect my PC's to shoot around each other, but then it simply became a natural part of the tactical challenge. (Why would I ever realistically expect NOT to be injured when someone standing right behind me opens up with a .50 cal in my direction?)
For anyone working on third-person sequels to this: please do something about the ladders and stairs. Make them more  fluid and accessible. I've had many a player character shot to pieces because the computer can't figure out how to send two of them down a wide staircase at the same time!

Played for free during the free 3-day period.
A luck/strategy board game where you choose a hero and try to complete your goal before time runs out in ~9 days (18 turns because of day/night cycles) and before your 3 opponents. Very nice sound/visuals and a couple animated story cutscenes.
There are three ways to win:
It's complex in a simple way. There are a bunch of simple mechanics that you have to learn but because they're pretty straight-forward it doesn't take that long to understand.
There are four core stats (each hero has a total of 16 points plus a passive ability): Fight (Combat), Body (HP), Wits (Card hand size), and Spirit (MP). There are six things to keep track of: Gold (for playing certain cards), Prestige (for the win condition/for choosing daily global effects), Cards (Actions/Equipment/Followers), Spirit Stones (for the win condition), Rot/Corruption level (basically lose hp but gain attack), and King's Bounty (Extra gold/prestige rewards on death & more targetted by guards).
The King is surrounded by palace tiles (which have Wits/Spirit traps/perils) and defended by Palace Guards (where Fight/Body to helpful in combat). Because the King loses 1 HP per day, it feels like you prepare for the first several turns and then rush the king at the final few turns.
This game is pretty RNG-heavy; stats determine how successful you are at challenges and heroes generally start with stats of 4-6 points (meaning 40-60% chances of success). The only way (I believe) to permanently increase stats is by doing quests that take several turns to reach. There are some card effects that temporarily increase stats (and some equipment cards that do as long as you use them) but you have to be lucky in drawing the right card.
In online multiplayer, on top of the RNG there's the human-BS factor. You're not going to find a 'fair' gaming experience all of the time. Whether by malice or ignorance, people will often group up and not take down the biggest threat to win, ensuring that solo players have little chance (unless blessed by RNG) to win and that those in the lead can sometimes just coast to victory.
It's a tough thing to address and I don't think the devs will address it based on no dev comments on a relevant Steam thread.
It happens in other non-1v1 games, too. For example, in any non-1v1 RTS/TBS game you could arrange an alliance before the game started, giving you an advantage against people who had to do actual diplomacy in-game. Or you could take a harsher route and make a 3-person game with a partner where the whole point was to make the stranger's life miserable.
The only thing you can do against this type of thing is play with a circle of friends that share the same game values and want the same game experience as you. Public games are like solo queue in League of Legends: you never know who you're going to get matched up with and you'll have terrible game experiences once in a while. If you don't have a gaming group then you have to do the public game gauntlet and create your own group by collecting Armello-friends to play with.
Single-player mode was fun enough to learn the game and face opponents who you know are just wandering around, randomly(?) fighting and questing until the king is low enough and then they to get the last hit. I've never seen them actually go for a Spirit Stone victory but I haven't played enough games to see. After playing 100% Orange Juice, public multiplayer games against randoms wasn't my type of thing. At least it's not as RNG-heavy and snowbally as that game (100% Orange Juice). This game has less rage-inducing/helpless moments than I remember that one had.
Worth a look if you like board games with a good amount of luck involved (card draw, die rolling, random events) and can handle winning and losing that way.

This is the game about war, its cruelty, love, friendship, death and normal people whose lives were destroyed by the rock of ages. So why you should play it? Let me tell you.
The game is set into the time of the Great War, WWI. This topic is interesting enough. But that is not where it stops. You are not playing as a heroic Rambo character. You are a man/woman made out of flesh who might get killed by shrapnel, bullet, falling tree or whatever. Pulsing eye and standing in the cover for a moment will not heal you. You are not professional soldier, you were born to work in peace and love, not to shoot. Like most of us. You are Émile, an aged man and French farmer. You are Karl, a young man of German origin and husband of Émile's daughter. You are Anna, a young Belgian nurse. And you are Freddy, an American guy who took part in this war to make revenge. Why? You have to play that. Ah, and one additional character which is not human. You will find out.
The story of Valiant Hearts is the main reason why you should play this piece. There are episodes from the battlefield, but also from another locations, e.g. Paris or training ground. Oh, and there are also Fast and Furious: WWI! In addition, the storyline is not fictional. It is based on the real events and real letters which were sent by the people captured in that madness. This is developed even more with varied items you might pick in each level. These might be helmets, tunafish tins, letters, etc. Every item has its own story which is written in the special menu. It brings me to another point - educational dimension of this game. Although I thought in know much about the WWI, I found out that this was simply not true. I also realized that the WWI is UNJUSTLY played down by the WWII because of its dynamics, warmachines etc. But the subject of the WWI has much to offer! Personally, I would demonstrate the topic of the WWI  taught in schools on this game. Like a homework and lead the discussion about it. How lovely does it sound: Playable homework...
Now something about graphics and soundtrack. Both are perfect. I love the UbiArt engine. I loved that in Rayman: Origins and I continue in loving it. In my opinion, this artsy engine played an indisputably positive role in this game. The soundtrack is mainly sad (thanks to that war, I suppose) but also cute and makes the atmosphere complete.
Conclusion...finally, you definitely think. Well, I think that I made myself clear on this topic - I loved this game and I completely recommend it. For Europeans it should be obligatory, but since there are wars wherever in this world. it should be played there where a war was or may occure. We shall not forget. 93/100.
PS: Point about the purchase. I bought this game 50 percent sale for 8 euros. This is the price definitely worth it. Normal price of 15 euros is the borderline. If it was 12 euros, it would be much better.

Developed and published by NodziGames, Gal-X-E is a shoot’em-up game from 2016 that does not stray too far from the already established arcade shooting formula we’ve seen again and again.

Not much can be said of Gal-X-E, that you couldn’t find already in dozens other Sci-fi arcade shooters. Perhaps that’s the biggest problem here. Not being able to stand out at all. If you played such games over the years, you’re not gonna miss absolutely nothing by skipping this. Do not get me wrong. It’s not a broken game. The gameplay is smooth and the mechanics themselves are fully functional. But is simply drags on and leaves much to be desired. You have unlockable ships and a leveling system to remind you of some form of progress. But without leaderboards or a multiplayer mode, what’s the purpose in the end?

The graphical details are standard 2D fare with some color and sprite  diversity to it but still looking like a bland mobile port. I wasn’t impressed and not even bored afterall. Just played it along, waiting for it to show any signs of innovation. None to be found, sadly.

To say the sounds are generic and repetitive would be an understatement. I preferred in fact, to mute them altogether and listen to my own selection of music tracks.

+ Steam Trading Cards
+ Decently priced

- Subpar sounds
- No Achievements

If it wasn’t for the perfectly functional side of the game and it’s Trading Cards for a decent price, I would have rate it below 6 and thus stop recommending it. This is the dev team’s second game on Steam and glancing over their debut, it looks just as generic as this one. You’re not going to regret not picking them up, unless you wish to support their future (and hopefully better) projects. I hope my constructive criticism isn’t mistaken for anything other than what it is. And do continue supporting indie devs. The gaming scene would be far worse than bleak without them.

My love for Indie horror games and such has led me to every corner of steam trying to find new good games to play and support and this one grabbed my attention the day it was released!
Sophie's Curse uses human being's natural fear of the unkown and possibly one of the most terrifying ambiances I have ever seen in all my years of gaming.
The Story
As it stands right now, you are the caretaker of an old man (who is fast asleep throughout the night) and you have to stay there and watch over him. Every 2 hours there is a checkpoint saving your progress as you go onto each 2 hour interval. The only form of electricity are four small hand-cranked devices that you spin to keep the battery from running out, occasionally the machines fail and have to be restarted via the laptop in the kitchen. All the while something isnt right with the house, an angry spirit for reasons unknown wants your booty and you have to keep the lights on and stay in the designated "safe zone" whenever possible to avoid getting your booty torn open by said spirit.
The game itself
Very terrifying, I wont compare it to other games because truly it is unique in its own right. It is a mixture of 1st person and point and click mechanics which works very well for what you are trying to do in the game.  The controls are very simple and easy to adjust to.
How is it terrifying? If the "Dead ghost girl" horror cliche doesnt spook you, the flickering lights, dark atmosphere and insanely horrifying ambiance this game has to offer will. It is quite possibly one of the scarriest games I have come across, the only downside is it relies alot on jumpscares and loud noises to set the atmosphere, but that can be overlooked in this case.
I would recommend this to anyone who enjoys a good scare and doesnt mind a few interesting puzzles, and micromanaging through the terror. Very good game and I cant wait to see what the creator does in the future, good luck and goodnight everyone!
EDIT: In future updates I would love to see new gamemodes, maybe even a difficulty setting, new enemies ect, and please please PLEASE add an options menu to adjust the resolution, graphics and audio.

In all honesty, I don't understand people who've downvoted this game because it's "just another platformer" with no unique elements whatsoever.
It literally says in the description that what you get is "a classic 2D platformer with old school gameplay - no puzzles, no punishment, just 100% pure classic platforming fun! Its most prominent features are HD visuals and beautiful hand-drawn art." Nowhere does it say that you'll get more than what you pay for. And, believe me, at a 4,99€ price tag, Oozi is well worth the investment, plus it's often on sale.
A decent platformer with 4 difficulty settings to choose from. I'm playing this game on the "hardcore" setting (this is apparently the right setting for experienced platformer players) and it does provide a nice scale of difficulty. You start every level with only one "energy bar" so if you get hit, it's game over... Well, not literally, as you restart the game from the latest checkpoint. Also, the game encourages you to collect as many stars as possible (plus 5 secret stars that unlock a challenge level), since they give you points, and you get an energy bar for every 2000 points. So, you're not collecting said stars for high scores alone.
There are 4 worlds (5 quite longish levels + boss level each), plus challenge levels, plus arcade levels. Also, the controls are amazingly responsive, which cannot be said for some high-budget platformers out there. All in all, a worthy title if you're in it for the platforming elements (like I am), and nothing else!

The episodes from Liberty City are alot like the expansions to the original Half Life game, both add a lot to the story of the original game, and add a good deal of new content as well.
The Lost MC Campaign: This story follows the Lost MC biker gang as their second in command (the player) is trying to keep the gang alive and prospering while the current leader is using the members for his own purposes. The levels throughout this offer alot of action and an interesting mechanic of staying in formation with your other bikers when riding. It reveals other perspectives to the main story of GTA 4 and gives plenty of backstory on characters that were not touched to much before. There are also a few new weapons in this and some fun motorcycles to ride, which oddly enough were easier to control than in GTA 4.
The Ballad of Gay Tony: This campaign shows you the life and empire of the club owner Gay Tony and his right hand man Luis (the plater). Everything from this type of campaign is present from drugs, to shootouts, and club adventures. This campaign does a decent job of exploring a few select characters backgrounds and offers tons of new weapons to try out throughout the game. The missions in this campaign are a lot more fun as the introduction of the parachute is present allowing you to jump out of helicopters and high rise buildings to escape danger. I would consider this campaign to be alot more fun gameplay wise than The Lost MC, while The Lost MC offers more story wise.
Both campaigns are phenominal, and short enough to keep you entertained while playing and long enough to enjoy them all the way though.

Gal-X-E was released on the 14th of May, 2016, and was developed and published by NodziGames. It's genres are Sci-Fi, Shoot-em-Up, Indie, and action.
Gal-X-E is a Sci-Fi shoot em up, and resembles what you might have seen in an arcade back when those were the cultural norm.
Enemy space ships, asteroids, flying garbage and... well, an eyeball that shoots missiles at you willrandomly spawn and attempt to kill you. Some are indirect and shoot in random directions, while others will target you and attempt to shoot you down.
As you play Gal-X-E, you will collect scrap which you could use to unlock better ships, in a fashion similar to unboxing in CS:GO or TF2. You use your scrap and unbox new ships, however, you can still unbox a ship you already own, effectively wasting your hard earned scrap, just like in CS:GO or TF2, only the ship is a crappy item and the scrap is your real money. Anyway, off topic.
From what I could tell, there is no storyline to Gal-X-E, your sole goal is to survive for as
long as you can. I myself am not good at Gal-X-E, however, I could not find any boss fights, which would have been very beneficial to the overall enjoyment of the game.
The graphics for Gal-X-E are very cartoony, but games in this genre all seem to have very basic graphics, not that cartoonish graphics are a problem. The controls feel very smooth and don't stick, leading to a very nice experience during gameplay.
There is one obvious downside to the game which the other reviews on steam don't the audio. The sound effects are decent and very fitting with the sci-fi genre, however, the soundtrack is, unfortunately, unoriginal. Like Girlfriend Rescue, another game I reviewed, the music used is creative commons. However, in Girlfriend Rescue, there was orchestral music that was ill fitting, but in Gal-X-E, the music is very fitting with the theme and is actually music that I like. Where does the music come from? NoCopyrightSounds, my favourite record label. One song I could easily recognize which was used in Gal-X-E is called Frag Out by DJ Assassin, and if you own Gal-X-E, listen to the soundtrack and compare some of the songs to those on NoCopyrightSounds.
Some suggestions I'd make to the game, although they aren't downsides, are that if I were the developer I'd include a pause screen, perhaps an online leaderboard (since the only game mode is survival), and steam achievements for completionists.
Gal-X-E is an interesting take on the bullet hell genre. It's a survival bullet hell that has an interesting unlock system for upgrades. I recommend Gal-X-E for those who enjoy bullet hell games, however, I highly suggest you check out
instead.

Gal-X-E is a space shoot em’ up/bullet hell game in asteroid style gameplay. The game is very difficult as is expected from a bullet hell game. It’s very basic, it doesn’t try to do something fancy.  There’s a lot of ships to unlock and each one plays differently, so depending on your playstyle you can choose your ship accordingly.
The graphics are pretty simple and sharp, colors are decent and for a space shooter surprisingly good looking. Usually space shooters look dull but not this one. The one problem I have with the graphics is the 4:3 ratio, seriously add an option for 16:9 ratio. This make the whole screen has black borders on the sides. Another problem is the lack of pause, seriously, why would you not include a pause feature is beyond me.
The music in this game is very good, most of the soundtracks are really good and pleasant on the ears. The sounds of the ships, guns and kills are also good and will remind you of the 8-bit era shoot em’ ups.
The game play is very simple. This game is addictive as hell as once I started playing I couldn’t put it down for quite some time. It’s one of those games which are so simple but super addictive, think Flappy bird, you just keep coming back for more and more. The game starts off reasonable but as you keep playing the difficulty keeps increasing, it even says so in-game “Difficulty up”. So as you keep playing more and more enemies will spawn and more bullets will start flying everywhere. The game will score you but there are no leaderboards, this sort of game requires that in my opinion.
You start off with one basic ship. There are 6 categories of ships. Light, medium, heavy, shotgun, sniper and chaingun. The ships speed/weapon power/gun type depends on which type of ship you choose, for example playing with a Sniper ship will have 1 very powerful shot then after a second or so you can shoot again. The Heavy Ship will have heavy rate of fire but a bit slow to move around.
You unlock more ships as you progress through the game. Since every ship that’s purchasable through the hanger requires scrap. These scraps can be collected by playing the game and kill enemy ships. Furthermore, there are 4 tiers of ships you can buy. Common, uncommon, rare and legendary. The common ships are the ones you start off with and to buy the other 3 tiers’ ships you will need to level up. For uncommon you need to level up to level 10, for rare, level 25 and for legendary, level 50.  This is a lot of grinding and in my opinion I lost interest in the Rare and legendary items. There’s a total of 24 ships which includes 1 of each type of ship in 1 of each tier.
There’s a large variety of enemies too, there’s an eyeball shooting huge bullets at you, astroids, invisible ships which can be only shot down when the re-appear briefly, non-shooting dashing ships, ships with random bullet spread shooting etc.  The enemies drop these stars which you can pick up to increase your score. Even if you go near them your ship should pick them up like a magnet.  If you don’t pick them up they will disappear. So, there Is a neat little risk/reward thing going on with this system. Some gameplay can be found below:
All in all, a very decent game and will give you plenty of entertainment. If you don’t mind grinding a lot you can also unlock new, much powerful ships. There's a lot that can be improves but the game is currently 49% off and at this price it’s a bargain.

Gal-X-E strives is a old school shoot em' up, developed and published by NodziGames. It seems that the game has a fair amount of content that is inside the game, however there are some issues with the game that doesn't really make it fun to play.
The gameplay itself focuses on only a single game mode, which is fine since this game is suppose to follow the kind of arcade style. Upon entering the game there is only one objective for you to accomplish, which is to basically shoot everything and get the highest possible score. That's it, now I feel like some people would argue that this isn't enough for a game but I feel like it is only fitting for the game to have one gamemode since it is following the arcade styled shoot em up.
I feel like this game had a lot going for it, I actually thought that the game was in Early Access when I first got to the main screen. Why? Well for a arcade shoot em up game like this your main focus would be to have a leaderboard to compete against your friends and others against the world. This game doesn't have this feature unfortunately, and therefore I feel like the game is lacking in that sense. I don't really feel the need to play more than I should because I only have my own high score to beat, in some games beating your own highscore is enough to make you play more of the game than you initially intended. But this game just feels like it really, really needs a leaderboard. I feel like without this essential leaderboard that the game itself hasn't got much replay value at all.
One of the main feature a game should have is the ability to have a pause menu. Well this game doesn't have that. Why I really don't know, but it just missing from the game. So if you are in the middle of a run doing really well but you need to take a break well your out of luck. Seriously please add a pause button for this game.
Something that they added to the game was the ability to level up and the large amount of ships that you can be. The ships have different types of shooting, so some of them have just a spray of bullets, while others are more accurate like the sniper class that has high attack but low reload speed. So the game is really nice in the way that there is a lot of different types of ships. This seems good, until you actually realise what you have to do in order to unlock all of these ships...
Now how does leveling up have to do with unlocking ships? Well the way that you obtain ships is by gather enough scrap, which you obtain by destroying enemies, and going to the Hanger and buying a ship. There are 4 different types that you can buy. Common, Uncommon, Rare and Legendary. You will only be able to buy from the Common pack to start with, in order to unlock the others well you will have to level up. Uncommon lv. 10, Rare lv. 25 and Legendary lv. 50. Now seeing as I have been playing this game for about 2.4 hours I am only just turning level 10. I'm not in the slightest bit motivated to unlock the other ship packs. I feel like this just drags the game on and forces you to play loads to unlock everything.
The graphics of this game are somewhat standard, the background when you play is just a still image. I personally would've really expected maybe twinkling of some of the stars so that it adds a bit of life to the game all together, The sprites of the ships are good, seem a bit plain at times but mostly all good.
The music of this game is a bit weird, sometimes the music would really suit the game that suits this type of gameplay sort of fast paced. While other times I feel like the music is just weird and really doesn't suit the gameplay at all. This is mostly for the music in-game. While on the other hand the music on the menu screen is a really nice opening to the game itself.
+ Nice retro styled shoot em up
+ Only one gamemode (a pro in my opinion following the traditional retro feel to the game)
+ Lots of different types of ships
+ Sprites of the ships are nice
- Needs a leaderboard
- Unlocking ships requires you to be a certain level
- Low replay ability
- No pause button...
The final verdict of this game, it seemed before I played this game that it was going to be a very fun and addictive arcade shoot em up. I guess my expectations were too high, the game is fun if you play it for short intervals but it gets fairly repetitive over a long period of time. The game does, however, have a nice variety of ships and a nice retro feel to the game. Overall, I would recommened this game if you are a fan of arcade shoot em up.

Drizzlepath: Glass is the 4th Tonguc Bodur game I've played (after Drizzlepath, Drizzlepath: Genie and Bottle) and I can see the improvement, in my opinion this is his best game so far.
There is more gameplay here, simple tasks and easy puzzles but this interactivity makes it really enjoyable. The graphics are nice, dreamy and realistic at the same time.
The story is quite captivating with a twist.
There were some interesting new elements such as the modern environment, the hallucination or the „horror house”, all nicely done.
The length of the game is ideal I think, the original Drizzlepath was too short, Genie felt too long (compared to the depth of its story), but Glass took just the right amount of time for me (as did Bottle).
The music is actually nice, fits the actual mood, relaxing when needed and sinister when you explore spooky areas, adds to the tension.
I enjoyed the monologues of the protagonist, she was a good choice for the voice-over.
And at last but not least: there were no platforming jumping puzzles, for which I am grateful, those were the only things I didn't like in the other games.
So if you like story driven, pretty walking simulators that also have some dark vibes, you probably will like this one.

A cute little game that I'd like to recommend, but as it is at the moment, it is somewhat unpolished.
I've so far got to the first boss, but it doesn't seem to be possible to beat him as soon as you get to him, unless I'm missing some trick.  Even if you've got one of the upgrades (and only one is possible to afford after a single runthrough of the four levels prior to him), he still kills you before you seem to be making any progress.  You can damage him for sure, but there's no indication of how much damage he still needs to take, so your efforts feel unconvincing.
The only option then seems to be to grind the four prior levels for coins to afford more upgrades - and I didn't expect to have to grind in a simple platformer like this.
There's also a few small glitches which make the game a little underwhelming to play - jumping near a ceiling is a little jerky for some reason, pausing very briefly on the upwards part, and colliding with the front of a moving platform causes things to pause again, until it finally delivers you to the floor (or spikes), and the platform is then delayed, which can make jumping between them more difficult.  And just hope you don't fall between two that are about to meet each other - you get stuck, and have to restart the level...!
There's also the small matter that once you break urns, you have to go a short distance away from the coins and then back again to be able to pick the coins up, which can be the difference between escaping enemies, and dying to them.
The artstyle is really nice however, and the "fallen city" concept interesting (if I could discover more of the story), and the simplistic take is refreshing - I hope it gets a few patches in the near future to address these issues, as otherwise this would be a pretty fun and relaxing game to play!

Although it was not long ago it released on Steam, Sven Co-op has been in the history of Half-Life since almost the beginning. It started as a Half-Life modification released in 1999. With the help of the community, it became one of the best Half-Life modifications ever released. The possibility to play the legendary story of Gordon Freeman co-op with friends was something incredible for its time. Not only that but there are hundreds of maps made specifically for this modification, creating an experience without limits... if you live in North America.
You see, if you live elsewhere it's most likely that there aren't server being hosted there anymore. Fun didn't last long for people like me who live in South America. I was able to play for some months until the servers were took down, perhaps due to the lack of interest shown by the community. Right now I'm writing this review being unable to play, so I guess you could call it a goodbye to this game. Now let's get to the technical aspects.
This is a game with undefined plot. Not because it's vague but because it depends on the map you play. Each map has its own story. You may even require other players to beat some maps. Despite that Sven Co-op has the original Half-Life campaign I can't take it into account since this analysis is about Sven Co-op, not Half-Life.
Gameplay is something that Half-Life defined in the industry when it was released, it marked a before and after in the history of video games. Sven Co-op inherits those elements and expands them even further with all its additional content (weapons, addons, maps). It's a pretty agile game to play, and despite being fast it doesn't go to the level of DOOM. Getting used to the controls takes very little time because of how simple they are.
The graphics aren't too different from the original Half-Life release. For its time they were considered excellent and even now they don't look bad at all. They have this special classic charm that personally I love.
The sounds are also the same although you may hear new sounds depending on the map you're playing. I guess it goes without saying that the sound and musical scope of the original campaign is simply outstanding.
In conclusion this is a game that I wish I could've played more. I don't think I've played the necessary to feel satisfied, but to think about all the missed opportunities.
It does really provide enough to have some funny moments, even more if you play this with friends. If you live in North America or any location that's still hosting servers I really suggest you to get this game, it's worth it. However, from my part I can't give a veredict based on more than my own experience.

GTA: Episodes from Liberty City is an expandalone (Standalone Expansion Pack) of GTA IV. They are a two-in-one game, with two sides of one story.
On one hand you have The Lost biker gang having gang and family issues, and on the other hand you are Luis Lopez, a part-time bodyguard at Maisonette 9, one of the biggest nightclubs in Liberty City.
I will be covering The Ballad of Gay Tony first, as I found it most enjoyable.
TBoGT has the most enjoyable missions in any GTA game ever, in my opinion. They are all action packed, interesting and never some sort of escort mission, or "drive there and come back" type of mission. If you've ever played GTA:SA then think of the mission where you board the cargo plane, "Stowaway". Now, multiply that mission about 30 times and you have TBoGT in a nutshell.
You get to own interesting and very fun weapons and vehicles such as huge capacity machineguns and... actually I won't spoil any more, I will just say that you will have fun, GUARANTEED, if you have one of those weapons equipped, or you are driving/piloting any of the special, new vehicles. Most of the new vehicles, if not all of them have been copy and pasted into GTA V, as they were too much fun!
The story of TBoGT is a bit lacking, but it's enough there to keep you going. The characters in the story, though, are the most crazy and insane in any GTA game ever! There is not one main story cutscene that doesn't involve someone really high on drugs, half-naked or drunk as♥♥♥♥♥♥ You just can't hold in a laugh every time a cutscene rolls!
Buuut, here comes the sad and disappointing part of the pack... The Lost and Damned.
Now, this might be a bit of a swayed opinion, but The Lost and Damned was just too boring for me. The first initial missions involve you riding with your gang, informing the player about who is who. The leader of the gang just got out of jail and you are picking up his custom bike from the shop. That's the intro, really, and it's a boring, long intro of just driving. The dialogue kinda made up for it, as it was semi-interesting. It is nice to hear the bikers talk to each other when they are in proximity.
You still get some extra weapons that you don't get to use in TBoGT, and even some vehicles, but nothing really stands out. There's a sawed-off double barrel shotgun that is incredibly useful at knocking off enemy bikers, as it only needs one pellet to do so, but it's inaccurate as hell and requires you to be at point blank range. I find melee to be more fun at that time. TBoGT has set the bar for that sort of stuff, and TLaD is nowhere near reaching it.
If you really enjoyed GTA IV's narrative and atmosphere, you might enjoy TLaD because it is much more slow and story-driven.
In the end, it's weird that it was packaged with a much more "mindless fun" type of game as TBoGT.
I will rate both parts of the expansions separately, but the game is so cheap now you might as well just buy it for one and have the other as a sort of nice bonus.
TLaD: 5/10 - Generally boring, uninteresting, but has its good bits, and come on it's still a GTA game!
TBoGT: 9/10 - Definitely takes the cake as it never gets boring until the end of the story.
(I have not touched upon the technical issues such as GFWL and such, but there is a mod called x_live_less (remove "_", Steam censors the name for some reason) that removes GFWL and may help you with any issues. I managed to play the game start to finish with GFWL installed and updated no problem, but this may be different for you. Keep in mind Steam refunds are a thing, and do not let this sway you from the purchase of this amazing expandalone!)

This is a competently made platformer which I can tell the developer put a lot of work into. The music is quite lovely, the coloring and smoothness of the graphics/art style are very nice and pleasing to the eye. Unlike some of the clunkier controls of many games on Steam, jumping around feels quite smooth. It is a very well-made game, and even contains minimal story elements in the form of 1-2 panel very brief/simple little comics. In fact, you get pieces of your spacesuit back after certain levels, which give you new abilities like smashing and bopping enemies you've stunned, which is nice as far as having things change a little as the game goes on. Before, metal-armored snailed couldn't be defeated, but with the stomp equipment, I could kill them instantly. Nice!
That said, the game itself got a bit stale for me. Each area is divided into (as I recall) 5 full levels with plenty of platforming, followed by a boss fight. The first couple of levels, things were just dandy, but by the time I was on the fourth level, I was a bit tired of the woods. The fifth level was more woods, and the boss fight, of course, was in the woods. The next few levels are set in caves with some ice, chain hoops, and wall-jumping, which were nice additions, but the platforming alone couldn't keep my interest. Choosing whether I should recommend the game or not was a huge dilemma to me. After all, the game is nowhere close to being actually bad. I would rate it as a huge "neutral", sadly it's not an option.
I got the game recommended by a few of my friends who told me it's amazing and loaded with feels. I downloaded it almost immediately as the screenshots looked very promising and I have to say that I love indie games.
I launched the game and fully focused on it, trying to get the maximum experience. At first it was a bit boring and I felt like the game and the story will become better soon. Sadly it never happened.
The story itself is rather sad and the game indeed is depressing. Despite this, it didn't move me at all. The game was very short, way too short to get immersed in the story and get to know the characters. I didn't have the feeling that those people actually "exist" - it's hard to explain, but playing video games, I perceive the characters as actual people. This never happened here.
I had a feeling my choices didn't matter at all. I couldn't relate to the protagonist as his personality seemed to be set from the beginning. I expected being able to include "myself" in this game, but all the answers you could choose from were basically the same. You don't feel like you control the game. It was comparable to a boring visual novel.
I barely finished the game, although as you can see I only played 30 minutes. It was enough to finish it and I don't plan on playing it again.
I would sadly suggest finding something else to spend your time on. This game is free, but it's not enough to save it from a negative review. I was disappointed, but if you especially like heart-breaking stories you might enjoy this game. I would say it would be a good choice for people who are very emotional and enjoy very, very slow paced games.

This is one of those games that is special. It isn't perfect, nor is it amazing, but it's definitely special. The concept is simple, your typical Diablo clone (though it feels more like Gauntlet) with a bit of Little Big Planet.
There isn't a whole lot of Little Big Planet influenced content. For example, the way you can customize your character is limited. You find loot and you wear it. The loot makes your character both look different as well boosts some stats, enable some abilities, etc. Little Big Planet wins hard by character customization. As far as level creation goes, it wins as far as I can tell. Maybe it doesn't win by content, for Little Big Planet wins hands down as far as content you can mess with, but this game wins as far as control to the point you can actually make some pretty fun quests.
The gameplay is simplistic. You attack, you level up, you develop a play style, you get better, you attack more. You finish levels for loot, coins, and xp. Loot and coins can both be donated to a "shrine" in your home level (or pod, if you're thinking little big planet, but you cannot customize it like you could your pod in LBP). When you donate enough and then pray, you then unlock randomly options you can choose from such as a better item, stamina boost, health boost, inventory increase, etc.
There is one thing unique beyond all of this, you're doing all of this for one major objective. You are leveling yourself up and grinding for better items so you can fight a dragon. Shocker, a game called Fight the Dragon and it's all about fighting a dragon. The catch is that it has a lot of health, 1 million HP to be exact, and your goal is to fight it and deal as much damage as possible. If you die, the hp doesn'treset. You can die and come back later, continuing where you have left off. This is a cool, interesting, unique game feature.
Considering how low of a price this game is, the fact it still has a four pack, and how enjoyable it is, I'd say it's worth full price easily. If you want, you can easily wait for a sale where it goes nearly half off, which is an even more incredible deal. The game might not get 100 hours from me, but I'll get my money's worth.
