When Ty the Tasmanian Tiger was released, back in 2002, I was 12 years old. I missed out on it because I didn't own any "nextgen" video game consoles back then. That's a shame, 12-year-old me would have loved it way more than I like it now, and I do. This is a game that's good and worthwhile, but features some problems common to 3D platformers from back in its time which make it not as good as it had all the right to be.
The game follows the story of Ty, a Tasmanian tiger (well, duh) who is supposedly the last descendant from a proud tribe that fought off evil avian fiend Boss Cass, foiling his ultimate plan of obtaining the five talismans of unfathomable power in his attempt dethrone mammals from the top of the food chain to honor his dinosaur ancestry. The game itself kicks off with Ty casually playing hide and seek with his adoptive family of bilbies when, suddenly, he falls into a hole and meets the spirit of an odd sage of sorts. The spirit tells Ty about his ancestors' deeds, and that Boss Cass is trying to gather the talismans again, and that Ty is the only one who can stop Cass's evil plans. There's something rather charming and nostalgic about the pre-rendered cutscenes used in this game instead of in-engine cutscenes that are more common nowadays. I really enjoy those, if only for the retro feel alone. As a main character, Ty strikes me as an awesome, enthusiastic, energetic and brave marsupial that is always ready to run around, hop on difficult platforms and land his boomerang on every baddie's face.
To aid Ty in his quest, he counts with a roster of endearing NPC friends, all based on Australian animals, each with their own charmingly exaggerated cartoon-esque personality. In fully voice acted (take note, Yooka-Laylee) cutscenes, they tell Ty about small missions he has to accomplish in order to gather special tokens, as well as hints about the controls and the game's mechanics, and warnings about the evil fiends and hazards that Ty may need to face ahead of him. Every character has an awesome Australian accent which adds even more charm to this radical outback adventure, and every cutscene and dialog in the game is rich in silly yet endearing humor. Among the roster of characters, there's the aforementioned titular character, plus an old cockatoo named Maurie who sounds like a wise yet slightly crazy old man, a koala scientist named Julius who acts in a stereotypical nerdy way that's rather endearing, and an awesome handful of others. I particularly like the mysterious Sly, and it saddens me that the game's story didn't explore this character in more detail at all.
Speaking of outback, the overall graphical design in this game is spot on, in spite of the low tech nature of it. Sure, they may look way too polygonal, pointy and unappealing for today's standards, but they're nothing if not effective in capturing that neat Australian feel, in both the scenery and the characters. Rainbow Cliffs looks and feels like a spot on Australian scenery, and every level represents, in one way or another, some kind of landscape that one may encounter in Australia, except with awesome platforming and treacherous traps thrown in for good measure. In his journey, Ty will go through rainforests, the outback desert itself, snowy mountains, beaches, and many other kinds of natural landscapes that occur in Australia, and that makes for an epic thematic experience I really enjoy.
As far as sound goes, I like the voice acting and the sound effects, they're appropriately comical and cartoonish, and fit well with the atmosphere of the game. The dialogs are particularly funny, always featuring some comedic exchanges and overall endearingly cheesy personalities. The music is nice as well, going for a mix between relaxing guitar music and some Australian tribal instruments (like the didgeridoo), always sounding appropriately upbeat when needed, and more calm and contained when the situation calls for it. It's always catchy, though, and that's a plus in my book. As I write this, I have the Rainbow Cliffs song stuck in my head.
Speaking of Rainbow Cliffs, I find the way this game deals with level design rather interesting. Rainbow Cliffs serves as an "open world" area of sorts, full of tiny secrets to be uncovered and serving as a hub area to enter the levels as well as a safe, open space for you to test out your movement skills. The levels themselves are an interesting beast: while some 3D platformers from the past went for straight-up linear levels with maybe a few secret passages (like the original Crash Bandicoot or the PS1 Pac-Man game) and others went for the open-level fetch quest style (like, say, Super Mario 64 or Banjo-Kazooie), this game goes for a mix between the two approaches. Every level has a linear-ish path that the player may follow from beginning to end, but along the path there are some more open-ish places that players may want to explore in order to find special tokens, discover shortcuts and special areas, accomplish certain missions assigned to them by the NPCs or rescue some bilbie friends. This semi-linear approach is effective because you hardly ever feel lost (and even if you do, every level counts with a map that you can look at by pressing the menu button) but it still gives you something more to do than simply going straight from start to finish. The movement mechanics themselves work fine, and the individual sections of the levels are well designed to the point where it's fun to run, jump, battle, swim, glide and do whatever else you need to do to get them Thunder Egg thingies.
This semi-linear design, however, comes with a price that I can't overlook: it sometimes tries to force the player to follow the predetermined path in the cheapest ways possible, like invisible walls and twisty, redundant paths. It feels realy cheap to not be able to jump to something that's right in front of you because of a stupid invisible wall that's disguised as a handful of foresty-looking sprites. This kind of thing was way too common in platformers back in the day, limiting the player's exploration possibilities, and it throws me off a bit.
Now, one thing I really like about this game's overall mechanics is the "key-and-keyhole" aesthetic of acquiring new skills and applying them to open new paths. Whether it's gliding with two boomerangs, swimming, or any other skill that Ty may get to learn during the game, learning new skills in a level always opens up new possibilities, both in previous levels where something may have been out of reach (or just hard to reach) in your first visit, and in Rainbow Cliffs, where you're finally able to access a rainbow scale that you couldn't get to before, or a new set of levels to play in order to obtain some Thunder Eggs. The feeling of satisfaction you get when you obtain a new power that allows you to get to a place that you previously located but couldn't reach is one of the things I like the most in games, as it gives the experience a sense of progression that no other form of media has. I do feel like this aspect of the design should have been explored more than it was, maybe adding some extra secret stuff that you can only open with the right 'rang, but that could have alienated portions of the target audience that prefer their games to be straight-forward, it's okay that they chose not to do that.
Now, I know I complimented the level design a lot, and while it's definitely good, it is far from perfect. One huge problem I have are the bosses which, while mostly fun, may sometimes be pretty close to impossible to figure out on your own if you're dumb like me. I had to look up walkthroughs for three of the bosses, including the final battle one, and I can't help but assume this is a flaw of the game itself. I mean, I never had problems figuring out bosses in any other 3D platformer, so maybe this one didn't care to make the bosses intuitive to figure out.

You know, every so often a game or series of games by an indie developer crosses your path and you really just have to dive in and see what there is to see. With Tonguc's games, my fascination is also filled with admiration, and as I play my way through his catalog of games, I find the quality of craftsmanship to be elevated with each new entry. Drizzlepath was a cool experience, Drizzlepath: Genie built upon that experience while becoming more focused. Bottle was a master class in taking a single concept and remaining focused throughout. With Drizzlepath: Glass, his mastery over the graphics engine and gameplay has become as evident as has his willingness to deviate from established style while still staying within a very true representation of the walking simulator genre.
Tonguc wrote the story for Drizzlepath: Glass himself and I think the evolution of storytelling in Tonguc's games is definitely apparent here. This is a more mature and yet also less verbose effort. The stories in the previous games were interesting as well, but I felt Glass was more approachable (for me anyway).
Drizzlepath: Glass takes on the topic of death, grief, and mourning, and while I won't spoil the story here, I will say that there were some pretty cool twists and turns that will keep you interested and also provide at least two distinct "Oh ####" moments as well.
While I hadn't specifically noticed this in Tonguc's past games, what I realized here is that there is a subtle and yet persistent erosion of the fourth wall. Rather than do so in overt fashion, the writing draws attention to what you are experiencing while keeping it within the confines of a personal, introspective dialogue from the protagonist.
I really felt the story in Drizzlepath: Glass upped the ante for this series. 8 out of 10
The gameplay in Drizzlepath: Glass is completely tight and responsive. The controls handle immaculately, there were zero issues with clipping or other common issues that tend to plague games in this genre, and it really flowed seamlessly.
The level design was very linear, and this is a definite noticeable direction Tonguc has been taking with his games. Yes, you can still wander about and check out the nooks and crannies within each chapter, but you are always encouraged to move forward along a singular path, and this is truly effective in my estimation. Too often, a lack of structure becomes an impediment to the story being told, whereas here, the obvious path forward really puts you in a good position to experience the game with proper pacing.
There are a couple puzzles in the game which are easily solved, but were nicely done regardless. There was also an interesting horror section which might seem out of place while reading about it, but within the context of the game made perfect sense and actually served to break up the pace a little and re-invest you in the experience.
9.5 out of 10
The graphics in Drizzlepath: Glass are a nice example of how a person can really refine the Unreal engine to craft a beautiful game. This game is stunning and with quite a bit of diversity, from the beautiful and flowing grasslands and forests to the ominous almost marshy areas and quite a bit beyond. There is also a lot of attention paid to distance within the game, and so things in front of you will be distinct and crisp while the objects further out will become increasingly hazy and indistinct. This game is a looker and you are almost certain to take copious screenshots as you explore the game's five chapters.
10 out of 10
I'm not sure who recorded this soundtrack, but the guitar pieces in particular were masterful. At times whimsical and at others brooding and dark, the audio tracks were not only consistent with the moods intended at various parts of the game, but indeed were pivotal in helping to instill and maintain those moods. Really, really well done. Quite a few of those tracks I could easily see myself listening to while driving or otherwise out and about.
Also, the voice acting in Drizzlepath: Glass has seen definite improvement from past installments in the series as well. This was an organic effort, and you really could feel an emotional attachment to the protagonist, which is quite important as she is both telling a tale and contemplating her attachment to it variably. Without that organic, natural feel to it, the story would not have been the same.
10 out of 10
Drizzlepath: Glass is really a success in every imaginable way. Everything about this game not only engages the player, but also serves as a clear demonstration that all involved parties have advanced their craft and continue to refine their abilities when it comes to video game development, story, acting, music, etc...

Drizzlepath: Glass is the third (and so far, latest) title in Tonguç Bodur’s Drizzle series. It is my favorite especially since it features darker and more mature themes than the previous two iterations. Throughout the relatively brief gameplay, even the developer acknowledges the long journey he undertook before reaching the current skill and experience in his storytelling and if you aren’t familiar with his fascinating walking simulators, then please get acquainted with his first creations. In order to fully understand Glass, you need to have experienced at least Drizzlepath: Genie beforehand.
The story in Glass, places players in the shoes of a nameless female “protagonist” on her journey to visit the grave of her husband, Eric. You probably wonder why I don’t really consider her a protagonist. It’s simple. Along the trip, the widow begins to share stories from her life and about her now lost, significant other. What begins as smalltalk, eventually becomes ambiguous enough to leave room for interpretation. It is heavily implied that she played a role in Eric’s demise.
There are a lot less symbols in Drizzlepath: Glass than in its predecessors but the marks of distinction come in the almost ironic absence  of a path or drizzle to “guide” players in their meditative journey. Both of these narrative and gameplay aspects played crucial roles in the original Drizzlepath or its direct sequel, Genie. The light type of precipitation you may refer to as “drizzle”, only shows up in the fifth and final chapter of Glass and there is absolutely no path whatsoever. Even when the landscape leads to narrow passages. This confusion may have been planned all along, so I won’t regard it as design oversight.
Unreal Engine 4 in a rather unstable rendition. Why am I calling it that? Because I couldn’t even hit 30fps on 4K in Glass, whether both Drizzlepath 1 and 2 would offer me between 35 and 40 frames in similar maxed out conditions and with the same amount of foliage and general effects. I couldn’t figure what was wrong and I had to play in 2K while even then, reaching stable 60fps was a rarity. That’s why I prefer Unity Engine. That one never lets me down, no matter what pixels get shown on-screen.
Don’t get me wrong, the game looks great. Unlike the previously mentioned titles, you even have a different stylistic perspective. More feminine, by the looks of it. Shades of purple and pink and far more peaceful wildlife than in the other Bondur creations. I couldn’t complain about the literal change of scenery and I still found the perfect occasions for 65 screenshots. I just wish it would have provided me the means to take 4K screens AND enjoy the game at that resolution. I’m not gonna play something at 25fps just for the sake of screenshots, like I presume most of those guys showcasing visual overhauls and PC mods do. Pure eye candy without gameplay stability/fluidity is a no go.
The soundtrack and the audio effects are a vast improvement over the past Drizzlepaths. The female narrator has a British accent and the OST is never interrupted under any circumstances. No flaws to be found here. The music shall make this imaginary trip all the more pleasant. And with no spoken riddles or abstract poetry, this time around.
Riddles are still an integral part of Drizzlepath and Glass doesn’t fail to deliver cryptic messages laying around your not-so-obvious path towards the cemetery. Visions of her husband, shall haunt out vocal heroine and there are a few instamces in which the game almost resembles a horror title. Don’t expect me to spoil them, since the gameplay itself is rather brief. You’ll probably spend less than 3 hours in Glass, if you won’t stop often for screenshots, like I enjoy doing.
No option to sprint, yet players walk at a brisk pace as it is. One aspect in this game that I truly found interesting, is the inclusion of modern buildings, either ruins or a subway section. No Drizzlepath before Glass, mixed modern elements with its otherwise fantasy setting. You must be fully aware that there’s no action or proper adventure features in this title. Nothing to kill or run from. You just take a walk from your surprisingly luxurious (on the inside) forest hovel to a dangerously-looking graveyard on a mountain peak. No NPCs at all, just various mammals and birds. I’m almost disappointed that the kittens you meet in the first chapter, only follow you around the house and won’t join you on your trip.
Bare in mind that it’s still as abstract as its predecessors. Drizzlepath: Glass seems to have received mixed reviews because potential players and customers were expecting more. Perhaps more action or the freedom of choice found in Geniue. Regardless of their reasons, you need to understand that Glass offers exactly what it advertises on its Store Page. Nothing less, nothing more. It has Cards and the type of Achievements which I truly enjoy. Only one and unlockable as soon as you finish your journey. The game is reasonably priced, yet you are free to purchase it during a Steam Sale or when bundled. Just don’t judge or accuse it for not being something it never claimed to be.
+ Abstract experience.
+ Gorgeous graphics and sounds.
+ Steam Trading Cards & Achievements.
- Brief and with no replay value.
- Abstract experience.

I ended my review of developer Tonguc Bodur's third game, Bottle, with an unfortunate declaration that it was my least favourite game of his that I've played thus far. I'm pleased to say that his fourth game, Drizzlepath: Glass, is by far my favourite, and easily his most accomplished work up to this point (though I still have two more games to go after this).
So what's improved? In a word: virtually everything. Wait, that's two words. Okay, I'm probably happy to change it to "everything", then. Which isn't to say that his earlier games don't have some rather lovely imagery, or are COMPLETELY worthless in areas such as story...but if you were skeptical and looking for somewhere solid to start, this would definitely be it.
Graphics and music are perhaps the only fronts on which nothing has particularly improved or worsened, but man...has that voice acting improved, and we finally have some footstep sound effects to provide that final layer of immersion we've been missing! Hallelujah!! The story and writing, while a tad choppy in places, is also the best of any Tonguc game so far, and the level of interaction with objects and environments has increased to the point where even those who complain about "no gameplay" existing in games like this will have to bite their tongues, at least slightly. (Actually, who am I kidding...those people will still bitterly complain. It's what they live for. Vive la "walking simulators", you whiney mother-♥♥♥♥ers!)
Oh, and a special word of praise about the mapping. The first two Drizzlepath games made it easy enough by providing fairly constant PATHS to follow - as in, clear dirt tracks on the ground - but this time, we're left with little more than intuition to guide us in the right direction. This game must do a fantastic job of this, however, as even I - who could get lost in a one-level shopping mall with ten shops - didn't get lost once. At least not notably. A minute or two in the wrong direction, tops.
Oh, and there's a small section in this game which is easily Mr Bodur's spookiest accomplishment yet, suggesting that he may well be capable of delivering a full-blooded "horror" game one day. In the meantime, though, we may just have to be content with his very beautiful "walking simulators", a genre which can proudly lay claim to this product as one of its finer efforts to date.
Verdict: 8/10.
(PS Those jokey, self-deprecating references to your earlier games REALLY aren't required, man. Just a tip for the future...)

Sniper Elite is a first person military shooter where you guessed it, take the role of an American sniper.  The game is a mixed bag and I feel as though it didn't get enough time to polish the game fully. What could have been a jewl ends up being just average. While not a AAA title, it fits somewhere in between the indie developers and the giants of EA, Ubisoft, and Blizzard-Activision.
The game is known for slow motion bullet kills, like Sniper Elite which also includes x-ray bullet kills.  The story and characters are well thought out and fit well. The game comes together well in an open world/zone setting that give you the freedom to explore and take on missions how you want. The graphics are good and bad. They look good in most cases and while not the fedelity of BF1, they do look good but you will run into some low textures from time to time and some bad models, like the wolf, that make you say WTF where they thinking? While most characters look good, you will see a lot of them that look like they have the same parents... The Ivan brothers are strong in this one. The optimization is not the best either and while most people will be able to run this, the game could use some TLC in the form of optimization, which was pointed out in the BETA and little was done to resolve the performance issues. The crafting system is also a mixed bag. On one had I like the ability to modify weapons and create ammo, but the cost to do so can be frustrating at times, especially when starting off.
The Good
The story and characters.
Weapons and crafting ability.
Open maps.
Freedom in missions.
Graphics.
The Bad
Bugs.
Optimization.
Graphics.
Cost of crafting.
While the game has its problems, they aren't enough to ruin the experience, especially at $30 or less if you pick it up on sale. I recommend picking this up and having some fun with it.

I had this on my Wish List, tried it during the free play days, then bought the base game on sale for a little over $10.
It's a reasonably fun board game solo, but the singleplayer is probably more useful for learning how the various pieces (avatar abilities, perils, gear, cards, etc) interact as well as doing some limited leveling of the same to learn good strategy so you can survive in multiplayer.
Matches have a finite time span of about an hour, as they last a set number of turns, and there are timers (which can be turned down or off in single player) to keep turns moving. The game is turn-based, but there is also a real-time aspect because you can play your cards at any time (subject to card-specific restrictions and available resources) when it's not your turn -- you could, for example, watch two other players fighting and then finish off the winner from a distance with one of your spells. In addition to the player-versus player, the game mechanics also encourage occasional, temporary alliances, some of which are parasitic in nature.
Multiplayer allows the inviting of friends and automated matchmaking with strangers. Match sizes are set at 4; it doesn't appear you can do two players and two AI in multiplayer (someone correct me in comments if I'm wrong, please), and there is no local multiplayer. I would like to see these features so I can play a more casual game with a single friend.
Production values are top-notch. I did notice a few grammatical and punctuation errors, but nothing horrible.
I'd love to see this as a boxed game.

Throughout my experience, this game really has been a buster for me, and I've always been a big sucker for all those board games that people call nerdy. They may call it nerdy, but at the very least it's exciting.
Anyway, throughout the few hours I've played through this, it really consumed a lot of time, that before I knew it, it was 6 PM! And I started playing that morning (Note the hours played thing. The rest of the hours, I played offline, because sometimes, your internet connection shuts down on you).
Characters are very fun, with an excellent selection. Rat Clan had already become my favorite, as soon as I started the prologue, and played as Mercurio, but he's not the only good guy you can find in the selection, there's also a couple of other interesting creatures that you can choose from.
There is a number of ways you can win the game, too, which gives more variety in how you want to take on Armello. You can choose from remaining as the most prestigious leader among your peers, and win by attrition, for the king slowly dies every morning. You can also cleanse the king of the rot that dwells within him by collecting 4 soul stones. This will also kill the king in the process, however. You can also let the rot consume you as well, and challenge the king to become the new king of corruption. And lastly, you can challenge the king and slay him manually.
Defeating the king is easier said than done, though, for everyone wants to be king, and you cannot just march into the palace without expecting anything. The king placed dangerous traps throughout his palace, and the king's guards aren't going down without a fight. These traps make it a lot more challenging to attack or cleanse the king, and leaves the attrition war as the most common and foremost way to win. It's unnerving that it's too easy to win prestige at some points in the game, and become the leader.
But, overall, this is a great game, with good graphics and awesome board-based gameplay. Do you want to lay a cake in your opponents plans, even when they have cake planned for their victory (Sorry, no cake exists in Armello)? Do you want to seek conquest and decide what happens? Do you want to be king? Do you like board games? This one's for you! (Wish it was free, though...)

Disclaimer: Played 4 games against the AI, PvP might be where the game shines. However, the game is too short. If you fail perils a couple times in a row and don't have many items, or if you die early or obtain Rot early, you're going to have a bad game.
Now, in a PvP game, the game wouldn't feel as short because human players will take much longer to take their turns. But each player still is only given a limited amount of turns, something like 24 turns each or thereabouts.
I'm a big boardgamer. I'm the guy that has a modest library of boardgames and is always hosting dinners to entice friends over to play them. I love boardgames, so any video game that seeks to function like one instantly catches my eye.
In Armello, the RNG is too prevalent for the game to be truly strategic, and the game is not long enough for strategies to shine through. In all games I felt like I was simply making due with what was given to me, not influencing the board the way that I would have liked. The decisions you make are out of necessity, not out of strategy.
Drawing cards is a HUGE advantage, and so is fighting. If you try to play a character that is low on Fight and Wits, you're already at a handicap. Each player gets only a handful of turns to make anything happen, so when your turn comes and your hand is already full, it feels really bad to not draw any cards. Each player should be afforded one card draw per turn NO MATTER WHAT. And I would go so far as to say that players can discard any number of cards to redraw from the same deck, it feels pretty bad to have 4 cards and every single one of them is a Rot symbol, I mean wtf?
The reason that fighting and card draw is so overpowered is because the easiest way to win is through a prestige victory -- the game will default to a prestige win for the player with the highest prestige when the King dies. The easiest way to gain prestige is to fight other players and creatures. A high Fight stat, and being able to burn cards, wins you fights, and therefore generates prestige. In one game an AI character was at 7 prestige before I had even 1, due to terrible RNG on my quests.
Without this review getting too long, the simple fact of me not recommending this game is because the RNG is too heavy, turns are either too few or too limited, and the balance is questionable.
Also, there are some head-scratching game decisions. For example, you can't even zoom your camera out to view the whole board, you can only see a few tiles at a time. What is that about? If the devs are worried that people would just play the entire game in a zoomed out view, then provide incentive to zoom in to see details. For example, provide hints on the board to inform the player about the tiles they wish to move into. That's just one idea.
Overall, Armello is a neat idea. I wanted to like it, but it really suffers from balance and design choices.

Drizzlepath: Glass is a semi-beautiful short walking simulator with an eerie theme.
I've played the 2 other Drizzlepath games and I like this one the most, it feels like a real step-up from the other ones.
The voice acting is great but sometimes felt a bit weird, it felt as if the voice actor was disconnected from the situation, from what you were experiencing in the game.
Great soundtrack but quite repetitive.
Graphics are nothing to write home about.
Performance wise, compared to the past Drizzlepath games, it is much better but the graphics feel more or less the same.
The lighting in the game is what annoyed me the most.
Yes, it is quite beautiful...
. Playing the game and having an extreme light source like that showed in your face makes for a bad experience, you have you kind of half-squint your eyes and look away from the extreme flares and such as showcased in that screenshot.
The game also has a lot of graphical bugs, mainly graphical bugs with trees and random splashes of water from miles away.
Instead of being faded out in the background with the fog over it, like everything else, the tree is black and stands out from half across a mountain.
The eerie theme this Drizzlepath game has is what made me enjoy it.
If it was
Drizzlepath game I wouldn't have enjoyed it I don't think.
It still kinda feels as if the developer somehow can't seem to stop making the same game over and over, but it didn't feel as bad due this game having a very different theme and actually having a story.
The world you walk in does not have 1 strict path you have to follow, don't get me wrong, it is a linear walking simulator, but it gives of the illusion that it isn't as restrictive due to there not being a line from point A to point B you have to follow.
The world sort of makes you naturally walk in the right direction.
One thing that sort of messed up the atmosphere I was in was the animals walking/running around.
Lets take the foxes in the game as an example.
Every now and then you see some foxes run around, they just run around in 1 static circle and do not react to you coming close to them, unlike the birds in the game that do fly away when you come close, these foxes stay in their drug induced trans of running in a circle forever.
Also the horses that run around
look like they have early stages of cerebral palsy.
All-in-all I enjoyed it, it's different from the other Drizzlepath games
and I hope the developer manages to disconnect himself from making the same game over and over and trying to sell them as different things.
But one must not forget, at the end of the day it is just a walking simulator where you have to follow a linear path while listening to a narrator.
The game took 1 and a half hours to complete.
I recommend this game for anyone who generally enjoys walking simulators, and people dislike them shouldn't waste their money on this.

is the third and latest installment of the Drizzlepath series. While the differences between the first game in the series (the original Drizzlepath) and Drizzlepath: Genie (the second game from the series) are quite noticeable, Drizzlepath: Glass closely follows in the footsteps of its predecessor, raising the quality bar by a notch.
While Drizzlepath: Genie remains my all time favorite of the three games, I vastly enjoyed discovering the new world created for Drizzlepath: Glass. The graphics are more detailed than in the previous games (the flora and fauna of the areas are more varied and chiseled, the panorama switches between plains and mountains to villages or abstract aspects) and the story is more palpable, closer to the style of Bottle.
In essence, Drizzlepath: Glass remains a walking simulator with the only 'active' gameplay (apart from exploring) being interacting with some objects. However, the game brings two novelty elements: a chapter structure and a fun and a not-so-short jumping puzzle. Each of the chapters conveys an unique and specific feeling, and the worlds are strongly individualized. The style changes over the chapters from calm exploration to heart-pumping, fear-inducing sounds and events, back to the mysterious 'calm after the storm', culminating in a surprising and unexpected ending.
Similar to Drizzlepath: Genie, the path is quite straightforward, although not always evident. The landscape offers more room for exploration and the path is not all the time visible - this way the game makes you run around a bit and discover the surroundings.
It's not a lengthy game - it can be completed in around 2-3 hours, depending on how fast you want to speed through it. Finishing the story awards the player with the game's only achievement.
It is a really beautiful game. Story could be better. For the price I say it worth the buy.

I've played both of the previous Drizzlepath games and Bottle. Drizzlepath: Glass is the best one in the series so far, but nothing has been improved upon, or changed up enough to win over people who didn't like the previous games. Don't be fooled by the open world claim on the store page. This game is linear like the previous entries in the series. The only difference is the areas have been enlarged enough that you can get lost in them now and the path isn't always clear. The narrator is understandable and does a good job narrating the story. The twist at the end was a much appreciated departure from that of the previous entries in this series. I enjoy Tonguç Bodur's games and enjoyed my time in this one. So I recommend Drizzlepath: Glass to my fellow gamers, but only if you enjoyed the previous games.

The Drizzlepath saga continues with Drizzlepath: Glass. Right at the top, I'd like to say that this game is much more enjoyable than Drizzlepath: Genie, but not nearly as enjoyable as the original Drizzlepath. Now let's take a look at why.
The basic structure of this game is very similar to the other two entries in the series. You walk along a path (don't let the "I swear it's open world this time" in the store page fool you), occasionally a woman's voice speaks, and you climb a mountain at the end, Dear Esther-style. BUT WAIT THERE'S MORE--this time, you can click on things. About ten times. Don't let the "hidden object-style gameplay" fool you, either. The gameplay is about as deep as a kiddie pool, and that's coming from a HOG addict.
Now, a little more about that woman's voice, which of course is the primary element of all these games. The actress is a British lady who is doing her best to faithfully bring to life all the hard-translated lines Tonguc can throw at her. She really is pretty good as an actress, but the lines just don't bring a lot to the table. In Drizzlepath 1, the writing was so baffling it was amazing. In Drizzlepath 2, the lines were so pretentious they were grating on the soul. In this one, they're just boring.
Now, a little about the story. Have you ever played Silent Hill 2? If you have, you've already seen everything this game attempts to do better than it can ever hope to do it. That's really all that needs to be said. As I found myself thinking over and over again while playing this game, no one needs to play this game. If you like walking simulators or horror, go play SOMA. If you like even a little bit of gameplay, go play Layers of Fear. If you like hidden object games, go play Theatre of the Absurd (which also isn't great but it at least has the stated gameplay style). Skip Drizzlepath: Glass so you don't corrupt and dilute your memories of the "heavily accented Spanish lady" (AKA the unintelligible South American woman) from the original. Oh, yeah, and if you haven't played Drizzlepath, go do that. It's great for a laugh. This, not so much.

I'll start off my review by saying this. The controversy with the Devs is stupid and if you're interested in playing the game and could care less about the drama, I highly recommend you ignore it. My 2 cents on the matter is that the nonsense between the ex Dev Solokiller and current lead Dev Sniper is more personal than related to SC. And the backlash by some defending one and then some the other is also emotional. Just saying.
Now onto talking about the game itself.
Sven Co-op started as a mod for Half-Life. because of it, it has everything Half-Life related from story, to weapons to the core gameplay itself. The reason for the mod existing however is the necessity to optimize the game for co-operative play, fix bugs and allow big mapping and scripting possibilities.
If you're looking for a decent time, there's a decent amount of servers to chose from with their own local communities. The Experience servers are a very common sight and will provide a basic RPG set for gameplay. Although a bit unbalanced, it should be fun if you want to mindlessly go through levels.
If mindlessly going through levels isn't your thing, there are vanilla servers or the option of playing with your friends. You can have a lot of fun playing together with someone you know and can speak with and maps get done a lot faster.
The Co-op element is overall well done. You get a medkit which allows you to heal other players and revive them. Barnacles will grab onto you and you cannot resist, your teammate has to kill the barnacle to save you. Shocktroopers from Opposing Force still drop the alien shock gun, however it has limited ammo and allows you to give armor to other players. You can see where I'm going with this. The new mechanics added around help you play co-operatively.
Map variety is also a fantastic thing and over a decade worth of maps will give you a wide variety of maps with playstyles. There are even Team Deathmatch maps available. And with angelscript, you should be able to easily add a lot of custom content yourself if you understand programming.
There are issues however.
Black Ops are brutal and the amount of grenades they toss can be frustrating. While most of the xen type enemies are balanced, gonomes are especially aggressive and are genuinely not fun to fight against in most maps. There are certain engine issues so things like ice physics are completely broken as of now. Certain weapons like the mp5 and the m4 are just a bit underpowered. Players will often rush maps on some of the public servers which is quite frustrating as some people will want to go through the maps at their own pace. Tor, a custom boss in the game can be quite brutal, as he tosses you in the air in open areas, instantly killing you. This only adds to the frustration factor.
Overall I think half of these issues will be fixed. I'm not sure if the other half will be given any attention but I do recommend this. It's honestly a lot of fun. I have about 400 extra hours on this back when it wasn't standalone. I can recommend it to you. After all, it's free and the only thing you're giving it is your free time and enjoyment.

In a gist, it's a fun top down action game that eschews stats and loots for a more tactical and visceral experience. The core of the game is planning your route through the campaign and mowing down hordes and hordes of aliens as you and your friends are barely hanging on to life. Sweet.
Some things in Alien Swarm that I would love to see in other games of this genre:
- Shared map where you can all plan your route.
- Minimal loot, minimal stats, focus is on loadouts and interesting effects (freezing, burning, electricity etc.). Going through loot is tedious when all you are doing is increasing DPS.
- That climatic end. Believe me, if you don't spoil yourself by playing on a lower difficulty, the finale is worth the wait.
- The tactical nature of the game. The game gives you a lot of tools and weapons. Bar the door, and the alien has to spend time smashing through it. Lay a wall of fire and watch the hordes melt before your eyes. But all the defenses are temporary, and the aliens can and will overpower/overrun them. You and your friends have to plan properly to use your limited resources for victory. Some of my favorite moments in this game is defending a point while hordes and hordes of aliens stream in from everywhere. All the defenses and traps we laid are exhausted but we do manage to pull through.
On top of that, with friendly fire on, you really have to plan things out so you don't end up shooting each other. You even lose ammo if you reload early! That's a feature that's missing on a lot of games.
There are some cool things in this game borrowed from third person shooters, like crouching (for cover) and calculating line of sight so you don't hit obstacles/the floor/the wall. Definitely makes the game feel more "grounded" and adds to the tactical layer, although I honestly don't remember if I ever used crouch.
Get some friends, play on brutal (yes, from the beginning), and have fun.

Valiant Hearts is  comic-art style adventure game following a small cast of characters and their trials in World War I.  It contains a endearing narrative that is neither naive nor overly melodramatic - the story isn't a "kid tailored" story as it deals with separation, trials, loss, with plenty of nail biting or tear jerking moments.  It is a wonderful story that gets the player emotionally involved - something that video games oft fail to do!  The gameplay is side-scrolling in nature and requires a bit of thinking and problem solving but is rarely tedious.
Additionally - if you are thinking of getting this for your kid - keep in mind - It contains plenty of interesting facts of WWI as well as conforming to the historical time line of events/conflicts of the time.  I bought a copy for mine and it sparked several conversations about the story and the history.  I can't recommend it enough.
In the end - a great game and experience worth going through.

Do I recommend this game? I would say yes. It has its issues, but in some areas it does really well and tries to establish its own identity. I'll start off with the cons first.
Cons:
Voice acting - The voice acting for a good amount of the characters are well done, but for other characters it feels like the performance was forced and didn't feel genuine. Like the first time you meet Lydia it made me cringe. Her actions did not match up at all with her voice and it’s like she was an emotionless robot.
Cutscenes - The cutscenes are dull and don't look very good. I'm playing in 1440p on a 1440p monitor and it seems like they were pre-rendered in 1080p. So not only do they look a bit blurry, but the scenes themselves look very dull compared to actual gameplay. Usually cutscenes look as good or better than actual gameplay, but in this case they look significantly duller and bland while actual gameplay looks sharp and great.
Outposts - Outposts are scattered throughout the map filled with enemies and loot. To clear outposts you must kill all the enemies. This sounds pretty standard, but the reason why I'm marking this as a con is because the enemies respawn if you die (they seem to respawn if you clear all the enemies but somehow die in the outpost even after clearing it [traps, turrets, etc]), reload a save, or exit the game (main menu/close game) and come back. CI Games said they made it so outposts will never truly be cleared because they didn't want the world to feel empty, but this doesn’t really make much sense which brings me to my next point
Lifelessness - Despite CI Games effort mentioned above, the world feels dead. There are no enemy patrols on the road and you don't see civilians driving around or even walking on roads. The only time you see enemies/civilians is in outposts, villages, and interest points. The space in-between these places are nearly devoid of life except for the odd wolf or deer occasionally. Not even Far Cry 2 felt as dead as this game does, and that’s not considering the respawning checkpoint guards in that game.
Crafting - It seems that the crafting system was put in for the sake of having one. You can buy ammo of all types and other things like grenades and health packs, and getting money is extremely easy because you can just basically farm outposts until you have enough for what you want. So having ammo crafting doesn’t really make a whole lot of sense because the same places you find the materials to craft will usually be filled with enemies you can loot for money.
Killcam - The killcam is a nice touch, but it doesn't make sense. Unlike Sniper Elite, it only works for headshots and there’s no x-ray vision. But this isn’t the con. The con is that when it activates time stands still and the person you shoot is always in a standing position. What I mean is if you aim and shoot at a guy who is crouching and the killcam activates, then the guy you just shot at will then be suddenly standing up as the bullet rushes towards his head. Also, if you aim just off center of a guy's head the kill cam will still show him getting shot dead center in the skull.
Spelling/grammar errors - I've noticed this in CI Games’ other title: Lords of the Fallen, where there are spelling and grammar mistakes in subtitles and menu dialogs. It really makes the game seem low quality to me as it seems that no one bothered to play through the game and perform basic spell checking and revising.
*Metric system - I put a star next to this one because it's not really what I would consider a con, and I think this really only applies to people that aren't European. While I don't mind that distances and speed in meters/km, it's just weird to see decimals and commas being switched around. Like when you get a long shot it'll tell you the exact distance down to two decimal places, but instead of it being something like 452.75 they write it as 452,75. I know this is a European thing, but being American and being taught the first way from grade school through college, it's just weird.
*Day/night cycle - This one is a bit weird. I put a star by it because I noticed this from dying often. While the game has a day/night cycle, it seems that dying always resets the time to night. Whether it's early in the morning, in the middle of the afternoon, or already in the dead of night, dying will always put you back into night time, or if it’s already night time then it won’t advance time to day/morning. You can change the time of day by sleeping in a safehouse, but if you die then you’ll respawn at the nearest fast travel point and it’ll be night time. It's a bit strange and annoying and I don't know if it's intentional by the developers or not.
Pros:
Graphics - A lot of comments I've seen on this game in some places seem to think the graphics aren't very good. Well I think that's ridiculous because it looks great. It's a very pretty game that owes its painting like sceneries to being on CryEngine. Only thing is, I wish there were better AA solutions because even in 1440p I still notice a bit of aliasing on things like railings, trees, vehicles, and buildings.
Leveling - There are three categories you use to put skill points into. The cheesily named Sniper, Ghost, and Warrior. Why would I put this as a pro you ask? Well you only get points based on how you play. Meaning if you mostly stick to your sniper rifle then you'll get points in the Sniper category. If you mostly go in guns blazing with assault rifles, shotguns, or LMGs (pistol kills count too) then you get points in the Warrior category. If you use your drone to tag enemies and take them out Splinter Cell style then you get points in the Ghost category.
Stealth/AI - Whether you go loud or stay quiet, the AI will not magically know where you are immediately if you mistakenly or purposely cause a bit of noise. They will search for you if you cause noise or if they find a dead body. If one guy finds you and you kill him with an unsuppressed weapon then the others will not magically know that you are there. They only go to where the shots were heard and if they can't see you then they will search for you. Also they will investigate if you come close to being spotted. I mean it's not MGSV level AI but it's pretty darn good.
Parkour/climbing - Being able to climb is a major plus as you can change positions quickly and make stealth more interesting and engaging. If you find a good spot and pick your targets carefully and at the right times, you can clear out most of an outpost without having to change spots. If you get spotted and enemies are converging on your location then you can quickly either climb up and stay out of site or jump down and quickly find a new spot for cover
Closing thoughts:
While it looks like there are more cons than pros, I decided to stop here as I don't really want to write out an extremely long review. As it is right now I think it's a bit much but I do try to be as descriptive and informative as I can. The two starred cons as I said I don't really consider cons and are more down to me being picky, but most of the rest of the cons I feel are attributed to this being CI Games' first open world title. For a first it's not bad, but it misses quite a few marks while hitting some pretty good ones at the same time. It's a shame that this game was so critically panned at release. I don't think it's a bad game, in fact I think it's pretty good for a sub-AAA budget. I don't think CI Games should abandon the open world formula for the next game, but instead take a few more notes from the games they obviously took inspiration from. If you can get this game for around $20 it'd be well worth the money. And if you don't mind its shortcomings too much then you might even find it really enjoyable.

Whether or not you should buy this game really depends on if you know how to enjoy it, and if you think you would enjoy it playing the intended way. This game is obviously dated, and has a lot of bugs, but they're usually concentrated towards a specific area (an example being that turn based mode is terrible compared to real time). For that reason, it's recommended to use a guide, and luckily, I found a really good guide that should help really anyone, if you're a newcomer to any fallout game or a Fallout veteran and anything in between, so I'll link it at the end of the review. For judgement on how this game stands on its own, ignoring comparisons to Fallout 2 (which is actually why most people dislike this game, they didn't get what they wanted, which was Fallout 3 and instead got this combat game), this game isn't really tactical, but it's pretty fun when played as a hack-and-slash sort of playstyle. Playing it with even more specialization than Fallout 2 and 1 is an important part of the game, and makes for a fun sort of roleplaying with how you use weapons and what sort of fighter you are. This gives good replayability, along with decent combat , more or less point-and-click but with some planning and all that.
Overall, this game isn't bad for what it is, but you need to know what it is to decide if it's something you'd enjoy. The game's kind of for a niche crowd and a lot of people don't understand that when they're buying the game, and that prevents them from enjoying it. As stated before, I recommend that you look at this guide, as it tells you the most fun way to go about this game, depending on if that playstyle's enjoyable to you.

Poor Oozi. The perpetually grinning yellow alien isn't likely to join peers like Mario, Meat Boy, Rayman, and Sonic among the ranks of the platforming protagonist elite anytime soon. Awesome Games Studio has indeed erected a vibrant and deadly world for its fledgling hero to charge through, but for all its visual creativity, Oozi: Earth Adventure is missing a certain spark to elevate it beyond its by-the-numbers approach to the platforming genre. It touches on all of the familiar bases without adding anything particularly interesting to the mix. That doesn't make it a bad game, though finding a reason to keep plugging away when the unflinching difficulty gnashes its teeth is a struggle.
Stars boost your health and your score.
Oozi is a likable-enough fellow. He's cheerful, slightly dim-witted, and prone to dying from the littlest of scratches. His day job as an intergalactic deliveryman hits a snag when he runs out of fuel and crash-lands on planet Earth--only this isn't quite the Earth you're accustomed to. Overrun by strange critters and humanoid aliens that are wrecking the place, Earth isn't such a friendly planet anymore. It's here where Oozi wakes up alone and without all of his high-tech doodads to help him. His quest to recover pieces of his missing gear and ultimately find his ship so he can be on his merry way starts off simple but soon ratchets up to a serious challenge.
At its core, Oozi: Earth Adventure is a no-nonsense 2D platformer that draws many of its mechanics from classic games of the past. Rather than innovating, it's concerned solely with testing your reflexes and your patience as you zip along and navigate your way through increasingly insidious stages littered with deadly obstacles. Checkpoints are liberally scattered at first, though they stretch out in the later stages that really push you to master the environments through repetition. Oozi can only run and jump to start, but recovering pieces of his missing suit grants additional abilities that change the gameplay up in mostly predictable ways. Before long, you can double-jump, butt-stomp, punch enemies, and wall-jump. But even as new skills are added to your repertoire, none of them feel particularly exciting. They're familiar to a fault; the constant recycling of old ideas saps much of the sense of reward you get from earning new powers.
Despite their mundane scope, these fundamental abilities are still handy as the environments get tougher and throw bigger challenges your way. Sneaky stage designs quickly scale upward in complexity to ensure your trek isn't an easy one. Spikes, monsters, lasers, platforms, and all manner of other obstacles are meticulously placed to provide maximum irritation. Reaching checkpoints becomes an especially grueling process in the latter half of the game.
Out of the woods and into the mad scientist's lab.
The fact that environmental dangers do get a little more inventive as you go helps balance some of the frustration of dying over and over again. Hauling and hurling timed explosives through long stretches to take down walls is an interesting and nerve-racking challenge. Ducking into the background to avoid monsters is clever too, and the screen-warping visual effect that kicks in as you approach running out of air in poison-gas zones is a nice touch. These accoutrements complement the overall excellent visual design. Oozi: Earth Adventure is a sharp-looking game.
Staying alive is a tricky endeavor. Oozi is a fragile fellow, but collecting a certain number of stars as you jump and pummel through each stage does let you boost your health. Hunting down special bonus stars also unlocks extra stages to play in Challenge mode. Infinite lives is the ultimate savior here, since death comes frequently--sometimes even seconds after your last respawn. Oozi's jump mechanics and midair responsiveness aren't always as tight as they need to be for certain maneuvers. Wall jumping in particular feels off too. Despite hitting the controls with precise timing, you won't always stick or rebound as you should, and these sequences turn into aggravating wrestling matches with the game mechanics that frequently end with a drop to your doom.
As a result, pushing through tough spots to hit the next checkpoint can feel grindy, though your reward for making it is not having to ever replay that same stretch again. That is, unless you're a true glutton for punishment. Arcade mode lets you revisit stages for speed runs that have you pushing to a high score as fast as possible. Challenge mode is more enjoyable, since it offers up fresh stages with primary and secondary goals to complete.
Who knew that such evil could leap from the sea?
It's hard to fault Oozi: Earth Adventure for simply sticking to what works within its genre, like so many other games before it. But there's not much here that feels fresh or exciting. The platforming action poses a formidable challenge and offers some nice variety across its diverse areas, but it's disappointing that this cartoonish adventure rarely pushes beyond the bounds out of its tidy, safe little box. Being generic and sporadically punishing doesn't totally outweigh the fun, as there is some to be found here, and the frustrating moments are pushed through with a bit of patience. Oozi: Earth Adventure just doesn't do enough to stand out in a crowd of similar games.
The Good
Nicely crafted visuals and art direction
Stages are cleverly designed
The Bad
Major game mechanics lack originality
Heinous difficulty spikes hamper the fun toward the latter half of the game
Movement controls are spotty when wall-jumping and in midair

All in all, the game looks and feels like it's in its early stages. I don't know whether or not it is or if there are plans for updates but it doesn't matter to me. What is displayed now is enough to keep my attention for hours and more being added in would only be a bonus.

Retro City Rampage
is an 80s homage/NES recreation of Grand Theft Auto. However, getting into the game, one will quickly realize that it's a dumping ground for pop culture references, with a game that cannot decide what the hell it wants to be.
Usually, faux-retro graphics is a kiss of death for indie games. Far too many developers use 8-bit homage as an excuse to make lazy pixel art. I am willing to excuse it in this instance considering that RCR was originally supposed to be an actual NES conversion of Grand Theft Auto. The character portraits are about what you'd expect from a higher-budget NES game, with the in-game art being fairly small
The music is good, but that's to be expected from Jake Kaufman. That said, he's done far better work for far better games (Check Shovel Knight, one of the few truly great retro throwbacks.) Not that you'd be able to hear the music unless you muted the sound effects, which is a very smart move because Retro City Rampage has some of the most ear-grating sound effects I've ever heard in a game. Every few seconds, there's digitized screeching, what's supposed to be sirens and constant white noise that is supposed to be gunshots.
Once upon a time in the 2000s, there were two directors named Aaron Seltzer and Jason Friedberg. After being part of the staff for the popular Scary Movie series, they set out to make their own comedies, such as Epic Movie, Meet the Spartans and Disaster Movie. Everyone
these movies, and deservedly so, because in lieu of making jokes about pop-culture, they would just reference the fact that it exists. Seltzer and Friedberg are now pariahs in Hollywood, because everyone hates them.
What does this have to do with Retro City Rampage, you ask? Because I'm convinced that this game's writers' only comedic reference were Selzter and Friedberg movies. The game does not tell jokes. The game tells references. Technically, the whole plot of the game is an *ahem* "parody" of Back to the Future. The tone of the game is set right at the beginning, where within the span of about six minutes, the game references Mega Man 2, Duck Hunt, The Dark Knight, Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, The A-Team, Contra, Mario Bros, Frogger, and Bill and Ted (or maybe it's Doctor Who.) See, the joke is that you probably recognize these things and they are there. The villain is literally Dr. Robotnik from Sonic the Hedgehog, except his name is Buttnick. There's a level where you go to a factory. The joke is that the robot is the Destructoid robot.

The story mode will showcase several problems with the game
1. There are several missions where you are faced with a ton of enemies, which showcases how bad the lock-on aiming is. It's inconsistent with when it wants to actually lock on.
2. The game has knockback when you are damaged, which
frequently kill you in later stages
3. The game will force you into random diversions, usually to show off another "parody." Want to ride a slow bike that can barely turn? No? Too bad! The developer remembered that Paperboy existed. Want to throw barrels at a wall and have to constantly douse yourself when you catch fire? It's a good thing that Tapper was a thing the developer knew about. How about having an automatic runner stage featuring a guy who can propel himself with his sweat? Don't know what the homage it, but you get it anyways! Then comes the last two stages. Now, in most video games, you would need to use all the skills you've learned in the game so far to the test but- hold the phone. The developer decided that for the final stages, the player should throw all their skills away and play freaking Outrun. I could excuse the arcade minigames because those were optional, but here, you are forced to play Outrun, while Dr. Robotnik fires missiles at you that are timed to hit you right when it's impossible to avoid them.

Prositives:
* More 80's refrences than any peice of media constructed in the past 20 years, brillliantly weaved together.
* Good NES music, thats available digitally and on limited vinyll.
* Comes with a in-game instruction manual that's just a joke.
* Free roam, with an emphasis on killing sprees. Basically, what GTA is built for.
* Chris Hoffman himself is a cosmetic in this game.
* A emphasis on retro graphics and style-you can even change the TV border (or turn it off)
* DX mode makes it easier than what you've heard (and is toggleable)...
Connatatives:
*...but it's still hard. Expect a lot of deaths and some frustrating levels.
* Once you finish the story, you're really only left with Leaderboarded-Challanges and Collectibles
* The story is about 16 hours. A little lackluster.
* If you're not familiar or from the 80s, the game's humor won't make any sense.
SUMMARY:
A radical jet-fueled love-letter to all things from modern gaming's birth, It's a satisfying yet challenging game for those who's hearts and minds are still with their NES. Anyone else, though, may simply be too young to get it.
8 bit GTA. The game is a good play, and takes points from the top-down GTA that started it all. Pretty entertaining, and a hilarous satire storyline that reminds us of the stories that games make.

Not that bad of a game really. I finished the campaign in 12 hours over the course of a few days and it even though it was linear, the story was interesting and pretty engaging.
Pros:
-Graphics are good
-Story was interesting
-Runs DECENTLY on most set ups
-Some missions challenging
-Perk system is good
-Options on how to complete mission (Sneaky or Rambo style)
-Open World
Cons:
-Not very many opportunities for long distance shots really, my longest is around 400 meters, kinda wish you could do some real long distance stuff but you get out of the area of the mission kinda quick or your vision is quickly blocked by trees/hills
-Campaign only follows one track, unlike other games where the ending varies depending on what you do
-Some rifle aspects unrealistic. Why do some 7.62 rifles do more damage than .338? Doesn't make a ton of sense sometimes
-Not a lot of distinct differences between rifles besides damage output and fire rate (Bolt/Semi). No real advantage to using .50 calibers bc they are unsuppressable
-Side missions are short and don't offer much towards gameplay after main campaign is finished
Note that I don't own any of the DLC for this game so I can't offer comments on how it impacts plot line or the weapons included in them.
All in all, I'd say the game is worth $20 and is pretty fun to play through. That being said, there were definitley things that the devs could have fixed or made more practical. I recommend this game but with a word of caution that this won't be the best game you play.

You already know the "Drizzlepath" series? Possibly even "Bottle"? Then you will know what to expect. More or less. In "Drizzlepath: Glass" your expectations may be excelled even, having more story, more interaction, so much – it had to be spread across several chapters this time.
If not, why should you be curious about it? ... Well, calling this game "just another Walking Simulator" would be an understatement. In good tradition since "Dear Esther", this game is better rated as "Narrative Game"; you don't just walk around in pretty landscapes (which are, how shall one stay calm,
– another demonstration of graphical features of modern engines and hardware; don't forget your camera model F12). And you are not just told a story while walking. You participate in it. You experience a story at the border between imagery and imagination.
In contrast to earlier games of this author, the path to walk is not so clear this time. You can explore wide fields, and you should, as you may discover confusing surprises now and then. Are they real or just visions of an ill mind? Shapes of a familiar person, leaving messages to you which may have a meaning, but in which context? Abandoned villages, a playground in ruins, a subway station in the middle of a forest ... the more you wander, the less you may trust your perception. Still, you can't get lost, eventually you will discover the direction to the next location.
Be warned, the hardware demands are rather high. A GTS 450 can barely handle it (below recommendation anyway). But it really shows off on recommended hardware. It will not only stimulate your eyes and ears (with wonderful music and a voice as pretty as the graphics you will see). It will also put you into different moods (which is always the greatest talent of its author). And it opens up a wide space of interpretation, more and more with every fact it reveals about the protagonist and the people she shared her life with, and with every reference to other places you may find (and remember if you know the other games already).
Finishing this game may not end its impact on you. How do you see the protagonist now, in contrast to the beginning? And how well do you know yourself?

Retro City Rampage is what you get when you combine a modern open world game with retro 8 bit gameplay and style. Oh, and with loads of pop culture and video game references. This combination of different gameplay and style works well, playing out like an 8 bit version of GTA and similar games with plenty of humor and parodies going on.
The story revolves around Player, the main character of the game, who is a henchman. After stealing a time traveling phone booth that takes him into the year 20XX, Player must work with Doc Choc to fix the time machine and also interact with other characters in Theftopolis to get the needed parts. In the game, the story is driven through missions and cutscenes. Along with the main missions for the story are optional side missions that provide extra narrative based on the main plot.
The game uses a lot of parodies and references throughout as seen with the characters and scenery, to name a few. With the sheer amount of references going left and right, it’s easy to be overwhelmed, but the parodies are a good laugh with a focus on video games and 80s and 90s pop culture. The references range from mainstream to obscure and subtle to blunt, and it’s a great experience keeping with the game’s theme and setting. The majority of the references lie in Story Mode, which really drives not just the parodies but also the overall style of the game.
Retro City Rampage plays much like a cross between open world games like Grand Theft Auto with some gameplay style from NES games. Like in most open world games, there is a big city to explore and missions pointing you to certain locations. The majority of missions focus on getting to a certain spot on the map and doing a certain task. There’s a great variety of different tasks to do, making the Story Mode missions interesting with different gameplay goals to complete. In addition to the structured missions that show each objective to be done, there are also arcade style missions with the goal being to get a high score. These arcade missions are quite fun in their own right, focusing instead on pure mayhem and causing as much destruction in the city.
As the gameplay borrows from GTA, there are some common elements in Retro City Rampage. Cars can be stolen, pedestrians can be attacked, police will attack upon seeing a crime, and there are a variety of weapons to use.  The game does deviate from typical open world games by bringing its own twist based on games from the 8 bit era. Jumping is performed like in platforming games with the intent to jump over obstacles and to jump on people’s heads. This jump attack can kill people and is a powerful unarmed attack. Objects and people can be picked up and thrown in a manner similar to beat em up games, where any object is carried over the head and thrown forward. Powerups can bestow different effects. These powerups must be bought unless a mission gives one that must be used, and they give a huge amount of power in a limited time.
In addition, the game is quite fair when it comes to trying to complete missions. After dying in a mission a few times, the game will offer some useful tips pertaining to that mission. If the game feels that the mission is quite tough for the person playing based on the many deaths that occurred, the game may change things around by giving a handicap to help complete the mission. This function of making the missions a tad bit easier is not in every mission, so some particularly tough missions must be completed at the default difficulty. Anyhow, it’s clear to see the inspiration from open world games, but there’s also a great combination with gameplay from NES games that works well as a game that is fun to play.
This game employs an 8 bit pixel style, with a very sincere approach in imitating the style of actual games from that era. The graphics are quite blocky and low resolution in the overworld, as if the game were on the NES. Character portraits are also similar in style, along with capturing the original character or person’s features from the parody. Only a few modern graphical liberties are used, one of which is the wavy screen distortion effect. In addition to its 8 bit style, there are various screen borders that slightly affect the presentation of the game, either by placing high resolution graphical borders that fit the game’s theme to even changing the colors of the game. With the 8 bit NES art style, the game treats the graphics quite well. It’s the same way that the parodies are treated with respect toward the original material, and the game goes great lengths into accurately portraying visuals as if it were an actual NES game with great results.
The music in the soundtrack is chiptune like the style of the game. There are some nice tunes played throughout, with the soundtrack being done by various video game musicians. Each of the songs work very well with the tone and style of the game, with a few parodies too based on some popular NES tunes. Overall, the soundtrack is quite catchy and stays true to the general theme quite well.
Of note is the sound design, which is done like the sounds of the NES. All the sounds are not realistic and instead go for the beepy electronic noises that were a mainstay of games in the 80s. This design choice perfectly matches what the game was going for, with almost every aspect of the game being lifted from an NES game from its original time. There are only a few unique things seen in modern games that this game uses, but Retro City Rampage does so well in staying true to the original retro video game style.
Retro City Rampage is in essence, an 8 bit version of open world games like GTA with lots of parodies here and there. The story is quite straightforward with the majority of parodies going there for a good laugh. The gameplay draws from GTA the most but throws in some gameplay style from NES games too. To top it off, both the art and music stay close to the style of the NES and holds its origins in high regard. Retro City Rampage is a fun game to play and oozes with respect for retro video games.

(Post-Fallout 2 Review) Fallout Tactic's story begins with a part of the West Coast Brotherhood seperating into another sect. The reasons behind this are political and moral as the West Coast Brotherhood are technology hoarders that want little to do with the people of the wastes, which conflicts with certain ideals. Thus creating a "Mid-Western"-esc Brotherhood.
You are introduced as an up and coming recruit for this new Brotherhood and take control of a new squad; With the sole purpose of completing objectives for the Brotherhood to expand it, and to later unravel the mysteries of the infamous "Vault 0".
Fallout Tactics focuses heavily on the "tactial" portions of their six-man-squad combat, rather than Fallout 1 and Fallout 2's open world RPG elements. The open world in Tactics has nothing much to offer other than some random encounters and the locations which are only unlocked via missions making it kind of underwhelming. Also Tactics suffers from a majority of its plot being linear, with the only real decision making being toward the end of the game.
This game however, is an extremely well crafted action-based tactial shooter with small amounts of RPG elements sprinkled into it and is a good change of pace from the previous iterations. Some of the missions that I played, were truly difficult and required a hefty amount of thinking power to push through them.
I had a tremendously fantastic time with this Fallout, and would recommend it to anyone that is a fan of the series or to anyone who enjoys cRPGs.

I suggest any prospective players of Fallout Tactics ignore the rose-tinted nostalgia contained in many of these positive reviews, and realize that even at the time of release Fallout Tactics had a well-deserved reputation as a mediocre knockoff of Fallout 1 and 2. At its core the game is a squad based, isometric RPG with a similar control scheme to Infinity Engine games such as Baldur's Gate and Icewind Dale, but it tries to focus almost entirely on large scale combat over the lore, exploration and storytelling that made the original two Fallout games so enjoyable. You generally use the same mechanics, weapons and abilities found in Fallout 2, and even can switch between real-time and the "classic" turn based combat, but the end result feels like a poorly balanced mess. My major complaints:
1. Inability to switch from real time to turn based mode outside of combat gives encamped enemies way too much of an advantage
2. Movement range in turn based mode is too small for the size of the maps you play on
3. Vehicles die too easily and are annoying to control
4. Some mission objectives are stupidly vague and NPCs don't give useful context clues
If it's not clear already, "needlessly slowing down the pace of the game" seems to be a reoccuring theme here. But there are other major areas the game has problems with:
5. The plot and characters are generic and unmemorable, and besides that, aren't even considered canon
6. Most of the skills outside of combat are useless
Despite these issues I'm not saying this game is all terrible. Being able to use cover and crouch is a cool concept that adds a layer of complexity to the combat system that the original Fallout games did not have. I like being able to play as other races like Deathclaws or Ghouls, they all have their own playstyle quirks that make them feel interesting and distinct. I also like the general concept of epic scale battles against heavily fortified groups of enemies- it's just that the concept was poorly tested and poorly executed. Because this game is not considered canon you are really not missing out on much as a Fallout fan if you decide not to play through it, but if you do I suggest not trying to ramp up the difficulty mode so you can stick with real-time combat (and thus minimize the pacing issues) as much as possible.

Want to relive the the glory days of IM chatting a la a faux AOL? Want a quick game that makes you think? How about a game that regardless of choice will leave you questioning your life choices and needing a bit of ice cream?
Whether or not you said yes to the last one, Emily is Away is a fantastic facisimile of IM that slowly sees you and your best friend Emily split apart over time until distance and time due their work. From being near best friends to utter apathy, you watch as every decision you make only pushes you farther apart. Frantically you'll restart the short game, thinking you obviously just input the wrong choices and can have your "happy ending," but no such luck.
There are a few problems that keep this froming being a perfect game, however. Controls can be a bit confusing, and the concept that you have to type for the text to properly appear on your end is unexplained (this should have been clarified). Also, in full screen mode, you cannot click directly onto things due to what I assume is a glitch. You must move your mouse to the left and somtimes diagonally to the left of the icon you'd like to click to use it properly. This makes it difficult to fully immerse in the game, but thankfully isn't a problem in Windowed mode.
Emily is Away is the perfect visual novel about loss, a "one that got away" story that perfectly encapsulates unrequited love and what distance can do to frienships. 9/10

I enjoyed the game for the few hours I played, so I would give it a recommendation. The reason why I wouldn't purchase it are reasons below which may contain spoilers of the game (strategy-wised).
Singleplayer's good for a few rounds. It becomes more of a RNG/luck game once you know which setup/character/victory paths to choose (Talking about Prestige). Of my 5 playthroughs, 4 of 5 games were won by simply being the prestige leader. Only one of those was by slaying the king (and even then, the king was at 1 heart, so it was 1 turn away from being another prestige victory). Collecting spirit stones by questing is a ton of hassle, let alone RNG from dungeons. Rot is risky and its just killing the king but with a 'side-effect'. So in conclusion, gathering prestige is the safest/easiest/reliable way of winning in every situation. Since you get prestige from killing everything but the king's guard, you may as well focus on combat stats. This means that many of the starting characters are rather pointless or underwhelming and there is just no reason to ever pick them (Sana). They are there to give yourself a handicap (or a challenge whichever you wanna call it) on your next playthrough. Again, singleplayer's only good for a few rounds because the AI aren't that smart. E.g. In my first game, the bot could have won from being the prestige leader, but instead, it picked a king's card that gave away most of his prestige.
Enjoy more than price.
