Factorio is a dirty, greasy, filthy, coal-powered dieselpunk game about material requirements planning, logistics, and that sweet sweet automation. It sounds nerdy, and it totally is, but god damn if it isn't fun and makes you feel smart. You see that sprawling matrix of countless mechanical objects in the trailers? You're going to build something like that. And you are going to fully understand it, and be proud of it, because you designed it, and it's yours. The amount of time and effort you put into your factory makes it feel like your baby. You raised it from the very beginning, and watched it grow, and were with it every step of the way.
45 hours, 2-3 obnoxiously long research projects, 300 adorable logistics robots, a train or two, and thousands of conveyor belts later, you'll finally launch that goddamn rocket... and you'll weep manly, manly tears of joy at your achievement.
And that's just your first playthrough.
...Though a second playthrough will, unfortunately, lack what made the first one fun.
Factorio is excellent, though it lacks replay value. The process of designing that automated production line to mine iron/copper/coal/stone/uranium out of the ground and process it into Science Packs to be placed into your labs for research projects is exhilirating the first time you figure it out, but doing it all again kind of feels like a chore, especially because of the insane amount of time it consumes. The only subsequent playthroughs I enjoyed were when the game had gone through significant updates since I last played it and a lot of the crafting recipes had changed. Even so... that initial 40ish hours I spent learning all of the tricks and making this world my ♥♥♥♥♥ is one of the best experiences I've ever had from a video game.
Now let's talk about the RTS elements...
I actually activated Peaceful Mode after a few run-ins with aliens, restarted games, and a lot of wasted time/resources building huge stone walls that constricted my factory's growth and ran counter-productive to the basic MO of the game. My first successful playthrough was alien-free. In my opinion, Factorio's RTS mechanics are currently unfun. The elements of setting up defenses for your factory against the various aliens actually doesn't mesh very well with the rest of the game's design. It feels like a distraction from the main game, and is not very well-integrated at this time, though this may change later, as the game is still in Early Access.
Overall, I highly recommend. You will absolutely get your money's worth as far as the dollars-per-hour ratio goes.

Short version: Cute cats, but the controls aren't that good. Crow will eat you for breakfast.
Long version: Purring Quest is a short little game wherein you're trying to return to your owner. That's the story, the main meat of the game is getting through the 5 levels, freeing cats and collecting fish bones along the way. The music is lovely and the art is pretty nice to look at.
It's a nice adventure/platforming game about kitties, and it's plenty merciful with unlimited continues. But there are some sore spots.
-The piano mini game abruptly comes at you at the end of level 4 and you're likely to get 5 misses before you figure out what the controls are. A quick pause before the mini game, showing the controls before it starts, would have been nice.
-The attack box is tiny and only usable on the ground. I got hit so often because I thought I was in range of an enemy.
-The crow boss will murder you. This is a fact.
-The storyline about random cats being abducted doesn't matter at all.
-The controls, man. I used the arrows keys but it was still awkward as I needed Q, Z, and Tab for other actions. Died using long jump. Had better results with double jump.
Despite these flaws though, I actually had a good time. In the last level. No more toads or rats or prickly plants, just platforming with only a couple gimmicks.
I kind of want to recommend this game, but...I wouldn't play it again. If you really must grab Purring Quest, then rebind the controls and good luck with your jumps.

Whoa boy, we're back in the Australian Outback again!
Ty the Tasmanian Tiger fits into the same niche as great titles such as "Banjo Kazooie", "Jack and Daxter: The Precursor Legacy", and "Croc: Legend of the Gobbos". In the game, you play as the Thyracine named Ty, who stumbles upon a cave of paintings depicting the destruction of the Outback by one known as Boss Cass, a Cassowary, who threatens to revert the Outback to prehistoric times, putting cold-blooded lizards at the top of the food chain once again. It is up to Ty and his band of fauna to put a stop to the stubborn bird's plans.
Having sunk 15 hours into the game, I was able to complete the game at 100%, including all Steam achievements (and this was at a relaxed pace, and knowing what to do due to previous experience).  I would say that a newcommer to the series would be able to beat the game to 100% in 24 hours. For the nice price of twelve dollars USD, I would say that it is money well spent, moving up and about the Australian Outback with a small Arsenal of boomerangs.
Parental Advisory: Ty's girlfriend is a Dingo, whilist Ty is a Thylacine. Interspecies relationships exist in this game. Be forewarned. If your child plays this game and expresses wanton for interspecies relationships, sit them down and explain why such things are frivilous.
Story: 7/10
You know what you are doing most of the time and you are given direction. Not a page turner.
Gameplay: 9.5/10
Better than most Collectathon controls. Would request changing boomerang switching to mousewheel, but is impossible.
Game progression is great. Technorangs can be very useful, especially if you are not quite so good at the game.
Graphics: 9/10
I've seen more visually impressive PS2 Graphics. The port does an excellent job cleaning up polygons, though.
Music: 10/10
Really puts you into the mood for crocodile wranglin'
Replayability: 6/10
You may go back to get the last cogs or last picture frames, but no way in hell are you doing it again.
Overall Score: 9/10

Note: As it stands, I can't really recommend it. I might play more later and this could change, but it is as it stands.
Fight the dragon is your base RPG formula. Pick a class, fight monsters, get gear, level up; and eventually hit the key component: Fight the Dragon. I won't go about telling you what classes there are, cause like all RPG's there is the main variety. You got your physical, your magical, and your dexterity.
What I want to get into the grit about is the gameplay. Playing the game feels a bit stiff or awkward in most cases, and it's mostly attributed to hitboxes. When you attack someone there's a good chance you'll hit them if you're so close to them you're clipping inside, but other than that you can seriously end up missing for stupid reaesons that can result in you dying very quickly.
Even when fighting skeletons in the tutorial, I found several times that I'd take swings at them and watch my blade go through them with no damage done, but they do the same in return and actually manage to connect to me. There's also been times where I'd attack and it'd hit, starting off a combo. But wait! The enemy was nudged back a bit, so I miss the rest of my combo by a hair, letting me take more damage.
The real struggle is with elevated platforms and ranged enemies. Did you know I honestly thought wraiths couldn't be hurt by basic attacks at first? Cause I'd get within breathing range and swing and they'd fly right through me without it connecting, but only after a few more attempts did I Realize they can in fact be hit. This was mostly because most of the time they were hovering above me just enough to have it not count.
Which brings me to elevation. A platform that's short enough to the point where you can walk up onto it without a climb should not prevent me from attacking an enemy that my sword is going right through their ankles! And when you are on a map with ranged way above where the player cant reach? You can ♥♥♥♥ right off. Especially with custom maps that like using these types of enemies.
That said, all the maps in the game are - aside from the provded - custom. This is the main key, and this naturally leads to some really unbalanced situations with custom maps, but dev maps are pretty reasonable for the most part.
Suggestions
Make hitboxes a bit more reasonable. You can size it out even half an inch or more and it'd be an improvement
Lower health on ranged enemies. It's bad enough they sprint away from you at twice your speed
FIX BLOCKING. Seriously, that thing is bipolar. Even at maximum health, it struggles to do jack♥♥♥♥♥♥half the time. Sometimes it feels like you need to block, and sometimes it feels like that axe needs to go past it into your face.

The entire premise is based around user-created maps, but they aren't curated whatsoever. Only a hundred or so good ones out of thousands. The only effective way to level up and make progression is to farm rats with +EXP gear in these custom maps. Abilities and combat are boring and uncreative.

One of the most cunning and beautiful games about family and friendship during the war showing the true horror of war and how ti rips you, your friends and family apart. How it will destroy humanity. Stop complaing about Uplay, there is no point crying over it and being a sook.

I like dogs. I like stories that make me feel bad. I like games that force me to make hard decisions. Can you see where this is going?
This game knits together neat historical facts about the history of warfare, (Chlorine gas? Well, I never...) with a collection of soldier-sent letters, building a point-and-click tale that encourages you to invest in your character/s. Some of them wanted to be there, others did not, but they had their reasons. Very, very, human reasons.
The game is short and linear. But it is poignant. It encourages you to buy-in to your character/s, selling them to you with heart and relatable motivations. It give you times when you cringe as a patrol marches by, or cheer at the plucky courage of your friend. The story is It's an incredibly well-written, and the puzzles are simple to understand, but can be challenging to complete. I paid full-price for it, and I'd pay the same again. It is a worthwhile investment in your emotional development, and I've seen no better story for telling the tale of warfare in an unbiased manner.
It's a beautiful story told from multiple viewpoints, all unified by a single common element. A dog.
It draws you in, keeps you fighting, pushing for that point where you can breathe... and then it twists the knife.
20/10 (I played it twice.)

What can I really say about this gem of a game?
It is certainly an acquired taste, and often people find it slow to start. That's because it is slow to start.
If you like a gritty unforgiving micromanagement RTS this is something you should look into.
One of the things that stood out to me is the insane difficult (notably for psychopaths) and the intense amounts of gore you can see.

-Charisma
It is possible to pass the game with 1 charisma with very little penalties, but it does have a use. It affects how quickly you rank up and also opens up some recruits earlier. I read somewhere that it allows you to take two of the best recruits in the game.
I've played the game as a sniper and enjoyed this game very thoroughly.
-If you're a melee user then you might be disappointed. It seems that melee is not really that great after super mutants show up, so you're boned.
TL;DR
It's an acquired taste.
Micromanagement RTS
Melee skills non-existent after super mutants
Very fun once the controls are down

I like dogs. I like stories that make me feel bad. I like games that force me to make hard decisions. Can you see where this is going?
This game knits together neat historical facts about the history of warfare, (Chlorine gas? Well, I never...) with a collection of soldier-sent letters, building a point-and-click tale that encourages you to invest in your character/s. Some of them wanted to be there, others did not, but they had their reasons. Very, very, human reasons.
The game is short and linear. But it is poignant. It encourages you to buy-in to your character/s, selling them to you with heart and relatable motivations. It give you times when you cringe as a patrol marches by, or cheer at the plucky courage of your friend. The story is It's an incredibly well-written, and the puzzles are simple to understand, but can be challenging to complete. I paid full-price for it, and I'd pay the same again. It is a worthwhile investment in your emotional development, and I've seen no better story for telling the tale of warfare in an unbiased manner.
It's a beautiful story told from multiple viewpoints, all unified by a single common element. A dog.
It draws you in, keeps you fighting, pushing for that point where you can breathe... and then it twists the knife.

There's a cliche, cartoony villian that takes this game from an interesting and emotional look into the horrors of the firt world war into a boring cliche. The puzzles are very easy so there wasn't even the challenge of a difficult puzzle to keep me going. I believe this would work well as a family game with children, since the violence is never very graphic, and overall is kept fairliy minimal considering the horrors of this war. Overall I'd say it's not for me but I could see it being a good family game and an educational tool

The story is fun, does not take itself too serious, but it is not deep, moving or particularly smart. The game is a satire and lives from its parodies of  old school games like Mario, Zelda and such, so it is definetly an advantage if you know those, but if you don't, it is still fun.  Some missions are definitly not easy, but usually doable, at least after a couple of tries, especially because the DX version features in-game tips (thank you dev). However, I would really recommend to play this game with a gamepad, I have not tried the keyboard control yet but I cannot imagine that it would feel as good as a gamepad.
So if you like retro games, cool 8-bit graphics and music and running around an open world shooting everything and if you don't fear an occasional challenge, I am sure you will enjoy this game for about 10 hours at least. I have played it only for 7, but there are still many things I want to do.
However, it is not a game that I will love in the same way as I love for example "Zelda: A Link to The Past" or "Cave Story". The world is not small, but it is also not deep, believable or full of charming characters, same as the flat main characters. A game can be a retro satire AND have a moving story with deep characters, as UNDERTALE proved. If you are looking retro game with a moving story, that might be more for you. However, the gameplay was definetly more fun in RCR, imo. I enjoyed it and will recommend it.

Let's start with positive things about Oozi. The art style is great, the main character and the inhabitants of the game world are both offbeat and vibrant. Everything is colorful, and everything has googly eyes. The controls are incredibly tight, to the point I was legitimately surprised, and collecting stars feels satisfying, mostly due to their large quantity.
Now, time for the design. The game is very, very, very simplistic. This in itself is not bad, but the developer seemed to have run out of ideas by the end of the first world. I had lost count of the number of times I'd seen the same hazard re-used. I'm not using hyperbole, here. If I see one more corridor where a spike trap bounces slowly from top to bottom, I will cry. It's not as though the developer didn't have plenty to work with.
He was aiming for simple gameplay and simple mechanics, but he treats said mechanics as though they're brand new, although they've been around for decades. The game doesn't even begin to explore the most basic platforming elements, including the double jump. There are one to three hazards -often reused- where the double jump is used creatively. To make matters worse, the game betrays its own selling point. It claims to be free of puzzles and gimmicks, but it frequently introduces new mechanics that are never explored thoroughly and quickly swept aside. Oxygen timers, bombs, security cameras, hiding in the background. They're all entirely one-note mechanics that are recycled throughout their respective stages and then discarded, rather than built upon.
If the game were say, an hour or two long, these flaws wouldn't be as noticeable, but entire levels sometimes felt copy-pasted, and they drag on for quite some time. I was pretty happy with Oozi at first, and it wasn't the simplicity that killed it, just the developer's unwillingness to explore his own mechanics. Nearly every other indie platformer has something unique or interesting to offer, even if their package as a whole is lacking. Oozi is entirely void of any distinguishing design, and I sadly can't recommend that.

A really great squad-based shooter set in the Star Wars universe. A short, but very sweet experience.
Republic Commando puts you in the role of the lead of an elite squad of Clone Commandos, sent to complete difficult tasks behind enemy lines.
The gameplay is fantastic, with the limited tactical options needed in order to survive against overwhelming odds. In most of the areas, there are certain places where you can assign your squadmates to perform a certain action, such as sniping, or throwing grenades into the area. Especially later in the game, proper use of these options is necessary, since the game gets quite challenging. Shooting and meleeing enemies feels great and extremely satisfying.
The members of the squad, your character included, are pretty much generic characters. You have the stern leader, the moody one, the comedic one and one who is the level headed guy of the group. However, despite their simple personalities, they are extremely likable and memorable, and their banter is a pleasure to listen to. The voice acting is absolutely fantastic, as well as the writing which allows the simple characters to shine.
But where this game really succeeds is the sound and feel of Star Wars. The music is absolutely brilliant, going incredibly well with the action on screen, making it feel truly epic. Small details make the game feel great, such as droid oil splattering on your visor when you melee a droid. Or if you shoot a droid in the head, the body will continue to shoot randomly around it until you shoot it as well. Geonosians fly around, being hard to hit, but feel incredibely satisfying to melee once close. Everything feels so  great to look at and listen to, which really makes it sad when it comes to an end all too soon.
The game has aged decently in terms of graphics, though the environments to get rather small at some moments, making it hard not to notice the blurry graphics.
All in all, a fantastic game, if you have doubt about grabing it, definitely do, especially if you are a Star Wars fan, and even if you're not, there is a brilliant tactical shooter under the Star Wars skin.

I remember the first time I put that disk, that artwork of Delta Squad giving me excitement, waiting for this game to finish installing so I could play as a Clone Commando. I was 15, perhaps, maybe 14. Being a Star Wars fan, spending hours playing Knights of the Old Republic, Jedi Outcast and Jedi Academy.
Got this on a discount a while ago, wanted to have my old games on Steam. - and still, this feels so damn good.
Nostalgia isn't a reason to still hype over this game. Republic Commando did define the First Person Shooter genre, combining a Squad-based Gameplay with a Tactical Shooter. You play your cards right, you don't die. Still, many shooters can't reach this level, they can't make a fast gameplay combined with team management in the middle of the combat. This game gave us a choice to place our commandos in the right places, managing our resources between having more firepower and getting the job done. Not the best variety of weapons, sure; still leading a group of four in various scenarios is enough to get yourself in a challange.
If anything, it's worth playing for the story itself. Being a "Deluxe Model" in a Clone Army, leading a squad of Clone Commandos with different characteristics. Listening to them trashing at each other, commenting on kills and reacting to your actions. Well-designed, well-thought.
To this day, Republic Commando is still one of the most feature-rich First Person Shooters out there. Still looking good, still has a damn-good story, still enojyable, still challanging. - Do you like First Person Shooters? Then, this is a must have.
They have to make a sequel...

Fallout Tactics emphasizes tactical combat and strategy but limited interactions with non-player characters, but they can still be traded with. Instead of towns, Fallout Tactics centers around Brotherhood bunkers and missions. The bunkers serve as a central point for the Brotherhood, and players can obtain the services of quartermasters, mechanics, personnel yeomen, and medics.
Combat in Fallout Tactics is a bit more complicated than the previous two Fallout games. Unlike those, which featured an individual turn-based system, Fallout Tactics features three combat types: Continuous Turn-Based (everyone can act at the same time, and action points are regenerated at a rate based on Agility), Individual Turn-Based (used in the original games) and Squad Turn-Based (each turn is given to a squad and include the ability to change stance, modifiers for height, and setting sentry modes).
Fallout Tactics is also the first of the Fallout games to feature a multi-player mode.
In this mode, each player controls a squad of characters and faces off against opposing players. During game setup, players are granted a number of points with which to purchase squad members and gear.
Although the main character in the single player game has to be human, recruits from the brotherhood and characters in multiplayer matches can be of any of the six races featured in the game. Humans, Super Mutants, Ghouls, Deathclaws, Dogs or Humanoid Robots.

I'd like to get this out of the way first. Yes, I know this game has pretty much been given up in terms of updates. That aside, I definitely recommend this forgotten game. Do I recommend this game to solo? A big NO. Get 3 friends and enjoy the game.
This game consists of only 1 campaign, a total of 7 missions/levels. It's a 4 player squad tactical co-op where you have a top view of your characters and using WASD to move and your mouse to shoot at targets. Though it is a rather very easy game on....easy difficulty, on normal and higher difficulties you require coordination with your teammates and even set up a team if needed. The fun, at least in my opinion, comes from attempting the speedrun achievements. The time spent in learning how to finish the mission in time without any of your buddies dying as well as keeping it within the time limit is fun. It's like learning how to fight a new boss properly with a party in your typical mmorpgs.
As said before, it is a forgotten game that does not receive anymore updates. But like it or not, it is still worth your time to try the challenge with your friends. I promise you will not be disappointed if you guys love learning ways to overcome difficult challenges.

Valiant Hearts: The Great War is a game over different figures who experience war in their own way, all trying to survive, but non of them are soldiers. Volunteers, sure, but not trained killers.
Story
The story is exellent, with an entirely different view on war. Unlike games like Battlefield 1, the characters feel emotions and have their own life. There is no conversation. No words, but some tones is enough.
The Graphics
Truely marvelous. The style is quite unique and sometimes morbid. Deaths aren't very often nor very graphic, but at some point in the game you can find a stack of bodies with feet blown off, etc. It is great to look at, the music isn't great, sometimes bland but adds to the atmosphere.
The Gameplay
Some puzzles feel oddly difficult while others are way too easy. The animation doesn't feel fluid at all times. The gameplay often feels bland and boring but gameplay is not too important in comparison (especially with other games).

It's a fun RPG isometric game.
The main objective of the game is to play and share adventures made by the players, and level up to face the dragon (the dragon is not really that important to defeat, he is a final objective but he will reward you with good loot, but you can get it also in the stages)
It has simple mechanics and good game mechanics, the editor is not so intuitive so you will need to check out tutorials on how to build your own stage and specially how to make switches and traps work correctly.
The bad? It seems little to no players play coop anymore (even though there is an active map creating community) and the enemy variety is very small. The graphics are also not the best, and some of the maps can have sections that are easily bugged.
I would recommend specially if you have someone at home to play split screen with, or if you like creating your own quests to share with others.

I give this a thumbs up, but only because it is priced at about the right level for the content you can expect.
In terms of gameplay, you work your way through hack and slash isometric maps, collect gear and loot, which you either equip or exchange for stat gains or better gear. Completing maps earns you tickets to "Fight The Dragon".
The maps usually involve a lot of clicking and running, as well as puzzles revolving largely around pressure pads and levers hidden within maze-like environments. Fighting the dragon is simply an arena against a boss.
This is reasonably fun for a short period of time, but it has little longevity.
The best part of the game is the creator, where you can design and build your own maps and campaigns. Despite the limiting graphics, there is actually a lot of freedom to build from the ground up, create relatively complex puzzles and interesting environments. Unfortunately, as always with these games, the maps you produce tend to get lost amongst a lot of crap, or go unnoticed beside those few early maps that received "thumbs ups" so show up in most people's searches.
I give this a tentative recommendation. It is fun but has little longevity.

Card Hunter is a free-to-play game that forgets to incentivise you to pay anything. The entire base game is available from the get-go and nothing is locked behind time or money gates, except for cosmetics. I have only played the base so you can see it makes up some 20 hours of content.
Leading your party of heroes through a variety of D&D-style scenarios, your equipped gear determines the deck of cards each of your characters draws from each game. Enemies will have different strengths and weaknesses such that your powerful load-out from last game could become entirely useless on the next level. This forces you away from being able to coast along on one overpowered strategy.
That being said the variety from the base items and enemies is not great. Most of the time you are not going to feel any difference between hitting something with an axe, or a lightning bolt, or fire. The underlying mechanics are quite simple so there is not much room for differentiation. If you don't enjoy the game in the first few levels I don't think things will improve for you.
Overall there is plenty here and as a free game, not much to lose. If you want even more of the experience there are plenty of expansions available to buy, but I cannot give any recommendation as to their value.

I give a very HESITANT Thumb-up. I'll explain.
I can't really judge this as a game, as much as I have to judge it as a toolbox. And, as with any game where you hand the keys to the kingdom to the playerbase, only about 1 in 12 actually knows what they're doing. :(
In Fight the Dragon you're given a battle arena against a red dragon with 1 MILLION health, and told to go questing from map to map to build yourself up and fight him. Any damage the dragon takes is cumulative, so even the 2 points of damage you do to him at lvl1 will stay.
So, you leap from player-made map to player-made map, fighting monsters and finding loot. As I said, most folks should not be given the tools to make game levels, as they don't know what is appealing, what flows well or even what looks good. I found myself with serious respect for the real industry after playing 50+ maps (there's an achievement for that), and only really liking about 8 of them.
But back to the dragon. Each time you finish a level you get a dragon ticket/scroll, which gives you three lives to fight the dragon in the special arena. As I said your damage sticks, so you run in and do as much damage as you can before he freaking annihilates you. Most battles last about 30 seconds, even with three lives. So you chip away at him over time as you level up Just remember:
-Fire Resist does NOT work on the Dragon
-You CANNOT bring your magic rings, arguably the best items in the game.
-Almost all the dragon's attacks have major push-back, so good luck if you're a melee character
The dragon fight is VERY unfair, and if that is the focus of your time in this game you're going to have a bad time. Instead, I spent my questing hours in search of a good map that felt like a real video game level, and not just something a 9 year-old threw together to mess with people. Not all levels are created equal, and it comes with a thumbs up/sideways/down function, and the ability to leave a comment on the level itself. I blasted a LOT of bad levels, trust me, and praised a few good ones.
Fight the Dragon is a cute rpg toolbox, but if you judge by the player-made content, not an especially good game. Get it on sale for a quick distraction, but this is not something to devote to.
TL:DR Version:
-Dragon has 1 Million HP, you chip away at his health over many attempts.
-Dragon fight does not respect fire resistance, magic rings, and allows you no health/mana items.
-Dragon can kill you three times in under 40 seconds, burning your Dragon Fight attempt currency.
-All the levels outside the tutorial are player-made, most of them are really bad.
-Cute, addictive, but not something you're ever going to finish. Only the INSANE will grind away the hours to ACTUALLY slay the dragon.

This is a first person Tactical Shooter where you lead a squad of four elite commandos. It has a high degree of versatility in how you and the squad interact or fight.
This game is for you if you like smarter first person shooters with a sense of humor.
    -    The fact that this game is set during the clone wars. Now, it hardly matters since the game has distanced itself from the prequels as much as it could. But it still worth mentioning.
    -    Limited amount of weapons.
    -    On higher difficulty enemies can take a lot of damage
    -    The game was made for 4:3 so you'll need to patch the game for higher resolution and correct aspect ratio. Links at the end.
    -    Changing weapons takes a few precious seconds.
    -    Whenever you get resurrected, it takes a few seconds too long to be able to move. This is really irritating when you're taking fire. Which you usually are if you're down...
    -    The game could've been a bit longer ...
    -    ...and there could have been a sequel damnit!
    +    I really like the dialogue and the sounds.
    +    I like how when 3 out of 4 of the team goes down, that one guy can still help the team up and turn the fight around.
    +    The maps have a really nice flow to them. You very rarely get lost or have to backtrack.
    +    The different campaigns have completely different settings.
    +    There's an easter egg or two around so the game does promote exploration
    +    The Commando AI works pretty well.
    +    There's little to no connection to the prequels The game is simply set in the Star Wars universe.
    +    There is no evil by designation. The game does not suffer from the polarization of e.g. Jedi versus Sith. This makes many games predictable. In Republic Commando it's simply you versus whoever intends to stop you from completing your mission
    +    I don't really think much about the music, which means that it does its job pretty well.
    +    There is no cover system (Not counting the fixed firing positions for your team). You just stand behind something to be in cover.

Retro City Rampage tries to do the whole GTA/Bethesda game/Ubigame thing of being a big open world that you get familiar with by driving around a hub, and that's a pretty modern convention. It also tries to do this while clumsily weilding about what they will assert is a very retro playstyle. The thing is, this ends up being a worst of both worlds scenario, strung with boring and repetitive combat scenarios spread across a pretty uninteresting city, with little motivating you to follow through with the dozens of side missions that show up on your radar. When I did try to do them, they felt like they were repeating the worst parts of the main campaign, which itself was largely juvenile in tone and design. They throw a million expendable cops, thugs, and soldiers your way, with a hundred invisible checkpoints and an infinite supply of lives so that you die a million times (97 by the end in my case) without losing a lot of progress. And I can't help but feel like that blind jab at "difficulty" is what they believed would make their game justifiable as "Nintendo Hard". RCR is less a game and more a hamfisted, halfhearted, and mostly unfunny collection of cheap references and gags.

At core, this is an interesting and somewhat tactical adventure board game. I like the different heroes and their playstyles, I like the challenge and the press-your-luck aspect, There's a lot to enjoy here, and as long as you don't examine the business or design decisions too closely you'll probably get a good number of hours out of it if you're a strategy focused player.
There's a few key problems that prevent me from being able to generally recommend it.
- The core reward/progression mechanic is based around randomly generated Quests. Quests become targetted to a specific space on the map, which you then become obligated to explore in order to receive a moderate reward and the choice to take a risk for something bigger.
The problem here is the fact that the quest location is set without any input from the player, and can in no way be prediced prior to making the choice of which quest to pursue. Logically this makes perfect sense and matches the questing model from the vast majority of RPG style games; however, here there's a very punishing random element to questing. Choosing one quest will permanently get rid of the opportunity to choose the other quests from that set, which means you're locked in to your target destination before you had any way to anticipate where it might be.
As the game progresses, the map gradually becomes filled with Perils which may cost you resources to overcome; additionally, the wandering monsters called Banes present a not insurmountable challenge, but it's a significant one. Unless you maximize your pawn's combat ability, the board can become a minefield as Banes get released onto the board. There's not many options for routing around them to get to your quest, because the long way around can easily involve spending 5 to 10 turns getting to the target location.
This results in 2 problems.
1.) Questing players are very much at the mercy of the RNG which spawn Perils and Banes and moves Banes from location to location. There is an element of strategy that becomes part of the equation when you're playing with other humans, but even then player ability to place Perils only really becomes pronounced in the later stages of the game, by which you should have developed your abilities to be able to overcome them or mitigate their effects.
2.) Of the four paths to victory, questing supports all of them; but one, the Spirit Stone victory, is specifically gated by questing and exploring dungeons. This means that heroes who are optimized for this victory route are even more strongly affected by the RNG as the game progresses, and will either breeze to their win condition or very quickly stall out and lose any hope of victory based on how banes and random perils propagate across the map.
This would seem to frame Armello as a game in which you need to keep your options open as much as possible and be prepared to take advantage of the opportunities that arise in the course of play, just developing your character as much as possible until it becomes clear you can make a try for one of the goals.
The problem with that interpretation is that there is a time limit to the game. Once a certain condition is met, the game will end and the player with the highest Prestige will win by default. This means that at any given time, the highest Prestige player is simply trying to stall the game, anyone in direct competition with them for the Prestige victory is trying to knock them out, and everyone else is rushing to complete a goal they may or may not have any chance at finishing based on conditions entirely out of their control.
The result of these conditions is that the only viable path to victory over which the player has any real control is Prestige. Prestige heroes are consistent, Prestige gain is reliable, and the Prestige victory is going to occur for someone 6 games out of 10. It's the only bet in the game that's actually worth making, and choosing a hero that is set up to aim for any of the other goals is essentially picking hard mode.
This would be fine, except it seems like the four victory paths are intended to be portrayed as being relatively balanced, and a relative balance between them is necessary for Armello to make any sense as a multiplayer game. Therefore, it simpy doesn't.
- The other main problem with the design is technical. The developers have provided the game with a zoom in/out function; however, they have independently and adamantly decided that the default level of zoom is the 'optimal' one for play, and that zooming out provides an unfair amount of information to players. They've supported this choice by adding a PS2 style fog effect that starts kicking in immediately as you start zooming out, and only gets progressively worse as you get higher above the playing field. Zoom out to the maximum level and you'll be wondering whether you booted up Armello or Silent Hill.
For a game with such beautiful art, the choice to provide the zoom function but make it functionally useless is utterly baffling to me; for a strategy board game, the decision seems even more strange. The models and terrain in Armello look great. Unfortunately, to appreciate them fully they need to be seen in context. If you zoom too close, you'll be looking closer than the distance they're optimized for. The detail shines at the top-down, distant levels, particularly at higher resolutions - or, y'know, it would. If you could see a thing. The default zoom level only shows off a few hexes at a time, and both from an artistic and a gameplay persepctive it's highly frustrating. It feels like the developers don't even know what their game's own strengths *are*, which is baffling, because clearly an enormous effort was behind the production of this game.
Armello is far from a solved game. There *are* different paths to victory. And because there's so much randomness, there is always the possibility for an upset to occur, for the seemingly impossible to happen, for the unlikely hero to take the crown.
But it's not what the design supports. Perhaps that off chance is enough for some players. As a strategy focused player myself, though, it's not. And at the too-close zoom level you're almost forced to use, the process of play is too frustrating to be enjoyable in the long term.

The prequels were flawed yes, but at least the Episodes II-III era (2002-2005) spawned some sweet SW games, for many the last great era for LucasArts (everything went downhill after 2005).
Republic Commando is "THE" SW shooter, by that I mean the best SW shooter of all time (unless Dark Forces gets a remake, which is unlikely next to impossible).
The Halo 2-Half 2 influence is evident (minus riding a vehicle and the gravity gun) and the game tries to be lean and mean (not bloody though). Explosions and melee attacks are everywhere, and the cheesy-cute humor of the prequels is nowhere to be found. Overall the game provides a solid Clone Wars experience.
The graphics still look very good for a mid-00s game and the sound design is superb.
But sadly, the game has some clear flaws, which put the game in a  8-8.5 out of 10 zone at best (it could have been a 10 out of 10)
a) too short (like 4-5 hours on easy). Also, some people will find frustrating that there are only three (extended) maps: Geonosis, Republic Ship and Kashyyyk.
b) the AI of the squad is not that great, they get killed easily on medium difficulty.
c) some enemies are ridiculously overpowered and hard to kill without heavy weapons (which are hard to find)
That said, the game was loved-popular enough so fans demanded a sequel, which never came due to the mismanagement of LucasArts that slowly killed the company until its 2012 disappearance.

This is a great game and you should buy it.
There. Now that we've got the most important part out of the way, let me explain why. This isn't a run-in-guns-blazing shoot-em-up game. It would be a solid shooter in it's own right even if it was, but Republic Commando more than holds its own, due to the strategic nature of the fights. The positioning of the other members of your squad around the environment (which will determine what weapons they will favour in the firefight) is critical to victory.
Take a sniper position further away from the action to provide covering fire?
Take a grenadier position to deal with tougher enemies?
Get in a turret and lay down heavy fire?
Most importantly of all, which instructions will allow your squad to cover each other and achieve the objective?
Make no mistake, the fights in this game, especially near the end, can get extremely difficult. You will die multiple times and have to strategise and experiment to discover which tactics will lead you to victory. And when you have to decide whether to take out the enemies in front of you first or sabotage one of two droid dispensers, every second it takes you to reach a decision is vital.
With four different weapons and four different grenades (plus whatever extra weapon you can scavenge from defeated enemies), the choices of a head-on assault, a flanking attack or a defensive position become very important and have to be judged carefully.
Although some today may consider this lacking due to not being based with co-op in mind, that is because this game is 11 years old, and was made when co-op play wasn't such a big deal. Maybe a missed opportunity, but not something that any Star Wars fan should hold against it.
Forget the new Battlefront. This is an excellent game, and I still hold out hope for a sequel or a remaster.

Alien Swarm is a game with a unique and interesting backstory to how it came to be. Sporting a top-down camera with an adjusted 60 degree view and set in a sci-fi realm, Alien Swarm arms you and up to three additional friends for some seriously fast-paced shooting and survival combat.
For those unaware of the history of Alien Swarm, it was created from a mod from Unreal Tournament 2004 by a team that was hired and supported by Valve. Originally, the game was produced by Valve, but unlike some of the more popular titles such as Counter-Strike, Team Fortress or the Half-Life series, it never really got the focus and recognition that the others did. In fact, there is only one official campaign in the entire game, called “Jacob’s Rest”, which is comprised by only a handful of levels. However, that does not necessarily detract from the overall appeal of the game.
An obvious downside to playing Alien Swam, as mentioned, is the one solo campaign. Within the confines of this one mission, your task is to land on a colonized planet, investigate what happened, exterminate all hostile alien lifeforms and rescue any survivors.
You’re given a choice between four classes: “Officer” – your primary gunner who earns passive damage and resistance bonuses as well as unique weaponry unique to only them, the “Medic” who heals teammates, the “Tech” who can deploy sentries, hack systems, weld doors with incredible speed and can carry class-specific grenades and auto rifles, and lastly, the “Special Weapons” which boasts massive damage output. Within these classes are 40 different equipment pieces that you can select based on your class, play style and need, making customization fairly simple and streamlined.
The game, as mentioned above, as a major drawback: that one campaign. However, the game included the software development kit [SDK], which, for those not familiar with the term, is the source code to it, allowing for full-scale modding and customization. This spawned a vibrant modding community that has made some truly fantastic campaigns to play, keeping Alien Swarm alive and well with new content and challenges. With the SDK included, users can play any of the user-created content, create their own or modify ones to their liking or specifications.
With all that said and as with other Valve products, Alien Swarm has a smooth multiplayer interface, full overlay support and integrated invitation options to invite your friends. While playing solo is fun in its own right, the game really shines when playing with a group of four, invoking the need for communication, teamwork and support of everyone involved; make no mistake, Alien Swarm can be extremely punishing.
A variety of difficulties, friendly fire penalties, tight corridors and waves of aliens means Alien Swarm will test both your reflexes, intuition and ability to work together as a team. Don’t get cocky, because when you die the game will freeze and slow motion capture your painful, premature death and let you know who killed you. So if you’re use to blaming your “friendly” fire on glitches, your friend or the enemies, the game will most certainly be there to call out your transgressions for all to see.
With consistent statistical data being tracked outside the game [much like other Valve titles], Alien Swarm provides an in-depth look at what classes you excel at, what weapons you prefer, your accuracy and how many times you sabotaged the mission with excessive friendly fire and much more. It becomes a handy tool when deciding who you want to complete some of the more excruciatingly difficult achievements the game has to offer.
Alien Swarm is one of those games I feel should really be re-examined because what is here, is wonderful. Smooth level design, crisp features, class customization, full source code and level design and a great atmosphere make it a great game to play for newcomers and veterans alike. There’s a severe amount of untapped potential within Alien Swarm. Did I mention, it is free?


Overall, Alien Swarm is often overlooked by other Valve titles. While the consensus among fans is that it is a worthy title to sit down and play, many people might not be familiar with it or know how it came to be. As more and more titles are being released every day, Alien Swarm still stands as something worth playing, even after all these years. Seriously, get out, recruit some friends and go blast some aliens. You won’t regret it.

This game promises to be a lot of fun if you have a lot of steam friends to play with. Unfortunately it suffers in a lot of areas. The AI is completely stupid. Several times I moved through the map, and one of my team got obsessed with killing the constantly (and in my opinion too quickly) respawning monsters and refused to follow the group, even though there was no ral need for them to keep killing the monsters. Ofcourse they get overwhelmed and die. At least once one of the team let themselves get stuck on the wrong side of a door and die as well, and you have to issue commands to them to make them do common sense things, or switch to them and control them directly.
The 'endless stream of aliens' thing in a game with no continues, save points or extra lives seems excessive, especially when you consider they also have massive swarms that attack in these areas, having built up behind some barrier before exploding through it in a giant wave. So far that I've seen, no weapon handles that kind of thing well... especially with friendly fire being a thing. It's also annoying that friendly fire can't be deactivated. t's basically impossible to know what a fellow player is going to do so you're constantly shooting each other, which, combined with the massive swarms of monsters and steady flow of incoming basically means you're GONNA kill someone you're probably really gonna need later.
The absolute worst thing about this game is the absence of a solo play option that actually matters. You can play practice sessions, but you get no experience for them, and can't advance through the stages; basically preventing you from learning the maps or developing a strategy for later stages by play throughs. Looking for a game to play is pointless, as you either run into locked, 'private' games that auto kick you, or groups of people running around three stooges style, headbutting monsters and each other until they die over and over with some seeming hope of leveling up as they die.
The good things about the game: despite all I've said, its got good atmosphere. You definitely get a good 'Aliens' feel from travelling down the corridors, or blasting your way through hordes of aliens. And it's always fun to just shoot things in these situations. So there's that at least.
If you can find a team of four who want to play this game regularly, it will improve quite a bit. Otherwise you're basically stuck struggling to make progress into the game, or playing with people who are seemingly trying to kill you as badly as the aliens are.

The following is a review of Sniper: Ghost Warrior 3 from a gamer that has played mostly FPS games for nearly 20 years and also was a veteran of United States SOF. I began messing with computers in 1984 with my first Commodore 64 computer. I was hooked. After that I started playing all sorts of games like Jane’s F-18 etc. What really got me hooked was when the release of Doom 3 and Xbox hit the market. To this day, it is my opinion that Doom 3 was the best FPS to ever hit the market for that time period. There was more to do than just “run and gun”, which brings me to Ghost Warrior 3. I am by no means a professional critic, but I do feel there are others that think like I do and have opinions that are similar.
I didn’t buy the game right away because the initial reviews were not very complimentary. In fact, I thought they were pretty brutal; enough to persuade me to beg off until release reviews. I am now on a fixed income so $59.99 is a lot for me to pay for a new game, but don’t get me wrong. If I know the game is really good, I will gladly eat Ramon noodles for awhile until I can cover the losses. Three months after release, I bought a used copy for my Xbox One at Gamestop. I had heard the nightmare stories of lots of bugs, long load times, unexpected crashes, etc. Before I started the game, I downloaded and printed a really good guide for the game which informed me of a blow by blow description on how to play the game, what bugs to expect and where, and how to avoid the unexpected crashes. While reading this guide, I became hooked on this game and I haven’t even started yet. Let me go back though. I have bought Ghost Warrior 1 & 2 on release day in the past and have been extremely satisfied with how it played. So I knew ahead of time what to expect basically. I knew the game changer was the open world aspect that they changed to for this particular title. So without further adieus, let me tell you what I thought.
This game is a great training tool because it is very close to the “real deal”. It shows how you really need to think ahead of your objective. You plan your equipment, arsenal, strike time, travel time and even allow for those unexpected side missions that you have the option of taking part in or not. You learn to listen carefully to your mission details so you can plan accordingly. A big part of your mission success is to know your environment and how to interface with it whether you are tracking, adapting to weather, or just solving a simple problem to alleviate a troublesome issue. The map you follow is a great beginners guide to topographic maps. All of this is in a huge open world gaming arena that scores and grades you on 3 major ironic points; Sniper, Ghost and Warrior skills. That’s right. It’s up to you how to accomplish these missions. You can go in guns blazing if you want, or just take your time and use stealth to sneak in and keep your presence unknown and body count to a minimum. You learn to be thorough no matter which way you do it.
It is my understanding that by the time I bought the game, most glitches and bugs had been addressed or fixed. Some griped that it didn’t have a multi-player mode and was put off by that. Sad as it sounds, I never play multi player. The reason is that there are so many people that cheat and take advantage of others, I don’t bother. I would rather sit down with a good game that has awesome AI, and play it differently each time to see what works for me. I like a game that rewards me for thinking and punishes me when I am not. Have I played the whole game yet? No, and with good reason. As I stated earlier, this is not a “run and gun” game. You savor this game like a good bottle of scotch, taking your time and enjoying its’ different “notes”.
So, overall, what do I think about this installment of Sniper: Ghost Warrior 3? Overall from what I see, the only real miscalculation that was made on this game was the release date compared to how many bugs it had. I realize it was pushed back on the schedule and problems arose, but I really think that if it didn’t have as many problems as it did, even the long load times would not have been as front and center as it was. Some say the open world should never have been used to make this different from the other two installments. I disagree. This was a huge difference to this game and made you feel less controlled in the environment. There was more realism than ever and lots of incentives throughout the game. The game play didn’t disappoint either. If you have no experience with ballistics, you can choose the normal mode, where it puts the dot where the bullet will travel. However, if you like the realism, then choose a higher level and learn to accept where you decided to put that bullet taking into consideration the ammunition type, the direction and speed of the wind, the distance, the target etc. That is truly what it’s all about. One shot, one kill. (or more) . This game teaches you to be responsible for your actions. The one thing I didn’t like about this game was that I couldn’t manually save along the way. So if you screw up, the last check point might be the beginning of the mission. It just makes you that much more careful and sure of your actions. I'm not sure whether to give this a yes or no recommendation.
Having played the pre-Steam version and now the Steam version, I have to say, this is a...decent platformer.  But I'd hesitate to call it any more than that.  It's certainly playable, basically bug-free, and accomplishes what it sets out to do, but it just...doesn't seem to feel all that fun, to me.
Specifically, the gameplay feels very, very linear and constrained.  There are few "creative" solutions possible to problems -- it's like, there's the obvious solution, and then that's it, and any attempt to try something less obvious will result in failure.
Pros:
+ nice, colorful visual designs
+ simple, easy-to-learn controls
+ vaguely interesting storyline, with visual details that correspond to it
+ secrets are easy to find (good for completionist nuts).
+ low basic difficulty (good for people new to platformers, such as children).
+ bonus challenge levels for more advanced players.
Cons:
- is too long to keep interest.  The gameplay stays largely the same, through all the levels.  While some enemies are defeated in different ways, and new stage hazards are introduced, the core gameplay of non-boss levels is essentially identical.  Each level drags on a little, and then having all these levels just drags it on even longer.
- some boss fights are rather tedious.  Example: the second area boss (the rock boss) -- if you screw up twice or touch the lava, then you just have to wait through that whole cycle again.
- gameplay doesn't lend itself to easy skipping.  If you screwed up earlier and respawned at a checkpoint, you'll still have to go past those same obstacles.  Though at least in this current version, stars stay collected and enemies don't respawn, which is a good thing.  (Bomb walls respawn, though.)
- controls are a little floaty in some ways.  (e.g. jump height)  Hit detection is pretty reasonable, though.
- some inconsistencies.  For example, red-aura enemies are supposed to be invulnerable, but some can be defeated, while some enemies without red auras are invulnerable.  If you're going for max points, this will annoy you.
- gameplay leaves very little room for creativity.  Moving faster is one example, speeding up boss fights is another.  You just can't do these things.  Crushing stone blocks are designed such that you can't run past two of them at once and you simply must wait for them one by one.  You can't move fast enough to pelt that boss with two bombs in one cycle, nor can you pick up bombs in mid-air.
The soundtrack is okay -- not particularly notable.  It becomes a little repetitive, but this is because (1) the same track gets used over multiple levels, and especially (2) the track starts playing from the beginning every time Oozi dies and respawns, making it more repetitive than is necessary.
Overall, this is a platformer with simple, straightforward, easy-to-learn controls, which are decent (albeit a little floaty).  I'd recommend this for people who are looking for a first-timer's platformer, especially for children given the flavor elements (i.e. the whole story about an alien visiting Earth, which looks nothing like Earth anyway in the game, haha), and it's a solid game in that regard, though there are probably better offerings out there, such as Mutant Mudds Deluxe with its very good learning curve which leads it from easy to more challenging gameplay.  Meanwhile, anyone who's played at least a few platformers will probably find this rather boring.
(Disclosure: I acquired this game as part of the Groupees Build a Greenlight Bundle.)

Wow, what a game. Many people write this off as a classic Lucas cash-grab, only there to entertain the kids. But as a huge fan of the Clone Wars TV show, I can honestly say that once I was able to put aside the sometimes clunky platforming, this was a pretty fun little Star Wars game. The story is your average kind from the show, a sporadic series of epic events that eventually are revealed to be one main storyline. With that said, however, it does a nice job of going from show form to game form, cleanly presenting you with enemies, levels, etc. In terms of aesthetics, this game is beautiful, a near-perfect art style matching the show, however back when the game was made, they weren't quite ready to efficiently utilize this style to it's full potential, as you'll spot when the game plays video from the show that isn't as smooth nor as clean cut as the original product; compare that to the game art style and the difference is clear. The camera is at times clunky, and you would swear the force is one with the ice, but overall this is an adventure that true fans of the Star Wars franchise should not miss out on despite it's flaws!

At core, this is an interesting and somewhat tactical adventure board game. I like the different heroes and their playstyles, I like the challenge and the press-your-luck aspect, There's a lot to enjoy here, and as long as you don't examine the business or design decisions too closely you'll probably get a good number of hours out of it if you're a strategy focused player.
There's a few key problems that prevent me from being able to generally recommend it.
- The core reward/progression mechanic is based around randomly generated Quests. Quests become targetted to a specific space on the map, which you then become obligated to explore in order to receive a moderate reward and the choice to take a risk for something bigger.
The problem here is the fact that the quest location is set without any input from the player, and can in no way be prediced prior to making the choice of which quest to pursue. Logically this makes perfect sense and matches the questing model from the vast majority of RPG style games; however, here there's a very punishing random element to questing. Choosing one quest will permanently get rid of the opportunity to choose the other quests from that set, which means you're locked in to your target destination before you had any way to anticipate where it might be.
As the game progresses, the map gradually becomes filled with Perils which may cost you resources to overcome; additionally, the wandering monsters called Banes present a not insurmountable challenge, but it's a significant one. Unless you maximize your pawn's combat ability, the board can become a minefield as Banes get released onto the board. There's not many options for routing around them to get to your quest, because the long way around can easily involve spending 5 to 10 turns getting to the target location.
This results in 2 problems.
1.) Questing players are very much at the mercy of the RNG which spawn Perils and Banes and moves Banes from location to location. There is an element of strategy that becomes part of the equation when you're playing with other humans, but even then player ability to place Perils only really becomes pronounced in the later stages of the game, by which you should have developed your abilities to be able to overcome them or mitigate their effects.
2.) Of the four paths to victory, questing supports all of them; but one, the Spirit Stone victory, is specifically gated by questing and exploring dungeons. This means that heroes who are optimized for this victory route are even more strongly affected by the RNG as the game progresses, and will either breeze to their win condition or very quickly stall out and lose any hope of victory based on how banes and random perils propagate across the map.
This would seem to frame Armello as a game in which you need to keep your options open as much as possible and be prepared to take advantage of the opportunities that arise in the course of play, just developing your character as much as possible until it becomes clear you can make a try for one of the goals.
The problem with that interpretation is that there is a time limit to the game. Once a certain condition is met, the game will end and the player with the highest Prestige will win by default. This means that at any given time, the highest Prestige player is simply trying to stall the game, anyone in direct competition with them for the Prestige victory is trying to knock them out, and everyone else is rushing to complete a goal they may or may not have any chance at finishing based on conditions entirely out of their control.
The result of these conditions is that the only viable path to victory over which the player has any real control is Prestige. Prestige heroes are consistent, Prestige gain is reliable, and the Prestige victory is going to occur for someone 6 games out of 10. It's the only bet in the game that's actually worth making, and choosing a hero that is set up to aim for any of the other goals is essentially picking hard mode.
This would be fine, except it seems like the four victory paths are intended to be portrayed as being relatively balanced, and a relative balance between them is necessary for Armello to make any sense as a multiplayer game. Therefore, it simpy doesn't.
- The other main problem with the design is technical. The developers have provided the game with a zoom in/out function; however, they have independently and adamantly decided that the default level of zoom is the 'optimal' one for play, and that zooming out provides an unfair amount of information to players. They've supported this choice by adding a PS2 style fog effect that starts kicking in immediately as you start zooming out, and only gets progressively worse as you get higher above the playing field. Zoom out to the maximum level and you'll be wondering whether you booted up Armello or Silent Hill.
For a game with such beautiful art, the choice to provide the zoom function but make it functionally useless is utterly baffling to me; for a strategy board game, the decision seems even more strange. The models and terrain in Armello look great. Unfortunately, to appreciate them fully they need to be seen in context. If you zoom too close, you'll be looking closer than the distance they're optimized for. The detail shines at the top-down, distant levels, particularly at higher resolutions - or, y'know, it would. If you could see a thing. The default zoom level only shows off a few hexes at a time, and both from an artistic and a gameplay persepctive it's highly frustrating. It feels like the developers don't even know what their game's own strengths *are*, which is baffling, because clearly an enormous effort was behind the production of this game.
Armello is far from a solved game. There *are* different paths to victory. And because there's so much randomness, there is always the possibility for an upset to occur, for the seemingly impossible to happen, for the unlikely hero to take the crown.
But it's not what the design supports. Perhaps that off chance is enough for some players. As a strategy focused player myself, though, it's not. And at the too-close zoom level you're almost forced to use, the process of play is too frustrating to be enjoyable in the long term.

It's a deep strategy game with attractive visual design.  The storytelling is all mechanical, which is something I appreciate in a game.  To be more specific, you play a hero vying for the crown of an endangered kingdom.  The king is slowly dying and also becoming more and more evil due to a dark mystical force known as the Rot.
The Rot can also take hold of the player characters, and one of the win conditions is actually to become even more corrupted than the king and overpower him through the raw strength of evil.  Another win condition is to become the champion of the good mystical force, known as the Wyld, and outright destroy the king with pure nature.  Another path to victory is simply to infiltrate the castle and best the king in single combat before he dies from his affliction.  Not as simple as it sounds.  Finally, there is the prestige victory.  Prestige is won and lost in many of the activities of the game, including questing and combat.
I would point out that the difference in difficulty of achieving the different victory types is unreasonably wild.  Nine out of ten games will be won with Prestige, the others will be won by assassination.  Rot and Wyld victories are unlikely, difficult, and almost entirely based on dumb luck.
Pros:
-Fun visual design
-Complex gameplay
-Abundance of playable characters (with DLC)
Cons:
-Games take a long time to finish
-When they say "easy to learn, hard to master," they really mean that second part
-Too much luck involved in determining victory

Fallout Tactics is a great game. Anyone who says this doesn't deserve the name "Fallout" hasn't played Fallout. The story is great, entertaining, and engaging, and straight out of the Fallout fiction. While the RPG elements of the previous two Fallout installments are mostly absent, Fallout Tactics gives you complete control of each member of your party down to the clothes they wear, the guns they carry, and exactly what they do. As you travel the wastes, you can pick up additional team members and types, making the customizability of this game and replayability immense. I have played and replayed this game multiple times, as the graphics and gameplay have stood up over the years quite well. My only complaint is the linearity of the storyline, but even then you can just go wander the wastelands if you feel like it, which is fun in itself.

This game is awesome.
As I write this, I am at the beginning of Act 3.  I played the game offline for a couple days (Hurricane Irma) so my hours do not reflect playtime.
In short, this game feels like an open-world Call of Duty with elements of sniper Elite.  A more forgiving far cry.
I loved Sniper: Ghost Warrior 2, which in my opinion felt alot like DICE games from the same era. (Battlefield 2: Bad Company)  The missions in this game have much the same feeling, (at this point There has only been one "guardian angel" mission, which I loved.
This time CI has framed their game in a Gorgeous detailed open world, rife with side objectives.  Cryengine produces such beautiful environments.  You can blow through the story missions or put time into the side missions and optional objectives.  I found a completionist take to be very rewarding.  The setting is stunning, woods and mountains, and I explored it in depth.
I have heard crticisms of the story.  Sigh.  It's an action game...  The writing doesn't need to break any new ground.  This game has what it needs to move the adventure.  Brotherhood.  Betrayal.  Vengence. Retribution....  (More to come, will update.)
Audio is good.  Voice acting good.
Over all, the game has a few bugs, but feels AAA.  Hats off to CI.
I got the season pass edition of this game, a couple months after release, for about $20.  I find this to be more than fair in a market that thinks a gamer should drop a minimum of $100 for similar content in the first few months after release.  Bravo CI.
Elements.
The gunplay.
Sniping is the main event here, refined and exhilarating.  (I lean heavily toward it.  I have 13 skill points over what I can apply to the tree) Bullet cam is well done, if it gets too repetive, you can shut it off.  I don't.
Secondary weapons are useful, varied and upgradeable.  You can engage in COD like gunplay, but you do not get nearly the sort of forgiving health setup.  Bring your A game.
Sidearms are good in a pinch, stealth headshots are their specialty.
Stealth.
Vital here.  You can crouch and go prone.  Sound is a factor.  Stealth kills are quick and brutal.  Throwing knife is useful.  In my opinion, stealth is well done and not to be negelcted.
Mobility.
Jon has a nearly Ezio-esque ability to climb and jump.  CI gives you plenty of opportunities to use them.  "Extreme navigation" can lead to rewards or help with objective infiltration.  A great addition to the game.
The drone.
I love this damn thing.  As a recon tool it makes far more sense than the "tower" trope or the balloons from mad max.  Also doesn't serve the same purpose.  Local goals only....  If you want to know what is in the world Map, go explore it.  The side objectives give you plenty to do.  Unlike many open world games, there are no pointless collectibles.  Weapon unlocks and supplies aacompany almost every "point of interest".
The music is great.  My fiance, who hates video games in general commented on the sweet music.  (Which shares roots with the Witcher 3 soundtrack)
If you see this on sale, i don't think you'll regret going for it.
PS- get the DLC.  Especially the car/rifle.  For a couple bucks, they are worth it.

This is not only my absolute favorite Star Wars game ever created, it's one of my favorite GAMES ever created. You control the leader of "Delta Squad," an elite group of clone Commando's. Each of these squad members is exceptionally voice acted, and they feel like real people. You will grow attached to them, and it truly starts to feel like a squad of brothers. I've played through this game over 7 times (only twice on Steam though), and it never feels old. The game came out around 2005, but the graphics and mechanics still hold up today. This isn't just a first person shooter. You actually have to think a little. You can give your squad orders (take up a grenade postion, disarm a mine, hack a computer, etc.) and depending on the situation, you might have to improvise, as it can get very hard very fast if something goes wrong. The story is very engaging, and a thrill to playthrough. The multiplayer felt like BattleFront 2's multiplayer, but without the ability to get into vehicles. (It's shut down now though).
Buy this game if you want an excellent Star Wars title with lots of heart, solid gameplay, an engaging story, and amazing voice acting.

If you've played Genesis and Super Nintendo platformers as a lad... heck, even Sega CD ones (I can't be the only one who remembers Wonder Dog... can I?)... this true-to-the-classics 2D platformer is calling for you!
What I like the most:
+ For slightly over a dollar, this is certainly much more than the bang for my buck. Without replaying for extra achievements, I put in 5 hours to beat it, so it only cost me somewhere around 20 cents for each hour played so far.
+ The art... both levels and characters... are excellent, and the goofier ones remind me of beloved cartoon characters and props, like the Three Eyed Fish from The Simpsons.
+ Much like the Super Mario series does with coins, collecting the abundance of stars gives you a sense of fun and satisfaction.
+ The length of the game is perfect, and although there are only 4 worlds, there is enough to explore in each of the worlds' levels that it feels as if there are more.
+ Upon completion of each of the first three worlds, you get a new powerup that helps you on your quest and provides a new gameplay mechanic (e.g. gloves that allow you to latch onto walls.)
+ Ever download one of those free Mario clones from Google Play? Imagine someone actually spent time on the level design, didn't throw a bunch of ads at you, and actually updated the gameplay mechanics as you go along (such as the aforementioned glove example.) Such is Oozi!
+ No gimmicky puzzles: pure platforming!
Some nuanced critiques:
- The difficulty of the bosses isn't the most balanced... I found the second boss to be much more difficult than the third and fourth bosses. They also can be time consuming to defeat, so it can be a little aggravating when you almost have your battle won, die, and then realize you have at least several more minutes to go to get back to being as close to beating that boss as you just were.
- Oozi's death groan got under my skin a little, and after awhile I found myself imitating it in order to cover up the game's loud and croaky rendition of it.
- The ending is really short.
Recommended: Absolutely. It plays like a classic 2D platformer, and though it doesn't reinvent the wheel, there's certainly nothing wrong with that.

- Quick time to kills with pistols being able to perform a 3-shot kill at chest high
- Almost no HUD on the screen
- Recoil where the weapon also moves around the screen as well climb
- Realistic damage where sniper rifles ALWAYS 1-shot light armored opponents

This has to be one of my favourite 8-bit games on steam. So what is this game exactly? Well it's exactly what it says it is. A 8-bit open world with a nostalgia feel to it, it really has a nice feel to the game. If Grand Theft Auto where made into a 8-bit graphic, with top down perspective, and some inapropriate humour then this is what you would expect from this game.
I really wasn't expecting this game to be as fun as it was. Although I have a few faults with the game play sid eof this game, overall it's rather impressive. As you would expect in any open world game there are quite a few missions to get through, and then there are side missions that may help you in  the actual missions later on. Some of the side missions are rather quite difficult, and the way that some of them are set out aren't really all that fun to play. After doing a few side missions I kind of just went on with the main story and left them out. They might've helped me in the main missions but I don't really think it would of all that much. As for the main missions, some of them where brutally difficult for me. The final boss wasn't really all what I thought it would be, moving from side to side and dodging whatevere that guy was shooting at you. I did rage a few times but beat it in the end. On a positive note, some of the missions where quite funny and simply just what  guy would do to waste time, for example there was a mission to waste time. So you get a hover suit and just bash people on the head instead of waiting. The characters where a little dull and boring, and the story really isn't ll that much, I basically knew what was going on almost all the time without the game telling me what to do. Get a sevral items for the
and then get back. Not really all that fun but kept me entertained with the decent missions to keep me playing. The game took me about 9 hours to complete, I still sometimes go on it just to run people over in a car and mess around.
The game (if you haven't already noticed) has a 8-bit styled graphic to it which really works well with everything that happens in the game. Everything looks like you would be able to play it in a old school arcade machine. Although some of the animations are a little lazy, for example the cars don't really have any wheel animation on the ground. This can sometimes make it look like everything is just moving across the road with the wheels not running across the road. I'm not really sure what you could've done to solve that but it was kind of annoying  to see that sometimes for me. Other than that nothing else to complain about the game graphics wise.
The music and sound for this game where both really good. The sounds for certain things weren't at all generic and really fit well with the 8-bit style of the game, the music also fits well with certain scenarios in the game. Whether you're killing a bunch of robots in a tower or just chilling along the road smashing everything in your path! The game really sets the music well.
This is probably one of my favourite 8-bit games on steam. With it's decent overworld map to mess about in, the music and sounds along with the awesome 8-bit graphics make it all feel like a pretty solid game. Do be prepaired though for some difficult missions that you might come across in the game that might leave you playing it for more than you want to. But some great humour and game play implemented into this game.
