A delightful computer board game with strong gameplay, colourful board and card designs and nice animations.
You play the role of one of the characters belonging to an Animal Clan in the Kingdom of Armello, working to overthrow the corrupted King Lion and becoming its new ruler. The game is always 4 players, and has 4 different win conditions which one way or another involve the death of the old King.
The game is easy to get into while retaining depth in the combinations of items, spells, trickery, follower and treasure cards that you acquire over the course of the game. The characters all have different abilities and interact with one another on their quest while adventuring across Armello to prepare to take down the King.
Would definitely recommend buying the game, it's great to play with friends and is generally completed in under an hour. The DLCs do enrich the way you play the game with new characters but the game works perfectly well without them, and the game is compatible to play with others regardless of owned DLCs.
One final note is that randomness plays a heavy part in the game, the makers of Armello make no secret of this fact! If you find randomness frustrating there are ways to play around it, but you will generally not do as well as those that take the bigger risks.
Every single player is still in with a chance to win right at the end, which actually is a positive feature of the game because it incentivises you not to give up!

After one multiplayer game, I can say this is one of the greatest board games I've ever played. The battle was incredibly heated up to the very end of the turn limit where anyone could've won. Each of us was approaching victory with a different strategy, but all of us equally able to win in our own way.
Each game is a story:
I started the game in the same area as Rabbit who tried to kill me two turns in, but we settled on a truce using the pre-programmed chat. Wolf was top. Bear was on the left. Very early in the game, Bear got all 4 spirit stones (super lucky), and thus he only had to reach the king to win. Wolf and I would have none of that, so we attacked and delayed him every time he came near the king.
After getting some prestiege, I used my new law-making power to give gifts to my ally, Rabbit, who later buffed me with spells in return. Once I had the bare-minimum attack power, I decided to rush the king before bear could win, which was essentially a risky all-in to win the game. Wolf was skepical, and continued to build his power.
Somehow got into the castle, rabbit buffed me with 3 spells to win the game (shoutout to Rabbit. Such a great ally), and WOLF came in with guns & spells blazing to rob me of my victory! We ended up killing each other, leaving the door to win wide open for Rabbit (who was behind at the time).
Naturally, I came in behind to buff Rabbit so she could claim victory, but WOLF used his prestiege to pass a law that struck down Rabbit with lightning and guards, opening the way for another face off between Wolf, Bear, and I. I made it to the castle first, Bear sat in the space next to me, and Wolf had the final decision. Kill Bear or kill me, thus declaring the other the winner.
For some reason, Wolf had a change of heart (or stuck to tradition) and killed Bear, Rabbit came in and buffed me, and I claimed victory ONE HALF a turn away from Wolf winning by prestiege.
Without Rabbit, Wolf would've easily taken the victory from me, so diplomatic victories exist too, even if they're not programmed in!
Really a fantastic game, and each mode of victory is just as viable (and fun) as the others. Easy to learn and easy to master, and very fun to play. (Note: This game was with internet strangers. Playing with friends is probably even more fun!)

Fun with plenty of strategy.  Refreshing and Steam needs games like this.
However, steam does not need devs like this.
The MP aspect of the game suffers heavily from collusion (players communicating through msging to coordinate/rig the game).  In a team game, that would be acceptable... in a Free For All game, it is not.  In a max four player game, it is unbalancing, and downright stupid when 3 of the 4 are in on it.  The game purposely restricts communicating to preset statements.  Temporary alliances of questionable trust are indeed part of the game - full game, solid teams are not.
But the devs do not do anything about it.  By contrast, look at the community hub for gremlins inc - the dev team remains active and involved with the player, responding quickly to investigate collusion claims that are provided with evidence, and taking steps to make sure those players are not rewarded.
The difference is reflected on the player base.  Constant game dev, expansion (and not simply p2w skin packs), frequent tournaments, servers for different regions, and easy to find games in Gremlins inc.
There are times in Armello where I can't find a game at all.  And no wonder - imagine waiting interminably for a mp game, only to find the players are colluding (and 3p teams cannot match other 3p teams in a 4p game) and you never stand a chance.  And there are no rewards for SP.  So why would you play this instead of something else?
Throw in p2w skin/char packs (in addition to the usual offering of paid cosmetic, map cosmetic, and chest/key microtrans...but even there, a paucity)... It would be hard to recommend this on anything other than a 'pay what you want' pricing, and even then you shouldn't pay much - because the game will make you pay in many other ways.

Half-Life with co-op?
♥♥♥♥ yes.

Sven Co-op is a Co-operative mod for the original Half-Life. It’s a simple premise: it’s Half-Life, but with your buddies. No competitive gameplay. No score streaks. Nothing fancy. Just play Half-Life with your friends.
You can share ammo with your co-op buddies, you can “boost” players up to secret areas or hard to reach areas by crouching down and letting them jump on you (a “quirk” of the Half-Life engine gleefully exploited by map designers). You can also heal your team mates with a medic kit that you all spawn with. You can gradually heal your team mates’ lost health, or sacrifice half of the med kit to revive dead team members. It’s a secret hidden treasure trove of untapped level design talent in the Half-Life community.
The official maps bundled with this release are of a wide array of crazy, from your very standard Half-Life rip off maps, to the more serious Afrika Corps maps (a kind of Co-op Day of Defeat) or the bonkers yet impeccably well made Toonrun maps. There’s even a set of maps set inside Tetris. However, it’s not all bright and shiny. To the newcomer, Sven Co-op is a confusing tangled web of spaghetti and confused design. It also doesn’t inform the player at any point in any of its finer details. There have been huge changes to NPCs and the like that are simply not documented well mid-game, and you’ll usually rely on the kindness of Public Server strangers to inform you, but that’s part of the charm. In my experience, Sven Co-op has always been an incredibly social experience, and I’ve found myself befriending total strangers on servers just because we had a complete blast on a maze map. You’ll find yourself opening up way more in-game than you would in Counter Strike where you’re more likely to receive racist abuse than anything constructive.
All in all, it’s absolutely fantastic – still. Download Sven Co-op now. You’ll barely know what’s happening, but somehow, someway, you’ll be swept up with your team mates in a crazy barrage of yelling, explosions, colour and sound. Sven Co-op is a welcome and beloved addition to the vast chapter in PC gaming known as the immortal Half-Life and I’m happy its received the boost in player count that this latest version will bring...

TL;DR is at the bottom.
Deciding to take a chance on this game after some real obvious problems during the public beta period & some other obvious problems with it's the company's staff I bought this during its current sale. $27 local currency down from a very unreasonable $55.
And... results are mixed.
The worst right off the top... after a 50 GB download I told the game to not use anymore data from the very start when it attempted to contact the internet... which turned out to be their worthless inclusion of denuvo rearing its ugly head right from the start. From a very much non-"AAA" game (though it doesn't qualify as "indie" either oddly). Restarting the game to re-allow internet access got me by the crappy DRM and appears to be the only thing it wanted from the internet... after the 2 week inital activation it did not try & connect to any other comptuers.
Once that was done I set the settings to high, made sure subtitles were off & went in game.
The game still has left over problems from the beta period which I don't believe the company knows how to fix despite there being several patches. However the game is improved from said beta period.
Built on the CryEngine the game is not a prime example of what the engine can do; proof that having a decent engine isn't all you need to make a decent game. But then anyone dealing with Unity engine based games should be familar with how that goes.
Examples where this particular game fails when using the CryEngine: the textures look some what washed out as if they forgot to disable a filter on their photo suite. Those are layered on decent but not great models; the hoods on the seperatists are a prime example... it looks like their face melted more so then they are wearing a hood.
Based on their gamma control prompt I'm supposed to play the game on maximum gamma setting... however I'm not doing so because this makes the game lack any sort of contrast. I don't know if that's a problem with their skull icon being too dark or what but I made up my own mind on gamma setting. It certainly doesn't help the graphics at all however to have it at maximum gamma which is why I'm playing only slightly above the middle setting.
Beyond making use of the engine the game has several programming/design bugs that fall directly to the developer.
One of the things that has been changed since the beta is the enemy AI. It's not as bad as in the beta however it's not great eitehr. The enemy no longer seems to have omnipresent knowledge of the PC location & don't all line up in a row like they did in the beta to get gunned down; now they sent out scouts... while the rest of them didn't move an inch inside the mission zone. They had 1 scout hunting which I killed & 2 more scouts went to the first scouts body... both died. By the time I was down off the hill I was on & into the actual mission zone the rest of the enemy NPCs had stopped being alarmed. Not great but still better then the beta.
Another item that appears to be changed from the beta is the bullet physics... it does appear to be more accurate though I still need to do more testing. The off hand feel however is that the shooting is more natural.
And with that on to something that hasn't changed from the beta. The horrible landscaping. This is a problem that seems to plauge CI Games & in this game it's to the point that a 1 inch hill can stop the PC from stepping over it. It's very imersion breaking to have to stop trying to walk over a rock face because you have to go a meter to the right to walk around the piece of rock that your shoe is higher then.
Other game play issues exist and are noticable but not game play breaking. Examples are climbing down a ladder... and watching the PCs thumbs clip through every, single, rung, of the ladder. Or how the paths in the weeds don't seem to exactly match where they're said to be in the mini-map's default settings (if they can even be changed... I haven't looked yet). And then there's non-realistic portrayal of things like suppressors & grenades. Suppressors that can only be taked off in the safe house using some unseen magical process & grenades that FLASH & BEEP before they detonate. I mean it looks nice but that's a totally useless anti-personal device right there.
The drone magically marks enemies... which is a good thing because trying to focus on anything with it is impossible... if this was a real drone there'd be class action law suits in the billions over it. A camera that sways when the drone is stationary instead of being rock steady, a drone that has some kind of lag delay on its input... when you stop moving it it moves a few more inches... it's like the developer never watched drone footage on youtube to see what a real drone looks like.
Audio wise the game is a mixed bag. Some of the voice acting seems decent while some of it is done by someone's older brother while home from college. The music is bland except for the main menu/radio's song which seems to be some licensed piece that I find quite catchy. One problem with the music is the radio... as indicated it appears to play the same song as the title menu. However turn the radio off & back on & be prepared to listen to the same song over again... from the start. The radio doesn't pick up where you left off earlier (like an mp3 player would) or even later (like the radio would)... no it starts the song from scratch. I think it indicates a problem coding the engine's mp3 player by the developer.
After all that there's the none game stuff to consider... specifically customer service. It is horrible; with one moderator constantly deleting & locking threads (to my preception in an attempt to make the game look better) to many customer concerns being unaddressed on the forums (I've seen multiple topics about distance problems etc. all of which go unanswered). While not directly part of the game it does effect any pleasure one may have with the product if they seek help and run into such behaviour from the company.
There's a nice selection of weapons; the map appears to be decently large.. the bullet physics do appear to have been fixed & honeslty a selling point for me is that there's some cleavage too. Do I regret buying it? Not yet... but I feel I over paid for it still.
However... after all that... do I think you'll get your money's worth game play wise from it if you buy it? Yes but with the very cautionary note of buy it while it's no more then $10 LOCAL currancy. You'll get that much play out of it.
TL;DR:
Grahpics: 5/10 - Based on engine textures are average or down right bad.
Audio: 6/10 - Music is boring & repetative. Environmental is mixed bag - some sound good to normal; others sound bad to horrible.
Gameplay: 6/10 - Pretty generic shooter with some major issues (like unable to sniper from where ever you want); lots of guns that feel somewhat different from each other but not completely realistic.
Story: 3/10 - It's wants to be something like a Tom Clancy novel however lacks any depth required
to be such. Predictable; plot twists that aren't twisted... characters you'll forget are supposed to be characters.. they're just talking cut outs.
Social: 0/10 - There's no MP. CI Games has promised it... there's not high hopes.
Performance: 5/10 - Some people are able to run it fine; other people can't run it at all on the exact same hardware.
Customer Service: 1/10 - It's gotten to the point where I think CI Games might be worse then EA.
Overall:  4/10 Average.
For now, based on that score & I'd say the game is over priced & to look else where if you want a decent shooter. To get your value's worth from this product do not pay more then $10. For the deluxe edition. The DLC is NOT value adding to the product.

TL;DR: a mediocre experience with some fun and satisfying moments which are sadly outnumbered by frustrating and cheap ones.
I pondered for a while if I should give this game a thumbs up or a thumbs down, I decided it simply doesn't deserve a "recommend" from me. The main reason is that this game is simply finnicky and frustrating frequently enough to ruin what little fun there is to be had here. Take the last boss battle, for example. Without giving anything away: it requires you to manipulate the direction of a certain object in a certain way, and 50% of the time, the controls for this manipulation just A) ignore your input) or B) randomly change the direction of this object so that you miss your mark by 90°. Infuriatingly cheap.
Another example would be the terrible platforming - this game was clearly made with a younger audience in mind, so platforming is literally "point-in-general-direction and jump", and it's easy and it holds your hand... except when it doesn't. Wall-jumps don't always work, the characters simply stop moving on narrow ledges if you're not pointing in exactly the right direction, you miss a giant platform pointing straight at it, sliding slowly off the edge etc. Long story short, it's finnicky and inconsistent. And don't even get me started on the fixed camera. When it's good, it does it's job, but when it's bad, it's just... SO bad.
Luckily, death is completely without consequence, but I actually also count this as a negative thing. Dying could at the very least deduct a few points from your score.
The game is also pretty poorly optimized, it looks decent enough on high settings, but the framerate just plummets. I have a dual core processor @2.5GHz (minimum req. single core 3.0), a 2GB video card (min. req. 256MB), 8GB of ram (min req. 2GB) and I could only get it to run @60FPS at the very lowest settings.
Another (minor) complaint is that the game rewards you with pretty much nothing if you 100% it. I got all Platinums, did all the challenges on Platinum, found all the collectibles and the reward for the collectibles is a Darth Vader hat/mask (actually pretty cool), but there is no extra map/bonus cutscene/all cheats unlocked or whatever for doing the other stuff, giving you no reason to replay the missions to max them out. Achievements don't work unless you're actually signed into GfWLIVE.
Speaking of hats, it would be a cool gimmick, were the hats not TOTALLY OUT OF PROPORTION with the character. With some hats, like the Republic Commando helmets or the Darth Vader mask, it's funny and fitting, but with others, like the Emperor or Yoda, it's just... jarring and plain ugly.
So.. are there any redeeming qualities here?
Sure, if you're a fan of the Clone Wars series (which I definitely am), it's nice to see the Jedi and Clones in action and actually get to play as many of them. The character selection when replaying missions is also a nifty feature. The story is standard Clone Wars stuff (which means it's pretty good), I read somewhere it follows right after S01E22 but it doesn't really matter all that much, I watched the entire thing and I didn't think I got any more out of the story than someone completely new to the characters.
The way the missions interact with each other is also done well, it does that classic Clone Wars thing where just as one subplot gets interesting, it switches to another one, the switches back to a grand closer. Props for the art design as well, it really feels like a part of the Clone Wars series.
Combat, while simple and a tad repetitive, is fun for the most part - I enjoyed the Clone Troopers a shade more than Jedi combat because it's more streamlined and consistent. That said, I'll admit that as a Jedi, force-pushing a whole platoon of clankers, slicing through a squad of Super Battle Droids then high-jacking a Spider droid to lay waste to anything left standing is IMMENSELY satisfying.
The sound design is also top notch, as is to be expected from a Star Wars game. The familiar music and bleeps and pew-pews all sound exactly as they should, and the voice actors are the same as in the series and they do a decent job (definitely on par with S01-S02 of Clone Wars).
Sadly, while there are fun and enjoyable moments to be had in this title, there are too few and far in between that the overall experience simply isn't that great. I got it as part of the Star Wars bundle (with the Jedi Knight series, both Force Unleashed games, Battlefront II, KoTOR I and II etc.), so I can't complain, but definitely don't get this game at full price, if you want to get it at all.

The Good-
If you like the show and simple casual gaming the game is great, especially if you have kids who like the show.  For all intents and purposes this IS the show, it has the same voice actors, including the narrator, and looks EXACTLY like the show.  I was really impressed with how true to the show they stayed,  I don't think a more direct TV/Movie to game translation exists.   They also have currency/point system to buy cosmetic or combat upgrades,  Anakin in Cad Bane's hat made me crack up.
The Bad-

I remember when this game first came out and my dad purchased it on the original xbox. back then, I thought the game looked cool just because it was starwars. well fastfoward roughly 11 years into the future and during that timeframe, I had sadly forgotten about this gem. Few things about the game.
The ai is fantastic, from having them man turrets to heal eachother and yourself (you'll need it) I found the ai to be some of the best i have ever experienced.

This game is a squad based ps2 era shooter set in the star wars universe set during the clone wars. it's no brothers in arms but the squad tactics are solid enough you can give basic orders and a lot of the time you need to use your squads abilities to continue the game. Besides that your squad abillities can be used in a tactical way. like defending a squadmate while he hacks into turrets to aid in battle, or opening a flanking route with a bomb. The solid squadplay is made better with the awsome AI that is put on display here. i mean this is awsome i have seen my squad heal themselves without being asked. Reviving eachother and deciding to kill surrounding enemies beforehand or not if the enemy is a big thing like a spider droid. The pathfinding works really well and the AI never broke on me once during my entire time with the game. besides that the game nails the look and feel of prequel star wars. There are a varied amount of droids and aliens to shoot that force you to use different weapons and tactics. the music has some shining moments with big orchesteral themes that suddenly play every now and then. This is on top of the expert sound designe that again help to make you feel like your playing a really cool Star Wars game. Also worth mentioning is the banter between the charachters while it's nothing shakespearian it's helpfull in giving the soldiers a little character they react realisticly to your orders. If you for example accidently give wierd orders that would not make sense IRL your soldiers will let you know you messed up with some dialoge. The level of polish is just great overall a game well worth playing.

This game is a sort of black sheep in Star Wars.  It doesn't focus very much on the Jedi, in fact, it barely references them at all.  But its definitely a game that kept me on the edge of my seat, leaving me wanting more at the end.
In terms of aesthetics, this game's age is showing.  However, it has aged well enough to still be pleasing to the eyes.  However, the real gem of this game is the combat system.
For much of the game, you are required to work with your squad.  You must coordinate your attacks, assign one or more of your men to choke points, concentrate fire on a big nasty unit, or assign your unit to slice a computer, destroy a machine, or even heal up at a bacta station.
This game definitely highlights on the use of teamwork and coordination.  And the only thing I think this game does wrong, is the coop...  or lack of coop.  This game easily could've got a benefit with a coop mode.  But alas, its far too late for that...  at least for now.
END OPINION:  It may be old, but it still shines on in the shooter industry as an underrated gem.  If your PC can still run it, then have a go at this game.

I was expecting this game to be dull and disappointing but was pleasantly surprised as I played.
Overall Oozi: Earth Adventure is a great platformer at a decent price. They've designed this game to appeal to all ages. There are several difficulty levels from Casual all the way to Hardcore. As you play you unlock challenging bonus stages--stages such as avoid the rising water or collect everything in a given time period.
The levels are varied enough and the occasional boss fights are great. There isn't much of a storyline but that is something common in platformers. Sound effects are okay but the music gets a little bit repetitive if you are trying for the high scores on some of the harder levels.
At normal difficulty you can expect to get through the main levels in about 6 hours and the bonus levels in another 3 hours. If you play at the hardest difficulties, and go for everything, you can easily expect to invest more than 20 hours in this game. Gameplay can get repetitive or feel like a grind, especially if you are trying to unlock everything, the modes and challenges available are varied but the levels you play on sometimes start feeling too similar.
They've taken the time to polish the game and add Steamworks features too. You'll find cloud save, working leaderboards, and even achievements.

Retro City Rampage might be one of the poorest attempts at cloning GTA in a long while. Developed by one man, which is cool admittedly, it's basically a Parody of both GTA and other games released throughout the years, which is its only saving grace. The parodies are funny! Everything from Duke Nukem to TMNT to Back To The Future to even Jean-Claude Van Damne are parodied and each one managed to get either a chuckle or a nice laugh from me at times. But that's the games only saving grace
The rest of the game is clunky, monotonous, and down right boring. It's main issue is that it plays its trap card too early with it's tutorial mission. After that, the game just copies itself to the point where even the jokes are boring. What hampers the game even more are the controls. Now I hate saying that the controls can ruin any game (I'm able to look past bad controls if the game is fun), but WOW! These controls are both bad and clunky! Not only is it a pain to move and aim, but the driving is what REALLY kills the game. I get the point that it's supposed to be emulating the NES in terms of gameplay, but come on! Even the driving games on NES had better controls then this clunker! When it comes to the shooting, it's even worse. There is supposed to be a lock on mechanic, but it's one of the worst ones I dealt with. Whenever you are shooting, you lock on to any near by targets and all your shots go there. The issue is that you STAY locked on when you are shooting and you can't freely aim at other targets without ceasing your fire and then firing again. This is a major hindrance when you are in gun fights when are you want to do is aim at another target but you keep targeting other stuff that AREN'T YOUR TARGETS!
Sadly, I can not recommend this game what so ever. Not only does it fail in trying to be a good GTA clone, but it sadly fails in being a parody at times. It does make me mad though...when I first got this game, I loved it. But now, the more I play it, the less I love it and the more I get frustrated with it. Save your cash and skip this game.
FINAL RATING: SKIP

I'm a science/math game junkie, and I couldn't wait to play Factorio, but for me it just doesn't itch that scratch.  It's a game where you try to avoid having too many parts on your assembly line or too few.  Great, I can work with that, except the variables change all the time.  One more drill here or one small loader here and you have to change your figures.. and unless you think small, you have to change your entire setup if you are a efficiency maximizer like myself.
One iteration of this is fantastic, but when you are doing it every few seconds on a system so large that even a calculator couldn't be of much help (a spreadsheet would)  it just becomes the chore-iest game ever.  You never reach plateaus of optimum, just struggling as you progress.
That's the negative.  That's what *I* have to say about it because it didn't meet my expectations. Although "Tactics" is built purely around combat, it's no less challenging than its isometric RPG progenitors. You will probably die a lot, and you will probably reload a lot if losing a squad member permanently is unacceptable to you. Mistakes are punished swiftly (and often brutally), and trying to just blast your way through is rarely a workable approach.
As a special note, be sure to save often and incrementally. I nearly made it to the end of the game, but was prevented when a defeated enemy blocked the only route to my goal. Unfortunately, I had made my only save just after the enemy was felled, which would have required me to roll back to the beginning of the area to try again. It had been such an exhausting process to get to that point that I just opted to stop playing. (Having put over 60 hours into the game, I figured that I had seen most of the show anyway.)
Anyway - this title is a classic example of game design, and definitely worth checking out. It won't "nursemaid" you, but that's part of what made it the experience that it was.

This is a platformer in which there is no penalty for death.  I played (and beat) the entire game, got platinum on all the challenges, found all the "hidden" artifacts, all in under 30 hours... Even on Hard mode, death is the most inconsequential thing in the game.  If a puzzle or boss is too tough for you, then merely keep at it... the game will never penalize you by making you start the level over, or by deducting points from your score.  The most that will happen is that you'll need to wait 2 seconds for a respawn and you -MIGHT- have to retrace 10 feet or so (super super rare to backtrack because of death... SUPER rare.)
Basically, if you like video games and enjoy a challenge, then stay the hell away from this game.  On the other hand, if you hate consequence and have a need to mindlessly click for 40 levels just to see what Obi and Annie are up to, then buy this game!  ...just make sure you get it on sale, for goodness sake.

A fantastic port of one of the underrated standouts among the character-driven 3D platformers in the PS2 era.  This is everything an HD conversion should be, as not only does it feature properly enhanced graphics for modern systems, but load times are blisteringly fast and both menus and controls have been significantly improved over the original release.
TY itself is an easy but enjoyable platform game with well-designed levels, tons of visual flair, and lots of stuff to collect.  There isn't much story and the game isn't terribly innovative, but it's crafted with enough polish to satisfy casual gamers looking for a few laughs over 5-10 hours depending on your acquisition  OCD.  It was infamous for rather twitchy controls which normally would not age well, but this update has addressed most of the serious control and camera problems.  I highly recommend playing with a mouse, though you'll need to tone the sensitivity way down if you value your sanity.
My major gripe is that the boss battles can be very confusing and have no continuity with either the character development or the story, but thankfully there's not many of them and they're not terribly difficult.  There are also some jumping puzzles that require pixel precision (par for the course in the early 90's).
Overall, well worth the entry fee and a wonderful nostalgia kick updated by the original development label.  Every classic game should receive this kind of treatment if a re-release is being considered.
TY 2 is currently in development, and hopefully the entire trilogy will be released eventually.  I eagerly await the next installment!

When I was a young boy, I had a love for board games but the problem was, having only one uninterested sister meant that I was to play alone for most of the time. I have kept this love with me since then and now, I am happy to say that I've some love for the digital board game that is Armello.
If you love board games that aren't too simple like Candyland nor too complex like Axis & Allies, Armello is the game for you. In some sense, Armello is like RISK. The dice can make the game or break it for you, but your strategy determines how fast you can exploit or recover from whatever shenanigans the dice result in. There's never really a single path to victory and the best victories are the most unorthodox ones.
Now, aesthetically, the game is a pleasing sight to the eyes. In terms of graphics, the game does well enough, and the score goes along with it. The art and animation for the cards are actually quite nice to look at, I have more than once actually visited the Card Gallery to admire the hard work put into them. The presence of anthropomorphic characters is of no concern to me, being long exposed to anthropomorphic in the media thanks to Disney and childhood cartoons. One critique I will reserve for the game at the time of writing though is the lack of lore for too many of the heroes. It's quite inconsistent. Among the Generation Two heroes, only Zosha has a backstory and the Usurpers get no stories at all. The Generation One heroes' backstories are very short blurbs whereas the Bandit Clan heroes get paragraphs of interesting details. Why the inconsistency? Did the lore-writers run out of ideas?
Also, pricing. Actually, I'm fine with the pricing. I have played many hours of it to make up for the price tag and the suggestion that the game is behind a paywall isn't that reasonable, considering the 8 non-DLC heroes are nowhere near crutched. You can win as easily with them as you can with the DLC heroes. That said, if you want to make your money's worth, wait for the game and its DLC to go on sale before buying them all. Could save a pretty penny or two.

For what it is, Armello is a great experience.
The art is beautiful - a real pleasure to witness as you play.
The gameplay is solid. Whether it's a plus or a minus, the game plays exactly like a board game.
I really, really wish the tutorial was like 100 times as long. Why? Not because I need to learn the game better, but because it was a fun tutorial. It felt like a mini campaign, and I really would love to have a full campaign to play in this game. Instead, the game quickly becomes a repetitive (though fun) experience - again, like a board game.

To some, it may look like just some so-so title that isn't worth a glance due to its small-time nature. But to me, I think it is a little (and I do mean LITTLE) gem in a sea of games of various qualities and polish.
Oozi is a humble platformer about a Rayman Wannabe who crashes his ship on a random planet, and thus is thrusted onto a quest to get his stuff back and return home. Storywise, it isn't much, but in this day and age, I suppose a simple plot is better than the overly dramatic stuff you get nowadays.
Once you get into the first level, though, the game certainly does start to charm you, with its lovely art style, its decent soundtrack (That is forgettable, but still nice to listen to throughout the game), and its easy to learn gameplay. It isn't a hard game persay, but it isn't a walk in the park either. I had times where the game did surprise me with some challenging platforming, which kept me interested and provided some satisfaction when I managed to survive past a difficult challenge to the next checkpoint. The game also throws out some interesting (if short lived) gimmics at you as well to spice levels up as you continue on your quest, from rock titans that can only be killed with short-fused bombs to security systems that require timing and smart jumps to avoid in order to progress through a part of the level. Sadly, many of these gimmics are often one level only, which is a shame they don't use some of these gimmics more often, because some of them really are interesting.
In the case of Bosses, there are four worlds each, with a boss in each of them. Ironicly, the first boss might be the hardest, because every boss I fought afterwards (even the FINAL BOSS) was rather mild. They still kept you on your toes, but they didn't seem awfully threatening. Really, the levels before the boss is where all the fun is, what with all the secret stars you can collect in each level to unlock challenge levels you can play to, well, challenge yourself, so there is at least a bit of replay value after the story is complete.
Sure, this game isn't the best platformer out there, it isn't gonna get any "oooohs" or "Ahhhhs" or even "11 out of 10s" out of you, but if you are looking for a decent little platformer that you can easily get into that'll provide a satisfying experience for a low cost, this is worth checking out. For anyone expecting something more intense, though... Look elsewhere.

Well, it's a beautiful and unbelievably charming game. The animation is just striking. Presentation is just flawless. It plays a lot like a board game, a mixture of cards and dice (D6 system). The board is hex based, where you travel around and get random loot from dungeons (you don't play dungeons though you just random roll for goodies), you tackle stone circles for healing and you claims villages to enhance your per turn gold income rate. There are three types of cards, item/magic/trickery and they work how you might expect, items enhance your character while magic typically does direct effects with either once shot effects or short term effects and trickery tends to maniplate the board most commonly by adding 'traps', events than when you walk onto the hex require you to roll a number of die and match all the symbols the challenge requires (usually 3 symbols). In theory the mechanics and system seem sound... However, everything falls through from there. The game is BRUTALLY hard and plain unfair, dice simply never roll in your favor. The dice are D6, so you should have a 1 in 6 chance of rolling what you want. I did the math multiple times through multiple rounds, it's actually closer to a 1 out of 10 chance, so that means the game is actively screwing you by rigging the dice rolls. Combine with that the AI is actively more focused on killing you than doing anything else, during play you get 'bounties' on you, basically rewards for people coming to kill you. However, bounties can be put on anyone not just the human player. This doesn't matter though, enemies will always bee line straight after you and ignore others even if they have higher bounties. Now, I love games like Darksouls, Dead Cells, Salt & Sancturary and This is the Police. I enjoy difficult games, as long as they're balanced in their own way. Sadly Armello isn't, it tries to cover up its design flaws by admitting in the tool tips "Armello is a brutally hard game" but that's a cop out, they failed to balance and released the game anyway.
Now, I'm sure there are people out there that love this and others still who think it is the easiest game ever made and can beat it while asleep and not even sitting at their computer. Goody for them. I've played a lot of hard games, this is so hard it feels broken. So badly in fact I ended up givng up before finishing the TUTORIAL, yes that stupidly hard. After what felt like an eternity of back and forth in the last part of the tutorial I finally just threw my hands up and accepted I wasn't going anywhere ever, I was going to continually run up to the wall, fail my roll and be instantly murdered by the 'guard' (basically player assassins) who are perfectly outfitted to destroy you. Afternumberous turns of this I was done, I wasn't having fun, I didn't feel 'challenged' because a challenge requires skill not dumb luck and dumb is exactly what this felt like after an HOUR of just walking back and forth, knowing I wasn't going to make the roll because that's how Armello works, you're fighting loaded dice, AI that hates you and basically a game that WANTS you to uninstall it and never return. I'm happy I got this in Humble Bundle, though I still feel a bit swindled, but that's because this got a ton of hype when it was released and I thought I was missing out on something great... I wasn't. Which explains why it was super popular for a month and then vanished from the public never to be spoken of again, this is for the masochists. Unlike other brutal titles like Darksouls and such which have a steep learning curve and a certain skill barrier for entry, Armello presents no learning curve, just blind luck because you really have no control over dice, that is the point of dice. Maybe my game is rolling super poorly compared to other people, or maybe other people just enjoy losing. Whether it's combat or a challenge, your chances of rolling what you need are pathetically slim. Even the tutorial doesn't know how to cope in some instances and just goes silent because it's waiting for you to get the rolls you need to move forward, which you're not going to get.
I wish I could recommend this, especially when people raved about this when it launched. But I just can't. If you want a board game like game, with great visuals, wonderful presentation, a serious challenge and awesome story, go get Banner Saga. It is very similar in many ways BUT is far more skill oriented and much less luck based. OR got get a Civilization game, again very similar in a lot of functional ways, just not insanely unfair. I'll continue to research this online, with how awful my first experience was I'm pretty determined I'm missing something here, as pretty as the game is I just can't believe something THIS unbalanced was so popular at one point, I just don't know what else you're supposed to do other than roll the dice and cross your fingers. Like most games today, if you suffer a set back you typically get penalized, which means every time you fail you are more and more likely to fail because failure handicaps you to increase your likelihood of repeating failure. IF I can figure out how to make this game work I'll return to edit this review, but as it stands, I don't think there's much else to see here. Skill games are skill games, Dice games are luck based, especially when the math proves that on a D6 you have lower than a 1 out of 6 chance of getting what you need, your luck is super bad. You can't improve luck, only skill.

Over and over, I've tried to give Armello a chance with an open mind, but every time I do I just want to vomit out all my disappointment for what this game could have been, and what they've turned it into: a pay to win game with a $20 paywall.
If you play this game by yourself, it's somewhat fun because all of the characters that you encounter are rather balanced relative to each other. However, if you step into multiplayer, not only is it nearly impossible to complete a full game without someone leaving and the AI taking over (by the way there is no way that I've seen where you can reconnect), but the matchmaing system is god awful and I have about a 20% success rate at even starting a match.
Okay, so let's assume the servers are having a good day and you get a connection, and nobody leaves. Well, maybe now you can have some fun with other people, right? Well, not really. You see, the game has 8 DLC characters, several of which are significantly stronger than the base game characters. Most recently, I've played against a Twiss (DLC character) along with a Barnaby and a Thane while I was playing Sana (all 3 are base game characters). The Twiss got 4 spirit stones (one of the two major hurdles in achieving a particular victory) before the dawn of day 3. From that point, it was a 3v1 against the Twiss (everyone used everything possible to kill her while ignoring other players), yet the Twiss still managed to win. This is just one of several examples where I felt cheated out of a potential good experience and victory.
Another issue I'm having is the crazy randomness. Pretty much everything is dictated by RNG, including the card draws, the questing, the perils (including palace entry, a crucial part of the game), and even the combat itself. As I often play Sana, many times I feel like I can't get a single spell that can deal even one damage, while players like the Twiss seem to get the one and only card that can win them the game (like a Hot Rot Wine on the last turn on the last night in order to cleanse the king having just entered the palace on the same turn). The feeling is so unsatisfying when you are about to win through hard grinding for the entire game, and someone else instantly wins because of just because the computer decided to let them win.
So if you'd not like to deal with the low quality servers, overpowered DLC characters, and painful RNG, then your only real option is to play singleplayer. But the okay singleplayer wouldn't be enough to justify the game's $20 pricetag. Sorry.

I love the concept of starting by doing everything yourself and working towards automating it fully. Factorio fully delivers on this concept with a quick ramp up of automation to avoid feeling like you're grinding for hours. The game is designed in such a way that each individual component you can build is extremely simple, and you can use these components in simple assembly lines. But these simple components' mechanics are such that you can combine pieces in ways that create complex systems with intricate timings and resource flows.
As far as Early Access goes, I'd just like to say that this game does not feel like early access at all. This is by far the most polished early access title I've ever played. The devs consistently release patches, mainly with bug fixes
(though I've never personally encountered a bug) with larger patches even introducing new content that adds more approaches to winning the game, all without complicating the starting experience for new players.
Overall, I strongly recommend this game to people who enjoy building/management simulation games, especially people who love playing Technic Modpacks and the likes in Minecraft.

This is a free to play game with pay elements in it such as extra content but in truth there is so much in the free game itself unless you are a real die hard player you won't feel the need to purchase anything.
It is without doubt one of best free to play games out there
Progress as much or as little as you like and be as casual or ingaged as you wish. It has a light hearted feel to it but does not fall into the trap of being childish and appeals to all ages.
The basic premise is that you gather 3 adventures and well.....go on adventures. You can purchase other adventurers or use the multitude of free content ones who are equal in everyway as far as i can tell.
A lot of developers have tried and failed with this formula but here it achieves on many levels as it doesn't try to pretend to be anything other than what it is and for many it brings back a lot of nostalgic moments of board game adventures.
There are only two issues with it as far as I am concerned.
1) RNG can ruin your playthrough from time to time but even then its not like its game over and you can often win even when you lose a companion.
2) You only have 3 in your party instead of the classic 4 man party of tabletop D&D which a lot of people compare this to; again this is not a HUGE draw back but sometimes you really do miss that 4th member.

This game is the perfect blend of traditional PvP and tabletop gaming.  The campaign is well-written, engaging, has a perfect difficulty curve, and has mild replayability.  The PvP meta is continuously evolving and changes every month with map rotations.
I've spent 658 hours in this game and only $10.  That should tell you all you need to know about its value as a free to play game.

Some of the negative reviews here are difficult to reconcile with reality; this is an open world sniping game, a very ambitious one with a boat load of features -- the Developers have made a lot of initiative to make this game interesting to a broader audience without dumbing the game down, and imho they've succeeded.
I'm going to take broad strokes here rather then focus on details; I prefer serious tactical realism games, am not a fan of game design and DLC that makes a realism title look and play like some sort of porn cos play or gay pride event -- this game keeps the aesthetic on charter and is fairly realistic.
It has it's shortcomings but if you like the genre and you're honest; you're well aware every game does. On the annoyances side you get something we're all either used to by now, or fed up with and triggered by: too much annoying narrative, and SGW3 is just as overboard as every other game in the genre and as annoying for all the same reasons of canny valley and terrible writing.
The AI isn't going to impress you either as setting a new state of the art, but it's better then what you'll get in any current gen Ubisoft game, and on par with or better than most everything else.  There are bugs, again all games have them, so if you don't anticipate them and a little frustration and teaking -- you you aren't buying and playing many current generation games...
The positives are SGW3 has been given lavish attention to detail, extraordinary even for a game at this price point, from the weapons and weapon handling, the 3D art and textures, the sound design, physics -- all are AAA quality. As well the game design itself shows impressive attention to detail and re-playability with losts of atmosphere -- something big publishing eschews more oten in their desire to create disposable commodity games to churn and asset strip customers as much and as quickly as possible in the crudest fashion.
I hope that SGW3 becomes a platform for future expansion, that CI Games takes a leaner meaner approach to narrative; perhaps along the lines of what Starbreez did earlier on with the PayDay games expansion -- with simple but high quality and well crafted mission descriptions with a short narrative, pictures, minimal animation and video  -- and focused on actual game content. CiG could promote their expansions as heavily as Starbreez does their expansions and have buyers!  A COOP option would also raise the bar and take the game to the next level, and keep more people playing.
Regardless, anything CI Games does with expanding SGW3, I'll be an enthusiastic paying customer -- easly worth the full-boat asking price!

Over and over, I've tried to give Armello a chance with an open mind, but every time I do I just want to vomit out all my disappointment for what this game could have been, and what they've turned it into: a pay to win game with a $20 paywall.
If you play this game by yourself, it's somewhat fun because all of the characters that you encounter are rather balanced relative to each other. However, if you step into multiplayer, not only is it nearly impossible to complete a full game without someone leaving and the AI taking over (by the way there is no way that I've seen where you can reconnect), but the matchmaing system is god awful and I have about a 20% success rate at even starting a match.
Okay, so let's assume the servers are having a good day and you get a connection, and nobody leaves. Well, maybe now you can have some fun with other people, right? Well, not really. You see, the game has 8 DLC characters, several of which are significantly stronger than the base game characters. Most recently, I've played against a Twiss (DLC character) along with a Barnaby and a Thane while I was playing Sana (all 3 are base game characters). The Twiss got 4 spirit stones (one of the two major hurdles in achieving a particular victory) before the dawn of day 3. From that point, it was a 3v1 against the Twiss (everyone used everything possible to kill her while ignoring other players), yet the Twiss still managed to win. This is just one of several examples where I felt cheated out of a potential good experience and victory.
Another issue I'm having is the crazy randomness. Pretty much everything is dictated by RNG, including the card draws, the questing, the perils (including palace entry, a crucial part of the game), and even the combat itself. As I often play Sana, many times I feel like I can't get a single spell that can deal even one damage, while players like the Twiss seem to get the one and only card that can win them the game (like a Hot Rot Wine on the last turn on the last night in order to cleanse the king having just entered the palace on the same turn). The feeling is so unsatisfying when you are about to win through hard grinding for the entire game, and someone else instantly wins because of just because the computer decided to let them win.
So if you'd not like to deal with the low quality servers, overpowered DLC characters, and painful RNG, then your only real option is to play singleplayer. But the okay singleplayer wouldn't be enough to justify the game's $20 pricetag. Sorry.

Retry City Rampage DX copies the core gameplay loop of classic GTA, with lots of arcade style minigames added, along with references and inside jokes. Some of the gags had me laugh out loud, while many others had me cringe. The main storyline is deliberately bad, bogging down in collecting arbitrary parts for a time machine over and over again.
So while this is not a great game, I can't help but give it thumbs up because I honestly had a good time for the 6 hours it took me to finish. There is enough variety and unexpected challenges at every turn to keep you interested, and the whole look and feel is rather authentic.
This could have been a much better game if the developers had taken the storytelling aspect more serious instead of relying on the audience going crazy over excessive referencing of established franchises and indie games. It's definitely worth the price tag, and if you catch it on sale or in a bundle, I say go for it. You won't regret it.

The PC's Mario Maker. Except instead of a platformer, it's a dungeon-crawler.
I think that about sums it up.
To go into more detail...
It's pretty enjoyable! The variety of handmade levels keeps things from getting too repetitive.
The random level chooser is pretty good about selecting higher-rated adventures, but you can also hand pick from the database. The only time I ever got an awful stage was from playing one of the optional "reward" stages that you are assigned daily. These are player-made adventures that are unproven, but give better bonuses for completion.
I'm still getting used to the map editor, but it's pretty cool. Haven't made my own adventure yet.
There's splitscreen! Good times with my roommate. The game is better on a controller. WASD for movement is awful for this.
Online multiplayer seems to have no population though. Oh well.
The combat is pretty okay, but not all that advanced. You have light and heavy attacks based on what weapon type you have. Up to four special abilities at a time, from a selection of much more that you unlock as you level up. You can block with a shield and dodgeroll. Some of these abilities use either your mana or stamina. It's not bad, but it's not very impressive either. It works.
There's not a large variety of enemy types. But they at least mix things up with various colors and "mutations".
If you're worried about maps that give you too much or too little loot, then don't. The loot system dynamically scales based on how many, and how often you encounter chests and enemies. Map makers are free to make adventures how they like without affecting your loot drastically. However, the strength of enemies also scales with you no matter where you go, so it kinda takes away from the sense of progression. But I can see why they had to do that.
The graphics look strange, but it's consistent, I'll give it that.

I'll keep it short: Oozi is a competent platformer, but it doesn't offer anything to differentiate it from all the other platformers that exist.  You could play it, and have an okay time, but why bother when there's more interesting platformers out there?

Oozi is a cute platformer that feels like it could have come from the N64/PSX era. The story is pretty much nonexistent, but the fun level is there. The game introduces new mechanics at (an almost too) leisurely rate. The challenge level overall is pretty average, but it can be significantly raised for fans of games such as Mr. Bree+ and Super Meatboy.  Enemies stay dead once you've killed them, though, even if you have to repeat a section, so if a particular area is giving you a hard time, you can clear it first before attempting to navigate the environmental hazards. 5 hidden "secret stars" on each level provide a bit of replay value.
The Good: Bright, crisp, colorful graphics,with beautiful detail. Controls are fairly responsive, although Oozi does do a tiny slide upon landing that can be a bit annoying on particularly tight jumps.
The Bad: No options to configure controls (what is this, 1996?). Does not recognize any controller except for Xbox 360. There is no way to see how many secret stars you've collected on the current playfield.
The Indifferent: Music is acceptable, if redundant. Hitbox is sometimes wonky, and the camera occasionally tweaks out.
Recommended? Yes, but I'd wait for a bundle or sale, as $10 seems a bit steep, especially with minimal configuration options and no way to rebind keys.

Just like with Call of Duty; World at War, every time I tried to play this damn game something happens and I’m unable to. Either computers blowing up or me lacking the interest to go through with it, I always stop. Well, I got this game on a gigantic Star Wars pack a good time ago and I finally went through it, to finally see what it has to offer. And as usual, I’m gonna talk first about what it does worst, then move up from there.
First and foremost, the story. They had a perfect opportunity to fill parts the movies didn’t really show about these damn iconic troopers. And what did they do? Waste it. Sure, you get to fight on the Geonosis raid on the first stage, but you never get to see anything else from the movies, no Samuel L. Mace Windu Jackson decapitating mandalorians or anything. And up from there, it’s just a few set pieces that are quite disappointing. I MEAN COME ON, I WAS SERIOUSLY HOPING TO GET TO SHOOT OBI WAN AFTER THE ORDER 66, BUT THE GAME NEVER GOES ANYWHERE!
Second, the weapons are… Meh. The initial idea is actually quite f#cking interesting, a swiss-knife kind of deal, your weird gun is actually a ton of different kinds of guns. I liked that! However it barely does anything original with that, the guns are the most uninspired cr#p you can think: generic spamming rifle, generic 1-headshot-kill sniper rifle, generic OP-Grenade launcher… And the worst part is that you can pick alien weapons and add them to your arsenal, which sounds cool until you notice how BAD they are at everything! I WAS HOPING SO MUCH THAT THE SHOTGUN COULD MAKE THE GAME FUN, BUT IT’S JUST THE WORST AGAINST DROIDS! AT POINT-BLANK RANGE! YOU DO MORE DAMAGE BY PUNCHING THEM!
Third, the squad mechanics. I personally think this game was ahead of it’s time on a bad way, this game SERIOUSLY NEEDED COOP. If it had, you would have Star Wars Left 4 Dead. However with just single player and a dead multiplayer mode (that kinda sucked anyway), it’s not so fun because their AI is as dead as progress with Half-Life 3. Giving them orders is cool at first, then you’ll notice how it never brings much new from what you see on the first 10 minutes of the game. It also doesn’t help that they’re stupid.
The PC version is also a weird port made in the deepest areas of hell. Some of the stuff the devs thought were okay for PCs make me want to look for them and shove my computer up their #ss.
Lastly, the stages themselves. I’ve already said that there’s not much to the story, right? Well, the stages are also quite small. And when I say small, I really mean small. What engine does this game use? Did they really have so many limitations? Every 2-4 minutes there’s another loading screen, and those 2-4 minutes were mostly just struggling to advance a large corridor. The game also barely has different themes going for it. There’s the initial Geonosis level. There’s an abandoned ship in space. There’s the Wookie planet. Another ship. And that’s it.
So, does the game actually have good stuff going for itself? Kinda. At times…
The characters themselves on your squad are not so bad. Sure they’re clichéd as all hell but I rather have 4 clichéd well written characters than a billion bad ones (LOOKING AT YOU, JAR JAR). Also the squad mechanics are cool when they’re first shown.

"The Purring Quest" is a cute little game about a cat trying to find their lost guardian. You play as the cat and have to jump and run through five different levels which all have a special kind of task at the end. You have to collect fish bones, jump over holes, fight different kinds of enemies, rescue caged cats, avoid unfriendly dogs and overcome other obstacles.
The graphics are simple but beautiful and each level has its own kind of peculiar charm. The cats you meet on your way have funny things to say and some of them are very relatable for me, especially Henri, because just like me he is mentally ill. I also liked to see blind cats in the game since one of my roommates is a blind cat.
I also like the small details in the game, like writings on the wall, mysterious eyes in the bushes and other little things which were nice to discover.
One thing I'd like to emphasise is the fact that there are several messages against declawing in the game. Declawing is something no cat should have to suffer and it's good to give people these messages in the game so they have the opportunity to educate themselves on the topic. I also liked the inclusion of several disabled cats. I'm the guardian of a disabled cat myself and it's cool to have that kind of representation.
It took me about 4,5 hours to finish the game with all achievements. It was difficult at times but it was not that hard to collect all fish bones, rescue all cats and find all of the items. Nevertheless it was a nice challenge and I really enjoyed playing it.
I bought the game for 2,49 € instead of 9,99 € when it was on sale. I'm not sure if I think the game itself is worth the full price but if you like cats and jump'n'run games you should definitely get this game when it's on sale. Since some of the money that is earned goes to animal welfare I think it's also worth paying the full price if you can afford it.
My conclusion: I really liked this game and totally recommend it for everybody who likes cats. :)

To support its more realistic approach to the subject, The Purring Quest has lively hand drawn graphics that look very fluid in motion and a music track that adds to the relaxing atmosphere. Levels have plenty of collectables and the learning curve is fair. Controls get a bit wonky at times, but luckily game doesn't demand insanely precise platforming and there is just enough checkpoints to keep you from becoming too frustrated over a difficult jump.
The Purring Quest doesn't do anything terribly wrong, but it doesn't give you that "whoa" feeling either. It's a cute and enjoyable game with a touching story. If you start the game with that in mind, you will get 1 - 2 hours of fun feline platforming, maybe 3 hours if you like to hunt for hidden items.

This game is incredible. The progression is challenging and the objectives are clear. The community is also amazing and full of dedicated people who seek to further push the game to the next level and are extremely welcoming and helpful. This game has occupied my mind for the past few weeks, and I have been able to go all the way up to automating rocket lanuches. When I finally was able to do that, It felt great.
But...
I didn't know what to do next.
Sure, I could keep on researching more technologies and get these cool weapons and demolish all the biters and spitters and worms that occupy the map.
Here's my problem...I turned off enemies from the start.
When I first got this game, I got it in a version that promoted enemies because they were rewarding. I used to have to destroy spawners and I would recieve purple orbs which I could craft into science and do even more research. In that version, it gave enemies a reason to be there, as a way to progress in the game. Almost every game with enemies would either give you items or help you level up as a way to motivate you to continue to work towards something through the killing of enemies.
When I first started in that version, I found the enemies too hard, so I turned them off in another save. Later, I needed to have spawners so that I could progress even further, so I started over again with enemies and tried to make it all the way through, but at the time, I fell off the game and didn't come back to it until recently during the release of 0.16.x updates.
The problem that 0.15 did to this game is made enemies virtually worthless in gameplay.
The game is built around building a factory so that you can launch a rocket into space. It used to end there and that would be it. But now with 0.15, there's even more research you can do after you launch rockets since they give you space science. And that can be used to research and increase stats in the game infinitely, and it gradually increases in science the higher it gets.
A lot of the researches are built around weaponry and combat so that you can create more weapons and do better in combat. There are some researches that increase bot speed and mining productivity, but other than that, almost all others have to do with combat. You get all of these crazy cool weapons like atomic bombs and get to increase damage to your bullets and things of the like. If you build a factory that is built around this and get to a point where you instantly kill spawners and enemies since you are so powerful. I never got to that point, but I have watched many people get there too.
But then what?
You're as op as you can get, and there's no more challenge. Yippie, you win. Pat yourself on that back. That about wraps up this game...
I want more.
Here's why.
There is no reward to killing enemies and spawners. This leads to some people seeing biters as annoying (as myself) since they provide a challenge without a reward. You can't expect people to face a challenge if there's no reward for being successful. Enemies were worthless, so I turned them off again in the new update and beat the game without them. But then I end up with a bunch of research that is meaningless because the endgame focuses so much on combat, when there is absolutely no purpose for it.
Blah blah blah, "enemies make it harder to get to the end", "enemies expand", "enemies get harder over time", blah blah blah, I get that. But for what? So that I could feel even better about finishing the game with them? If you're that type of gamer, go ahead, I won't stop you. If that's rewarding to you, then I highly reccommend it.
However, if you could give me a reason, if you could give me a purpose, if you could make enemies rewarding in advancing in the game, then I would be more than happy to turn them on again.
The problem is that there is so much emphasis on combat in the late game without a reason for it. If I were to recommend anything to help advance this game to the next level, maybe add some bosses and other challenges that are difficult to motivate the player after launching the rocket to something further. This would give the combat researches a lot more purpose after launching rockets since they would help you increase your stats to make it easier to fight these bosses.
I would also reccommend a leveling up system based on combat with the natives all the way through, that could also help you increase your stats on top of research, which would give enemies even more purpose all the way through the game. I would also reccommend making the researching of said stats more valuable than combat. This would motivate players to keep building an extensive factory to increase your stats, but also avoids causing players to shy away from enemies, since they do help you even the slightest bit, which in any game, people will be motivated by. If this were to ever be implemented, and since I'm just one guy with an opinion, probably not, I could see an even larger audience to that this game deserves. Until then, I don't see a reason to go further. However, I will gladly get involved in the modding community and see what fun I have in store there, as well as other challenges and scenarios.

This is unfortunately a weighty blotch on the reputation of the Star Wars gaming franchise.  What strikes me more than anything, given the fact this is an official Star Wars title, is how overwhelming 'budget' the entire experience feels.
The sub-seven hours I spent with it became all the more wearisome as it went on, revealing more and more horrible design decisions and a blatant lack of any sort of meaningful playtesting.  I sincerely did try to enjoy this, although it was with a mighty sigh of relief I breathed when it was all over.
Now a little disclaimer, I haven't actually watched any of the cartoon show, but from the clips I've seen the art style does seem quite faithful.  But what is puzzling is how poor the graphics are overall, given that the game is only half a decade old.
I thankfully had no problem in getting the game to run, but to those still struggling, I implore you to not waste your time.
The dialogue is suitably inane and suits the Saturday-morning-kids-cartoon feel that they were aiming for.  As you progress through each level the characters will jabber back and forth at one another.  However, combat is not paused during these exchanges, and to skip through these conversations, you press left-click.  To fire, you also press left-click.  And given that you have very little to do in the game beyond firing, odds are you will blaze your way right through these conversations, with broken audio fragments punctuating your battles in a very jarring staccato-beat.  Though as a small mercy I'm fairly sure none of the conversations would have turned around my enjoyment of this train wreck.
The game is separated into 3 acts, each separated by a rather well done movietone-esque war news broadcast updating the viewer on the current events.  Between level cutscenes are not quite so well done by and large, and are overlong.  Thus the brevity of the 40-odd levels (some clock it at 3-4 mins to complete) means any sort of meaningful flow is brought right back down to earth constantly by the recurring cutscenes.
The gameplay is fairly boring and repetitive, with the designers playing it safe with the generic action-adventure style of running, jumping between platforms, and blasting or slashing enemies as they rear their heads.  However the platforming sections are horrendously bugged, with the game completely misinterpreting the jump command altogether and plummeting you to your death ad nauseam.  Thankfully you jump between most characters in the game level to level, which stops it being a complete snore-fest, and the ones where you play as clones give you a welcome respite from the awful platforming.  However, even these sections are flawed as the camera angles chosen are woeful.  And countless times I was shot down by unseen enemies off screen but I wasn't able to return fire!
Various other glitches abound, such as where you would get permanently stuck on scenery or the next area/cutscene would fail to trigger, forcing a level restart.
RPG elements are laughably token, with the majority adding nothing to gameplay whatsoever.  You can also do challenge missions to gain more upgrade points.  In these, you have to complete certain actions within a time limit such as killing a bunch of enemies in a certain way or collecting as many free-floating points as possible, and these pop up as you clear certain areas.  But after I completed a few and realised they were all just pointless busy-work, I skipped doing them altogether.  And even at that I still managed to buy all upgrades well before the game's end.
Now I know, given the fact this is aimed at children, I can't expect a Dark Souls-like experience.  But the game is ridiculously easy, and dying in this game doesn't stop combat or respawn enemies, your partner keeps firing on and then you appear beside them, fully healed, a matter of seconds later.  I believe they must have decided to go this way when it was clear the jumping and camera angles would induce countless unnecessary player deathes and if they wanted people to finish they had to make the constant death less painful.  It also removed any sort of challenge and made me even less enthusiastic to play on.
Now there are moments of sporadic genuine fun to be found but they are smothered under the weight of all the issues the game piles upon itself.  Do yourself a favour and pick up virtually any other Star Wars game available instead.

All I can say is that I am glad I did not pay the full retail price for this game and for what it's worth here is some advice based on my experience.
The minimum specs cited for this game mean nothing - the game is extremely poorly optimized and unless you have a pretty high end rig, you are going to have problems, no question. Even people with GTX 1080's , I7 processors and boatloads of RAM have experienced game breaking lag, freezes and poor FPS.
Strangely this does not seem to be true for everyone but it does leave you with the concern that buyng the game is a bit of a lottery - you might get to play it, but you might not and a decent rig doesn't appear to guarantee anything!
Admittedly I only have a lowly GTX 750 ti, but having seen others play the game on this ageing but popular card I decided to give it a go. Even on the games lowest settings with my resolution cranked right down to 720P, the game will not run. So don't believe the YouTube videos - I tried every optimization suggestion out there for this game and it remained unplayable due to horrible fps drops and freezing. The prologue ran as smooth as butter on medium settings at 1080P but once into the "open world" those without really high end CPU/GPU combinations will probably have issues.which may or may not be game breaking. If you're close to the minimum suggested specs the likelihood of serious issues is pretty high.
The first major patch released then broke the game for people who had not been having major problems and since then there have been no further patches/fixes.
So, as of the time of writing, this game is broken and quite badly too. I can say, hand on heart, this is the first ever game my PC has been unable to handle and that includes many recent and current AAA titles as well as poorly optimized indie stuff and plenty of stuff that uses Cryengine. So yes, Sniper Ghost Warrior 3 really is a bit of a howler as far as technical issues and bugs go. I still think the game looks like it could be fun if you can run it but as it stands I certainly cannot recommend it.
Additionally, based on what I've read and things that the devs have reportedly said, I think it is unlikely that most, if any, of these issues will ever be fixed.  They have moved on to their next game apparently, having admitted that they bit off way more than they could chew with SGW3's ambitious open world setting. They say they will support the game through 2017 which suggests that after that their paying customers can expect no more from them. As requests for help are already apparently falling on deaf ears, holding your breath for a properly functioning game might not be the best of ideas.
If you still feel you want to risk it, Caveat Emptor folks. There are certainly far better uses for 40 gigs of your HDD space.

Back in the day I was dissapointed Fallout Tactics wasn't a 'real' roleplaying game like Fallout 1 & 2. Being a huge fan of the series I still gave this game a try and I wasn't dissapointed to say the least.
Fallout Tactics, like the name already says, is a tactical game in the Fallout universe. You start by creating your main character and give him/her the skills you prefer. You start out with 2 other squad members and as the game progresses your squad members level up so you can adjust their skills like all (PC) Fallout games. After each mission you enter the worldmap to go to different locations like you're bunker where you can recruit new squad members and/or buy/sell equipment. Squad members can ofcourse die and won't return (unless you load your savegame).
What sets Fallout Tactics apart from other tactical games for me:
1. The variety of enemies. Sometimes you'll be battling Bugs, the other time you will be facing Super Mutants and several other enemies I won't name here (spoilers). Every enemy calls for a different approach.
2. The variety of missions. Sometimes you will have to rescue people, sometimes you have to do an escort mission. Also in most missions you've got a vehicle at your disposal.
3. The variety of weapons. Fallout Tactics has a huge range of weapons, both realistic and unrealistic but they all fit in the game nicely.
4. The use of skills in a game. Lockpicking, Healing, Defusing... it's all there.
5. Different 'races'. Your squad may also contain different kinds of races like ghouls and Super Mutants. All of them ofcourse have their own speciality/skills.
6. Gameplay. The tactical combat just works really well in this game as a tactical game should obviously. Everytime you make a clean kill feels very good.
7. Graphics. The graphics have aged very well in my opinion. Blood and gore is ofcourse included and every kill feels satisfying.
8. Last but not least; The Fallout universe.
Simply put in my opinion Fallout Tactics is still the best tactical game out there. Although I have to admit it's partially due the Fallout universe. I have played the XCOM series and Jagged Alliance and this game is still number 1 in my book.

The closest thing I can compare this game to is Gloomhaven the analog board game.  You play as three (singleplayer) or one of up to three (online multiplayer co-op) dungeon adventuring heroes whose equipment forms a deck of cards that are played as your actions in small skirmishes in the plot-driven quest for better loot.  The base gameplay evolves as you level up to include fun mechanics and there are a number of themed expansions as well as a player vs player arena for competitive deckbuilding and strategic play.  Initially this game was frustrating to me but revisiting it later many improvements to the content has lead to a strong title.  No money is required to enjoy this clever title, but the ways you can spend money to support the developer are rewarding without being game-breaking.  In many ways this is a pay to show appreciation title and you may still find yourself tapping that wallet.
