Armello takes a new look at the digital fantasy board game. It incorporates RPG elements, card games, strategy games, turn‑based combat, and dungeon grinding.
The character art is reminiscent of Disney’s animated Robin Hood, with the weapon-baring animals conjuring the same nostalgia. It’s a fantastic aesthetic that adds a lot of personality, charm and uniqueness to the digital board game. Furthermore, an enchanting soundtrack does a great job of portraying the medieval setting.
The combat is a mixture of random dice rolls, character stats, and any cards you have in your possession that you’re willing to play. It’s an ideal balance of luck and tactics.
With the adventuring, the medieval fantasy setting and the fight for the throne, Armello invokes "Game of Thrones", "Magic the Gathering" and "Risk", and delivers precisely the kind of experience you’d expect from such a combination. The acts of cruelty you can perform are devious, the adventuring bold and heroic, and the twists as you flit between victory condition paths unforeseeable and sudden. It’s a great drama to witness and play.

Co-op gameplay is my absolute favorite category of game.  It is incredibly satisfying to work together with other players with seamless teamwork.  Unfortunately there are very few games that provide a good co-op experience, nor are there many players who enjoy co-op gameplay.  This game provides one solution to the first problem.  As for the second, well, good luck.
This game has simple controls, yet there is always more to learn.  The weapons are interesting, quirky and fun.  Most have a role to play.  There are plenty of options to customize gameplay, workshop addons, reskins, and maps to keep things interesting for years to come.
The only downside is the players, who despite the fact that they chose to download and play a game that was entirely built around the concept of team play, have no such concept themselves.  Some players join multiplayer games only to basically try soloing.  Why they play this game is beyond me.  There is no shortage of toxic players of the usual variety either, but that is to be expected.

The most gut-wrenching experience I've ever had playing a video game. Every piece of this game's design - the rough, ink-like art style, the muted color scheme, the powerful score, the panic you feel as you frantically try to cut through wires to escape gunfire and run from incoming shells (on top of how slow the characters feel sometimes) - builds the horrific, sobering image of the Great War. This game should be required playing in school, and for anyone even a little curious about the sheer scope and awfulness of World War One.

There are a lot of games out there who have a cool artstyle, a captivating story and rewarding game mechanics.
But none have touched my heart, like this game.
I honestly believe, that 50+ Years, when I turned from a young meatbag to a old meatbag, and I look back at my life, this will be one of those very few games that I'll still remember.

I will preface this by saying that though I try to review games in a light-hearted and humorous way, this time humor fails me.  Like "This War of Mine", this is not that type of game.  Instead, I will ask you serious questions more related to the story, but also inherit in the mechanics of this game.
Do you want to experience the catastrophy of the 20th century that spawned so much war, and so much conflict around the world?
Do you want to see how the things that drove men apart brought people together?
Do you want to see how attempts to bind people as one ironically drove apart the peoples they sought to bind?
Do you want to experience war not as a heroic soldier, but instead by striving to survive the meat grinder of the chemist's and machinist's war?
Do you want to see your friends fall, you family fall, and understand the tragedy that started a hundred years ago and continues to today?
Do you want to, even so, and indeed despite such obstacles, strive to keep what family you have and attempt through this conflict to, if not achieve glory, than to achieve humanity?
Do you want to experience a war where no side can be truly and completely said to be right, and yet the moniker of great is rightly attached, not because of a measure of good, but just from scale?
Do you not just want to hear, but to experience and feel Charlie Chaplin's speech in The Great Dicator?  And at the same time feel the struggle and the striving and the failures against such a system that turns men unnaturally against one another, turns men into machines and cannon fodder?
Do you want to learn about the world?  Not the world we imagine, or the world we are told, but the world that once was, and that can be, and that should be, and that was, and that was wrong?
If so, this is the game for you.

Valiant Hearts is not a game you play for the challenge or great graphics or realism. It's a narrative/puzzle game you play mostly for the narrative, and at that, it excells. The game does have it's minor tecnical issues and once I had to reload the level to correct a glitch, but only once. Most of the time it works just fine and let's you immerse yourself on the story.
The puzzles are often easy and the collectable itens come with bits oh historic facts about the life during the Great War. Most are fairly easy to find for a veteran player who knows how to explore a game level. There are some very fun action sequences (my favorites are the ones on Anna's cab, syncronized with the music) and the gameplay is very simple (there is a trick with the arrow keys on the first aid minigame, if you're playing on the keyboard, though).
Now the narrative. It's immersive, it's sad, it's touching, it's very, very good. You can learn and get a good idea of the War by reading the facts the game chapters presents. Collectable objects also give some good aditional facts. It's well worth the hours invested, as the characters are very charismatic and lovable, the pace and story are engaging and the sound track and animation are impecable.
All-in-all, the game is money and time very well spent.
A really charming puzzle game with a strong story which gives you a lot of historical and emotional insight into the war. A very sad ending which stays with you.

I've played my fair share of this game, Completed alot of the campaign and defended the game since day 1 (Pre-Ordered for $59.99) all the while sticking it out up until the release of the new DLC for the core issues to be fixed. Sadly, They did not. The Developers admitted they have failed at launch which was fine but it seemed that they chose to give up development and abandoned ship. There are some pros but the cons far outweight any enjoyment one can have. I will list only what I've experienced and won't be biased or will attack the game.
Pros: The game itself is more open world than previous Sniper games. It's FarCry like controls make it an easy transition. The ballistics are challenging and fun. The variety of not only the weapons but the optics and ammunition types made me have hours of fun.
Cons: You will not be able to shoot 500+ meters unless at certain spots in the game when the enemy AI just happens to render or you happen to see silhouettes. I was able to achieve the 500 meter achievement by shooting from a hillside aiming nearly straight down using the night vision in the second act. The open world environment is empty. You'll see a few deer and a few wolves but that's it. It was to mock a FarCry environement where every animal is trying to kill you. The last but certainly not the least. Turn off the "bullet cam" It's not Sniper Elite and you won't see X-rays of how a rifle round rips everything apart inside of the human body. You will see the trajectory of the bullet as it soars only to see it hit a general spot (i.e A headshot at a higher angle from the target will appear as if the shot came from the same level as the target.) It made me limp as if taking a cold shower.
** The development team shouldn't give up on this game and what could be a very awesome and enjoyable game. Stop releasing DLC and fix the F@#king game. Until then, I will stick with Sniper Elite V2,3,4 and the Zombie Spinoff. **

Whomever said this game looked better than FarCry was an absolute moron.
The game feels like FarCry, tries to look similar, and while some of the game mechanics are good, the overall game really isn't that great (and not nearly as optimised as FarCry is). The bullet cam is a bit overdone in games, this doesn't show the X-ray that another popular sniper game does, which I'm thankful for when sniping multiple enemies. You can disable it as well, also good.
The multiple classes or skill trees, while interesting, doesn't really do much for the overall asthetic of the game. You carry a sniper rifle of your choice (you start off with one, then get another in chapter 1) And you carry a carbine of sorts. So, you are always adequetely prepared for long range or med/short range combat.
Then...there's the storyline. What the dev failed to do was establish a relationship that the player can get behind. Starting with a short prologue and then jumping into a mission where things go awry! At least do couple missions than let us go through hell with them only to have them become the object we need to get back the rest of the game. Or switch between the two. So, is it worth full price? No, absolutely not. Am I upset I got the game with the season pass and all dlc (minus soundtracks) for only $25? No, I will still snipe the hell out of npc's.

It could have been really good ... But alas, many bugs (such as mysteriously resurrecting enemies) and other glitches. Apart from that there is no quicksave, so you have to start over again from basically the beginning every time, or whereever the developers have made a checkpoint - very annoying! And lots of meaningsless driving around to unlock fast travel points - I did not buy a drive-a-car game, seriously! And the waste of time climbing mountains, all while scout mode is not always working properly ... Really? And the dialogue is ridiculous and an insult to intelligence. However, if you can live with these flaws, the game is good though, so I will recommend it at a reduced price! But these developers could learn a lot from e.g. Deus Ex.

If you're looking at purchasing "Fight the Dragon", you are making a pretty wise investment with your funds.
This title is a dungeon crawler, similar to the games like: "Diablo", but with a more light-hearted look and feel to it. However, there's a bit of a different twist to it. For, while you'll start off playing some basic developer created levels, to get aquainted with how the gameplay fully works, you'll soon find that the rest of the game is playing stages that other users have designed.
This aspect, in itself, gives the game massive amounts of replayability. As there are new maps (and even campaigns!) being created, by people around the world, each and every day.
But, sometimes, we don't want to play other people's levels. So, alongside the gameplay elements of this title, there is also a built-in level creator (Which you probably already guessed at, thanks to the above statements). And, my god is it a good one!
The level creator gives you massive variety on what you can build with, and every tool that the developers used when making their stages as well. At first, it will feel a little overwhelming, as there are so many options to choose from, when looking at the blank canvas. However, the tools provided to you are so easy to learn that, as you practice (and play around) with them, you'll find yourself becoming more and more adept, and soon will be making stages that even the devlopers would be jealous of!
All these good things said though, there are a few issues that I do have with the game.
1 - The difficulty to this game is pretty low, once you get a single good weapon and piece of armor. Allowing you to solo "Extreme" difficulty stages, with little problem.
2 - You can not fight the final boss (aka: the Dragon) in multi-player. Though, this was likely due to coding reasons, it still takes away a little bit from the feeling of an adventure, when most of the time, you're going to find yourself fighting through levels with your friends, or random allies.
3 - The soundtrack isn't that varied, and is limited to maybe a total of 5 or 6 different tunes (Though, what little tracks there are, are still amazing).
Despite these small issues I found with the game, "Fight the Dragon" is still an AMAZING game! One of which you'll find yourself putting many hours of your life into, just as I did when I played an almost non-stop 24 hour spree of the game.
Yes. It's THAT addicting.
Final Score: 8.5/10

I would give this game a 5/10 but since there's not a "meh" option for Steam reviews I'll go with a recommendation.
This game does have its flaws. Most folks will need to download and install Microsoft Games for Windows Live in order to play the game and there is an annoying bug where the game will start with Co-op turned on and you won't be able to progress until the other player character is moved.
But once you get into the game, it evokes memories of the Playstation 2: Lord of the Rings the Two Towers and Return of the King games in that you control characters through a sort of gauntlet from one end of the map to the other, racking up kills as you go. The graphics are very close to the CGI animation of the Clone Wars TV Series and has all of the original actors. There are moments where you feel like you're watching an episode of the Clone Wars.
That said there are some annoyingly frustrating sections where due to camera angles you end up missing jumps for small platforming areas and falling straight down a bottomless pit. The bugs mentioned above and this issue are the biggest obsticals for this game.

Republic Heroes is a fun arcade game when everything is working properly. The problem is that it's a rare occurence when everything works as it should. No camera control creates a terrible environment where you'll spend more time dying trying to figure out the angle to jump than what the actual mission length requires. Controls are somewhat awkward and combat generally becomes the same process. I didn't encounter too many bugs, but when they occured, it was horrible.
On the bright side though, the game has a fun, typical Star Wars vibe and the plot is actually good. There's the ample amount of foreshadowing for what occurs later in the film series and the voice acting is the exact same as in the TV show Clone Wars.
Overall, I wouldn't recommend that anybody purchase the game unless it's on sale. Even if you're a die hard Star Wars fan, the game will frustrate you more than the game itself is worth. Buy the game when it's on sale, no other time.

Now, I do enjoy this game quite a bit, but the fact remains that they've never patched some of the game-breaking bugs that can get you stuck when revisiting a special encounter - such as Bazaar Day or Phil the Nuka Cola Dude. Another issue is the slow-paced combat when using the turn-based options, while the continuous turn-based isn't so bad, but it has its drawbacks. For instance, you might be moving two separate groups in an area and might forget another group for long enough for an enemy patrol to come by and open fire on them.
Traveling on the world map is another bad experience due to the frequent, almost constant barrage of random encounters. This makes it absolutely vital to level somebody's Outdoorsman skill to 100 or more to give you the option to skip them and continue your journey.
It's a decent game, but it has a few nagging drawbacks that keep it from comparing to the first two Fallout games. If you play it, keep these things in mind, as they're quite frustrating at times.

Armello is a great game built on an RNG system that you will sometimes love but will most of the time you will hate it.
The way Armello represents the RNG is straight forward, suns hit in the day, moons hit in the night, swords always attack, shields always defend, worm die do nothing, wylds attack and rolls another die unless you become corrupted then the wyld and worm switch ability. The RNG is all presented in a very nice looking screen where you throw your customizable die with your cursor. The biggest issue is that you will often find yourself in a situation where you rolled full attack like your opponent, and you both die or even just throw five worms while you have zero rot, this happens far more than it should, even if you have the proper equipment.
The game is otherwise good, great even. The aesthetic is beautiful, the characters have great quotes, "What's harder X? Your skull or my shield," the quest are good, and when the RNG is even slightly charitable, the game is a blast even if you don't win. Just remember that it isn't over until there is a new king, so many times has someone been so sure of victory I walk into the castle and become King.

I want to recommend this game so much, because if it weren't for this one huge problem it would be a must-buy. but...
it's not full RNG. the AI cheats, and it cheats a lot. whether it's having a near infinite amount of cards to burn so they have the upper hand in (only very important) battles, exceptional luck with the exploding die that give them an extra dice roll (getting insane extra die rolls up to 5 per die), or always having that one card they need to kill you from across the map and send you back to your spawn point, the AI cheats.
and even if it's not the AI cheating, all you need to do is a bit of save scumming to realize that it's not RNG. every move the AI  makes is already pre-determined at the start of the game, every peril you fail or succeed in is pre-determined when you enter it, and every battle is pre-determined when you begin it. don't believe me? alt+f4 right after the results of a battle or peril and then reload your save. it'll have the exact same effect every time.
it's sad. it's really sad because if it had true RNG, like hand of fate or any other similar board game-esque strategy game, it would be one of the best.
Edit 8/8/2017: After a friendly conversation with one of the developers in the comments below, he  admitted that the AI is not completely random: "The AI, however, is not random - similar to human behaviour. They have a hidden set of values that sways their decision making. They will still pursue their same objective even if you reload. It aint perfect but they seem to do a pretty good job!"
While I understand the need to avoid save scumming, there's other ways to do it than making the AI completely scripted. And in a game that is constantly screaming how everything is RNG based, why isn't the AI random too?
If you can get past the AI's blatant cheating perfection and just focus on the fantastic characters, artstyle, music, and general feel of the world, then go ahead and get this game. I just can't personally get over how a game that shouts how everything is random can also have predictable non-random AI that will cheat if it gets too far behind.

Factorio is a time-eating game that plays like a single-player RTS. For an early access game, there's a lot of gameplay to be had in this indie game. At the time of this review, I've put 39 hours into it in just 3 and a half days. I've enjoyed my time playing so far, but Factorio still has some jarring flaws that I hope are fixed before the game officially releases.
This is a big game. There's a lot to learn and experiment with and many shining moments to be had while playing this life drainer. It's extremely satisfying to see your factory grow from being just one man mining coal to a massive industry with robots, train systems, nuclear power, and big deadly weapons. Players who like a game with grind and progress will get a kick out of Factorio. It's easy to get consumed in the game, always wanting to make your factory bigger and more efficient, researching new technologies and building units by the thousands.
Factorio is a good game but, holding an incredible 98% positive review rate, there are some big problems that most players are aware of and forget to mention. First, this game has a learning curve that will cause every player disappointment at some point or another, since it can take HOURS of gameplay before you realized how much you're paying for a mistake you made earlier. Take me for example: I'm currently on my third game save. I had put 8 hours into my first game save and 17 into my second one before deleting them and starting over because, once I realized I was doing something wrong, it's easier to start over than to try to fix the problem while relocating equipment after the available resources have been drained. That's a combined 25 hours of progress lost because I made mistakes and didn't realize them. I enjoy complex games that can take some time to learn, but players should never stop and say something like "I used all of my resources to make something I thought I would need, but I have no use for it and now my game save is ruined." It's not just me that feels this way. Most instructional videos online are about half an hour. I watched a 25-minute video twice to understand how I'm supposed to gather and use oil and the video's comments are full of thanks from people who couldn't understand the process otherwise. Look at the Factorio forums, players are asking for help on things that should be straightforward. The game's tutorial is okay, but it only covers the VERY basics of the game and, more importantly, doesn't teach the player about efficiency, which is necessary for progress.
Second, for what is, at the very least, an open strategy game, there aren't very many choices left to the player. In other words, if you're not playing one particular way, you're not playing right and you're probably just going to lose. Factorio is such a big game with so much to work towards that you can feel that the possibilities are endless, but they're not. You win the game when after you build resource Z. You need resource A and B to make resource C, then you need resource C and D to make resource E, and so on until you get to Z. That's how you win. If you don't get resources A-Z, you don't win. You can't try to make a strat where you get a whole lot or resource C and E without focuing on everything else, even if you don't need it for anything else but resource Z. The fact that Factorio is a grinding base-building game that doesn't give the player choices is what keeps it from being a great game.
The developers don't intend on ever putting Factorio on sale or on any retailer/key selling sites, so the game will always be $20. I still think this price is pretty steep and it wouldn't kill the developers to give some kind of discount for holidays and the like, but I understand their reasons for not doing it.

EDITED (07-09-2017): removed the minor spolier alert. Edited some comments.
Gameplay:
Though very straight forward, the game mechanics is actually interesting. I'm not a big fan of plantformers because I don't enjoy jumping puzzles and testing my reflexes. Valiant Hearts have some of these elements, but mostly it's at your own pace relaxing puzzle solving. Yet, for those hardcore gamers, this game is also not childplay, but there are over 100 collectibles which should challenge those who strive for perfection.
Please note that there are some minor bugs where you could get stuck. Simply restart from checkpoint and they are nothing gamebreaking.
Graphics:
I believe the sample images should say enough. Please pardon me for my limited knowledge in artistic terminology, but this game has very artistic sytles. Characters are very cartoon-like but backgrounds are simply realistic in its own way. I've been a fan of realistic graphics in games for years but this game's style still amazes me.
Audio:
I would say the audio for this game does even better than its graphics. Every BGM fits so well for the scene and you can really fell the mood while playing. The soundtrack is available on Amazon and I won't urge to buy it because you will do so after finishing the game.
Story:
Let me put it this way: even without the amazing soundtrack, this game's story already guarantees its highest rating from me. It's hard to comment on the story without spoiling anything, but it's a war story that you don't normally see in other games.
Verdict:
The total playthrough is around 6 hours. I suggest you find a day when you don't have any rush to other things and play through this game immersively. Try to pay attention to all the cutscenes and examine any collectible items you come across. I promise you'll fall in love with this game.
100/100 recommend.

I first played this game way back in the day on the Playstation 2 before i could even understand english (It´s my second language). However that didn´t stop me from fully enjoying the game, it´s very simplistic and someone that don´t even play video games on a regular basis can play this game with no problems.
The Story:
This story takes place in Australia and you play as a Tasmanian tiger called Ty. Ty´s family has been trapped in the spirit world by the evil Boss Cass (The Main Villain of the story). It is now up to Ty to save his family and friends from Boss Cass who wants power from the ancient Talismans that trapped Ty´s family in the spirit world. You will be travelling across multiple different enviroments of Australia to find them including the forests, the outback and the great barrier reef. Along the way you will be facing Boss Cass´ goons that include kangaroos, frill lizards and blue tongue lizards as well as mini bosses like a bull, a cyborg shark and a massive mountain monster.
The Gameplay:
The gameplay isn´t too advanced. Combat consists of you throwing boomerangs and techno boomerangs at foes as well as biting them. You will also be gliding, swiming and jumping a lot since the game is a 3D platformer after all. In each level there are different tasks that include finding and saving your friends, collecting all opals and collecting all golden cogs that will unlock technorangs. Each level all have a main quest that can be something like escorting someone to safety, finding lost children or finding someone of interest.
The characters:

The Purring Quest is a 2D Cartoon Looking Platformer
STORY: 8/10
In my opinion, the story here is extremely simple; however I feel the game was more intended to be allegorical in nature. It shows the life of a cat, meeting other cats, on a journey to reunite with his or her owner. It's extremely cute, well written and not over-exhausting. Each meeting gives the story of a real-life cat and a small integration into the story.
GAMEPLAY: 8/10
You play as a cat, collecting dead fishy bones, and various other hidden collectables throughout each of the 5 levels. The platforming is not overly difficult, nor do I believe it was intended to be. I believe it's just the right amount of platforming for this type of game; and was quite enjoyable.
DIFFICULTY: 7/10
If you plan on being an achievement completionist, you should expect this game to last you 2-3 hours for the genuine most. It is very short, and definitely left me with a feeling of wanting more. I wanted more levels, more story, and more kitty fun. The game is not difficult, and I believe even children would find the gameplay enjoyable.
TECHNICAL: 8/10
At times the controls are a bit non-intuitive, but nothing you cannot overcome with a bit of patience.
I will give props to the developer for one major improvement. I was an instant purchaser of the game, and the controls were quite difficult. I was often missing jumps, and they were simply not responsive. In a relatively short period of time; a patch was released to correct the controls and it was significantly improved.
GRAPHICS: 10/10
All graphics are hand drawn by developers, I cannot be more complimentary. Backgrounds are beautiful, characters are based off real-life cats. Absolutely wonderful.
CONCLUSION
Recommended gameplay for a simple platformer, with cute graphics and in illustrative story. Worth the time for all types of cat people alike. 8.5/10

After replaying the whole game again after it left early access to become the full version, I'll now rewrite my review, whether that changes much or not, to represent the final product.
Ty the Tasmanian Tiger is a game for fans of platformers. It's a classic collectathon game with not a lot of emphasis on story or graphics. In terms of difficulty, it's quite frankly a game for kids, as it is for the most part very easy to progress through. Somes bosses may stump you unlike the rest of the game due to a lack of guidance combined with very unobvious tasks you must do (Particularly the Fluffy's Fjord level).
For the most part, Ty's level design is done quite well. Many levels are very linear, but with enough twists and turns to make them fun to play, while several are very large and open. One might call the larger levels rather empty, but this is expected given the limitations of the time this game was made in. So for what they did accomplish, these levels are still impressive, and even beautiful in some cases.
Graphics are obviously nothing to write home about. They're kept relatively basic as the game is focused on gameplay instead. None of the textures, effects, etc are pixilated or unnecessarily blurry, so they're really not a cause for concern. Lighting and shadows are nicely done in the remaster, and the remastered version allows you to see things MUCH further away than in the original, which makes for some amazing views and nice spotting points to search the map for collectables you might be missing.
Ty the Tasmanian Tiger's soundtrack is excellent, featuring mostly great songs and some that are just downright amazing (Two Up). There are a couple odd balls, mainly the boulder minigame theme, but you'll rarely find yourself immediately hating a song (Only after you've spent an hour trying to find the last opal).
The occasional quirk you might encounter might include the infra-rang sound effect or camera trouble. The infra-rang is just down-right annoying, and as for the camera, there are settings you can use to adjust it closer to your liking. If you still have trouble after that, it's probably more your fault than the game's, being that I myself never had problems with the camera as bad as others might describe.
Regarding bugs or oddities of any sort, I've found only two things so far while playing the game. I'm unsure whether this is the game's fault or not, but it seems to have potential for slight incompatibilities with some computer settings. I changed power usage settings at some point before finishing my second playthrough found that the lighting effects were too strong and some particle effects had boxes around them. While these errors are not at all severe and won't distract you much, they are still errors nonetheless. However on the level "Lyre, Lyre Pants on Fire", there is a possibly gamebreaking bug. It is possible you may comb the level and still be missing a few opals. This is because there Y coordinates can glitch out (Or are just flat out incorrect, I'm not sure), making them impossible to reach and/or find. Fear not though, for they can also glitch out again by reloading the level (Or this is Krome's idea of a fix), and spawn in a respawned crate, from which you can acquire the missing opals. Finally the weird landscape at the end of "Beyond the Black Stump" isn't bugged out or anything. It's just lazyness or a lack of time for polishing.
For what the game is trying to be, it's very well crafted. It's certainly nothing less than at least a descent game. If you enjoy platformers, Ty the Tasmanian Tiger is definitely a title to pick up.

I really wanted to like this game, I mean it's got sylvanian animal characters as heroes and really colourful art and animation that brings the lore to life. However after spending several hours on the game, I can't help but feel that the game is really inbalanced and that lots of times, the game depends more on luck and chance on getting good cards early on than on your skill and management. You will find that winning is easier with some characters and extremely difficult with others.
This is a turn-based strategy game that has minimal storyline, with four players trying to win by getting rid of the Corrupted King and ascending the throne. One can do it in four ways, either by slaying the King, gaining prestige while waiting for the King to expire, collecting Spirit Stones or gaining rot and challenging the King. It may seem that there are many routes to victory but winning via Spirit Stones and Rot is really difficult. And victory usually goes to characters that are strong using the Kingslayer or Prestige route.
Personally, I'm not much for multiplayer action, so maybe someone who enjoys multiplayer games may have a different viewpoint. I like the world of Armello though, and would really like to see a single player turn-based strategy RPG game with full storyline based on its characters and lore.

Valiant Hearts is a sweet little narrative-based game with puzzles as the core of its gameplay. The art style, puzzle difficulty, and story are all simple enough to appeal to any age range and any player but they are not so dull or boring enough to be unchallenging or uninteresting.
Overall, Valiant Hearts is a nice and cute game with stark moments of race-against-the-clock terror mixed in as reminders that this is not a dream, and the ending will remind you that although these characters are all fictional, they are based on real people, millions of them, and the millions that they knew, who did not live through or die in a video game with a cutesy art style and fun puzzles, but in the real world in a horrific conflict that did so much damage of the kind that can never be undone.
This game is a beautiful monument to and teacher about the Great War and a wonderfully fun game at the same time. I will be recommending it to everyone I know, gamers and non-gamers alike.

The game is childishly cute and the story is kept simple. The sound fits in very well with the game's atmosphere. You jump around, gather stars, stomp funny looking creatures on the head while avoiding falling into lava, water and being crushed (among other things) on your way to the exit.
There are 4 difficulty levels to choose from, ranging from being immortal to 1-shot you're dead. However, loads of checkpoints make dying a minor issue so if you got some experience from this type of games then hardcore's the way to go.
As you progress in story mode you'll unlock extra bonus levels that offer new, unique challenges that'll keep you going once the story's over.
Something I believe to be very important in this type of game are the controls and I'm glad to say that they were excellent. Easy to learn and the little alien do as he's commanded (and yet I somehow managed to drown it in lava more than once).
I wouldn't recommend this to a hardcore gamer who's looking for something difficult to sink his or her teeth into because the game's not that hard. If you're looking for a fun, casual platformer however then it's great!
I would also definitly recommend this to parents who seek a game for their kids but don't like all the blood and gore that's so common in most games today. If your kid is old enough to understand the controls then this is a really good game!
Personally, being of the NES-generation I actually did have a lot of fun with this one and although I'd never give it a 5 I can't see any reason as to not give it a 4 =)

Oozi: Earth Adventure is a game for children, including those that have never played a video game before, who have little to no expectations. The game is focused less about quality and more about being able to let players freely progress through a game without constantly dying. Fortunately enough there is a kid specific difficulty level suited for these players.
There is no charm here, at least none that would satisfy and keep the attention of a child. No idle animations, no funny voices or sound effects, no memorable soundtrack (which is on a very noticeable short loop). There are DOS games that are filled with more fanciful flavour and variety than this and it doesn't help that Oozi: Earth Adventure does absolutely nothing to progress the tired, old, trope-filled platforming genre; floating platforms, ground spikes, climbing up vines, stomping on monsters, enemies who fly side-to-side, etc.
The controls are clunky and unresponsive. Climbing walls is an absolute chore and you will often find yourself flying into a deadly trap or another enemy due to the floaty control scheme. Every level slowly progresses with a variety of enemies and each chapter concludes with a boss fight. Once you've started the next chapter you soon come to realise that the new enemies you're facing now are just reskinned versions from previous levels. The camera system does you no favour as it sticks to your character, rather than allowing any wiggle room, and it generally will not be able to show you any nearby traps or enemies if they happen to be just a few pixels out of its field of view. This will often cause you to go bouncing into roof spikes or falling into an enemy just off to the side.
These issues would be perfectly fine if there didn't happen to be a thousand other games that do the platforming genre more justice than Oozi: Earth Adventure. Most children are more likely to have their first gaming experience with the Mario series, so by the time they discover Oozi: Earth Adventure they will very quickly realise just how inferior this game is in comparison.
Edit: I've now discovered that the more you play this game the less smooth it will run. Whether it is due to a memory leak, I do not know. This has caused the game to drop its frame-rate to less than 20 frames per second, unacceptable for a 2D sidescroller that depends on reaction time for most of its puzzles. There will also be times where the game will seem to suddenly stutter for a split second. This wasn't happening when I first started playing the game. There are also bugs with one of the enemies. If you die, respawn, and come across the enemy again, they will spawn in their death state and automatically die. It's almost like no one tested this game before release.
Slidy controls, unpredictable jumping a poor hitboxing makes this platformer a must-buy for people who hate money.

This game has some of the most interesting design I've ever seen in a zombie game OR an open-world game.
The biggest conceit is that rather than playing with one character, you play as characters from a survivor community, and if you die (or get bored) you simply swap to another surviving member. This is a great mechanic that both adds serious weight to death and avoids creating a frustrating experience where you need to repeat gameplay until you can do things without dying at all. Community members all have character traits that can help make them more (or less!) useful members of the community, and you can upgrade them with specializations too - these gameplay differences between characters help make each person feel distinct.
You can dynamically relocate your community and infrastructure across several pre-designed sites, too, and set up outposts in just about any building to create tiny safe zones. There are tons of neat little ideas in this game aside from that - for example, the "survey" mechanic where you can climb tall buildings and scope out nearby areas to fill in your map is a great idea. The noise mechanic for drawing zombie attention is common sense to some degree, but it's taken much further than other games would by combining it with other gameplay systems; for example, rummaging through abandoned houses and supplies makes noise, and you can rush the generally slow search process by creating even more noise. It's a brilliant touch that adds tension to the otherwise boring act of looting.
State of Decay is tons of stuff like this - little and big design ideas about how an open world came could be different and systems-driven. There are scripted story quests too, which do the job but mostly serve to structure the arc of your playthrough. Combat is rough and draining. Stealth is tense. You worry about using guns or cars because of the noise they'll cause. You need to keep your people supplied and medicated and happy enough not to get into fights.
If anything, I wish there were a bit more internal struggle to keeping a settlement functional - about halfway through the game I started feeling like my settlement would be fine without much attention. But most of all, what I want is a sequel that builds on the unique ideas for open-world design presented in this. And, luckily, there's a sequel on its way!

This DLC introduces nightclubs where you can dance with women and work as a bouncer, previously introduced to the GTA series in San Andreas (2004). Ballad also introduces several new helicopters, including the Buzzard which is somewhat superior to the original Annihilator. Both DLC games feature the ability to Gang/Drug Wars, which reward you money and weapons every 10 wars. If you haven't played the original GTA 4 however, then you SHOULD NOT play this game, as you won't understand the storyline as well and missions too, as they cross over with the original GTA 4 missions occasionally. Excellent tactical game.  Can be played either as either Turn Based or Real Time, or better yet, a mix of the two.  I love the turn based combat from the first two Fallout games, but in this game, I generally stay in real time, or Continuous Turn Based, as they call it.  There is a ton of combat, so the CTB is much faster unless you get to a particularly hard part.  Even in the CTB there is plenty of tactics and positioning before you engage.  Having your squad sneak up behind a barrier in a crawl, then have them simultaneously pop up and burst AK47 fire and shotgun blasts into the enemies face is great fun.  Get caught off guard and find yourself swarmed, don't panic, simply hit Return and enter turn based.
The campaign is interesting, and all the leveling and character customization from the Fallout RPGs (1/2)  is here.  Throw in the scavenging feel of a post apocalypse world and you can't lose.  Strongly recommend this game.

I know that a lot of people had problems with this game because it differed from the original fallout, but I'm going to attemp to explain to people why this game is great and you should probably buy it. First off I'll admit, yes, this game is WAAAAYYY different from fallout 1 &2, But not all the changes are bad, the graphics have substantially improved, and character customization is almost as strong as in the first 2 games. However, the main reason I feel this game is worth buying is because they focus on the combat. A lot of people will disagree with me, but I think combat is something the original fallout games should have focused more on. This game focuses almost entirely on it and somehow manages to pull it off. The fallout series most notable feature is its dynamic choice system, in that choices you make directly and indirectly influence the world around you. This game has very little of that, so if really want a diverse range of choices that can effect you negatively and positively, then you probably won't find much here to entertain you. Choices are very limited, at best and charisma influences nothing but your availiable recruits. This means that most of what makes up a fallout game isn't present in a fallout game, treason, I know. BUTTTTTTTTTTTTTT, the combat is so fricking awesome that I can't help but recommend this game, if you enjoy turn based or RTS combat with a touch of non-canon fallout lore, this game is definitely for you.

As a gamer, I generally have a good feel for which games I will find fun and which I will wish I had never bought.  Any game with a good plot usually falls into the former category for me, regardless of the genre.  And while I like FPS games in general, I never bothered with games like Call of Duty, which were, in my opinion, shooting solely for the sake of shooting.  So, when someone gifted me Battlefield: Bad Company 2 on Steam, I decided I might as well give it a try.
To begin with, I will give the developers credit for integrating the tutorial with the opening mission, and at the same time, not turning it into a “tutorial mission."  Learning the controls was integrated well with the mission, and I didn’t feel like the mission was custom-tailored to teaching me.
The plot however, was exactly as I expected: a mildly-coherent excuse for more shooting.  I vaguely remember something about the Russians having some evil doomsday weapon (which sounded like some kind of giant EMP generator) and my squad somehow being the only ones qualified to stop/find/destroy it.  And it being excuse for more shooting, the plot must always take the route of greatest enemy contact.  I found the weapon once, but of course it was only a fake weapon, and I then had to go to South America and kill some local militia-folk in order to find the real one.
As the plot is usually my principal motivator in FPS games, I quickly grew frustrated with my plot-to-death ratio playing on the Normal difficulty.  I had one mission where I had to make my way down a mountain in a blizzard, and not only did I have to avoid bullets and RPGs, but I had to avoid dying of hypothermia by taking shelter in strategically placed small homes.  I eventually got to a bridge with scores of Russians on the other side, and I could not, for the life of me, make it across without either dying from being shot too many times or dying from hypothermia by staying in my cover too long.  It was at this point that I got fed up and switched to the Easy difficulty.  After doing so, the rate at which I was dying became far more tolerable for the relatively ♥♥♥♥♥♥ plot I was being served.
Overall, I don’t know if I can say that Battlefield: Bad Company 2 is a bad game, but I do know that it’s not for me.  The plot is completely token, I die way too often, and even on Easy difficulty there’s too much shooting and not enough plot-advancing for my tastes.
P.S.: If you want to hear more about Battlefield: Bad Company 2, along with some of the other gripes I had with it, check out Yahtzee’s Zero Punctuation

Okay, so I really, really had high hopes for this game. I'm a huge fan of board games and I've got a pretty big collection of my own, so I'm always on the lookout for digital board games to help scratch that itch. At a glance, this is a fantasy board game with a huge variety of heroes, charms, cards, and would have tons of replay value, right? Right?
Well, let's start with the story. Or lack thereof. I was really hoping this game would have a story mode, especially once I booted up the prologue and played through it. The prologue itself wasn't very compelling, but I figured that I would expect that from a tutorial. But no, the tutorial is basically ALL the story you'll ever get for this game. I guess that makes sense because every game is the exact same setup, so making a narrative with this limited of cotent would be practically impossible.
The lack of a story and the overall surprising shallowness of the game (having only one mode to play) isn't what kills it for me though. Oh no, what kills it for me is the gameplay.
The best board games I've played can be beaten with a level head and a solid strategy. Usually there's something of an element of luck which has to be there, but in general, those who play the best will win. Not here. Oh, no. This game is ALL luck. Good luck trying to focus on a win condition right out of the gate. If you don't have rot cards, the Rot condition is never going to happen (and the rot cards are fairly rare. Even if you do get them, getting enough rot to take down the king is extremely unlikely. You can get killed by the rot creatures to gain rot but... yeah, getting killed by somethign isn't a great strategy in general). The spirit stone condition is completely up in the air. Getting spirit stones in dungeons is super unlikely, they spawn on the map super randomly (meaning that they're far more likely to spawn nearer to one of your three opponents than you. Oh, but you can always just pick a quest with a spirit stone as a reward, right? Haha, no, of course not. To get the spirit stone, you need to pass a skill check which means, yet again, MORE random rolls. Even if you're luck enough forthe spirit stone quest to land on your best attribute, you likely won't have better than a 50-60% chance of getting it early game, and failure means that you wasted your time and probably got hurt for no better reason than the dice fell poorly.
The prestige victory is probably your best bet, done by having the most prestige by the time the king dies of Rot. you get prestige by killing other players and monsters, and by completing quests (and certain other ways). But the real important thing here is that by killing other heros you get prestige. So if you're a combat focused character and find a not combat focused character, it's pretty easy to kill them. Then you can spawn camp them for as much prestige as you want. Yeah, for some stupid reason, every player has a fixed spawn point, so camping is absolutely a thing that can happen to you, as horrible as that sounds/is. Prestige leaders also get to pick the modifier that happens at the beginning of each day so... yeah, that's great, right?
And then you can also just kill the king in battle. This is also pretty viable, since you can high roll early for good loot with a combat character and then just stomp the king and his guard into the dirt early on. That is easier said than done since the king is a very formidable opponent (especially early when he has a ton of health) and is protected by his guard and powerful perils in the courtyard. Still, it's certainly more viable than the ♥♥♥♥ing rot or spirit stone victories.
It's not just the random spirit stones you have to worry about. Randomly drawing terrible cards, randomly having rot monsters spawn on top of your head/raiding your settlements, having the king slap down random perils in your way, or just rolling crap in combat.
The game also doesn't sound great. Music is basically nonexistant, there's little voice acting (and that which is there isn't great), and the soudn effects are pretty bog standard.
There are some good things. The game is colorful and looks nice, the cards are well animated, there are LOTS of cards to mess around with, heroes to play (but a lot are hidden behind a pay wall), and starting bonus' to unlock.
But when it comes down to it, Armello is the worst kind of board game. It understands nothing of what makes a good board game, mistakes luck for skill, and is something of an insult to the genre. There's a lot to see her, but it's too shallow to be worth trying. Just leave this game to Rot.
I give Armello a 1 out of 5.

"Fight the Dragon" is a casual, 3D isometric, hack and slash, RPG, dungeon crawler; in which greater than 99% of all stages (dungeons) are player made; difficulty varies based on the stage creators' imaginations.

The first dungeon the player starts in is scripted to be 3 Sprockets' tutorial stage.  He or she begins with a one-handed sword and a shield to fight with, and is taught what they need to know in order to play the game.  The stage is short but gives the player a general idea of what the overall game is like.

Combat is action-oriented; attacks and skills must be aimed (players and monsters) and dodged/blocked.  Some players may be turned off by the number of hits it takes to take down some monsters, which is usually about four for a standard monster; although, they come in many difficulties and varieties.

In "Fight the Dragon," players receive loot from slaying monsters, opening treasure chests, or trading in donation points from the Loot Shrine.  Loot comes in 5 different grades:
Brown > Junk
Purple > Common
Green > Rare
Orange > Extraordinary
Yellow > Legendary
Each player's own loot that is received from monster and chest drops is affected by the player's own luck (LUC) stat; higher luck yields greater chances for better loot grades.

Lower grade items are not completely useless.  In the over world/lobby area, there is a structure called "Loot Shrine" to the North-West, which allows players to sell (donate) items, they do not want, for donation points; the value (VAL) assigned to each item determines how many donation points are received when traded in at the Loot Shrine.  These points can be used to obtain higher grades of random gear, stat points, inventory slots, health power-ups, or stamina power-ups.
On a side note, the Loot Shrine also functions as a bank, allowing players to store items they want to keep but not yet use.

Players of given all of the building blocks necessary to create a plethora of possible stage themes via the many terrain types, props, npc options, and more.  Some players may be turned off by the shallow quantity of monster choices or the inability to place more than one object on each block.
The ACK is fool proof in many ways.  Players can easily figure out what each feature does by tinkering + play testing a few times.  It is impossible to make a stage's overall monster difficulty to checkpoint and/or potion chest count too high.  There is a limit to the number of treasure chests that can be placed in comparison to the overall difficulty of the monsters.  The player is unable to submit (publish) a stage if he or she cannot complete it.

Two or more people can band together via an internet connection (online), one of whom is the host, or split-screen mode.  Online mode is done peer-to-peer, so having a high internet speed and strong connection is mandatory, otherwise players will seem to be teleporting every now and then.
Multiplayer mode does have a feature that allows players to directly teleport to one another, should someone get stuck or lost.  Players receive their own loot, so if someone wants to give an item to another player, all he or she needs to do is drop the item.
The basic controls consist of WASD for movement, basic weapon attack, special weapon attack, ability to rotate the camera clockwise or counterclockwise, sprinting, blocking, dodge-rolling, and the 4 class skills.  All of these can be customized with the "key mapping" feature.  Jumping is performed automatically when a player walks towards a one space gap or sprints towards the side of a ledge.
This game is an example of the phrase "poor graphics do not necessarily mean a poor game."  Although they are not impressive, they are not repulsive either, but of course beauty is in the eye of the beholder; basically, an expensive PC is not required to play the game.

When in idle parts of each stage, the music is rather lax, but when the player approaches monsters, the music intensifies.

Most of the sound effects are appropriate for the action that takes place for each of them, however, the same cannot be said for a majority of player projectile weapon attacks.  The lack of variety for sound effects may be unappealing to players and can get stale quickly.
For what "Fight the Dragon" is right now, I can strongly recommend this game to people who get utility out of creating their own stages and/or stories.  I also recommend this game to people who like action-oriented combat, loot based games, and/or adventure variety.
I strongly do NOT recommend this game to people who like PVP, because there is no PVP.  I also strongly do not recommend this game to people who want end game content; after reaching level cap, there is not so much left for the character to strive for other than gathering more loot and gathering more health and stamina power-ups.
Pros and Cons said, I have to say that I love this game; I like being able to apply my creative side in a fun way.

If you enjoy puzzles, you would like this game a lot. The whole point of the game is using time travel to get through the puzzles, where you have your characters go through portals into the past during the same puzzle, essentially causing other events to happen simultaneously.
The game is a handful of hours to play, depending on how well you are at figuring out the puzzles. The game does not really give you much direction for most of the puzzles, though sometimes you will know how to start out (i.e., you will see that you lose the puzzle if a given character goes in any direction except for one at the beginning, etc.).
There are 4 different sets of puzzles, with different gameplay mechanics. Each puzzle set has 15 levels, where the first 10 "complete" the set, and the other 5 are bonus levels with more difficult puzzles. I think that the last set of the game is almost the easiest, actually, because of the mechanic it adds into the game. The enemy makes it more obvious what directions you cannot use at different times.
The graphics of the game are simple, but interesting. Minimalist, essentially. I do not really remember much sound or music from playing a few days ago, so I guess that is not really a big part of the game.
Causality can be really, really difficult to figure out, but it's worth trying.
A great little puzzle game with one of the best time-travel mechanics I've seen in ages.

Causality is a 2.5D puzzler where you control the passage of time. Your astronauts are perpetually running along a network of catwalks and you have to use the arrows to redirect them to avoid monsters and open/close barriers to allow everyone to reach their own destinations before the timeline runs out.
You can use LT/RT on the controller or simply drag the mouse to rewind or ff, both methods feel easy and satisfying. There is no real-time clock so you can take as long as you like. Move it forward a bit, decide that's not gonna work, go back a bit and try something different etc. I imagine a dance choreographer would be good at this.
The graphics are nothing short of stunning. There are not a whole lot of elements but it's all presented with subtle reflections and transparency that really gives it a smooth, rich ambiance.
There's no music but a haunting, spacey sound with robotic sound effects which all suits the mood nicely.
The level overview looks good too, with sparkly tiles floating in starry space. There's volume control, fullscreen or configurable window sizing, language options - yes, you can change to various languages just for the few words on the options screen - and a colour blind mode. They clearly want the game to be accessible to everybody... even Mac and Linux users (like myself)!
There are 60 levels divided into 4 sections. Section 1 is a lot of fun but didn't give me too much trouble. Halfway through section 2 I started to struggle and from there it gets steadily tougher. These are hard puzzles, not for those looking for a quick and easy route to 100% achievements.
The teleport function deserves a special mention. It has a variable time setting so that sometimes you have a ghost of yourself travelling at the same time, other times not. Wrapping your brain around this is a task in itself.
The only downside is the linear level progression. You have to solve one level before you can move on to the next, so if you get stuck (which you certainly will at some point) you have no option to try a different puzzle to refresh your brain and then return to this one later. It can get frustrating, knowing there's a lot more of the game available but out of reach.
[UPDATE] You can now skip ahead one level! Thanks devs!
This is RIDICULOUSLY underpriced! It's worth 2 or even 3 times the asking price. OK, so it doesn't have too much replay value but the production quality and level design belongs in a much higher price bracket. The hard challenge of later levels will keep you occupied for many hours.
Achievements - one for each completed section plus several for completing certain levels in a limited number of moves. Steam Cloud. No Trading Cards yet.
I have to say, the Steam store page doesn't do this game justice. I was expecting a quick, cheapo puzzler with a clunky menu system to keep me amused for an hour or two then forgotten. I was gobsmacked at the high quality of the whole thing. It really does have a WOW factor as soon as you launch it.
Needless to say, I STRONGLY recommend Causality. It's a tough challenge with creative level design, it looks gorgeous and the price is a bargain.
If you do like this game I also recommend Induction, another good quality timeline-based puzzler.

A neat little puzzle game :)
Impressions:
The mechanics do an awesome job with screwing with the player's mind. There's weird time-traveling and cloning teleports, paradoxes mixed with somewhat more classical switches and falling tiles. This is probably how I'd sum up the game in one sentence actually. A proper mind♥♥♥♥ery of a mix of calssic and modern puzzle game mechanics. Causality definitely tries to do something new here but builds it on solid foundations of the genre.
Content:
There's 4 sets of puzzles, 15 levels each. You need to beat first 10 puzzles of each set to progress to another one. The levels are designed in a way that the obligatory 10 are somewhat easier than the optional 5 which can really force you to spend more time on them. That said the game isn't long and doesn't overstay its welcome. It took me just a few hours to beat the mandatory 40 puzzles.
Graphics:
Visualy it's simple but good looking. Slowly animated backgrounds don't distract you from cracking the puzzles presented to you in the foreground. It feels rather minimalistic but that's all that's needed.
Issues:
Now onto the flaws. For a game that does a good job at steady pacing of the difficulty curve it really sucks at explaining things to you. It could *really* use some form of an as-you-play tutorial to explain some of its more innovative mechanics. Meanwhile you’re thrown into it and left to figure it all out by yourself. Which might sound like a fun sort of a challenge but sometimes leaves you guessing and making random choices just to “see what happens” instead of thinking what to do next. And that’s what puzzle games should be about.
Performance and ethics:
Technically everything is perfect. No framedrops, no bugs or crashes. Great job on part of the devs here. Also kudos for no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t with pre-order stuff. It’s a good game that doesn’t need silly marketing to appeal to the fans of the genre.
Summary:
Overall, Causality is very solid, especially at such an attractive price. If the devs have even more creative mechanics in mind I’d definitely like to play some downloadable content for it.

Having slogged through so many puzzle games recently, Causality managed to reinvigorate my interest in isometric puzzles with its novel time manipulation mechanic. This bittersweet feature will have you pulling your hair out as you try to navigate multiple characters through time paradoxes, butt loads of switches, death traps, enemies, teleporters and more. This 60 level pit of glory and frustration is sure to provide veteran puzzle solvers a unique and tough challenge.
Starting out, Causality’s time manipulation seems to be just a glorified rewind mechanic. Initially, clickable directional tiles are the major challenges, populating the levels to help redirect oblivious, auto-moving astronauts to their destinations. As you progress, crazier obstacles will be added, compounding to create some semblance of difficulty. Several levels later, you’ll be crying when you see spatial teleporter tiles. What makes these tiles so unique is that they aren’t quite teleporters in a traditional sense. Causality provides a clone image that will eject from the teleporter’s exit
you actually step onto the teleporter’s entrance. Sometimes the clone will eject 3 spaces before the original enters, while precise finagling may get the clone to eject 10 or more spaces ahead of time. This clone is essentially a fully-fleshed character that is free to interact with anything. Naturally, you may be thinking that it’s odd to create a clone if you haven’t entered the teleporter yet. What if you decide not to go into the teleporter after positioning your clone? In adherence to the law of time and space travel, in agreement with any logical thinker, Causality will erase the clone if you decide not to commit to the teleporter. Furthermore, the game’s leeway with the time you get to spend with two copies of one astronaut may lead to a time paradox – a situation where both copies (original and clone) head towards the teleporter entrance.
At the bottom of every level is a nodal timeline, outlining how many steps you have remaining to get to the goals. The timeline also notes the points at which certain traps or static hazards will activate. One of the biggest uses of the timeline is determining the beginning and end of a teleporter “feedback” loop – how many steps you have with your clone before the original disappears. In addition, the complex nature of teleporters will, more often than not, suddenly create clones in the middle of the level while you are altering directional tiles. The timeline helps visualize things and allow you to go back to the point at which the clone spawns on the teleporter exit.
Do NOT refer to this walkthrough unless you’ve tried everything; it’d definitely ruin the fun.
From what I can remember, the majority of the levels will be relatively easy (YMMV), able to be completed within minutes. A bulk of the levels will take a bit longer to solve, upwards of 15 minutes or more depending on whether you can or can’t see a viable path. The remaining handfuls/bonus levels will take quite a while – they doubled/tripled my overall playtime, and I still haven’t completed every bonus level (I got stuck on the final level for ~3 hours until I was spoonfed a path). These devious levels are extremely much more complex than the standard levels.
Although I really enjoy the teleporters, they unfortunately seem to be the only true time-manipulating challenge. I definitely wish there were others, like something similar to Ratchet & Clank’s Time Puzzles, but for such a neat and novel game, I can’t find too much fault here. A part of me wants to recommend this game to others just so they can experience the hellish levels I managed to overcome, but setting my ego aside, Causality is much more than its mind-wracking torture. The colorful backgrounds create an immersive experience and an optional color-blind mode adds some nice polish too. This makes it easy for me to recommend Causality to any fans of novel puzzle games.

In Card Hunter, you play a party of 3 adventurers in a grid based map. However, your equipment isn't actual weapons, but a deck of cards. Each item you add to your equipment is associated with several cards, which are added to your deck when you equip said item. The aggregation of all the cards of your items will become the deck of cards you play with, and that deck controls everything you do during the battle: move, attacks, heal, and other special abilities are all done by playing one of your card.
Each turn, you get dealt 3 cards per character, and the 2 teams alternate playing 1 card each. Once you're done playing cards for this turn, you can pass, and once both teams have passed, the turn ends and new cards are being dealt.
Though there are a lot of concepts to grasp, the lengthy tutorial will help figure things out one by one, until you're ready to go on your own. You should master most concepts of the game within a few games played.
Finally, each mission you complete (or each multiplayer battle you win) will reward you with a loot chest, containing 4 random items, that you will be able to equip on your characters if you wish. With a wide array of weapons, items, shields, skills, etc. available to collect, you will soon be able to create and tweak your characters' equipment the way you want and make powerful decks that suit your playstyle.
The game can be played solo or in coop, playing the main campaign of the game, or in 1v1 multiplayer arena. Each mode is available for free, and each is great in its own way.
The base campaign is huge, with 40 missions to play, entirely for free. Though the difficulty is rather low at the beginning, it will slowly ramp up, until the final missions which should be an interesting challenge even for veteran boardgamers/tactical video gamers. Several missions are clearly intended to help you master one or more concepts of the game that will then be helpful for the final challenges.
While playing coop, you will be playing the same campaign against the AI, but instead of controlling 3 characters, you will only be playing one character of the party and your teammates will be playing the others. In case they are only two of you, you play with only 2 characters, but you will draw an extra card every turn to balance that handicap out.
Finally, the multiplayer is a great opportunity for people who want the ultimate challenge. Characters in multiplayer are automatically set to max level, able to equip any item in the game (within restrictions). You are thus free to make the most powerful decks you can think of and then face off against other human opponents to see how good your deck building and your board play actually are. Once again, the game will help you get your bearing in this mode, by having you play at first against AI and then only matching you against players of a similar multiplayer rating to yours. That way, you will be able to fight interesting battles and climb the rankings at your own pace.
With any free to play game, there is always the question of what is the monetizing model like and do players need to pay in order to actually enjoy the game (or be successful at it). Fortunately, Card Hunter has an extremely player-friendly monetizing model. You can play for free the 40 missions of the campaign (which would probably represent something like 20h of play even if you were only playing it once), as well as playing multiplayer battles as much as you want.
What money brings in Card Hunter can be labelled as "More Card Hunter", and has 3 main usages: More missions, player figurines and club membership.
* Additional missions can be bought, usually offering new settings and new monsters to fight against.
* Player figurines are simply what is used to represent your characters on the boards. If you don't like the default ones, or want to change them, you can buy several of thoses for real money. They are cosmetic only, they do not affect the gameplay and once you buy one of these, you can use it on any number of your characters, as please you.
* Club membership is the only non permanent thing that can be bought for money. You can buy one week, one month, etc. of membership, with decreasing price for increasing commitment. What it does is offer you more loot when completing a mission or winning a multiplayer battle. By default, everybody get a chest with 4 items in it. Club members get an additional 5th item. Since item drops are random, club membership doesnt guarantee you will get great items, it's just a slightly faster way to get more items.
So, on the whole, what you get with money is just additional content, for those who enjoy the game and want more of it. More missions, and a slightly faster growing collection of items. You can play this game dozen hours without feeling the need to buy it, but if you do spend money on it, you will probably enjoy all the new stuff you've unlocked.
With its accessible tutorial and its coop play, Card Hunter can be enjoyed casually by a wide variety of people.
However, the game is most likely to appeal to players who like turn by turn / tactical games. The kind of players who enjoy trying to find the optimal combination of items, and the right set of moves to play. With its large array of items, Card Hunter allows you to create many different parties (group of 3 characters), with widly different playstyles, and tweak them obsessively until they perform as well as you expect it.
But having a good deck is only part of the game, and it's how you play it once you're on the battlefied that will decide who is the winner. Figure out the opponent's strengths and weaknesses, move to cover if necessary, push when you have the advantage, and withdraw when you don't: Card Hunter's actual gameplay is all about tactics, lines of sight, and using the cards timing to your advantage.
Card Hunter is free to play, it's great and it has a ton of content, so stop wasting your time reading this review and try it for yourself ! ;)

OOZI: An Earth Adventure.  An evenly paced colourful plat-former, about 5 hours in story mode but provides additional length through challenge stages unlocked by maximizing designated hidden in game tokens.  The Steam leader-boards are an exceptional touch.   Not in the vein of Super Meat Boy or any other punishing plat-formers, OOZI is a plat-former that you can actually finish and have a pleasant time while doing so.
Difficulty selection ranges from "Kid" to "Hardcore" though the latter just makes the game slightly more challenging.  Players are not punished for failure and retuned to checkpoints with previously collected assets intact, which means that for example, discovered secrets persist on restarting checkpoints.

There are numerous game play mechanics which vary the experience.  Additionally, OOZI introduces "Quantum Ghosts", holographic recordings of other players that appear in your game.  This also means that your game-play is being recorded as well for an appearance in other OOZI instances.
The layouts of the levels are homogeneous and are only distinguished by theme and obstacles.  More diversity in this regard would of been welcomed.  The controls are tight enough for precision movement though I felt that the wall mechanics could of been better implemented.
OOZI: An Earth Adventure featuring a nice array of Steamworks features; Steam Achievements, Leader-boards, Cloud Save, Trading Cards and Full Controller Support.  The developer is also very responsive.  I reported a broken achievement and it was fixed in 10 minutes.   Their hard work is apparent by the high level of polish and Steam features that have been applied to this adorable plat-former.

I first finished this game around May or June 2013 after I got it from a Greenlight bundle. I loved it for the art direction, the simple mechanics that induced nostalgia in me, and the comfortable gamepad controls (I would not play a game like this with mouse and keyboard, out of personal preference).
Having grown up during the old age of "jump & run" games, or platformers, I felt right at home with Oozi. It pulled all the right strings for me, and made me remember my old Sega days with all those simple yet enjoyable games.
Oozi has 24 levels in its story mode (whereas the story is just a basic framing on loading screens and between the four zones), of which 4 are boss fights. That may not seem much compared to games like Super Meat Boy or A Walk in the Dark, but it certainly is enough in this case.
Levels can last a good amount of time, depending on difficulty and skill level. You'll definitely get many more hours out of the game than out of pretty much any modern shooter.
On top of the main levels, however, the game also comes with an Arcade Mode, which puts you back into those levels with a more specific goal than reaching the end: Collect as many stars as you can before the timer runs out. If you die, start from the beginning. Checkpoints replenish a bit of time, which is very tight all the way through the level. If you finish the level, you will get a rating from one to three stars, depending on the amount of stars you caught.
This is quite tricky in a lot of levels, and will require almost perfect runs to get 3 stars.
There are also Challenge and Bonus missions, with varying goals. From reaching the end of the level while avoiding rising water to "kill all enemies" missions, you'll get a lot of action. Additionally, those, too, have two additional goals each. All three goals need to be met for a three star rating. And they run on a timer!
These missions are tough as nails, and will probably infuriate you a lot. However, they are satisfying to beat, and well-designed - if you are good at platformers, test yourself on them!
The overall level design of Oozi is simple on first glance, without any elaborately hidden secrets (not unless you run through levels blindly), but the trap and enemy placement really builds a nice difficulty curve.
While you start out with only your basic double-jump and can only knock out basic enemies, every zone delivers a new set of skills and mechanics. This ranges from stomping over wall-jumping to picking up bombs, punching stunned enemies and hiding in shadows. The traps get more mean as the game progresses, and while a lot of them and the enemies are similar or just visually different from previous encounters, the sheer variety of things that may kill you is a plus.
Truth be told, the game still has some glitches and bugs here and there (restarting one challenge mission would get the objective stuck, for example), but nothing that would really deter from the game's enjoyment. Those things are easily fixed and worked around.
As it stands I would recommend Oozi: Earth Adventure to fans of platformers, and oldschool platformers specifically. It is a refreshingly enjoyable game without any of the more "pretentious" elements or big stories, and simply focuses on challenging the player. Which it does excellently! Purchase recommendation given.
