Story
The tale of the Purring Quest is one that has not been highlighted by the developers. They sell themselves short by saying it is a game about meeting cats famous on the internet when the real story is buried in dialogue with cats and optional conversations. Kimchi begins his journey for unknown reasons in a cemetery teeming with rats and patrolled by hounds to meet a cat who tells Kimchi looking for his owner is silly and his owner must be very emotional. Once Kimchi is done being lectured by this philosophical cat, he treks farther in search of his lost owner. According to the wise cat, Kimchi is different than other cats in the fact that he is looking for his owner and not the other way around. According to the cat, cats should be the masters of the humans. Nonetheless, Kimchi still looks for his owner. Not much more can be said about the story without spoiling everything, but just know there is a darker evil afoot.
Gameplay
As a platformer, a game should have a fluid a consistent moving system and should not feel off. This is something The Purring Quest fails to achieve. The game feels very weird to control, especially in the beginning. The first area in the game was one of the most frustrating times I have ever had with a game- it gave me bad flashbacks of Sonic ’06 from my long lost childhood that I had never wished to recover. Moving around in the first level brought me to killing myself at least 4 times and getting beaten to death by small rodents twice. I was extremely upset with how weird the controls were made for the game and thought they could do better. You have to hold S and then press Space bar in order to do a higher jump. What kind of control is that? I did not play the game on controller at all and cannot say it would be a horrible experience on there, too, so I would recommend trying it out if you do purchase the game.
Other than the awkward movement and “combat” system, the game also has straightforward stealth mechanics. You can press a button on, say, a bush while the enemy is looking away and they will turn around and pass you, allowing you to continue the level. There is a small window for error and if you time it correctly, you can leap over the enemy and progress through the level. Maintaining stealth in this game quickly gets boring and you just end up wanting to sprint past every enemy encounter in order to make haste.
One key factor that struck me as odd about the game is the lives system. You have 8 lives and if you run out of them all, you simply go back to the last checkpoint and regain them all. There doesn’t seem to be any consequence to losing all your lives in any form other than your own pride.
Graphics/Performance
The pixelated graphics in The Purring Quest are pretty but in terms of the platforms themselves, are not easy on the eyes. Sometimes it can be difficult to tell platforms apart from other things in the surrounding area and may take a few moments of inspection or trial and error. For me, it was frustrating realizing I had not walked on to another platform but that there was indeed a gap in between two platforms and I plummeted straight to my death. Things like this happened multiple times and made me take breaks from the game out of anger.
I can happily say that I did not encounter a single bug or crash throughout the entirety of the game and this is something that made my experience more pleasant. No progress was ever lost unfairly and the game runs like butter.
Music
At first the soundtrack was pretty mediocre but by the third area I was enjoying listening to the tunes presented to me. Nothing I would listen to outside of playing the game but still, The Purring Quest has a pretty chill soundtrack overall.
Overall
Pros:
•	Pretty Artwork
•	Collectibles for Completionists to Pursue
•	Interesting & weird story
•	Humorous characters that can be found
•	Optional conversations with cats bring out the story
•	Not a single bug or crash
•	Nice soundtrack
Cons:
•	Awkward movement and combat
•	Frustrating first level
•	Basic, monotonous stealth mechanics
•	No consequence for running out of lives
The Purring Quest is a fun adventure that I can only recommend for completionists who will willingly collect all 200 rotten fish in each level and look for the side objects and cats. If you don’t try to get everything your experience with the game will be very short and shallow, devoid of much story and lore. I recommend this game heavily if on sale and you have a few dollars floating around on your Steam account. The game does have soul and it is obvious the developers put time and wanted to make the game as good as they could. I personally support a sequel with smoother platforming attributes and more levels.

This game is a good example of why it's important to also check the negative reviews on a game that have a lot of positive reviews.
As many others have expressed, this game shoves parodies & references down your throat every single moment and that seems like all the game is good for and even then, it does get annoying especially if you're familiar with all those since it's like- where the hell is the new, fresh content we haven't seen & experienced before?
The dev can make an excuse saying it's meant to be a homage to retro games but I think that's cheap if it doesn't have much of it's own content & flair to back that up. I know it's a parody, but at this level it's just plain cheap reuse of existing  ideas & scenarios from other games put randomly in it. That said, it tries hard to be funny but you'd just get a few chuckle here & there. That said, newer gamers who hadn't played the games it's parodying would not get most of the joke and to me, that's bad since like a bad parody (either games, films, cartoons, etc.), it fails to make the joke happen for those unfamiliar with the source material.
Moving on, even with the story, parodies & jokes aside, this game is still♥♥♥♥♥♥ It's just like the most of those pseudo-retro games with retro graphics but in terms of gameplay, it's anything but. A run-of-the-mill collectathon platformer that's a bit like if you mixed a bunch of Sonic OCs with Mad Max Kidz. A very, very Australian game, to the point where if it wasn't actually made by Australians it would come off as grotesquely racist. The main character, Ty, speaks almost entirely in stereotypically Australian exclamations like some kind of tourism board mascot, which given that everyone else in the game speaks mostly-normally leads to him coming off as a touch surreal, like he was originally written as a silent protagonist who had dialogue hastily added into conversations held more at him than too him.
Story-wise, the game is as thin as it gets. I almost get the impression that the game was based on some sort of Saturday Morning Cartoon, the way the backstory is vaguely alluded to, characters come and go like we should know them already, and side characters go through cliche story arcs at breakneck pace. It's not that I didn't know what was going on - everything about the story was incredibly by-the-numbers - but it felt like somebody wrote a story twice as long and had it edited down.
Gameplay is basically passable, if annoying. You only gain two new moves throughout the game, aside from your ever-growing collection of boomerangs with increasingly redundant functions. The boomerangs themselves are fairly clumsy to use, despite being your primary weapon, as their range is extremely vague and their targetting is inconsistent, leading to many situations where you can throw one at an enemy five feet away and it'll whiz harmlessly past him and leave you unarmed for the next few seconds. However, the game's difficulty is almost nonexistent - the hardest achievement in the game is the one where you have to lose all your lives - largely due to Ty getting nearly 10 seconds of mercy invincibility every time he takes damage, meaning it honestly takes effort to lose a life to a single threat.
Ultimately, though, the game is honestly inoffensive. It was a functional timekiller, but I'm not going to give it a recommendation on the grounds that I wouldn't actually suggest anyone else go out of their way to play it. It's not bad, but it's hardly anything good either.

Ty the tasmanian tiger, released in the 6th generation of video games in the year 2002 for xbox original, Nintendo gamecube, and playstation 2 was a platformer collect-athon in the vain of games like Banjo Kazooie and Super mario 64. Though bear in mind the flaws it has, are mainly due to age.Games of its era had the same flaws due to the transition from games being mainly 2D based to 3D. People still learning the extra dimension, can't expect it to be perfect.  The sequels are most likely on their way provided krome studios can get the funding. So support them for their hard work <3

TL:DR will be at the bottom
One of the greatest games i have ever played, AND it's free. I've had hours of fun playing through this game, and it's best played through with a full squad of friends. The amount of weapons in game is very large, including a flamethrower, dual SMGs, a tesla gun that only targets enemies, shotguns, and many others.
This is on top of the passive or active equipment you get to bring with you, from armour, to flares, to shock armour that kills parasites and stuns enemies, and even hellstorm missiles. Some of these weapons are class specific, such as the vindicator shotgun being only available to the officer class, or the prototype assault rifle only being available to the technician, and the minigun only being available to the weapon specialist.
The unique weapons and skills useable by these different classes means that you will need to balance your team properly for the mission ahead; if you're clearing infestation use a flamethrower; if you need to hold out somewhere bring sentry guns and mines. There are surprises everywhere in this game, and parts of the map that can be used to your advantage, such as doors you can weld shut, weapons closets the technician can hack, and hidden items that can give you an edge over the enemy.
The enemies you face in this game include the normal swarm aliens, who aren't much smarter than "charge the marines and hit them", spitter aliens, which spew acidic balls at you, large three legged sacks that lumber toward you and then explode, shield bugs that have 4-5 large armoured leg plates in the front and a bulbous weak spot in the back, so you need to co-operate with your team to distract it while another person shoots it's weak spot. enemies like the parasite can bring a grinding halt to your progression while you need to stay in the healing bubble of a health kit, but enemies like the artillery bug can shoot timed bombs that do massive damage at you, making you need to keep moving. combinations of these enemies, such as a mix of spitter bugs and shield bugs. the shield bugs can hold your team off while the spitter bugs spew acid at your team, doing damage while the shield tanks for them. or things like a mix of parasites and artillery bugs; the parasite makes you stand where you are to heal and live, while the artillery bug will force you to leave the bubble and die, or get hit by it's projectiles and die anyway.
Whenever I and my team died in this game, we realized it was our fault; every time we died there was a part that we messed up, e.g. seperating in a nest, getting cornered by a shield, or forgetting to weld the door at our back shut.
TL:DR, get this game and play through the campaign with 3 other friends.

When I first played this game years ago on the xbox, what struck me then and still does now is the fact that the game had friendly AI who were actually competant and capable of dealing some real damage to the enemy. They're not just background pieces made to look good while you go Rambo on the enemy.
The gameplay is still solid now, with few glitches, if any. Your teammates can be directed in battle to perform various actions and use specialized weapons against the enemy. The game doesn't give you freedom to choose where to set up these weapons anywhere you please.  Instead, it places those locations strategically, which isn't surprising with how old the game is and how revolutionary the AI design was for a singleplayer campaign at the time. There's good level design and coupling that with hard difficulty will make players cautious as they advance towards their objective. You can have your AI partners arm bombs, hack doors, and other various tasks, or you can do it yourself and have the AI protect you (which they actually do, though you still need to be alert of enemies that slip by). If you royally screw up (maybe you threw a grenade and it bounced back into your face, or you took an anti tank round to the chest) and get shot down, it's not game over. Instead, you have a chance of getting revived and back into the fight.
Sound assets are still good. Subtitles are recommended if you want to know what everyone's saying since blaster fire and explosions can drown out certain pieces of dialogue. The soundtrack consists of a mix of star wars music and the same music mixed with a bit of a choral-like singing which adds to the dark atmosphere of the game. Your partners will sometimes say funny quotes, some scripted, some not, depending on who you have doing what (quoting Sev, "Sir, you sure you don't want somebody who can shoot straight?") Overall sound is good.
The graphics of the game hasn't aged well over the years but the game's still running smooth on my system (Windows 7). I still haven't seen many graphical glitches in the game. Not much more to day.
Overall if the game still works on your PC, it's worth taking a look at Star Wars Republic Commando.

If you like squad based games ...AND a darker take on Star Wars then this is the game for you. You play as one of four elite storm troopers that are specially tasked with covert missions during the timespan of the clone wars leading up to Star Wars Episode III: Revenge of the Sith. While it is a dated game, with clunky combat and incredibly incompetent AI, the story is intriguing and the characters are memorable. Each Commando has his own personality, and while that may seem out of the ordinary for clones, they were specially grown to develop their own personalities. This does not account for each Commando's different voice, however; for every clone should sound like Jango Fett like in Episode II. I understand why the developers made this change because they wanted to give greater depth to each Commando. This did add to the overall game in a positive manner, because hearing the same voice over and over again from each Commando would get rather irksome. I mentioned at the beginning that this game is one of the "darker," in the series of Star Wars games out there. What I mean by this is that you play as a very vulnerable and mortal soldier during the clone wars, unlike many games where you play as an all powerful jedi or sith, in Republic Commando you have to play strategically in order to survive each mission in the game. There aren't many missions in the campaign, but each mission spans the length of a couple hours. I find the balance between the clones and their enemies in this game slightly ridiculous (it takes about 2-3 grenades to destroy a Super Battle Droid,) but then again, it is a game that really shows how close you can come to death as a clone, and gives you the feeling of playing smart and strategically...which I really enjoy. While you have little command of your squad's general movement throughout each campaign, when there is something that needs blowing up you can prompt any clone to set a bomb. You can also prompt clones to find cover in certain situations, and each clone in your squad has a specialty. Think of your squad as a TF2 lineup and you cover all the bases (one heavy weapon clone, demo clone, support, etc.) I have not cleared the entire campaign, but what I have played I have found challenging on normal mode. pick it up when it goes on sale and have fun playing one of those hidden gem Star Wars games.

The Purring Quest is a much cuter game than it is an enjoyable one to play. It seems worth getting that much out in the open right from the onset, as whether or not developer Valhalla Cat’s feline focused platformer is worth any sort of consideration, depends on how much its premise can carry it for you. If you exist at the center of a Venn diagram consisting of cat related paraphernalia, armchair philosophy, and graffiti calling for substance legalization, The Purring Quest is able to provide at least some amusement for a very distinct audience. For those less immediately taken in by celebrity cat cameos and catnip jokes, The Purring Quest quickly becomes more chore than delight.
For every adorable cat on screen, The Purring Quest’s presents a dozen screens painfully plain and flat. This is as much a frustration due to how it contributes to The Purring Quest’s uneven appearance, but even more so as it is often impossible to read a level for platforms and hazards, resulting in many cases where the player must leap blindly and rely on trial and error to navigate to the end. As a strict platformer with zero objectives to contend with beyond running, jumping, and picking up fishbones, it’s hard to excuse The Purring Quest for screwing up such an integral portion of its design. Poor jumping controls and clipping issues further exaggerate The Purring Quest’s mediocre mechanics, to a degree that is the digital equivalent of kicking someone while they’re down.
This feeling of sadness more than disappointment comes across primarily on account of how clear it is that Valhalla Cat’s legitimately love their game, and despite all its faults put their all into making it at least a little charming. I can’t fully recommend The Purring Quest in any capacity, in fact I feel insincere even saying it may be worth an hour of your time, but I do wish the best for Valhalla Cat’s future projects. They have a long way to go, but I’m willing to give them the benefit of the doubt that they’ll get there someday. Until then I will have to advise you to get your cat fix elsewhere.

Imagine an 8-bit Grand Theft Auto clone and you've got Retro City Rampage pretty much thought out. If you took a GTA protagonist and had them take a Forrest Gump-style tour through 80s videogames and cinema, the result would be exactly what you get here: A lot of thievery, swearing, ultra-violence, explosions and generally just a complete mess. But hey, you get the high score. The odd thing about RCR is that it's generally more fun then any of the games that inspired it, and manages to be much more forgiving in difficulty besides. Accompanying its relentlessly entertaining and reference-laden campaign is a series of bonus levels, including rampages that test just how well you can do what a GTA player does best- tear♥♥♥♥♥♥up. There's also plenty of unlockables, including a number of extra playable characters, a huge variety of weapons and vehicles, and that chiptuny goodness you expect from one of these retraux titles. If you like virtually ANYTHING from the last, like, 35 years of nerdery, you're likely to find something in Retro City Rampage that makes you smile. I know I did.

This review of course was written without playing online, which I imagine will change this strategy quite a bit!

There's nothing particularly wrong with Armello (aside from maybe the microtransactions) so I'm going to give it a thumb up.  But be aware it's not a 4X game, nor a game in the vein of Heroes of Might And Magic.  Instead, it's more of a board game.
More specifically, it is a combat board game for 4 players (with AI opponent support).  Since the board is pretty small, you will frequently be fighting with your three opponents, encountering traps, running afoul of the "rot" demons, those pesky royal guards, and whatever their ailing boss the king throws your way.  Expect to die a lot, but fortunately this just ends your turn and returns you to the start.  The goal is to succeed the king by either killing him without being killed or having the most prestige when the old lion kicks the bucket through means other than a successful assassination.
Games of Armello last about a half-hour, roughly 20 turns, so it's a good lunch break game.  There's some between-game accumulation mechanics in that playing certain characters or doing certain things in the game will unlock trinkets you can bring with you in the next game to give you a slight edge.
One thing that annoys me about Armello is that the random number generator has been given too much power.  All tests (combat, perils, whatever) are conducted with rolls of six-sided dice where the goal is to have the dice come up on specific faces.   One of the die sides is essentially "succeed and roll again," (also known as "exploding" dice) with "success" in fights meaning a successful attack point.  Two other die sides will result in a successful attack point.  One die side is a defense point, and the remaining two sides are duds.  In short, 3 sides are an attack, 1 of those attack sides include a reroll, 1 side is for defense, and 2 sides are duds.
For example, lets say you have 10 "fight" dice and your opponent has 4. Your roll comes up 5 attack, 1 attack and reroll, 5 duds, no defense, for a total of 6 attack and 0 defense.  Your opponent rolls 2 attack, 2 attack and reroll, an additional 2 attack with his rerolls, for a total of 6 attack.  Assuming both you and your opponent have 6 hearts or less, you both just died, some good having more than twice the dice did you.  The odds of this happening aren't all that low, in fact it's not too uncommon to "explode" so many dice that there's massive overkill even with relatively few dice in play, and that kind of resolution is just too random for my liking.
That is not the only way in which luck heavily influences the game.  Getting the bonuses on completing quests is completely random, though weighted with higher odds for having certain stats.  Given that the main victory condition is successfully commiting regicide and living, combined with the highly random combat resolution I just mentioned, every time somebody has a throwdown with the king it's a gamble one of three things are going to happen: 1. they win, 2. they lose, 3. both the king and assassin die and so the winner is the player who has the highest prestige.  In most games, it seems to me that the dice gets to decide who wins.  Even Mario Party isn't this random.
Can I recommend Armello?  Well, if you like the art style, like board games, and are not too bothered by dice rolls being game changers, then this game is for you.  If you would rather play a 4X game, this is not one of those.  If you absolutely hate it when a random number generator snatches away victory, you might want to give Armello a pass.

Fantastic. Still my favorite Battlefield game. I'm not all that into the single player campaign but the multiplayer is where it's at.
The main Battlefield series has always seemed just a little too "big" for me to get into - I'm looking for a more condensed experience, and that's exactly what Bad Company 2's online mode is. All of the awesome, epic battles that occasionally take place in the larger games, condensed into an almost endless onslaught of insanity from the time the match begins to the time you're convincing yourself "just one more round".
The maps, while not always balanced perfectly, are still extremely well designed to induce a very chaotic sense of "tug of war". It's like a perfect combination of map size, available weapons, player count and class balancing - any team that makes an effort can hold their own against a team that is more skilled. There are tons of ways to turn the tide of battle at any given moment as long as you don't get too comfortable in one particular role.
Can't capture B? Well, take the fight to A or C. When the enemy is focused on protecting those, your lone wolf Recon soldier can capture B. There aren't so many players in a match that all capture points are easily squatted - the teams are constantly moving back and forth, and that's what makes it fun.
Camping isn't really a problem. Sure, it's annoying when you're constantly getting sniped by a Recon solider, but there are ways of dealing with that. The best way is to use the marking feature, an ability that lets you tag enemies you spot with your own eyes so your entire team can see their location.
Even if you're unable to kill that enemy yourself, marking them all but ensures several of your teammates will turn their sights toward the enemy and take them down. It's beautiful to watch that Recon sitting in the trees who has killed you 3 times in a row suddenly flee in panic as 5 of your teammates converge on him, all because you simply tagged him.
I don't know how much more time this game has before EA shuts it down, but until that day, it's an experience you shouldn't miss.

I have the latest patches on both games. Everything is vanilla except for the Visual IV Mod. If you don't have it, you might as well install it. It makes the game look a lot better and apparently includes a "fixed rendering code" to make playing smoother.
I run EFLC on the same settings and results were pretty much identical. Everyone is aware that GTA IV is a ♥♥♥♥ port, but I think I've managed to get a somewhat consistent framerate. It still drops to >30 for a few seconds, occasionally. This happens no matter what I do. It's still completely playable and doesn't annoy me at all, but it's something I noticed; It's still miles ahead of the console version. If anyone is able to get a constant 60+ in this game, let me know what you are doing.
R* Social club isn't a big deal. GFWL is useless and I don't like it, but it hasn't caused me any trouble so far. Over all, my experience with this game has been really good. The only thing that would make it better is if multiplayer wasn't dead, would've made a nice mod-friendly alternative to GTA: Online.
Edit:
I felt inclined to update this review after finding out a little more about the graphics settings for this game. GTA IV is not necessarily meant to be maxed out on current hardware, the intention of the developers was that the higher graphical settings would be for future use, and when GTA IV was released on PC back in 2008 there was a disclaimer of some sort that advised players to use medium settings. I'm just learning this now and I had purchased GTA IV in 2012. People are criticizing the game for being a terrible port and having framerate issues because they believe they should be able to max out a 7 year old game. Gameplay: 7.5/10
Level Editor: 9/10
Sound & Music: 6/10
Replayability: 8/10
VERDICT: 8/10
To put it short, this game has one of the best and easy to pick up level creators I have ever played with. The combat on the other hand is decent enough and actually has quite enjoyable platforming and puzzle elements.
The thing is that it won't be as interesting if you don't have an interest in the level creator nor have a friend who is an avid level creator. I really enjoy making levels for me and my friends to play together, so I indulge in that part of the game very much.
Note that the game is still updating as I write this review!
If I were to put it in bullet points, it would go something like this.
Pros:
+ Fun and simplistic 4-player dungeon crawling experience
+ A fairly good selection of classes to play with, could use some more though
+ Somewhat interesting rogue-inspired dragon main boss fight, accessible any time
+ A unique and ever-expanding community driven experience
+ Incredibly simple yet capably advanced level creator in the right hands, with lots to work with
+ Well thought-out criteria for publishing an Adventure
+ Randomized Loot System keeps finding loot interesting
+ Some decent workshop support to make your character look more out of the ordinary
Cons:
- Inability to 'Fight the Dragon' cooperatively, even though the ability to feels implied in the title screen
- Combat remains somewhat repetitive, particularly with the lack of variety in skills (updates may change this)
- Enemy AI regardless of enemy 'difficulty setting' remains predictable (an eventual update, perhaps?)
- Editor's Building Point and Difficulty systems somewhat strict, making it hard to create expansive and difficult single-adventure experiences
- Editor only allows selection of regular and 'miniboss' enemies, no real boss-type enemies, resulting in massing enemies to create a sense of difficulty or dangerous boss-rooms
- All enemies, logic nodes, and props handled on the same layer in Editor, creating some disappointing set-backs (I can't place enemies on top of destructible walls?)
- Sound effects and music are somewhat limited
- Needs a bigger community, join us!
--- The Long Review ---
To say it beforehand so that I can get it out of the way,
I love this game. I understand that it is still being developed and I hope it has a bright future ahead of it.
COMBAT AND GAMEPLAY
The combat is extremely simple with a simple attack button, use button, and skill buttons. There are also potions to use, whether healing or mana which can be found in chests placed by creators. The interesting part about the gameplay however, is that creators can incorporate platforming, traps, and verticality into their maps to build a more stylized playthrough. I appreciate a map that tries to put in a decent story, as well- seeing as the game itself at the core has pretty much no particular story in any way.
Creators can also include switch, key, pressure-plate and enemy kill puzzles into their maps, making a level more than just fighting all the time. By nitpicking through the creator, I could even create these miniature cutscenes or sequences with whatever's available right now, too.
This game has some super-simple and really effective drop-in, drop-out coop that takes no effort at all. Multiplayer really does make this game worth playing, and enemies try to scale in health and power.
CUSTOMIZATION
Character customization allows you to choose from a variety of heads, and hair- allowing you to scale and position them how you want. Using the Steam Workshop, there are a selection of things there to make your character look more unique than the choices that are given to you by default (I love my pyramid head). If the community were larger, there would be such a great selection of things to turn your character into.
LEVEL EDITOR
The level editor is among of the best I've seen, while being easy to get into with many advanced things you can learn. The game offers many different kinds of tiles ranging from many different stones to sand to snow and etc. There's also a wide variety of props to help spice up a level design. Enemies with varying difficulty that can be placed in a level are varied enough so that there's enough to make diverse kinds of levels with different monsters to face- but more would be greatly appreciated.
I won't go in depth, but where the editor gets fun is the inclusion of logic blocks, logic switches, gates, key doors and all that jazz. Utilizing the game's verticality also makes it more fun- being able to set up platforming areas or places that you need to jump or climb to reach.
ABOUT THE CONS
Even though there may be many cons in that list, I believe that many of them can be solved with future updates to the game, so long as it gets continuous support. Many people are still disappointed by the fact that you cannot cooperate to fight the dragon, though- myself included. Something needs to be done about the Fight the Dragon aspect of the game, but I don't think that's what makes the game special (even though it's the name of the game). The game however, is a little too easy overall and it'd be nice if there was more of a curve that isn't just putting a bigger handicap on.
WE WANT MORE
I would love for this game to be updated more and more so that level creators can make truly unique adventures between map-to-map- with things like tons of different enemies and dynamic environment objects like drawbridges, moving platforms, slippery blocks, catapults, water currents, rolling boulders and the like. Other things like the inclusion of friendly combat NPCs, vehicles, pets, and even tilesets would be great. I noticed a weapon label for each enemy in the creator, will we see enemies like Ghost Armour sporting a greatsword or giant flail at some point?
There were more than enough times while I was in the creator where I said things like 'I wish I could do this' and 'I wish I could do that', but there just isn't enough yet to allow it. One of the biggest problems I faced while making maps was the building point limit and the difficulty limit, needing to add more potions or reduce/shuffle enemies around when I felt it was completely unnecessary takes up a lot of my time making a map. Campaigns do remedy this in certain ways though.
Just give us more, FTD crew. I'm not expecting this to happen overnight, but we want more because we want to make even better maps for everyone to play- and I don't see anything wrong with that.
THE PROBLEM AT HAND
Much of the problem remains in the fact that this game is fairly unknown, with none of my friends knowing this game even existed until I told them about it. Considering that this is almost a purely community driven game, this game needs to be supported by many people and this is a problem that may need to be addressed before it's too late.
A WORD FOR THE FTD COMMUNITY
The last thing I can really say is that the community itself also needs to step up to the plate when it comes to making levels. There are many levels upon choosing quick-select that are simple hack and slash, very plain easy levels that aren't particularly unique in any given way. Being on a grand quest to fill out the map, I feel that using the quick-select is the best way to get that 'I'm on an adventure' feeling, otherwise I'd use the Gallery a lot more. I don't believe that this is something the developers can fix, but it would be preferrable to find some more of the great blood-sweat-and-tears adventures out there.
FINAL THOUGHTS
I really think that this game deserves more attention to bring out its true potential, and I want to see this game have a bright future because I think it has tons of potential to be expanded on. Buy this game- buy it on sale if you have to. Support the developers and contribute to the FTD community because there is the potential for something incredible here.

I finished the game in two play sessions. Mainly because I've played the game when it was still on Gamecube.
Now that I've beaten the game, I'm just going to go over the pros and cons:
+ The music never gets old, even with the loop. That says something about the sound design.
+ The gameplay is actually solid for a collectathon title. Hell, even the swimming controls were pretty good, from a genre that generally has crappy water levels...
+ The dialogue is witty, and screams Austrilia. Also, NEVER play Ty without sound, because you might miss some of the adlibs the characters make separate of the subtitles.
~ While not a major concern, the game doesn't run all that well on low end PCs. If you are worried about performance, just reduce all graphics options to their absolute minimum, then lower the resolution. Lowering the resolution only shrinks the screen, not the resolution itself.
- The controls can feel floaty at times, and it may take some time getting used to.
- If you end up missing anything in a level, it is a pain to find out what exactly you missed. Fortunately, every level except the first can be completed in one go, so don't feel as if you need to backtrack later in the game.
- I didn't test the game with Keyboard and mouse, but the game wasn't designed with this in mind. If you want the best possible experince, you have to play with a controller.
Now, let's get the rest of the series on Steam, and I'll be sure to creamate those games when they come out! (In other words, I'm going to 100% them)

Some tips to play this in co-op without having to deal with setting up a server and trying to figure out how to play the Half Life campaign in co-op.
Download and install:
- Its free and lets you get a "Local Lan" going that is super easy.
Friend with the best internet connection should be host.
Invite your friends, create an active party and have friends join it. They will all get a IP address that will be close to yours.
Now start Sven Co-Op.
Play Sven Co-op
Start New Game
If you want to do the train ride: hl_c00
Map: hl_c01_a1 (right after train ride, door will open after a few seconds)
Click "Game" tab and select "Lan Game"
Name Server
Set Max Players
Set Difficulty
Set Server location (no idea what this actually does)
Start Game
Any friend that wants to connect to your game they go into "Join Game" click on the "Lan" tab and hit refresh. The friend that is hosting the game will now show the game listed.
Each new map has to load. write down the map name by holding tab and looking in the top left corner if you are done playing so you can select that map when you want to continue.
Playing this game with survival is pretty fun as you can heal and rez each other with the health tool on number 1. Sometimes though it becomes a pain cause of stupid "old school" game tecnology.
To disable survival mode: Host will open command window with ~ key.
as_command survival_enabled 0
This will disable the survival mode for the current map only.

The story is lame and shoddily conveyed, and the ending is lackluster, but the open-world exploration and base building are pretty fun. For a while. The world is interesting enough to wander around in, the combat is fairly good - and so are the aesthetics. The game can be a bit buggy, and is prone to the occasional glitch though.
The biggest gripe I have with this game is that it has a lack of variety - which is a shame. There are actual quests (main quests and side quests), but you mostly end up doing a lot of recurrent randomly generated side activities over and over again.
-This survivor is angry, kill some zombies with him.
-We need this thing for our base, get it.
-This survivor is in trouble, help them.
-This house is infested, kill the zombies in it.
Again and again. Sometimes you're lucky and some actual quests come trucking along, but mostly you'll be exploring and doing shallow activities. The game loses a lot of longevity because of it, sadly. And you don't get that much from the activities either - but you have to do them from time to time, otherwise things get pretty bad. And the survivors will annoy you on the radio. And die.
Still, it's a pretty fun game, and a decent SP zombie survival game to mess around with for a good chunk of time. I got my money's worth at least.
I do recommend it. To the right people. Just don't expect the holy grail of open-world zombie games.

Epic Snails is a multiplayer shooter based on the perspective of a snail. Epic Snails has been created by Rocketsnail.
It is set in a garden theme where you have 2 teams that shoot eachother with guns attached to their shells. You will earn coins to buy hats to wear in and out of battle.
Now, for this review I am going to split this into six parts, they will be:
In this review we are gonna start straight off the bat with gameplay. In this game the gameplay is amazing, I love the way it is set up and how I am coming back for more. The way they make it oddly satisfying to use the homing missiles from a distance is what I love. They have 3 guns to choose from to fit your desire, to add on to this you can buy hats to wear during battle and in the lobby - which I'll come to soon.
In between matches you hang out in the well designed lobby; I really don't know how they do it but the map is so well designed the lobby takes hours to have enough of. There is so much to see and find if you look closely. You can try bug finding and you'd be suprised how hard it is to let it go stale.
Now a big part of a multiplayer or singleplayer game these days is the community - a potentially un-welcoming community can completely change the way new comers see the game. The majority of the players in this game are not rude or anything and they talk with you and start a game, this is from my experience but they will nearly always be happy to play a game!
At this time personalisation is what Epic Snails lacks. They used to have 3 guns, multiple hats and 4 tombstones. As of a recent update they changed this, removing the tombstone feature and adding 2 more hats in the shop. In this game customised snails would be a great idea due to how simple your snail is and how easy it is to copy it.
In Epic Snails the options contain all you need. Sensetivity controls, 3 sounds controls, screen resolution and fullscreen on/off, 6 quality settings + a custom and a recently added setting, the option to change the control keys. Epic Snails has what you need for a game that can deliver this much enjoyment.
Now this is where the staff team comes in. From my experience the staff team are amazing people. They will fix found bugs in the next patch OR - as shown before - if it's a bad glitch they pump out an emergency fix. The owner Rocketsnail is a great guy, he listens to the community and what they want. The staff team arrange events with timing and all after all this, I don't really think there is much more that I can ask for.
I think Epic Snails is an amazing game, I have listed all there is from this. This game kis an amazing product from all of the developers experience. It is almost perfectly put together, when the game works it is fantastic. Overall I can't get enough of it! I'm usually always online - my username is "fishypeter" - unless it is school hours or late at night (in gmt). The youtube community is growing bigger, from YouTube and Discord I can see many people waiting for the game to be released. Epic Snails is amongst the best games I have ever played, so much fun comes in a neat little package; I can't wait to see it in it's true glory. I don't think I can give it a proper rating while it is in closed beta but until Open Beta - here is my rating.

This review of course was written without playing online, which I imagine will change this strategy quite a bit!

There's nothing particularly wrong with Armello (aside from maybe the microtransactions) so I'm going to give it a thumb up.  But be aware it's not a 4X game, nor a game in the vein of Heroes of Might And Magic.  Instead, it's more of a board game.
More specifically, it is a combat board game for 4 players (with AI opponent support).  Since the board is pretty small, you will frequently be fighting with your three opponents, encountering traps, running afoul of the "rot" demons, those pesky royal guards, and whatever their ailing boss the king throws your way.  Expect to die a lot, but fortunately this just ends your turn and returns you to the start.  The goal is to succeed the king by either killing him without being killed or having the most prestige when the old lion kicks the bucket through means other than a successful assassination.
Games of Armello last about a half-hour, roughly 20 turns, so it's a good lunch break game.  There's some between-game accumulation mechanics in that playing certain characters or doing certain things in the game will unlock trinkets you can bring with you in the next game to give you a slight edge.
One thing that annoys me about Armello is that the random number generator has been given too much power.  All tests (combat, perils, whatever) are conducted with rolls of six-sided dice where the goal is to have the dice come up on specific faces.   One of the die sides is essentially "succeed and roll again," (also known as "exploding" dice) with "success" in fights meaning a successful attack point.  Two other die sides will result in a successful attack point.  One die side is a defense point, and the remaining two sides are duds.  In short, 3 sides are an attack, 1 of those attack sides include a reroll, 1 side is for defense, and 2 sides are duds.
For example, lets say you have 10 "fight" dice and your opponent has 4. Your roll comes up 5 attack, 1 attack and reroll, 5 duds, no defense, for a total of 6 attack and 0 defense.  Your opponent rolls 2 attack, 2 attack and reroll, an additional 2 attack with his rerolls, for a total of 6 attack.  Assuming both you and your opponent have 6 hearts or less, you both just died, some good having more than twice the dice did you.  The odds of this happening aren't all that low, in fact it's not too uncommon to "explode" so many dice that there's massive overkill even with relatively few dice in play, and that kind of resolution is just too random for my liking.
That is not the only way in which luck heavily influences the game.  Getting the bonuses on completing quests is completely random, though weighted with higher odds for having certain stats.  Given that the main victory condition is successfully commiting regicide and living, combined with the highly random combat resolution I just mentioned, every time somebody has a throwdown with the king it's a gamble one of three things are going to happen: 1. they win, 2. they lose, 3. both the king and assassin die and so the winner is the player who has the highest prestige.  In most games, it seems to me that the dice gets to decide who wins.  Even Mario Party isn't this random.
Can I recommend Armello?  Well, if you like the art style, like board games, and are not too bothered by dice rolls being game changers, then this game is for you.  If you would rather play a 4X game, this is not one of those.  If you absolutely hate it when a random number generator snatches away victory, you might want to give Armello a pass.

Fight The Dragon is a simple hack and slash with light rpg elements and user created content that can be fun in short bursts for the right audience.
-while simple, the graphics are quite colorful and charmingly cartoonish
-frantic and simple combat is easy for everyone pick up
-most adventures take 10 to 20 minutes to finish, meaning you can just fire this up and play one even if you're short on time
-a good amount of different equipment options, all appearing on your character model when equipped
-a ton of user created maps and campaigns to play
-a nice and easy to learn adventure editor allows you to create your own contentand share it with other players
-lots of user created character customization options in the Workshop
-very fun in coop, also has a splitscreen mode
-its simplicity eventually makes the game repetitive and hurt its longevity
-fighting the dragon is actually pretty dull, you just go against it over and over (using scrolls given to you whenever you finish an adventure) slowly plinking its lifebar before it kills you
-user created adventures vary wildly quality-wise: some are pretty unbalanced, a few might be broken and a good amount of them has bad english
-the classes have not enough differences between themselves save a few exclusive abilities and equipment
-enemy AI is pretty bad, I often saw them getting stuck on the environment or running in circles
-enemy balance is a bit over the place, some have way too many HPs and/or damage-making kiting the only option-others summon way too many extra monsters
-multiplayer is pretty dead, so you'll have to rely on friends for coop
Overall Fight The Dragon isn't a bad game at all, it's just a bit bland overall and perhaps too simple for its own good: the fact only one player in ten has ever reached level 10 with one character is pretty telling when considering the long term longevity of the game.
Still, if you're looking for something simple to play every now and then and that won't take too much of your time this game is surely a good purchase at its usual sale price (3 to 5 dollars): it's basically a snack when compared to fully fledged hack and slash games but it works well enough. If you're looking for a good story, deep character progression and engaging combat you can safely skip this one instead.

I bought this game during the Steam Summer Sale, figuring if I didn't like it I didn't spend too much money on it.
I fired it up and played a little while, figuring out the combat and loot system, as well as trying out the random and player-made adventures.  The next thing I know, 6 hours had passed and I still wanted to play more!
THIS GAME IS FREAKING AWESOME!
Fight the Dragon is an action hack-n-slash RPG, but one like no other you've ever played.  Sure, you get stat upgrades, tons of loot, and you fight strange mystical creatures.  FtD, however, has something I've yet to see in any other game - player made adventures!  Thousands of them, too, for hours upon endless hours of replayability!  Add to that the four unique character classes, and you're getting far more than your money's worth from this title.
My personal rating?  The graphics have a cute charm to them, and while the controls can be a bit slow or clunky at times, they're very manageable.  The gameplay and replayabiolity is where this title truly shines, however.  I can see myself sinking 100's of hours into this one, and maybe even creating a few adventures of my own!

Let's get a couple of things out of the way...
1 - This game uses UPlay. For some this won't matter. For most it will. This game is notoriously difficult to get working. Please see my post in the forums for how I got it to work.
2 - For those pulling their hair out trying to get this game to work, stick with it, it's so worth it.
Now for the review...
The first thing that wil grab you about this game is its art style. Wow does it look great! Ubisoft know what they are doing when it comes to 2D art (Rayman Origins, Rayman Legends) and this game is no exception. The carefully crafted hand drawn asthetic perfectly captures the gritty horrors of war and the beauty that can be found in times of strife.
The second thing that will grab you are the characters. The wonderful 2D art really brings them to life and you quickly bocome invested in each character as their paths cross in a wonderfully serendipitous storyline. Each character has his/her own distinct personallity and you really grow attached to them as the story progresses. This is especially noteworthy considering there isn't any real voice over work here. The characters speak in gibberish and it is truly suprising how much emotion they can display using this limited form of communication.
As for the game mechanics they are varied and expertly crafted. The puzzles are all fairly straightforward and most border on the easy side. I don't really see this as a detriment to the game thought. It keeps the pace brisk and you are never frustrated by getting stuck on this or that puzzle. The way the characters interact with each other, relying on each ones specific skill set to takle the puzzles, is terrific.
The music is equally stunning. Using classical peices to evoke a time and place. It's really quite beautiful and extremely effective.
So as a final verdict I can't sing this games praises enough. For those willing to endure the headache that is UPlay you will be pleasantly rewarded for your effort with a stellar gaming experience. A true gem of a game that really deserves more attention than it has gotten from the mainstream gaming media.

is just as a game as an artistic form that express what almost every man can relate to. A friend that we care, but with life being so overcomplicated, we just lose track. Life changes, and sometimes feelings remain, it's what we do with them that matters.
Based on 2002 and forward to 2006, the years where instant messages were popular, modems were smooth, and Windows XP was the best operative system ever. If you met the internet in this timeline, this game has even deeper value to you, and I'm sure you'll easily relate to.
The player talks with Emily during each year, and every year something important happens. Whatever the actions of the player were, the events mark the future options, as Emily remembers certain important decisions and dislikes.
Emily portraits something that doesn't really have a name, it's a Jane Doe of feelings, a ghost that haunts every man who ever went online and met a nice girl whom things didn't work out. Some relationships are meant to never return, but they never really die. You keep thinking what if things were different, if your actions were others, what would've happen? This game portrays that feeling like a naked canvas waiting to be painted by the owner of your own feelings, it's just that sometimes you're not the one holding the brush.
is also an experience on how impact can have based on the player's memories! Emily is a girl that has feelings towards the player, but her personality and habits change throughout the years, leaving the player with a mixed feelings, and being far from each others can easily relate to long distance relationships.
An interesting concept, well executed, but lacking more conversations throughout each year, and maybe more interactions? The mechanics work almost as a visual novel, but the player can still browse the contacts and read their descriptions. It's definitely interesting and amusing to see what was relevant throughout the years.
The player can also select avatar's, and for the first year, Emily will comment on them, which is a nice detail considering on how many there are.
A fantastic free and unique small preview of what we sometimes left behind, friendship, or that special someone that moves along.
7/10

This game is an RPG take on a board game. Each character has a skill that is unigue to them
A once lovable and fair ruling king gets consumed with rot and goes mad.

There are multiple ways to win the game:
You can have the most prestige, which is obtained by defeating fellow players in battles, completing quests, or just stealing it with cards you draw as you play. You also lose one prestige every time you die.
You can win by challenging the mad king to a battle if you manage to survive the battle and kill the Mad King, ultimately you become the king slayer ( Sound famaliar Game of Thrones fans?) and the victor of the game. You can win by obtaining 4 Spirit Stones, which are obtained in various ways, and use the stones to banish the king without needing him to battle.
This game also features card you draw each turn. the cards vary some are battle perk, some are personal perks, some are traps are spells to either place on the board or u//se on other players. The only draw back so far is the game can be kind of lengthy depending on the setting but you can change them to your liking. There are paid dlc and character skins but they dont give you an advantage just different playable characters or board and dice skins.
I recommend picking this up you wont regret it. 9/10

Just got through my first game of Armello (against the AI, should that even matter), and I have to say I'm fairly impressed. Originally, I had decided to close my wallet to this game when I'd heard the Bandits would be locked exclusively to backers and were more powerful than the base 8 characters, giving everyone who hadn't backed at the Bandit tier a blatant handicap. However, with the Bandits available to purchase for $10 (my first intended DLC purchase, with the Usurpers coming after that), I figured now would be a good time to dive in.
So, having only finished the tutorial and knowing the different ways to win, actually being released into the realm left me unsure of just what I should do first. Which clan do I like? Which character is the most interesting? How do I want to win? How will I do what I plan to achieve? I enjoy the backstabbery rogue-like appearance of the Rat clan, so I chose to side with them first, with Zosha as my character. My opponents were Amber, River, and Sana, to which I didn't pay much attention or care. I didn't know whether to go for Prestige or Rot, but the game ended up answering that for me, thus beginning my lengthy journey to win the King's ear and his throne upon his (un)natural demise.
Things did start fairly poorly, with River having 3 Prestige before I had even finished my second quest, at which point I had considered switching tactics, but I stuck with it. I focused on quests, buffing myself to - at least what I think to be - a fairly decent 8 Fight and 7 Body, at which point I allowed my daggers (and the occasional bit of magic, if I drew the right spell) to earn their keep. My equipment helped as well, ensuring I entered every combat encounter with the odds, even if slightly, in my favor.
I bullied River a bit, as she had the King's ear up to this point, but my first actual hero kill went to Sana, who I had burned to a crisp as she only had 1 health. I then waited in the shadows, picking off targets as they limped away from nearly lost fights, and my Prestige continued to grow. In a short time, the King came to me for his royal decrees, and it stayed that way. My daggers and magic made sure of it. 6 Prestige, then 7, then 8. Up, and up, and up it went, killing heroes, saving settlements, and fighting the Rot. However, by now Amber had started to get a little brave, perhaps from the Rot flowing through her, and started attacking the palace with alarming regularity despite losing her life to either a guard or the King himself. With each passing day, the King grew weaker and weaker, and my victory drew closer. When all was said and done, I sat comfortably upon 12 Prestige, far out of anyone's reach, but the assaults on the castle continued.
At long last came the night of the second to last day. Just one more sunrise, and victory would be mine! But the walls continued to be assaulted. Amber from the South, River to the West, and Sana to the North. Sana was dealt with quite easily by the guards I had ordered to be summoned, but that left two more targets to worry about. Amber easily broke through the walls within the daylight hour, killing a guard and regaining her strength to a full 7 hearts. She HAD to die. I followed suit as night fell upon the land, setting a perfect ambush but angering the King as I set foot into his domain. I slaughtered that precious little rabbit without so much as a scratch, sending her back to her home for the third time. Sana, once again, fell to the guards before managing to lift a single finger. However, I had forgotten about River. Somehow, she had slipped within the castle's walls with no trouble at all as I chased Amber about. She then stood there, right before the King, and let loose a single arrow, piercing his fragile heart. All my work, the Prestige I had earned, undone in an instant. Perhaps, had I betrayed the King and plunged my dagger into his back, the Rats would have ruled the land. For now, the Wolves shall enjoy their victory, though I do not intend to make the same mistake twice.
Simply put, I'm enjoying this quite a bit.

The Purring Quest is an indie platformer where you assume the role of Kimchi, a cat who is on a mission to return something lost to their owner. The graphics are cartoon-y, but both background and animated felines alike are done very well. The cats are adorable! The shining light of the game is the introduction of several famous "cats" - the dialogue is befitting of their "humanistic" personalities and written well.
While the animation is smooth, the platformer mechanics are simple, but clumsy. You have the opportunity to have two jump styles, which I thought interesting. The game is not long at all, so the clunky mechanics did not detract from how I enjoyed the game. You'll find yourself having missed a platform (or dying) for really no reason at all - but all levels have multiple save points. . . so like I said, game is short enough and the difficulty easy enough to let it slide.
I'd really like to see more from this developer - so if you enjoy "cat pop culture" and want an easy, funny, and short platformer - give it a try!

Controls are just awful. Sometimes the cat run even if I'm not touching any buttons (it happens after jumping). The animations are very simple, the double jump doesn't work too well. It could be a lovely game for one evening, but the controls are too frustrating.

Super cute game, though several of the fishbones are nigh-invisible against the background and I had trouble with some of the jumps. Also a little hard to tell what areas are active places to stand, particularly in Level 5. Not too difficult to get all the achievements with a bit of patience, though!

First things first, The Purring Quest is a very short game. It took me 2 hours, of casual play, to complete the game and all achievements. The last 30 minutes were probably spent on replays looking for a single fishbone I had missed. If you only play longer games, you can stop reading, as you'll be frustrated with the lack of content.
That said, the game is cute, and imaginative, putting you into the role as a cat, The game at it's core is a platformer, with a total of 5 levels. At the end of each level you get a "boss" fight, where the gameplay shifts drastically. It causes a little confusion while you figure out what you need to do, but the game is forgiving in that you get plenty of lives, and should you run out, you can choose to "continue" and you refill all your lives.
I still don't have a good sense of the target audience. The puzzles themselves are single and straightforward, so a child could play confortably, but there are also time bassed sessions and quirky controls that are better suited to an adult.
The game offers keyboard or full controller support, but I found I had to keep switching back and forth. For general play, the controller was a lot easier, but when I reached a music "boss" fight, where you notes scroll from the top of the screen and you hit the appropriate button at the right time, I found the controller was almost impossible to manage due to the way the screen presents the info. Switching to keys, I aced the fight in my first try.
I do recommend the game, and had a lot of fun playing it, but if you pick it up, just be aware that you'll get a max of two hours and find yourself wanting a little more.

This game is worth playing if you enjoy any sort of fantasy hack&slash. Gauntlet* and Hammerwatch are the comparisons that come to mind. WIth community driven content and online multiplayer, the re-playability of this game is very high. It's not without it's bugs or faults, but the developers are also active on the forums and within the community; They are quick to address concerns the playerbase has with the game, replying frequently to questions posed by the community. The Workshop content is also a nice touch, allowing much more customization of your character than offered by the vanilla game; Levels, though, are found in game and not on the Workshop.
The editor is simple and uncomplicated (as much as an editor can be), but don't expect to be able to do too much with it. There are some nice adventures out there, but this isn't
. It does what it says on the box, and hopefully the devs add more to it as time goes by (and I believe they are?).
Play this game with a controller as playing with the keyboard requires a bit of hand contortion, or quick relfexes and finger accuracy, to access all the controls.
*: I've played classic Gauntlet and Gauntlet Legends, but not the newest remake on Steam. From what I understand, though, it is still an apt comparison.
While I assuredly like and recommend this game it definitely needs that something more to make me
it.
I also wish the editor was a bit more robust. You can't move props you've already placed, instead you have to delete and remake them. Variables and flags would also be a godsend, especially if values could carry over between maps in a campaign (Imagine if later maps could be changed depending on choices earlier in the campaign!). It could also use a bit more variety: pressure plates that don't have large skulls on them and are easier to hide, a variety of switches (perhaps even hidden ones, like wall sconces or torches), pressure plate triggers that aren't barrels... Things that allow the community to
dig their nails into and get creative with. Right now it all feels a little cookie cutter.

I liked this game, and keep wondering why there isn't a sequel out given *spoilers* *spoilers* *more spoilers*. I'm hardly a fan of the Star Wars prequels, but the characters and plot are interesting and solid. I especially love the first half of chapter 2, with its "haunted house" feel. I can even get over the fact that Scorch is voiced by Raphael Sbarge (that guy who will forever be Carth Onasi to me and who only has one acting style), given that all the squad's personalities are both clearly defined and show development across the plot-arc. For instance, I love how Fixer is incredibly straitlaced but sometimes the facade cracks, just a little.
I also don't play a whole lot of shooters, but I really enjoyed the feeling of being in charge of a squad that reacts to me without a whole lot of complicated keyboard commands to memorize. In fact, there's only one button to direct every terrain-contextualized action, and that's okay with me! A little odd that the boys will get infinite ammo of whatever type they're using while they're in a terrain position, but hey, Scorch lobbing unlimited grenades is also okay with me. The graphics are also fine for how old it is, and I like the little details like the visor windshield wiper for rain/blood/oil/scratches(!?). It was a little frustrating at times when running low on ammo or health and with no way to get more before having to survive difficult waves of enemies, but that's almost certainly because I'm not very good at shooters. :P
Overall, I really got the feeling that I was part of a team while playing this game, and it was really awesome.

Fallout Tactics changed the focus from a role-playing game (rpg) to squad-based strategy game. With this shift in basic gameplay most rpg aspects from the two first Fallout instalments have been removed, e.g. sequence of missions is fixed and linear, no cities, limited exploration and character dialogues.
One of the greatest changes is the introduction of the squad-based combat system, which gives you complete control of each member of your party (up to 6 members). With each story-related mission, you can pick up additional team members with different talents, allowing you to customize your team to suit your preferred tactical approach.
In addition you have the possibility of the continuous turn-based (ctb) combat mode, which for the most part should be called real-time mode. From a strategic viewpoint the game lives up to its title, in providing a captivating tactical gameplay with several ways to successfully complete each mission.
The fan community has released one mod called Redux (hosted on No Mutants Allowed), that fixes most problems of the game. It can be downloaded on the link below (thanks to Cory?killer).

In Armello, the current Lion King is Infected with Rot and is dying. It is up to you to save the day by killing the current king and taking his place, waiting for him to die and taking his place or save him by purifying him of his Rot. Choose a hero from one of the 5 races and pit your random skills against 3 other players.
The gameplay is fairly straightforward with each player taking 3 actions on their turn. There are 3 different cards to draw from, Items, Spells and Trickery. There are 2 other types called Treasures and Followers. Each card requires a different type of resource to play. Items and Trickery require Gold while Spells require Magic. Item cards also require 1 of your 3 inventory slots. Some cards may even require a special type of resource called Rot. Confusing?
Conclusion, it isn't as fun as it is advertised due to the pseudo random number generator. You might as well have decided who wins by rolling dice at the start of the game. The skin shop is another money grubbing scheme that irked me. You have a buy to play game so it's not free to play. Why are so selling more DLC? However, the artwork and animation is pretty decent and I think that this is its saving grace.
Note: Armello is done by League of Geeks cofounded by Trent, Blake and Ty.
1. Guaranteed End
Maximum of 18 turns due to the King having 9 health.
2. Beautiful Visuals
The art of Armello is wonderful. The different artist names are revealed for certain cards. Yet, the style is somewhat consistent.
3. The 5 Races
Pretty interesting. You have Bears, Wolves, Rats, Rabbits or Bandit. It's a pity that there has been no new release of any race after the Bandits.
1. Zooming Out to Clouds
Why do I zoom out to clouds? I want to zoom out to a strategic view so I know where all the other heroes are at a glance.
2. Pseudo Random Number Generator (RNG)
I am not here to play a game based on feelings. I don't want to play Armello the game that makes you feel this way and that way. It sucks. I want to have planning, not dice rolls deciding the victor.
3. Small Map
It's small at 4 hex rings. You just don't get the feel that it's an epic quest. Rather, it feels more like a claustrophobic cluster ♥♥♥♥. It doesn't help that there is no reliable method to reach the opponent on the opposite side of the grid. Since the castle is in the way, it takes far longer to go around.
4. Dice Design
There are 6 faces on the Armello dice.
a. Miss
b. Explode (Score and roll again)
c. Defence
d. Attack
e. Sun (Only counts as hits during the day)
f. Moon (Only counts as hits during the night)
By default, you are meant to fail 33% of the time. If you want a specific face like defence, you only get it 16% of the time. This wasted dice is akin to doing nothing in the game. There is no strategic play just an empty dice that you might as well have not rolled. The variance is very large. You could roll all misses compared to all infinite explosions.
5. Random Everything
Combat - RANDOM
Dungeon Explore - RANDOM
Perils - RANDOM
Followers - RANDOM
Quests - RANDOM
Card Draw - RANDOM
Political Decisions - RANDOM
Stranger Follower - RANDOM
What choice do you have?
6. Dungeon Explore
You wonder what you explore the dungeon for? The rewards can only possibly be +4 Gold, +2 Magic, random teleportation to another dungeon, summon a Bane or get a follower.
7. DLC, DLC, DLC and Skin Shops
What the ♥♥♥♥? This is not a free to play game. Why are you charging for skins?

This would be a great game for someone new to action RPGs--maybe a budding game designer in middle school or high school who hasn't played this sort of game before. It's got a whole construction set for building maps, isn't complex, has a bunch of social features, etcetera. They'd eat it up.
But I have a hard time recommending this to someone who's played many games before, as it's been done better many times.

The game model functions very well - controls, stats, loot, combat (for the most part), and co-op.  The premise of the game is to adventure in community-created campaigns, finding keys, unraveling small plots, looting better items, and making your way to fighting the dragon by collecting Dragon Scrolls.  It's almost like Shadowrun Returns, but without the developer-created campaign.  There are some REALLY good adventures to go on by the community.
However, it's like finding needles in a haystack - the majority of GREAT community-created scenarios are far and few between.  Many fall short between amateur DMs and wannabe writers akin to middle school English class.  75% of the adventures you will partake in often have glaring issues like loot balancing, confusing or short level design, awful dialogue and spelling mistakes and more.  It seems like anyone can create a dungeon with 5 rooms, 50 potions, tons of easy enemies and enough loot to make the game not much fun.
This game is AMAZING for DM's and really shines in the way of quick pick-up and random co-op play.  It falls short in the way that the majority of the content is shallow or just bad.  If you dig hard enough, you'll find gold though.

I don't get why people trash this game so much, I personally enjoyed my time playing it and it has plentiful of content as took me over 30 hours to do everything and get all of the achievements in the game.
Some people have been saying that the game has huge running and crashing problems, personally the game only crashed twice during my 30 hour playthrough (and even those crashes were due to the fact the game had been running for more than 5 hours nonstop). Also when it comes to FPS I kept it open too see how high or low it can get in VERY HIGH graphics settings. The game stayed solid at around 60-80 fps depending on the location and only dropped to high 50s during some storm sequences or when using the drone. Don't let the console reviews fool you when talking about this game, even though this is a CONSOLE PORT it's actually much MUCH BETTER on PC.
The game, while CI games tried to make it into a AAA title really slightly misses the mark and at times you can see the lower budget going on with it. However if you can get past this you can easily have fun while playing the game.
Pros of the game:
- Large open world  with enough change in between the 3 areas of it
- Gunplay is... really good IMO, especially the sniping (duh)
- Variety in weapons (you have almost 40 different weapons too choose from
- Crafting system for ammo and gadgets is helpful and really good.
- Variety in locations and missions
- Multiple options on how to do missions, will you recon the area and find a good sniping spot, or will you run into the
middle of the shooting all rambo style.
- If you care about achievements the ones in this game are not too hard or too easy (you will most likely need to grind
for a few of them in order to get them done as you will most likely either not use or even think of doing certain things
while just playing the game.
Cons of the game:
- Story is Meh and very gliche
- some texture work, especially on the enemies could have been better, then againn you will be shooting those fools
regardless so who cares?
- if you get spotted then good luck fighting your way through the enemies as their aim is spot on and getting completely
mowed down happens easily.
- Mission lenghts (this being a pro or a con depends on what type of a player you are): the thing with some of the
missions is that if you know what you need to do OR at times you happen to start them from a direction the devs did
not think of you can finish some of the missions in less than 5 minutes when its supposed to take 20.
ALL IN ALL:
If you are already interested in the game I would suggest atleast trying this one out, if you can choose the platform you use ALWAYS pick the PC version as its superior to the console versions. I also recommend getting the game from a sale. In general getting the Season Pass edition for under 30 bucks is a good price IMO and the base game for 20 or less. The game highly feels like a budget Far Cry and you need to keep that in mind whilst playing.
HOWERER if you are not certain about this game but you want to get a good open world game, get far cry 3 or 4 as those two games are superior to this one and cost around the same amount if not less. If you want a similar setting, get Far Cry 4. If you want a good Sniper experience and you are willing to throw in more cash get Sniper Elite 4.

Now, allow me to provide a little backstory. I got this game back when I was roughly 9? 10 years old? Back then, it was around the time the PS2 era had hit a spike in popularity, so naturally, I got this game as a Christmas gift, and I fell in love with it. Maybe it's because furry animals are a guilty pleasure of mine, but that's a story for a different day.
Naturally, when I saw this game was on sale on Steam, nostalgia got the better of me, and I bought it in a heartbeat. Playing it as an adult, as one would expect, is certainly different from how it was when I was a kid, and that's putting it lightly. This is both a good and a bad thing, and I'll go ahead and break it down so I don't waste more of your time with unimportant backstory.
It's... About what you would expect from a platformer on a PS2 at the time. You jump around, collect stuff, complete objectives to move on to the next level, kill enemies, and has some side missions on the side. It doesn't necesarrily deviate from the 3D platformers at the time like Spyro, Crash Bandicoot and other games,  so if you're looking for something revolutionary, this definitely isn't it.
I would say that in terms of gameplay, this game is pretty close to Banjo Kazooie, in the sense that most of the game revolves around collecting stuff to get more stuff.
This isn't to say that it's BAD, or COMPLETELY unoriginal. One thing that does set this game apart is a few things, such as replacing double jumping with gliding, using Boomerangs as weapons rather than fire or, well, your fists, and the fact that there are very few levels with "unique" mechanics that change the gameplay a bit.
There are times, however, where the objective is not clearly communicated. For example, in one level, you are supposed to use coconuts to get across some quicksand. This is not properly explained or hinted it unless you decided to just randomly throw some boomerangs around. The game stops nearly all hand holding about halfway through, so if you don't understand how to do something, you're on your own in that regard.
I give the gameplay a solid 6/10. It's nothing really special or out of the ordinary, but it's by no means boring. The game has just enough for you to do and kill so you won't be left wandering aimlessly and figuring out what to do.
The story is cheesy, that's all there is to say about it. It's a pretty by the book "you're the chosen hero that has to save the world" scenario that's typical of games around this era.
The story also relies on a lot of ex-machina scenarios (An antagonist showing up when you least expect it, falling into a hole at the very beginning and finding out the entire backstory completely out of the blue, and so on), so at times, it does feel like things happen out of the blue without any reason.
Really, there isn't much to say about the story. It's fairly predictable despite things happening seemingly out of no where, character development is near enough nonexistent, and... That's it.
For a PS2 game, the graphics aren't bad. They aren't GREAT, but they aren't abysmal, either. Much like its gameplay, it's what you would expect from a PS2 era platformer: low renders and flat angles.
At times, the game does feel a little empty, but that's only in the first couple of levels. Nothing is really boring to look at, and aesthetically, the game is pretty pleasing. You have rainforests, snow areas and ocean areas, and each level has pretty good lighting and scenery that gives it the feel it's going for.
The game is definitely much better as a child than as a fully grown adult. While it does have enough to keep someone interested in terms of gameplay, and it doesn't really get stale, it suffers from playing things a little too safe. Nothing about it is extraordinary or revolutionary in any way, which isn't necesarrily a bad thing, but it makes the game ultimately forgettable.
I recommend this game for younger audiences, since I am sure that younger folks will find a lot more enjoyment out of it than older. If you are an older person looking for a good PS2 platformer, I can't really say that this is what you're looking for. If you want to try it out, by all means, go for it-- it's not a bad game by any means. There are just other PS2 games that do what this game does but better.
