I both love and hate this game!

I love the way it begins so simply and accelerates to to both complexity and madness. I love the mathematics and the ratios. Factorio gameplay seems familar to me. As an engineer, I have managed many factories. So designing and constructing he perfect factory only to get side tracked or discovering a better way rings true to life.
I hate that this game never ends. There is alway one or two or eight or twenty things to improve or protect. I've watched smarter player then I, often set an objective at the begining of each episode. And wonderful players like Colonel Will who never stop until the fps falls so low it becomes unbearable. Then there is always an option to add one more train and upgrade the computer to..... ahh this is Factorio!
Factorio has become such a great game because of three groups of people; enthusiastic players, responsive devs and dedicated modders.
I have seen some players lose enthusiasm for the game only to have it reignited by the next release. So many enthusiastic players. Negative Root set out to break the game, Arumba, xterminator and so many others pushing Factorio to the limit with new types of gameplay. JGGames shear pleasure in building and tearing down structures. KoS a joy to hear even when she is chatting with Ellenor. And Nilaus so open hearted building elegant designs. So many players finding new ways to play Factorio.
I am sure the devs never envisaged how many possibilities could develop from such a simple concept. The devs relentlessly develop the game and incorporate new play styles where possible. The devs have also created some of the most interesting builds.
The modding comunity? I tip my hat in respect of the range of mods, from convenient to new games to madness. As to the latter I thank Angel and Bob for the many times I walked away from my computer frustrated and confused. Only to return with more determination to move forward.
What next? I am still having fun with V0.16. Perhaps next with Angle and Bob's megafactory.
I dislike killing the biters for no other reason then they are annoying. After all we are the invaders. I miss collecting allien goo for research. Perhaps the allien goo could be reintroduced for military science. Or for planet specific science; electric barriers, pollution miigation, deep mining, tree and biter farming, ....
Finally, there are two things missing from a real factory building experiance, equiptment reliabilty and maintenance. I am unsue that this would add to the gameplay. Certainly reliabilty and rate of deteriation could be added to production/engineering science but would this be fun? In the later game robots would do all the repairs and replacements so this would just bring an overhead cost making larger factories more expensive to build and adding complexity to outposts. It would also make belt only builds very difficult.
I still have many more hours of fun exploring Factorio V0.16 and watching others play the game with more or less frustration.
My thanks to all the dedicated Factorio players, devs and modders for hundreds of hours of fun and frustration.

Okay. This game got a lot of hype leading up to its release, and I think it was rightfully so. The gameplay is fluent, the graphics are crisp, the shooting mechanics are fantastic and the weapon customisation is fun... but it could do with some work. The entire game is not without its flaws though, and I'll do my best to list a few here for you to consider. Number one is the story line. A lot of the missions can be fun, but the majority of them are a little bit on the tedious side, which again makes me a bit sad because the game has a lot of potential for greatness. The ending to the game was one of the weakest, most cringe worthy and pathetic endings of any video game I have ever played! I can sum the story line up quickly by saying that I am glad I didn't spend huge amounts of money buying the game - or I would be even more disappointed than I already am. A re-write of the final mission would be a great gesture from the Dev's!! One massive thing that annoyed me is that the game stooped to the level of including big boobed bimbos as pretty much the only friendly AI that you interact with. The girls are boring, uninteresting, overly sexed up and a total waste of time. Which is a shame because you see them all the time in the game. Another is the driving mechanic - it's bad! The sound of the engine has a noticeable looping spot that totally ruins the immersion and trying to drive anything with a mouse and keyboard will see you spiralling off of a cliff very quickly! The shooting mechanic is this games main redeeming feature! If you can see past its obvious flaws, and you enjoy taking the long shots with some amazing weapons - then this game is still going to be a "must have" in my opinion. Nailing the perfect headshot is extremely satisfying and will keep you wanting more.
Overall I would give this game a solid 6/10 - with the story line being the games biggest flaw.

Cons: Dev admits they screwed up, but still hasn't learned enough of a lesson to fix simple bugs after 3 months. Repetitive. Slow, both in pacing and physical player speed. I don't feel invested in the story because I have absolutely no clue what's going on or why. Save system that isn't a save system due to respawning enemies and fast travel checkpoints in an open world setup, meaning if you have to leave the house in the middle of a mission, you best leave your game running or else expect to start said mission from scratch upon return. Can't comment on the multiplayer or the drama around that, as I don't do MP, but what I've read elsewhere is pretty stupid. Also it's another game with an open world collect-a-thon of random stuff to gain resources and in game money to craft and buy weapons and gear.
Pros: Pretty (like, *really* pretty; I'm on mostly high, a few medium, and one or two very high/ultra settings on a mid/upper-mid tier rig and it STILL looks *gorgeous* and runs at 60 fps). Best sniping mechanics in a FPS I've seen to date. Even on Normal (lowest) difficulty there's a good challenge due to player health and damage ratios (although this also lends to not being able to go into 'assault mode' if you want to, you're basically *forced* to be stealth 100% of the time, which makes the AR weapons kinda pointless and the one LMG completely pointless). Good selection of rifles to choose from, with a half decent selection of customization options.
Jury's out: The UI. Personally doesn't bother me too much, but I can see how some might have issues.

Alright, this game is AWESOME.  Star Wars Republic Commando is an FPS based on the lives of Delta Squad, 4 elite clone commandos who are sent on the most dangerous and imperative missions the republic has to offer.  Each one has his own distinct personality and all 4 of them (you play as squad leader) are pretty likable characters.  Here are the commandos in order:
38 "three-eight" aka "Boss" or "Sir"- the squad leader and the player character. He is fully voiced by Temuera Morrison, the voice actor for Boba and Jango Fett in the films.  38 (said literally "three-eight")  is a no nonsense commander with a head for strategy and a dry sense of humor.  He leads the squad (obviously) and is able to issue orders to the other 3 commandos, for example, he can tell them to set up sniper positions, anti armor, mount turrets, use healing stations, etc.  (btw these are actual game mechanics, issueing orders to your squad is a huge part of the game).  He has all the weapons that the other 3 commandos are capable of wielding but unlike the others he is capable of using special, enemy weapons that can be found off certain foes.
40 "four-oh" aka "Fixer"- Fixer is the tech specialist of the squad and specialises in hacking and computer interfaces, he is very useful for hacking terminals.  While all the commandos have the same skills and abilities, some are better than others at certain things.  For example, Fixer can hack faster than the others, Scorch is more accurate with grenades and can set explosives faster and Sev is a deadeye with a sniper rifle.  Fixer takes his job verrry seriously and doesn't talk about much other than the mission or how to accomplish it, but he does have moments where he loosens up.  Fixer is exceptional at melee combat and dispatches melee using foes with ease.
62 "six-two" aka "Scorch"-  Scorch is the squad demolitionist and explosive expert and his outlook on life relfects that.  He loves danger and has a very positive, optimistic viewpoint on any sitution, using humor to deal with even the most harrowing of missions.  He is the squad funny guy and his upbeat personality is definitely helpful when things look grim.  Scorch's preferred weapon of choice is the anti-armor grenade launcher and grenades themselves.
07 "oh-seven" aka "Sev"-  Sev is the designated marksman and stealth fighter of the squad and revels in war and battle.  He is a deadly sniper and the best shot in the squad (other than the player).  He is probably the most mandalorian out of the squad and by that I mean he lives for war.  62 finds his fervor for killing to be a bit creepy at times but he is a good soldier and a good friend... and a truly terrible enemy.  Sev's weapon of choice is the sniper rifle, which he uses with pinpoint accuracy.
The game's combat is pretty good and the squad AI is amazing even for today, the commandos feel very human and real.  The game even has multiplayer which I'm not sure if there is anyone on it anymore but it was good in its own way as well.
The story is pretty good and involving and gets pretty hectic at times which keeps things interesting.
All in all this is one of the best star wars games out there and I highly reccomend it for any star wars fan.  I know I spent most of this review talking about the characters, but I did so because they are  the game's strongest attribute.

The initial difficulty is partly about learning effective tactics and combat, and partly understanding a couple things that aren't explained:
- The 100g shrines are way better than the 15g shrines, so save up for the 100g upgrades first.
- Monsters continually spawn at a distance from you, so don't rush through unless you're just running for the exit.
- The rock monsters are indestructible, just avoid them.
Things I wish were different:
- The difficulty drops off sharply after level 5 if you farm gold and pick up all the upgrades.
- If you don't exit at level 10, playing levels 11-18 feels kind of pointless. It's fun to be an unbeatable killing machine, but doing it for 8 levels is a bit much.
- The final boss cutscene isn't skippable.

A unique, pleasant cat-themed game with an emphasis on platform jumping and collecting. Enemies such as rats and birds can be dispatched by your claws but more serious enemies such as dogs and old ladies need to be nimbly dodged or sneaked past. Those mutts can be avoided byhiding in a box, Metal Gear Solid style :)
Animation is absolutely top-notch, it's no wonder the animator has experience with Disney and other major studios. Music is pleasant and relaxing, mostly piano and classical type tracks. "Boss" encounters incude an interesting take on the whack-a-mole game, a battle with a giant raven and a perilious climb to the top of a chapel while dodging pigeon ... projectiles.
Famous internet cats make cameo appearances and the entire game is full of references cat-lovers will enjoy. The humor may be lost to those unfamiliar with these characters though. Play time is short (about 3 hours if you don't collect everything) and there are no bonus modes or quests aside from collecting everything and freeing all of the cats, which then become permanent residents of your main menu screen. It's a nice touch!
A portion of the proceeds go to various animal welfare organisations. I strongly encourage you to check out the developer's official website for lot's of interesting cat stuff.

It's a pretty basic platform game – jump, attack some enemies, avoid falling things, collect items for bonuses. You can also hide behind specific objects from enemies like dogs, but it's not really necessary and you can also just jump over them and run. Later in the game you get a hiding box (like in Metal Gear Solid), which allows you to hide anywhere, anytime you want.
It controls like...well, almost like in Lion King (1994). You need to get used to it.
As for the difficulty, the game was much more punishing than it is now, but the sudden difficulty spikes are still there. Practically all levels are basically a walk in the park (maybe except that mole boss fight), but just before the final level it gets much more challenging (with extremely frustrating piano mini-game and spotlight chase). Speaking of that mini-game, it appears out of blue in the end of 4th level and it may seriously hurt your experience or even put you off the game. It's very similar to Guitar Hero and it's pretty fast. It could work, but not in the way it was implemented and definitely not with the controller.
If you play the game with controller, you simply wouldn't be available to get past that mini-game at all. Imagine pressing buttons on Xbox360 / XBone controller pretty fast just seeing colours of controller buttons on screen, not even letters. Playing it with keyboard is definitely less frustrating, because you can put your fingers on it like on a piano, but it's frustrating nonetheless. In the end I managed to beat it (and even getting an achievement for doing only one mistake) by tricking my brain. It's hard to explain, but it was about dividing the screen into two areas inside mind and expecting hands to follow.
At least you can switch between controller and keyboard on the fly.
Also, if you play it on TV, be prepared that the dialogue font is quite small and overall the game was designed to be played in front of a monitor.
As for the options, there is a standard Unity launcher where you can change resolution and graphics quality. You can only change volume of sounds and music inside the game itself.
Music is really great, relaxing and good to listen outside the game. Sounds are just as good and fitting, cat sounds specifically are very charming. I also like how the cat you play (Kimchi) makes “meow” sounds from time to time.
Story is about cat returning a medallion to the man which looks after him (I won't say “owner”, uh-huh). The intro is sad and can be heartbreaking, but the “cutscenes” (both intro and ending) are made in form of a slideshow and don't feature any kind of animation. The pictures change very fast, it looks quite rough and can be distracting.
On your way through the game you will also meet characters based on real life cats (such as Nora and Oscar).
The game is short and can be completed in 1-2 hours (standard walkthrough) or 2.5-3 hours (completing / collecting everything). Which is great for me.
Made by passionate cat lovers, it's a must-have game if you like cats. Despite the mentioned mini-game and the game itself still being rough around the edges.

Every once in a while a game comes out of nowhere that is so complete and works so well that it makes all the other games in the genre look idiotic.  Tons of guns, working vehicles, AI companions, rpg elements,  silencers, explosives, resource management, castle defense, complete integrated campaign, and most importantly it is a game that runs properly.
Pros
-Very good map design. Feels like a real place.
-The graphics are excellent, medium quality textures but very well done textures and the day/night cycle is smooth.
-AI is good. Your companions do a good job at following you without getting in your way
-Zombies are awesome, the devs really know how to get your heart racing when you are inside surrounded by zombies.
-Actual sensible zombie population system, if you clear out all the houses and setup outposts the whole town will be safe
-Works with reshade completely even gives full depth buffer acess to apply your own ambient occlusion.
Cons
-Console porty. Blurry. 8X FXAA anti-aliasing is on by default. Need to create user.cfg to disable it manually. However it looks like a crisp 1920x1080 pc game after the fix however.
-Reloading system in SOD is the worst i've ever seen. A game like this should have rapid
-Lily or whatever her name is wont shut up. She keeps telling me to do things every 30 seconds.
-I dont notice any visual differences from minimum to ultra graphic settings
-runs at 60fps easily but somehow manages to not feel 60fps smooth (tried nvidia vsync too)
But thank the heavens you can make advanced tweaks on your own. Simply make a user.cfg file and put it in the same directory as the game executable and you can fill it with all sorts of commands. The only command i use are
r_UseEdgeAA=0 (Disables games atrocious anti-aliasing blurriness completely. 100x better)
r_HDRGrainAmount = 0.0 (Not sure if this does anything)
r_DrawNearFoV = 75 (Increase fov)
r_HDRBloomMul = 0.0 (disables atrocious hdr bloom that makes white wood objects glow like a medallion in the sun)
r_PostMSAA = 0 (Not sure if this does anything, disables anti-aliasing)

Atmospheric:
The aliens in the vents make their noises,
and the motion scanner bleeps kep you on the edge of your seat,
and make you fall off when you wander into an ambush.
Hard:
This game requires tactical eye and teamwork
between you and your squadmates.
You must play smart and look after each other,
because that is one less gun in the game,
and your chances of survival become very slim at best.
Fair:
If you get eaten it means 'you dun goofed up'.
Tie game doesn't resort to cheating.
The alien AI is quite smart and they can
easily outsmart you if you aren't paying attention.
Fun?:
Alone:
It can be fun, if you are skilled enough
and are used to RTS games. But it can be
frustratingly hard solo.
With 1-3 friends:
Two-player game is quite fun, but this game shines
with a full squad of human players as you struggle
on towards your objective, counting on each other,
and hoping you can pull it off without any hirches,
and that everyone survives.
Of course, this is where friendly fire comes into play.
'Friendly fire is not'. You WILL take damage from squadmates.
In the beginning you are more likely to die from
a squadmate trying to shoot an alien trough you
than the actual alien.
In this game players need
good communication and discipline to make it trough
while still being ready to take action at any time.
This doesn't mean this game is meant for twitch players.
I'd say it is quite the opposite.
You can survive by playing the game as a twitch action shooter,
but you can negate need for reflexes with some
tactical awareness and being in the right place at the right time
and anticipating the enemy.
The only negative things I can say about this game is
that there aren't many enemy types and the
main campaign included is a little short.
I really do wish they added more official maps to this game.
Overall?
This game is hard. But incredibly rewarding. And free.
Definitely worth adding to your Steam library and giving it a spin.

=EARLY ACCESS REVIEW=
*Klunky but fun*
In a nutshell, "Pain the Town Red" is a first person Voxel chaos brawler that plays like a cross between the Royal Rumble and Mortal Kombat.
There are no alliances.  Enemies will only chase you so far before they decide they'd rather beat the snot out of the nearest person.  This includes the bosses, who may find themselves mobbed by the mobs.
Most things can be picked up and swung, jabbed or thrown at your enemies.  You're given a few moments to get a feel for the map and then regardless if you start the fight or not, eventually everyone will go crazy.  Certain bosses will not be hostile until enough of the normal thugs are dead (and you can use this to your advantage) but they will eventually come for you.
Game play wise, it's deceptively difficult.  While the enemies are as stupid as the day is long and you are far, far more agile with many more abilities, you can't take many hits -- the player seems only as sturdy as a normal enemy.  If a weapon kills an enemy in short order, you can bet it will do the same to you -- so awareness of your surroundings is paramount.  Balancing this is how free you are to do whatever you'd like, exploiting the map for all it's worth.
It will be interesting to see this develop -- hopefully the lag issues and bugs will be patched up and it could be a very interesting multiplayer brawler.

Rewritten after spending 75 hours in the game, finished the main campaign, done all the side missions, story missions, finished the hitman (most wanted) list, collected all the collectables, found all the point of interests on the map, finished the DLC - The Escape Of Lydia and still busy with the DLC - The Sabotage (but close to finishing that as well). - 06/09/2017
ACT 1 has a lot of bugs, glitches and other weird stuff which forces you to RESTART your game. ACT 2 has them too, but a little less dominating. And certain elements in ACT 3 can give you an error which crashes your game entirely. But all of that doesn't happen again at the same spot, so they are not gamebreakers and everything is forgiven because how awesome and beautiful this game is.
The DLC - The Escape Of Lydia was a waste of money, I paid 4,99 for it and while the fun was rising, it was already done. Way too short. I know it was a bonus DLC if you pre-ordered the game but yeah, I bought it yesterday together with the DLC - The Sabotage for 9,99.
The DLC - The Sabotage is AWESOME!!!! They said the DLC's difficulty settings were a bit notched up, oh yeah, they were not lying! I died a few hundred times and loved it, a challenge! Gonna play this game again in a special challenging mode and combine it with a drinking game, for every death I take a shot. Finally a game that is worthy for it!
PLUS POINTS:
1. Challenging against AI which is alert and point precise
2. Tough terrain to reach certain locations
3. Collectables
4. Most Wanted Hitlist
5. Side Missions / Points of Interest
6. Rich Story between two brothers, enough documentation for deeper contrast
7. Big Maps
8. Interesting usage of Drone, Tracking, limited ammo (scout sense)
9. A map filled with not only enemies, but also animals and civilians doing their thing
10. No health regeneration, minimum health packages
11. Upgradable perksystem for Sniper, Ghost and Warrior
12. Driving to your locations, with fast travel points
13. Weapons/Drone upgrades; silencer, camo paintjob, ammo clips, scopes, hacking, nightvision
14. In highest setting game looks awesome, in lowest setting, the game STILL looks awesome!
----
MINUS POINTS:
1. Long loading time when you start up the game (understandable per open map)
2. I fell through the world
3. Getting stuck when jumping on assets or climbing up a tower (only in ACT 1)
4. When you get stuck, you need to restart the entire game
5. Out of range, all enemies teleport back to orginated location (so basically you can cheat your way in when the mission is too hard for you)
6. Not many enemies at certain locations (for example the rocket base)
7. Certain locations not always reachable, like they forgot to place one extra climbspot
8. Constant repeating "don't shoot, I am unarmed, I am no threat, I don't have a weapon" from civilians that you want to play this game in the upmost stealthy way so they finally SHUT UP!!!
9. The robot voice (don't want to be a spoiler here, but OMG! And I thought the civilians jabberjabber was horrible)
10. Voices from enemies sound sometimes SO LOUD while they are like still miles away, it's confusing sometimes "are they right behind me or...?"
----
If this game is any similar to Far Cry 3 then I would say The Witcher 3 - Wild Hunt comes much closer to it. Because once you liberated an area, the civilians are taking it over. Not in Ghost Warrior 3; You conquer it, you earn XP from it, you come back to it and the enemy is back. Has also the tracking with a special "sense".
----
SUGGESTIONS:
Make more DLC's and upgrade the game:
- We need more big maps, more point of interests (those question marked hot spots), more puzzly situations! Absolutely adorable!
- I understand for the story driven part, options are running out. But you can expand it a lot with more exploration maps.
- Add a Find-And-Shoot-The-Bottle for achievements (like at every base location you can find 3 bottles, if you shoot them all, a bonus mission gets unlocked or a question mark location.
- Add more Most-Wanted hitlist personages (or combine it with the bottles, for every bottle you find and shoot, you unlock another hitlist personage - just suggestions)
- Add like, sniper mercenaries in the game who are hired to take you out, if your health is low, you die instant, but if not, you have a chance to redeem yourself or you have a chance to spot him before he spots you.
----
OVERALL THOUGHT:
This game needs more optimalisation and less bugs for sure, especially when there comes a seperate multiplayer part in the future (like Modern Warfare 2). The game is awesome, adds a lot of extra details like with the drone, examining tracks and having those classes (sniper, ghost and warrior) for perks.
If they are making this multiplayer counterpart, I REALLY hope they put a pixelsizer in the settings menu so EVERYBODY can run this game without performance loss. (if you don't know what I mean, check the settings in the DOOM game)

The biggest change comes in the speed of combat; there are modes in this game now that makes combat freaking mad fast. Rather than controlling one unit, you can now control Squad members which significantly increase combat depth. In return all “choice” in the rpg aspect of this game is gone, npc dialog interaction doesn’t exist. I find this game to be closer to the Commandos series than Fallout, which is not necessarily a bad thing but if you’re playing this out of love of the first two Fallouts, stop now. Gameplay wise, this game is superior by far. Story and immersion wise, this game is nowhere near the level of Fallout 1 and 2.

Great spin-off, although it has fewer role-playing elements than previous two titles from the Fallout franchise. Fallout Tactics is more of a strategy game that puts the emphasis on realism in the fights. The elements of the combat system present in both Fallout and Fallout 2 such as the line of sight and cover have been improved. Skills like sneak or traps now have a meaning. Vehicles have more implementations now, you can hide behind them for protection, shoot at them to initialise the explosion or ram your enemies while driving. Characters in Fallout Tactics can also fight while crouching or crawling. Aggressive and defensive stances allow you to prepare effective ambushes. Combat can be played out in turns or in real-time. It's a really polished game, one of the best out there compared to other games that require tactical thinking.

Star Wars: Republic Commando is a tactical first-person shooter set in the Star Wars universe, developed by LucasArts and published by Activision and LucasArts in 2005. The game uses the Epic Games Unreal Engine.
In Star Wars: Republic Commando you play as an elite Clone Commando accompanied by three other squad members through three main missions with submissions included. In the game you investigate hostile areas and search for enemy Intel. You are Delta RC-1138 (Boss, orange suit), the leader of Delta 38 who meet up with Delta RC-1262 (Scorch, yellow suit), Delta RC-1140 (Fixer, green suit) and Delta RC-1207 (Sev, red suit). These elite Clone commandos are created at the clone factories on Kamino. As a squad leader you can order your squad members to attack, defend a position or blow up blockades and each squad member has its own abilities. During your military operations you will find yourself at Geonosis (Rocky desert planet) where droids are manufactured, at the Republic Assault Ship (RAS) and at Kashyyyk (Wookie Forest/Swamps Planet).
I highly enjoyed this game because tactical functions and of the HUD (Head Up Display) interface which is built inside the Helmet of your character. Also the weapon designs are well done, for instance the DC-17m Commando Rifle Model which is an adaptable rifle of the Galactic Republic. You can change parts of the gun while in battle and switch a modular sniper- or anti-armor grenade launcher attachment when you progress into the storyline. I also liked the hidden blade (Knuckle Plate Vibro Blade) which comes in handy when you are out of ammunition or just for dealing massive damage in close-combat. The voice acting is great and the interaction between squad members makes the game feel lively.
I highly recommend this game to people who like the Star Wars Universe or tactical first-person Sci-Fi shooters with great gameplay, certainly when the game is on sale!

I've had Armello on my wishlist since it released back in 2015. I was hoping to one day pick it up on a 50% off sale but finally just pulled the trigger during the 2017 summer sale (40%). Anyway Armello is good fun, especially if you can find a group of three friends to run with. I play with a full group and we are able to share the two major DLC packs (Usurper and Bandit) with only one of us having purchased them. I thought this was a nice feature, especially since the base game and associated DLC are a bit pricey for my admittedly very cheap tastes.
The game is much deeper then it originally appears and can be pretty addicting. We played for several hours in the days after purchasing the game. There are many avenues to victory, lots of strategy, and plenty of different characters to fit how you want to play. You can really mess with each other during the game which is really nice. Currently we are playing this game with people that live in three different time zones, so it's nice to feel like we are still sitting around a table and interacting a bit. If you feel like making things interesting you do have the ability to tweak the rules via "house rules", which changes everything about the game but prevents progression or achievement gain. I'll briefly say that the achievements in this game are actually pretty sweet. They make make me want to put in some time to not only get them but also just get better at the game itself. There are some nice RPG/progression elements in the game, and we have had plenty of "wtf how did that happen" moments too.
Now for the downsides. It has a bit of a learning curve. I wouldn't say that this is a "casual" board game, though it could be certainly played as such. It feels more like a competitive game to me. I think they could actually get away with putting in some sort of ladder. Anyway it's not a quick game either. I think our games run 45 minutes to an hour each, depending on how much people are thinking and what the turn timer is set to. The camera is pretty bad. You're playing on a map and want to zoom out and get a good look at everything but when you do the clouds get in the way and everything is blurry. There is no way to rotate the camera that I have found.
Bottom line the game is worth a buy and gets better the more you play and experiment. The unlockables, developer support, and progression will keep you playing for quite some time.

A decent sniper game with a huge Far Cry vibe to it, think of it as a less polished Far Cry 4 with sniper rifles, they share similar mechanics and it's very familiar to me.
The game has a much different presentation to the 2nd game, the game isn't based on linear missions, it's an open world game where you capture outposts and drive to the missions yourself, meaning you can approach the mission however you like. It uses a similar style to Metal Gear Solid 5, there's an awful lot of freedom when it comes to it.
The graphics look great due to it being a CryEngine game, but CryEngine comes with extreme pitfalls, such as poor performance with constant FPS drops, even on a 7700k and a 1080Ti. I get high frames but they're CONSTANTLY dropping. But overall the environments look great, gun models are good and the whole game does look like a 2017 release. Although it should be noticed the voice acting/syncing is absolutely diabolical for a 4 month old game.
The story is very cliche but it has a decent twist to it that grabbed my attention. At first I didn't really care about it and just enjoyed the sniping, but it does grab your attention in a big way by about Act 2-Act 3 (There's 4 Acts in the game) The terrible voice acting doesn't help.
The gunplay is strong and impactful with a huge variety of weapons, there's over a couple dozen sniper rifles, assault rifles and handguns with varying stats, calibers and firing type. The sniping is a lot of fun with slow motion bullet effects, kind of like Sniper Elite, also has a decent amount of gore, so you definitely feel like your shots are doing a ton of damage.
The missions are well laid out, although simplistic. You drive to a place, execute a few people, maybe gather some intel and extract from the area. But the complete freedom of the missions really does add to the experience, and makes every mission unique.
Overall, I would recommend this game if you can get it for a decent price. The technical bugs aren't awful (I've had one crash in 8 hours but that's about it) You will also need an above average PC to run this game at high framerates. I cannot hit my 144hz cap on high 1080p with the highest end GPU on the market. So just be aware of the CryEngine issues.
I would give the game about a 6 or 7/10, I picked it up for £12.99 with the season pass.

This is surprisingly a very good game. I bought it without any major expectations when it was on sale but it provides an interesting approach to sniper games.
It's an open world game, where you have to go to your missions yourself. the world is filled with other stuff like collectibles so you are free to do what you want. Snipping experience is very good as well. You have to account for wind speed and direction, gravity and elevation. Every shot counts. You don't have unlimited bullets and they don't refill after every mission. You have to buy them or craft them in your hideout. I didn't have the need to craft them as I always had extra money but anyway that option is there provided. Talking about bullets and weapons, there are several types of bullet each for specific weapon and purpose. You can have anything from tagging bullets which just show the enemy to explosive bullets of multiple calibers. You can upgrade your weapons as well by installing modes on them so basically, you can play this game how you like it. To aid that there is a skill tree. It has three categories
, however, you gain separate points for each of them dependent on the action you do so it really depends on how you approach each task that is given to you. Finally, the music in the game is atmospheric and it's good especially in the main menu.
The only downside I found is the car. Textures are quite bad and driving experience is horrible. It doesn't feel like a real car at all though, it's not a major negative as you can use fast travel.

Star Wars Rebublic Commando is set in the early stages of the Clone Wars. You are a clone commander in charge of Delta Squad, the republics deadliest soldiers. You and your squad are sent behind enemy lines and must fight the droids of CIS (confederacy of independent systems) However, the droids are not the only threat you must face.
When I first dove into the game, I was expecting a squad based system which would be confusing, similar to Red Orchestra 2. The system was actually pretty simple. It did not take long to learn the mechanics. You have just a few buttons which you can use to give your squad commands. Commands such as defend this area, follow me, advance (search and destroy), cancel orders. You can also order your men to different highlighted positions like, sniper,anti armor, turrets and grenade. Might sound confusing, but it really isn't. I was surprised of the good physics in this game and the gameplay itself was fun, but only for a couple of hours. The maps and basic gameplay got a bit repetitive and I got bored after a half an hour or so each session. Still, it was fun and entertaining.
the story was not as good as I hoped. You get a short prolouge cutscene that tells you about the clone commandos. The story jumps from one place to the next. At first you are at Geonosis and suddenly you are investigating a lost republic war ship. So it is not a direct storyline throughout the game. What I did like was the chatter between your men. It was funny at many occasions and you got more feelings about your men. It also ends with a cliffhanger and since republic commando 2 was cancelled I doubt that there will be a sequel anytime soon. Though, the developers leaked information about how the story would continue, so the ending is still there.
It was a game ahead of its time, so I can't complain about anything really, except the story. Other than the story being very loose I would still recommend bying it, especially if you are a Star Wars fan. The music is top notch.

It's free, it's clever, it's unique, and it's fun. Yes, you should play Card Hunter.
Card Hunter does a truly phenomenal job of taking common trappings - turn based tactical combat, old timey D&D, deckbuilding games, Diablo-esque loot 'em ups - while both using their familiarity and also turning them on their heads. In brief: adventuring earns you equipment, each piece of which is represented by a combination of 3 cards that you use to move and act in battle. Leveling up increases your number of (and power of) equipment slots. Add that up, and you have a sneaky deckbuilding game, where each of your three units' decks are assembled with just a handful of actual selections. Combine that with an extensive cast of monsters that each have signature deck strengths, and you've got a thoroughly complex game that comes together pretty intuitively, especially since none of this would
with real-world cards.
And it bears mentioning separately: the free-to-play elements are extremely subdued. The benefit provided by real money payments notable but far from gamebreaking, and the game avoids the typical problem of desperately showering you in ads.
If there's a downside, it's that equipments tend towards side-grades rather than upgrades. While that seems like a positive at first glance, it does eventually mean that you'll be drowning in hundreds of equipment options that, while maybe not
viable, offer a dizzying array of possibilities. It's an easy game to pick up, but a difficult one to get back into if you've been away for a while.

Do you like deck-building? Do you like collecting stuff? Do you like free games? Do you like annihilating your enemy with an all-out pulverizing bludgeon? Go ahead and try this game. And there is a co-op mode and I would like to have more people to play with. :)
In card hunter you complete missions using your three characters. Each character has its own deck from which you draw cards that make you attack, block, move, heal or annoy the enemy.
The missions each consist of a group of enemies to defeat and sometimes also victory squares that need to be conquered and defended. The enemies all have unique strengths and weaknesses which forces you to adjust your strategy. Goblins can block weaker attacks and come in large groups, wyverns are immune to electricity, have high armor and can fly, monkeys draw many cards and don't care about blocking terrain, etc. You can use AoE attacks for the goblins, boil the armor of the wyverns and punish the monkeys for having so many hand cards.
Your party is even more diverse than the enemies. You can crush, slice, impale or bash your enemy. You can drain their life, make your friends invulnerable or put everybody in a frenzy. You can turn the ground into lava or acid, burn, freeze or electrocute the enemies. Or you simply shoot them with lasers.
Each character is either a dwarf, a human, or an elf and belongs to one of three classes: warrior, priest, or mage. Dwarfs are tougher, elves more mobile, humans benefit your team. Warriors have more hp and do more damage, but haver to get up close, priests can heal, protect and curse, mages can use their crazy spells from afar.
But that's not everything. You build the decks of each character on your own using items that you get through playing. This means that you can make a dwarf warrior that jumps around like yoda, always attacking from behind. You can make a vampire elf priest that is evasive and feeds on the pain of his enemies. Or you can make a human pyromaniac who draws many cards and unleashing firestorms that will even kill your own party if you don't watch out.

In a tragic love story you play the role of the ever present pet cat. One of your masters, the woman, passes away suddenly, and you are left with the man. The problem is that the man has fallen into deep depression, and starts to forget about all the good times with the woman. This is where you really come in, you see you have the ability to help him retain the memories that he is losing, but there's a problem. He sees someone, while visit the grave, that looks like his lost love and disappears leaving you alone in the graveyard.
In The Purring Quest, you will now find yourself playing the role of the cat, you will have to navigate through stage after stage, dodging dogs, birds, flower pots, water, and more. You will be tasked with collecting fish skeletons along the way. You will also meet up with at least one cat per level that will help try to guide you back to your human. There's also a cat that is trapped in each level that if you set them free you get bonus points.
Graphically this is a side scrolling game, that looks good, there are a couple of levels in which the background and the foreground get kind of confusing, and it is only when you try to make a jump to a ledge, that isn't really on the same plane as you are that you learn what is available and not to maneuver on.
I would have liked to have seen the different cats that you interact with be voiced, I would have really enjoyed that aspect of the game, and I think that it would have definitely allowed the gamer to be pulled further into the game.
Up to this point in the review, I've basically had a good things to say about the game, but now comes the time where I've got to talk about the flaws, and there are some pretty glaring ones that need to be talked about.
Let's talk first about the tutorial, I do like the fact that there is a tutorial piece to the first level that basically pops up the keys you'll need to use to perform actions in the game, the only problem is that this game allows for gamepad input, and the tutorial does not switch over, so trying to figure out how to jump high, attack, climb, hide behind an object, and other such actions is a trial and error activity, which is never a good thing.
There are no options in the game, outside of first choosing the overall language. I would have loved to be able to control the volume in the game, and it might have alleviated the controls issue if there was an option to select keyboard or gamepad.
Speaking of controls, they just don't feel right, there have been too many times in game where after playing the game over and over again, I'm still having issues remembering what to hit to perform some actions. There's also the fact that there are some precision movement pieces that will have you slamming your head on your desk because of the collision or the slightly too high perch you just can't reach.
Let's talk about bosses, there's a boss at the end of each stage, and I've learned that each fight has been different, which is fine except that these don't feel crisp. I know this is a spoiler, but I'm going to help you out, the frist boss is a crow, you can ONLY hit the crow when its not moving in the middle of the screen, if its moving you're going to take damage.
Speaking of damage, you start off the game with 7 lives, or times you can get hit. Does it not bother anyone else that this number is not 9? I mean Cats equal 9 Lives, when the hell have they ever been 7 lives? I know that's nitpicky, but it bothers the crap out of me.
In the end this is a cute game, it definitely has its moments. If you are looking for a stealth game starring cats, you are going to need to at least take a peek at this game. For me, however, there was just enough flaws in the game that I just could never truly enjoy myself, and so I've got to give this game a 5.2 out of 10.

Ailen Swarm: Reactive Drop. From my understanding its a fan remake of the game "Alien Swarm", if you liked the orignial you will LOVE this. All the original content, plus 10 times as many campagins, 5 new guns, 8 player missions, new aliens, a pvp mode for some reason, new challange modes  and colour coded drawing on maps so now you can tell who is drawing smiley faces and... "other" things. And easily the greatest feature, which killed the original by not being included, steam workshop support! The original died of a lack of new content, running the same campagin over and over and over gets dull quick BUT NO LONGER! the community can now give life to the game! The community may be a bit unforgiving to new players, but it doesn't take long to figure out what your doing and the community will show you nothing but friendliness once you figure out what to do.
The Game is a coop, top down shooter. Great with friends, but beware friendly fire, or just grab a chainsaw and run at someone (if you are friends, you dont wanna be kicked for screwing random folk over online). It is lots of fun and you can tell by the turret designs how much Aliens inspired the original creators. Its a challanging fun game, pushing teamwork, alien slaughter and coordination to their limits. The original campagin is still there for beginners and will show you the ropes, slowly building up to parasites and mortar bugs. There are 8 characters and 4 classes to pick from, each character's class is already chosen for them. The Tech marines can hack doors and objectives (they are vital to some missions, you will infact all lose if no tech marine lives in them). The Weapon specialists can carry autoguns and the new devastator, the real hard hitting guns. The medic can bring healing equipment which can be used to cure the infestation mechanics in later missions (there are enemies called parasites, they touch you then you will die unless healed), making them vital in later missions. Lastly the officers, they can carry the powerful vindicator a nice one shot, big magazined shot gun that can launch fire grenades as well. They also have access to fire mines which create walls of fire nothing can live walking through. The officers also have passive health buffs for the team and makes your team more resistant to damage. Each character has different stats, Wolfe deals more autogun damage and his bullets are more likely to pierce enemies but wildcat the other Weapons specialist deals more damage with conventional weapons and moves faster for example. Another example is the officers, Sarge buffs your team more but jaeger hits harder and deals more damage. Its all about making a balanced team comp that can deal with the different challanges.
The new campagins are great, each one as i played had something unique about it that made me say "WOW! thats AWESOME!" The clearly with out a doubt was a lot of love and effort put into each one. I have a special place in my heart for "lana's escape" the puzzle campagin, while not super hard puzzles, and being a bit light in terms of swarm, it was a great change of pace dealing with non-swarm threats for once and the missions were all creative.
The new guns are great, they range from powerful to decent, but every new gun fills a nice niche, take the devestator for example, now Weapon specialists dont HAVE to take a autogun and can opt for a fully automatic shot gun. The new rifle is decent not amazing tho but it also fills the niche of late game weapons. in the original you would prob take a flame-thrower or the starting guns and the last gun unlocked was a grenade launcher. Now a grenade launcher is fun and all but its so situational, you wouldnt take it as a primary weapon would you? But now you have a late game rife/shot gun hybrid giving player a bit more freedom and reliable non-situational late game choice. And now there is a new upgraded medi-gun to unlock that can give playes 2 times damage as well as heal so now you dont just max out healing options early on and have a new weapon which allows higher levels of skill and gameplay.
Sure the aliens arent too impressive to look at, but its a FREE GAME! And what you get is amazing fo the price, who caes about a few minor problems.

To preface this, I own the original State of Decay and all expansions on Steam and Xbox 360. I also own the State of Decay Year One Edition on Xbox One just so you know where I'm coming from and why this game isn't in my Steam library. That said, let's talk State of Decay.
This game is insanely addictive if you're a fan of zombie survival and base building type defense games. It was developed by a new studio at the time, Undead Labs, founded by Jeff Strain of Guild Wars fame and a number of other developers passionate about zombie games. That's one of two things you need to know. The other is that this was originally released as an Xbox 360 Arcade game and was limited to the 2GB download on that platform at the time. And given the job these guys did with it, I would love to see what they could do without some of the restrictions and a bit of a bigger budget.
There are 3 modes for this game that are included by way of the base game and Breakdown and Lifeline DLCs. In the original story mode you start right in the thick of things as the outbreak is happening on the Trumbull County map. It's a pretty good size and comes with a number of optional base locations. You start in the church, which is ok, but later you'll want to expand to one of the bigger locations, which will be opened up during the storyline and also come with a few prerequisites.
The characters all have voice actors, but as you might expect being a budget game they reuse some of them. As you build onto your base you'll eventually have the chance to help out other survivors in enclaves. Earn their trust and they just might join you if you want them. But you might want to be a bit picky as each member has some useful skills, some useless skills, and other personality traits and flaws. Some might be great motivators to keep your community’s spirits high, while others are complete♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and cause problems.
As for the zombies, you have your garden variety shamble, runners, and your specialty zombies.  A shamble or two alone isn’t much of a problem, but runners are fast and if you’re not careful they can grab a hold of you, allowing the others to catch up. In small numbers they’re not too dangerous, but if you get the attention of a horde, you better have explosives, plenty of ammo, or the ability to run long distances without getting winded too quickly. Otherwise, you my friend, are about to become a Manwich.
Specialty zombies come in a few flavors. I don’t want to deprive you of experiencing them first hand, so let’s just say some are big, some are mean, some are loud, but most can make sure you make a gruesome décor in whatever area you’re standing in.
As for the DLC, Breakdown is a repeating play of the Trumbull County map. You start the map at a little outpost and have to establish a base and build your community. After a while you’ll locate an RV or get a call telling you where it is. Repair that and you can move to the next map with a few choice survivors from your community to tag along. The next map is the same but the difficulty continues to ramp up with each move over to the next. Certain challenges are also available each new map that if completed will unlock one of the hero survivors for you to recruit to your community. These are characters from the original story and the Lifeline DLC. Some of which have special traits that can be very handy like calling in an artillery strike, a surveillance drone, etc.
The Lifeline DLC takes it up a notch and introduces an entirely new map and story. This DLC focuses on a military outpost as the outbreak is happening. You start with all the resources you could need, so make use of them quick because as the story goes on and the zombies encroach on other areas, you will lose specific perks. Luckily, you can recapture them by way of establishing outposts.
Lifeline also has a 3-stage hazard challenge. You start at Stage 1, then stage 2 hits, which is your warning to haul♥♥♥♥♥back to base. When Stage 3 hits, zombies will assault your base. You will want to be there when that happens; otherwise the base will be a bit of a mess. That and you will probably lose some people you might rather keep alive.
The base has a set of defenses that can be manually set back up after each attack. So make sure you do that. After a successful defense, you’ll be able to resume your activities of scavenging for goods and saving survivors. By the end of this one, you’ll have a choice to make. And that choice can have a bit off an impact.
Overall I can’t recommend this game enough if you like zombie games and base building/defense. As of writing this it’s on sale through Steam and if you’ve been on the fence, I recommend you buy it. State of Decay 2 is coming up next year, so if you haven’t tried this yet, now is a great time to do it.

TinyKeep, by Digital Tribe (pretty much a one programmer company), Kickstarted back in 2013.   It's changed a bit in theme and appearance over the development period, and though delayed in polished completion, has actually delivered a playable product.  It's a *simple* rogue dungeon crawler that relies on permadeath and a few amusing mechanics to provide entertainment.  There's not a lot off complexity, but if all you need is 5 or 10 minutes distraction then this won't require a great deal of commitment from you to have fun.

After you complete the game for the first time, which takes a few deaths to get used to it, and a run of about 30 minutes if you take the obvious steps, you'll probably feel like giving it a bad review.
But, you should really find all 3 of the endings (
) and you'll realize that you missed 90% of the game, as one of them is actually not the end ("The End
" in the credits
a hint).
You shouldn't think of this game as an RPG or hack 'n slash (even though the promotional videos may make you think that), because you'll never level up your character and obtain cool armor and sword (
), but rather as a puzzle, whose mysteries are awaiting to be revealed. If you look at it from this perspective, you'll see what this game is all about.
The only complaint I have after experiencing the (almost) entire game is having to hold TAB to display the level map, which covers the entire screen. It would have been much less frustrating if the map was constantly displayed in a corner of the screen.
In summary, this game cannot compete with other games in the same price range (I got my copy for 1€, so I got good value for the money), but is definitely different from anything I've played so far, so I would encourage you to try it.

I don’t write reviews. I also don’t play free-to-play or multiplayer games.
Yet I spent almost 75 hours and 100$ worth of pizza on this in under three weeks. What the hell’s going on?

First, to address the sharkbear in the room; yes, this is F2P in the modern sense; some content is locked behind a paywall, there's a premium currency with which to purchase cosmetics, a VIP system, and there's systems to "encourage" daily logins.
So it's not free?  Well, the price for all the paywalled content is not egregious, and if you believe game devs don't deserve any money at all, you and I are in fundamental disagreement.  The simple fact is, once you've paid for the extra adventures, they're available permanently, so that's fine by me.  The VIP system is nice enough that I've subscribed a few times, but considering the loot earned is so amazingly RNG-based, and the fact that some of the best items are easy to get hold of (bejewelled shortsword, I'm looking at you), calling the game pay-to-win would be lunacy.  As for cosmetics, well, if you've got spare cash and feel like supporting the devs, why not?  I'd sooner spend my cash on the VIP system now and again, but everyone's got their own priorities, right?
Right, so, is it good?  Well, I wouldn't have bothered writing all this if it wasn't.  It's fun as a game, with a healthy dose of goofy self-deprecation in its writing.  The mechanics of the card game/board game crossover are well thought out, and while you'll definitely lose sometimes due to the RNG, you'll also have some lucky saves and hits (which won't stick in your memory as well).
The community is generally positive, at least in cooperative PVE (I've barely touched PVP), and most people are helpful, rather than aggressive.
About the only major issue is that there really is a degree of grind to this, despite the protestations of some long-term players.  As the loot is completely RNG-based, and many adventures (or even particular levels) require quite specific approaches, it's easy to reach a point where you simply cannot beat a board because the equipment you have is either massively inappropriate, or just too weak.  The only way to get the appropriate equipment is to repeatedly re-run earlier levels (or have a go at PVP).  I'd guess this is where accusations of P2W come in, but the bonus equipment merely expedites the grinding by a small amount.  There is a certain satisfaction in honing efficiency in different levels, particularly as you gradually get equipment that suits each level piece by piece, but I've sometimes found myself wishing to program a bot to re-run levels automatically.
All in all, it's great fun, but sooner or later, you'll find that you can't progress without grinding (even with the VIP system), and at that point you may find the fun rapidly runs out, or you might enjoy experimenting, improvising and getting help from a good community to make further progress.  For me it was the latter, but I don't doubt that it's not the same for everyone.

If you had asked me before I played this game how good my knowledge of obscure internet cat memes was I'd have said it was pretty top notch. The Purring Quest has taught me otherwise. The Indie Platformer based around internet felines only had maybe one or two moggies that I recognised!
The stories introduction places you in the role of a cat chasing after its owner. From here you platform your way through five different levels to reach him and return his locket. Along the way you meet some famous cats who. I'd say they encourage you along but they really don't do anything other than recite a few lines which presumably are based on what they're famous for.
The best thing about this game is the aesthetic, it's almost cutsey and reminded me almost instantly of 102 Dalmatians on the Gameboy Colour which is a game that I played a lot as a child. Everything is hand drawn and has a consistent theme to it. The animations are also fantastic, especially the one you do to hide behind things, but they often transition awkwardly ruining the flow of them.
The platforming itself is difficult thanks to some pretty nasty controls, you lose any momentum immediately and the jumping feels too heavy especially when you use the high jump. Some levels, the final one most obviously, also have a few issues where it can be difficult to tell the background from platforms. The levels themselves however aren't very hard to get through and the majority of the games difficulty comes from collecting all the items around the level. With 200 'fish bones' throughout the level and a couple of other things hidden out of the way there's maybe 3 or 4 hours of content in all.
Each level also ends with a different style of 'boss' from a combat based enemy to a difficult Assassins Creed like climb. The last two of these, a guitar heroes type piano playing section and a speed run platforming section, were enormous difficulty spikes compared to the rest of the game and would likely cause many people to give up on it.
In all the Purring Quest ends up being an unfortunately median platformer in an oversaturated marketplace. It's core theme isn't strong enough to pull it through the occasionally dodgy platforming and the general difficulty of the game will leave a lot to be desired. Still; there's far worse out there and every purchase will send some of the profits through to animal charities so you  might want to give it a look.

In a word, charming. As another review said, playing this game is therapeutic (at least if you like cats and melancholy).
This grabbed me from the opening scene. It seems odd to have a full-out platformer and story based on being a cat. Yet there it is, and competently at that. A few things are contrived (it is a game after all) but it really felt like a cat's journey to find/help his owner, coming across the caged cats and celebrity cats really added a lot of flavor to the whole journey feel. A great story (I'd say with the same emotional impact as the entirety of How I Met Your Mother), told effectively in the short span of 2 minutes and with only a few animations. Proof that you don't need million dollar, epic sweeping cutscenes to deliver a powerful emotional punch. Unrelated thought, but the scenes in this were way better than in Starcraft 2: Legacy of the Void, in my opinion. The 'secondary' storyline isn't really related to the main story, but it also helps add some subtle meaning to the journey.
Music/Graphics: Beautiful. Everything is hand drawn, with a lot of extra details in the foreground/background like trilobites, funny graffiti, even the fish bone collectibles have flies buzzing around them. The title screen music (main theme) instantly makes me melancholic, and the other music suits each level perfectly. Ranging from calm for the quiet forests/cities, to a sort of 'suppressed urgency' for the last. Would be a good idea to have a separate soundtrack if it's not already in the files.
Controls: The weakest part. Kimchi is responsive, but sometimes overly sensitive when jumping (seems to have an initial deadzone for moving left/right, then suddenly accelerates). Also, with default controls I couldn't do a high jump while running to the right, so I had to change the control settings (which weren't a great choice to begin with). Changing the controls isn't the easiest thing in the world, it seems like *every* single option for every peripheral type is thrown into one big list, and you need to find your particular peripheral, taking some guesses. Also, the 'tutorial' messages don't seem to update buttons to match your particular setup but I could be wrong.
Gameplay: I bought this game somewhat as a 'joke', but it's a surprisingly capable platformer. There isn't a huge variety in the platforming puzzles and a few sections can be frustrating (largely due to controls), but overall it's very satisfying, helped in part bythe desire to collect every item. Finding everything will make you work a little bit, but generally isn't difficult and won't make you spend 50 hours which fits the theme (as interpreted by me) of this game being more of an experience. Each level tends to have its own flavor as far as specific platform arrangements or moves. Also, the end sequence (or boss battle) for each level is a unique experience (first boss seems weakest designwise). The levels aren't too long, any longer and they'd be a drag in my opinion. The overall game length is quite short, but it still felt right to me.
It's clearly an indie game and there are a few rough edges, but this is a great complete package with everything tying in to each other making it greater than the sum of its parts. It's apparent that a lot of care and love went into this game, from the selection screen all the way to the credits. The premise seems a little bit silly at first, but a game hasn't struck me as much as this has in a while (enough to make me write my first game review).

Really an amazing experience, don't let the cartoon facade fool you. It's a bit like dark souls meets your-favorite-isometric-camera-arpg, with a built in map maker.
The combat is what brings the game to bear similarity to dark souls (for me). You can dodge, roll, block and stun enemies with certain abilities. You then have selectable abilities that can enhance combat and really make your class shine, unlocking their true potential. It also feels relatively balanced and consistent in how it scales difficulties that gameplay never feels stagnant. Actually, gameplay feels quite rewarding. Upgrading stats or putting on new gear. You work hard for those first few rare pieces and it feels like a small accomplishment.
The map maker is where the online portion of the game thrives; all players can make and submit their own unique creations using a very intuitive and simple development interface similar to voxel based construction games. You can set traps, create false doors, use movable objects to hide switches and levers, create npc's who trigger events, create anything and make it trigger an event, set up boss monsters and create pools of phat lewt; possibilities are endless. The magic comes in the creation of adventures (these are what the maps are effectively called in Fight the Dragon) and exploring other user's creations either solo or with friends. I'm about 6 hours into the game and have spent half of my time making my own mazes and arenas. It's addicting and fun.
At under 10$ (I got this for 5$ on a steam sale), I would gladly pay full price for a title like this. If you are an arpg fan, or a dungeon maker fan of anykind..you must try to Fight the Dragon.

There are so many great classic games out there and granted this game isn't that old compared to other games that you can pick up on steam. However, I chose this game because following the BF squels 3, 4, Hardline and 1, this is still my favorite of the the battlefield games and I enjoy playing it just as much today as I did when I first played it. And this carried over to the great console download exclusive Battlefield 1943, which was made using the same engine and was much like the BC:Vietnam DLC only WWII (I'd love to to see 1943 on PC). Bad Company 2 feels like and old shoe while the other games in the franchise are like a new pair of shoes that never feel like the old pair. I've been playing a lot of BF1 because I invested $60 into it and it's fun for what it is. It may have the current-gen graphics and a few new bells and whistles, yet it's still doesn't even match the quality of BC2's gameplay.

A good title for "TinyKeep" could be "brutal without merits".
Tiny Keep is a 3th person roguelike game with a nice graphic, and a couple of cool mechanics and ideas, but still doesn't manage to succed.
As other roguelike games, like nethack, angband & Co, this one is pretty punishing: it's possible to restart from the last visited level, but you start with no extra equipment or perks, and this makes permadeth a rule "de facto".
However, unlike nethack and angband, where I get hooked despite the spartan gameplay and (often unfair) difficulty, there is just not enough (variety? fun?) here to worth my time.
Starting the game from the first level is a boring chore, grinding and collecting every single coin waiting to have enough to activate some altars, while resuming at successive levels makes the game harder, so the game turns into a kind of trade-off between unfair difficulty, and boredom. Not very enticing, right?!
I guess this could be a nice diversion, when you get bored between other (more satisfying) titles, but it's not the kind of game you work hard from start to finish.
EDIT: tried to use this game as a diversion, a game here, one there. Still a boring and frustrating.
EDIT2: this game is now 0.99 Cents. For that price, I guess it's more than a fair deal, so I'm changing my judgement

I think it went without saying from the early trailers and press that this game was going to try and play at your emotions with its grim story concerning the First World War. As a history buff, I was worried that it would fail to deliver. I must say, having played through it a few times now, that it succeeded in bringing across its story in a rather compelling way.
Graphics/art/look: Valiant Hearts works on a 2D axis (with slight variations to give a 3D illusion), but it plays perfectly into the gameplay. The art style has a deliberate comic book art style that you would think would not fit into the grim setting of trench warfare, but in fact plays into it perfectly in a dark graphic novel sense.
Gameplay: Valiant Hearts is not pushing any boundaries in a gameplay sense. Most levels consist of solving item and throwing puzzles in order to proceed in one direction. There are some other variants, such as moving to avoid artillery shells, driving around obstacles to a musical tune, or completing button sequences. The main takeaway is that the gameplay is more indicative of a point-and-click adventure game. In fact, I don’t think it has a single segment where the player uses a firearm as in a shooter game that is usually associated with a war themed game. While this is not a bad thing, it does mean that the gameplay is nothing to write home about, but it makes up for it in other areas.
Story: Well, this is the big one, and is what makes the game worth the recommendation. Without explaining too much, the story focuses around a few individuals caught up in the war and their personal struggles. What makes the story work so well (for me) is that the story is not about the war. It is about the people, and the war is this awful thing that they have to live with and occasionally engage with. The tone works a nice area between pleasant areas and small fulfilling tasks to gut-wrenching warfare and environments. Between this and the coverage of several areas of the western-front during the First World War, this game more accurately depicts the horrific monstroscitiy World War 1 than any shooter (or other game) to date has.
Ubisoft: Well, it has U-Play. This is a (understandably) total deal breaker for some people. If you need any more info on the issues with that, other reviews do this subject more justice than I can ever hope to.
I recommend this game to any gamer open to the experience. Given the price, it is absolutely worth your time to give it a shot.

At first The Purring Quest seems like it would be a game for children, but that idea is put to bed early on by the first cut scene and the difficult controls. Since nearly all the positive reviews mention control awkwardness, and some mention console controls being the solution, I went straight to console controls. That just raises another frustration: there's no controller layout diagram, or even a list of bindings. You receive control instructions the moment you first encounter the necessity to use a control, and it's for the keyboard control. You have to hunt around on the gamepad to figure out which button S and W are mapped to (they're the bumper keys, by the way). It's not the sort of intuitive thing that you'd automatically go to. To save you some frustration if you do decide to try this game, use the left bumper to jump higher, and that same key makes you hide (where available), but the right bumper makes you climb (when available), and unhides when hidden.
Boss fights are all around terrible and just shoehorned in, because side scrollers need boss fights? There's no life meter, and really no indication that you've just entered into the boss fight that feels like it doesn't belong there to begin with. Health and lives are at times interchangable, with some things taking one health away and rebounding you back, and other things taking one health away and sending you back to your last checkpoint. Regardless, when you're out of health, you just continue back at the checkpoint with full health (so why not just give all health back any time you're sent back to the checkpoint?)
The artwork is fine, but it seems like level design is artwork-based instead of playability based. Terrain is spaced out for the artwork, not for playability. The Purring Quest feels very much like a clunky collaboration of a single first time game developer and a single first time game artist, with a very amateur feel to a well drawn game. There is no story to speak of here as any sort of saving grace.
There's nothing of value to be found in The Purring Quest, especially at a $12 price tag.

Overall : 7/10
A lot of potential but far from perfect!
The core mechanics (sniping, assault rifles and sneaking) are spot on.
The game is lacking on the story mode and the multiplayer aspect is missing at the moment.
To be continued as new updates will come out during 2017 ...
Graphics : 8/10
Three big environments exist (moutain, snow and woodland). These are developed well.
The open environment really adds to the sniper-ghost-warrior gameplay.
You can choose how to play, which is very important for me.
The maps have a lot of points of interest. I recommend to explore them, sometimes you encounter interesting locations!
The good thing is that while you are exploring, more points of interest pop up. This drives you to explore the map.
Optimization : 6/10
Not really optimized, outside 60-80 fps on 1440p-low on a gtx 980 (overclocked). Inside safehouses i get 55-60 fps.
Story : 6/10
Main story line is ok. Not very much unforseen plot twists. This could have been better.
Side missions are bland, and dont differ that much from the main story line.
I was expecting a FPS-RPG experience, thats why this aspect is lacking for me.
A lot of collectibles and unique sniping rifles (only for decorating your safehouse) can be collected.
Length : 7/10
25 hours on medium, with a lot of exploring (100% completion)
I do not recommend to pay the full price for this, to achieve my 1 euro for 1 hour of gameplay goal.
Update:
I've put in around 40 hours now. All singleplayer dlc content has been completed and all achievements have been unlocked.
Still waiting for the multiplayer though ...

One of my favorite fps games with some of the best soundtrack pieces I have ever heard in a video game. You follow in the footsteps of Delta Squad, and elite group of Clone commandos who are sent on various missions in a few different points within the Clone Wars timeline. Much of the game's content is original from the films, and even those who despise Attack of the Clones might appreciate this game.
The game is decently challenging with a few spikes mainly towards the end of each major campaign. The story is somewhat short, taking an average gamer on normal to finish it in about 10-12 hours. The story follows through 3 campaigns, featuring covert operations of Geonosis during the initial invasion, an investigation of a derlect republic warship, and assisting with operations on Kashyyk towards the end of the Clone Wars.
Despite its length, the gameplay doesn't become super repetative, and the large amount of encounters in which Delta Squad is ambushed, outnumbered, or split up create a very tense and enjoyable experience.
To be honest, the game didn't age well, but if you're used to playing old games it's actually a good game.

TinyKeep is an interesting game that I honestly really wanted to like. It has a cool art style, its gameplay is quick and full of action, and the controls are snappy. When I first started playing, I honestly thought I loved the game! Then, after awhile, I beat a couple levels, and realized I was SO BORED.
TinyKeep is a "rogue-like" in that you have to make muliple runs through the dungeon/prison you are escaping, learning enemy types and traps, and honing skills that you will need to complete the game. The problem is, there isn't enough of those things for you to stay interested in playing and there aren't ANY permanent elements that carry over between plays (until you beat the game)!
Enemies/Traps
There are only something like 10 enemies in the entire game, and a few of them play identically to each other. That being said, it gets worse because only a couple of those 10 enemies are actually any threat past your first play through! After only a few hours, you will easily defeat or avoid all enemies and really the only reason you might die is if you are trying to grab some tricky loot. The traps are exactly the same: ~10 different types, a few are nearly identical, and only 1-2 actually pose a threat.
Upgrades/Items
There are NO items past the sword and shield you get in the beginning (I am NOT counting items you get after you beat the game). The main way you defend yourself is by buying abilities/buffs at shrines with gold you have collected. There are different level shrines and about 20 different buffs. The problem here is threefold: 1. the abilities/buffs do not improve the gameplay in any significant way, 2. the buffs are completey random, and 3. the buffs are not permanent through multiple play throughs. Problem number one is the biggest. A couple buffs give you special abilities, but overall, you will be playing this game exactly the same way in level 20 as you were in level 2. Most of the upgrades just beef up your character so you can take damage from enemies. Problem number 2 is very annoying, because buffs cost money and they are completely random, I have spent 300 coins to get the same one THREE times! Granted, some buffs stack, but the game should prioritize new upgrades with a higher probability when purchasing. Finally, problem 3 is actually no that big of a deal, since you can become OP by level 5 (out of 20) and never have a problem for the rest of the game.
What TinyKeep boils down to is grind. For the first few hours you will have genuine fun as you figure out the gameplay mechanics and storyline, but after that its the same experience over an over: attack monster, bait monster into trap, avoid easy trap, collect coins, buy repetitive upgrades, rinse, repeat...
