As a fan of tabletop RPG's, boardgames, and card games, I really like this game. I could explain the mechanics, artstyles, variations in playstyle to help you understand why, but I think I'll share a story.
I like to grind achievements, I think it leads to some very interesting outcomes that wouldn't happen if you weren't trying to do a certain thing in a certain way. On this one occasion I was trying to get two achievements at once, equip three treasure cards from dungeons, and have three treasure cards and three followers equiped as Amber, a character who has extra luck when exploring dungeons. I play the game, grinding the same two dungeons over and over for these treasure cards, the outcome of which you have no control over, the game just randomly gives you gold, an enemy, or cards, and fighting anyone who comes too close for ♥♥♥♥♥ and giggles. Near the end of the game, I have three followers and two treasure cards, and am in second place because while I'm doing this I'm using cards to kill people and gain "Prestige", so that I can try and scrape out a win (prestige is the point system that determines the winner if the game ends before anyone can kill the king). This has lead me to be one Prestige point behind the winner, but its the second to last turn before the game ends, and me failing to get my achievements. On my very last move of this turn I get teleported across the map to another dungeon, because that is one of the possible outcomes of exploring dungeons. The leader, comes for me, but he had to cross across a dungeon tile to get to me, and this randomly spawned an enemy which attacked him, and prevented him from getting to me, and its his last turn so he can't try to get me again. I have two last chances to grind the dungeon, and the first one produces nothing. I do for my last one, I shout "Praise GabeN", and roll the dungeon one last time. As you probably suspect I get my treasure card, but not only is it some treasure card, it's the royal banner, which gives me three presige points when I equip it, which places me in the lead. Win the game, I get my achievements, and I laugh my♥♥♥♥♥off.
And that's why I really like this game, because only in a game with such a high emphasise on luck can such absurd things happen, which lead to really memorable moments, and a really memorable game.

Take GTA and make it 8-bit and silly as hell!
Graphics:
Retro fans will drool over the 8-bit look of the game, which is nice to look at.  Lots of vibrant colors and detailed areas to enjoy.  And the cutscenes are well drawn and fit the feel of the game.  Nothing much to complain about here.
Sound:
8-bit sounds all the way!  From the sirens and gunsfire to the music, it's all 8-bit bliss.  Much of the music is also nice to listen to, but you have the option to shut it off it it's not your thing.  The game also has options for different filters and boarders to make it feel like you're playing it on an old tv back in the day, scanlines and all.  Some of the colors filters, while nice options, can hurt the eyes after a bit.
Control:
You can use keyboard/mouse or controller, but controller is HIGHLY reccomended.  Controls are a bit of an issue, as the default keybinds feel weird and rebinding them is dificult.  Once you get past that though, the game plays fine and control is responsive.
Gameplay:
This games, despite the cartoony look, retro graphics, and hilarious story, is still a GTA clone at heart.   You can mug people on the strees, collect weapons and carjack people.  There are paint shops and pickups to lose the heat, and shops to buy skins and weapons.  But you also get a few tricks that GTA doesn't, like speed boots, the ability to jump on enemies, add weapons to your cars, and even a time machine!  The wackiness really sets this game apart from GTA!  The story is also a full on omage to old retro games!  The game's missions doubly so!  You even have to go visit an imfamous dam from a certain turtles game!  The only issue I have is that some of the missions are QUITE long and due to random difficulty spikes, will often take more than an hour to complete, and repsawns during the mission are unforgiving.  I have ragequitted a few times because of this.  Still, this fact does not limit the overall fun factor of the game.
I recommend this game to anyone who has or had enjoyed a GTA game, but want something more light-hearted and crazy!
This GTA parody includes a ton of classic game references, particularly from the NES days.  Anyone who is not aware of that era may want to look elsewhere though.

Retro City Rampage is a wonderful homage to all things 80's.  Expect references to 80's movies, games, pop culture, and much more.  The gameplay itself is like a 2D, 8-bit version of the 3D Grand Theft Auto games, split between on foot combat, and vehicle segements.  There are 62 story missions, 23 weapons, and tons of vehicles.  The game has a pretty good difficulty curve starting very easy and building up to extremely difficult for the final sequence of story missions. The game is very generous with checkpoints so dying is almost never that big of a deal.  Aside from the main story there are 14 "sprees" and 23 "second rate sprees".  The sprees involve trying to get a high score while under various effects such as drunkeness, invulnerablity, explosive sweat, normal stuff.  There is one second rate spree for each weapon and they just involve killing as many people with that weapon as possible.   There are also 70 collectibles hidden around the game world (similar to the packages, magnets, oysters, etc. from the GTA games) along with plenty of other hidden easter-eggs giving plenty of reason to explore the game's overworld.  Overall the game was very fun, very funny, and highly recommended by me.

This is a basically an indie version of Grand Theft Auto. Retro-graphics with chip-tunes, all pixeled out. Its a fun idea and the references are all great. It is chalk full of homages to all the greats (and not so greats ;)). There is obviously alot of love put into this game with constant updates, since I have owned it anyways. If you are into it, there is also several game modes that will get you plenty of hours.
One problem for me, and why I ultimately do not recommend it, is the controls. I mainly play with an X360 Wireless. Driving is obnoxious - its the style where 'up' on the controller = 'straight' regardless of your current orientation. It also forces you to map your own controller instead of recommending a default config. I mean the devs should find a tried-and-true setup and just recommend that (they surely can recommend something from all the time they spend playing it).
Second problem is the core gameplay. After you strip away all the clever references, you are left with some really bare-bones game mechanics that requires little skill or learning, and is mostly short little epidsodes that you plow through with little grace. They certainly try to have a strategy angle, but I don't think it matters too much. Maybe it does if you are trying to get top scores or something, I cannot speak for that.
When it comes to indie love, this game has it all, but falls short with core gameplay and controls.

What can I say? I love this game. I can’t even write from an objective standpoint here to make an honest and fair review with this one. I’ve spent over 20 hours with this game here on steam, gotten every achievement- and even then- I didn’t quit. I took the time to Gold Medal all the optional missions too. I seriously can’t get enough. I tried for hours to put my name up on the leaderboards. I’m in the top 20 for lots of the missions and I’m quite proud of that. But enough about me.
Since I can’t really come at this from an unbiased angle I’ll just try to explain what’s it like. It's a retro-inspired Grand Theft Auto-esque homage to everything that was popular before I was born- and I can definitely respect that. I grew up watching movies and playing the games of the 80s- even though I was born in '95- just because of the way my parents were. It’s a top down shooter in some ways- a bit like Smash T.V. (a game which is actually referenced in a rather obvious level) The game is indeed open world- and has the very same mission based structure you’d come to expect from an open world experience. The cars in it drive in a couple different ways. One is akin to an RC car (a bit like R.C. Pro-A.M) and the other is one of those “Drive in the direction you press” things. Oddly- I usually prefer the latter- but mostly because I find it more precise. The story is goofy and out there- but fitting for the game. And there’s even a few cameos of a few other popular indie games.
This is the kind of game that you might be skeptical of when you see it in action- but when you actually play it you’ll see what makes it appealing- surely. Whether or not you’ll like it is entirely subjective in this case- but if you have an interest in retro games or games that resemble the kind of gameplay you find in Grand Theft Auto- you’ll at the very least get a kick out of it. If you grew up in the 80’s with the games and movies of that decade- I’d almost universally recommend it.
I can’t imagine a situation where someone will buy this game and feel entirely disappointed. I’d imagine you’d want to pick it up during a sale- as with most things on steam- but I feel the game is entirely worth the full price. Especially if you want to support the developer- who’s a pretty awesome guy by the way.
I can’t wait to see what Brian Provinciano has up his sleeves for the future.

I originally got State of Decay and then, later, when it was on sale, picked up the YOSE version.  This is my updated review for the YOSE version.
The game is a single-player third-person zombie apocalypse sandbox of sorts: while the main game has a storyline to follow, you certainly don't need to follow it and the story won't advance until you do, giving you a lot of time to just poke around.  I have enjoyed the game very much. It's certainly interesting enough to play and while it starts out reasonably tame, it can get quite difficult.
The main game begins with your character and a buddy returning to the more civilization-adjacent parts of a national park after a two-week fishing trip only to find that, while you were gone, civilization kind of had a major meltdown. From there, the game focuses on stealth and survival by building up friendships with others and establishing a base from which to operate and outposts to reinforce that base and provide small "safe zones".
The criticisms I have are somewhat picky. To start, the story is very simple and somewhat shallow — it would be easy to play through it relatively quickly and then be just done with the game. A lot more could have been done, but, as I understand it this was Undead Labs's first game, and it was made for XBox Arcade with all the limitations that requires — so we will perhaps see more story development in SoD2.
Second, there just isn't enough information in the tutorial; you feel bombarded with information (because a lot comes in through your Journal) that you can't make much sense of — and then lost because basic information (such as the benefits of establishing an Outpost, or whether it's wise to leave resources in Outposts or loot them thoroughly before setting one up in a location) can be a little difficult to find.
Third, there are too few voice actors, meaning that you end up with the same voice actors' lines being used for several different characters who end up sounding exactly the same while they say (verbatim) the same things; get two of them with the same voice together on a mission and it can get kind of weird.
Finally: the driving physics and UI aren't ideal. The game was set up for XBox, so maybe this is where PC players like me start to have problems. But while I can play Saints Row and Grand Theft Auto and drive just fine, I find the driving in State of Decay frustrating — especially because the smallest mistake can send a car sailing through the air as though it suddenly weighs nothing. And cars that turn over always explode, so there's that.  I can't tell you how often I've been driving along just normally, hit a small rock, and the next thing I know, I'm frantically trying to get my supplies out of my car before the thing goes boom — it's ridiculous.
Meanwhile, though, State of Decay is nice to look at: the colors are just muted enough to evoke the proper autumn-at-the-end-of-the-world feeling, and there has been a lot of attention to detail in filling out the large area (Trumbull Valley) in which your character gets to roam.  There are three small towns to explore, as well as a lot of countryside, with a ton of interesting things to look at if you appreciate the details.  (Bonus points to you if you find the homage to Plants vs. Zombies in Spencer's Mill.)
The game also makes you take a step back and figure out how to survive. Your character can go stealth or maniac, or pretty much anything in between. But don't count on the zombies to cooperate since that's sure to get your favorite character eaten nearly every time. And since death is final in this game, that really makes a difference.
Strategy and sound are important, which I really enjoy, and on top of that there is also resource management to deal with: you've got a base full of survivors who need food, medicine, and ammunition to remain survivors, and construction materials to keep their base up. Scavenging through the zombie-infested, burnt-out world is a constant necessity.
In the end, the game is definitely worth a few bucks (especially if you can catch it on sale), and I look forward to other games from Undead Labs.
I've played several hours of the Breakdown DLC, and it's been a lot of fun and a lot of frustration, but the frustration really seems to be the point of it. It's primarily the sandbox version of the base game, with a couple simple tasks to do to "move to the next level". Each level, the zombies get more numerous and more difficult to deal with and the scavenge-able resources get harder to find.
If you don't mind that sort of challenge — the one where you are pretty sure you'll ultimately fail — it can end up being a lot of fun.
The Lifeline DLC introduces a new area — the outer belt of Danforth — and a new set up.  In it, you're in charge of what military forces that remain in the area, and you're tasked with holding down a base against periodic zombie sieges while also trying to locate and extract important assets.  There's a storyline of sorts in Lifeline, too, and a resolution at the end.  As with the main game, it's a bit short and shallow, but it's entertaining enough, and it provides enough of a scenery change from the other two game modes that it makes things new and fresh again for a little while.

Tiny Keep is a wonderful, well-polished game that could have been much, much more.  Another good one to put on your Wishlist in case a nice discount comes along, but honestly an incomplete game at most prices.

My friend and I tested this and while I don't have definitive proof, it seems like the game actually skews the random components to interfere with the more sophisticated Win avenues.
A group of us have played roughly 10 multiplayer games, and I've spent a number of hours playing bot games, all in the quest to figure out what strategies would work given the other people in the game -- should I go speed? Try to kill the king early? Focus on stones? It doesn't matter.
It all amounts to the same thing, and the outcomes feel highly manipulated.
I wanted to like it, but it just kept slapping me down. Bad balance, bad RNG. Don't buy it.

PROS:

CONS:
- a bit short campaign
- some weapons become useless
- enemies always focus fire on you
- sand/snow storms blind a bit too much?
- EA account needed for multiplayer
Comment:
The logo looks like BF3 which might get people confused. Because, unlike the main BF franchize known for seriousness, Bad Company is lovably goofy. Best way to describe the mood is "less serious CoD:MW" mixed with "a parody of an american action movie". Unlike the previous Bad Company game we can enjoy this one on the PC too, although it is missing one DLC on the PC (Onslaught expansion which is a multiplayer co-op game mode). We are greeted with a WW2 intro/tutorial mission but the main game is played within a USA vs Russia conflict set in the present. The campaign is cool, fun and it keeps this tone for the most of the game. You will probably find your two or three favourite weapons and play those. First playthrough is good but once you unlock all the weapons you get to choose how you want to play. Which in my case was running around destroying everything with the rocket launcher. Unlike the collectable weapons that unlock for later use (or to have them already when replaying the campaign) the m-com stations serve little purpose than to distract. There could have been perhaps less (or more?) enemies if you find and disable one of these stations ... or at least extra dialogue. Your team buddies can actually kill enemies although the focus stays on you so you don't get bored letting your (immortal) mates do all the work. You all make a stereotypical gang - the smart one with glasses, the tough one, the sarge and the basic/vanilla one which you play. The slightly dated graphics still hold their charm though there are some graphical hick-ups - like tank threads that do not move. And I know it's kind of stupid to say but sand and snow storms hinder your vision a lot more than they maybe should. Because of this you either have to know where your enemy is or you have to be lucky. These storms are also annoying when driving around in vehicles and avoiding cliffs. The multiplayer is a blast and is still one of the best FPS multiplayers (even more if you have the Vietnam expansion). The playerbase is still good so check it out. There are more players in the default multiplayer than the Vietnam expansion but try that out too, it is awesome. Overall this is not a perfect game, it has flaws, but these can be overlooked due to the sheer fun factor of it. Get the bundle!

During the 26-mission campaign in Sniper Ghost Warrior 3, I went from infiltrating a mob wedding to scouting a block of abandoned flats for a drone which took me hours to find. There is an equal amount of everything in Sniper Ghost Warrior 3, and it was this unique gameplay that I loved the most. Bar the terrible cliche and boring story. I went from holding my breath and taking down an enemy 300 meters away from me, to pulling out an AK47 and filling them all with led. I did not expect this sort of diversity while playing the game, and when I needed to go loud compared to silent but deadly in the distance, it worked out just fine.
Sniper Ghost Warrior sees you take on the role of Jonathan North who gets involved in a civil war in a Georgian countryside. While this plays as the main host of the opening act, you will find yourself going around different locations throughout the game's act-based campaign. Jonathan's main goal in the game is to search for his brother who was kidnapped after a mission gone wrong, but the story never fully plays out as dramatically as it begins. Some parts and characters felt too cliche to be noticeable, and the whole premise felt dull from the opening act. While the narrative might be lacking, the game does make up for it with a great collection of mechanics that makes you feel like one badass sniper.
Every act takes you to a new location, and instead of littering the world with objectives, you select a mission and head off to that area to complete it. Every mission can be completed in any way you want, and there are no restrictions to how you approach the objective.  Keeping your distance and taking some enemies out one by one from 200 meters away is great, but you can also do that and then head into a compound with a loud assault rifle and clean things up. Not before you scan the area with a wobbly drone first though. I always found that the sniper route was best for most missions and it felt awesome as my bullet went through the mercenaries head.
At times I would plan my way into an area and then pick off the enemies along the way. The real feature is how versatile the game is in terms of how you can go about this in any way. The tools at your disposal also make a big difference like the drone that can fly around and tag enemies, as well as the night vision goggles and grenades. While most of these cool devices are barely used when going the sniper and silent route when the game messes up, or I did, then they come in handy during close quarter fights. Needless to say, the missions are all exciting to some degree, and the game never feels too repetitive to want to stop playing and move onto something else. Your safe house acts as a hub for all things you need. Here I crafted ammo, equipped new guns, and kept up to date on the mission I was on and what I have done in the game. Sleeping would advance time, and the skill system in the game would change the way I would approach a new mission and gear loadout.
Skills are only unlocked depending on how you play, so "Ghost" is mainly for silent approaches, and I levelled the "Warrior" trees faster when I went in guns blazing. The only thing here is that most of the time, well maybe the entire game, I felt that the skill trees were just there, and I never felt compelled to unlock any of the skills. With nine skills in each tree, it never felt like anything worth investing in and some of the skills only helped at times like the 50% bigger loot and gadget slots. The thing here is that the best skills were often in the skill tree I never unlocked, so it was a case of me losing out on them. The same can be said for the weapons and gadgets, as I never changed any of it and stayed with the starting sniper until half way through the game. You unlock new weapons and mods after missions, but the starting stuff felt great, and when I did change equipment I failed the mission due to the silencer being weaker than the last, which led to it breaking.
While the shooting and sniper feeling is on point in Ghost Warrior 3, the game does suffer from some lacklustre moments. The open world feels like a Fallout 4 DLC as it is filled with nothing but a dead wasteland of sadness. Going out of the safe house and heading towards a mission was a drab, with next to no collectables or activities to complete along the way. It was literally a case of "drive to the mission, complete it, go back, select another one and rinse and repeat". While there are some visually appealing moments, the safe house looks gorgeous but other than that the world is dull and lifeless. The CryEngine has not had a good run with this generation of consoles it seems as Homefront: The Revolution also suffered from the same bland look and feel. I did not come into contact with many bugs, besides some NPC glitches that saw people running around in a circle.
In the end Sniper Ghost Warrior 3 is a great shooting game, but its story and its underwhelming open world left me in a dull state of mind. It has a Far Cry feel to it when running around the large open area, but nothing to keep you busy besides the handful of missions and some collectables. Its story is uninspired too and left me needing more. However underneath it all there is a great sniper game here if you can get past all the features that hold the game back.

Card Hunter's a very unique CCG that plays like an top-down tactics RPG, ala Dungeons and Dragons. However, all your actions are tied to cards you draw from a deck, and your deck is built from sets of cards that come from the gear you loot and equip onto your characters.
This creates an extremely interesting deckbuilding scenario. Some items have bad cards on them, but to compensate any other cards on the item are often far more powerful. Rather than simply picking out the best cards possible like any other CCG often has you do, it becomes a becomes a question of careful balance. Do you want to take a lot of good cards, and take the risk of playing around the bad ones? Or do you aim for a consistent of evened-out cards? Either way, you are presented with a complex problem that you'll be thinking about long after you've put down the game.
As far as F2P goes, this is the most F2P-friendly any CCG has been in the couple past years, especially looking at games like Hearthstone. The game's leagues allow you to earn what is essentially 3 card packs for doing nothing but putting in a 50 gold investment, and there's a lengthy, fleshed-out and expanded campaign that you can grind infinitely until you are satisfied. In addition, the game has a very strong enforcement that rarity is not equal to power, there are many common and uncommon items that are far more powerful than their rarer counterparts. And thus, even players who are just fresh out of the campaign have a shot at competing in the competitive multiplayer's metagame.
The game even offers the campaign in co-op multiplayer, allowing you to share the game with your friends. It's a little clunky around the edges, but it does exist for anyone who is interested in it.
One major downside to the game though is that it gets very difficult very quickly. Some of the earlier campaign maps present enemies that are substantially tougher than you, and without thinking through and understanding the game mechanics, you'll quickly find that you'll be stuck on the same map for possibly hours. In addition, there's very little readily available guides to help you from this point.
Regardless, I believe that anyone who can persevere through that will find themselves playing for far, many more hours, as this game does not present difficulty without reason.

At 6 years of age, while my mother was manning a food stall with her siblings at a funfair, my cousins and I explored the foyer where Microsoft was marketing and showing off the original Xbox. Of the many games they set up to let players try out for free, Halo was a staple and of course my cousins brought me to play it.
But right next to Halo was another console station, where an older boy was manoeuvring a strange orange rat-creature through wooden bridges and collecting red glowing balls. Not to mention, the rat thing was throwing something that whacked green lizards and flew right back to him. It was outright fascinating. I got my chance to play after watching the boy. As a child of that age, I didn't fully understand what to do, where to go, or even
to play it.. but I had fun. A bit too much fun, in fact - I spent the rest of the day at the foyer, testing out all the games but ultimately coming back to the orange rat thingummy.
I was 7 when my parents gifted me an Xbox of my own. Along with Halo and Star Wars, Ty the Tasmanian Tiger was part of the 'Console + 3-game bundle' they were offering way back then, and you can imagine the absolute JOY I felt when I recognised the character on the cover of the game case - it was the orange rat! Whose name I then understood as Ty, who is a Tasmanian Tiger (which is extinct in the real world. Thanks mankind :c). Needless to say, for the next 6 to 7 years of my life and ownership of the Xbox, I always went back to TTTT, even when I wasn't able to buy the sequels.
My Xbox took its last breath in 2009, the same year I began living without console gaming. Yeah, I went to PC some time later, but never really played any games (I didn't know what Steam was back then). Fast forward to 2016, more mature and having a Steam game or two under my belt, random memories popped up and I decided "Hey, let's search that game I always played as a kid.." So I did. *scroll...scroll...scroll...*
That's when I saw it. "...as of March 2016, TTTT being remastered for Steam". HOLY MERRY MOTHER OF JOSEPH. MY CHILDHOOD WAS COMING BACK.
Immediately searched for their Facebook page, reading through all their updates regularly. It was just sheer excitement! And the best part? It released while I was in AUSTRALIA, the HOME of Ty (p.s I was sitting in Parliament as a guest when I bought the game. Lel). The child in me pretty much took over.
When I finally flew back home 2 days later, sleep was nowhere in existence; I spent the entire night playing through all the levels and worlds, collecting every single thing I didn't collect befoer, and most importantly
. I was even happier when I got to the final world and boss, because that was the one thing I never got to do before my Xbox died. Simply... Simply magical...
And now I hear they're planning to remaster the other two games? Krome Studios is fulfilling the wishes of the child in me. I'm elated. Excited. Grateful. Insertotherwordshere. Just.. thank you so much, Krome, for bringing back our childhood!
TL;DR = Had this game with original Xbox. Super happy when they remastered for Steam. I'm nominating it for a "Nostalgia Lives!" Award. c:

A few warnings and tips for new players:
- The game has a learning curve if you want to perfect your builds. However, the beauty of the game comes from your own learning and experiences in my opinion. Use trial and error, make a base that looks like complete spaghetti, and learn from it. You can learn a lot of optimization tricks on your own just from trying new ideas. Once you have played on your own, you can really appreciate the efficient and optimal designs that other people have created.
- The biters can be unforgiving. I suggest playing in peaceful mode your first time. Once you learn the building aspect of the game, move on to combating biters.
- Lastly, and possibly most important, don't get overwhelmed. BREAK EVERYTHING DOWN INTO PARTS! This makes the game much more manageable. Lay out what you want to build, and work backwards to get there.

TL;DR: Good comedy multi-genre game with horrible controls.
Rest of review:
Retro City Rampage is hilarious.  It has so many pop references around every corner that I can't help but laugh at the cameos from Paperboy, Sonic, Mario, Ninja Turtles, Bill And Ted, Back To The Future and so on.  It also makes light of the game development process by giving the player a "ROM City Rampage" prototype version of itself inside the player character's room.  The game relies on its humor and does a good job of keeping me entertained.
The controls are a different matter all together.  For starters, you're not given controller support, even though the game's store page and the game itself both say you should be able to use a controller.  I was tempted to map the controls with XPadder, but I didn't feel like going through the trouble of that.  Regardless, the default keyboard control scheme is not very comfortable, and I found the mouse useless.  Aiming at enemies without stepping into bullets was difficult because I could not control where I was looking while I was moving.  The auto-aim system doesn't work well, and I can't auto-aim at everything.  Overall, the game is frustrating to play because of the control scheme.
If you don't mind a little frustration and are looking for a funny 2D RPG shooter, Retro City Rampage should be your first choice.

This game never fails to relax me. It's my go-to game when I have that "unmotivated sunday I don't know what to do" feeling. It can get pretty intense and competitive though but all in a nice and well-handled manner.
Firstly I really want to complement the artstyle, design concept and music.
They all add a lot to the atmosphere! The artstyle for characters and the landscape look really smooth and cute, kinda like a fairytale, but as soon as you are ingame you will find out that there is a dark twist.
The whole setting and music are really calm. The design of the cards is really gorgeous and I like that the cards also feature the artists signature.
Secondly the game concept is a lot of fun and simple! It's basically a boardgame rpg where you have one goal: Be the new King or Queen of Armello. There are 4 different ways to achieve this and there are also 4 players on the field.
Different stats, abilities, starting boosts and cards add a big variety to how you can pursue this goal.
Especially the cards offer a lot of utility when it comes to giving yourself some boosts or hinder your opponents.
There are 3 types of cards: items, magic and trickery.
All the characters exel in different aspects and the cards can help you to improve your strengths or minimize your weaknesses.
Thirdly, and this is really important to me: This game and people are not toxic!
They can't be toxic because there is no ingame chat! I love this option and i think this adds a lot to the game.
You can use predetermined phrases to express some basic emotions and react to or show what you feel about different actions ingame.
It is turn based which makes the pace of the game pretty slow but that is nothing bad in my opinion. Near the end of the game it's getting pretty intense when everyone is trying to go for the king and claim his throne.
The only thing that bothers me sometimes is that magic and wits seem like the most viable stats. It is nothing crazy or something that i would call broken, but it gives the most utility which is a big factor in this game. A high wits stat enables you to draw a lot of cards and a high magic stat gives you the power to use more or stronger magic cards.
I rarely use the trickery cards which is a shame in my opinion but maybe that is just because of my character preference.
There are 2 character dlc packs which increase the number of playable characters by 8 in total. (So double the included characters). They add some nice new strategies to play with them because of their abilities but nothing that doesn't fit into the game or makes the balance an issue. The standard characters are really enough if you want to enjoy the game, but the dlc's can add some diversity and freshness. I feel like no character really stands out to be particularly stronger than the others.
Lastly I want to talk about the "drop system" in this game.
After every game you can either get a chest or a key (The chance for each seems to be 1/2, so it's super fair. (I applaude for this because i have never seen someone add KEYS as drops so you don't actually have to spend money)
From the chests you can get new die to throw at your enemies faces when you end up in a battle with them.
I strongly recommend this game and if you feel like it's something for you, it's definitely worth it!

The Purring Quest is a game by cat lovers, for cat lovers. Valhalla Cats, the Spanish studio behind the game, proudly state on their website that each member of the team has at least one cat. However, the game’s tag-line “have you ever wanted to be a cat?” is not entirely apt. The Purring Quest is not a sim game, nor does it offer the multitude of interactions found in the PS2 adventure game Dog’s Life, with its similar tag line: “It’s great being a dog.” Rather, It’s a somewhat old-school platformer, with increasingly difficult stages ending in a boss fight or similar encounter.
You take control of Kimchi the cat, jumping on window ledges, climbing trees and chasing birds and mice, and each stage has a number of collectible items like fish bones (warning: don’t feed your cat fish bones). Kimchi has two kinds of jumps used to reach these precious fish bones and ultimately move on to the next level. A regular short jump and a high jump, done by holding a left shoulder button then X. This choice of button press seems unintuitive at first, but it soon becomes second nature.
The game’s enemies are the aforementioned mice and birds. Kimchi’s only attack is a single swipe of her claws, but that’s more than enough to send these foes bursting in to a puff of smoke…yeah, the enemies literally burst into smoke. This was confusing at first, but it may have something to do with the family friendly nature of the game. There are also dogs which must be avoided at all costs. Early in the game you get a cardboard box (perhaps a nod to Metal Gear Solid?) which can be used to hide from these dogs which are prowling the streets.
The boss fights have some interesting ideas built in to them; like knocking rocks on to moles heads as they pop in and out of the ground. In practice, the control scheme just isn’t quite as responsive or fluid as you would like it to be and it makes the fights quite frustrating as a result. In that fight, there are cactus plants between the moles, forcing you to jump around them. The jumping is just not accurate enough to be able to avoid these cacti completely. Then there’s the final encounter which is basically a race to escape the boss. The difficulty spike here is gargantuan; the jumps come thick and fast and must be executed with pinpoint accuracy. Expect to retry the final boss many times.

For what it is, this game receives an odd amount of universal praise, and it's frankly strange there isn't more criticism. I suspect this is because most don't play more than an hour or two, which is when freemium games really start to reveal themselves. So here we go:
Difficulty. The game starts off as a very easy ride, before suddenly gutpunching you with a huge difficulty spike when without warning you're going to find that you constantly need to customize your deck to each fight. This isnt necessarily a bad thing in itself, but chances are you simply don't have the options you need to actually carry out the strategy. Building a specific type of deck to counter a mission can become downright impossible because you simply dont have the cards to make it. The loot system is completely rng (though you can inject money to expidate the process).
But hold, you can buy items from the in game shop! Too bad the in game currency to buy these items is also only obtained via rng. So you have to grind to obtain it. But you can only play each level once per day. So fine, maybe you'll go into that mission with only a couple of counter items. But whoops, you didn't draw the right cards. Back to the start for you.
As the game goes on, it's clear that they gave up on any semblance of caring about balance and just throw a dozen enemies with hands 4 times the size of yours with blatantly overpowered cards. Maybe you decide you'll use a lot of cards that push your enemy back so you can avoid damage. Too bad, the enemy has all range cards and tons of movement along with armor cards. You need to reach the end of the board before the enemy can call for help? Build a movement heavy deck. Oh wait, the enemies inexplicably have cards that do 12+ damage. Guess you better go back and do more grinding. And if a single one of your party dies, it gives the enemy enough points to win instantly.
But what's that? You got a piece of powerful gear? Too bad, you can't use it until you're a much higher level. And on the off chance you recieve more than one of these, you're gated from using them through 'power tokens' so you have to grind even more to use it. The level ups do not come quickly after you've played to this point.
I hear tons of people claim that game is in no way pay to win. So lets go down the freemium checklist:
-Forcing daily logins to make progress
-Time gating content
-Premium currency
-In game currency that's worth far less than than premium currency to the point it's a joke
-High amounts of content locked to free players
-VIP Scheme
-Guaranteed strong gear for paying players
-Horrendous real money to currency ratio
You can try to excuse the gear issue as 'anyone can get the rarest gear', but it is an incredibly time consuming and rng process to those not willing to drop the excessive amounts of money the game wants you to. The game might well have been good, if they'd just bit the bullet and put a price on it. But as it stands, free to play claims yet another victim.

The campaign mode is fun and doesn't take long to get through; each dungeon has a gimmick and you have to change your card deck often if you want to pass the level.  There is payment for extra dungeons and extra loot, but it's not needed.  The game has challenge as you have to figure out how to position your pieces and move around the board just like chess.  But it has very annoying RNG for card drawing and this really shines in multiplayer where having a bad draw (no attack cards) can turn the tables and snowball for the entire game.   But also moving your pieces around the board without thinking can end your game even with good cards.  It takes time and some decent playtime to really build up your deck, and like other card games, some cards are much better than others.  A lot of people will end a game early if they see your a more experienced player because that means you will have better cards and no chance of winning.  But reset still gets you loot.  I liked this game, but the RNG got on my nerves too much and I'm ready to move on to another game.  Try this out if you want a fantasy card game mixed with dice rolls and board game environments.

Retro City Rampage (DX) is a typical "retro" game which isn't afraid of making fun of itself and the whole 80, 90's genre of gaming with many reference to TV and movie from that times as well. In fact the whole game is full of references everywhere , some obvious , some more obscure which will only make sence if you have knowledge or even better experienced the shows or games they are making fun of.
The graphics are over the top retro 8'bits and many gameplay mechanics reminds me of the games of that era, packed in a GTA aspirated but of course over the top game-frame. The creator of this game used a lot of time to give you the feeling of playing those antiquated systems .
There are also many funny commentaries of the state of gaming both practical and moral which can even apply today. At one point the hero of the game regret one of his past transgressions, the other character listening to the "player" (yes the player's name in the game is "player", another pun) comments ironically that he should maybe stop routinely running over and killing innocent bystander while he is at it.
This is a funny comment on heroes in games (and medias generally) sometimes committing large scale genocide in order to "save the day".
The gameplay is actually ok and refreshingly diverse, but it's obvious the creator prioritized putting references and puns in almost every frames of the game. As a result, the game itself might feel too short and small, the city especially could have been a tad larger,  and I can understand the criticism. I still would recommend the game for the well done retro feeling , funny puns , especially but not only if you grew up in the 80's and 90's.
It's not very expensive to begin with but if you get a discount at some sales, it's really worth it as long as you have some interest in game culture and ready for a game that doesn't take itself very seriously.
Buy it.

This game is a NES nostalgic dream. It isn't however, an NES game (just to make that clear)! It is a spoof of every game possible and it does a good job of synthesizing it together. Just get ready for both good and bad (lame) jokes.
The
follows a person named "The Player" in which he is essentially a thug for hire. A bank heist goes wrong and The Player ends up stealing a time machine which flings him years forward. Doc Choc (another spinoff of a well known persona) comes in to help The Player recover pieces of the machine to get him back to where he belongs.The
is like the first version of GTA. You are able to move in 9 directions and shoot relatively to your position. Weapons are in abundance and in variety from golf clubs to shotguns to the bionic commando arm. Why is there? Why not... why not. There will be situations where you will need specific weapons to accomplish certain tasks. I prefer to use the shotgun over automatics when it comes to being overwhelmed by a lot of characters. The player can choose to free-roam the city or do main missions or side-quests. The game is really over-the-top with everything it does and isn't scared to loosely knock off and ridicule other games.
Any car (or bicycle or motorcycle) can be stolen. Some cars can be modified to be given a jet engine at the back or some kind of armaments. The more you progress in the game, more modifiers become available. If you do happen to break the law, cops will chase you if you break but it isn't as tedious as the GTA series. To get the police off your back, the player needs to find a special police token that will rid them of their wanted level. This token appears randomly in areas or can be dropped by eliminating a certain amount of police forces. In addition to modding cars, the player may mod themselves as they please. Again, progressing through the story will unlock more styles. There isn't much the player can change but hair is definitely one of them as cut-scenes will show "The Players" face. Throughout the game, there are power-ups that can be picked up to give the Player some neat abilities. These abilities can come in the form of speed or in some obscene form such as a Super Mario cape allowing your character to fly.
The
are quite basic and provide basic 8-bit fun. If graphics are imperative to you, this might bug you. Although the graphics are simplistic, it seems that the smallest of details were paid attention to. Sure, it is a simple color with a simple outline but the thought of including as much as one can is appreciated. The
follow a NES scheme. The music station can be changed (there are about 10 stations to choose from) and the sounds are appropriate for the setting. Don't expect to hear triple A explosions but you'll definitely hear everything going on in the game.

Amazing strategy type board game gameplay is smooth and the artwork is beautiful i would highly recommend Armello to any real time strategy fan or a board game fan of any age.

I am actually quite enjoying the mechanics of the gameplay. It's a classic, uncomplicated strategy game. My only complaint is that the Prologue gets tedious watching all the battles between AI's (but I can see why they've done it to cement game mechanics). The AI also feels evenly weighted, challenging you without any infuriating rigged feeling (like the one you get in Talisman for example which I still love anyway).

If you enjoy board games & RPGs, like animals, and are fascinated by the intrigues, stand-offs, and backstabbing in Game of Thrones, then there is no reason for you not to own this game. Most games of Armello will last between 60-90 minutes depending on a wide array of factors. I've also played one game that barely went 40 minutes and another that went well over 2 hours.
The game's art may come off as cartoony and possibly even childish, but don't be fooled for a minute; there is a very dark and scheming underbelly to Armello. There are numerous roads to victory, none of them particularly simple, and different heroes may have an easier time pursuing one path versus another. I have often found that starting a game with one strategy in mind often falls apart very quickly depending on the play styles of your opponents and what cards come out. It really helps to understand your chosen hero's abilities, strengths, and weaknesses and how they may succeed or fail against your different opponents as you go along (your and everyone else's "character sheets" are always available for viewing in game).
Try the different clan heroes out and learn the mechanics in single player mode, but at some point definitely play multiplayer - that is where the real fun & intrigue of this game lies.
One feature I like is the ability to watch another player's battles and peril challenges. You click on an icon and you can watch what cards are drawn, who the dice get rolled, etc.
I think the third video in the Steam ads for this game captures the essence of Armello the best - the one that starts with "From great horrors, great heroes emerge." Every game begins in a similar demeanor... the players tend to all greet each other, but within 3 or 4 turns it all turns delightfully ugly because in the end, just like in The Highlander, "There can be only one."
I think you will find Armello is an extremely satisfying game experience in a maddening sort of way. $20 very well-spent.

I gave it a thumbs-up because I am really hesitant to thumbs-down a game that can easily be fixed with a few tweaks.
Pros: The game is done in a really nice aesthetic; I feel the graphics and sound are very nicely done. The theme is cool, and from what I've heard thusfar of the soundtrack, it is rather nicely done. Some cool mechanics (like hiding) etc are nice.
Cons: Game might be a little simplistic for some, but then it is a 2D sidescroller.
What needs fixed:
1). XPadder for some weird reason does not like this game. This is the only program that can tell XPadder is running. I have never seen any program or game be able to tell the difference between keyboard input and XPadder. I bound the Q button and the spacebar (attack and jump respectively) to different buttons on my joypad using XPadder (because the game ONLY allows 360 controllers). When I pressed the button for jump I'd sometimes jump, but sometimes attack. This obviously wasn't going to work, so I was forced into using WASD controls instead. (Side-scrolling on a 360 analog stick is a huge "NOPE!"). Not sure what to suggest here, other than perhaps looking into enabling more controllers than just 360 controllers.
2). The first stage's boss's hitbox is really wonky. In fact, the character's attack hitbox seems a bit off. The first boss is very erratic, it seems to be entirely random if you hit the boss, or the boss hits you, or you trade hits. Given that he takes more than 6 hits to kill and you can only take 6 hits yourself... yeah, good luck with that. I think the best thing to do here, is to give the player character a slightly bigger hitbox with his attack. Also, it'd be nice if we could attack in mid-air, the first boss seems a bit frustrating when you spend most of the fight waiting for him to attack you (and you'll probably just get hit in mid-swing anyways, no matter when you time it). Also for some weird reason, the boss's hitbox seems to be "off" too -- when he flies side-to-side, he was "hitting" me even though he wasn't actually touching me.
3). Sound/Music FX sliders would have been nice in the first config dialogue popup before you actually get into the game. I have a strong pair of headphones, and most programs I need to turn the volume down considerably or I get my eardrums blown out. Being able to set volume levels before actually entering the game is a godsend, so it'd be really nice if you could include that.
The gameplay is pretty slow and boring in my opinion. The fun part is supposed to be player generated content but there are quality control issues there.

If Steam had a neutral rating, I would probably give the Purring Quest a neutral instead of a yes. The Purring Quest has some things going for it but also has some issues that prevent it from being anything more than an average platformer.
The standout in the game is the presentation. The artwork and music in general are really well done. The story is not bad but I wish there was more to it. The game is filled with cat jokes and puns so if you are a big cat fan you should enjoy this aspect of the game.
The gameplay is solid overall and I had some fun with the game. Unfortunately the game doesn't really do anything unique with the platforming genre. Being a platformer featuring a cat as the protagonist I was hoping that the game was going to have some unique mechanics that I hadn't seen before.
The biggest problem that I had with The Purring Quest was the jumping controls. While they might get fixed with a later update, at this time they are imprecise. Regularly I would press the jump button and nothing happened or it took a lot longer to jump than it should have. This leads to some frustrating moments since I can probably attribute at least 95% of my deaths to the jumping controls.
The other problem with the game is the length. To finish the game to completion only took me two hours. The game is short since it only has five levels and outside of the troubles with the controls the game is not particularly difficult. I didn't collect all of the collectibles which would add some time to the game. I don't really see The Purring Quest as the type of game that I would replay though.
At $12 I would maybe recommend the game for people that are big cat people. If you don't love cats the game is just not worth $12. If you like platformers I would probably pick up the game when it is on sale though.
Note: I received a review copy from the developer but received no other compensation for this review.

Opening this game I was quite excited as I'm a huge fan of kittens, cats and meo-re. If you want a preview without too much spoilers I have added my video above, as I'm not too great with words. Feel free to watch that instead for a better idea of the game.
The game begins with a very heart wrenching cutscene, upon this cutscene I paused to question "how long do cats actually live? Surely not this long?!" But anyway- Politics aside... upon finishing that cutscene you are then brought to the main menu where you get to choose from English or Spanish languages. On the main menu there were only three options 'New, Continue and Quit' which troubled me a little bit as I do love volume control. The reason I love volume control is because this game is very loud. Luckily upon starting a new game you can open the menu and get volume option sliders! Yipee!
When you start the game you are presented with an overworld layout (like Mario) where you can choose levels. There are 5 levels ranging from villages to a cities. When you get into the game it has all the functions of a platformer - as you'd expect. There are several checkpoints in the levels which I feel are too spaced out because sometimes the game can be very cheap with killing you. You die from insta kills - such as falling down pits or being spiked to death or from being hit by rats and enemies which in turn takes away 1 cat head which you have 7. (You can see them to the top left in the screenshots.) In control of the cat, you have a normal jump, a normal attack, a high jump, hide button and a climb button. The reason you need to have a hide button is because of those pesky dogs which I found frustrating, If they touch you once you restart at the last checkpoint.
In the levels you have collectibles too - there are smelly fish bones (which are the most common scattered everywhere), hidden objects such as paintings which can be tough to find and the final collectibles are trapped cats in cages which you swipe to break them free. They then have a fascinating discussion and whenever I spoke to them I always imagined them to speak french back. (Don't ask why)
Moving on, I don't blame how cats are after playing this game. It makes me realise that everything is out to get them! Dobermans, Chihuahuas, Pitfalls, Pugs, Electrical Cables, Frogs, falling plantpots, moles and the most frustrating of all Cacti. They caused me many deaths. (And I have only got to level 2). The reason I stopped there was because I'm pretty bad at platformers, the high jump mechanic feels a bit off (like I'm not sure if it's just me, but would love someone to clarify that) and those blasted Cacti!
I had to stop there because my blood pressure would've gone through the roof otherwise. I would've really appreciated if they added difficulty options or life collectibles. Even more checkpoints would definitely suffice. Getting killed cheaply and then resetting quite far back was annoying. So please, if you are annoyed easily enter at your own risk.
I recommend this to all cat lovers, cats, platformer appreciators and those down for a good challenge. I would however not recommend it to those who get agitated/annoyed easily because this game can easily set you off with its cheap tricks of killing you.
In the end, I feel it's farrrr from purrfect but if you do find enjoyment in the game it is a very pleasant experience indeed.
Thanks for reading and let me know if I can add more/or if you have questions feel free to post below :)

Tiny Keep is a rogue-lite dungeon escaping experience. The art style is
simplistic, with basic options that may or may not appeal to your taste. The
themes of the individual levels stay mostly the same, but unfortunately the balance
of difficulty is uneven. This can deter newer players or those who enjoy a slow buildup
of difficulty as they progress.
One difference from level to level can be found in the
layout of the map levels. There are traps on each level, and while not a deterrant,
you can use them to your own advantage to trap or kill your enemy. The traps break
after so much damage has been done to the traps, which I appreciate.
The camera angle is a mix of third person and top down; that tied down with the
screen shake of the camera can lead some to become dizzy or nauseousas they progress.
The camera angle also can be very disorienting as you try to find your way through the
levels.
The gameplay itself is very simplistic; a hack and slash primal kill experience. If
that's what you're looking for, it can be good. There is very little in the way of tactics
or combination of gear sets or powerups. The game accomplishes what it sets out to do very
well, but it pushes the difficulty level too fast too soon, combined with the seasick feeling of the camera angle makes me hesitantly recommend it.  This would be a good
purchase to get on sale.

watch if you are looking for a more in-depth review.

Alright, I don't like when a review gives a whole intro and everything saying what the game is, what it's like- no. Just no. I'm gonna start right off and say that the game's not worth it, for many reasons. First off, the game is bland. It's a roguelite game, so it meets the standards of randomized levels, obviously. What it doesn't meet is entertaining replayability. When you start off the level is all new and randomized, whoop-dee-doo, but what is never randomized one bit is the combat. The combat style is a constant. The combat style should never be a constant in a roguelite game. You always find and use the simple shield and sword through the whole game. There are no upgrades, no changes, no new items. They're the same equipment. The fighting style was bad from the start, though. You click to slash the sword and position your character in the right way so that the shield is in front of you to block. There isn't even a block button. This is bad combat for
game, not just a rogelite! To top it, the enemy variety is abysmal. You can fight a human with a sword, a human with a bow and arrow, a skeleton with either
. There may be more but I never bothered to make it past the third level. Then there are the bosses, which aren't randomized either. It's always the same boss with the same gear and same look and same A.I., with the fight being either harder or easier than the last run depending on how the level was generated.
I'm going to take advantage of that great segue I just made and move onto level generation, which remains on the topic of randomization but still deserves its own paragraph. The level generation can create some terrible maps or some simply average maps depending on how pleased Lady Luck is with you. There can be some very tight areas with tons of enemies piled into it which make for a terribly unbalanced and difficult fight, or a large mob of enemies that back you into a corner where they maul you until you're dead. There's also a problem with the randomization of the levels. Each level has a certain theme to it, and with those themes come some rooms or objects or enemies, etcetera, that are unique to it. These characteristics are employed every playthrough of the game. Take the third floor, for instance, which has a theme of
This takes away from the "new playthrough" feeling a great deal, and honestly feels like you're playing your previous run over again, this time more boring because last time was one less time you played the game than now. Only when you reach a new floor do you get that "new" feeling, and when you die and have to work your way back up to that floor again, it won't feel new anymore because you already got there last time, and it's essentially the same floor.
Yet another great segue. Getting back up to that floor again most likely won't happen because the game is
Seriously, TinyKeep is balls hard. I can say from experience with both games that it's harder than Super Hexagon (currently I'm halfway through Hyper Hexagonest). It's not only crappy because it's very, very boring, but because it doesn't provide you with sufficent means to defend yourself in many situations. There is not a single thing that would qualify as an asset for video games in Tiny Keep. Here is the problems I encountered.
- No options. Having only resolution and "Graphics quality: good bad best" options for a pc game is pitiful.
- No controller support. I was using a ps4 controller (one of the best out there) and the game couldnt handle it. It's funny how in the store page they dare and say "Full Controller Support". HOW THE HELL YOU HAVE CONTROLLER SUPPORT WITH NO KEY BINDINGS!!!!
- No key (re)-bindings!!!!! Wow!!! How can you make a game without key bindings. Not keyboard OR controller key bindings.
- Worst map/minimap in gaming history. The game's map artstyle is ok. But the disign is so bad. The maps are always very bad, I have never come across in a good map. Also the minimap....... So the minimap is unhelpful and most of the time you cannot understand where to go within 1 second. And 1 second is much more than you'll ever have to check the map in this game. Furthermore the "Sprint" button is tied (unchangably) to Shift and the minimap to Tab. So
you cannot see the minimap and sprint at the same time. Neither you can leave the minimap on in someway.
- Zero gameplay complexity. In this game you can only attack with your sword through left click and block with your shield with right click. There is no chain attack progression. That's it. You will never ever have any different way to fight than JUST ONE SIMPLE SWORD ATTACK WITHOUT PROGRESSION!!!!
- Zero visual updates to your character. So, you only got one sword attack. But also get the same da,m sword. Ah, a funny thing as well: See at the begging of the game you get a sword from maggy. In each run the sword looks different until you pick it up. Then it looks the same after you pick it up. LOL
- Zero progression complexity. You only get some passive upgrades like %double damage etc. There is no originallity here and the whole system is pitiful.
- Boring as hell. Blunt, unoriginal. Not even the artstyle is original. The music score isnt anything special either. Overall not something you would gladly give your time.
In the end I would give this game 2/10 or 1/10 since like I said, you can't find something and say "Well at least this game has THIS THING going for it...". No, there isn't any "this thing" in Tiny Keep.
I am really grateful I got it in a package from Humble Bundle. I would never buy this game for more than 1 euro.

The campaign mode is fun and doesn't take long to get through; each dungeon has a gimmick and you have to change your card deck often if you want to pass the level.  There is payment for extra dungeons and extra loot, but it's not needed.  The game has challenge as you have to figure out how to position your pieces and move around the board just like chess.  But it has very annoying RNG for card drawing and this really shines in multiplayer where having a bad draw (no attack cards) can turn the tables and snowball for the entire game.   But also moving your pieces around the board without thinking can end your game even with good cards.  It takes time and some decent playtime to really build up your deck, and like other card games, some cards are much better than others.  A lot of people will end a game early if they see your a more experienced player because that means you will have better cards and no chance of winning.  But reset still gets you loot.  I liked this game, but the RNG got on my nerves too much and I'm ready to move on to another game.  Try this out if you want a fantasy card game mixed with dice rolls and board game environments.

I don't often write reviews, but I  thought I'd write this since there are many that are totally slamming this game. I got this during a Steam Sale (I refuse to pay full price for games anymore, I'll wait for a sale everytime), but it's been heavily on my radar since I heard they were making a third game with an open world.
So far, I'm having a blast with this game. This is what I thought the original SGW was going to be when it came out. Anyone who's played the previous two knows that they were very linear and didn't offer much in terms of player choice. This game is a great first step in the right direction. During missions, there are suggested sniper hides, but you can really set up anywhere you'd like. Missions are varied, and fun to play. Even better, during play, I could see several different ways that situations could be handled, so I'm looking forward to replaying through the missions using different approaches.
The enemy AI has impressed me so far. Should it be discovered that their allies are dropping, the remainder will take cover from the direction that the shots are coming from. They don't stand out in the open waiting to be picked off, so you'll need to do a thorough recon with your drone to formulate a plan on how to take the enemy out. If they do know where you are firing from, they'll use diferent tactics to attempt to flush you out and destroy you. After being discovered during a mission, half of the compound's forces stayed behind cover as I tried to draw them out. Unbeknownst to me, the other half had made their way into the woods, flanked my position, and took me out. On another, while assaulting a fuel depot, several of the enemy laid down cover fire in my direction while their buddy ran to a mortar. Within seconds, motars were impacting around me, forcing me to reposition. Pretty fun emergent gameplay.
The game advertises three core pillars of gameplay; Sniper, Ghost, and Warrior. I've stuck mostly with sniping, but enemy numbers and placement, terrain, and situation will generally dictate. For me, sometimes the ghost pathway is the most satisfying approach. Few things are more fulfilling than sneaking through a small town with a suppressed pistol, taking out the enemy one by one with said pistol or knife, stacking bodies enroute to your target.
The game isn't perfect; it's got its share of bugs, but so far they've been few, and nothing gamebreaking. Even though there have been some reviewers that didn't like the open world, I'm all for it. It is extremely detailed, atmospheric, and downright gorgeous to look at. I'm the type of player that loved Far Cry 2 above its sequels, and part of the fun in that game was the lack of fast travel. The movement to the objective was where most of the tense, atmospheric fun was at, and I treat this game the same; fast travel doesn't exist for me. Plus, you miss a lot of the side areas using fast travel.
Some things I wish they would implement in future updates:
- A co-op mode so you and a friend could truly play as sniper and spotter. Picture the fun and coordination a team would need as one player scouts with the drone providing real-time intel to his buddy whom is moving through an enemy occupied town or compound. Imagine the challenge and gratification of acheiving your objective without alerting anyone or firing a single shot
- Real night-time. One annoying aspect that this game shares with Far Cry 3 and 4 is they all have super luminous nights. Always a full moon, and extremely bright. It's pretty much daytime with black skies. The night vision and thermal optics serve no true purpose in this, as you can see better without them. Implement darker nights, and I'll actually have a reason to use these tools. Arma 3 and Dying Light do night pretty well and force you to rely on flashlights or NVG's to see in darkness. I wish they'd do something similar. I want nights so dark I can't see the bushes in front of me.
- More detailed wind reading mechanics. Instead of using a meter displaying wind direction and intensity, the player actually has to judge this for themselves using environmental indicators ie; swaying trees, flags, streamers, etc. Using mirages to read wind would be awesome as well, but that's probably asking too much.
- More detailed with sniping mechanics in general, such as MIL or MOA scopes, ranging using mils, etc. I understand that this game is already more realistic than most other shooters out there regarding long-range precision shooting, but it would be neat if they included a hardcore difficulty that indludes details like this with no on screen indicators. Everything must be calculated by the player.
Overall, I'm very happy with this purchase as the game is quite fun with beautiful, large, varied environments. I was super bummed to hear that CI games "admitted" they were too ambitious with this project. I disagree, and think they did really well. This is a good stepping stone to the next one. If this series goes back to the linear template they used before, I won't be buying the next one. Here's to hoping they stick with the open world, and improve upon it.

This game is a NES nostalgic dream. It isn't however, an NES game (just to make that clear)! It is a spoof of every game possible and it does a good job of synthesizing it together. Just get ready for both good and bad (lame) jokes.
The
follows a person named "The Player" in which he is essentially a thug for hire. A bank heist goes wrong and The Player ends up stealing a time machine which flings him years forward. Doc Choc (another spinoff of a well known persona) comes in to help The Player recover pieces of the machine to get him back to where he belongs.The
is like the first version of GTA. You are able to move in 9 directions and shoot relatively to your position. Weapons are in abundance and in variety from golf clubs to shotguns to the bionic commando arm. Why is there? Why not... why not. There will be situations where you will need specific weapons to accomplish certain tasks. I prefer to use the shotgun over automatics when it comes to being overwhelmed by a lot of characters. The player can choose to free-roam the city or do main missions or side-quests. The game is really over-the-top with everything it does and isn't scared to loosely knock off and ridicule other games.
Any car (or bicycle or motorcycle) can be stolen. Some cars can be modified to be given a jet engine at the back or some kind of armaments. The more you progress in the game, more modifiers become available. If you do happen to break the law, cops will chase you if you break but it isn't as tedious as the GTA series. To get the police off your back, the player needs to find a special police token that will rid them of their wanted level. This token appears randomly in areas or can be dropped by eliminating a certain amount of police forces. In addition to modding cars, the player may mod themselves as they please. Again, progressing through the story will unlock more styles. There isn't much the player can change but hair is definitely one of them as cut-scenes will show "The Players" face. Throughout the game, there are power-ups that can be picked up to give the Player some neat abilities. These abilities can come in the form of speed or in some obscene form such as a Super Mario cape allowing your character to fly.
The
are quite basic and provide basic 8-bit fun. If graphics are imperative to you, this might bug you. Although the graphics are simplistic, it seems that the smallest of details were paid attention to. Sure, it is a simple color with a simple outline but the thought of including as much as one can is appreciated. The
follow a NES scheme. The music station can be changed (there are about 10 stations to choose from) and the sounds are appropriate for the setting. Don't expect to hear triple A explosions but you'll definitely hear everything going on in the game.

While it feels like several indie games these days attempt to play upon our nostalgic love for the 80s and 90s era of video games, Retro City Rampage takes the trope to levels that I don’t believe have yet been reached. Pixelated and chiptuned, you’ll know that exact feeling from the minute you start the game and hit the start screen.

Retro City Rampage plays more like an NES game than any other recent title I can remember, and not just from the style. The controls are tight and limited, but jumps are very hard to land. This becomes frustrating later in the game, as Mario-esque head stomps are required to dispatch certain foes. This does not translate well into 8-direction movement, as you tend to slide all over the place trying to land on a character the size of a dinner plate. Vehicle controls are fine, however, which is a benefit since you’ll spend an extended time zooming around the town in the various cars you snatch, GTA-style.

While I felt that Evoland took a good idea and didn’t take it far enough, Retro City Rampage doesn’t have that problem. The creators of the game seem to have first-hand knowledge of the golden era of videogames, and pop culture references come flying by – I’m very sure that there were several that I missed completely. Saved By the Bell, Back to the Future, Terminator, G.I. Joe, Sonic the Hedgehog – the list goes on and on, right up to recent memes that still managed to find a way in. With this amount of references, it would be an easy thing to feel inundated by all of the content being thrown at you, but I never felt like it was too much, or going too far.

There are a few difficulty spikes that are frustrating, particularly with the combat, as some enemies are simply bullet sponges that will require you to strafe and jump and shoot like a madman. There is a simple lock-on feature, but I felt it was somewhat unreliable as I tried to clear rooms of enemies. Wide-spread weapons, such as the rocket launcher, gained primary use for me, as I just had to aim in the general direction of some foes. When it came time for me to face those same weapons, however, I felt almost helpless. Plus, the end boss of the game doesn’t fit into the rest of the game’s dynamic at all – the end stages are completely based upon Rad Racer, which really serves as a knuckleball to the game’s pacing and would have served better as a side-mission somewhere else in the game.

The game has a healthy amount of content, with a few side-missions and some achievements to chase as well. You can play through the game once again in Turbo Mode once you’ve completed the adventure at least once, though personally I felt like I had my fill after the first play-through. I may return to the game down the line, for achievements, although I am satisfied with the time I spent with it.

I wanted to like this game, I really did, and I pushed myself beyond my own will to continue playing this game. I love the Far Cry series, which this game is heavily "inspired" by and I do enjoy the sniping mechanics SGW and Sniper Elite offers.  Eventually, I surrendered.  The TL;DR of this review is : CI Games was up to something good here, and I wish Ubisoft would baptize this game and polish (Eh? Get it) it up to make it worthwhile.
Now for further thoughts....
SGW3 tries to be a Far Cry clone, but strikes out on optimization. Although I never had any framerate issues on my higher end GPU...Sudden Pop-Ins, awful collision boxes,  poor physics,  delayed input responses, and an AI that can only be described as offensive, makes this experience dreadful. Its a glitchfest. Not to mention the corny writing and voice acting. The graphics are pretty damn decent however, when the game behaves properly.
The game itself feels repetitve. (1) Go to the safehouse (2) Upgrade equipment and select mission. YOU HAVE TO BE AT SAFEHOUSE TO GET MISSION (3) Drive through a endless, empty, boring and lifeless dirt road to reach your mission site (4)  Search and tag your enemies with a drone that controls like a stumbling drunk (5) Snipe, with the option of using a hinting system that trivializes the bullet trajectory mechanics set in place (6) Infiltrate the site just for the sake of pressing the "use" button on something (7) Maybe have a sluggish gun fight on your way exfiltrating the site (8) Go back to the safehouse and repeat.
Lastly, the controls feel like they were a last minute thought. Too many damn in-game menus to select different gadgets and ammo, grenades and what not. The devs could condensed some of this.

Have you ever played around in a sandbox game and thought, "Man, I wish I could just automate this part."? Did you ever dabble in logic gate simulations like Redstone in Minecraft or similar?
If so, this is the game for you. The entirety of the game revolves around managing and manipulating resources scattered around the map. The further into the game you get, the more ways you have of automating and streamlining things you've been doing by hand.
It's an extremely satisfying and organic progression moving from a schmuck picking up rocks with his bare hands to having a fully automatic mining operation generating thousands of smelted iron plates every minute.
The only downside to this game is how incredibly absorbing it is. Be prepared to lose several hours out of your day every time you launch this game.
