- Music and FX are not the best, but are not horrible.
- Unbalanced matches (sometimes). Sometime you're team will be full of low level players against really high level players making it totally unfair.
- Lag, sometimes. This is bad because the game doesn't seem to be complex so no idea why there's lag sometimes.
So for the big letdowns I'd say the terrbile MKB controls (considering this is a PC port), but probably having a proper configuration would be and advantage over the mobile gamers, so maybe that's the reason (or devs were just lazy).
But afterall is a nice ligth MOBA for guys like me that don't have too much time for big MOBAs like Dota2 or LOL and just want to kill some time and have a lightweight MOBA experience.
Just remember to USE an Xbox360 controller.

TinyKeep is not at all a Roguelike game despite what the developers and others might try to convince you, in reality TinyKeep is a straightfoward action game with RNG elements. That's it.
So let me explain by TinyKeep not qualifying as a roguelike game, it only has procedural generation and permanent death that can even barely and I mean barely qualify itself as a roguelike. The reason for this is simple: Permanent Death can be removed from the game once a certain item is obtained which removes a huge staple of the roguelike genre. Secondly procedural generation means jack in this game. Yes the dungeons are 'randomized' but if they always consist of the same things for each level, in my opinion it should not count as procedural generation.
Now let me explain why it should not count as Procedural Level Generation. In the Binding of Isaac as a popular example, each floor has a semi-random amount of rooms with random enemies, a random boss, a treasure room with a random item, and two secret rooms for the bare minimum. The only floors that stay somewhat consistent are the last two floors along with the floor for Mom's Heart.
In TinyKeep the first level will always involve
Floor 1 - Prison, find Sword/Shield, only Archers/Brawlers with 1 Treasure Chest
Floor 2 - Prison, Boss at the end once you reach the door note with 1 treasure chest and 1 throne
Floor 3 - Prison unlock the 3 colored doors, unleash the skeletons, go to door and beat the big skeleton
Floor 4 - Dodge stone guy and hit the end everyone is orcs
Floor 5 - Orcs with 2 stone guys, 3 colored doors, unleash skeletons
Floor 6 - Skeleton Boss, super short with nothing in it
Floor 7 - Flames n demons have to have fire proof perk
Floor 8 - Flames n demons w/boss
Seriously I can go on. Every floor is the same. I can't qualify this game for being Procedurally generated if every floor has the exact same qualities barely moved around. TinyKeep also has a whopping total of 6 enemy types (I'm not counting the fact that there's a goblin/skeleton/human archer as three different types, let's face it they're all reskinned versions of the same thing). And you know what floors you face which.
I don't believe only having a floor layout randomizer should ever qualify as a roguelike, which is all that TinyKeep has.
At any rate the game suffers from far more than the two elements I listed above. The only 'power up' of sorts in the game involves buying blessings for either 15g, 7 - 100g, 1 - 500g, and 2 - 750g. (The latter two are endgame).
The 15g blessings can be bought up to at least 15 times in a row, at a complete RNG chance as to which of many skills it can give you will power up. The 100g blessings can only be bought one time each and are easily the most needed blessings that every player needs, and the last three (500g/750g) are for secret/broken powers.
Here's the problem with these blessings. Most of them are worthless at the 15g level,
-There is one for running faster which has diminishing returns because you only need to move so fast
-Multistrike which is worthless past level 2-3
-Serrated Edge which is an RNG chance of doing more damage
-Arrows to Ether which is an RNG chance to dodge an arrow
-Able to run backwards faster
-Run with a shield faster
Out of all of these the only TWO skills that aren't complete garbage are the Tank skill and the Lightning Reflexes skill. None of the other skills are even worth leveling up but since it's RNG it'll probably happen if you want it or not.
Also RNG only exists to screw you over in this game.
-Chests can be empty for no reason
-No vase spawns in a level
-RNG for any of the 15g blessings
Another problem with the game is the inclusion of a physics system of sorts, where walls will blow out throwing blocks on the floor, and enemies bodies will become obstacles when you kill them. It just gets frustrating especially in the latter levels of the game with the amount of clutter everywhere. Especially when the giant skeleton bodies seem to never go away getting me stuck numerous times.
Finally one of the last problems is that 'farming' exists which essentially completely breaks the game. Essentially levels 1-4 are the scariest part of the game because it's so hard to get your hands on money, at that point in the game it's possible to only have around 300 coins. Once you hit level 5 you can get every single 100g power up and level up most of the 15g ones to 10 with ease. This is because the skeleton invasion never ends and you can infinitely farm them for however long you please.
Overall the game acts like I'm having more fun than anyone could ever possibly have. It's really not fun to play through this game more than a single time and the game expects you to play through multiple times. The game is downright confusing with some of the 'secrets' such as the cauldron which is completely ignored until the loop begins. This makes no sense because there is another shrine which was kept out of the early levels to not confuse beginning players. Why this was included is beyond the scope of my knowledge.
If this game had done the blessings differently I might not have such a problem with it, perhaps make them like Isaac to where they are powerups you can find throughout the level. Maybe even make it to where you could CHOOSE which one you wanted instead of rolling the dice each time.
The game should also stop being so persnickity about secrets. It's cute that you want to include secrets, and I think most games should do more of them BUT it's stupid that the second half of the game is locked behind a 'secret' of sorts and I know most people who have reviewed the game probably don't even realize it exists.
The bigger problem with that is that the second-half of the game is complete garbage. Again too much clutter and♥♥♥♥♥♥flying around everywhere making progress a chore. Furthermore it's even sillier that if you make it to the 2nd half of the game and die, you are forced to replay through the first half just to get back to the second half.

The greatest asset to this game is the pricepoint.  Apart from that, there is little draw to it.  Granted, *it has potential* to be very fun, but currently it does not meet standards.  Though this game has a nice concept, the absent replayablity, simplistic elements, and awkward design break this game's worth.
First and foremost, this game doesn't have much replayability.  Granted, it's worth stating that no level is the same (other than the elements (different enemies, objectives)).  The layout is different every time, which is cool.  And I understand the rogue-like design of a hard-restart upon death (I love FTL).  But there is a huge difference in difficult and tedious.  You CAN skip a level once you beat it (e.g. go to 6/20); but if you do, you WILL lose.  This is because once you die, you lose any perks.  Later on, you can't really win without having a lot of those vital perks.  Having to go through levels 1-5 the first three times is okay.  But those get boring, FAST.  The gameplay is not exciting enough to get me through it each time.  The developer should at least allow a checkbox that let's the player keep perks upon death.  This would at least give me incentive to come back.
--Honestly, I cannot see myself coming back after one or two more plays.
I love the idea of a dungeon crawler that forces the player to use speed, cunning, and logic.   This game has some of those elements, but they are repeated and way too simple.  Hack, hack, block, hack.  Run away behind the enterance; wait for archer; kill archer.  That's the game.
This is an indie game.  Bugs are too be expected; I get that.  But in a rogue game, where death means another 20 minutes wasted, it isn't easy to forgive.  Getting stuck on a random pointless vase or stone and getting swarmed is so disappointing.  I'm used to being disappointed in myself; don't make me have to change my thinking.
Overall, it's a nice idea, but I can't really say I enjoyed it.  I kept waiting for it to improve and give me more, but instead it only got repetive.

Paint The Town Red is a game that could be compared to games like Party Hard and Hotline Miami in the fact that you jump into levels and kill everyone there. The difference between Paint The Town Red and those games is that the game takes place in a 3D Voxel system that allows individual bits of skin, bone, and other bits to fly off them when you hit them. The camera view is also from a first person perspective, and your character can take more than one hit (Obviously, more differences than these exist, but these are some of the very significant ones.)
Pros:
-Paint The Town Red has highly replayable levels, and some of them have secrets to discover
-Almost every item that isn't nailed down is usable as a weapon, this includes apples, oranges, frozen slabs of ham (Which are surprisingly good at blowing people's heads apart,) and basketballs. This leaves a ton of experimenting open to the player on how you want to destroy the enemy.
-The 3D Voxel system makes killing enemies very satisfying. Stabbing an enemy will leave gaping stab wounds, while punching them will leave bloody bruises. Hitting them enough times with a blunt weapon in the same place will eventually go through their skin into the muscle and bone layer, and some blunt weapons, if you're lucky, can blow apart an enemy's head in one swing. You can also cut people in two with a katana, and several enemies can be hit with one swing if your weapon cuts through the enemy.
-The level design is generally good, with areas such as a prison, a biker bar, and a disco dance club. Some levels are better than others, however.
Several Pros are likely unlisted, but these are what I thought of important items
Cons:
-This could be me personally, but the game can have decent FPS lag when a lot of things are happening on screen. The Arena level seems to cause this a lot.
-Nitpicking, but some levels are better than others as stated before.
Several Cons are likely unlisted, but these are what I thought of as important items.
Altogether, I'd reccomend Paint The Town Red to just about anyone who doesn't have an aversion to massive amounts of violence and gore. Those who have slower PCs, like me, might experience some slowdown on the more CPU intensive levels, but this isn't a massive issue.

It is difficult for me to write a negative review for this game because I find its goal absolutely admirable. The Great War is a notoriously difficult topic to approach due its complexity and, to a contemporary observer, absurdity. As such, the AAA industry is frequently guilty of 'WWII-fying' WWI (actually Valiant Hearts is also somewhat guilty of this to some extent). Incidentally I believe that some people will vehemently disagree with my assessment and believe me, I really wanted to love this game. At the very least, I would like to see other attempts at the challenge Ubisoft Montpellier set before themselves. Eventually somebody is bound to succeed at it.
The main problem of Valiant Hearts is the extreme inconsistency between the tone and the subject matter. This is the single worst conflict in human history, as horrifying to the people of last century as is to us today and yet this war is stylized here as a Franco-Belgian bande dessinée. You may argue that the cute cartoony style is used to attenuate of the sheer unspeakable terror of the war but if so, the stylization goes too far and robs the scenes of their impact. Valiant Hearts does attempt to redress itself towards the end with the mountains of corpses and hellish landscape of Chemin des Dames but this actually sends the wrong message by implying that the Nivelle Offensive was somehow worse than the rest of the war (if you disagree with this particular point, I invite you to compare this chapter with the depiction of Verdun earlier in the game).
While the story is at least serviceable, there are several things I wanted to point out. First of all, it is quite strange that the protagonists of Valiant Hearts include an old French farmer, a German expatriate living in France, an African-American who volunteered to fight in the French army and a Belgian faculty of medicine student in Paris. You can see the pattern here, right? Walt the dog is basically the only character who is not affiliated in any way with France. You may argue that this was a deliberate decision to allow the characters to meet sooner in the story but, by taking clear sides in the conflict, Ubisoft Montpellier made a big mistake. After portraying Germans as sausage-munching, beer-guzzling mustachioed villains throughout the first half of the game the developers did only token attempts to undo this stereotyping by the story’s conclusion. While I can’t blame a French developer for siding with France in a fictional depiction of WWI, the war requires a more nuanced approach and Ubisoft’s partisanship contributes to an industry-wide misrepresentation of WWI. It is downright irresponsible to draw from WWII archetypes to characterize Baron von Dorf. I don’t care that a 20th century French peasant is somehow fluent in English and appears to be the strongest man alive. I draw the line at Baron von Dorf however: the character belongs in Wacky Races, not in a historical drama.
When it comes to the gameplay of Valiant Hearts, I admit to being something of a fan. The list of influences is wide and varied, including titles such as The Incredible Machine, Commandos: Behind Enemy Lines, Metal Slug and the Sierra/LucasArts classic adventure games. Despite the simplicity of the controls scheme the game was quite varied and enjoyable, save a few trial-and-error action sections towards the end of the story. I do not actually have many complaints here. The annoying hint messages, which appeared whenever you stopped to admire the multi-leveled level art, were completely unnecessary and got in the way. Admittedly this is a minor complaint and in fact I can only think of one major gameplay issue: Anna’s QTEs. QTEs in general are something of a lazy shortcut, used whenever the designer wants to keep the player engaged in the game but can’t come up with anything better than timed button prompts. In Valliant Hearts Anna’s rhythm game sections are initially harmless but quickly overstay their welcome. More importantly, the ‘game-ness’ of QTEs actively distracts from the unpleasant nature of Anna’s actual tasks, which include applying stitches and even an amputation! In fact the game's finale is particulary impacted by these obnoxious QTEs. Fortunately the ending still has emotional impact due to the strength of the overall presentation.
Like I wrote at the beginning, I really wanted to like this game. It certainly has a lot of merit but for me the bad ended up outweighing the good. I think the aesthetics and 'game-y' aspect of Valiant Hearts clashes with the message it tries to convey. The desperation and misery of the human condition as it is conveyed through context, collectibles and historical footnotes throughout the game is frequently undermined by the chunky and friendly exaggerated art-style, silly mumbling voices and Walt’s disarming charm. I applaud Ubisoft Montpellier for attempting to convey the tragedy of the Great War to a wider audience but I find the results unconvincing and difficult to recommend.

Star Wars: Republic Commando is a Tactical First-Person Shooter set in the Star Wars universe, specificly during the Clone Wars. We play as RC-1138, leader of the Delta Sqad - one of the few commando units under the command of GAR. Yeah. War wasn't won by the Jedis only.
We see Deltas since the very beginning of their lives on Kamino, and through 3 Operations: during first asault on Geonosis, retaking the missing Acclamator and preparing the Kashyyyk for liberation from CIS (you know, blowing stuff up). Every member of the team is well-written, which makes us really connected to them. We have Scorch "if we are all clones, why am I the only one with the sence of humor?"; Fixer, focused on the objective, not leaving any place for jokes and chit-chat; Boss (you): just the leader, pretty self-explaindatory; and my personal fav: Sev, squads' own little psycho. Although everyone has different specialisation, it doesnt really matter in game: you can assign each squad member to every task (of course, you can do it on your own). Why Tactical FPS?
During gameplay, you will encounter numerous places, in which you will have to hack some console, blow obstacle or some driod dispenser up or so on. Sure you can do it yourself (well, most of the time; it appears that some activities can only be performed by squadmates. In others you need to stand with your face in the objective not to accidentally assign teammate to the task), and count on your squad to cover you, or you can cover teammate which you will assign to it. So thats for detonations and slicing into consoles. Other commands include: recieving bacta (just healing; no self-regeneraiting HP), focusing fire on single target (helps with SBDs and droidikas), and breaching the door (which comes with a grenade most suitable for the situation from one of deltas; they have unlimited ammo). There are few more, but i will get to them in a minute.
Gear. As for every FPS, there ale plenty of toys. So you have always present pistol: unlimited ammo and quite weak shoots; DC-17 rifle: nice rate of fire and damage, useful against... everything; and two attachments for your DC: Sniper attachment turns your weapon into... A SNIPER RIFLE! (i know you expected a pizza, but that would be useless here) - every enemy has a weak spot: hit it with this beauty to deal maximum damage; and Anti-Armor attachment, extremally useful against SBDs and large groups of enemies. Unfortunatelly, both attachments have rather tiny ammo pool (Sniper has 20 and AA - 4), so you cannot run happily scoring headshoots and blowing droids up. Sorry. But additional ammo and bacta dispensers are pretty common sight, so you should have right ammo for right task. There are also explosives: we have regular thermal detonators, acting like typical frag grenage; we have Sonic grenade - works just like thermal detonator, but explodes on impact with the enemy. There is a flashbang, leaving enemies vulnerable for a few seconds, and lovely EMP detonator: just one drains droidika and SBD health to the point in which all you need to do is land a few shoots to finish them. They become extremelly useful during last few missions. What else... a melee attack is OP, but same as with personal interaction: face in the enemy :/ . Also, stabbign enemy will splash his blood or oil into your HUD, making it a bit harder to see anythign for a second or two - but what else have you expected? There are also some episodic weapons, dropped by enemies, like SMGs, Shootguns and minigun, but they are present just sometimes, nevertheless, pretty handy.
But wait, rest of the team sould also be able to use these weapons! - bet you will be asking. Not all of them; sure they have DCs with unlimited ammo. But they cannot freely use anything else. Freely. I said earlier about door breach in which they will use grenades; there are also pleny places in which you can assign them to use their DC attaachments and grenades. This mostly happens when there will be lots of enemies rushing but no worries: assignin 3 of them to sniper positions in a narrow passage will destroy any number of enemies weaker than droidika (have i mentioned unlimited ammo?). So whenever you can - assign them to these. Also, watching their melee takedowns is addicting.
I shall continue with AI. Teammates can fight well, and unless surrounded, or fighting against some powerfull enemies, they will handle themselfes. In other case they will get downed. it's not the end - would be quite a shame if they could die thanks to your incompetence. You can revive them, or assign alive squadmate to do it. If not in full health, near bacta dispenser and without orders, they will go heal themselves. Of course, nothing is perfect - during playthrough, I had to restart level twice, because teammate glithed during command and couldn't move or complete the task :/ Also, enemies sometimes were trying to shoot through the walls. But it's all ok, when listening to squadmates' comments. Few examples:
1. Scorch: Man, this place gives me the creeps.
Sev: Ah, Scorch... Nothing better than a jungle hunt. Hiding in the bush, putting a plasma bolt through a hostile's cranium...
[sighs wistfully]
Sev: Makes me feel alive.
Scorch: Okay, now Oh-Seven's giving me the creeps.
2. Boss: [dying, while the squad is under fire] Need bacta... commandos...
Scorch: Can you die later, sir? It just isn't a good time now.
There are many more. Just buy it, I won't spoil the fun.
Finally, enemies: we have CIS droids, ranging from weak B1 droids, through Super Battle Droids to huge and OP Spider Walkers (gotta have nightmares after fighting them :/ ). There are also trandoshans (if you kill trando merc, shoot his backpack to turn them into angels going to the heaven. Just a hint) and geonosians of various ages: straight from the eggs up to blue flying bugs with beam weapons (also, terrible to fight against). But they are all killable, with some effort.
To sum up - this is a solid game. It has humour, challenge, good story, characters, effects and physics (last two - up to the 2005 level). I could hazard a guess that even  if it wasn't part of such franchaise, it would be great. Also, try reading Karen Traviss' Republic Commando novel series before or right after finishing the game - it expands the history of republic commando squads and makes the game even more awesome when you know more about it's characters.

Ahhh, Factorio. It is finally time to write my long overdue review of you.
As of the time of review, I have had this game for over 4 years when it wasn't even on steam, hence why I actually have pretty low hours compared to some, and just to prove I had this back all those years ago, the old character was taller, no visable axe or guns being carried and was blue.
But now is not the time to compare old and new, so let the review commence.
The main pros to factorio is that you can automate literally EVERYTHING, what the basically means is that when you get tired of manually mining coal for example, you can build machines that will do that mining for you, same can be done for crafting of ammo, spare tools and more machines to automate, which is just so much easier than going mining, building the thing needed and going mining again.
There are also a whole logistic side of it aswell which includes robots, logic chests (active, passive etc), automated repairs, train signals and enabling/disabling or certain factory areas automatically to save fuel and electric.
On top of all this, It is ****ing addictive
Now for the bugs
This may seem surprising, but with me currently running the experimental (0.16.x time of review) I have found ONE issue with the game and that is the simulation speed command and a crash when it was set too high by me while waiting for the map to be revealed.
Now this is classed for your computer specs, after building for a while on a single factory, autosaves will start to take longer and longer, that is only due to the computer saving everything, including the known map, all particles, where every item is and what buildings are where, if there are trains moving and at what speed and what is currently in the pipes and the progress of everything being made, with my current factory (thousands upon thousands of items lying around and easily over 70 things happeing at once) the longest autosave has only taken 3-4 seconds which is impressive due to how much is going on that it needs to remember, but as I said it really comes down to what specs your computer is, a good, high end one will easily do the same thing at a much faster rate while a lower end one may take ten seconds to autosave.
Overall I definately recommend this game, and even more so to people who are bored of something like Minecraft being repetitive

An enjoyable action-RPG. The game is initially somewhat difficult due to a lack of ranged weapon availability. Once you pick one up though things become much easier. It's WASD controls with keys assigned to weapon swap, dodge and block. You have a special meter that allows you to use skills you unlock at 1st, 5th, 10th, and 15th. Each class has specific weapons it can use along with 4 skills. There are generic weapons / armor etc. that all classes can use as well. There are four classes from which to choose with a variety of loot to collect and equip. You earn dragon scrolls by playing new adventures that you can use to 'Fight the Dragon'. This beast starts with 1 million HP and you can use multiple dragon scrolls to whittle down his health. You will die multiple times but are rewarded based on the amount of damage you can do before biting the dust. The dragon's HP is persistent so next time you'll whittle it away even more...The adventure creation kit is fun and easy to use and is the real draw of this - creating, sharing and downloading adventures. There is an excellent feedback system so you can see how many folks have played your adventures, the ratings they provided and any feedback / comments they have to help you improve. Online multiplayer co-op is available as well though I have not tried it.
TL;DR : Enjoyable loot-based ARPG. Easy to use adventure creation kit that you can share with friends to play co-op. Persistent dragon HP mechanic is interesting as you do all you can over the course of your adventures to take it down.

Its been very seldom in my PC-gaming life that I have discovered a true gem of a game. FTD is such a game. I will break it all down into three parts: single player, online play ( multi-player), and creative. But first one thing that strikes me from the start: the graphic design of the game is such that it will ( or should) run on low-end computers. The visuals are, for lack of a better term- quirky. Its like a cross between Legos games and LBW with a dash of WoW.
*Single player- In single player you go to an "adventure" screen where you can bring up an incredible assortment of maps to play on. It should be noted ( im guessing here) that over 90% of the availible maps are created BY OTHER PLAYERS. This is both a blessing and a curse: Player-made content is wide and varied. You may get a great and fun map; you may get one that was obviously made by a ADD 12-year old.
If you enjoy a player-made map, you can choose to "follow" that creator. This is a wonderful feature that highlights other maps made by favorite creators. Very nice feature.
* Multiplayer- I cannot honestly say I have much exp with this. Problem is that most of the games going are "closed" ( ie friends only). I have only been in one MP map and I got there near the end of the run. Overall it was ok.
* Creative- Now THIS is the reason why I think FTD is easily one of the best games in years; The UI that is used to make maps is very user-friendly. I have exp making maps for other games and its usually a bad learning curve. With ACK ( the map editor) I was making a map within 30 min of starting. You can "publish" ( make availble to other players) your creations via a simple-to-understand vetting process. This process ( I assume) is used to keep junk maps from being offered. It works....most of the time.  You may still come across just plain bad maps.
The bad side ( there has to be one right?)- The selection of enemy ( monsters etc) to place in maps are VERY limited. For a sword & sorcery game not to include enemy human casters? There are no, say, "friendy" men-at-arm NPCs to use. The list goes on. I can hope that all this will be added in future ( and free!) DLC.
Overall- Simple but effective combat system, graphics that are cute but not kiddy, an incredible creative tool, and MP options to boot.
I hope the devs of FTD get really REALLY rich, because they actually DESERVE it!

I really enjoyed this game (played it for 89.5 hours). It is a simple strategy/operational level game, but you have to think and build your units for tactical level warfare.  I enjoyed trying to build the French armies as close to possible to the historical ones based on the various French Corps commanders.  You do need to keep a standing army to watch your backside/coastal regions or the British will land behind you.  I also built a reasonable capable French frigate fleet and denied the Med to the British, which helped.  Watch out for diplomacy, know who is allied and protected by whom, and try to pick off any independents you find ASAP (though that makes everyone else like you less and less).  Definitely worth it when it is on sale, for those who enjoy this sort of game.  I was also able to mod it to add different units and to tweek the strength of certain units (after which they came out with the unit packs, British and French).  The programmer even answered an email when I got stuck at one point trying to mod something. He has moved on to their later WW1 and WW2 games, but I was impressed.

TL;DR An excellent digital board game with solid tactics and a bit of RNG.
Pros:
+ Beautiful environments
+ Good soundtrack
+ Fun strategy
Cons:
+ Expensive character/expansion ownership
+ Occasional poor frame rate
Armello is a lovely digital board game with good lore and characters. The game is very strategic in that there are several different ways to win, and several different tactical methods for winning each way. This variation provides great replayablility options.
This game heavily involves dice rolls, so be sure to keep that in mind when considering a purchase. I’ve found the RNG to be solid-truly random, which is great.
I have occasionally encountered drops in frame rate, nothing incredibly significant, but worth mentioning. Owning all of the characters (DLC) is a bit pricey, but well worth it if you enjoy the base game. Additionally, the base game includes 8 different characters with different stats and strategies which gives you ample playing options to help you decide if buying the DLC is worth it for you.
All-in-all, I definitely recommend this game as a fun, engaging, and well packaged table top game.
Happy gaming!

I was introduced to this game by a friend and I fell in love with it from the moment I started playing it. It is a tale of a kingdom's tragic spiral into chaos and the fight to end a king slowly dying upon his throne, sick and twisted by a foul corruption, The story made me feel sorrow and pity towards the denizens of the kingdom because I felt like I could connect to that conflict. "No matter who wins the struggle for power, the strength of the kingdom is still lost as the bond of those who formed it disipates into the fires of war".
As for the gameplay, it brought back the enthusiasm I had in tabletop RPGs long ago. Everything is easy to understand for beginners, but still provides a challenge to long time players. The choice of characters and their traits actually makes me feel like I could play as any of them with ease and no matter how south things go in a game, there's a way to turn it around thanks to there being multiple ways to win. The constant threat of royal guards, perils set by the king, and corruption kept things interesting every game. Get some friends together and the chaos will ensue as the game gets more intense as the days pass.
I know this isn't much to say about the game considering that I love it, but Armello is my go to game when I need to get my mind off of things or when I just feel like playing a game. The story connects to my heart and the gameplay reminds me of the joys back when I played D&D when I was younger. I'm getting everything for this game because the devs definatly deserve the support.

So summary, fun game a bit glitchy, if you like board games like these and can look past the glitches go for it it's not that bad.

Or the main logic loop will freeze up and the gameplay halts entirly.  For the technically inclined, this is likely due to bad IPC or multi-threading.  That's an educated guess, I did not spend time dissembling,
However, great art and game design with gameplay that's very unique and a breath of fresh air.  But not one of those companies willing to own up to their downfalls.  Instead releasing new content (which costs extra, fyi).  This is coding 101.  Bugs first, everything else second.  But that mantra does not appear to exist here.
Is the game good?  Absolutely.  Is it stable?  No.  And that will kill your otherwise fun gaming mood in a heartbeat.  If there ever was an abandonment or the code open sourced (unlikely IMHO) then they could easily be fixed.  Until then I would stay away.  I'd create a community patch but I would likely be met with hostility, where other companies would welcome it.
Hats off to the game designers and artists.  Credit goes where it's due.

Before I bought this game I was sceptical for various reasons. I've read most of the reviews on Steam and elsewhere, but  even though it's praised for the incredible visuals (obviously), little is said about the actual gameplay - specifically after the early access release. Also, some of the reviews make it seem like the gameplay is only enjoyable when playing multiplayer.
Having now spent the best part of a Sunday playing single player mode I really feel happy about the game.
The only real story time in the game is a brief tutorial (acting as a prologue) that introduces you to the 4 main characters and the surprisingly easy gameplay mechanics. You *will* find yourself wishing for more, and that's okay, but this is where Armello stays true to being a digital boardgame - you have to make your own story.
The first time a little critter died I was pretty shocked, but then it respawned and all was well with the world. Needless to say you get used to dying... a lot.
Apart from the awesome cut scenes (that's no doubt the thing that caught your attention in the first place), there are over 100 collectable item | spell | trickery cards that are beautifully animated. As you play the game over and over again you discover more and more cards and it becomes quite a challenge to find new ones.
This is a world akin to Brian Jacques' Redwall. It has also been compared to Game of Thrones for some reason... it's probably all the dying and the creepy king. But really this is something quite unique. The collectible cards mentioned before really help to flesh out the world of Armello.
According to the developer forum they are planning and actively working on content for the game, like a Bandit Clan DLC that will introduce a new clan of 4 heroes and
- Scheduled to release Q2 2017.
Buy the game. Be patient. Enjoy the small things.

I read the reviews on this game and held off for some time as both Sniper and Sniper 2 were, frankly, bad.  Sniper 2 improved a little but it was still stuck in 1990's in terms of polish and mechanics.
Once the sales started I decided to take a punt on this game and I'm actually glad I did.   I'm from the "Sniper Elite" camp so this game needed to be up to scratch for me.   It actually is.
(Side note: The theme tune for this game is actually stunning.  I listened to it for some time before actually playing the game!)
As most people are saying, you need to play this game on AT LEAST HARD mode, this will open up the weapons and make you think about your shots.  You don'y get much ammo early on in the game, so those 20 shots must count.
The bullets arc as you would expect and taking down a target from 350m+ brings a smile to your face as you watch the bullet snake and dip into the target.   From a gun play point of view, this game is lots of fun.  I've only played 3.2 hours, but it was all spent exploring the map and finding the longest shots I could, to take down rebels.
The bullet cam is a nice touch but it does not quite have the impact, visually, that the cams in Sniper Elite do.  They feel like pre-rendered animations rather than how a person taking a round to temple would drop.  They either fall forward, or fall back - no real dynamic intertia model here. Even taking someone out from the side has the same animation, slight sideways wobble and then either falling back or forward.   Oddly, when not in "bullet cam" the deaths are far more convincing.
The Drone mode is a nice touch and really does help you plan take downs and long shots.  The way it hovers around and circles feels like a real drone and is a joy to whizz around the tree tops.  You get about 250m range but you can zoom in so you can survey up to around 1km when you have a clear view.
You can craft items in this game from items you find on the map, but I've not played with that too much.  I don't quite understand what it's trying to do as you can'y craft anything you cant buy, so it seems a bit pointless.  It might bear fruit later in the game maybe?
The campain is "so so" - I have to admit I lost interest straight after the prologue and the characters are just plain odd and don't seem to gel well to "why they are there"   The voice acting is just awful and sounds like it's being read from a story board.   The swearing in the game is oddly placed as well.  I'm no prude by any stretch, but the overuse of it just dumbs down the game for me.  I know it's supposed to be "Boo-yah!" and "F**k yeah", but come on!  Lets have some actual dialogue that helps the story along??
The villager NPC's are awful, they just stand around looking off into the distance and muttering inane drivel.   You can walk right up and nothing happens, no interaction, no moving away.  Bizarre.
GFX wise, it's a nice game to look at and the sounds are well thought out, like the slight squeak of a vinyl seat as you get in and out of the jeep you can drive.    On that, The driving is dreadful but functional.  I didn't buy it for that.
The maps are huge and you will find plenty do in the side missions.
In closing, If you enjoy the Hitman games and Sniper Elite you will get enjoyment from this game for sure.  Just ignore the voice acting (if you can) and take adavantage of the open world, then its a really enjoyable game.  Just get it when it's on sale!

Grand Theft Auto IV, a game that blew everyone's minds just because of the graphics. And then you realized San Andreas had way more to offer with less graphics. So what would be a solution to making a game seem so great with limited variety? Add some Downloadable Content that probably should of been in the game since Day One but at the same time make you feel like it is optional. Well I guess that's not entirely how Episodes of Liberty City was formed, just most DLC in general. Although this DLC I'll give some credit, you don't have to buy the original game to play it, which is pretty neat. Though makes you kind of wish all the content in Episodes of Liberty City would be indluded in the orignal game. I'll explain later on that but for now let's talk about the Episodes starting with the first one mostly everyone picked first, The Lost and the Damned. Okay maybe I picked it first.
So the Lost and the Damned, what's it about. It's about a Biker named Johnny, who's no way related to a Greaser named Johnny back in another Rockstar game called "Bully," who all he wants is to ride with his Biker Gang and assist. The name of the Biker Gang is called "The Lost," who's runned by Billy who was in rehab for drugs. Supposably Johnny and Billy were great friends but since Billy's return it appears to not be as strong anymore. You even get a sense of betrayal is coming up. Well Spoiler Alert that's kind of what happens. The Lost and the Damned is basically Bully just shorten with blood and guns. Oh yes, the episode itself is not as long as the original game which is kind of dissapointing especially since these episodes are playable stand-alone. What's more the story of each episode takes place during the original game's timeline. So you would think there would be more going than just helping a mere Biker Gang with the Leader getting arrested all in attempt to get rid of Johnny. Though it may be short in story, it does add new weapons and do they play the part in a Biker Gang. From Automatic pistols to the classic sawed-off Shotgun. As you progress you'll gain other new weapons not seen in Grand Theft Auto IV, but since the story's short, it won't take long at all. Oh and Johnny has a problem playing dress-up. Yeah if you were thinking of making Johnny wear something other than a leather jacket for the whole game, I'm afraid that's not possible. Although I wouldn't mind the same kind of Jacket being worn by Niko Bellic, oh well next Episode.
The other is known as "The Ballad of Gay Tony," and I won't lie, I thought you was going to play as Tony, but this Episode has the "Legend of Zelda Syndrom" meaning you play as another guy. And this guy is pretty much a Dominican Quagmire who goes by the name "Luis." Tony is the man you work for due to personal reasons that involve Luis' history with Tony. No nothing like that, more like Tony helpped Luis when Luis needed help though most. So Luis feels honorbound to help and work for Tony no matter what. Unlike The Lost episode, Ballad feels more lively. And it may not be as short as The Lost (though still far shorter than GTA IV) but there was much going on. Also like The Lost, this takes place during Grand Theft Auto IV's timeline, more specifically right after the Bank Robbery. You soon meet Tony and you're off to some meet, which ends up in a big fire fight trying to get out the door. Though this also introduces you to one of the new weapons in this Episode, but soon later in the game you realize both episodes have their own exclusive guns and weapons. As much I like The Lost in style, Ballad has my vote for most content. I mean there's a bunch of guns in it that really should have been in the original game from the start. But doesn't matter which one you like, it's an automatic hands down that the Shotgun in this game is Over Powered. Why? Explosive Rounds. The Ballad of Gay Tony is the only episode part of the GTA IV timeline that features Explosive Round ammunition. And boy could it do damage to EVERYTHING! Also early in the game you get to high jack a new Helicopter, a buzzard which unlike the orignal or the Lost features Rockets and Miniguns. The moment you started piloting it, you just didn't want off. Also Parachutes are in it. Guess what, they wasn't in Grand Theft Auto IV, big suprise. And where as Johnny didn't like playing dress-up Luis has no problems with it. Though doesn't like buying clothes so might as well wear what you have. I mentioned before how both of the episodes are part of the same timeline, What you might be wondering is what is Ballad's part of the story other than being bossed around by a gay guy. Well really this is the Episode that explains a bit on the whole Diamond thing that partially was around in Grand Theft Auto IV and as well in The Lost episode. But this shows how it started and how it ended which you know, I'm glad. I'm glad because those Diamonds seemed useless to the story in Grand Theft Auto IV to begin with, and the fact you didn't get them in the end was like "What was the point?" This Episode gives the point but I still think the Diamonds shouldn't of been a thing, but it works only for this Episode.
Is Episodes of Liberty City worth getting? Not alone, I would get this along with Grand Theft Auto IV just to understand most of the story. Also with both episodes quite short in story, you may end up feel like "what else to do?" There is a Multiplayer option which has the same options in the orignal Grand Theft Auto IV, however customizing your character is more limited in customization. This is not a Bad DLC / game, just I wouldn't recommend buying it without getting the original. It's fun to play as a rage fueled biker along with a sex crazed bar manager. And the content given is very nice. But the Story length for both is not really enough to get this alone. Now if you are planning to get Grand Theft Auto IV, then yeah get this just to experience a little bit more.

I have found out that PVP does not require max level characters. All PVP characters are set to level 18, rather, where characters are given 8 power tokens, four blue and four orange.

I would give a positive review for just about any Paradox title (yes, including Victoria II and Hearts of Iron III, as buggy as they may be), but this is a title I simply cannot baby for its mistakes.
To get one thing off the board immediately, I would NEVER recommend without this mod:
The reason for suggesting that mod is that it takes you, instead, back to pre-Napoleon era just prior to when he became First Consul, thus there is more time to play and less satellites of France (aka more countries to play as). Plus, the mod offers new technology and an uncommon chance to gain cores on conquered provinces--thus the freedom to build units/ships there.
----------------------------------
That being said, I cannot recommend the game in its vanilla state for reasons of simplicity. This game wins favorable points for its astounding combat system; I absolutely love watching battles go on, regardless of the size, and what the generals can make of situations. ...which brings me to my first issue: Generals. Some countries get an abundant amount of generals, receive a few, and some receive NONE. You have to give me credit, I pulled off a save as Egypt where I conquered all of Africa, Spain, and the Ottoman Empire; easier said than done when you only have ONE general and NO admirals to work with. In this sense, the game's only friendly toward countries like France, Britain, Austria, Prussia, and Russia. Fair enough, those countries are the center of attention, but I shake my head at the disallowed freedom to TRY and rise up as a lesser power.
For me, quite a significant issue is the lack of countries that can be freed; specifically, countries like Scotland, Norway, Iceland, Finland, Hungary, Romania, Serbia, etc. do not exist in the game, so they may not be liberated. AT THE VERY LEAST, Norway couldn't have been made available to liberate? Why not!? I don't give a horse's♥♥♥♥♥if "Norway didn't exist until 1905"; this is a game of imagination and 'what ifs'. If as France I wage war on Denmark, conquer Norway; I want the freedom to pretend that as part of the terms of peace I'm enforcing, I insist on a "Norwegian Norway". If conquering everything is how I'm going to play the game I'd just go play a more amateur title, like Supreme Ruler; I expect much more from my all-time favorite development studio.
Lastly, let me argue that the coalition system is confusing beyond comprehension (at least to me). Yes, the coalition leader must subsidize its members, but even so, if I'm at 200+ relations with France and in a PERFECT geographic and militaristic position to strike an enemy, why is Napoleon so anal on letting me in? I wish I could have a summary of reasons returned to me like in most other Paradox titles. In this sense, getting a coalition invitation is like a surprise birthday gift to me; only that I most often decline when I do receive an invite on the grounds that I'm unprepared for war.
Overall, I admit, I am almost on the fence on this one. With the mod posted above, I would recommend this game for one gold reason:
March of the Eagles may be overpriced, amateurish (compared to other titles), and essentially a mini game title. Be that as it may, it is a SUPERB game to gift a friend who's new to grand strategy titles. Want someone to start playing EUIV/CKII/Vicky with you but they're unsure of whether they want to buy such expensive titles? Send them this way, this will give them an idea of what to expect in the better titles.
Treat this game like a mini game title or "get to know Paradox" game for newcomers. Admittedly, $60 for the 4-Pack doesn't sound that bad, if you have 4 people you'd like to trick into the unresistable allure that is grand strategy.
Criticize, debate, ask, praise, as you desire.

Fight the Dragon is a hack-n-slash RPG-lite. The game is centered around custom-content. Things like custom heads, hair, and levels. The customization only goes so deep, though. This leaves custom levels feeling shallow.
The game has a large identity issue. There are several poorly explained and poorly used mechanics that are only there to make the game feel more like other games. For instance, some weapons require you to have a certain level to equip. This is fine and good, and it fits the gameplay very well. The game complicates this by adding skill-points that you unlock everytime you level up. This would be fine if it gave you more than 1 skill point per level, but instead your left with a restricted and overly complicated leveling system. It ruins the flow when you pick up an awesome weapon, only to find that you don't have high enough Luck or Strength to wield it.
Combat is your traditional "Click-Click-Click-Heal-Click" style of combat. It has the illusion of deepness, giving each class unique heavy attacks. These heavy attacks all boil down to about the same thing. You throw something, and in a second or two it explodes. Not a very original combat system, but it works well.
Customization is a mixed bag. You can customize the textures of your body, head, and hair. Basic stuff, not very hard to grasp at all. For more advanced people, you can customize the meshes of only the head and hair. This frustrates me a bit, but it doesn't really affect my view on the game.
The level editor is frustrating as hell. The controls require you to forget everything you know about good level editors, because none of it transfers over. Basic stuff is just omitted for no reason.
Overall, the game is fun. As of writing, I've put in about 4 hours into the game. 3 of which were spent on multiplayer. It's a little boring, but if you get it on sale it isn't bad.

If you ever decide to buy a Grand Theft Auto game for modibality, this should be your first choice. You are all probably familiar with Grand Theft Auto, shoot stuff, run over people, kill police officers and perfrom other violent, sadistic fun actions. This game does have a plot which crosses over with Grand Theft Auto 4, so some things may be unclear if you have not played it. Aside from all that, the amount of mods for this game, good God! You can get legitimate real life cars, have more traffic diversity, get an entirely new map, be a police officer, the sky is the limit. If you ever finish the game or get bored of going on rampages while taking countless lives, then the mods will increase your play time, there are so many! The excellent modability is what makes this game truly worthwhile, the money you will pay is a small price to pay for the endless gameplay capability. There are a few compatibility issues with Windows 8, and you need a nuclear powered computer to run this game with full graphics and all the mods, but frankly I have an adequate computer and I am able to run the LCPDFR mod and a couple car mods at medium settings quite well. In the end, this game is fantastic not only because of the mods, but because of its good plot, and wide lively envirnoment.

It's a fine, decent, average, playable 3D collectathon platformer. If you need one on PC?
Well, try playing Mario 64 and the Banjo games first, then come to this. Maybe start with Banjo Tootie if you want something weirdly morbid.
Anyway, there's not much to say. I wouldn't recommend this for 100% completionists because the placement of some of the opals (think coins from Mario) are really, horribly obscure and unsighposted, and you need to collect EVERY SINGLE ONE in order to get the corresponding thunder egg (Star/Jiggy). And leaving the level before collecting them all resets your collection. And there are 300, THREE HUNDRED, TROIS HUNDO, in each level. I once played through a level for about an hour trying to find the last 3, which were in a crate covered in snow on the side of a mountain with nothing else around it to make it an interesting area. What the criminy.
But, it has snappy controls, a fun setting, interesting music, creative achievements, and... a couple cute characters. Mostly the fat parakeet guy. He's great.
No alarms and no surprises. It's a 3D collectathon platformer.

Never has a game been more appropriately named than Satellite Reign. It’s a isometric, real time squad based RPG that focuses on upgrading your agents bodies (kidnapping civilians and police) and upgrading them (cloaking devices, muscle upgrades, spring legs ect) to take back control of a city from Dracogenics, whose crimes are worse than yours. It plays much like Syndicate (the old games, not the FPS version), but with enough differences that you know that this is not some knock off version.
There is no base in this game, you have 5 city blocks, and that’s your entire world. While you can do op’s in each city to make your life easier, you are never safe, and the areas are never under your control. Your weapons are never overpowered, you can’t just waltz in with a squad of agents kitted out to the teeth and hope to come out of it alive. This is where the tactical part comes in- each agent has a role, and their gameplay is based on that. While everyone can fight, there is a unit with a dedicated role for that. The hacker is who you want taking down camera’s and opening doors ect. This adds quite an element of thinking to the game, and if one of the agents makes a mistake (falling off a zip line, setting off a camera) then things hit the fan very quickly and can easily end up with the loss of most or all of the team. In most games that would be a reload, but in this the worse-case is some of your agents will respawn with lower stats at the closet satellite uplink you have setup. This makes for an enjoyable, slow planning stage and a fast and frantic action stage, usually including a very large firefight. Upgrading your agents isn’t as easy as picking out one upgrade in each category, as each affects your gameplay style, from stealth/hacking, soaking up damage, to respawning.
The world and background are slowly drip feed to the player, but other than the immediate parts relating to the game not much is explained (other than the company is evil and you are being paid to destroy them). There are logs around the world to collect, but again other than the CEO you are trying to kill, they don’t mean much as you don’t know who anyone is (if you pick up the Novella then all your questions are answered- I would recommend it as it adds so much to this game and is a good read anyway). It’s a bit of a shame that a lot of the plot isn’t explained as well as how the Novella puts it- if it was the sense of urgency and righteousness would be a lot higher. Also, a lot of logs would make much more sense other than the interesting back and forth between a few characters.
The city looks cyberpunk- all neon lights, faceless corporations, and futuristic weapons and abilities. Its looks stunning, and runs very well at 4K. the sound is excellent, and music suits the game as well.
I’m sure you can get 100 % achievements but looking at the grind it would involve I gave up- and I’ll usually stick through anything for 100%. I’m not sure if they would be easier with co-op but I didn’t like my chances in solo play. And the ending….that was good.

TL;DR : Screw you, game. You made me feel things. My twitchy, explosion-loving, FPS-playing gamer mind can't handle more feelings than "kill" and "murder". How dare you make me care about human lives. And dogs.
Pros:
+ The art. The animation is simple once you pay attention to it, but not in a "bad" simple way. It's 'minimalistic' (I can hear art majors screeching in the distance as I misuse that word). It does exactly what it has to in order to be expressive. The inked aesthetic of the art itself reminds me of a few indie graphic novels I can't put my finger on at the moment, but it's at once gritty but clean. Color is dull and vibrant at the same time. Oxymoronic, I know, but it's true. Characters are also immediately recognizable.
+ Gameplay. I was honestly surprised by the two "minigames" that you play, both evoking the DDR-style rhythym games I enjoy. Once I noticed the car chases were in time with the music I was actually smiling -- it was honestly super creative. I'm not good at puzzle games, so I'll admit there were times I got stumped. I imagine the rest of the gaming world can actually play games like this without using the hint system (which is another plus) so you can discount my stupidity if you must. A few of the puzzles were very smartly done too -- the ones where you have to open a vault with a number code are pretty cool. The "physics" puzzles involving grenades/dynamite are well done.
+ Characters/Story. Despite the speech being either a) speech bubbles with Spy vs Spy-esque levels of telegraphing what they're saying, or b) mumbled words (they are actually speaking, just super mumble-y), you honestly care about them. Each character has personality, and you care about each of their goals. One thing I should point out is that, because this is "The Great War" and not "
World War 2", you end up hating and loving both sides of the war. Yes, you end up caring about both German and French characters, mostly because this was a war fueled more by tangled alliances and shin-kicking rather than racism and gun-ho nationalism. At one point a German soldier (who only has a few minutes of screen time) dies in an artillery blast and I actually felt bad. You feel bad for everyone -- except, of course, the ridiculously characature-ized (I think I spelled that wrong) main antagonist. Finding real-life paraphernilia and reading about it in the journal definitely makes this a poignant adventure. Sure, there are definite liberties taken with the time period, inventions, battles, characters, etc. but it never feels... fake. It's a story, but it's steeped in realism, and you can tell.
+ The dog. The dog is wonderful. You can pet the dog. Any time the dog brings you something, you automatically pet the dog. Good dog. I will now, from here on out, rate games depending on if you can pet the dog or not. You should too.
Cons:
- I feel like saying "it's short" is a cop-out. But it is. I finished it in 6 hours, and this includes me getting stuck on puzzles and hunting around for as many secrets as possible. I'd say for the average person, this game will be about 4-5 hours long. If you're the kind of person that does a money-to-gametime ratio, you're paying 3 bucks for every hour of gameplay. (Many people try to shoot for a one-to-one ratio at the very least). The short length means that some parts feel exceptionally long and others extremely short, though not rushed, thankfully.
- A few really tough segments. And no, not puzzle ones either. There were three or maybe four parts that were extremely intense. Rarely does this game ever time you on anything (even when someone's screaming for help), but the times that you are, it's hard. Stuff like the screen automatically moving to the side and you have to keep up with it while dodging artillery. Or a part where you have to dig through a massive pile of dirt filled with un-exploded bombs while artillery falls from the sky putting MORE bombs in your path. It can be very frustrating.
- When you're facing Evil Von Wurstkopf, the tone goes from chillingly sad to kind of silly. It's good to break up the tone every so often but the villain just feels so... out of place. I mean, you HATE the guy, but he's over the top and silly. He's like the Chaos Space Marines from W40k: overcompensating their evil through yelling, crazy outfits, and murder. Except in this game, the Blood God is the ever-churning machine of war.
- U-Play. Thankfully I never really have problems with it like others do, but I still roll my eyes and sigh when I see the box pop up saying "opening uplay". I get that this game is from Ubisoft but, y'know, UGH.
ALSO NOTE: PLEASE DON'T READ THE U-PLAY ACHIEVEMENT LIST UNTIL YOU FINISH THE GAME! It sounds obvious, and thankfully I didn't check until the game was done, but there's a few spoilers in the list. If you're an achievement hunter, wait until your second play-through to get them all.
Oh yeah, another Con.
- Achievements on U-Play but not on Steam.
Basically, buy this. If you like historical games, WW1, or dogs, you'll like this. Also, check out Verdun on Steam too (the battle of Verdun is actually in this game too!). It's a WW1 shooter that's actually pretty good if a little tough at first. Since Battlefield 1 is coming out in a week or two and it looks like it might rub history buffs the wrong way, then Verdun is a good way to nail headshots while still wearing a tweed jacket and smoking a pipe like the historical nerd you are.
So basically you get history, sadness, dogs, gritty violence (though there's no gore), and small little vignettes of people's lives as they struggle with one of the most terrifying and brutal wars in human history. You will get shot. You will get hit with artillery. You will choke to death on chlorine gas. You will walk over piles of corpses to push the assault. You will see enemies as friends, and friends as enemies. You will see death. And you
pet the dog.
6 hours well spent

I read the reviews and was a little cautious when I bought this game, but after playing a little bit I am pleasantly surprised. One of the reviews I saw described it as Far Cry with Sniping elements. I think that description nails it on the head. The gunplay is fun with weapons feeling different enough for me to switch between them. The stealth and stalking aspects have their ups and downs (as is with any game with open world AI), but overall I enjoyed it. It didn't feel unfair and it didn't feel too easy. I've only put in 5 hours so far, but I'm having fun and can't wait to get back to it to complete the story and side missions.
Pros:
- Bullet time - It's cheesy, but I like it.
- Graphics - I have a 1080ti and a 4670 so I am  able to max out the settings. The game looks great, especially when I'm climbing a snow covered mountain to get to a good sniping spot
- Gameplay - Go places, kill things how you like. The game is all about what you make of it. You can easily run and gun sections with an AK, but the game truly shines when you use all of the sniper tools available to you (drone, marking, luring, etc.)
- Season Pass - Knowing that there will be more content to come is always nice.
- Gun Variety - Like snipers? There are a ton of sniper rifles with different customization options.
- Open World - Reviews say the open world is largely empty, but the environment isn't necessarily a metropolis. You're in the back country with worn down buildings and churches. I feel the population is apt for the environment. I enjoy fighting vehicles, humans, and even wolves (you get to collect resources from all of these).
Cons:
- Tutorial - The game doesn't hold your hand and you'll figure things out as you go. Not really a bad thing for me, but a lot of people expect to learn a good portion of the game in the tutorial
- AI - The AI will randomly do some wonky things, like run right into the open to get shot in the face. Most of the time they find cover that will benefit them, but other times they will see a mate die in front of them and hide in an open area.
- Repetition - I enjoy the gunplay and resource collection, but others will not. Understand that you are given tools to play this game in a variety of ways and you'll do just fine.
Overall, I'd say the $25 is a bargain for a game with as much content as this. I've been putting more hours into this game than Sniper Elite 4. The kills and environment just feel more genuine. Again, just my .02.

Long Story short: Yes, I do recommend this game.
Why? Read.
Short introduction:
Star Wars Republic Commando is a rather short FPS where you take the role of a clone Commando-Squad, the "Delta-Squad", consisting of four Elite clonetroopers: Boss, the squad leader (which you control), Fixer, the heavy arms guy, Scorch, the guy with the "l33t hax0r skillz" (actual quote), and Sev, the Sniper. In the course of the game these four troopers have to fulfill various objectives, such as stopping the Separatists from extracting from Geonosis.
Story:
As much as I'd like to tell you otherwise: The Story is rather irrelevant. It does help to know the sorroundings just a little, but in the overall game it is irrelevant. That's mostly because the sorroundings have either no effect on the Gameplay or are explained to you when relevant.
Sound:
I'll quote Wikipedia on this one: "Republic Commando features a darker and more militaristic soundtrack " than the rest of Star Wars. What this means is: You can hear that it's Star Wars, it's just adapted to the setting of the game.
Regarding the overall sound: The weapons sound authentic, not that it would be hard to make a blaster sound like a blaster, especially heavier weaons, for example the cannons of Republic Assault Ships. Futhermore background noises exist, e.g. the battle on Geonosis and the Fauna on Kashyyyk. Also: The enemies sound like enemies and not just random AI. Why? The Super-Battledroids complain about being hit and some enemy classes keep on complaining about their weapons always being empty. So: breddy gud.
Gameplay:
Oh boy. Now comes the interesting part.
As mentioned before, you control Boss, the squad leader. This means that you can/have to order your squad to do certain things, such as taking position to use a Sniper or planting explosives, so that you can advance to your objective. All this while being overwhelmed by enemy forces, who obviously try to stop you.
There are several points to make, though:
1. Your squadmates are absolutely loyal. Tell them to revive you while under enemy fire; they'll come to help you, complaining about "recommended protocols". Tell them to plant a bomb amidst four to five Super-Battledroids, they'll do, even if they die trying. What does this mean? The AI may not be dumb, but it certainly does not improvise.
2. You are always overwhelmed and under pressure. Just like a true SpecOps team.
3. No medkits. You can only regenerate health at Bacta-tanks, which are rather rare. You do have a weak energy-shield which stops you from taking damage directly for a few hits, though.
4. You are always in dire need of ammo (atleast if you waste as much ammo is I do). Although you can pickup some enemy weapons, you can only pickup one at a time, and that weapon may not be that helpful (e. g. Wookie rocket launcher).
Multiplayer: I'll skip this one, as it requires a workaround, because GameSpy is dead.
Conclusion: This game is pretty fun, if you can survive a little anger, although I'd recommend buying it on sale, as it it took me only ~3 days-ish to complete.

Some games are short but sweet, concluded after a single, glorious play session. Others require a few sleepless weeks of dedicated play to unlock all of their mysteries. Then there are the very few games that take on a whole digital life of their own – that become a part of the player’s daily ritual for years to come, with more to gain and accomplish than you could ever truly quantify. Animal Crossing: New leaf is one of the latter. It’s also one of the most charming, addictive games I’ve ever played.
There's a whole lot of "new" in New Leaf, but before I get to that, rest assured that the core mechanics that have kept gamers playing for years after the release of prior installments are as strong as ever. The main idea behind any Animal Crossing game is that players move into a new town and spend their days building up relationships with villagers, harvesting fruit, fishing, catching bugs, decorating their house, and tackling the almost innumerable other activities that comprise one’s Animal Crossing life. It doesn’t sound like a to-do list that would necessarily make for the most enthralling game, but that’s exactly what it amounts to. There’s something about the relaxing rhythm of each activity that keeps you coming back for more, bolstered by the subtle yet effective way the game incentivizes you to keep playing, keep collecting, and generally keep on keeping on.
What sets New Leaf apart - and makes it a cut above the rest - is that the barriers laid down in past entries have largely been lifted, allowing for a sense of freedom, creation, and ownership like never before. As the acting Mayor (a first for the series), you’re now able to decorate not just the inside of your house, but the outside too, as well as your whole village. From the very outset you have a hand in deciding the layout of your village and the placement of your house, and eventually it’s all on you to decide the location of certain establishments (like The Roost and the Police Station), as well as to determine what decorations will grace your town and where they’ll go. You can place a miniature Stonehenge by the beach, a Zen bell by the train station, some streetlamps by your favorite villager’s house, or even surround your own place (which can be a castle, if you like) with fountains. The possibilities expand the more you play, as villagers keep making suggestions for possible Public Works projects to improve your town. You can even personalize specific pieces of furniture by taking them over to Cyrus at the resell shop, ensuring that your home and village will be quite distinct from anyone else’s.
Evolving your stomping ground in this way is irresistible, as over time you watch it grow from a simple collection of houses to something truly amazing and unique. Having this freedom to shape your village to reflect your personality like never before truly enriches the experience. It’s always been easy to fall in love with your village in Animal Crossing games, but now it really feels like your village, like a place you helped build from nothing, somewhere you really have a personal stake in. You’re not just a museum patron, you’re the one who funded its growth and filled its halls with fossils, fish, and bugs. You’re not just a club-goer, you’re the one who spear-headed the campaign to bring the music venue to your village in the first place. It’s a delightful improvement that makes the experience impossible to put down, as there’s always another project you can help fund and  another thing you can do to set your village apart from the rest. The brilliant thing is that Nintendo found a way to expand upon the gameplay of past entries without compromising the simplicity and charm that made the series so beloved to begin with. This is the evolution of Animal Crossing, and it’s an absolute wonder to behold.
One of the most astounding things about New Leaf is how much there is to do. In just a few weeks I’ve put in well over a hundred hours, and there’s still so much I’d like to accomplish. In addition to the familiar activities, new additions like diving and swimming allow you to explore and interact with your town in a whole new way. It’s refreshing, and a whole lot of fun. Completing public works projects, customizing furniture, and visiting the variety of shops across the tracks will also take up their fair share of time, and Nintendo fans will be pleased to know that there’s now a whole range of Big N items you can acquire to decorate your house with (so if you’re interested in getting a Triforce or Metroid for your living room, be sure to buy those fortune cookies on sale in the Nook brothers’ shop). Throw in new holidays, new characters (like Reese and Cyrus from the resell shop), new clothing options (pants!), new furniture and so on, and you’re left with an experience that is fresh, yet familiar. Simple, yet refined.
Then there’s the multiplayer, which is far beyond anything the series has ever attempted previously. As expected you can visit your friends’ houses either online or locally – dropping off gifts if you’re a good friend or chopping down their trees and messing up their flowers if you’re a big jerk. But that’s just the start. You can also visit “dream versions” of other villages in the Dream Suite. This allows players to upload their town for friends and strangers alike to visit. The genius part is that nothing visitors do actually affects the person’s real town since it’s just a dream. So you can go crazy stomping flowers and♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off neighbors without paying the consequence of never being invited over again. Getting to be so bad without any negative repercussions is cathartic to say the least, and is a great way to encourage you to open your village to outsiders without the risk of a rude visitor ruining your town (and your day).
For players who crave a more corporeal form of interaction, you can also engage in a series of delightful mini-games with players across the globe on Resort Island, headed up by the former Animal Crossing mayor, Tortimer. The island’s perpetual summer is rather relaxing, and provides a great opportunity to stock up on seasonal fruit, beetles, and sharks for the selling. It’s also convenient that you are fully able to enjoy the island and its diversions all by yourself if, for whatever reason, you don’t feel like going online. Finally, StreetPass has been utilized to allow you to view the houses of anyone you pass who has a copy of the game. It’s really cool getting to see everyone’s different decorating styles, as well as being able to purchase the items that catch your eye. In a way, it creates the illusion of a persistent game world for you and your StreetPass friends, which is a nice touch.
While the customization, variety, and multiplayer are certainly the highlights, pretty much everything in New Leaf has been refined to make this as delightful an experience as possible. The simple graphics have been touched up so that fuzzy animals are now actually fuzzy and larger animals tower over the smaller ones. Little things like being able to group fruit together in your inventory so you can carry more, donate multiple fossils at the same time, or tell which flowers you’ve watered thanks to a new sparkling effect go a long way towards making the small chores that pack your day-to-day life easier than ever. These might seem like small details barely worth noting, but anyone who has ever played Animal Crossing will likely agree that, much like in life, it's all in the details.

Very nice, very niche game, gameplay is a solid RPG-flavored turn-based strategy board game with an emphasis on dice rolling, card/hand management, item collecting and adapting your playstyle on the fly since there is a heavy amount of RNG; how the map is laid out, what quests you get, what items you get, what spawns where, etc.
While there isn't much of a story, the setting is immensely thought out, and the art style of the game is undeniably charming and amazingly detailed. I would pay a lot of money for a graphic novel or animated film set in this world.
Online multiplayer is somewhat barren, but it's easier to find a game than you might think and if you can convince three friends to buy it for private games, it will last you quite a few - thought, admittedly, the gameplay can get somewhat repetitive as the roster is small and the overall structure of the game is fairly simplistic.
Definitely worth it if you're into strategy and/or RPG games, and like multiplayer.
