I love Armello, I really do love it, both the gameplay and mechanics it has to offer and the characters's designs with their unique abilities. The skins are a good implementation (though I haven't gotten any of the character things, and I'll explain why later) and the random events that form part of your adventure's development are one of the things I love the most from this game.
I like that you can wear different types of rings and amulets at the start to have a bit of your own customization, and that you can act with 3 types of decks, get followers that aid you, etc.
The music is nothing too original or anything like that, but it's not annoying and it fits well regardless.
I like that you can have multiple ways of winning a match, some more risky than others, but all of them are interesting to try if you like finding your own way to victory through different paths.
I can say that this game is worth buying and playing, if a friend is recommending this to you so you can play with him/her, do it. Hell, if you have more than 3 or 4 friends who have this game and who would like to play it with you, then buy it. This game is great when it comes to multiplayers.
Now, since this is a game meant for multiplayer, here are some flaws that you HAVE to consider if you really want this game:
-First, sometimes people will ragequit and MAY make you or another player be stuck where they are, forcing all of you to leave the game, this can anger some people but it's not something that will happen 100% of the times, since when someone disconects, they are replaced by an AI. (I personally haven't found this too bad of a flaw and it just happens like 5% of all the matches I've had)
-The game rewards you for playing online, giving you keys or chests at the end of a match, this is a great concept that unfortunately is affected by the first flaw, so I wanted to mention that this bug will mean that the match will be stuck and that no one will earn the rewards that you use to get skins, this can be bad but as I said before, don't think it's something that is going to happen that often.
Now... this is my biggesst complain, I was really thinking on relunctanctly not recommending this game, that's how bad it is but it's not really the game's fault:
-This game has a growing community, meaning that most of the time there's going to be around 190 people playing and you will most likely not find anyone joining, like I do. I really want to play this game, but during this month all the times I've tried playing online have resulted in me not finding absolutely anybody. Maybe this game has region blocking or something and that's why it's harder for me to find people (that's my guess at least), but I really CAN'T FIND ANYBODY ONLINE, meaning that I can't play the most enjoyable thing about this game anymore cuz I can't find people online that easily.
I used to just click to play online and I wouldn't wait too much before entering a match, now it looks 97% impossible to find someone, in fact, after looking for people for the 9th time I've opened this game, NOW I just found someone online, JUST ONE person... they left 10 seconds later... ♥♥♥♥ you if you are that person, by the way.
I do recommend this game cuz it's fun to play with friends, wich is why I said before that if you got people who play it or who would like to play it with you, thn it's worth buying, the more people you got that play armello the better the possibilities you'll enjoy this game, but if you have no friends who play this game then MAYBE you'll have a harder time getting to find people online.
However, if you get this game, you do help the community to keep growing and in time it'll be easier to find people online to play with, THAT was the only reason I changed my mind from not recommending to recommending this game.
So yeah, with nothing else to say, buy it so this game keeps growing and specially if you got friends who have this, it's a great game but the lack of people keeps it from being one of my favourite games.

An excellent game based on the archetypical Paradox Interactive 'Europa Universalis'.
Nonetheless the experience is quite different.
The game is made more thematic and focussed on the Napoleonic Wars. The periode is also far shorter. (20 years roughly)
And the game manages to reflect the flavor of the period through the 'coalitation' system an era specific techtree and a focus on warfare between allies.
The events are thematic although I'd have loved to see more of these.
War will be almost a constant and victory is achieved by obtaining key areas for land or sea dominance.
The best part of this game is the combat system. For the first time you have an indepth control over troop composition, formations, tactics, generals and subcommanders.
This impacts the game greatly and you can end up having your armies specialize. Concepts such as experience, frontage, supplies etc are very important.
In conclusion if you're a Napoleonics fan, enjoy the EU engine and you want a quick, fun strategic experience then go for it.
Wait for a small discount and pick up the 2 DLCs that'll add some more visual flair. And you'll be set to go.

This game has some really great potential, but there are a lot of issues holding it back that really hurt the experience.
Firstly, the AI. It's ridiculously grabby and cares little about what it's grabbing. France, for example, can and will take anything from stripes (yes, stripes) of sweden and finland (problematic for obvious reasons) to a chunk of northern portugal, while England, meanwhile, is happy to take Norway, Hannover, or even parts of Bulgaria.
Additional AI issue include ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ diplomacy choices (in a game as Saxony, my Prussian overlord declared war on Sweden without reason, and followed it up on a war with Bavaria - inexplicably allied with both the English and French while they were coalitioned against eachother, only to white peace with Bavaria). And it's extremely rare to see a proper coalition war, sadly, where many of the greats get involved.
Regarding the combat mechanics (which could stand to be better explained, since the tutorial doesn't do a good job of telling you how to keep armies efficiently supplied or how that at least works), armies tend to fight to the death much of the time and it's sometimes difficult to tell what's going on (ck2 may have spoiled me there). Sieges can be very random as well, with morale not having a good amount of consistancy (ie, france seiging a high-level fort that suddenly goes from maximum morale to surrender - it may be more realistic but the events need to be more visible, and I honestly prefer the EU4 & CK2 methods better). Additionally, in costal provinces, even if you have a substantial amount of artillery, there doesn't seem to be anything preventing sailing in reinforcements of a fort, to the point of aburdity, where you DON'T want the siege to end, since the army will then pop out and engage you (which can be very bad - the besieged army somehow isn't disarmed at all or even impeded in any way, resulting in a besieging army that lacked some supplies being routed if you aren't careful).
Another gripe I had was how prestige determines the winnder when the year hits 1820 and there's nobody with complete naval and land dominace, which, while it mostly gives the win to the nation actually winning, it does sometimes get it horribly wrong. Some combination of factors (such as multiplying total dominace with prestige, military strength, and/or other factors).
I'm a big Paradox fan (I love CK2, Hoi3, and EU4), but I can't reccomend this to others. If you want Napoleon, consider the EU4 bookmarks.

This is a game judged harshly for what it isn't and what people thought it was instead of for what it is and what it was meant to be. What this game isn't is a grand strategy game seeking to model every cultural and economic aspect of running a nation in Europe in the early 19th century. What this game is, to put it simply, is a Napoleonic version of Hearts of Iron. It's purely a war game and that's all it aspires to be, and as a war game it's pretty enjoyable. It's a masterpiece completely underrated and neglected by paradox, with the mods and dlc's their other games get this could be one of their best games, yet it's good anyway, unlike Europa Universalis it's completely focused on combat, so forget politics and marriages, it's time to BATTLE! The possibilities are endliess and no two armies are alike. Unlike every other Paradox game that isn't Hearts of Iron, this game's combat isn't a simple matter of just shoving two doom stacks into one giant province, watching floating numbers for a few seconds, and the other one scurrying off. It's about creating highly customised and unique armies commanded by countless possible commanders in order to give yourself a tactical edge. Combat is deep, nuanced, constant, and satisfying.

My previous review was the salty reaction to a save game gone horribly wrong. I am going to write an unbiased review now that I have a better understanding of this game.
WITH that being said, this game is still awful. It's a mini-game, a small sliver of a time period that you can actually enjoy in Paradox's flagship title, "Europa Universalis IV," with proper DLC. The difference is, you can enjoy many, many more hours of gameplay in EUIV than in this game. Reason being, is that you can actually play that game more than once and feel like you're having a different adventure each time. In this game, it's the same exact scenario every time; which would be okay if it was executed properly.
I'm a huge fan of most Paradox titles. This game, however, is a title I cannot recommend based on several factors.
- This game is very unfriendly to those who wish to play as a smaller nation.
- There is a very small selection of countries to play as (of course, unless you want to play as a puppet of France or Britain, but no matter who you play as that might as well be the case anyway.)
- There is not much to do except for watch France and Britain declare war on each other every five minutes.
Good things about this game:
- Combat! Yes, this game has a very good combat system. I was immensely impressed by how much depth there is to combat in this.
- Having a historical figure as menacing as Napoleon tormenting Europe. While this partially goes against what I wrote before, it is very engaging to try and create an army large enough to combat him, even if it is kind of impossible.
- It's true that this game feels like a mini-game, but from a certain point of view, for some players, that could be a good thing. Perhaps this game can be seen as a decent introduction to Paradox games for those who have never tried them before.
In conclusion, if you think the goods outweigh the bads, then it's worth trying out. Maybe you'll find enjoyment in this game. I personally don't recommend it because there are better alternatives and this game is very frustrating with the things it lacks.
I would also like to point out that a fine fellow politely informed me of something I was wrong about in my previous review. I had for whatever reason convinced myself (I am an avid lover of history, by the way) that this game did not in fact last the length of the Napoleonic era. That was wrong of me, and I must admit I do not know as much of the Napoleonic era as some do. But that's why we have peers! To point out when we are wrong and correct us in an ever so polite manner.
Thank you for reading, and please understand that the opinions expressed in this review are my own and you may have a completely different gaming experience than I had.

That being said, I can't help but feel they really dropped the ball on combat and movement.
Pros:
The loot system in the game is fairly well done. Judging by a few of the items I saw, some late game items will modify playstyles significantly enough to justify tags such as legendary. I love that you have a reason to pick up all your trash. The loot alter is a fantastic way to deal with that, although I'm not sure what else gold is used for, and as a result it feels tacked on as a system for getting trash loot without actually picking it up. It's certainly convenient but feels underwhelming as a whole. I'm not sure how I feel about Dragon Rings, but it's not a bad idea per se.
One of the best features of this game is the fact that the community creates content. To be honest not a ton of it wowed me, but there was quite a bit of it that was well done and as a result each run felt much better than a standard randomly generated run would.
Cons:
The game features an incredibly simplified combat system that gets repetitive, fast. It's not an issue by itself, but when coupled by the sliding, non-grounded movement the game just feels very poorly made from a design standpoint. It makes the game feel a bit fast and frantic, with almost no tactics involved. When you throw in a few more players it becomes awful trying to navigate through small areas due to player collision, which simply does not work in a game like this in my opinion. I can only assume most dungeons are designed for one player.
On a similar note, the game's difficulty does not scale well at all in 4 player groups. We were picking "extreme" difficulty missions every time and I don't think any of us ever took much damage. The only deaths we had were when we had to commit suicide because we jumped into a part of a dungeon we weren't suppose to be at yet and couldn't progress, or we knocked each other off of terrain from collision due to latency issues. It also doesn't seem like there's a lot of actual content in world building. Perhaps some content is level-gated, but we were seeing the exact same sets of environments, enemies, traps, and levers the entire time. If the community is able to bring in new art assets to worlds, this will likely be a non-issue, but the core game feels lacking in diversity.
Despite the name "Fight the Dragon" along with a tag for mutliplayer, you cannot fight the dragon with friends. It's just your standard ARPG run around getting loot game with no real bosses (at least that we've run into), which gets a bit boring. (to me at least, some people love that as a core)
tl;dr - Fight the Dragon has a great core idea, and I'm sure a ton of people will love it. I just can't help but feel the simplicity of the combat system mixed with the weird floating/gliding movement is holding it back from being an actual great game.

Worth playing for a few hours because the campaign is quite challenging and fun in places but probably not worth getting really into. It's got quite a good strategic element to it but it is quite heavily based on the luck of the draw. For instance in one battle against the final boss in a stage I drew nothing but movement and defence cards for three turns in a row and it was able to fully heal itself back up whilst I was left with no option but to run away, regroup and hope against all odds that my priest actually drew one of his dozen unusued healing cards still left in the deck and my mage would finally get a couple attack cards.
Admittedly it was satisfying when I finally managed to kill it after running around the whole level avoiding it for ten minutes but then on the next boss fight my mage drew three powerups at the start and then all my most powerful spells on the next go and just nuked it immediately.
It often doesn't seem particularly clear why this happens when my character's only have one additional movement card in their decks on top of the default one yet have a tonne of attacks and heals that rarely ever seem to appear.
The strategy comes from playing the hand you have as well as you can and that is good but it can be a little too random and unbalanced in this regard. I'm sure the multiplayer would be very annoying as a result but then I also suspect it is simply a pay to win job and not worth bothering with at all.
Like all 'free to play' games the in-app purchases are completely extortionate and not even remotely sensible. Rather than buying all the extra single player levels you could buy two or three good games on here which don't try and bleed you for money. If they were sensibly priced at $5 for ten levels or something I might be tempted to unlock them but the day I shell out $20 multiple times on in-app content is the day I want someone to shoot me in the face because I'll clearly be braindead...

As a fun game to kill time, i can't recommend it, because it's Luck: The Game.
Your cards are drawn randomly, so you can get, for example only moving cards when you need to kill last enemy, or only attack cards when you are far away from any enemy. And since you need to discard all but two cards in hand, at the end of the round, you can't do any elaborate tactics, if you lack the walking/attacking card.
Also some (i mean most) cards have random chance to activate, eg: roll +4 to block attack; for some reason enemies can roll 6 all the time, which means your attack does nothing, while your block/parry get 1-2, means enemies get all the damage on you.

Difficulty and game-design of this game is just tribute to good old video-game machines - tough difficulty, dozens of secrets,  score multipliers, memorable characters, unblockable characters, crazy weapons, aliens and sh*t.
If you looking for nostalgia, and wants to go back to your childhood, go for indies, Playstation 1/2 or Retro City Rampage.

Christ Almighty, what a buggy game. However once it's patched, there's a lot of fun to be had.
Overall, the game is quite enjoyable, but has some serious bugs that just ruin it.
The game plays more like FarCry than Sniper Elite, and apart from the prisoner rescue, there is no permanent clearance of enemies. So that rocket base you spent 45 minutes diligently sniping clean of soldiers is restocked next time you load the game. Great way to up your XP; not so good if you're wanting that feeling of making a difference.
Real life sniping concerns do not appear to be in effect, such as cold barrel shots, but I haven't played on the hardest level yet, so may yet be discovered
Things they really need to fix
+ Ladders that hold onto you. Occasionally you can launch a drone to break the climbing animation, but most times, it's a reload
+ Stealth kill animations. There you are being a Sam Fisher Sniper Ninja, and suddenly you find you're locked in an eternal struggle with the hapless soldier. Naturally, any roaming enemy will ease your dilemma by shooting you dead. If you've killed them all, and this was the last guy - heh, it's a reload.
+ Deciding not to reward you for your shots. Your 630m, no breath headshot was perfect. Game goes 'Meh'
+ Bouncing betties that will not trigger inside, but sure as hell will kill you outside. Guess who found out the hard way
+ Shots over 600m seems to have the ♥♥♥♥ You effect, where the target will flinch *every single time*, even if before they've stood there for several minutes, idly contemplating life
+ Occasionally, the rfile refuses to fire.
+ Unable to reload in the aim. Or launch drone.
+ "Criminals will not shoot you if you are not hostile" Criminals unload into your face.
+ Even though you have a bipod equipped, whilst prone, the reticle is still doing crazy eyes
These issues aside, there's a lot to like about this game, and lots of roaming, climbing and, of course, shooting to be had.
The storyline is paper thin, and overly jingoistic (think America World Police), and the noob mistake of saying 'Over and Out' is in the first part of the game, making any military folk cringe.
Line of Sight seems to be contextual. Sometimes, you can see targets at over 500m, other times, they only pop up at 150m.
On top of that, the rifle appears to be mildly passive-agressive, and will occasionally fight aginst you when you're trying to line up a shot. To get around this programmed deviance, hold your breath, line up on the forehead, release your breath and fire. Gives you extra XP too.
Not sure I could recommend this at full price in it's current state, but if it's on sale, it's well worth some comfortable hours, blowing peoples heads off.

This is a game judged harshly for what it isn't and what people thought it was instead of for what it is and what it was meant to be.  What this game
is a grand strategy game seeking to model every cultural and economic aspect of running a nation in Europe in the early 19th century.  What this game
, to put it simply, is a Napoleonic version of Hearts of Iron.  It's purely a war game and that's all it aspires to be, and
a war game it's pretty enjoyable.
Thus the mechanics of everyting relating to the military are deeper than most, if not all, Paradox games barring Hearts of Iron itself, and everything else is simplified.  You can't adjust taxes (though can take out loans in an emergency), you don't need to justify declarations of war, war begins almost immediately after you unpause the game, and technology is represented as a linear set of techs organized by category that you purchase with "idea points" that accumulate each month.
The entire point of the game is the military and that's where the depth comes in.  Similar to Hearts of Iron, provinces are very small to allow for maneuvering, and most importantly, armies are extremely customizable.
So you could have a right flank that entrenches and stands their ground, a center flank of line infantry that conducts a feint, and a left flank of elite guards that conducts a counter punch to enemy troops caught in the feint, each with the perfect commander to accentuate the tactics.  As an added bit of Napoleonic immersion, it tracks the number of enemy flags captured for each brigade, which had an deep impact on troop morale.
The possibilities are endliess and no two armies are alike.  Unlike every other Paradox game that isn't Hearts of Iron, this game's combat isn't a simple matter of just shoving two doom stacks into one giant province, watching floating numbers for a few seconds, and the other one scurrying off.  It's about creating highly customised and unique armies commanded by countless possible commanders in order to give yourself a tactical edge.  Combat is deep, nuanced, constant, and
.

March of the Eagles is Paradox Interactive's attempt to squeeze the era of the Napoleonic Wars into a grand strategy title. Though MotE succeeds in its ultimate goals, the game itself stands on uncertain ground. It struggles to find its place in the library of other grand strategies as it focuses solely on the military and geopolitical aspects of the Napoleonic Wars. While some consumers may find this acceptable, fans of the Europa Universalis series (which closely resembles MotE in both style and mechanics) may be disappointed by lack of political depth. On the other hand, being a grand strategy title with large barriers to entry and a sharp learning curve may keep casual strategy gamers at bay. In completely unrelated culinary terms, March of the Eagles can be perceived as too lean for hardcore Paradox fans while also being to beefy for newcomers to the franchise. Despite this, the game still remains enjoyable and fulfilling to those who stick with it. Though most of the game involves preparing supplies and armies for the inevitable attack of the French, some smaller moments also break through. Having my 5th Portuguese Dragoon regiment march from Algeria to Sweden collecting the banners of defeated regiments was great fun. All-in-all, March of the Eagles is a pleasant experience for those gamers who want to experience the military side of grand strategy and have always wanted to reshape the history of Europe.

As a level editor, Fight The Dragon is excellent, with simple, easily understood UI and an intuitive map editor.
As a diablo-style RPG, the game severely lacks content, story, or skill progression.
It's too easy to find levels that use every monster/mechanic in the game, which leads to everything afterwards feeling repetive. So after 4 or 5 levels or shooting/slashing mobs, collecting keys, and placing barrels on switches to open doors, it gets quite dull.
If you're looking for a chance to make your own (short) RPG dungeons to show off to your friends, this is a fine game to pickup.  But, if you're looking to play through a MP adventure with friends, well, you're better off sticking with games that advertise their game, not their editors.

Fight The Dragon is a simple, community-driven dungeon crawler for up to 4 players, populated with maps designed by the players themselves. There are twelve customizable character slots, and four classes to choose from, each with different weapon proficiencies and four unique abilities: the fighter, the rogue, the ice wizard, and the pyromancer. If you've played a fantasy-themed game before, those classes shouldn't be unfamiliar. The playstyles are all a tad different, but early on, it becomes quite apparent that ranged combatants are considerably easier to play, and arguably more effective as well.
The look of the game is a bit classic. It isn't voxel, and it has smooth textures, but the shapes of the in-game models look quite crude in a few cases. Controls are fairly simple, and the mechanics of the game will come naturally to anyone who is familiar with the genre. The gameplay itself is smooth, if a tad unbalanced; it's rather easy for a map designer to make an area too difficult, whether intentionally or not, by saturating it heavily with certain, more powerful monsters. A good example is a trio of enemy pyromancers- they deal so much damage in such a short time that they will instantly kill you with fireballs and pillars of flame if you stand still for more than a thoughtful moment. Loot appears rather frequently, so it isn't too difficult to find a decent set of gear that compliments how you choose to play. A feature called the 'Loot Shrine' acts as an alternative to the typical store you'd find in the 'safe zone' of a dungeon-crawling RPG. Rather than buying and selling items, the game allows you to 'donate' all of your gold and unwanted gear for a chance at progressively better loot- the more you donate, the better the rewards, which come in the form of rare armor and weapons, extra stat points, increased inventory space, or other miscellaneous character upgrades. Although the game offers you three choices (typically one item and two 'other'), the choices are completely randomized, so you may end up finding some unattractive offers when you decide to cash out. I find this feature to be a refreshing change from the norm, and i've abused it quite a lot in my own time playing.
The gimmicks that make FtD stand out from similar titles are it's trademark Adventure Creation Kit, and the titled battle against the Dragon. The Adventure Creation Kit(ACK) allows a player to construct a dungeon, then play in it against his own creation, or upload it to the server to share with friends or the community as a whole. The ACK is very user-friendly, and it's fun to play with. The design options that it gives you allow you to make maps of all sizes, or even chain multiple dungeons together to create a full campaign with multiple levels. The designer truly allows for an impressive amount of customization and creativity.
Fighting the Dragon, as many would assume from the title, is an integral part of the game. At any time, provided your character has recieved a Dragon Scroll by completing a dungeon, you may challenge the dragon arena. The Dragon itself is extremely strong; with a massive, constant HP pool and tons of damage output, he's an extremely tough opponent, only killable with determination and lots of patience (and Dragon Scrolls). Each scroll you use gives you three lives to deal as much damage as possible to the Dragon, before inevitably getting massacred and sent packing back into the player-made dungeons. Fortunately, the Dragon's health bar is consistent through attempts, so the damage you deal in each battle will carry over to the next time. Each time you reach a certain point of progress(by consistently putting tiny dents in his health), you will get a shiny red piece of Dragon loot that has a very special effect, but will disappear after you've used it for a certain time. I find that these two features really do make the game a special one, and it allows the player to take a much-needed break from the constant loot grind.
Overall, the game is put together well, and only suffers from a few minor bugs and glitches. The biggest issue I have with the game is a lack of balance and character development; aside from getting a new ability at level 5, 10, 15, etc., your gear makes your character what it is, and there is very little variance between two characters of the same class. Ranged weapons and kiting tactics seem to be the way to go most of the time, especially when the difficulty ramps up so quickly in most cases. The enemies deal a legitimately high amount of damage per attack, and some fights can cost the players a few lives before they can get a grasp on the situation. Aside from those few complaints, however, this is a gem of a game, would recommend to fans of the genre and RPGs in general.
Appearance: 3.5/5, basic textures, mostly attractive, sounds get repetitive and could have more variety.
Controls: 4.5/5, easy to pick up and play, mechanics aren't too hard, everything works how it should.
Gameplay: 4/5, bugs are few and far between, the ACK is fun, character building could use more options.
Replayability: 4/5, the ACK keeps the game fresh, but enemies get a bit repetitive.
Overall: 4/5, a good, solid dungeon crawler with some fun gimmicks and extra tools to make the game unique.

I find this game to be very fun and I recomend it as a time waster or relaxing game. What I will list next are not complaints, but suggestions that could be added in the game to make it even better.
These features might be welcome (especially if they are toggle on/off features):
- Collision Based Damage: This would make tossing an enemy against a wall or furniture more relevant.
- Fall Damage: Similar to the above it would make kicking enemies and falling off heights relevant.
- "Realistic" Blood Mode: In the game's current state just punching an enemy causes him to bleed profusel. A mode that made the blood spurts more adequate to the damage done would be welcome as well. Bleeding profusely would be achieved by stabbing an enemy, "breaking his nose" or caving his head in, but still more tame than the current more cartoonish mode. This would also make it more challenging to paint the maps RED. Requiring more violence to really get that bloodbath result.
-Dangerous Unarmed or Bruce Lee mode: Although there is the Hard hitter mode (makes enemies fly further) I find that I would like to replicate Kung Fu movies and go through a stage bare handed. It is possible to do so in normal mode (if played carefully), but I would really like a mode that caters to that specifically. Higher damage and Easier Stuns with fists would be nice in this mode. Some visual and audio aditions might be nice too. Like Chinese Kung Fu characters and sound effects.
-Kung Fu Themed Map: Regardless of the previous item, it would be REALLY nice to get a kung fu themed map. Like a shaolin temple or a tournament setting.
-Counters Attack: Would make for an interesting gameplay  shift to have the possibility  to steal the enemies weapon or counter attack them if timed right with a block.
-Better Collision When Tossing Items: Maybe it's my PC that's not really that good, but the collisions when tossing items seem a little wonky. Making the items bounce according to their type and knocking down the enemies would be a nice visual response. Sometimes solid items, like billiard balls, just fly through an enemies head as if they were bullets.
I really do recommend the game. Just tons of mindless fun.

Wow. This game is...it's something else, that's for sure. I bet it'd be pretty fun if you were god. However, I am a human, I am not god and I am not omniscient, which I feel like is a requirement to play this game.
I'm gonna do my best to explain the central problem I have with this game, but if you don't think my criticism is valid, that's fine. Maybe I just don't "get" factorio.
However the way this game is laid out, I wonder: how long does it take for one to "get" factorio? 6 hours? 20? 50? 100? 1000? A lifetime? I don't know. This game seems to have the highest learning curve of any game ever. It explains the very basis of what the gameplay should consist of but not how you should play it. For a game about automation, I felt the need to do everything manually because coal (the main resource I used during this game) kept running out once I had so many machines and it just wasn't possible to keep everything automated.
Look at this playlist
This is a 93 video guide explaining how to play the game. I'm sure it properly goes into detail but this thing takes several dozens of hours to watch. This is an indie game! If your indie game is so unapproachable that a player must watch 60 hours worth of content in order to understand it you did something very wrong! It's just not reasonable for someone to invest time like that in order to have fun.
So is it awful? Well, no. While I find the game to be far too complex to actually be fun it's not unbearable to try it out. And you know, it's hgihly likely that some people will be able to approach the game in a way that they can make sense of the trillion things to do here. Any game is allowed to have deep and intricate mechanics but you should start out small and have the game introduce each element one step at a time.

A board game with beautiful art, music and characters. Much like any game with dice, it heavily relies on RNG. The end result feels very similar to games just like 100% Orange Juice. Let me make this clear: this game may present itself as a strategy game based on how it looks, but it truly is a board game at heart. The only difference is you can play it online with friends. The store page DOES say stuff like "deep and emergent strategy" to describe Armello, and that is only PARTIALLY true. No matter what, there will be some actions you can think about taking that will probably benefit you in the long run, such as *attempting* to kill your character to make it to your quest faster, but you always have to consider RNG instead making you blow through what you're trying to die against. You can easily have a game where you reign supreme with good card draws and luck (Hot Rot Wine is extremely overpowered in any victory scenario, the steal others cards power should be cheaper and more common), and some games you accomplish nothing because someone else already screwed you over very early on (also making them highly unlikely to win if they also die) or the game RNG just hates you very much.
The point here I'm trying to make is that you get a varied, different game in each session. Some will be really ballsy and take on the King early (watch out for the Sana), and some trip into a rot victory, although it is unlikely. Sometimes a player can get 3 Spirit stones in a span of fifteen minutes because no one interrupts them, they get a lucky stone circle spawn, and the stone circle luckily has the random quest that allows you to get yet another spirit stone. There is no competitive in this game, and there never will or should be because of how the game works, so I'm also baffled at how people complain this hard about how the game works. This isn't like XCOM where the entire rest of your game is screwed because the game decided it should be, Armello isn't continuous. It's an about-hour session that is separate from every other.
In my last statement, I'm going to specifically call out the people leaving negative reviews just because now there are seven dollar skins that neither look impressive or cool enough to purchase. Who gives a♥♥♥♥♥♥ There's no doubt in my mind that someone is stupid enough to buy them, and regardless, they do not impact gameplay in the slightest. Same with the dice skins - you know, unlike CERTAIN OTHER GAMES with the chest/key system, in Armello you get a chance for a key and chest every single multiplayer game, win or lose. I would say this is very fair.
TL;DR Please don't purchase Armello imagining it's probably some unique take on Civilization or grand/strategy. Instead, purchase it because of the fun you can have from the unexpected, even better with friends.
P.S.: Please integrate the Steam feature "recent players" into Armello so you can probably make friends off of this game.
Edit: When the hell will the mobile version come out

I play a variety of board games weekly, which is what attracted me to Armello. I can sum this up quickly:
It's pretty.
It's somewhere between simple to moderate in complexity.
It has a consistent theme.
It involves a good deal of luck.
It doesn't take long to play.
End of summary.
If you're looking for something to do in an hour, that's easy on the eyes and somewhat challenging, Armello is a nice option. If you're looking for a rich strategy game, this isn't for you.

What can I tell you that hasn't been said already and isn't immediately apparent from looking at screen shots and videos? It's a great pick up and play, relaxing, and oh so clever. It feels like playing a table top board game but with elements from rpgs, adventure games, and card games like Magic, and Gwent. After the initial learning curve of how to play, it's very easy to hop in to a game and just get to playing it. Armello doesn't bog it's self down in complexity, yet there is still many layers to it and many ways to go about playing and attaining a victory in game. Highly recommend!

Sniper Ghost Warrior 3 was a really good sequel to the other two predecessors.
You can really feel, that City Interactive tried to implement things, which Sniper Ghost Warrior Fans wanted to see in the next game.
One of these things were the tunnel'esque Levels from the predecessor and the Spotter, who always told you, who to shoot first. They removed the spotter and developed 3 big areas, where you decide, who to shoot, when to shoot and how, or even IF you have to shoot. That's where City Interactive copied the Formula, most of the Shooters nowadays have, and implemented a 3 class System; Sniper, Ghost and Warrior. You get points on each style, when i.e killing someone with a sniper rifle, storming at the front with an assault rifle or sneaking from behind, avoiding detection and silently taking enemies out with the knife.
You always get some points on each class during your missions, but you get more, when you act in a way.
Also they implemented a very important feature for every Sniper Player: The paralax adjustment.
Players from the predecessors know that issue: Always measure how far below the crosshair is the target?
Aaand, you miss. Always happened to me in Ghost Warrior 2 and it was annoying.
In Ghost Warrior 3 you can now adjust your scope that it is aligned with the target you want to hit, even if it is Hundrets of metres away! That is a big improvment on realism and fun; at least for my side.
The Rifle-Repertoire is solid. Nothing special, but enough to choose from.
You get SVD's, 50. cal Rifles, MSR's, SR-25's and more to choose from, but don't be surprised; due to copyright issues, the original or real names from the weapons aren't shown, so they have invented names.
A thing which kills the immersion a little bit for me, but well, it not so bad for.
Sure it is no Battlefield or Call of Duty, but you get Sniper Rifles for every range; 50 Cal's for long, MSR's for Mid-Range and VSS' for low ranges for example.
Again nothing special but it gets the Job done.
The same can be said to the sidearms and secondary weapons.
Now we should come to the story.
Even though City Interactive tried to invent a better storyline, they still failed to surpass the "cringey B-Movie'esque" Stories. Every Ghost Warrior Player, who played the predecessors know, that the Ghost Warrior Games aren't known for their deep and meaningful stories, but at least the third part is not as cringey as the two games before.
They tried to bring a touching story of two brothers in it, and for some moments you feel with them, if you are generous, but most of the time they stay dull. The same can be said to the sidekicks; they stay dull and fulfill their roles in the story, but deep charater building is missing in that. Don't expect an Metal Gear Solid, Deus Ex or The Last of Us. Still, it is solid.
The missions mostly are pretty repetitive: Gather intel, sneak into a building, killing a target, and the same again on an other level. And the same can be said to the secondary missions. Nothing special, but nothing bad either. It gets the Job done.
The AI is pretty dumb, but once alarmed they have an insane accuracy and kills you even hundrets of metres away with their Assault rifles.
Now we should come to the last part: The Open World/Graphics/Sound.
Graphics are thanks to the Cry Engine pretty good. You have beautiful Sunrises/Sunsets, farsights on hills and amazing work of Details. Especially the amount of Details to the rifles is pretty good, but the lack of character details is on the other hand dissapointing.
You have 3 Areas, one urban/wood area, one Mountain, snowy area, and again a more woody area.
All 3 are beatifull made, with outposts to eradicate, villages to visit and other points of interest to investigate, which is really fun to dive in thanks to the Cry Engine.
Sounds are very good. If you fire a shot, listening to footsteps, or staying in a forst, while a river is floating by, really catches the immersion of a living open world.

I really have a zero tolerance policy to games when they crash - I mean, you wouldn't think it was acceptable if a book randomly shut itself while you were reading, then you had to find the page you were on again.  That being said, Republic Commando left such a good impression on me that I still recommend it despite that!
Every aspect of this game is pretty lackluster by itself - your weapons don't feel particularly powerful, there's very little enemy variation, missions are very linear, etc. - but everything comes together to create something unique and memorable.  Each of your squad members has an individual personality, all of your weapons have clearly defined roles, and the little windshield wiper that cleans your visor every time oil gets splattered on it from punching a robot in the face is so satisfying to watch.
FAIR WARNING, THOUGH:  the fact that you have a squad does not mean this is a tactical shooter in the same vein as Rainbow Six Vegas - quite the contrary, this is an old school, circle-strafing FPS with enemies that will teach you what the true meaning of "bullet sponge" is.  If you set your expectations right, you'll have a lot of fun!

Tinykeep is a topdown hack and slash Rouge like, featuring a lot of physics elements, traps and monster factions that battle eachother. While that sentence makes this sound  like a must buy, it has some issues preventing it from reaching it's full potential.
1: The phyiscs objects keeps getting in the way, and at some point the massive piles of bodies just make it a sludge getting through rooms. I had to walk to the farthest corner to despawn the ragdolls during one level, because the corpses was lagging my game to a crawl. Floor traps sometimes break and fall off, i'm not certain if that is a bug or a feature.
2: The maps are confusing, and the lack of locked rotation meant i got lost at many points. The map screens paint function makes reading the map quite difficult. The 3D enviorments sometimes gets in the way of seeing the character and the monsters he is fighting.
3: The game is structured like a rougelike, with random level generation, random monster placement, and semi random powerups. However, the structure of the game dosen't really support this: There is nothing to do on a second run. All rooms are functionally identical, either containing traps, enemies or not. There are no special rooms, or random powerups to find, and very little reward for exploring but more enemies that might yield gold. You pay for the powerups using coins, but these are plain, and unintresting. Faster movement when your holding a shield, running backwards faster, jumping higher, increased damage towards certain types of enemies. Nothing that will change the way you do your run, and most runs you will simply have most powerups at the end anyway.
But having it a rougelike means no save function, which means that if you die you have to start over. Which is fine, except 90% of the game is very very easy! There is really no problem defeating the first three "bosses", they are no harder then regular enemies. The last boss however, can basically kill you in a 2-3 hits, especially when your acid sword hits you both, making you slow and draining your health. If you die then, you have to play through 90% of the content.
Which i just did.
"Fun."
You could also jump ahead at try to defeat him with the starting sword and none of your powerups. Which kinda defeats the point of the rougelike anyway. Why not just have a save system?
Still, worth the 3 euros, fun if flawed little experience.
This is pretty much exactly what I always wanted in a rougelike, fast responsive controls, good graphics, and a difficulty level that makes it just frustrating enough to qualify.

"Tiny keep" is a treasure to behold and a somewhat interesting game to play. However, This game is lacking a variety of things to a rogue-like procedural death/dungeon crawler. ! SPOILERS !
If this is a game, I'm afraid it's not a very good one.
Emily is Away has a story to tell. One story. There are choices that let you choose how you approach that story, but it is still only one story. In a different genre, this linearity would be absolutely fine, but here, where choices are supposed to matter, I believe the linearity is a hindrance.
In games like this, I play myself (or as close as I can get to myself as possible while still enjoying the game and my character). In situations like this, I tend to respond by listening, and offering advice where I feel it is wanted, and giving the person space if they want it. It is difficult to play that way in this game-- not because of any emotions felt, but because of the sometimes limited scope of choices. It is even more difficult to feel satisfied in this game by doing that-- I felt, at the end, as if I had missed out on the main plot.
I decided at the beginning that since I didn't have any backstory for Emily, I wasn't going to treat her as though she was a close friend or love interest or anything. I was going to make conversation, and listen to her problems if she wanted to share them, and help if I could, but sorting out her life and/or trying to get in her pants was not my responsiblity.
The game did not prepare for this.
A frequent topic, and one that I considered the main character to have unnatural obsession over for someone with my choice of relation to Emily, was her love life. If it was abusive, I would absolutely have wanted to help her, but that didn't seem to be the case. If she wanted to vent, I would have listened, and in fact she did vent, and I did listen and try to be supportive. But still, the character seemed to want to break Emily and her boyfriend up. I did not want to do this.
As I continued in my quest to be Emily's acquaintance, or at best, old high school buddy, the game pushed and pushed in the direction of making me want to date her. When she finally asked me why I hadn't kissed her, I noted quite heavily that I at the keyboard had had no such chance to do or not to do so, and then decided that my character would not have noticed that she was interested, because I feel as though I am the sort of person who would not have noticed. It was at this point the game decided to make my character have sex with her off-screen. You can imagine my reaction, I'm sure.
I decided to apologise, or to try to, anyway (the game actually only let me apologise for my character's actions upseeting her, not the actions themselves, which I felt was a cop-out, but Emily was apparently okay with), because she was clearly upset. This was the point where the game seemed to finally "get it", ostensibly, at least, and let me have a normal small-talk conversation with Emily in the final chapter. There was, however, a distinct sense of pouting to it, though, as several of the options were dramatic things like "can things ever go back to the way they were before?" (paraphrased), as a last-ditch effort to get me to cry over some unrequited love. Eventually, I had to be the one to sign off, which just felt like the game was telling me to get out of its house if I wasn't going to respect its teenage romance drama. I was not impressed.
It is now clear to me, from reading reviews and comments by other people, that this is a romance game. I did not know that at the start. I was expecting some sort of horrible crisis to have to help her out with, or a horrible twist that would make me a bad person. (To be fair, I'm glad that didn't happen.) But a romance game has to make the player feel invested, through empathy specifically, in order to be successful, and empathy requires as little linearity as possible. This is why I have to say that as a game, it just doesn't hold up.
However.
If this is a storytelling experience, then it's absolutely fantastic.
I can tell that each piece of dialogue was written with care. The choices and references felt straight out of the early 2000's (which I have to admit is a period of time I don't remember very well). The UI and artwork is excellent. And I'm sure the AIM-like interface will have quite the significance to anyone who used to use it.
I suspect that the story is linear for a reason. I further suspect that reason to be that this is something from the developer's own life. An experience they have had, a personal tragedy they wanted to share. If that's the case, great. But perhaps this game would have been better as a video.
You see, I made a comment earlier that for a romance game to be compelling, it has to tap into empathy-- feeling the same things as someone else, and relating to them that way. This is difficult, perhaps impossible, in a video game with a linear story. This story does not inspire empathy, at least not to me, but I'm sure it could inspire sympathy, which is a lot easier to work with. You don't have to match someone else's experiences as closely, you can just remind them of some things and they'll be able to understand how your character feels, without actually feeling that way.
I am not a believer in the concept of the "friend zone". I believe that concept only exists because people do not want to do the right thing, the hard thing, to get over it when something like this happens, but instead blame the person they desire or obsess over their desire for them. However, I understand that some people do believe in the concept, and that I am not going to change their minds. This is fine. But it seems to me that in order to enjoy this game, you need to be a believer in the "friend zone". You need to be accustomed to asking awkward questions because you just want to date someone so much. That, or you need to be accustomed to answering such questions and not getting annoyed by them. I do not fit this description. I do not look very favourably on the traits in this description. And so, this game was, and is, not for me.
But it might be for you. It's free, and quick, so you might as well try it. And if you come away finding the story as poor as I did, well, at least the experience is pretty nice.

Insurgency is one of the most unique tactical shooters I've ever played.
It's even different compared to Red Orchestra 2.
It's the only proper tactical FPS setting the bar between ARMA and Call Of Duty.
As much as I love this game, I believe that this game is entirely underrated. It's surprising that no one would play such a cheap game like this that will deliver more than an AAA title.
The game may be simplistic at first, but trust me. This game is somewhat complex at times when it comes to tactics.
Insurgency allows you to play a variety of playstyles, dependent on what kit you're using and how much supply points you'll usually spend. Because of this, you're able to make the impossible of possible, as I've seen unique and outstanding plays through servers.
Insurgency also has unique gunplay, which is overall amazing and pretty authentic.
Looking up to spice up your game? Look no further towards the workshop. The workshop has a crapton of content to reskin and resound your game. Hell, you can even have custom weapons in this game.
The modding community in insurgency are well talented and well dedicated people that I have respect for. I respect their dedication for creating content for such a small community to admire their beautiful hard work.
Honestly, to truely experience insurgency, you have to play it. Insurgency is like the only game you can find to fit the modern day middle eastern war setting for tactical shooters. It's the most proper and grounded one to play.
Pro Tip: Use AP Rounds on your primary always

I... actually binged the game for about 12 hours. I've owned the game 12 hours and spent 12 hours playing it. Wow.
Well, needless to say, if you're the type of person who enjoys very precisely and meticulously building assembly lines, if you're into efficiently laying out power lines and challenging yourself to create the biggest and best factories you can, you'll like Factorio. I wasn't too into the $20 USD price tag, since that's a bit much for an indie game to me, but I bit the bullet and it was well worth it.
I think I just summed up the game too. It's all about putting down equipment in the 'best' way, stuff doesn't take too long to rip back up so you're not penalized in any way for reorganizing. It's quick and painless to lay down new stuff, and the satisfaction from zooming out and taking a good look at this giant monstrous factory you've built... something special.
This is really just Minecraft's IndustrialCraft 2 mod focused to a razor sharp point, and followed through with to the nth degree. This is all about automation, where IC2 actually sort of tried to curb that in some ways. There's a sense of progression here where you're always building bigger, more advanced, more complicated machinery that needs way more parts, so you have to build more parts to get the automation to build those parts so you can build more automators so you can build more parts so you can build the stuff you want faster.
There's just so many little optimizations you can do to get stuff going at every stage of the game. And, it never really feels wasted... something as simple as setting up a 'safety net' fuel supply or something just in case you're away from it long enough, an overflow box to store excess product, whatever, you're always capable of doing something to make your machines work a little bit better.
Very good. I think this game could just be released right now, it works well enough, feels polished enough... but I hope to see the devs add more content, more machines in the future and more layers of complexity all the same.

If you've ever done any programming before, this game is a must. Building, expanding and optimizing your own factory can be very time consuming and very fun. It's a game that I always come back to after I think I'm done playing it. They update it regularly and have a great subreddit where the devs are active. Would recommend.

Armello's a fantastic game. Strategy combined with beautiful art, characters, soundtrack makes for an excellent and well balanced game. I've got over 300 hours under my belt and I'm sure I'll have many more, as it always keeps me challenged. I love this game and have a lot to say about it, so if you want to read a full review check it out here:

I had mixed feelings when starting Armello.  However I am a big board game fan. That tag got me interested in Armello.
However I was rather concerned by the fact that it never was a real board game.  In the board game world that is the equivalent of a strait to DVD release.  They tend to be kind of poorly done.  I purchased this intending to use steam refund.
However the game is one of the better games in the non-RPG adventuring genre.
Like most games in that genre there is a ton of dice.  However Armello, unlike most, give a player a choice in what they want to do, instead of mandating go here fight this, etc.  It provides a variety of things to do and avoids a grind.
But were Armello really shows its glory is the card play.  The game has great hand management.  There is definitely some tactics to when and how you play your cards. I even found myself debating if I should wait for optimal use or just play the card to get another draw.
The game is competitive and does it correctly.  Most let you either just race or perhaps slow your opponents down.  In Armello you can actually hurt your opponents, but never remove them from the game.
The theme for Armello is fine and I like the graphics.
Now for the weakness --
The game requires you keep track of the other players (at least to play on the top level). However what a player is doing is sometimes done so fast that if you blink you'd miss it.  Other times another players turn can be painfully long while you mostly sit there.  The game needs to speed its turns but also keep a log or make it easy to see what they did.
In conclusion. This is a good game.  It is relaxing and crafted with a professionalism you do not normally see in this style of computer board game.  Solid graphic, solid game play with a solid recommendation.  Although sometime I wonder if my opinion is inflated due to low expectations.

A great little role playing strategy game with cute graphics, excellent mood music and lots of replayability including online multiplayer.
Armello is a well designed game whose main game mechanic revolves around traversing a fixed map of varying terrain and obstacles with your player character.  It is a turn based game which allows you build deceptively complex strategy with a little bit of luck.  Any person familiar with table top role playing will understand the mechanics of Armello well.  Gain cards in your hand and play them with the appropriate resources (money, magic and in some circumstances prestige or even health).  Move through the map gaining resources and doing quests (by landing on the quest tile and passing a short game of chance).
The story behind the game is simple.  Armello's ruler, the king, is dying of rot, an evil infestation making him go mad.  4 seperate factions are vying to take control (wolf, bear, rat and rabbit) through their agents.  The base game comes with 2 agents for each faction.  They are well balanced and will require unique game play strategy to win.  The gameplay is relatively short when you get the hang of it.  Online mutiplayer is not a mode I have tried therefore I can't comment on this aspect of the game.
That said I very much like this game.  It isn't an expensive game but the developers have contunually been adding elements and tinkiering with game play.  There are expansions which add 1 new agent for each faction and a soundtrack, but these aren't neccessary to have many hours of fun playing the game.

TLDR A game that's trying to position itself (almost successfully) as a lunchbreak RPG Roguelike, can be picked up by casual gamers and fairly hard core ones, but gameplay may be too difficult for casual gamers.
Gameplay
You've been sent to the bottom of dungeon, and must escape through randomly generated levels, following the footsteps of your cell mate, who has left the odd item and clue behind for you.
3rd person/topdown view with a wide fov, but a very narrow draw dsitance, meaning you can never see very far ahead of you, although this isn't really an issue, and actually adds to the claustriphobic feel of the game.
It's trying to simplify many things, RogoueLikes, RPG's, Dungeon Crawlers, and Lunchbreak games (games that can be completed in 1/2h or under). And it largely does a good job of this. It's actaully a good intro game into many of these genre's, as it simplifies many of their elements into sometghing almost casual. I say 'almost', as the difficulty puts this game out of reach of a Casual gamer.  This game is going to kill you and send you back to the start. a lot.
Death is a thing. Perma death, level 1. no progression.
Mechanics
Dungeon generation is similar to another game, Spelunky - that is, each level is made according to a formula, so you'll see the same obsticals and content each time on any given level, only the order of the rooms may shange.
Items in the world are also obsticles - knock a vase over now and you'll have to jump over it later. this will get you killed more than once.
enemies can swarm you, and you pretty well cannot escape once this happens.
RPG elements are randomised, so that there is no overthinking about what skills to unlock, it just gives you skills, and you have to adapt your gameplay style on the fly. one run you might get a few speed buffs, the next, might be defensive buffs... etc.
Graphics
Tiny keep, Big heads. It's a cutesy art style, seems to suit the game well, and is beautifully drawn.
Will run on even a modest computer.
There is blood spatter, despite the cutesy - it's not gory, but it is there.
Controls
standard FPS controls for kb/mouse. I've hear of Xbox controller support. The game is simple, so the controls are too. they work well, feel responsive, but you can pick up on the controller thing, as the camera can float a little (isn't) directly connected to the mouse like an FPS)
Audio
Wasn't working for me, sadly. I'll update this later.
Interesting stuff
There's no Wiki - So how do you look up whether the big bone guy that 1hits you can be killed? Do the Skellies ever stop spawning>? I don't know, I haven't lived that long.
Overall
I actually kinda like it, but I'm not very fanboi, yet. It's a good pick, a solid game, one you wouldn't regret buying, as long as you have a idea of what you're getting into first.

The game is a lot of fun, and with proceedurally generated levels you will never have the same run twice. Challenging enough to keep you coming back for more and it not being a cakewalk without being so difficult for you to ragequit entirely.  6 hours in and I've only got to level 6 of 20, and there's still a new game+ mode and other secrets Ive yet to figure out.
Definately reccommend that you buy it if you like what you see.

Alien Swarm, released in 2010, is one of the more neglected Valve releases and a very underrated free-to-play game on Steam. Alien Swarm: Reactive Drop, released this past April, is a completely free, stand-alone expansion to the game developed by a group of fans and given Valve's blessing.
Reactive Drop offers absolutely all of the content in Alien Swarm, plus a host of new weapons, game modes (including PVP!), leaderboard functionality, singleplayer, expanded 8-player coop play, and most importantly, over 4 new campaigns to play; as well as Steam Workshop support, which means the sky is the limit for your content needs.
If you got bored of Alien Swarm a month after launch, then Reactive Drop is a great way to get back in and remember what you were missing, as you definitely won't run out of content this time - and if you've never played it before, then don't hesitate to download it. It's a ton of alien-killing fun, all for free.

There's just something about the setting of a cyberpunk story (book, movie, game, etc) that speaks volumes, essentially warranting the setting as a vital and important character in its own right.  The setting needs to be believable and accessable (sure, you can have a far distant future as the setting, but it needs to have some commonality that we here in the real world can connect to) in order to transition from mere decoration into a uncaring and unforgiving giant on which the players are mere pawns.  Okay, I know this sounds like a crazy review, but bare with me.
So the Syndicate games were influential on me as I grew up: as a video game interpretation of the wonderful cyberpunk novels I was devouring in my teenage years, and as catalyst for me to plunder the secrets of how to make a clunker of a PC into a gaming rig - thus causing me to become better acquainted with IT in general and as a skill for our new era.  I lived, breathed, and imagined fantastical stories based on this series of games (more than one friend can recount how I spent a whole camping/hiking trip discussing in detail various aspects of the games).
And then the world of PCs shifted away from DOS and Syndicate seemed to be a relic of the past, as each succession of Windows seemed to make it more difficult to dance in my beloved dystopian cyberpunk world of yesterday.  There would be other games to come about and soften the loss of such a titan, but memories would hold true for the almost anarchic freedom one could play out in the Syndicate series (yes, I know that there was limitations, but one only needed to be creative in his/her play).
Finally, whispers of this game began to emerge and I was sold when I saw the basic premise and concepts that would eventually coalesce into Satellite Reign.  The atmosphere, with all of its harsh neon and umbral starkness, served as a wonderfully dismal backdrop for my agents to ply their trade through.  One of the things I loved about this game was how simple a minor infraction could erupt into a full-scale firefight, often requiring a quick and tactical retreat to lick my wounds, reassess my target, and plot a counter-strike.  "Long is the way and hard, that out of Hell leads up to Light." (Milton, Paradise Lost)  This game made me take my time (still playing through it, on hiatus), but with each success I had earned more resources, tactical prowess, and some new loot (agents, weapons, gear) off of the fallen.
Would I recommend this game?  Yes, naturally for the reasons I stated above.  This game is a game I play because I love the atmosphere, the freedom, and the tediousness of the missions.  It's a long game that allows me to play out my story of being a rebelious "syndicate" struggling to eek out an existance amongst corporate giants, as I claw and devour my way to the top.

"Back to the past!" 9/10
This game could not be more appropriately titled. Rampage you say? You're damn right it is and I couldn't be more happy about it. To picture it, imagine a mashup of your favorite 8-bit video games from the 80's with some early 'Grand Theft Auto' thrown in for good measure. Which is totally awesome if you ask me, and makes for one of the best retro gaming experiences of all time; in my opinion, of course.
Playing through this game, you're sure to pick up on various themes and obvious and also obscure references to old Nintendo classics such as levels taken directly from Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles (that damn water level, for instance), sounds from the Mega Man series, and the track design from one of the best racing games of all time: Rad Racer, to name a few. The plot is also a mash-up of sorts as it's basically taken directly from 'Back to the Future' with sprinkles of 'Ghostbusters' and other popular 80's movies as well. Can you imagine, both 'Ghostbusters' and 'Back to the Future' in the same game? It doesn't get much better than that, folks.
Actually, now that I think more about it, this game is just one big barrage of nonstop old-school references to video games and movies from the 80's. But as I said, there's nothing wrong with a little nostalgia. And if you grew up playing games like 'Link to the Past', 'Mario Bros', or any of those fantastic early NES titles, then this game will make you feel like a kid again; in a good way. You know, like having no responsibilities other than to wipe your own butt after using the bathroom, or brushing your teeth before bed, or doing your homework the night before, or...hell, just pick this game up already. You will not be disappointed. And even if you are, what did you expect from a kid?

After finding that I enjoyed the base building aspects of Fallout 4, I thought I'd give another game that emphasizes this element a try, so I purchased State of Decay: Year One Survival Edition. I liked the focus on building your base and defending your group of survivors, collecting resources, and fixing stuff. I liked the ability to switch between characters and level them up. In fact, I was looking forward to that: a mix of multi-character RPGs and FPSs. Overall, however, my impression of the game is mostly negative.
First of all, this is a "permadeath" game, which means that if one of your main characters dies, you can't restore a previous save and get them back. The developers and afficionados of the genre would call this a feature, and, for those people, it should be available, but it should also be possible to turn this off. Just tell the player that having a permament character death be part of the authentic survival experience, but offer the option to restore. With permadeath, your game play has to necessarily be very conservative, just like, you know, in real life. You can't experiment: What if I just rush in and start slashing? What if I enter via this door or that? Sure, but then you could lose the character you spent hours building up. Ugh.  Isn't the point of a sandbox to experiment?
Second, the game mechanics are buggy. Zombies in walls, PC and NPC occupying the same space (e.g. when climbing ladder), awkward attack animation, ice-skater walking animation, etc. There are also nuisances that may well have been intentional, such as the inability to trade items with another player-controllable character or to drop items. Once you pick up an item, you either have to stash it at your base or destroy it. You can't put it back into a container you're looting or drop it on the ground for another payer-controllable character to pick up. Lots of things that the developers should've fixed for their Year One edition.
Third, the player gets inundated with quests that don't have a clear sense of priority. This may be intentional or not, but it leads to a frustrating first-time experience. In most RPGs, you have a choice of when to accept side-quests; in SoD, tasks (problems) just keep getting added to your journal. Should you deal with the character who is sad or angry first, because they are causing morale to drop, or help some trapped survirors because Lily said, "better hurry," or advance the story line via main quest, or ... ?
Overall, the game is built on a great premise, but sloppy execution and adherence to the permadeath doctrine made it unenjoyable for me.

This game reminds me of some Disney films, like Hunchback and Hercules. The similarities are drawn most frequently in terms of tone. The tone yo-yos back-n-forth between deadly serious and playful comedy constantly (think Hellfire vs singing gay-for-goats gargoyles). Dead bodies litter the screen, but there is little blood, the characters speak in cartoonish mumbles, a change of clothes hides a German accent and outlandish coincidences that rival Les Mis. Sure, suspension of disbelief, but this is a game about history and real lives that were lost, yet we’re supposed to believe that these soldiers are so nice that they wouldn’t shoot a dog? Dogs were used in warfare and often to carry messages, so were likely shot at just as carrier pigeons were. Even the divide between historical facts that the game provides the player and what was happening in the game itself seemed to be on opposite ends on the office, refusing to speak to each other. The villain was again a lot like Disney; he was given a dumb name (Baron von Dorf – a fictional figure made up for the game. Real life tragedy, death and finality not good enough, clearly) and traits that didn't make him appear threatening, but rather weak and cowardly (e.g. Scar from the Lion King). So, I didn't feel anything when we defeated him. I don't see how this game's story is so highly praised. This is a topic that could have been handled much, much better. Like if Hunchback didn't have those damn gargoyles or the Lion King without the comedic relief jumping in not 5 minutes after Mufasa’s death. The story writer’s and dev didn’t need to treat their audience like Disney-going children. However, Disney is successful for a reason and this is the same reason that this game has done so well, I imagine.
It was difficult to get past how "gamey" the experience was. The puzzles were ok, but sometimes unclear, didn’t fit the tone or were made more difficult to just pad them out (e.g. solution off-screen, very narrow margin of error). They’re not too bad though and I didn’t use the in-game hints very often. These hints are time-locked and are delivered after a set amount of time, so the game doesn’t hold your hand in terms of the puzzles. However, you can’t really fail Anna’s medical QTEs, so the game still reminds you that it’s for a casual audience. Just like Disney pandering to the lowest common denominator. As an aside, I also found the pigeons super cute. Pigeons > Dog.
Additionally, the game has a few technical issues. Most notably with Anna’s taxi driving sections were the sound would cut out or stutter or loop. Indeed, the main reason I’m writing this review is due to a technical fault with the game in one of Anna’s sections. In Chp 3 there is a known game-breaking bug that, from looking up solutions, has been known about since at least 2014 and yet has not been solved. The solution given online is to play in 800x600 windowed with all in-game sound/music off. Why has this not been patched? Why do I have to modify the way I play my game to get past this? In fact, playing in windowed 800x600 with no sound did not solve this for me, neither did updating drivers. And I honestly don’t care. This game is ok at best. I’m glad it was a birthday gift and I did not pay money for it. I’ll watch an LP on YouTube to see how it ends.

WW1 has broken out and you play through the game as a collection of characters on both sides of the war. The most important concept to know here is that they’re just focused on surviving the war and wanting it to be over. Rather than glorifying the war or making it seem like it’s a fun shooter, it takes time to setup character motivations and desires so you can get some closure for their arcs at the end of the game. The most striking part of the entire game really revolves around the fact that the war is shown as a never ending grind and in the end, the characters just want to go home. It shows war as being ♥♥♥♥ed up and chaotic and the characters change to show that. Most importantly, this is a game about characters going through war not a war game with characters it in. The people are the focus and they are what you care about.
I’m being vague about the game because the story is really good and you should experience it for yourself.

I felt sad at the end of the game. Not because
but because I cared for the characters. In my eyes, if you can do that by the end, then you’ve been presented a story that is worth experiencing. Is it a gameplay masterpiece? No. Does it deliver a convincing story that war is super ♥♥♥♥ed up? Yes.

This game is great, the reset of progress is a little much, but thanks to the modding community it was no problem, This is a really nice game for something that's Free To Play, Difficulty isn't entirely based on how much damage you do or how much health the swarm has, its more: Are you alone? Are you playing with bots? How many Swarm aliens are in your immediate vicinity? These questions don't seem important when choosing difficulty, but these questions are actually extremely important, a swarm will take down an unprepared team on any difficulty, on higher difficulties they do more damage and have more health, making certain enemies you'll find down the road an absolute pain, The only bonus to choosing higher difficulties is getting more XP, so you could cut down a long grind on a singular mission by upping the difficulty, The best way to play in my opinion is play every mission with AI on the easiest difficulty until you know what you're doing, because when you enter multiplayer, people are going to want higher difficulties and everyone knowing what to do is essential for survival, Anyway, Multiplayer is fun when your team is coordinated and having 8 available marines (while low on character selection) is great to smash the swarm with an abundance of ammunition and medical supplies, The last thing you need to know is the Commander class is essentially worthless, You will almost ALWAYS need a Tech, Special Weapons are going to be your go-to to swarm killing, and your lives will always be easier with a Medic.
