So let me preface this by saying that I was a big fan of the original Alien Swarm game, I praised its format, level design, atmosphere and sound direction. Alien Swarm was the first game I ever genuinely tried and managed to speedrun, achievement incentives helped to do that, but all in all the original game is fantastic and quite frankly is utterly criminal that it was free to play, I've met people on the original game that I still talk and play games with to this day.
But Alien Swarm had a lack of content, A single campaign telling the story of Jacob's Rest, a colony on the planet of Vereon XII which had an unfortunate incident resulting in a rather nasty alien occupation. Alien Swarm maintained a solid playerbase regardless of this lack of content even after all these years, But there was so much potential for the game that the community just accepted that we were never going to get.
Until now.
What we have here, is a huge expansion, Reactive Drop adds everything that Alien Swarm fans wanted. We have new weapons, new campaigns, an 8-player mode, fully fuctional bot support, Deathmatch, Bonus missions for those hungry for more and even workshop integration to allow for even more campaigns and personal customisation.
To talk about the gameplay, Alien Swarm: Reactive Drop is a top down squad based game that is played up to either a 4-player or 8-player maximum, you have 4 classes and 8 playable characters. First up are the Officers, Sarge and Jaeger, the mere presence of these men make everyone perform better, they lead and have access to the all powerful Vindicator shotgun, capable of bursting down the toughest the swarm have to offer. Secondly we have the Heavy Weapons specialists, Wildcat and Wolfe, using Miniguns and heavy fully automatic shotguns, you'd be hard pressed to find a better way of clearing and locking down entire hallways of swarm in mere seconds. Thirdly we have the doctors, Faith and Bastille, the all important Medics, capable of fortifying defensive locations with beacons that can heal the entire squad, or equipping a medi-gun for more concise on-demand healing. Last up are the Technicians, Crash and Vegas, outright required for any missions that task you to obtain information, these men hack terminals, bring motion trackers and have access to a special auto-aim rifle with tesla grenades.
Every Marine has a trait that makes them different from their counterpart in someway, For example: Sarge and Jaeger both share varying levels of the Leadership buff, Vindicator damage bonus, an explosives bonus and a health bonus, but their 5th traits are different. Sarge has a personal damage bonus, making his abillity with any weapon he is capable of using significantly better, where as Jaeger has a melee damage increase bonus, most likely instantly killing any swarm that dares get close to him. Wildcat is faster than Wolfe, but Wolfe is capable of taking more punishment at the risk of being significantly slower.
There is alot of depth that goes into team picks if you take the time to look at the soldiers individual stats, something that I never really noticed until recently, although team picks wont matter much if you're in an 8-player server, where every single marine will be present.
For teams that wish to succeed, it's important to stay together and be mindful of your ammo, some eyes watching your front, moving the squad slowly, some eyes watching your back, to prevent nasty flanking attacks, the game is extremely well designed for both the players and the aliens, there are choke points that teams can hold while they wait for alien waves to end, but there are several entry ways for the aliens to use to keep the team on their toes. If you divide? You'll get conquered. There are few instances in the game when you are generally "safe". Players can weld doors shut to relieve some pressure, but the aliens can knock them down given enough time, players can use combat stims to give your tech those precious extra seconds of hacking while you hold off seemingly endless waves of swarm that don't want you looking at manifests.
I mean...I'm typing all of this, but I'm just going to end up repeating my original review of the older game...It's Alien Swarm, it's fantastic, Guns sound great, levels are very well designed and generally fun to go through, the marines have some unique dialogue between each other, there is tons of equipment to obtain and unlock and the game as a whole is very atmospheric.
To say that this is the definitive version of Alien Swarm would be an understatement, the fact that the original game was free was a steal, but this huge massive expansion pack that has added so much longevity, free as well? The quality within this game exceeds that of what we're getting from our Triple A titles nowadays. I can't not recommend Reactive Drop, at least not to people who don't like top down shooters...But I urge you to give it a try, it's one of the most underrated games on Steam.
And one final time, it's completely and entirely free.

A Top-Down Strategy akin to Commandos meeting a Cyber-Punk dystopian feel.
The game really is fun, albeit, takes a lot of getting used to. The sneaking is 100% easier to accomplish but sometimes you just wanna hold a full on heist, with the only problem being that you need some good micro-skills to achieve this.
Which partially takes away from the game which is a shame because this game does deserve a larger player-base than it has.
The visuals are great and set the tone perfectly with the cyber-punk esque game play, and some of the features (such as hacking a person and using their DNA as clone material, granting you status bonuses) is also really exciting to use.
The level design could use a fair bit of tweaking, if the stealth class weren't able to go invisible on a whim as an ability some of the areas are impossible to sneak through, and even then, it won't always be a saving grace, requiring your hacker or soldier for certain skill checks, which is a real shame.
So you end up being railroaded into doing some areas full-blast loud, and it's usually these areas that are hardest to do in that vein as well, leading back to the issue of micro-management, which is pretty necessary if you want to survive a loud heist of pretty much any of the areas.

For fans of the Total War series who like looking at the bigger picture. Or an excellent entry level Paradox Interactive grand strategy game.
When I bought the game I was a complete Paradox Interactive noob but I always liked the idea of their truly-grand strategy games. However, having played the demos for Europa Universalis III and Hearts of Iron II, I was convinced I would never be able to get my head around the complexities of Paradox's games. This all changed with March of the Eagles. The era in which the game is set is right up my street and the scale of the campaign map was like nothing I'd experienced before ('scale' is a relative term here).
People familiar with strategy games will be fimiliar  with the basic concepts here. You destroy your enemies and take their land, simple. However, in MotE the immediate gains (land) you make are much smaller than those in other games such as the Total War series. This may sound boring to some but I assure you the opposite is true. Because you have to fight harder for every inch, when you eventually destroy a nation it is all the more satisfying.
Every nations on the map is playable from launch (no DLC is a rarity these days) which adds replayability to the game. I had the most fun playing as a lesser nations and working the larger powers against each other. Personally I recommend one of the Italian nations.
What suprised me is what you
while playing this game! If history/national geography interests you then this game is great. I can now name a lot of lesser Germanic/Burgundian nations such as Nassau and Hessen which I didn't know once existed. There are also event pop ups which add little to gameplay but provide educational fun, such as I never knew that Napoleon named his brother the King of The Netherlands. Fun fact!
The diplomacy element and associated AI is not the greatest in any game ever to be honest but it does the job perfectly well. There is a 'coalition' mechanic in this game which is a unique concept as far as I am concerned. This basically means that you and a bunch of other nations rally behind a super-power (Prussia, Austria, Russia, Ottomans, French or British [and Spain, but not really]) to defeat another super-power which results in an unbreakable alliance. This is a nice idea and historically relevent and probably the best feature in the game.
Let's be honest. You auto-resolve most of the battles when playing Total War and that's why you're here.
Basically the meat and potatoes of the game. If you're not planning on going to war there is not much point in playing the game. There are no live battlefield engagements in the style of Total War or Age of Empires but frankly they are not needed. While nine times out of ten combat boils down to who has more men, there are still other elements that effect the outcome in subtle ways. There are a variety of units avaliable to build but they are essentially pictures which represent statistics. But specific army composition is not necessarily what the game is about for me (though the right balance helps). For me it is not the who, but the where and when.... and also who a bit. Having the right amount of men in the right place at the right time is how you are going to win, not by numbers and blitzkrieg tactics. Also, with the exception of Russia and the Ottomans, you are not going to survive alone.
When you build an epic alliance as Britain with Naples, Prussia, Bavaria and Piemonte against the French this is where the game shines. It's even more fun to watch all those nations instantly turn against you for their personal gain as soon as the war is over. In this respect the game is extremely Machiavellian, and I love it!
The combat is further complicated by the need to balance resources such as money and manpower. Compared to other Paradox games this level of resource management is childs play, but it is still on a par with other conventional RTSs.
Famous historical characters such as Horatio Nelson and Napoleon make cameos which is a nice touch. They come with combat bonuses and can lead you armies/navies.
Acceptable. There is not a lot to be said here as the game essentially consists of a map and a few character models. It looks nice, don't get me wrong, but it is what it is. If you're going to be persuaded either way by graphics for a game like this you're probably in the wrong place. Be warned, there are a lot of menus but that is fine. You find your way pretty quickly.
The sound effects are passable to the point of being simply passive. Again, there is not much to report. Music on the other hand is where Paradox always delivers and this game is no different. It feels thematic but also extremely epic. The music adds further grandeur to the game which may not exist otherwise.
The way Steam works the chances are this game will come up in a Steam sale soon enough. If it drops below £10 ($13ish) and it sounds like it might be your thing just get it and blame me if you're disappointed. I doubt you will be. If you want to get into Paradox grand strategies but don't know where to start then this is the one for you! It's simple enough to pick up easily but deep enough not to be considered a glorified tutorial for the other games, yet it introduces you to the essentials of Paradox grand strategies. For me it was a gate way drug and now Paradox is one of my all time favourite game developers.
The downside. To be brutally honest after playing Crusader Kings II and Victoria II, among others, I don't see why a seasoned Paradox fan would buy this if they don't already own it. It brings nothing new to the grand strategy table. It was so good for me because it was my first expericence with the genre but if you know the genre already then there is little for you here. It's good, yes. But there are other Paradox games which are better (the aforementioned Crusader Kings II is my favourite so far).
For the uninitiated Paradox virgin: 8.5/10 (buy at any price)
For the Paradox veteran: 6.5/10 (buy at a reduced price)

Tiny Keep is interesting - a roguelike (going up instead of down), Tiny Keep has some nice features too it - it's cute, good sense of humor, and does a good job of randomizing levels. I found not starting with a weapon a bit annoying, and the controls a tad diffcult to control, but I overall enjoyed the game.
Here's a video of me trying it blind for the first time, if that may be of use to you:

Fiendishly addictive. TinyKeep hearkens back to the method of gaming that started it all in the arcades. Permadeath. None of that pansy♥♥♥♥♥♥♥handholding and coddling that you find in so many modern games. This is pure, distilled challenge. Easy to learn, difficult to master. You can complete the game in a few hours... but you aren't likely to. You get one life, and have to bust out of a randomly generated dungeon. You encounter tougher and tougher enemies along the way. There's a real sense of accomplishment when you have a good run, even if you don't win. The game stays fresh due to the random level generation, and the fact that you're always finding quirky new ways to kill enemies or interact with the environment (my favorite is to get an enemy chasing me, then jump over a fire pit... knocking fire onto the ground, which the enemy runs into and burns to death). Lots of fun little details to discover.
The character design is charming as hell. And the audio and voice acting are all top notch. There is a lot of character and love put into this game. Sometimes the orcs dance when they're idle. Different types of enemies will often have conflicts and fight each other. What does that bubbling pot of green stuff do? (you'll find out eventually)
In short, I cannot recommend this game enough.

We’re back with yet another review. We just keep going, don’t we?
Today, we’re having a look at TinyKeep!
A dungeon crawler with randomly generated maps, you play the part of a prisoner who apparently sleeps so deeply that his cellmate, one “Maggie”, decided to abandon him, and leave a load of (somehow voiced) notes around the place to tell the story and help you out.
Featuring fairly simple gameplay, you have to explore and click the guards to death before they manage to kill you. Not much to say on the gameplay front that hasn’t been done before, but it’s done well enough to remain entertaining. Sometimes the tried and true formula IS the good one.
The sound design is decent, the graphics are perhaps a bit simple, but nice and cartoony, so all in all, the game scores fairly well with us. Enough to make us want to keep playing, at least, and what more could you want?
Recommended!

The logo looks like BF3 which might get people confused. Because, unlike the main BF franchize known for seriousness, Bad Company is lovably goofy. Best way to describe the mood is "less serious CoD:MW" mixed with "a parody of an american action movie". Unlike the previous Bad Company game we can enjoy this one on the PC too, although it is missing one DLC on the PC (Onslaught expansion which is a multiplayer co-op game mode). We are greeted with a WW2 intro/tutorial mission but the main game is played within a USA vs Russia conflict set in the present. The campaign is cool, fun and it keeps this tone for the most of the game. You will probably find your two or three favourite weapons and play those. First playthrough is good but once you unlock all the weapons you get to choose how you want to play. Which in my case was running around destroying everything with the rocket launcher. Unlike the collectable weapons that unlock for later use (or to have them already when replaying the campaign) the m-com stations serve little purpose than to distract. There could have been perhaps less (or more?) enemies if you find and disable one of these stations ... or at least extra dialogue. Your team buddies can actually kill enemies although the focus stays on you so you don't get bored letting your (immortal) mates do all the work. You all make a stereotypical gang - the smart one with glasses, the tough one, the sarge and the basic/vanilla one which you play. The slightly dated graphics still hold their charm though there are some graphical hick-ups - like tank threads that do not move. And I know it's kind of stupid to say but sand and snow storms hinder your vision a lot more than they maybe should. Because of this you either have to know where your enemy is or you have to be lucky. These storms are also annoying when driving around in vehicles and avoiding cliffs. The multiplayer is a blast and is still one of the best FPS multiplayers (even more if you have the Vietnam expansion). The playerbase is still good so check it out. There are more players in the default multiplayer than the Vietnam expansion but try that out too, it is awesome. Overall this is not a perfect game, it has flaws, but these can be overlooked due to the sheer fun factor of it. Get the bundle!

This could have been a good game.  I wanted to like it.  It has a sense of humor about old style RPGs, y'know.  Pencil & paper ones.
But I can't like it.  The game play, while simple, is too frustrating.  In pretty much every single player scenario, luck rules the day.  You can design your gear as best you can, but drawing cards is random, and you can't save many from round to round.  Use em or lose em, regardless of any sense it makes to do.  Interestingly, while you get random draws, the AI seems to have a lot of very small numbers of options, so it -always- has exactly what it needs to kill you.
Every time.
So scenarios that claim they are for level 10 parties actually means you should be at least level 16 to have a chance of winning without trying it three dozen times, and it only lets you replay a certain number of times a day.  Then there's that pesky luck based award system that sometimes means you need to be even stronger than that.
PvP is completely broken, with pay2win players dominating everything.  Even if you chance upon a less broken player in the completely random matching system, if you weren't lucky enough to have found decent equipment in the solo play, you are again screwed.  And when I say completely random, I mean it.  Your arena ranking number means absolutely nothing to the game and it will happily put you up against players who are far superior to your meager crap cards repeatedly.
Good concept, good writing, wish I could see the rest of the story line, but I hate the game play too much to keep it installed on my computer.

So let me preface this by saying that I was a big fan of the original Alien Swarm game, I praised its format, level design, atmosphere and sound direction. Alien Swarm was the first game I ever genuinely tried and managed to speedrun, achievement incentives helped to do that, but all in all the original game is fantastic and quite frankly is utterly criminal that it was free to play, I've met people on the original game that I still talk and play games with to this day.
But Alien Swarm had a lack of content, A single campaign telling the story of Jacob's Rest, a colony on the planet of Vereon XII which had an unfortunate incident resulting in a rather nasty alien occupation. Alien Swarm maintained a solid playerbase regardless of this lack of content even after all these years, But there was so much potential for the game that the community just accepted that we were never going to get.
Until now.
What we have here, is a huge expansion, Reactive Drop adds everything that Alien Swarm fans wanted. We have new weapons, new campaigns, an 8-player mode, fully fuctional bot support, Deathmatch, Bonus missions for those hungry for more and even workshop integration to allow for even more campaigns and personal customisation.
To talk about the gameplay, Alien Swarm: Reactive Drop is a top down squad based game that is played up to either a 4-player or 8-player maximum, you have 4 classes and 8 playable characters. First up are the Officers, Sarge and Jaeger, the mere presence of these men make everyone perform better, they lead and have access to the all powerful Vindicator shotgun, capable of bursting down the toughest the swarm have to offer. Secondly we have the Heavy Weapons specialists, Wildcat and Wolfe, using Miniguns and heavy fully automatic shotguns, you'd be hard pressed to find a better way of clearing and locking down entire hallways of swarm in mere seconds. Thirdly we have the doctors, Faith and Bastille, the all important Medics, capable of fortifying defensive locations with beacons that can heal the entire squad, or equipping a medi-gun for more concise on-demand healing. Last up are the Technicians, Crash and Vegas, outright required for any missions that task you to obtain information, these men hack terminals, bring motion trackers and have access to a special auto-aim rifle with tesla grenades.
Every Marine has a trait that makes them different from their counterpart in someway, For example: Sarge and Jaeger both share varying levels of the Leadership buff, Vindicator damage bonus, an explosives bonus and a health bonus, but their 5th traits are different. Sarge has a personal damage bonus, making his abillity with any weapon he is capable of using significantly better, where as Jaeger has a melee damage increase bonus, most likely instantly killing any swarm that dares get close to him. Wildcat is faster than Wolfe, but Wolfe is capable of taking more punishment at the risk of being significantly slower.
There is alot of depth that goes into team picks if you take the time to look at the soldiers individual stats, something that I never really noticed until recently, although team picks wont matter much if you're in an 8-player server, where every single marine will be present.
For teams that wish to succeed, it's important to stay together and be mindful of your ammo, some eyes watching your front, moving the squad slowly, some eyes watching your back, to prevent nasty flanking attacks, the game is extremely well designed for both the players and the aliens, there are choke points that teams can hold while they wait for alien waves to end, but there are several entry ways for the aliens to use to keep the team on their toes. If you divide? You'll get conquered. There are few instances in the game when you are generally "safe". Players can weld doors shut to relieve some pressure, but the aliens can knock them down given enough time, players can use combat stims to give your tech those precious extra seconds of hacking while you hold off seemingly endless waves of swarm that don't want you looking at manifests.
I mean...I'm typing all of this, but I'm just going to end up repeating my original review of the older game...It's Alien Swarm, it's fantastic, Guns sound great, levels are very well designed and generally fun to go through, the marines have some unique dialogue between each other, there is tons of equipment to obtain and unlock and the game as a whole is very atmospheric.
To say that this is the definitive version of Alien Swarm would be an understatement, the fact that the original game was free was a steal, but this huge massive expansion pack that has added so much longevity, free as well? The quality within this game exceeds that of what we're getting from our Triple A titles nowadays. I can't not recommend Reactive Drop, at least not to people who don't like top down shooters...But I urge you to give it a try, it's one of the most underrated games on Steam.
And one final time, it's completely and entirely free.

I love Paradox games, which is why it pains me to pan this one.  Clocking in 200 hours with the likes of a
or a
game is easy for me to do, but at the 18th hour mark I decided this is simply a flawed game concept.  The problem is that the
.  Nowhere is this better seen than in the process of battles.  The somewhat generalized battle system may be fine for a game that covers hundreds of years, but a game that only covers decades demands a more involved/detailed battle system.  They make an attempt by allowing you to choose battle tactics for example, but you never get the feel for the difference as the battle zips by, typical in Paradox games.  Napoleon's never ending pursuit for the definitive battle never feels fully realized.  The player is left wanting more once the battle engages.  The game desperately needed a sub system - or mini game if you will - that allows the player to engage in some tactical choices in the battles.  In this way the building of the army and the choices you made in unit structures feels more important.  And honestly, some of the other things so important and necessary in a long time frame game just seems like a distraction here.  The diplomacy and coalition building system holds promise, but in practice seemed more tedious to me than fun or interesting.  Once again, the engine that makes history dabbling sandbox play fun just does not scale as well in a game covering less historical time.
I really hope they take another shot at the era but next time take the time to design or better modify the game engine to better reflect the uniqueness of the simulation.

That dirty old Napoleon was a true son of a ♥♥♥♥♥.
For a game to choose such a narrow slice of history, the Napoleonic Wars, and do it so well is truly a hidden gem among strategy games.  With one exception , this is a game you can pickup quickly and move into battle / conquest mode with minimal reading / tutorials.  The tutorials are there and cover every feature in detail should you need them.
Pick your country wisely when you play this game.  Starting off on the wrong side will test your patience and mettle for battle.  I started as Great Britain and ruled the seas...but those pesky French kept drawing my ships and transports into battle.  I would end up winning but these spoiler attacks slowed me down a lot.  Enemy AI is competitive at the strategic level and in combat.
The one daunting task is understanding the military units.  You can make upwards of twenty different types of land combat units in MoE.  TWENTY.  Knowing the difference between a Marine brigade and a Dragoons brigade is a must.  Knowing that armies, during that time, needed supply trains as much as they need fighting brigades is a must.  Knowing how to position your troops and their fronts for maximum effect is a must.  Put too many troops in a single front and you incur an attack penalty!
Given the narrow slice of history involved, MoE is probably a niche strategy game.  Still, I'm very, very happy with my purchase.  If you play Hearts of Iron III, Crusader Kings II, and / or EV IV, you should add this game to your collection.

After ~21h of gameplay I can say, I'm very satisfied by this game. It's certainly not perfect, it has many bugs, but nothing gamebreaking - at least for me. I played alternating on my both rigs (specs on my profile), without any problems like crashing. One time a building didn't show up, after reloading a checkpoint and another time an objective marker didn't vanish, after a mission was completed, but as I said, nothing gamebreaking.
But other than that, it's a very nice singleplayer experience. Sniping feels challenging and rewarding on hard difficulty, the large open world leaves room for many ways to encounter enemies, AI is okay.. I've seen worse, but also better. Story was also very interesting in my opinion and oh well.. I got even surprised (maybe I'm one of a few here, but I didn't see that plot twist coming).
All in all I would give the game 7 out of 10. Considering the game was made by a relative little developer with limited budget, compared to Dice, or something, the game is very well designed.

Performance still needs work, and there's some Eurojank, but this is a surprisingly solid Far Cry 3 clone. AI is decent, guns are great, and there's a sense of tension to combat encounters. The open world design is quite good, too, with "points of interest" adding detail to the world.
Hopefully the devs keep patching the game. Would be nice to have some stuff like a chromatic aberration toggle, for example.
On the negative side, the storytelling and voice acting is a massive mixed bag. I don't think any of it is "bad", per se, but the voice actors needed better direction, and the pacing of the story is pretty screwy. It's pretty jarring playing Homefront: The Revolution and then playing this because HFTR's actors put their heart and soul into their performances. These actors seem to be unable to decide whether they're confused or angry half the time.

Sniper Ghost Warrior 3 is a game that was aiming for AAA tier results and fell short with a mixture of mediocre design and story elements that would redeem itself in certain ways that allowed me to enjoy 17 hrs of the original campaign (normal difficulty, skipping side missions) playing stealthy. I will definitely return to the game to play the upcoming DLC missions.
Pros that I feel are neccessary to highlight:
+Arriving at your mission and planning them is a lot of fun, especially marking enemies, objectives and alternative entry points with your drone.
+Sniping is very fun because of the distance and wind factors that you have to take into consideration, along with choosing the best rifle along with the right optics, attachments and ammo.
+Sneaking up behind enemies unnoticed allows you to interrogate them to learn enemy positions.
+Close quarters fighting is fun when you want to pick off hard to reach unsuspecting guards with your suppressed sidearm or rifle.
+The Georgian countryside is a cool and visually interesting place for a video game and CI games incorperates some of the Georgian music and architecture well. I don't think I've seen a game take place in that region since the early Tom Clancy games (Splinter Cell, Ghost Recon).
+You can choose to go in quiet (best and most fufilling option), or guns blazing without getting penalized heavily.
+ There is a lot of extra side content that you can grind out if you enjoy doing that (I do not, personally).
Cons I feel neccessary to point out:
-The writing for the campaign is simply awful. I had zero emotional attachment to any characters and many plot points that were meant to make you feel empethetic towards the characters had me in tears laughing over how cliche and mediocre the writing and delivery was. I suppose you could look at this as a pro if you're looking for a comedy aspect to the title.
-When sneaking around populated bases, your character will often make loud grunting noises when dropping down a small distance. This didn't alert enemies, however it does kill the stealth immersion. Another big stealth immersion killer is when you pick up dead or unconcious bodies: instead of setting the bodies down quitely, your character either drops or throws them, making a loud noise. Fortunately this never alterted any enemies, but it is still annoying.
-Load times are very long for whenever you launch the game or load a different map area (I remember a woodlands mountain region and a snowy mountain region and you only switch between the two a few times).
-I literally had no interest doing any of the side missions or investigating the points of interest on the map. The main missions of the campaign overshadowed the majority of the extra content.
Side note: this game borrows a lot of the open world ideas from the Far Cry franchise. I haven't had an interest in the Far Cry games since Far Cry 3, and Sniper Ghost Warrior 3 kept my attention because of the more fleshed out sniping and stealth elements that I wanted out of the Far Cry series. This game could have run better on my GTX 970 on high settings, however it did not detract from my enjoyment of the game.
Conclusion: I got this game at around $30 (all DLC included) and I feel that that is a good price for this game. If you like stealth games that allow you to dominate a mission without being seen, you will most likely enjoy this game. Just don't go into it expecting AAA gameplay and writing.

There are a lot of comparisons to Far Cry (3 and 4) with this new version of Sniper and it's open world setup.   On paper, this is the perfect game for me, as the taking over bases undetected with a sniper rifle is my FAVORITE thing to do in Far Cry 3 and 4.  The problem with the Far Cry sniper rifle model is that 250 meters or so is your max range, even with the 50 caliber, which in real life can do 1800+ meters.
This game has the guns and, I feel pretty decent weapon modeling.  To be successful in this game, you do have to make scope adjustments, but its a relatively quick action.  I have forgotten to do this, missed the target, and had a whole base after me.  And, similar to Far Cry, if you keep shooting from the same spot too long during an alert, the mortars will find you.  And hiding bodies is more critical.  They start looking for you if they see a body.
So the bad. . if you take out a base with your elite sniper skills, it does not raise a flag in your honor. . in fact, next time you drive by it will be fully populated again, which I guess is handy if you want to build up some cash and gear, but it doesn't really make sense.  They're are very few vehicle types, never any on the road unless you're driving it, and the damage modeling sometimes feels like its whole hog or none. . only  a few times did I get some smoke to signify that I was doing some damage and I better stop hitting trees.
The voice acting isn't the worst, but what they're saying is sometimes helpful, other times just keeping me from getting to the good stuff.  I mean, Far Cry 3 is an award winning game, but the whole time your character is like "They killed my brother! I must have justice!" and then you go to the market to trade a bag of sex toys for bullets.  I mean, what???
I rarely encounter dangerous wild life.  It exists, but last time I was driving to a mission I passed the wolves so fast I may have run over them.  I also like that aspect from Far Cry. . . a patrol could just be hanging out and a bear comes out of the woods and starts to tangle with them, so you'll hear gunfire, and vehicles arrive, and all of it feels a little more alive.  Sniper 3 is missing that "alive" feeling.  The villages have about 10 residents, 10 enemies, and some birds flying over occasionally.
I liked the other Sniper series games, and they were linear.  I'm a fan of the series and I like this game. . but Far Cry has spoiled me with how well it does open environments.  This game needs more traffic, pedestrians, and wild life so it feels like I'm actually in a countryside somewhere and not just the alleys between different arenas.

Valiant Hearts: The Great War takes you on a journey through the intertwined lives of characters through the first world war. As the player progresses through the story, the game captures some of the ills fated for those who lived through the war and how it affected the lives of individuals. The music at times is a bit hokey, but overall the audio in game helps. Game play is fairly simple and nothing is too complicated. Anyone should be able to enjoy this game. The comic book style of the art at first was something I wasn't very interested in, but grew on me the more I played. Game is worth the price, but has been on pretty good sales before. But for just under $2/hour definitely worth the asking price.
Story: The story in Valiant Hearts has been exquisitely crafted to bring together the lives of several individuals including one who cannot truly speak for themselves. Watch the trailer if you want to know what I mean by that. Time after time I was angry with the game for sending the feels in after me and dragging me out of my cold little hearth where I nurse my jadedness at the world... not because it was contrived, but because it succeeded in dragging me into the feels zone. Stupid game. :P
Gameplay: Super simple, nothing to it. Easy to play though sometimes you're not entirely sure what the game wants from you. This didn't really happen till much closer to the end though.
Audio: Overall great, but sometimes the music made me laugh a little. I get that symphonys were still big things back then, but just made me giggle a bit.
Graphics: The comicbook style of the game is very well done, with backgrounds and details lending to the overall immersion into the story by the player. Contrasts in some scenes help express a complicated feeling that you grasp instantly, instead of having to read words to get what is being communicated.
Final Notes: Definitely worth the play and the money. The game has been on some pretty good sales and one major knock against it for me at least is the Ubisoft DRM that's required to play it. Game is pretty short though, about half 6-7 hours of my play time were from me having walked away and left it running while I went to do something else. Still... an excellent game.

I couldn't recommend this game more. The action is fun, the story is heart-breaking, the graphics are really nice and atmoshperic, the 100+ collectibles should keep you busy, and that's about it.
The only thing about this game is the price (I bought it at a sale, which I recommend you do too, because 5€ is a fair price). 15€ is a little bit too much for 6 hours of gameplay, maybe more if you play this game more than once.

If you're looking for the modern incarnation of '90s games like Syndicate Wars, Satellite Reign fits the bill.

I missed out on the Syndicate games in my youth, but know enough to understand the comparisons Satellite Reign draws to them. I also know now those aren’t favorable comparisons, despite efforts to imitate key parts of the design. Satellite Reign is very much its own thing though, a mix of real-time strategy, stealth, open-world exploration, and team management. It’s a bold and impressive mix, held together with a magnificent aesthetic but dragged down by flaws in its weakest elements.
Dracogenics has perfected a cloning system that can essentially allow a person to live forever. Using this as leverage they’ve become the de-facto ruling body of the dystopian cityscape the game takes place in. Obviously not everyone is happy about this, and you happen to run a terrorist cell with access to stolen cloning technology. With your functionally immortal squad, you begin a long campaign to amass the hardware and resources necessary to infiltrate Dracogenics and blow their hold on society. And if that means burning a few research labs, gunning down a few hundred security guards, and kidnapping citizens for their genetic material, isn’t that the price we pay for freedom?
It’s important for cyberpunk games to nail not just the look but the feel of their setting, and Satellite Reign succeeds here admirably. You are very much not the good guy here for reasons that will be expanded upon in the mechanics, and that narrative integration with the game systems does a lot for immersion in a grim and gritty world. Corporate grips on the world are apparent from the vast tracts of private holdings you’ll need to infiltrate and the proliferation of company soldiers out on the streets. You’ll also catch glimpses of life in this dark future, like the desperate folks charging the district checkpoints without passes and being mowed down by the unyielding automated turrets.
With the aesthetics well in hand we can focus on the mechanics, which are solid in their arrangement if not in their execution. The tutorial portion of the game helps you build a team of four agents, each with a specific role like hacker or infiltrator. Your agents gain experience to level up their unique skills both active and passive, everything from brutal takedowns and scanner sweeps to health boosts and zipline proficiency. They can be outfitted with weapons, armor, attachments, and cybernetic augments all customized to fit the type of soldier you wan to field. Gear is obtained as prototypes from successful raids, and can either be equipped immediately with the risk of being lost if the agent is killed, or researched for mass production.
Elements like funding and researchers are where the team management ties into the open world of Satellite Reign. Within the four vast districts of the metropolis are public areas full of citizens, data terminals, ATMs, and security forces keeping the peace. Your team can hack ATMs to provide a small but steady funding drip, building it into a deluge once you compromise most of the city’s banking. Scientists can be recruited from the crowds if you can locate them, usually by scanning. Scanning also reveals stats on civilians which links into the most interesting and darkest aspect of the game. Your agents are clones, and every time they die their base stats degrade. To get around this you can kidnap people and harvest their genes to create stronger, fresher clones to house your terrorists. This side task can be surprisingly engrossing, scanning and tracking prime specimens until you can isolate and black-bag them without alerting anyone.
All of this serves to build up your team to take on the corporations, which means infiltrating their compounds and stealing their stuff. Secure areas are winding mazes of roads, alleys, catwalks, ziplines, air vents, and balconies separating you from the structures you need to raid. Your team is kill-on-sight in these zones, so you have the option of going in guns blazing or taking more stealthy avenues. Stealth is highly dependent on skills and can be a harrowing experience, as the map is designed more with realistic layouts and patrols in mind than clandestine access. On the other hand, once you’re spotted and the alarms go off you’ll be facing near-infinite waves of soldiers, making your infiltration more of a slog than a shootout.
This right here is the core problem with Satellite Reign, situated in the very heart of the gameplay and aggravated by every contributing aspect. The real-time combat engine lacks a real pause function (there’s a skill you can upgrade to slow time but it’s a poor stop-gap), leaving you with little time to exercise the fine control needed to execute stealth. That causes most missions to devolve into shootouts against crushing waves of enemies. To give you some wiggle room here, your agents are quite beefy once upgraded even a little and take plenty of sustained fire to bring down. But to balance this out, enemies are similarly beefy and take tons of shots to dispatch. Instead of intense tactical firefights, you end up stuck focusing one enemy down at a time and hoping they don’t melt your armor before you melt theirs.
It’s not enough to sink an otherwise deep and stylish game, but it sure as hell is a major drag on it. After a few hours I began dreading new missions into the sprawling compounds, because try as I might I simply could not stealth the whole way through and always ended up losing an agent or two trying to pull everyone clear of the target. Victories felt strained and stolen, not hard-fought or masterful like they are in other tactical games. I absolutely adore stealth and tactical games but their combination here felt so much rougher and hard to manage than something like Invisible Inc, and it’s the adherence to the real-time control that does it. But even with a dedicated pause function you’d still be struggling against ever-present patrols and ridiculously armored enemies every step of the way.
Satellite Reign gets so many things right, it makes the one thing it gets wrong all the more painful. It’s got an amazing look, opting for the clean neon approach to cyberpunk but drenching it in melancholy rain and walling it off behind brutalist architechture. The sound design keeps up with appropriately crisp effects and a moody soundtrack. The writing is on point, the missions are many and varied, and the interface won’t take long to master despite containing tons of options and information. It’s only the infiltrations, the combat and the stealth, where the game stumbles hard, and that just happens to be the cornerstone of the gameplay. If you’ve got the patience to push through it and master it to a greater degree than I did, then perhaps you can fully enjoy the grim and glossy future to be found within.

Disappointing and confused gameplay.
I was a backer for this on Kickstarter, and I was excited at the ideas behind it, but the product ultimately ended up disappointing.
Genre:
Is it a roguelike? No, not really. The levels are procedural (I think), but are same-y enough that it hardly matters. You either have room with spike trap/spin trap, or room without trap.
Is it an RPG? Not really. The gameplay is strung together on a bare story, which deemphasises the player's role and emphasises another character.
Action? Things feel too slow to be 'action'. Sword swings and jumps are sluggish and the rubble is annoying and slows you down.
What about speed runs? For some reason the developer emphasised the time taken to play the game, making me think it is only for speed runs. If you like speed running, maybe this is for you?
Gameplay:
There is very little to the game. Run around, hit bad guys. No levelling of any sorts. No variety in items. No variety in player. Bonuses are passive, so not noticable in terms of appearance.
I was excited about the AI behind the game, with many updates during the Kickstarter placing emphasis on this. But it amounts to enemies swarming you and attacking, or attacking other factions (which doesn't happen enough in the game).
The game is insanely difficult for the first part until you farm enemies for cash and then it becomes too easy. The permadeath is incredibly annoying, because every run is practically the same. Using the traps against enemies is fun, though.
On the plus side, controls are tight and responsive, but the physics-based gameplay just makes everything sluggish.
Graphics/Sound:
Graphics are ok. A bit basic, but the cartoony look works. The sounds are good too.
Price:
As a Kickstarter backer, I didn't pay the Steam price. And I'm fine with giving my money to the dev. But the Steam price seems FAR higher than the amount of game warrants. Perhaps at 25% of the price this game would be worth it.
I'm sad the AI wasn't a bigger focus, that the gameplay is so basic, and that the basic genre is confused and cannot make up its mind.

I'll qualify this "Not Recommended" by saying that with some tweaks and a bit more content, the game could be quite a bit of run. Right now, though, it is a Roguelike with only two Roguelike elements: Randomized areas and YASD ("yes another stupid death"... you die a lot). However, it is missing the plethora of interesting options that make lots of playthroughs worthwhile.
In the first level, you run around until you find your sword and shield. This level is entirely uncessary and should be removed. You have no other actions beyond attacking and blocking, and thus failing to acquire both of these items cuts down on your decisions by a lot. You can't even punch the enemies.
Secondly, the name TinyKeep is apt, as most of the rooms are cramped. This isn't such a big deal until the later levels when you are faced with (seemingly) unkillable enemies and retreat being one of your main strategic options. However, when every broken pillar and box slows you down, and when fire-shooting enemies cause you to permanantly slow down (by the way, if I were set on fire I'd be running FASTER... for at least a little while) and when getting hit caused you to flinch and stay in one place rather than continuing he direction you were going... it's all a bunch of self-negating feedback loops.
I very much hope the developer continues to update and support this game. He's got something good here, and could unearth a real gem with a bit of refinement. But right now he misses the mark.

TinyKeep is definitely a game with a lot of promise and it has some really cool features, but ultimately it falls short of being anything more than just a distraction for a couple of hours. Let's start with what turned out good.
The gameplay is fast and frantic, yet simple, giving it a very adrenaline filled arcade type feel. The art style is both audibly and visually charming even if the characters faces are a bit dead and lifeless. Every, chair, table, crate, cup, and bone in the game has full physics to it, which makes the environment feel messy and alive.
So where does TinyKeep fall flat? Lets start with the big pink elephant in the room, Permadeath. When done right it can make a game feel challenging and suspenseful. When done wrong it can make it frustrating and repetitive. Tinykeep falls into the latter category.
The gameplay is simple hack n' slash with no room for differing play-styles or player choice. The dungeon layouts are random but the content of each floor has little to no variation. These issues wouldn't matter for most games except your expected to play through the same levels over and over and over again every time you die.
Other games featuring permadeath offer enough variation to keep each playthrough different. The player will have a chance to try a different strategy or approach, and they may discover new enemies, items, traps, and environments that they didn't see last time. TinyKeep offers very little in this regard.
Short of that, my other complaints are merely nitpicks. Sometimes the camera angle and the clutter on the dungeon floor can make movement cumbersome and unnecessarily difficult. The map is hard to read, which is a real pain considering the layout is random. Traps are sometimes  hard to avoid, yet they do little damage, so oftentimes you will find yourself just running through them without care if they hit you or not. I could go on, but I'm sure the problems will be smoothed out with later patches.

It's GTA IV, but with more fluid game mechanics. What you probably want to hear is whether it's worth getting, whether it fills the gap until GTA 5 hits the shelves. So in a word, yes. In two words, sort of.
The game engine is still the GTA IV engine, of course; don't expect any dramatic changes between GTA IV and Episodes From Liberty City (EFLC). The only discernible differences are better driving (motorbikes! yay!) and cover taking mechanics, as well as slightly better AI and new radio content.
The graphics are still the same ones that taxed the hell outta all our PC's back when IV was released; this old engine seems to have been optimized quite a bit since then, even if the physics are still a bit buggy in large scale explosions or bridge traffic pileups (yup, they still periodically do that weird stacking thing on the bridge).
The AI as mentioned before has better cover taking, especially when in a firefight with allies. But, when♥♥♥♥♥♥gets real, you'll quickly realise that the AI can't handle certain things. There were moments in my playthrough where i'd be in a firefight and just move myself behind a solid object that i could still fire over or around, and find myself then being able to systematically slaughter any bot that had the temerity to walk into my fireline.
The soundtrack to the game is pretty decent. The LC Rock station with Iggy Pop in particular was to my mind the best thing about the Radio stations. There's a fair few gems in the limited new content the radio stations get, but after a while you'll probably find yourself adding your own music just to keep things fresh.
The storyline is alright; it fills in gaps between key events in Niko Bellic's story. In terms of the quality of the storytelling it's more or less your usual GTA fare. Lots of violence, swearing, racism, homophobia and misogyny coupled with explosions, gun fights and chase sequences. EFLC is just as cheesy, offensive and satirical as GTA has ever been, so if that's your bag you're in for a fun, nostalgic ride through that familiar virtual cesspit that is Liberty City.
To summarise, there's nothing really *new* here, and whilst it's certainly a lot of fun revisiting LC through the eyes of two very different characters, after the 30 or so hours of gameplay it takes to rinse through it all, you can't help but feel like it was fun, but you've done it all before. You'll almost certainly find yourself very quickly forgetting the characters and their stories, but at least you'll have enjoyed the process.
Overall: 3.5/5
Audio: 3/5
Graphics: 3/5
Gameplay: 4/5
Nothing groundbreaking, revisits a lot of old ground, but it's still an exciting sojourn through a living, breathing city.

So you want to be a hero, huh? Armello gives you the opportunity, ‘cause one way of the other, the rotten King is gonna die. You get to decide if you have the sword in your hand or not when he drops.
I had seen the advertising for Armello for a long time, but passed it by. The art style with the animal characters was initially off-putting to me. But Steam advertisers wouldn’t give up. They continually presented it as a game that I might like and sure enough, I do.
Armello is a digital board game. You are a clan champion in the land of Armello and the king is going mad from “The Rot” and slowly dying. To save the realm, you need to take King ‘Scar’ down. Even if you ignore him, he’s going to eventually die, the only question is whether you win or not.
The game is turn-based, which I prefer, and is a virtual dice rolling, animated card playing nail-biter where anyone can win.  Games last around 30 minutes for single player on “quick” mode, to an hour or so on Multiplayer mode. There are built in times in multiplayer in order to keep the game moving along.
There are four different ways to win the game and that adds some welcome diversity.
I found that I do like the art style, the cards are really nice with a light humor that I appreciate. You unlock new cards as you encounter them in game, so (so far) there are no additional cards to buy. That may change with additional DLC. You can purchase a seasons DLC for $5 which add spring, fall and winter to the board color mix. It’s a nice touch and I recommend it. Some may feel that it is a money grab and that the seasons should have been added for free or been part of the base game. To that charge I respond, this isn’t EA, LoG is a small Australian studio – don’t be a hater. Help them feed their kids.
You can play single-player against the AI or multiplayer against three human opponents. The single player experience is solid, although the AI is not terribly clever. Once you know what you are doing victory is common. There are four different character choices at the start, but with the Usurpers DLC expansion the list of choices grows to 12.
I have experienced problems with the multiplayer game. It is not terribly smooth or reliable. I’ve been dropped from starting games, if two people choose the same character to play, that can be problematic as well.
There is a decent choice of pre-made multiplayer communication options depending upon the character you play, but no open chat feature. This means that there is no dealing with the trolls of the internet and the filth that spews from their lonely chat box. This is a refreshing feature that I would like to see in more multiplayer games.
When you complete a multiplayer game, win or lose, you receive something. Presently it is either a chest or a key. Combine both to receive a different, stylized digital die that you can use in future games or sell on the Steam community market. I find it a nice motivator to keep coming back and play through to the finish, even if you feel that you are losing.
While the board is slightly randomized for each game, the whole is so similar that you may not even notice. As a result, many may grow tired of a similar experience after a while and find the game somewhat repetitive. Multiplayer games are the counter to that, it’s just a shame that they do not function perfectly.
As a whole I recommend this game. If you like board games this one is an easy pick up. The rules are not difficult and you can pick it up and play a quick game. You can play with your friends and Steam helps to facilitate that. If only LoGs can remove “The Rot” in the multiplayer, this would be a real gem.

I was incredibly excited to see a spiritual successor to Syndicate, a game that is still one of my favorites today. In fact, I installed DOSBox entirely to play Syndicate. I was especially thrilled when I saw the review "...does Syndicate better than Syndicate ever did." Then I launched the game, and felt the uncontrollable urge to vomit.
Nothing in this game is Syndicate except that it's isometric. That's it. No more the incredibly tense shootouts between your squad and endless police, or your squad and enemy agents (I had to reload my save dozens of times due to death via enemy agents.) Instead, you just... click once. That's not gameplay, yet that's the combat. The entire point of Syndicate was the cool mechanics (for example: Mind control device) and the innovative drug system and dependencies that made the game fantastic, and the excellent combat, and the fact that even though your agents were part machine, they were still human.
Now you just click, and BAM! They're dead for you.
Because your agents literally just all open fire at one click.
You don't need to play the game!
You just need to click once.
Done.
Also, the game crashed each time I loaded a new level, and, in addition, none of the keyboard commands worked.
Joy.

I am so glad that I gave this game a chance! This is the spiritual successor to the PC Syndicate series That I have been looking for! Controls take some getting used to, but I really hope this gets a sequel or at least more DLC.

The combat and most everything is ruined by finicky mouse controls and a lack of auto-targetting. In general, just avoid this game and go buy one of the earlier Syndicates (readily available).

I really wanted to love this game, and I persevered for a while with it, but the choice to make the game an open world one was not a good one. I was a huge fan of Syndicate Wars back in the day, so I was chomping at the bit for this. Unfortunately it just lacks the same magic. I think that the closed, linear progression style of the originals worked so much better than this open-ended style.

After a fair bit of playing this game, I thought I'd write an honest review about it (almost unheard of with me).
A lot of people are saying how GFWL has broken this game and how it is the main reason to not buy this game. Honestly, GFWL doesnt affect my gameplay nor should it affect yours. I have gotten GFWL to work from the first day, but I never use it because literally no one plays multiplayer on this game anymore. So, therefore, GFWL is not needed.
Also, people are saying that the PC version of this is broken. No, its not. So far, I have seen no extra bugs from what the other platforms already have with the exception of two problems - the fact that if you have a graphics card with 2GB or more for video memory GTA IV is not going to pick it up, and that The Lost and Dammed lags extensively. For the garphics problem, all you have to do is create a 'commandline.txt' file in the game directory increasing the 'availablevidmem' size. A lot of people dont know this and therefore, label the game as "broken". My computer has a nVidia GeForce 830m with 2GB of graphics, and it runs like a dream on the highest settings. For the extensive lag in TLaD, its unplayable. Even with the graphics turned down to the lowest possible settings, it lags from anywhere between 5 and 12 frames (for me personally). Also, the reaction times are severly affected due to the fact that the game will delay the action you want it to for at least 3 seconds. For example, if you go to shoot someone, it will not register the mouse click until 2-3 seconds later. Same for the keyboard input and mouse movement.
The number one reason I bought this game was to mod it with the LCPDFR mod. But since then, I have installed multiple mods and it makes the gameplay twice as fun as with no mods. I have also clocked The Ballad of Gay Tony two times as I really enjoy the storyline. For me personally, its a game that will never get old.
The computer I have used to help with this review:
HP Pavilion 15-P008TU laptop
Intel Core i5 @ 2.6Ghz processor
nVidia GeForce 830m graphics card
8GB DDR3 memory
Win8.1 64bit
Not a lot is required to run this game, as I could run it on medium graphics on a machine that was three times as weaker as this one above, using Win7 64bit.
I legitimetely think this is a great game and I would seriously recommend it to anyone who is looking for an awesome game with a great storyline and freeplay as well as good modding capabilty. Just use TLaD at your own risk.

I am glad Ty the Tasmanian Tiger was released on the PC for the first time ever! The game was released multiplatform on PS2, GC, and Xbox on the release date of September 10, 2002. The PS2 version was developed first then ported to Xbox and GC then released at the same date. I can't believe I missed out on this early access of Ty having a HD remaster on PC in Steam. While the Xbox ports were the best, the PC outshines all the ports! I should have bought the game back in March! But now I know and due to many updates the game now runs smoother and looks beautiful than before!
This is how a 14 year old cult-classic platforming game should be ported and released on PC! I love funny animals or you call them anthro animals. While the Crash Bandicoot series, Sly Cooper series, and Ratchet and Crank series are more well known and popular compare to Ty. Those who played those games will also enjoy Ty the Tasmanian Tiger series since it was remastered for the first time, which was needed for a long time.
The Ty series were hard to access due to being on legacy six generation of home video game consoles: PS2, Xbox, and GC at that time. Each and every year, the games are becoming more rare and harder to find in physical hard copies in great condition. But, I am a proud owner of the original Ty trilogy on the original Xbox in mint condition. Because I still love the original Xbox and still play the console along with the exclusives, I've a decent collection of Xbox games with most that will never be released on PC or remastered to the current generation of consoles.
Play as Ty and help his friends out to defeat the evil Boss Cass who threatens his Australia outback home!
The original ports of the game have bugs and some annoying things, but they're going to be fixed on this release.
I do hope the Ty series will be released for the PS4 and Xbox One as three games in one! Becausing playing a awesome game series like this on consoles is the true experience.
Amazing job, Krome Studios! I can't wait for Ty 2: Bush Resue to be next on the HD remaster! Ty 3 included too. The sequel is actually my most favorite in the series.
